message: , taught by Prof Kenneth Dean No webcast for lectures. Note: Please take this in whichever semester (usually Sem 2) that has Prof Dean assigned as the module coordinator. The workload would be alot manageable and Prof Dean's lectures are pretty interesting. His slides were mostly pictures. However, if you are pressed for time, I would say the lectures were skippable, except for the last lecture before finals, since more information on final quiz would be given. The recommended lecture reading materials felt more useful for exam revision. Tutorials (20%): - 10% class part: Must participate, just ask question or reply question. Easy 10% - 10% for assignments: 3 short (~2 pages) written assignments. 1 on family history, 1 on response to a film (It's a great great world) and 1 on ghost story. I needed to put in more effort for the film response assignment out of these 3, but nothing too difficult. Huiguan visit oral presentation (10%): - Presented after Recess Week. Easy as it's essentially what you have learnt from an assigned huiguan visit with your group members. Each member can do about 2-3 slides each before compiling and it would suffice. Huiguan visit written report (35%), submit by Week 13: - Descriptive report (team grade 20%): Most, if not, all of the content can be reused from the oral presentation done earlier. Easiest group report I ever did. - Max 2 page individual reflection on huiguan visit (15%): Relate it to themes discussed in the lecture notes or reading materials. Nothing too difficult. Quiz (35%) in Week 13: - In-class, handwritten, open-book (no electronics), choose 2 essay questions to do (I think 4 to 5 would be given), 1.5 hours. For my year, huiguan-related topic and amusement park topic were tested, which many people picked to answer, given the prior work done in terms of the huiguan visit and the film response assignment. Revision-wise, I just did my own notes by summarizing the recommended reading materials and assignments I did and brought those to the quiz. For those rusty to essay-writing, might want to watch the time and write faster. I reckoned this 35% was the most important factor to determining my final grade outcome. Overall, very light workload, interesting content and great lecturer. What more can one ask for? Recommended for all. Expected grade: B+ / A- (because most seemed to do equally well for everything aside from the 35% final quiz, which we didn't know the marks) Actual grade: A

Prof: Dr Zhang Weiyu Mid-Terms: 35% Class Participation (Weekly tutorials & IVLE posts): 25% Finals: 40% A friend warned me beforehand about how dry and boring this module was, but I headed straight towards it anyway like a stubborn bull (because it fit perfectly into my timetable ha ha ha) and got away with an A, unscathed. I really enjoyed this module quite a lot, although I tended to fall asleep (a lot) during the lectures. I blame the U-Town lecture theatre and its dim lighting lol. In all seriousness though, as long as you're willing to read and understand the textbook, this module isn't hard at all. Exams merely comprised of MCQs and Short Questions which you will be able to answer as long as you understand your stuff. I suggest making notes out of both powerpoint slides AND the textbook; they are equally important. There's also quite a bit of irrelevant content in the textbook, but Prof only tests what she covers in her lecture so you don't have to remember the other stuff. This module is not made up of pure memorisation, there is actually quite a good bit of understanding as well so just try your best to digest the concepts. The textbook is quite good, but in case you are still confused, Google and Wikipedia are your friends. NM Majors, don't look upon this module as a compulsory one that you dreaaaadddddd so much. Coming from a sociology major, it's quite fun lol.

CN2121 was taught by Dr Jiang Jianwen and Dr Lanry Yung Lin Yue, 2 committed professors. There are weekly tutorials. The module covered the following topics. Dr Jiang's part: 1) Basic Concepts 2) First Law 3) PVT 4) Second Law 5) Thermodynamic Properties of Fluids 6) Thermodynamic Analysis Dr Lanry's part: 1) Thermodynamic Properties of Systems 2) Multi Component Systems 3) Phase Equilibrium 4) Chemical Equilibrium The compulsory textbook is : Introduction to Chemical Engineering Thermodynamics by Smith, Van Ness and Abbott.Highly recommended to get textbook - that's assuming you actually aim to pass this module since its open book. Exam Format: The mid-term had 2 open-ended questions and made up 30% of the course. (Open book) There are tutorial presentations that count for 10%. Your group basically does the assigned question and presents it as a power point. The finals (5 open-ended questions) accounted for 60% of the module. (Open book) Comments: The lecturers are pretty good but the module is so conceptually draining that you will get lost here and there (and pretty much everywhere). However, if you study, the mids and finals are quite manageable. The lecturers also double as the tutors during their respective portions. Tutorials are CRAZY. Takes a full day to complete each tutorial (many needing matlab and all). Study hard, can pass.

Taken under Prof Tagore AY 2014/15 Sem 1 What it's about: Arguments for and against existence of God, issues related to God such as miracles, potential conflict between divine foreknowledge and free will. All of this is covered in the compulsory small textbook by William Rowe. Assessment: a group project + 700 word assignment + finals For group project, you are randomly assigned to a group. The group topic will be released to you 2 weeks before you are due to present(if i rmb correctly). Mostly, it's about summarizing contents covered in textbook and lecture and so it isn't THAT taxing as you might expect out of groupwork. The 700 word assignment is for anything under the sky related to philosophy of religion. Though that is the case, it is recommended (by Tagore) to choose something that is briefly mentioned in the textbook and dwell into it. Do consult Prof Tagore or your TA if you are unsure if the topic you have chosen is good. This can actually be done all the way at the start of the module. You probably would be too scared to but I assure you after the recess week your picture of what to write won't get much clearer because it's really write on anything you want. Ah finals. The format was a little different from the past: 2 sections of '2 choose 1' essay topics. Refer to PYP. Exam questions are very standard and can be predicted. It's a lot about rote memorization and regurgitation during the finals. Finals (for the first time I think) are closed book, which is good actually because otherwise it will literally be a copy-paste exam. And also potentially weeds out ppl who don't understand the arguments at all. Final comments: I will recommend you take it. The fact that you are searching for this module shows you are interested in the contents. You will get a better understanding of the philosophical arguments than if you relied on Wikipedia/Google. Prof Tagore is quite entertaining at times and the workload is quite light really.

NOTE: NUS student. Taken in 20/21 with Dr. Derek We covered a LOT more than the description. Basic theories of specific heat, Drude theory, Phonon waves, Tight-binding hamiltonians, 3D real-space and reciprocal-space geometry, X-ray diffraction, nearly-free electrons, Bloch’s theorem, conservation of crystal momentum, semiclassical equations of motion, semiconductor physics, semiconductor devices, and even the Boltzmann transport equation. A module I enjoyed a lot more than I thought, given that I had little interest in SSP as a whole before this. The starting part was kinda boring to be fair (really it is just a review of basic stat mech, and could be covered a lot faster) but the second half of the course is both challenging and interesting. I found out that solid state physics really boils down to one thing: the study of periodic potentials. This periodicity leads to so much interesting structure (the separation of the k-subspaces in the bloch eigenfunctions, for instance, which basically are the eigenvector solutions to Schrodinger’s equation for a periodic potential lead to the nice energy bands that we know and love). I also finally learnt semiconductor physics properly (now I can finally answer Prof. Ariando’s EP1 viva questions xD), and now I finally know what a MOFSET is (I hope i spelt that correctly). Huge shoutout to Dr. Derek who was incredibly helpful and very passionate about teaching, replying to my long emails with even longer answers. The test and exam are pretty easy. HW is not too difficult either but can be a bit long sometimes. The textbook that we followed was Steve Simon’s book, which is full of witty footnotes and quips but IMO lacking in depth. I liked Ashcroft and Mermin more, where they don’t hide the rigor behind either some exercise question or some handwavy explanation. A new experience for me, taking a mod at Yale-NUS. Was a nice experience, the campus is beautiful and the physics section of their library is a nice little secret, the books are so new! and their collection is good.

I took this module in 2015/2016 semester 2, and I really enjoyed the module. The module has a good mix of utility, workload, and appeal. It is useful for people who are interested in reading financial statements, which would be useful in investing in the future. The lecturer (Dr Aimee Shih) is interesting and the workload of the module is fair. It took me about 2 to 3 hours a week to read the notes and complete the tutorials. I also had a really good TA, as she was caring, and dedicated in teaching her classes. This module, however, requires effort. It is NOT for people who want to get a quick A. It is a module that requires you to put in effort, and rewards you fairly for the effort that you put in. My favorite part of the module is the project, where we have to read and analyse financial statements. Research done to answer those questions deepened my understanding for many financial indicators.

AY2017/2018 Y1S1 Lecturer, tutor: Robin Loon Don't let the other module reviews fool you. This module is an absolute disaster. Sure, it's fun and interesting. If you're taking in purely out of interest, then good for you! But if you're like the rest of us who want an easy A, think again. No, in fact, think hard, because TS1101E is NOT an easy module. You spend HOURS practising and rehearsing, only to fall short. Your CA is the one that will kill you, not finals. Each performance rehearsal weighs 10%, and the actual one is 20%. You are required to perform Undercover by Tan Tarn How (a short skit), and another 20min long play. Fair warning, Dr Robin Loon DOES NOT SPARE YOU. He grades you according to your abilities. If you don't have a natural flair in acting (like me), you will suffer greatly. Heck, if you're good at acting, you'll still get marked down, because how then are you supposed to improve without any constructive criticism!!! Your supposed A- standard will be brought down to a B so that you can be made AWARE of your flaws, which gives you room for improvement. TS1101E does not give you the opportunity to grow and learn. Sure, you will see yourself improve, but only because you don't want to have your grade suffer. You'll then realise that it will all be meaningless, because your other TS friends would have already been consistently moving up the ladder. But i'm probably just salty, because Dr Robin Loon isn't a very fair tutor. If possible, try to fight for the other tutor, Ms Samosir (if i recall). She's leagues better, and less biased. According to my other TS friends under her, they did relatively well, and far better than Dr Loon's students. But if you're still stubborn and thinking to yourself, WELL i think i'm PRETTY GOOD AYE i bet i can conquer TS1101E and penetrate Robin's Loon ass, here's a tip: Don't overthink. Forget about "alienation" or elaborate mise-en-scene, or the semiotics behind every action. The prof just wants something simple. He likes simplicity. You want to score? Think like a primary school student and I you'll get your B+. Wait, were you hoping for an A? Nah bro, should've went to Ms Samosir's class. TL;DR - Don't, it's not worth your time and effort (unless you're a theatre prodigy)

under Prof Soo Yuen Jien (aka Uncle Soo). This module covers the various parts that come together to form an operating system, including process and memory management, file systems, and synchronization (e.g. semaphores, mutexes). It explains why each process on your computer can execute independently of all the other processes. Some C programming knowledge is assumed - CS2100's coverage of C is generally sufficient, but more experience with C will make lab assignments easier. This module is rather content-heavy, but logical reasoning might be useful due to the style of exams set by Uncle Soo (the questions sometimes require creative thinking, and cannot be directly regurgitated from your help sheet). I would liken this module to CS2100. Uncle Soo makes lectures really engaging and easy to follow - amongst all the lecturers whom I have had, he is amongst the best (in terms of teaching ability). There are weekly tutorials and fortnightly lab sessions, and each lab assignment consists of a in-class demo to the lab TA and a graded homework portion (which requires writing C code). In general, I've quite enjoyed this module (both the lectures and labs). Midterms and finals are closed-book (with help sheet). There are no group projects for this module.

Took this module in AY2021 Sem 2 First of all, if given the opportunity, please do not take this module under Prof Bryan Low unless you already have an intuitive understanding of machine learning concepts like concept learning, neural network, etc. For the most part, throughout the module, we went through quite a bit of stuff that were theoretical, abstract and sometimes even mathematical in nature. This sounds fine but Prof Bryan has this habit of making things seem a lot more difficult than it actually is. There are several instances during the lecture when he could actually use diagrams to explain certain concepts but decides to use very technical words to explain. And don't get me started on the analogies he gives. This tends to make things very confusing since it is very difficult to understand what he was trying to get at. And to further make things worse, every so often, you will meet some tutorial questions you have no idea how to start on. And when you eventually look at the tutorial answers, it's like they are pulling answers from the air (looking at you information theory). And guess what, the tutorials are graded, so glhf if you are soloing the module and not strong in the theories. Last but not least, when it comes to the exams, it appears that what is taught in the lecture != what is taught in the tutorial != what is tested in the finals. Honestly, I have no idea why he focusses sooooooo heavily on concept learning. It just isn't interesting nor useful at all in the practical sense. Also, the neural network question was quite useless and pointless. It's already made known to us that most of the time, neural network is a black box model, yet he wants students to list down the weights that make the neural network consistent. Just extremely pointless. I guess one thing that is great (for experienced students) is that the exams are very grindable (except for the Find-S/ Find-G concept learning questions), making it very possible to get good marks. Ultimately, a few takeaways for someone like me who is not very interested in the underlying math and concepts are EM algorithm, Naive Bayes, Decision Trees. Apart from that, the other topics are just extremely boring and sometimes pointless. End of the day, please consider if you are willing to put yourself through the mental torture before signing up for the module. Expected grade (After seeing midterm grade distribution): D/ F Midterm grade distribution: 75th percentile : Don't bother 50th percentile : 40/60 25th percentile : 33/60 What I got : Way below 25th percentile Actual grade (Guess my finals hard carried me): B-

Taken in AY 15/16 Semester 1 Lecturers: Assistant Professor Deron Raymond Herr, Assistant Professor Pieter Eichhorn, Associate Professor Tan Chay Hoon Expected Grade: B Grade: B- (Used my 2nd s/u here, disappointing) Assessment and workload - 50% midterm test (60 questions 5 options each) I got 30/60 for it, which was terrible and far below median of 36. - 50% final exam (60 questions 5 options each) Unknown score here. I thought I did well for this part but I guess the cohort did well too. - No helpsheet for anything, pure memory module. - Lectures are webcasted, and thus attendance decreases as time progresses into the semester. - No tutorials, no projects Experience: - This module is deceptively light. It's only 2h a week on Wednesdays with no tutorials. Best of all, webcasted lectures! What a dream for all (lecture skipping) students. Especially to science students who have lessons on Monday, Tuesday, Thursday and Friday and seek a Wednesday break day. That was what I thought and hoped. I did not skip any lectures as I like live lectures. - This is a pure memory module. It is the first of its kind that I've taken. I'll likely not do such modules again. It was such a terrible experience as I'm really bad at MCQs, as evident from the midterm test score. Basically all you have to do is memorise every single word from the lecture slides and be sure in your answers, then the A will be guaranteed. There is no secret. Just pure memory work. Concepts are not needed here. However I have to concede that some parts of the module were extremely useful as it has indeed allowed me to understand common medications better. - About the lecturers. Dr Herr is the module coordinator and he takes on most lectures for the 1st half of the semester before recess week. He tends to mumble sometimes so get a front seat. He injects adequate humour in his lectures as well. His lectures are moderately technical. Be prepared for unpronounceable medicine names and many intersecting medicinal effects. Also the terms and conditions that certain medicine can be used. I found it really difficult and I could not memorise those despite spending the entire recess week on this. Dr Herr is also approachable and can be consulted through email or after lectures. - Dr Eichhorn takes on lectures from both halves of semesters and he is an excellent lecturer. He lectures in a partial casual style and yet formal when it matters. He makes jokes and shows us adorable apps like mouse party for the drugs of abuse topic. However his lectures are very technical and there's lots of mechanisms to memorise about the medications that he introduced. Intersecting effects of medications are present also, thus requiring more memory power. Dr Eichhorn is also approachable and can be consulted through email or after lectures. - Dr Tan would be the best lecturer out of the 3 in my humble opinion. She is enthusiastic and very engaging. If she takes this module again, I beseech readers of this review to attend her lectures. You won't regret it. It's very rare to have such engaging lecturers. Her lecture slides are also easy to understand and can be easily related to. Things like cough/cold/depression/pain medications were covered by her in an engaging way with activities in the lecture as well. She also makes the effort to chat with students before lecture starts to get a grasp on how she should deliver the content. She's also very approachable and can be consulted through email or after lectures. - Mid-term test for me was a killer. The unspellable drug names and intesecting effects of blood pressure/diabetic/hypertension drugs basically killed me. I got so confused in the midst of the test that I panicked and forgot even more. It doesn't help that the MCQ questions are extremely cunning. An example would be: Heroin: A) Effect A B) Effect B C) Effect C D) All of the above E) None of the above These questions are the norm and I got so frustrated with them. My sense of insecurity doesn't make things easier either. If you're good at such questions, by all means takes this module. - Final exam is similar to the mid-term test. By this time I was demoralised and I just did my best memorising the easier part of this module. 10 questions out of 60 would be similar to the mid-term test. (In fact from my memory almost all of them were the same.) 50 questions were based on the 2nd half of the semester. I thought I managed to do most of the questions, and hoped that I could salvage a B, but I didn't... Questions again were similar to the one given above, with more giveaways than the mid-term test. Conclusion: - This module is a killer memory module. You get a small taste of what medical students experience on a daily basis. I concede that it is moderately useful, especially at the parts when Dr Tan lectures. Ultimately not worth taking if you're bad at memory modules like myself. Still, the choice is yours!

Hi, there are more module reviews here too: CS2103T Software Engineering Difficulty: Hard Grade Obtained: B+ Lecturers: Prof Damith This is a 4MC core module for CEG students so there's no escaping this. CS1020 is a prerequisite for this module. This module is basically an introduction to group programming projects. The content is all online and you are expected to be self-learn it and attend tutorials to go through the content and clear up doubts. You can also go for the lectures by Prof Damith, which is exactly the same as the content online but with more sharing of examples and real-life experiences. All the content is here Here's the high-level overview of the topics taught: Software Engineering Requirements - for the project Design - design principles, modeling, architecture and design patterns Implementation - IDEs, code quality, documentation, integration Quality Assurance - testing Project management - revision control, project planning, teamwork Tools - UML diagrams, IntelliJ, Git, Java, JUnit This module is graded this way: Project (50%) Participation (10%) Final Exam (40%) The project component refers to Phase B. This will be a major pain to your team and suck up all of your free time for the second half of this semester. In groups of 4, you're supposed to set your own the requirements for the final product you want to have at the end of the module, modify existing features and add new features to an existing code base: addressbook4 to make those features happen. And at the same time, each person will play different roles in the group e.g. project lead, code integrator, project management, documentation. You're also expected to apply the content mentioned above (design principles, design patterns, proper project management, maintaining high code quality, write good documentation) with deadlines on a weekly basis (your v1.0 to v1.5 project milestones) There are way too many things for a single person to do but that's why you have 3 other group mates to work with. And that bring us to the next point, choosing team members. It's best to choose teammates that are motivated and capable. So, see those exchange students who are here to party, travel the world and do the bare minimum? Yea, probably not them. That person notorious for consistently submitting substandard work late? Nope. You get the idea... One quirk is that unlike other NUS modules, the peer reviews here counts as part of your grade so don't expect to do nothing for the whole project and still expect good peer review scores. Finally, with 40% of the grade in finals, your team can only help you so much. You'll still have to depend on own effort. Apparently, the exam format was changed this semester (133 true-false questions with negative marking + 4 open-ended design questions) so it was much harder to predict. I guess the best thing would be to practice drawing the UML diagrams and getting your foundation concepts right. Bell curve rating: This module is supposedly not bell curved Helpful resources: Module Website: Module Rating: Way too much work for 4MC

AY2015/2016 Sem1 Lecturers: Dr Ong Ee Cheng (Micro), Mr Chan Kok Hoe (Macro) Didn't intend to take EC1101E but it was the last few mods left in last round of bidding. The pre- and post- lectures are damn mafan to remember to do so I didn't bother. IVLE doesn't keep archives of quizzes you don't do. Textbooks used are more useful for understanding but if you want to know how you'll be tested, lecture slides will be of greater use at zoning in on the math involved. Ah yes, be prepared to buy a scientific calculator for this mod and do pri-sch level math. Apparently not indicative of level of math to come so don't be fooled. The Economist Strikes Back 1&2 are interesting reads but if you're low on cash, not worth buying. In exams, only comes out as 1-3 questions. Time management during exams is crucial because almost everyone was complaining they never finished the paper. Also, you won't get your scripts back because Dr Ong claims students in the past were known to sell exam questions to outside vendors and she can't keep coming up with tons of new MCQs each year. You'll only have one slot after exams to review your paper for 1hr and learn from your mistakes on the spot. Be prepared. I preferred Mr Chan over Dr Ong's lectures because his questions are not correct/wrong but "what's your reasoning" sort of type. He's also less passive aggressive during lectures. If you're buying second-hand textbooks, make sure its the same edition as the one specified. Won't make a difference for micro but for macro, Mr Chan suggests not to use other editions as different writers write about macroecons differently. Overall, I hated this module because it says "Introduction to Economics" but they might as well write "Introduction to Mathematics". Examinations barely test your analytical skills which was what first drew me to Econs in JC. Be prepared to be disappointed. MCQ format also quite insulting to intelligence because everyone has 20-25% chance of getting it right anyway but with so many people taking it, they need an easy way to assess the whole bunch of us. *yawn* My suggestion: Take this during Sem 1 so you can just S/U it anyways and just have fun learning the content. Great module for people who hate going for lectures because web-lectures are uploaded. You won't meet any interesting classmates in this mod though.

Taken in AY 16/17 Sem 2 under Prof Zhao GongYun I think it was Prof Zhao's first time taking on this module? He didn't seem familiar with some bits of the slides, which were based on Prof Pang's notes. But yeah there were the same symptoms of reading off a lot from slides, and students turning up to copy down extra annotations (some even just showing up for the final recap lecture). Sometimes the Prof himself got a bit lost trying to recreate the derivation of the proof/lemma from scratch. And it felt like a portion of the applications of network optimisation were rushed through or even omitted. In the end I found myself often cross-referencing other online resources on the same topic to clarify the slides' contents. Tutorials and homework assignments maybe helped slightly in terms of practising the algorithms, but still left lots of students lost when it came to proofs or derivations, I feel. Also wow the midterms were a massacre. Even the median grade was a failing grade (can't remember how low). I think because out of nowhere quite a number of proving questions popped up that didn't really resemble anything we've seen before? The finals seemed way less intimidating, but still kinda difficult in my opinion. Frankly I think you might be able to get away with self-learning rather than attending the 7-10pm lecture, despite the lack of webcasts. The content itself is interesting and pretty useful, but the presentation still needs ironing out. Just be wary of the different conventions that other resources may use compared to Prof Pang's / Prof Zhao's, e.g. preference for minimisation versus maximisation.

Taken in AY20/21, Sem 2, under A/P Vincent Tan. Assessment: - Weekly HW, to be handed in (10%) - Quiz 1 (12%) - Quiz 2 (18%) - Finals (60%) Topics covered: - Probability review - Poisson Processes - Finite-state Markov chains - Detection Theory (Binary Hypothesis Testing) - Estimation Theory (Statistical Inference -- Score function, Fisher Information, Cramer-Rao Lower Bound, Loss functions etc.) In my opinion, the first chapter on probability was the hardest, but arguably the most important for building the necessary foundation for tackling future topics. The chapters that came after were more interesting, with the topic of markov chains being the coolest. The focus of this class seems to be more on breadth rather than depth. That said, there's little compromise on mathematical rigour. Prof Vincent does not shy away from presenting proofs, but generally does not expect their reproduction during assessments. As Jaywai mentioned, Prof Vincent is an incredibly dedicated educator. He comes for lectures extremely well prepared, and is readily available and prompt in answering questions over email, after class, and during office hours. He even created a WeChat group-chat to facilitate discussion (upon a student's request). Considerable effort also goes into the setting of exam questions, which can be quite creative. Each week, Prof Vincent produces a set of handwritten lecture notes (which he writes as he lectures) and avails them after the class. Taken in AY 20/21 Semester 1 Lecturers: Professor Sharon Tan and Zhai Yingda Assessment Structure: Online Quizzes and Datacamp Assignments: 15% Graded tutorials (1 per week from week 3-13, best 10 to be counted): 35% Online Assessment on week 9: 10% Online Final Assessment: 40% As the name of the module suggests, BT1101 is an introductory module to business analytics, specifically covering the three types of analytics - descriptive analytics, predictive analytics and prescriptive analytics. Descriptive analytics was covered by Prof Sharon during the first half of the semester (before recess week). The content here can be split into two parts. The first part of the course gives an overview of business analytics and how it can be used to generate value in different contexts. It also serves as an introduction to the programming language R and how it can be used as a useful tool in data visualisation. This is not only done through weekly lectures where Prof Sharon will have live demonstrations where she will code in R, but also via Datacamp lessons/assignments which serves as a more OTOT hands-on form of learning. The second part covers statistical concepts which are often used in descriptive analytics. Some of these concepts would be familiar (mean, median etc.) while others would be rather new (for instance, skew and kurtosis). While I personally did not find the content in this half of the course difficult, I felt that the biggest challenge was the learning curve in efficiently coding in R as I had no prior experience. Predictive and prescriptive analytics were covered by Prof Yingda during the second half of the semester. Predictive analytics covered 4 main concepts – Linear Regression (simple, multivariate and logistic regression), Time Series Forecasting (ARIMA – AR, MA, I models), Data Mining (forward and backward model selection, data dimensionality reduction and principal component analysis) and Monte Carlo Simulation. The content in predictive analytics felt a lot more difficult as I found it less intuitive (I remember the lecture after time series forecasting, I had no clue what was going on HAHAHA and it wasn’t just me, quite a few of my friends also shared similar sentiments) so I would say one should put in more effort here to grasp the concepts. That being said, the coding in R for predictive analytics felt a lot more straightforward as compared to descriptive. As compared to descriptive and predictive, prescriptive analytics did not have as much content and we managed to finish covering it in the final two lectures. Prescriptive analytics in BT1101 covers two key areas – Linear Optimization and Integer Optimization (which is simply just a subset of the former). The content here is also pretty straightforward but do note that one needs to be careful when coding in R as it can get very messy when coding the constraints in the optimization problem. Some personal tips: 1. Manage your time well when preparing your weekly tutorial submissions! The tutorials were due every Monday so might not be a good idea to begin your tutorial late on Sunday night. Personally for tutorials with slightly more challenging content (yes predictive analytics, I’m looking at you), I allocated more time to prepare them so that is something you might want to consider doing. 2. The online quizzes and datacamp assignments rewarded effort (participation) rather than performance so just attempt all the quizzes and assignments to get full marks for this component, otherwise it’s likely that you’ll lose out. Note that the quizzes and assignments have various deadlines as well, so once again manage your time wisely (that being said, I do not encourage chionging them all at the last minute because that isn’t exactly the best for your learning) 3. Prof Sharon and Yingda/the undergrad TAs conduct weekly consultation sessions where students can ask questions related to course content or even about coding in R. If necessary, do make use of these sessions as it really serves as a good platform to clarify your doubts as understanding the concepts in BT1101 is key to doing well. This module was definitely one of my favourite modules this semester due to how useful the content here is in the field of analytics and I would highly recommend anyone who is unsure whether to take a second major/minor in BZA to take this module to determine if you want to take it up!

Taken in 15/16 Sem 1 This is a compulsory module for many majors such as Maths and Physics. Don't be fooled by the name Calculus though. It sounds simple but that is not necessarily so. Topics covered: Functions, Limits, Differentiation, Integration and ODE (a bit only) Basically this is a major extension of whatever calculus you learnt in H2 Mathematics. The first few chapters are the hardest to grasp but are essential as a foundation for understanding the rest of the topics covered. Note that the main point of this module is not for you to chuck random formulae at a question hoping it works. Depth is more important in this module as seen by the emphasis of rigour of proofs and understanding how each and everyone of the formulae you have learnt comes about. (Essentially they all stem from the understanding of limits). You will have a greater appreciation of how many mathematicians before you derived the formulae we are so familiar with today and it will be essential for you to understand this as you go on to study calculus in further courses. Personally I found the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus the most enriching and enlightening. The depth of each topic is quite large so do go in detail of understanding each topic, ESPECIALLY LIMITS. Another warning is that although the concepts might seem easy to grasp, you will find that you have grasped nothing at all when faced with the questions. Prof Farooq Shamsuzamman: Flash Distillation (Binary and Multicomponent), Binary Multistage Distillation and Special Cases, Absorption and Stripping, Multicomponent Multistage Distillation, Column Sizing Prof Suraj Vasudevan: Extraction (Immiscible Systems and Partially Miscible Systems), (Revision) Mass-Transfer Analysis, Rate-Based Design for Distillation, Absorption, and Stripping, Humidification, Cooling Tower Design TLDR (long review ahead): THIS. MODULE. IS. HARD. Might be one of the HARDEST CN mods you will face in your candidature as a chemical engineering student (excluding hard project mods like CN3101A and CN4123R Design Project). However, it is also one of the most critical modules you will learn in your candidature if you are an aspiring chemical engineer, as it deals with separation units, arguably one of the most common and critical unit operations in Chemical Engineering. This module will make you reconsider your interests in Chemical Engineering again. This module will form the bulk of your study workload in the semester. Consistent revision is needed to understand loads of concepts taught in class, BOTH the lectures and tutorials. LOTS of conceptual details within each separation process unit and you need to have a really strong grasp of Mass and Energy Balances to master this module well. Exams are tight on time, both the quizzes and final exam, and you REALLY need to master the concepts well to ace them. PRACTICE through the past sample papers that they give for quizzes and final exam. This module discusses the different separation process units that are commonly used in chemical industries. For our batch, the main separation process units that were discussed were distillation, absorption, stripping units, extraction, and cooling towers. Prof Farooq will teach the first part of the module, which deals with mostly equilibrium-based separation processes. He started off with binary and multi-component flash distillation, which is the foundation to understand the subsequent topics which are multistage distillation and its special cases. The finale of this topic would be multicomponent, multistage distillation columns, which would be the foundations for you if you are really interested to enter the oil and gas industry. This is more like an “introductory”, as understanding the operating temperature and pressure of distillation columns and the preliminary calculations to determine the required number of stages for the distillation column was the highlight for this module. Further understanding of distillation column calculation would need HYSYS simulations which would be taught in CN4122 Process Synthesis and Simulation. Prof Farooq will also discuss distillation column design and sizing. Next, Prof Farooq would discuss binary and multicomponent absorption and stripping. The second part of the module discusses other separation units like extraction and the relations between separation units and cooling towers. Prof Suraj will start with extraction, both immiscible (which you will find surprisingly similar to stripping) and partially miscible systems. You will hurt your eyes and brain understanding both the equilateral and right triangular diagrams for partially miscible extraction. Then, Prof Suraj will move on to explaining rate-based separation processes for distillation, absorption, and stripping and how the concepts correlate with the equilibrium-based concepts that we have learned in the first part of the module. Prof Suraj also discussed column diameter calculations for rate-based design. As rate-based design uses concepts from interface mass transfer (from CN2125), a quick online video gave a recap on this and there was a small quiz regarding this topic. Lastly, he touched upon humidification and psychrometric charts (from CN2101) to explain cooling tower design, which although does not sound like a separation process unit, the graphs are similar to stripping and it is also one of the most common unit operations in Chemical Engineering. I would consider this module as the hardest CN module you will encounter (with the exception of CN4123R Final Year Design Project) throughout your candidature as a Chemical Engineering student and in my opinion, this module will test all your fundamental basics regarding your Chemical Engineering knowledge. The analogy is this: For Computer Science (CS) people, they have a hardcore big brain core module which is CS3230 (Design and Analysis of Algorithms). For Data Science and Analytics (DSA) people, they also have a hard big brain core module which is DSA3102 (Convex Optimization). For Computer Engineering (CEG) people, they have a very important but taxing and heavy core module which is CG3207 (Computer Architecture). In the case of Chem Eng people, we have our own big brain and extremely crucial module, which is CN3132. Understanding the contents of this module is essential for aspiring chemical engineers as in this module, you will learn about one of the most important chemical engineering process units, which are separation units. If you see the list of TEs and Pathway modules, you can also see that CN3132 (together with CN2116) are prerequisites for a LOT of TEs and Pathways. I would go as far as to say that CN2116 (Chemical Kinetics and Reactor Design) and CN3132 would be two of the most important modules you need to master to be an aspiring chemical engineer, as these two modules are the modules that separate Chemical Engineering from other engineering disciplines. Thus, these two modules are conceptually challenging (if you read my module review in CN2116, I considered that module as the hardest CN 2k module in NUS). In this module, you will integrate what you have learned from CN2101, CN2121, and CN2125 (Material Energy Balances, Chemical Thermodynamics, and Mass Transfer) to learn about separation process units and integrate them with knowledge from CN2122A (Fluid Mechanics) and CN2125 (Heat Transfer) for the pumps, reboilers, and condensers operating conditions, using some tools to help in calculations from CN3421A (Numerical Simulation). This module really has LOTS of details and concepts, mostly based on thermodynamics and mass transfer and understanding various graphs regarding operating and equilibrium lines of several separation process units. To be honest, the calculations are not really too extensive, but I was overwhelmed with the tons of concepts introduced in this module. If you made it this far into your Chemical Engineering degree and not really enjoying it, this module will make you reconsider your life choices by making you ask yourself: Why am I in Chem Eng? During the module feedback exercise, I describe what I liked/disliked about this module as follows: “This module has the difficult conceptual understanding approximately the same level as CN2116, integrating concepts from CN2101, CN2121, and CN2125 and giving them steroids to understand separation units, integrating them with knowledge from CN2122A and CN2125 to design the pumps and reboiler/condenser and touched upon safety concerns from CN3135, with also a sprinkle of CN3421A added to the mix.” There’s one 2-hour lecture slot and a 2-hour tutorial slot every week, with tutorials starting from Week 2. Lectures are recorded, but the tutorials are NOT recorded . As the tutorials are not recorded, you NEED to come to the tutorials, as the tutorial questions are set in such a way that it gives extra insights regarding what you have learned in the lectures. The tutorial solutions are longer compared to other CN mods like CN3121 as the professors wanted to give extra insights regarding what they have taught in the tutorials. Once you lag behind, you will DIE (like I did during the second half of the sem :”) ). In addition, you need to watch some extra videos (they call it online lectures) before the lecture timing as it serves as a “prelude” to the lecture. Practically speaking these online videos felt like another 1-hour lecture that you need to watch in your free time (although the videos take at most 30 minutes) as these videos always introduce new concepts and (at least for me) need some time to digest. Please revise and don’t be afraid to ask questions when in doubt, as sometimes the concepts inside this module make your brain ache hard, and you better get your concepts right before getting NUKED in the quizzes and final exam. Again, I should emphasize that the difficulty of this module is in the tremendous amount of details and concepts that you need to understand. The calculations are not really very tedious, and if you’re more of a math person, you might find CN3121 and CN3421A much more of a breeze compared to this extremely difficult module. The reason you need to get your concepts right is because of the examination format. The quizzes and final exam are done using Examplify without backward navigation . For thee quizzes, you will have approximately 2.5 minutes per question, and these questions test regarding your conceptual understanding and a bit of calculations. Thus, again, if you don’t get your concepts right by the time of the quizzes, you will DIE . The final exam was basically a speed run. Compared to much older batches, our questions were a LOT easier, where you can roughly see what should be done. If you try to see past papers from 19/20 Sem 1 and older, you will realize that this module’s final exams were MUCH tougher. They kid you not when seniors say CN3132 Final Exam has been one of the most KILLER final exams throughout their candidature back then during non-COVID days. However, now there were MUCH MORE questions for our batch, and if you need to flip the lecture notes a lot to find the right concepts, you will waste lots of time and won’t finish the entire final exam (in other words, get NUKED ). So I would guess that the professors now want us to understand the concepts thoroughly and quickly remember them to solve the problems. I would suggest making a cheat sheet for all the details and formulas so that you can get quick access to them during the final exam (personally I made another 18-page cheat sheet for this module like CN2125). I find that a lot of people didn’t manage to finish the final exam as they flipped their lecture notes round and round to find the required formula/procedure to use. The professors give sample papers for the quizzes and final exam so you have something to practice to prepare for the quizzes and/or final exam. My reaction when I saw 2019/2020 CN3132 Final Exam PYP for the first time the day before the final exam: “... if these questions come up tomorrow, I will surely die . Let’s just assume that the final exam was similar to 20/21 PYP as the format is similar.” Thank God it did. Before ending this VERY long review, I would like to give a comment regarding the professors who taught this module, Prof Farooq and Prof Suraj. These two professors are two of the most knowledgable Chem Eng professors I have ever encountered throughout my candidature as a Chemical Engineering student. Prof Farooq has been teaching this module for DECADES (as a fun fact, Prof Suraj was an NUS student back in the early 2000s, and the lecturer for CN3132 when he took the module was Prof Farooq). I heard that some Chem Eng profs in NUS said that Prof Farooq is one of the smartest professors in the NUS Chem Eng department. He’s indeed, very, smart, but he wants his students to learn by doing. Thus he expects you to do the tutorial questions yourself and if you have any discrepancies with the prof’s answer, you can ask. Oh and sometimes if your questions are… quite basic (not to offend anybody), Prof Farooq sometimes asks you back the question and lets you think for yourself. So, think first before you ask your question. His voice might be quite monotone and compounded with his “coldness”, some people don’t like his way of teaching. Prof Suraj, on the other hand, is much, much kinder. Although the contents might be quite hard to digest, his explanations are thorough enough. He also sometimes promotes the TEs/Pathways that he teaches like CN4215R Food Technology and Engineering and CN4221R Control of Industrial Processes. Overall, excellent work from these two professors.

Taken in AY 15/16 Semester 1 Lecturer: Associate Professor Han Fei Tutor: Associate Professor Han Fei Expected Grade: B+ Grade: A- (Pleasantly surprised by this grade) Assessment and workload - 5% Tutorial attendance (Free marks) - 5% Tutorial participation (I'm sure I got the full 5 here since I presented 6 times in 10 tutorials, my tutorial group was so passive that I had to do it. -_-) - 20% Homework (There's 1 set every week, totaling 11 sets. Each homework has 3 questions. Homework is submitted in piles of 3 sets.) - 20% mid-term test (I got 83/100, very surprising to myself and my peers) - 50% final exam - NO calculators allowed for any test nor exam. - 1 A4 size helpsheet written on both sides for mid-term test and final exam - No webcast. Experience: - I have mixed feelings about this module. It is a difficult module, no doubt. It's an introduction to mathematical analysis and I suppose is considered as a pure math module more than an applied math module. We start off with basic set theory and revision of mathematical induction (which should be easy for people who did MA1100 under Associate Professor Chin Chee Whye like myself...) Things escalate into being more abstract when infimum and supremum are introduced, along with the axiom of completeness of real numbers. Simple sequences and series we love from Secondary school and JC become monsters after sequence analysis is introduced. Things like square root 2 become abstract. Theorems are abstract and the proofs are difficult to understand mostly. We also have to face our fear of epsilon delta definitions and concepts from MA1102R here, as that concept can be used to do many kinds of proofs. It helps to revise a bit of that before epsilon delta is introduced in proving limits of sequences. IVT, EVT will be covered again as well. The hardest part for me was gauges. I just do not understand the concept and I can't visualise it. Also the questions in homeworks, tutorials, tests and exams are 90% proving, which I do not have a knack for. Lastly another difficulty for me (in fact many of us) would be that I tend to get the idea of what the question requires, but I do not know how to phrase it in words to write the proof. - Prof Han is a decent lecturer. He knows his stuff well. Lectures can sometimes be boring as I find mathematical analysis to be rather theoretical, abstract and dull. The lecture slides are also wordy and Prof Han sometimes reads word for word, causing me to zone out sometimes. Prof Han also does a recap before each lecture which is very much appreciated since lectures are not webcasted. Prof Han is also approachable and willing to answer trivial questions from students. He also prompts participation by asking questions in lectures and often it is usually the people seated at the front who answer it (Like my friend and I). The only grouse I have is being unable to get the midterm papers back. Up till now I have no idea where I went wrong and how to show a sequence is Cauchy using the definition. - Tutorials are very important in my opinion. It gives you the free 5% if you attend all of them, and also the opportunity to learn from geniuses that surprise Prof Han himself. It is done seminar style and the 3 questions in each tutorial are free for all. To obtain some marks for the participation, I suppose a student has to present at least once. I volunteered 6 times and got my mistakes corrected, which is a good thing since Prof Han himself examines your proof rigorously. Homework is also returned during tutorials. Prof Han also asks thought provoking questions in each tutorial in addition to the tutorial questions, and 1 question out of the 3 usually require some divine intervention. Tutorial solutions uploaded are also brief and it is best to attend the tutorial sessions to copy and listen to his explanation. - The mid-term test was manageable and very similar to the tutorial and homework questions, with exception to the last question which I could not do. Thus for mid-term tests, understand the concepts deeply if possible, and try tutorial and homework questions earnestly. We had 1.5h to do 100 marks worth of questions. - Final exam is difficult. It took me totally by surprise. There were about 15 marks free from lecture notes, which I did not copy into my helpsheet. 10 marks were allocated on proving the harmonic series diverges and alternating harmonic series converges. Both were in the lecture notes but I did not copy them and thus lost the marks. We were also asked for 2 definitions of supremum, which I only remembered 1. Thus, make use of the 1 A4 doublesided helpsheet as efficiently as possible! 40 marks of the paper were easy, with the last 3 questions of the paper being undoable in time constraints for me. In addition, 1 question came out exactly the same as 14/15 Semester 1 exam and 1 question is extremely similar to 14/15 Semester 1 exam. Prof Han also asked the thought provoking question that he asked for 1 tutorial in the exam, which was to find a function that's discontinuous at infinitely many points. Thus it pays to think about the questions he asks in tutorials as well. I suggest copying some difficult tutorial questions into the helpsheet and the presentation required. Also, try out the past year papers than Prof Han sets under timed conditions to get a feel of the difficulty. Conclusion: - This module is difficult, abstract, not fun and yet a little interesting at the same time. It is core for all mathematics majors so we have no choice. Statistics majors have the option to do this but I suppose it is not a good idea. Remember that it is a 90% proving module so concepts are critical.

Taken in AY21/22, Sem 2, under A/P Vincent Tan. *Disclaimer*: took this as an audit student, so I did not attend tutorials, nor sat for the exams. As He Yuan and zx have mentioned, this class focuses on traditional (and statistical) machine learning algorithms. The class is taught in a mathematically rigorous way with a good number of proofs. I'd say that a good grasp of undergraduate probability & statistics, and some familiarity with Linear Algebra, are essential to following and appreciating the material taught. During lectures, Vincent writes as he delivers the content. He usually uploads these handwritten notes after class, but also shares the LaTeX-ed version prior to the start of class on LumiNUS. These notes are quite self-contained, but one is also encouraged to look at the reference material: Jaakkola's MIT Machine Learning notes. Vincent is an amazing lecturer. Although the material can get dry at times, he never fails to bring the concepts to life. I think he does a great job at linking the different concepts together: for example, by introducing slack terms and augmenting the loss function, the progression from the perceptron, to the SVM, and then logistic regression, was done in an illuminating way. Besides connecting the dots, he tries to show the algorithms in action by running code snippets in class. For example, he shared an example of how Adaboost would classify and assign the costs to misclassified examples. I thought this was a brilliant way to engage and shed light on the inner-workings of the algorithms. (Honestly, by the end of this class, I think one would be equipped with sufficient knowledge to code a number of algorithms from scratch.) Still on the topic of lecturing, Vincent has this incredible ability to elucidate his thought process, which he exercises as he writes his notes. I've found his pedagogical style of *thinking out loud* very helpful in refining one's intuition for approaching problems, in addition to deepening one's understanding of the material at hand. I feel that this is one huge push factor for attending his lectures, and probably tutorials as well -- watching him articulate the content is more effective than just referring to his notes. While mathematically rigorous, I'd say the class has more breadth than depth. There are quite a number of topics that he covers, ranging from classification algorithms, to graphical models. Hence, a delicate balance between breadth and depth is necessary. However, he did spend considerable time on SVM and graphical models. If you're interested in these topics, I'd highly recommend taking this class. But if you show even the slightest interest in Machine Learning, I'd encourage giving this class a go! This was my second Machine Learning class, and even then, I gained a lot (!) of insight from this iteration of MA4270. Lectures aside, Vincent is very open to answering questions, discussing the material, and even concepts beyond the scope of the class. Although I did not take this class for credit, he entertained my questions and thoughts without fail. He's very responsive over email and the LumiNUS forum, so feel free to reach out to him whenever you have questions! Even better if you can attend office hours! (Don't be afraid to show up -- he takes genuine interest in students' learning, and you'll learn a lot from him!) Finally, just some side remarks: if you are interested in Stochastic Processes, you can also consider enrolling in EE5137, which is taught by Vincent. I took that class and thought it was also very well delivered (and cool). You'll definitely be in for a ride!

CG1108 AY2016/17 Sem 2: This module, compared to many other engineering modules, is much more manageable in content and concepts wise. You will find quite a lot of flexibility in this module due to the many methods you are taught which can be used later on in the harder parts of the module such as DC & AC Transients. But you must know them all, as questions can force you to use a certain method. The exams are quite challenging at times, but there will always be very manageable questions which you can do with a good grasp of concepts. This is one module you don't really have to practice until the time comes (just before the exams itself, I did my practice 2 days before finals). The first lecturer is Dr Soh Wee Seng, who is a very nice lecturer, is very pleasant to listen to (his pace is very comfortable) and works out example problems on the spot which are very easy to follow. His lectures are usually quite packed (but the cohort size is small anyway). The second lecturer is Dr Sahoo, who in my opinion isn't as good as Dr Soh, but is willing to explain the concepts in detail if you consult him after lectures. Tutorials are optional to attend. And they REALLY are. If you know how to do all the questions perfectly (answers for each question are given), there's no point in attending them. However, if you get stuck, do attend the tutorials as the tutors are the professors themselves. My tutor was Prof Soh who maintains the same standard in lectures in tutorials. The module also has lab sessions. The individual lab sessions can be fun, or frustrating when you don't know what's going on. Go around the lab and ask literally everyone you can find for help. But individual lab marks are very easy to get, just copy your friends if you really can't get the results. My experience with the group project is frustrating, as the instructions on the lab sheets can be confusing. Also, I was the hardware engineer for the team, dealing with almost all the hardware on the line tracking car we have to make. MAKE SURE YOU SOLDER PROPERLY, else your connections can fail quite badly. You can get the lab assistants to help you out. Also the software portion (which uses Arduino, which has similarities to C) is NOT EVEN taught at all. Integrating the software and the hardware can be a nightmare. The final week before the car demonstration was spent debugging both software and hardware. Luckily TAs are the ones evaluating the project, and they are quite relaxed since so long the car has the capability to perform the requirements relatively well, they'll let it pass (You don't exactly have to go through the whole course smoothly). TL;DR The module is very manageable, concepts are quite easy to master, lecturers are good, the individual labs are ok, the group project requires considerable effort though. Exams can be a little challenging. Expected Grade: A / A- Actual Grade: A Unfortunately, this seems to be the last time they are conducting the module, as the syllabus is changing for CEG. :(

(covid -- 100% zoom) Prof Damith Expected: A Received: A+ I can't remember the weightage already, but there's 3 main components: individual project, team project, and final exam. As you'll see below, the assessment is mostly a joke anyway. Again, I'll preface this by saying that I don't find Prof Damith to be a bad lecturer. As is this case with most (MOST) of the profs in NUS, they're good people, but there's just something wrong with the course content or delivery. In this case, it was a mix of both. I can't remember what I wrote for the "official" module feedback, so I'll paraphrase from memory here. In essence, this module should really be called "Object Oriented Software Engineering, Sponsored by the UML (tm) Mafia". Java, OOP, and UML really go together like flies, rotten fruit, and a bad aftertaste. Starting with a high level overview of the problems: (1) Objected Oriented. ------------------------- To put it in short: if I were an average student with not a lot of prior programming experience of *differing paradigms*, what would I walk away from this module with? I'd walk away with the idea that OOP is the One True Paradigm, because (a) all the tools and environments are already setup to be OOP-friendly and everything-else-adverse; (b) the module, the professor, the tutors, they all keep endorsing OOP, whether implicitly or explicitly; (c) the starting code given (for the TP) is written in OOP, and is even said to be "well-written"; (d) all my friends are writing OOP code. I'd graduate with a warped view of programming, with the idea that large software projects invariably end up being OOP. In fact, given the structure of the NUS compsci curriculum, all you'd graduate with is "OOP", and "Java Streams" (thanks Prof Henry). Tragic. This module completely does not cover any other kinds of programming paradigms. From day 0 and the individual project, it's all objects, classes, OOP OOP OOP. One of the deliverables for the individual project (henceforth IP) was literally "More OOP -- implement more OOP". This gets worse for the team project (TP). As you might have read from the other, less scathing reviews here, it is a brownfield project, so you start with some existing code. And let me tell you, damn is that field brown. It's not dirt, by the way. Let's just say it's... fertiliser. The code you will be given is your typical, enterprise Java OOP garbage codebase. Full of classes pointlessly abstracted out, code that is a sort of "implicit spaghetti", and classes that literally have no state (only methods), and yet are instantiated -- all for a program that doesn't do very much. About that spaghetti -- because of "abstraction" and the "Single Level of Abstraction Principle" (abbreviated SLAP, how fitting), the code *looks* neat, but you'll soon realise that in order to actually grasp the program (AddressBook 3 -- AB3 ( , you end up jumping all over the place. It's bad. In short, this mod pretends to be software engineering, but in reality it is OOP engineering. So if I don't write OOP code, am I not a software engineer? Do I not qualify for the $5k median starting pay of CS graduates? (2) Sponsored by the UML Mafia ------------------------------------- You better get used to UML, because so much of the finals will be testing UML. Guess what -- after this module, I couldn't tell you what the notation for interfaces are any more. Does it matter? No. Just like the MIPS mafia (which you will be familiar with if you took/take CS2100), the UML mafia is another shadowy organisation that somehow manages to get schools all over the world to push UML and treat it like it's the holy grail of program structure/organisation representation. (Hint: it's not). Here's my personal take: 1. for a high level overview, nobody needs such a rigorous, over-specified notation like UML. Does it matter what specific methods this specific class has? No -- that's what your IDE is for. In fact, the 2103 textbook even states that there isn't a standardised notation for architecture diagrams in UML. god bless. 2. for a low level detail, nothing beats reading well-documented code. Here's the problem with UML: it's not code. Having outdated documentation is already a massive, known problem in the software industry. If programmers can forget (and/or be lazy) to update documentation that's literally right next to the code they're changing (eg. Doxygen, Javadocs), do you think they'll update a bunch of silly UML diagrams that need to be compiled to silly pictures by a silly tool? Probably not. UML will get outdated so much faster than documentation, that the one true source of information is the program source code itself. I won't get into too much detail for the rest of the mod, as the other reviews cover it pretty well. The other thing I want to say is that the mode of assessment frankly sucks. As you might gather, there's 3 main components: the IP, the TP, and the final exam. (I think there might be class participation -- would explain why the tutor keeps name-calling us). Here's the thing: literally 90% or more of the class will get full marks for the IP. Yes, full marks. As long as you submit a working program that meets the specification (which isn't very hard), there's literally no way you can get below full marks. There's a component where you need to add a GUI with JavaFX, but guess what? There's literally a tutorial that you can copy-and-paste code from, and there you go. All you need to do is change a few pictures and you're done. Guess why 80% of the submissions for the IP literally look like reskins of each other? The IP component had weightage of ~20%. What does that mean? It means that it's literally worthless. Unless you're a good student, there's no need to put in so much effort into your IP -- just the minimum will get you that 20%. (putting in extra effort, eg. differentiating your program from the rest, probably won't get you any bonuses either). Next is the TP, which is ~45% (?) of the grade (more than the final exam). Again, given that this was a brownfield project with an existing codebase, from what I could tell, there were 2 kinds of groups -- the kind that basically came up with an entirely new program, and the kind that didn't really change the existing code too much. There was hardly any middle ground, from what I could tell. Where does that leave you? it means that even if your team really puts in a lot of effort to make a good submission, there's tens of other teams that are submitting comparable projects. and that means that this bunch will get mostly full marks for the TP component as well. Finally, the final exam. So, after getting full marks for the IP, and full or close to full marks for the TP (because you're a good student who put in a lot of effort, and had a good team to carry you, right?), you're still fighting for that A+ with lots of other people on this end of the bell curve. Remember how I said you had better dissolve UML paper in water and drink it? In the end, your grade might be determined mostly by the final exam and it's mere ~30% weightage. So what does the final consist of? UML. Yes, UML. Sure, there's other components like code style, conceptual questions on testing and other stuff, but... UML. seriously, go memorise your UML (or get a good cheatsheet). There's graded components for documentation as well -- on the CS2103 side, the developer guide. Because this isn't 2101, it doesn't need to be *THAT* polished -- just make sure your UML is correct, and it doesn't look too shabby. It's probably a good idea to designate one person in your team to be in charge of formatting and error-checking, and another to be in charge of polishing the UML. Finally, there's the bug-testing part of the assessment, which was... an interesting concept. (not a bad one, mind you). There's 3 parts -- (1) attack other people's TP to find bugs; (2) attack other people's TP documentation to find errors; (3) defend your own TP against attacks by refuting their bogus claims. The problem is that sometimes you might get a group that either (a) is simply too good that there's very few "high-severity" bugs, or (b) the group simply didn't add that much functionality that there are very few new bugs at all. (bugs from AB3 don't count). When other people file bugs against your project, your team does get to give a rebuttal (including downgrading severity, rejecting it, etc. -- with appropriate justification), and you can counter-rebut a team's justification against your bug reports. The teaching team uses some magical orb of wisdom to decide who wins, and it's not very transparent here. Sometimes you get truly stubborn people who insist that your program should work the way they want it, and not the way that you have clearly documented in your user guide. for some reason. Of course it's not all bad things; you do learn how to use git+github with a forking workflow, intellij idea (personally i didn't use that piece of bloatware), and how to write tests with junit. the textbook also does *SKIM THROUGH* some code quality fundamentals (like the SLAP thingy, as well as basic SOLID stuff from 2030), but not to a great degree. It's not *all* useless. Team wise, as others have said, it's better to get together with people you know beforehand, and try to get into the same tutorial group. You get to choose (with caveats), so choose wisely. There's some restrictions that remind me of HDB racial quotas -- can't be all the same gender, needs at least one non-singaporean, etc. -- so either have that token group member already part of your decided group, or form a group of 3-4 people and literally cold call the remaining people (that's what we did -- zoom chat and email "yo you wanna join us") to fill up the 5 people. And don't just pick people you know -- make sure they're competent too. If you end up with a bunch of people who are lackadaisical, the project won't turn out well. TL;DR: uml. it's compulsory, you can't escape this. uml. get good teammates. uml. it's not that hard in a practical sense, but the final exam is important. uml. Taken in: AY15/16 Sem 1 Lecturer: AP John Christian Holbo Final grades: A First off, don't take this module if you 1. Hate reading (around 50 pages per week of reading is normal) 2. Hate writing (bulk of the grades comes from six 1000 word written assignments) 3. Hate science fiction (it's in the name of the module, duh) With that out of the way, this is the complete syllabus for my semester, including assessments, assignment topics and readings for the week (yours will probably be different, but not too much since this module is taught by a single professor and he does reuse most of the syllabus every semester): Content: This module is a lot of fun - half philosophy, half media studies. The content this module covers is incredibly broad, so it mostly skims the surface on the topics covered in the description, but hopefully it should whet your appetite for more. The central tenant of this module is that science fiction works can act as thought experiments - intuition pumps, as the assigned philosophy text calls them, to tweak and expand our intuition so we can think about difficult problems. Although it's not in the module description, the module also goes into media study quite a bit too, going into the nature of genres and the history of science fiction. Readings: There are three books assigned for this module. Stories of Your Life is a short story collection by Ted Chiang, one of the best contemporary science fiction writers. It's available as an eBook for USD10, or cheaper off bookdepository.com ( ). The Wesleyan Anthology of Science Fiction covers SF short stories from the early 19th all the way up to the 21st century. It's a pretty good anthology, covering a lot of household names as well as less famous writers and stories in a variety of styles, topics and subgenres. It's fairly expensive, but if you plan to take this module you can get it more cheaply online before term starts. Intuition Pumps And Other Tools For Thinking is the recommended philosophy text, but I think it should be required. The text is very accessible and tackles a good deal of the topics covered in class, and will help inform your assignment writing and tutorial discussions. NLB stocks many copies of this book, so you should have no problem getting one. Coursework: Workload is relatively light - other than the readings and assignments, there's no other work required. Every week you get 2-3 assignment topics. Over the entire semester you are required to pick six and write a 1000 word essay/paper/story. The assignment topics themselves are broad, and your word limit is tight, so try to narrow the topic you're discussing. It's also good to talk to the professor before and/or after each assignment to see if your topic will work. My advice is to do one every two weeks, so you can get the comments from the previous assignment before starting on your next one. Assignments are graded relatively - you'll get a 3/5 if yours looks like everyone else's. If you need someone to proofread/review your assignment, or want to see what a 5/5 paper looks like, I'm available at e0011848@u.nus.edu. Lecture/Tutorial: The lectures are a lot of fun. There is no webcast, but instead you get a podcast (audio recording). I would recommend going to the lectures in person - the lecturer has a great sense of humor and the slides are often worth being there for. Tutorials don't usually require preparation. Just turn up, and the tutor / professor will prompt the class with discussion questions. Overall, this module has been a lot of fun, and I feel that I've learnt a great deal from it. If you have even a passing interest in science fiction, pick this module up. PS. Do you like ponies?

Hi, there are more module reviews here too: Taken in AY16/17 Special Sem Difficulty: Varies wildly, Tedious for me Grade Obtained: CS Module Coordinator: Prof Zhao Jin Orbital is SoC’s self-directed, independent work course which is done over the summer break. Students get to learn software development skills on their own (google and stack overflow are your best friends now). You also get to clear 4MCs of Unrestricted Electives though you probably don’t need them to graduate. Here are some of my tips for orbital. These are only my opinions so they might not always be right or applicable to you. 1. Even though it’s stated that Orbital is only for Year 1 SoC students, this is not true. Students from all faculties and years are accepted; my partner is a Year 2 Mech Eng student. 2. I feel that it’s better to partner somebody you already know beforehand, preferably also in your course. Since you’ll probably see them more often and it’s easier to meet up to do work on the project. 3. Communication is a very important, a lack of communication can really slow down your pace of development. E.g. when your partner has a much better and faster method of accomplishing the task than you but you have already sun k many hours in to a task. 4. Be decisive. Even though you have to listen to feedback and modify your project to meet user’s needs, don’t pivot too much or you’ll short on time to complete your product. My partner and I changed from making a mobile app to making a webapp halfway thought Orbital so we ended up spending tons of time learning new technologies and rebuilding. 5. Use version control. Use git, seriously. Nobody likes to deal with multiple copies of the same file on your desktop or in dropbox. That’s a definite no go. Also, you’ll need that git reset –hard HEAD when you screw up your code. I’m pretty sure that dropbox cant do that. 6. Having enough data is very important. Think about where you’re gonna get the data for your webapp/mobile app before you set your project. For my Orbital, I did a navigation webapp for NUS that requires data on amount of stairs and whether a path is sheltered for every path in NUS. Needless to say, there was no data and we had to hard code a lot. We also wanted to solve that by letting users provide the data but we didn’t have the time to do it (refer to point 4). One of my observations is that though the ideas and implementations of the other groups are solid, they all face the same problem of not having enough data in their apps for them to be truly effective and usable. 7. Just have fun! Don’t forget to walk around and look at all the apps/games your friends have made during Splashdown in Sem 1. Here’s my webapp if anybody is interested: Helpful resources: Google, Stack overflow, any online tutorials Orbital website Module Rating: Very chill and good exposure to software development but also very time consuming

Taken in Special Term 19/20 with Dr. Wei Khim The course covers basically exactly what is in the description; unlike PC2130, where we focus on describing and solving the dynamics of highly artificial systems exactly, in this module we introduce a wide range of approximation techniques to come up with near-perfect solutions to real(er) life problems. Do know your harmonic oscillator and hydrogen atom inside out when you go into this course, because they will appear time and time again. In our term (being the special term and with less time), we mostly breezed through the WKB approximation (not really much in use nowadays), spending only an hour and half on it, and it was not examined (not that it can really be tested, either: it is a mountain of algebra). I think Sakurai is a good companion -- and regardless, I think every physics student should have a pdf of this -- if you want extra problems/ a few extra topics to apply your brain to. The development in several chapters follows the book. Most of the assignments were easy, bar the last one, which was meant to distinguish the A+ from the A students, and one on the variational theorem, which required hard work and a lot of Mathematica. But this was a special term in coronavirus times, so it is a highly irregular situation to say the least, and usually there is a final exam where you can flex your perturbation theory skills. Overall, a fun(?) mod. If you are a Physics major, you have to take it anyways; I don't think many non-Physics majors get this far in the sequence, but if you want to learn why exactly energy levels of atoms split in magnetic fields, and why the 1s and 1p orbitals have different energies in Helium but not in Hydrogen, this module will teach all that and more.

This year's programming project was actually a reasonably interesting one, namely to implement a word-pair disambiguation classifier, in which the program needs to choose the right word of a given pair (like adopt/adapt) to fill in the blank in each test sentence, after learning from training data where the correct answers are provided. The word pair is of course not known in advance, so the program must be able to learn from the training data alone. We submitted both source code and a short write-up explaining our classifier. A significant portion of the marks went to our classifier's performance on the unseen test data, which is fair enough, but some marks also went to the classifier's performance on the sample test data that Prof Ng provided, which I felt was a bit wrong since some people might tune their classifier to fit best the sample test data.
