AY 18/19 Sem 1: Lecturer: Dr. Tan Ban Pin This module extends ideas about permutations and combinations from high school, and topics covered include Binomial Coefficients, Principle of Inclusion and Exclusion, Generating Functions, Recurrence Relations and Graph Theory. Although the topics themselves were easy to learn, the style of the problems made the course somewhat difficult . Combinatorics and Graph Theory problems tend to require a lot of "ad hoc reasoning" in order to solve them. This made the tutorial problems difficult to solve properly, and it became hard for me to tell whether I really understood the concepts well enough to solve exam problems. Dr. Tan Ban Pin's lectures tended to be informative and systematic, but were also quite mundane, boring and were scheduled very early in the morning (8 am). My tutorial was also scheduled at 8 am, and that was probably the reason why only 3 or 4 people attended. While I didn't particularly like Dr. Tan's lectures, I highly recommend the textbook for this course (Principles and Techniques in Combinatorics). The book is a great source of problems, and the worked examples and style of the book really bring the concepts to life. The assessment structure was also not well designed. Although there were only two assessments (30% mid semester exam and 70% final exam), it put a lot of pressure on students who didn't do well in the mid semester test, and it deprived us of other learning opportunities. The mid semester and final exams weren't too hard if you had seen similar problems before, but were very difficult if you didn't have much time to study anything other than lecture notes and all the tutorial problems. Overall, I wouldn't recommend doing this unit unless you have to, or you really want to learn Combinatorics/ Graph Theory. However, I did learn some useful tricks (e.g solving recurrence relations, pigeonhole principle, bijection arguments) that ended up being useful in other units. Grade: B

PC2230 Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics For more reviews, visit Taken in AY20/21 Semester 2 Lecturer: Dr Loh Huan Qian Grade Distribution: Tutorial 15% Quizzes and Polls 10% CA Test 1 25% CA Test 2 25% CA Test 3 25% Contents: Zeroth and First Law of Thermodynamics Microcanonical Ensemble and the Second Law Maxwell Relations Heat Engines and the Third Law Canonical Ensemble Grand Canonical Ensemble Identical Particles Lectures (Two 2 hr Lectures / Week): Huan Qian first goes through all the hot things that you've seen before in PC1142: The usual laws of thermodynamics, heat capacity and so on. After a couple of weeks, things get whackier. We started delving into statistical mechanics - using probabilities to determine the properties of a system. Things only get weirder and weirder from there on. The microcanonical ensemble begins with dealing with an isolated system, considering all possible states of a system and finding out the most probable outcome. Here, ideas were frankly not too far out. We then moved on to the canonical ensemble, where we consider energy being free to exchange with the surroundings. At this point, things started getting stranger, although it was all still grounded in the same ideas. Finally, we reach the grand canonical ensemble (Sounds like a FGO final move), where not even the particles of the system are constant. Along the way, we also made a few pitstops, looking into Maxwell relations and heat engines, before wrapping up with Bose-Einstein condensates. Huan Qian is a meticulous lecturer. She thoroughly dives into the concepts of TSM, explaining every step of the way so that we do not end up too lost. Her lessons involve working through examples and derivations, which are very helpful when doing her tutorials. Nothing that she teaches ends up going into waste. She also engages the class with PollEV quizzes. Don't miss out on lectures, even if only for the quizzes. Tutorials (Assignments) : HQ's tutorials are usually very similar to the content covered in class. The questions are usually direct applications of concepts, or a reapplication of an example she went through. Not too difficult, although there may be some that require a little out-of-the-box thinking. The questions are usually quite interesting, about some funky phenomena you might not have heard of before, or some application of some problem in her lab, or just neutron stars. It makes the questions less of a chore to do, and more fun to apply what you've learnt. She also includes some questions that require the use of programming to solve. Do take some time to brush up on your python skills if you can. What was especially tricky was graph plotting. This wasn't explicitly taught in CS1010. You would have to look up how to do it and implement in yourself. Exams The CAs were alright. I was a little pressed for time, but honestly, not challenges that can't be done, or a complete bolt from the blue. Expected Grade: B+ Final Grade : A Thoughts One of the more interesting modules I've taken so far. At some point in my education I've just come to believe that physics is either equations that describe exactly what's going on, or approximations that break down at the extremes. This module covers the in-between, where we use probabilities of states in order to describe systems far too complex to consider the exact solutions of. Using probabilistic methods, we can arrive at answers that manage to be very close to what we see in the real world, even closer to the extremes. The idea that what is likely to happen, rather than what will happen, is not something we see used thus far in our physics education. Coupled with quantum mechanics this semester, these two modules opened my eyes to another way of seeing the world. I really appreciate the broad range of questions hurled at us. The use of programming in our tutorial questions especially. Programming would definitely be a necessary and useful tool when applying physics. Having an early exposure to using programming to visualise and problem-solve, and having to learn how to self-source for ways to implement is, in my opinion, a very meaningful lesson to have. This is the last of the 2000 physics module reviews I am writing, and so I'll conclude with a ranking of my favourites from the ones I've taken so far: PC2134 > PC2131 = PC2230 > PC2193 = PC2130 > PC2132

Prof Farooq Shamsuzamman: Flash Distillation (Binary and Multicomponent), Binary Multistage Distillation and Special Cases, Absorption and Stripping, Multicomponent Multistage Distillation, Column Sizing Prof Suraj Vasudevan: Extraction (Immiscible Systems and Partially Miscible Systems), (Revision) Mass-Transfer Analysis, Rate-Based Design for Distillation, Absorption, and Stripping, Humidification, Cooling Tower Design TLDR (long review ahead): THIS. MODULE. IS. HARD. Might be one of the HARDEST CN mods you will face in your candidature as a chemical engineering student (excluding hard project mods like CN3101A and CN4123R Design Project). However, it is also one of the most critical modules you will learn in your candidature if you are an aspiring chemical engineer, as it deals with separation units, arguably one of the most common and critical unit operations in Chemical Engineering. This module will make you reconsider your interests in Chemical Engineering again. This module will form the bulk of your study workload in the semester. Consistent revision is needed to understand loads of concepts taught in class, BOTH the lectures and tutorials. LOTS of conceptual details within each separation process unit and you need to have a really strong grasp of Mass and Energy Balances to master this module well. Exams are tight on time, both the quizzes and final exam, and you REALLY need to master the concepts well to ace them. PRACTICE through the past sample papers that they give for quizzes and final exam. This module discusses the different separation process units that are commonly used in chemical industries. For our batch, the main separation process units that were discussed were distillation, absorption, stripping units, extraction, and cooling towers. Prof Farooq will teach the first part of the module, which deals with mostly equilibrium-based separation processes. He started off with binary and multi-component flash distillation, which is the foundation to understand the subsequent topics which are multistage distillation and its special cases. The finale of this topic would be multicomponent, multistage distillation columns, which would be the foundations for you if you are really interested to enter the oil and gas industry. This is more like an “introductory”, as understanding the operating temperature and pressure of distillation columns and the preliminary calculations to determine the required number of stages for the distillation column was the highlight for this module. Further understanding of distillation column calculation would need HYSYS simulations which would be taught in CN4122 Process Synthesis and Simulation. Prof Farooq will also discuss distillation column design and sizing. Next, Prof Farooq would discuss binary and multicomponent absorption and stripping. The second part of the module discusses other separation units like extraction and the relations between separation units and cooling towers. Prof Suraj will start with extraction, both immiscible (which you will find surprisingly similar to stripping) and partially miscible systems. You will hurt your eyes and brain understanding both the equilateral and right triangular diagrams for partially miscible extraction. Then, Prof Suraj will move on to explaining rate-based separation processes for distillation, absorption, and stripping and how the concepts correlate with the equilibrium-based concepts that we have learned in the first part of the module. Prof Suraj also discussed column diameter calculations for rate-based design. As rate-based design uses concepts from interface mass transfer (from CN2125), a quick online video gave a recap on this and there was a small quiz regarding this topic. Lastly, he touched upon humidification and psychrometric charts (from CN2101) to explain cooling tower design, which although does not sound like a separation process unit, the graphs are similar to stripping and it is also one of the most common unit operations in Chemical Engineering. I would consider this module as the hardest CN module you will encounter (with the exception of CN4123R Final Year Design Project) throughout your candidature as a Chemical Engineering student and in my opinion, this module will test all your fundamental basics regarding your Chemical Engineering knowledge. The analogy is this: For Computer Science (CS) people, they have a hardcore big brain core module which is CS3230 (Design and Analysis of Algorithms). For Data Science and Analytics (DSA) people, they also have a hard big brain core module which is DSA3102 (Convex Optimization). For Computer Engineering (CEG) people, they have a very important but taxing and heavy core module which is CG3207 (Computer Architecture). In the case of Chem Eng people, we have our own big brain and extremely crucial module, which is CN3132. Understanding the contents of this module is essential for aspiring chemical engineers as in this module, you will learn about one of the most important chemical engineering process units, which are separation units. If you see the list of TEs and Pathway modules, you can also see that CN3132 (together with CN2116) are prerequisites for a LOT of TEs and Pathways. I would go as far as to say that CN2116 (Chemical Kinetics and Reactor Design) and CN3132 would be two of the most important modules you need to master to be an aspiring chemical engineer, as these two modules are the modules that separate Chemical Engineering from other engineering disciplines. Thus, these two modules are conceptually challenging (if you read my module review in CN2116, I considered that module as the hardest CN 2k module in NUS). In this module, you will integrate what you have learned from CN2101, CN2121, and CN2125 (Material Energy Balances, Chemical Thermodynamics, and Mass Transfer) to learn about separation process units and integrate them with knowledge from CN2122A (Fluid Mechanics) and CN2125 (Heat Transfer) for the pumps, reboilers, and condensers operating conditions, using some tools to help in calculations from CN3421A (Numerical Simulation). This module really has LOTS of details and concepts, mostly based on thermodynamics and mass transfer and understanding various graphs regarding operating and equilibrium lines of several separation process units. To be honest, the calculations are not really too extensive, but I was overwhelmed with the tons of concepts introduced in this module. If you made it this far into your Chemical Engineering degree and not really enjoying it, this module will make you reconsider your life choices by making you ask yourself: Why am I in Chem Eng? During the module feedback exercise, I describe what I liked/disliked about this module as follows: “This module has the difficult conceptual understanding approximately the same level as CN2116, integrating concepts from CN2101, CN2121, and CN2125 and giving them steroids to understand separation units, integrating them with knowledge from CN2122A and CN2125 to design the pumps and reboiler/condenser and touched upon safety concerns from CN3135, with also a sprinkle of CN3421A added to the mix.” There’s one 2-hour lecture slot and a 2-hour tutorial slot every week, with tutorials starting from Week 2. Lectures are recorded, but the tutorials are NOT recorded . As the tutorials are not recorded, you NEED to come to the tutorials, as the tutorial questions are set in such a way that it gives extra insights regarding what you have learned in the lectures. The tutorial solutions are longer compared to other CN mods like CN3121 as the professors wanted to give extra insights regarding what they have taught in the tutorials. Once you lag behind, you will DIE (like I did during the second half of the sem :”) ). In addition, you need to watch some extra videos (they call it online lectures) before the lecture timing as it serves as a “prelude” to the lecture. Practically speaking these online videos felt like another 1-hour lecture that you need to watch in your free time (although the videos take at most 30 minutes) as these videos always introduce new concepts and (at least for me) need some time to digest. Please revise and don’t be afraid to ask questions when in doubt, as sometimes the concepts inside this module make your brain ache hard, and you better get your concepts right before getting NUKED in the quizzes and final exam. Again, I should emphasize that the difficulty of this module is in the tremendous amount of details and concepts that you need to understand. The calculations are not really very tedious, and if you’re more of a math person, you might find CN3121 and CN3421A much more of a breeze compared to this extremely difficult module. The reason you need to get your concepts right is because of the examination format. The quizzes and final exam are done using Examplify without backward navigation . For thee quizzes, you will have approximately 2.5 minutes per question, and these questions test regarding your conceptual understanding and a bit of calculations. Thus, again, if you don’t get your concepts right by the time of the quizzes, you will DIE . The final exam was basically a speed run. Compared to much older batches, our questions were a LOT easier, where you can roughly see what should be done. If you try to see past papers from 19/20 Sem 1 and older, you will realize that this module’s final exams were MUCH tougher. They kid you not when seniors say CN3132 Final Exam has been one of the most KILLER final exams throughout their candidature back then during non-COVID days. However, now there were MUCH MORE questions for our batch, and if you need to flip the lecture notes a lot to find the right concepts, you will waste lots of time and won’t finish the entire final exam (in other words, get NUKED ). So I would guess that the professors now want us to understand the concepts thoroughly and quickly remember them to solve the problems. I would suggest making a cheat sheet for all the details and formulas so that you can get quick access to them during the final exam (personally I made another 18-page cheat sheet for this module like CN2125). I find that a lot of people didn’t manage to finish the final exam as they flipped their lecture notes round and round to find the required formula/procedure to use. The professors give sample papers for the quizzes and final exam so you have something to practice to prepare for the quizzes and/or final exam. My reaction when I saw 2019/2020 CN3132 Final Exam PYP for the first time the day before the final exam: “... if these questions come up tomorrow, I will surely die . Let’s just assume that the final exam was similar to 20/21 PYP as the format is similar.” Thank God it did. Before ending this VERY long review, I would like to give a comment regarding the professors who taught this module, Prof Farooq and Prof Suraj. These two professors are two of the most knowledgable Chem Eng professors I have ever encountered throughout my candidature as a Chemical Engineering student. Prof Farooq has been teaching this module for DECADES (as a fun fact, Prof Suraj was an NUS student back in the early 2000s, and the lecturer for CN3132 when he took the module was Prof Farooq). I heard that some Chem Eng profs in NUS said that Prof Farooq is one of the smartest professors in the NUS Chem Eng department. He’s indeed, very, smart, but he wants his students to learn by doing. Thus he expects you to do the tutorial questions yourself and if you have any discrepancies with the prof’s answer, you can ask. Oh and sometimes if your questions are… quite basic (not to offend anybody), Prof Farooq sometimes asks you back the question and lets you think for yourself. So, think first before you ask your question. His voice might be quite monotone and compounded with his “coldness”, some people don’t like his way of teaching. Prof Suraj, on the other hand, is much, much kinder. Although the contents might be quite hard to digest, his explanations are thorough enough. He also sometimes promotes the TEs/Pathways that he teaches like CN4215R Food Technology and Engineering and CN4221R Control of Industrial Processes. Overall, excellent work from these two professors.

ES1531 AY2016/17 Sem 2: Screw this module, I don't even know what the heck am I doing. It's supposedly a critical thinking and writing module meant to equip you with the said skill. Unfortunately, to me it feels more like a module that needs good English and throw in some funky tools you have to incorporate into writing. This is probably due to the engineering nature of this module. (It's a module that is COMPULSORY for all engineering students I believe) I describe it as an irony of having to stick to using a set of tools while having the need to write freely in order to express your critical views. You are introduced to tools which you have to utilize in your writing to make it sound like a critical writing. It also teaches you to respect the author's work (it is a critical thinking module after all, you are expected to critique people). ES1531 is entirely sectional teaching, so there are no mass lectures or tutorials. The quality of teaching you get is entirely dependent on what tutor you got. My tutor was Ms Wati. While she is very good at knowing the skillsets and can answer your questions with confidence and clarity, she can be overly critical (not exactly that bad) and sometimes expect too much out of us as engineers (when we are all only Year 1 students!). I do not blame her for not enjoying the lesson and the module, since this module doesn't make much sense to me anyway. This is consistent workload module, where you have 2 major assessments to hand in, and even has to incorporate a final exam. All 3 components are worth a whooping 30% of your grade. The last 10% deals with class participation, which probably means how much you contribute to asking questions in class. In Assignment 1 (A1), you are supposed to read an article, write a summary of the author's main claim and key arguments, as well as writing a critique of any ONE key argument of the author. And what's worse, you have to substantiate your point of view using external sources on the internet. Yes, it feels like A Level H1 GP all over again, except you have to do so using the set of critical thinking tools you are taught. Now you understand the irony I am talking about. My suggestion is to start early, because the research will take some time. Going over word limit for the summary is an issue, while being under word limit is an issue for the critique. That irony. If you run out of words to write, you can write about the ethos / credibility of the author. In A2, you will be teamed up with 2 other teammates of your own choice in order to write a paper on a certain topic, which is likely to be a problem the world is facing today. You are to evaluate existing solutions and come up with your own (and evaluate your own solution too). Like A1, you need substantiating data to support all your evaluations and feasibility of your solution, and you'll need a LOT more than A1. Like proper research papers, you will need to cite your sources properly in APA style. And ABSOLUTELY DO NOT PLAGIARIZE. Like A1, the research is going to take a LOT of time, and is probably why this module is such a burden. Get good teammates, and capitalize on each other's strengths. My group was a well-balanced group with one person good at finding research materials, one good at writing in general, and me being more towards writing, but with an eye for detail, looking out for tiny discrepancies. After finishing A2, there will be an Oral Defence between 2 groups. While it sounds scary, it actually isn't at all. Most importantly, NO NEED for FORMAL WEAR. (because we are engin students, screw attire :P) It's also not graded so there's no need to come so prepared for the Oral Defence. However, it is supposed to help the tutor on marking your A2, so at least know your project well. In fact, it is even possible to collaborate between the other group you'll be with for this by coming out with questions both teams can ask about their paper. (and you should, you don't want your tutor to bomb your team with unexpected questions) The last component is the final exams. It's like A1, however you not only have to critique one key argument, but THREE. (and yes, you still need to do the summary) Fortunately, you are not expected to use all your critical thinking skills due to the time constraint. Also, whether is it fortunately or unfortunately, due to the exam condition and the absence of the internet, you are expected to know some of your research material you've done in A1 and A2 to help you in the exam. You are not required to quote the source properly, but you do need to indicate it is from your research or external readings. But see this in a good light - you can use your general knowledge to throw in some facts that JUST SEEM somewhat relevant to your evaluations. Yeah, basically just some smart bullshitting. :P If you write fast, there shouldn't be much of a problem to finish the exam. But to properly follow the requirements is sometimes questionable.

While taking the test, the software locked us from other applications in our laptops, and we couldn't even "ctrl alt del". The second midterm was a traditional written test. The first midterm was quite easy, and I felt that an excessive amount of time was given (90 mins for 15 MCQ, that's 4 mins per question!). Most people left the test early. The second midterm was harder than the first, but it wasn't too hard either. 90 mins were given for 3 questions, and counting the part (a) part (b) etc, that's about 6 parts. The paper also felt more like an algebra paper, as most of the questions can be solve by writing down expression using definitions and simplifying it. A lot of hints were given as well. For example, they gave you the identity needed to simplify the equation, so you just had to modify your expression to fit the hint's identity. Lectures were webcasted. In fact, half the time, live lectures weren't even available as only a video was available. The LT would be empty. It's a flipped classroom kind of module, so the prof would go through some questions on alternate lectures and webcast them as well. I did not go for lectures, and neither did I watch the videos. I just read the notes. The video explaining the concepts were made by the prof, not recorded from an LT. The video is usually about 10-20 mins, which is much shorter than a traditional lecture, but it's also a bit boring. Those videos felt like listening to the prof reading a script while pressing next on the PowerPoint slides. He didn't even use a marker/pointer to show which point he is at on the slides, and instead, would say stuff like "as you can see from point 2". Just reading the notes without watching the video should be sufficient. My senior recommended me to take it in sem 1 as it was taught by the math department instead of the stats department, which I unfortunately couldn't due to missing prerequisites. By the end of the module, I felt like I didn't learn much because I just copied everything to my cheatsheet without understanding. Multivariable calculus is required for a deeper understanding, which I have not taken. Final grade: A

Took this mod in Semester 1 of AY2014/15 under Prof Chew, Dr. Cynthia He and Dr. Wu. The topic is mostly covered by A level genetics except for Prof Chew's portion on population and quantitative genetics. If you've read through Campbell and Reece it shouldn't pose much of a problem. Each professer gave a CA at the end of their 4 lectures, plus one final exam with 75(?) MCQ questions. I skipped all lectures save the 4th for each prof when they gave out the CA at the end of the lecture, and all lectures were webcasted. The biggest problem a lot of my classmates faced was with Dr. Wu's strong Chinese accent (I am fine with accents), but his passion for the subject he teaches is endearing with lots of self-made props to express concepts such as chiasmata formation and holliday junctioning. His CA was the hardest though, and involves reading two papers. While it is open-book (notes, the two papers can be brought in, and the papers should be brought in for reference), it ultimately tests your skills at drawing the main concepts from the papers. Dr. He's portion was probably the easiest, involving transcription, translation and replication. Her CA was also the easiest, with fill-in-the-blanks and name-the-enzyme questions. There were some tricky ones with concepts that she taught in lecture 4 like determining the minimum amount of codons needed for a fictional species with X number of amino acids etc, but otherwise it was a breeze despite it being closed-book. Prof Chew's portion is the heaviest of the lot, and he compensates for this by utilising the lab slot to make up for lectures (he essentially has 8 lectures). His CA is open-book, discussion and research and basically gives you a situation to which you need to come to a conclusion with regards to a question in population or quantitative genetics. The question was disappointingly easy compared to previous years', but be sure that he has a lot of tricks up his sleeve. His lectures need to be experienced in the flesh though: on webcast they just seem to be nothing but a continual divergence from his main line of teaching, and only make sense in the lecture environment. Labs were graded, with the components of 2 individual lab reports, 1 4-man group proposal and 1 lab book shared between partners. It basically involved DNA extraction and purification, gel electrophoresis, transduction and mutagenesis, but is very straightforward. Exam was equally so, though with the occasional wtf question and paranoia that comes with an option E that says "not enough data to conclude or none of the above", which seems to be a possible answer for a whole lot of the questions. Got an A- for the module.

My favourite FASS module, hands down. I'm very, very impressed with the NUS Japanese Studies department, and I'm so glad I dropped the English Language exposure module to take up this one. I think this module is one of the easiest Asian Studies exposure modules in FASS to handle. Firstly, you're only studying one country, which should make things easier to remember in your head and seem more focused in general. Secondly, the final exam is multiple-choice, and will be very easy if you study your lecture notes and at least finish all the readings (60 pages a week, but they're interesting and varied readings). The most stressful thing about the module (besides, well, panicking about content, but trust me it's not actually that much) will likely be the coursework, which consists of a 3000-5000-word research paper done in a group, and a 600-word forum post that provides an overview of anything Japan-related. These will require a lot of effort, but will also be very fun - if you try hard enough, you should be able to tailor at least one of these to your specific interests. I'm not sure how people who aren't interested in Japan at all would take to this module, but for a casual mainstream animanga consumer like me, it was thoroughly enjoyable. The department makes sure that the subject matter covered is digestible for the uninitiated - they frame the content in terms of disciplines of study (what is history? what is material culture? why do we use art to analyse society?) and they keep larger concepts in mind while delving into minute details and anecdotes they find interesting. It also helps that the lecturers are clearly passionate about what they do and want to share their knowledge - the passion becomes contagious at times. Dr Chris McMorran and Dr Scott Hislop are the best lecturers I had this semester. In fact, I was in one of Dr McMorran's tutorial groups, and he's probably the best FASS teacher I've had overall. They speak very well, are very coherent, and almost invariably finish their lectures on time. They're also very human, for lack of a better word. Dr McMorran remembers each student by name, every year. Dr Hislop talks about his nightmares about the Nara Daibutsu (big Buddha) and his experiences in Zen Buddhist training. They come across as people, which is so important when you're teaching. So yeah, very good, best module, everyone should take it. Difficulty: content-wise, just study; for the rest, depends on how good you are at research. Workload: 60 pages a week, but manageable IMO Assessment: the best Asian Studies exam ever (MCQ), but research essays can be a challenge depending on how good you are at essays. also group project Interest Value: will probably cover at least one Japan-related thing you're interested in; if it doesn't, you have the excuse to research it yourself for one of the assessments Teaching Quality: ace. literally ace.

I would definitely recommend this module.

Taken in AY18/19 S1 with A/P Reuben Wong As part of the UTCP, this fulfils the requirement for Junior Seminar (Pre-requisite for Senior Seminar) and it is exclusive to students of College of Alice and Peter Tan (CAPT) at the moment. This module discusses about theories involving thinkers who question and analyses society: mainly the ruling class, distribution of powers, the dominances of ideas and reasons why it is so. Theories would involve understanding theories by Karl Marx, Michel Foucault and Antonio Gramsci. Some theories would include Hegemony, Marxism, Freedom of speech. What makes this class interesting is that we would apply these theories to everyday situations such as Meritocracy, Age of Majority, LGBTQ, Mental Illnesses and Social Inclusion. So, every week, there will be a presentation by a pair to the class and how can these theories be applied. Presentations tend to be very informal and chill. Sometimes, Prof Reuben will bring us out on a field trip. This semester, we went to enabling village to see how individuals both with and without disabilities can co-exists through empowerment and accessibility features built into infrastructure. I found this most enriching because it has not occurred to me how much effort and planning is needed. It is simple changes that needs to be made, but then it is often overlooked. And at the end of the semester, we have to submit a final paper of 1500 words (reflection or expository essay) to demonstrate our understanding and what we have learnt from this module. Topic is free for you to decide. Personally, I wish I wrote on a topic that I was unfamiliar (such as social inclusion as experienced from my trip of enabling village) because this is a CS/CU mod that is safe for me to really learn something new. This class is highly sought-after by English Literature majors, especially if it's taught by Dr Susan Ang, and it's easy to see why. Carried out in small groups of about 20+, you sit in a circle and attack a poem/story/short novel for an hour, then repeat according to how much time you have. Basically, it's very hardcore close reading with graded class participation. My class was, according to Dr Ang, a "high-performing" group, and I found myself not being able to slack for an instant. It was like taking the eight most vocal members of my IB class, multiplying them by three, and grading them on how much they talked. Though I wasn't pressured as much by the grade as I was by keeping up with everyone else. It was super intense. Dr Ang is probably the most respected teacher in the NUS English Literature department; if she isn't, I think she should be. For those in my previous school, she's like Mr Connor and Mrs Goh in one, combining astute responses and observations with a rapid-fire pace. She's very good at identifying students' individual tendencies and pointing them out so you know what to improve on. She has a reputation for being quite prescriptive about grammar, but try not to let that get you down too much; she's otherwise very good. She also has a reputation for only engaging with high-ability students, but since my whole class was apparently "high-ability", I don't know how to comment on that... Oh, by the way, Dr Ang lets you type your final exam if your handwriting is bad enough! I think it saved my grade in the end. Difficulty: It depends on how used you are to close reading, but Dr Ang does offer extra tutoring sessions in her office that a lot of students took up. I didn't, though, so I can't talk about them. Sorry ): Workload: The classes themselves are intense, but the homework is very light. Two essays (two drafts for each, with opportunity for one-on-one consultation), and the one novel you have to read in the middle of the semester is very short. Assessment: If you took IB, it's just a lot of Paper 1s. If you took the A-Levels, it's a lot of whatever unseen paper you had. The final paper is three hours long, but it's meant to be ample time. Snacks are provided at the back of the lecture theatre when you take it. Interest Value: You're already a literature major, so there's no turning back now. But each class covers different material, which helps to keep things fresh. Teaching Quality: Dr. Ang won the NUS Outstanding Educator Award for a reason. Grade: A+

Taken in 16/17 Sem 1 Lecturer: Kelvin Seah (Micro) / Georgios Georgiou (Macro) Tutor: DIng Gong Yi Having no prior background in Economics, I thought it would be helpful to write a module review based on my experience. Chose to do this mod in my first semester because I am doing a double major in Mathematics and Economics and I can advance to other modules in the following semester. (since there is only 1 level 1000 econs mod) The module is split into two parts, Microeconomics and Macroeconomics. In Micro you will learn about the theory of Supply and Demand (this is every important and will be the foundation of every other topic in this module) and different types of market structure and the rationale behind decision making in these market structures. In Macro, it is the study of productivity at the national level and also how various 'natural mechanisms' and government policy plays a role in regulating the economy. Personally I feel that micro is way way easier to understand than macro because it is a lot more intuitive albeit for some parts, for instance, why a firms makes the most profit when the firm's Marginal Cost (MC) Curve intersects with the Average Variable Cost (AVC) Curve, are not very well-explained and feels quite arbitrary. For Macro I felt that there were many leaps of logic when we are moving from concept to concept and takes more time for concepts to sit in (for instance, purchase of goods improves the economy and central bank purchase bonds creates more money for the country) But after learning about Macro, you'll be able to better appreciate the issues surrounding issues of global economics. I feel that one should try all the pre-lecture material as well as attend all lectures because there are participation marks given out for both. On tutorials: In general, the type of questions that comes out for tutorial will not come out for tests and finals. Aside from calculation questions, the other open-ended, non-calculation tutorial questions is more 'application-based' - in the sense that they'll give you an atypical scenario and expect you to apply the concepts you learnt in this scenario. I feel that my tutor, Gong Yi has done a fantastic job as he usually recapitulates the key concepts in lecture before each tutorial and also reinforces his explanation of tutorial questions with more advanced knowledge if necessary (to cover for the leap of logic in macro content because he mentioned to us that its really watered down as opposed to the previous years). Last but not least, he is also always willing to help and also sends us a summary of what we've learnt in the previous week on the weekends. YMMV depending on tutor. Mid-Term Tests and Finals: As others have mentioned, bell-curve is rather steep (but the definition of steepness depends where you're coming from). The median was 31 for mid-term; was quite satisfied with the 38 I received for MTT. Content-wise, Mid-term would generally cover all of Micro and finals will cover some micro (generally the last one and a half chapters of micro) and all of Macro. In general try to read every question properly and do every question meticulously. There are some clever play of words and terms in the MCQ questions which may make you lose some marks. To prepare for MTT and even finals one should also forgo your intuition and try to stick with definitions (although in case of Econs, a lot less rigorous than mathematics) - especially so when there are so many counter-intuitive examples in economics. Personally, I feel that to achieve success in this mod, it is mandatory to have a good understanding of the underlying mechanism of various market structure and Macroeconomics Model. MTT feels more time-tied compared to the final examination - I had about 5-10 mins to spare after finishing the MTT paper and one round of checking whereas for finals I had around half an hour left after finishing and checking. Final note: Dont be deterred by the 3 hours lecture slot! Lecture usually lasts an hour and a half or at very best (or worst), two hours. For students trying to clear UE: Since it is not too difficult for a non-H2 econs student with no Econs background so I think those who enjoyed Econs at JC level would certainly do well for this mod. Expected grade - A Actual grade - A+

Lecturer: Dr Wu Shangyuan Tutor: Ms Sim Ee Waun Grade: B (S/U-ed) Course Weightage: Class Participation – 20% News Article Pitch – 20% Feature Story – 35% Press Release & Social Media Writing – 25% My biggest disappointment this semester has got to be 'NM2220 - Introduction to Media Writing'. We were taught the theoretical basics of media writing such as: news writing, web journalism, broadcast journalism, photo/video tips, lateral reporting, writing for public relations and advertising. We also touched on topics like ethics and media law. However, in my opinion, this module tried to cover too many things without actual guidance on how to write a news article or craft a press release, which were the main graded components. Coursework wise, as someone who is already working part-time and freelance in the media industry, I felt that this module focused too much on the nitty-gritty that is not an actual representation of the working world. Firstly, we had to do a pitch of 3 stories from one local news article. Sounds simple but the unrealistic guideline was that the angles have to be fresh and original. In the real newsroom, ideas are tweaked slightly from others because those are what get the eyeballs instead!! Next, we had to write a feature story on something interesting about NUS students. Once again, we also had an unrealistic guideline – this time that it has to be 700 words... No feature piece is 700 words in the real world. We also had to take our own pictures but in the newsroom, there are professional photographers for that. Moreover, the marking was rather strict. Lastly, we had to write a press release and several social media captions on a fictitious health campaign. This was okay if not for the fact that the tutorial on press releases was after the assignment deadline so we were basically left in the deep end of the pool. Overall, an unrealistic and poorly organised module. It is better off as two separate modules that go more in-depth – one on basic journalism (news writing) and one on writing for public relations. No wonder they said don't bother with journalism school. Now I know why...

AY20/21 Sem 2 Seems like I'm the first review for this module, and I hope this helps provide a brief overview of the module. Make a new app? - Learn new tech stack as part of a project - Decide to take CS4242 right after so you clear 2 modules in 1 shot on Mondays - Want to end lessons around 6pm so you can hit the gym right after before dinner (post-workout gainz JKJK unless ;) ) This module is an extremely interesting module and one of the only modules in NUS involving sound and music in terms of Computing (apart from the basics learned in CS2108). A must take module for students who want to delve into the world of Music, Speech, and the like for Computing. Also, please try to at least recap on Fourier Transform and the intuition behind it. Strong mathematical concepts are not required, but good to have to understand intuitively what exactly is going on. Or you can just be imaginative and recognise patterns. Anything, really, since there aren't any final exam papers or midterms papers, with the module being more project-based. Oh yeah, and tutorials are mainly QnA sessions to clarify doubts or ask about your assignment/projects. Usually ends early or not compulsory (depending). Also, class size was ~30 when I took it, but honestly, I think this is because no one knew much about the module (well not anymore! ;) ) The prof basically covered the entire required syllabus in the first half which involved the main concepts, such as Fourier Transform, Encoding/ Decoding/ HMM-GMM, and some fun bonus topics like music production in studios and etc hardware stuff which we didn't really touch in our project. You'll also learn music representation in computers as MIDI. The second half of the semester was basically given to us to do our own projects, which for reasons of diversity were to be done in teams of 3 and highly encouraged to have members from different countries. Glad to have my buddies Ronald and Dolly who were solid in their work and we produced a CAPT System for training people to speak Korean, which I believe is someone's FYP this coming academic year. Nonetheless, although the content discussed in the 2nd half was not the core content, it mainly consisted of the prof inviting guest speakers from other global and local universities and research labs, who shared their own domain of expertise. Pretty awesome if you ask me, because we touched topics from machine translation (different languages) to music production (synthesising music from just a very short sample clip that sounds almost natural) to synthesising speech (making computer voices as similar to humans as possible). Assessment: - Project (v big percentage, think ~45%) which spans from proposal, to code, and report and demo. - Presentations: You will need to be able to #1 pitch your project idea to your classmates and prof, which is an essential skill for many research projects and entrepreneurial stints today, and #2 demo your final project to the same audience and not only capture their attention, but also communicate your ideas succinctly. I recommend 1slide/min, evident by my team scored 14/15 and 15/15 using a small number of slides. - Assignment: done in bash, using kaldi. Took a ridiculous amount of time to install as I tried installing it on windows. Ended up just using virtualbox to install a specific version of ubuntu and kaldi ASR toolkit. Note that you MUST use a specific version of ubuntu iirc 16.04 (and not the latest) else some components won't work and the whole setup will just fail to build/compile. The assignment mainly consists of just understanding how kaldi works (and in the process knowing the main steps of ASR) and tuning parameters. You'll need to write a report. Also, although you might be new to bash, please don't make the same mistake as me and forget that you can use loops LOL - Midterms and Finals: essentially just surveys and feedback on the module LOL free marks hahaha just answer as truthfully as you can, pay attention in class, so you'll be able to provide good and insightful suggestions in improving the module. , taught by Prof Michael Yoshitaka Erlewine (mitcho) This is an ideal introductory module on linguistics. As I am interested in different languages, I totally enjoyed this module. All the lectures were nicely presented, fun and engaging. As we write or speak, we tend to follow certain rules, although oftentimes unaware of them. For example, a native speaker of English would find the sentence “more than two students except John came to the party” weird but may not be able to tell why it is ungrammatical. In fact, although this sentence is syntactically correct, it involves an underlying contradiction and is thus not allowed in the English language. This module covers various interesting topics on linguistics like this, and I feel that I have gained a better understanding of human languages after taking it. The workload of this module is not very heavy, as there is only one lecture and one tutorial each week. The essay (15%) may take a little bit of time as it requires reading a linguistics paper or book chapters, but it is manageable. In the tutorials, we were split into groups and each group was responsible for presenting one of the problem sets (10%) and uploading the answer (5%) -- it was a good opportunity to practice presentation skills. Also, if the lectures and tutorial problems have been well understood, it is not difficult to perform well in the quizzes (10%) and exams (20%+30%). Overall, highly recommended. Final grade: A+

Taken in AY 2020/2021 to fulfill my GEH requirement under Prof. Brian Farrell This module is pretty much exactly what it says on the tin. The course explores what a civilian is and why many civilians were killed in war. The course was split into four parts - Defining the Combatant, Making War on Societies, Making War on Nations/Peoples, and Making War on Cities. Each part was structured such that the first lecture of the part would be a broad overview, then the next few lectures would be looking at specific case studies in history. The tutorials occurred on Weeks 4, 6, 8, and 12. We'd have to read some readings that was related to the topic before the tutorial and then we'd spend the tutorial discussing it. The readings can be a bit long, especially since one of our 'readings' was a 90-minute movie, but since we had only four tutorials the workload wasn't too bad. Outside of the tutorials, there are other optional readings. I didn't do any of them and they aren't necessary for the assessments but it might be helpful. Assessment Breakdown: Participation, online tutorial and online forum: 20% Two Midterm open book Take Home Tests: 25% Research Essay: 25% Final Take Home test: 30% If you're good at writing history essays this mod will be a breeze. If that doesn't sound like your thing then you might not want to take this course. For the participation, just make sure to post in the online forum and give your own input in the tutorials every now and then and you should be good. Final Grade: A- TL;DR: 1 is worst, 5 is best Enjoyment: 4/5 Usefulness: 3/5 Prof: 4/5 Difficulty : Content isn't hard to follow, assessment difficulty depends on how good you are at essays Workload: Not a lot outside of the Research Essay Should You Take It: If you don't mind researching or writing essays and the course description interests you, sure. AY19/20, Sem 2. 30% Mission Report A 60% Mission Report B 10% "marksman bonus" Profs: Lu Wei Quan, Yang Lu Here are the things that I've learned: 1. IS1103 violates my natural rights to life, because it is soul-sucking, making it unethical. 2. IS1103 is unethical under utilitarianism, because my aggregate utility has drastically decreased after taking this module. The entire foundation of this module is frankly horseshit. It's branded as an "ethics" mod, but there's literally nothing applicable to ethics in relation to computer science. So why in god's name is this mod compulsory for SoC students? Why? Here are some examples of the quiz questions that they ask: According to Layer2.txt, it is mentioned that The Pawnbroker relied on Security by Obscurity. Is it ethical or unethical for The Pawnbroker to rely on Security by Obscurity? The correct answer: Under any of the ethical views mentioned in this question's suggested answers, it would be ethical ----------------------------------------------------------------- According to Layer5.txt, it is mentioned that The Pawnbroker relied on Security by Encryption. Is it ethical or unethical for The Pawnbroker to rely on Security by Encryption? The correct answer: It is unethical under Contributing to society ----------------------------------------------------------------- As you saw from Exhibit A, although many organisations require its members to abide by "strong password" policies (eg. use a mix of alpha-numeric and special characters, don't write the password down, use a different password for each website etc.), many of such policies are in fact very difficult to abide by, and if they are abided by, this tends to create difficulties for users in their daily lives (eg. forgetting the password). Is it ethical to have such policies in the first place? The correct answer: It is unethical under all the ethical views mentioned in this question's suggested answers ----------------------------------------------------------------- What kind of nonsensical Q&A is this? Encryption is a contentious subject in the world of ethics, because on the one hand you have people defending its use for privacy, but on the other hand you have people making backdoors to catch criminals or whatever. There is so much depth to a discussion about the ethics of encryption, and yet all we get is some stupid nonsense that it's unethical under contributing to society? What absolute garbage. That's just for the quiz; for the mission reports, the mode of assessment is that we need to justify *THE "CORRECT" ANSWER* of the quiz. Not the answer that you wrote, but the answer THAT THEY GIVE. What kind of backwards teaching methodology requires you to posthumously justify answers that weren't even your own? Did you submit an answer on the quiz that you felt was correct? Well good luck to you, because you have no chance to even begin to justify yourself or your point of view. How bloody ethical. Furthermore, each "justification" can only be a few sentences, because you have to literally write hundreds of them; 4 options per question, 5 ethics questions per quiz, 10 quizzes in total -- you do the math -- spread over reports A and B. I might not have come out of NIE and taken some weird course about "experiential learning" or whatever, but I do know that in the 8000-9000 words required to write out those justifications, we could've had 8-9 long-form essays, which lets people defend and expand -- with rebuttals, counterpoints, and examples -- their viewpoint of ethics. Instead we get this half-assed mode of assessment which benefits nobody except the people marking the answers, because they don't need to use their brains to actually evaluate the arguments made by students. How can you teach a module saying that ethics is up to the interpretation of the individual person, when the entire structure of the module is in such a way that nobody even gets to express their own views? Next there is the "world setup"; it feels like the profs watched john wick over winter break and decided to add artificial drama to the module, which contributed nothing to the students' learning experiences. Maybe if the questions asked about the ethical implications of the fella's actions or something, but instead we just get nonsensical labels like "adjudicators" and "high table" and whatnot applied to the quiz. If you gotta try so hard to make your module seem "cool" to a bunch of 18-20 year old adults, what does that say about your teaching methodology, and the content of the module? Finally, there is the question of the absolutely condescending Lu Weiquan. After a few weeks there were expectedly people rightfully complaining about this module. In response, he sent out an email to all students, "explaining" his motivations with so little tact, and with such a belittling tone to the students, that I really wonder what the intention of that email was. Here's an excerpt -- the email "answered" some "grievances" that students had: 1. In response to the question "Why not just make everything like every other written test/exam that you've ever taken in your Primary/Secondary/JC/Poly/etc school life?" The way the question is phrased already paints a negative picture of the response, but I digress. All these quotes are taken directly from the announcement on luminus. "As IS1103 is an Experiential Learning module, the learning happens when you experience what you need to experience in the module. In other words, unlike other modules / classes / courses that you have taken, in which all the answers can be found in a textbook, Experiential Learning is about finding the answers through your own personal experiences when doing the missions." Indeed, experiential learning means learning through experience. But, I cannot say with a clear conscience that, in the course of this module, i have actually "experienced" anything. Second, is it feasible to understand why flipping through a stack of papers is troublesome, as compared to simply doing a Ctrl-F on a keyboard for text search in a word document? Third, is it feasible to understand the difficulties in making ethical decisions if you have never experienced the pain and sweat and hunger and anger and frustration and jealousy and joy and happiness and love that goes into making such decisions in the real world?" What can I say, except that I completely agree? Unfortunately, this is not the reality of IS1103. It is not feasible to learn about riding bicycles by reading a book, just as it is equally impossible to learn about ethics by doing quizzes about contrived scenarios without avenues for creative discourse. Furthermore, I am sure that it can be justifiably unethical under some of the ethical frameworks, to make students flip through papers to essentially "teach them a lesson" that physical data is harder to aggregate than digital data. Also, arguably, students were not asked to make any ethical decisions, so this entire point seems barely relevant. "If you answered yes to any of the three questions stated above, you're not being truthful with yourself, and scientific research backs that up". This translates to: your personal experiences and opinions are invalid, because "scientific research" is never wrong. Is it ethical to be so condescending and dismissive towards a student like that? “Scientific research” or otherwise? ---------------------------------------------------------------------- 3. 2018/19 Sem 1 with Prof Dilip Raghavan. 4% Homework 23% Midterm 1 23% Midterm 2 50% Finals The focus of MA3205 under Prof Dilip is purely undergraduate set theory at an introductory level, and this is shown by his usage of an axiomatic system stronger than ZFC (MK with modifications). The workload is fairly light, even for a math module, as technically you only have to submit solutions to one (1!) question every week. As Ruomu stated earlier, the helpsheet is extremely helpful for tests and exams. Using the correct theorem from notes or exercises can simplify exam questions by a lot, and there's way too many theorems to remember. Most of the test/exam questions will be fairly technical, like applying a theorem from notes, or an induction proof. Technical proof techniques like induction or element chasing become mechanical with enough practice so make sure you do most of the exercises. However, there will be a few questions that really push your creativity; my peers who solved it will usually come up with various different solutions. Also, if taking this module under Prof Dilip, do go for his lectures. When talking about set theory, Prof Dilip is an entertaining lecturer. Unlike the notes, Prof Dilip in person focuses less on the dry technical details and prefers to draw pictures for us on the whiteboard, which might help you understand the what the proof is trying to do better. Set theory as covered in MA3205 can be very useful for undergraduate mathematics. On one hand, knowing the different forms of Axiom of Choice (Zorn's, Teichmüller-Tukey, Well-ordering theorem) and how they relate to each other can be useful in analysis and topology, while some other concepts and constructions covered (ordinal numbers, back-and-forth method) can prepare you for mathematical logic. Final Grade: A+

Taken in Semester 1 AY21/22 under Prof. Chan Chee Yong. Components: 4 individual assignments (20%), team project (40%), final exam (40%). Topics covered: Database design, Storage & Indexing, Commit Protocols, Concurrency Control, Data Replication, Raft Consensus Algorithm, Data Consistency, Query Processing/Optimization. Somebody wrote in their review for CS3223: "For those who think CS3XXX may be easier than CS4XXX: THIS IS A TRAP". That wasn't a joke. This module is twice as intense as CS3223. (It doesn't require much prior knowledge from 3223 though even though the latter is a prerequisite) All lectures are long and will take the full allocated two hours or even more. There are a lot of protocols and you are expected to understand all well. Once you understand the concepts they should be intuitive, but before that they are torturous. Each tutorial is right after a lecture where the Prof will discuss a question sheet from the previous week, or continue the lecture itself. No attendance is required for both lectures and tutorials. The project is super heavy. Be warned. You will need 5-person effort to not tank this component so make sure that everybody is on the same page. It requires each team to implement a database application using two different DBMSs, one of which is likely Cassandra. Unlike in CS3223, there will be no template code provided and all design options are up to you. You will need to conduct experiments on your application and write a long report detailing everything in the end. Expect to spend 300-500 man-hours in total. Each assignment is released on Examplify as a take-home exam and consists of some simple calculation questions. Try to not lose marks to careless mistakes. The final-exam is closed-book with one A4, double-sided cheatsheet allowed. Good luck trying to cramp that much information into such a small estate. Luckily, the paper turned out to be manageable if you did the tutorials/ follow the lecture examples. Questions are mostly short and do not require a lot of recalling. Grad and undergrad students do different papers so I can't say much for CS5424. Prof. Chan is pretty good. 10/10. I think most if not all DB modules in SoC are well-conducted and the profs know what they are doing (as do you <:). TL;DR: Do not solo this module.

Lecturer: Dr Gilbert Yeoh Assessment: - Midterm (open book): 15% - Essay/Short film: 35% - Class participation: 20% - Final exam (open book): 30% Class format: Weekly lectures and tutorials, typically with a film screening (optional but highly recommended to attend) that takes place immediately after the lecture. This was one of the more enjoyable modules I've taken, but it really helps going in if you have at least a passing interest in film critique and understanding the techniques used in film-making. Each lecture usually revolves around a film that the class has watched in the previous week, using that film as the context for (1) discussing specific film-making techniques (e.g. The use of mise-en-scene, motifs, cinematography, etc), as well as (2) analyzing the themes of the film and how they are conveyed. The class also serves as an excellent opportunity to watch some classic films like Psycho and Citizen Kane on a "large screen" (the LT screen). Some of these were a chore to sit through (Greed) and others I loved (Wong Kar Wai fans get to watch 2 of his films), but of course art is subjective so your mileage may vary. The tutorials were conducted by Dr Yeoh and 2 TAs, all of whom really know their stuff and are pretty passionate about the subject matter. Practicing tutorial questions is important for scoring well during the midterm and exams, which have an interesting format where short clips from various films (known and unknown) are shown several times, and thereafter candidates have to answer essay questions based on those clips (e.g. How does director X use cinematography in this shot). In general I found that the questions tend to test one's understanding of film-making techniques and how they are used , rather than on analyzing the themes of the film. MCQ questions are also present which annoyingly test on recall of certain scenes in the films studied (E.g. which of the following items were not present in scene X), without those scenes being screened during the exam. The essay component is a fun exercise in applying what you've learnt so far in a 1200-1600 word critical analysis of one of the films you study during the course. The essay questions seem to be recycled each semester (not confirmed) and Dr Yeoh provides sample essays for reference. In general, I think many people tend gravitate toward the questions on the 2 Wong Kar Wai films or 2001: A Space Odyssey as they are among the more thematically rich films screened during this module, so there are more things to potentially analyze. I can't comment on the short film component, which one can opt to do in lieu of the essay. As for Dr Yeoh himself, as mentioned earlier, he is really passionate about what he's teaching and it shows during the lectures. The lectures might occasionally get a bit dry, but I think that has more to do with the content being taught rather than his teaching style. TLDR; This module serves as an excellent starting point for those at least somewhat interested in the subject of film, without being overwhelming. 8/10 Expected grade: A- Actual grade: A

Only difference may be definitions being more specific and other subtle differences etc. I think it is only in the second half where you learn new things like ordinal and cardinals numbers, well-ordering, and an more in-depth discussion on the axiom of choice which in MA1100 (at least in my memory), where there wasn't enough time for proper treatment/discussion. I think discussion in Prof Yang's class is pretty much 2 ways. Content can get really dry sometimes because the proofs are quite technical? Also, Prof Yang focuses more on the big picture than rigor and axioms. Which I personally think it is not a bad thing; without ideas, creativity and motivation, mathematical ideas would are just mere exercises in logic. but funnily enough, he still requests for proofs to be rigorous (LOL) Ever since my time as a freshman (cheh only 1 academic year ago), I was intrigued by set theory and despite how naked and simple it is, it manages to hold much of mathematics together. When I attend Prof Yang's class, it still never fails to amaze me and I legitimately look forward to every other lesson. Do take this module if you want to know more about set theory that is not covered in MA1100.

Dr Tang Wai Shing I like analysis for its rigour and logic in proofs. The module is a bit harder than MA2108 because some concepts are less intuitive. Difficult proofs usually appear in Mean Value Theorem, application of Riemann/Darboux integration criterion, construction Riemann Sums, and finding an explicit formula for a series of functions (can be very tedious). Easier parts include applications of differentiation, Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, and using various rules to test the convergence of series/sequence of functions. The most interesting parts could be the proof that Riemann integral is exactly Darboux integral, that all monotone and continuous functions are Riemann integrable, the Darboux Theorem, usw... Please don't cram at the last minute! One should be very continuous in effort to absorb all the concepts and develop a sense of intuition in the mind. (Continuous in the sense of limit at a point=value at the point...) Also, although the module allows cheat sheet, they are not really going to help as there is little time in exams. I think there are 3 lecturers that teach different batches in turn. My prof is Dr Tang Wai Shing. He is very skilled at explaining theorems but his voice is monotone. So sometimes I can't concentrate. His finals are also the hardest among the 3 profs. #justsayinglol Learning with friends helps a lot. There aren't many people taking the module so we got to know each other quite well after the sem. I managed to get an A+. My efforts seem to pay off! Will take MA3209. Just remember to work hard and steadily to understand! Analysis is cool in the sense that it is intuitive. Wherever in doubt, drawing a picture may help. Difficulty: Hard but managable through effort. :)

to Sem 2. This module is taken in place of CP4101 BComp Dissertation for those students doing a double honours programme and whose home faculty is the School of Computing. The workload of this module is meant to be 1.5 normal modules (6 MC) per semester, but varies wildly since it is an open-ended individual project. It is essential to choose a good supervisor (usually a professor who has a similar research area to your project), especially for research projects where you require significant guidance from your supervisor. I recommend choosing a supervisor whom you already know or who is recommended by students working on projects with them. You may define your own project topic and scope, or let your supervisor suggest topics that they think may be useful. For research projects, it may be beneficial to let your supervisor suggest topics, since they may be more aware of current research areas. You may also want to approach multiple potential supervisors, hear their suggestions on project topics, and then choose a project that you find interesting. The defining difference between XFC4101 and CP4101 is that an XFC4101 project is double counted for both your first degree (i.e. the computing degree) and second degree. This requires you to have both a supervisor from your first degree programme and a supervisor from your second degree programme. However, these two supervisors may be the same person (i.e. a professor who holds a joint appointment in both departments). It is said that even if the two supervisors are distinct professors, usually only one of them will play a major role in your project — in this case, the advice in the previous paragraphs would probably apply just to the supervisor playing the major role. Graded requirements and deadlines are exactly the same as that of CP4101; the requirements of the equivalent final-year project module of your second degree are to be ignored (at least for my case, where my second degree is applied mathematics).

Taken in Fall 2021 under Prof Vincent Yan Fu Tan. TL;DR: probably best module I've ever had at NUS math/CS so far. Take the module if mathematics does not scare you. Otherwise I guess CS3244 is more than enough for CS people. Prerequisites: Mostly you need to be familiar with probability theory, basic linear algebra (1000 level) and a little bit of optimization theory such as KKT conditions. Although numerical analysis is listed as a requirement, it is not actually used in the course. Contents and teaching: This module covers traditional problems in ML from a mathematical lens (as they are indeed math problems), such as perceptron, SVM & VC dimension, regression, active learning, SRM, model selection via BIC, feature selection via Naïve Bayes, AdaBoost, EM and graphical models (Markov chains, HMM, Bayesian network and trees). As you can see, that's A LOT of stuff and they are all covered with great mathematical details during the lectures. Despite this, Prof Tan went through everything with great passion and patience and he is probably the best educator I've ever met at NUS so far. He induced most of the results rigorously during the classes and explained their math motivations very clearly, so it is very easy to follow and understand the contents throughout the semester. Practice questions are given during the tutorials and Prof Tan taught all the tutorial sessions himself, with detailed scripts (the same as his lectures). In conclusion, I really enjoy listening to his lectures and I'll say the contents are "quite easy", not because they are actually easy, but because Prof Tan really taught that well it's that easy to understand. Assessments: - Programming assignment (10%): I'm not sure about other terms but this year the programming assignment is about perceptron and SVM. If is released on week 3 and due right after recess week. You will be asked to implement some algorithms from the lecture in python with code skeletons given to you. The assignment itself is not hard but I have to admit some of the instructions are quite confusing and slightly inconsistent with the lectures. Make sure you post your questions in the forum if you are not sure since Prof and TAs will answer almost all of them. In the end, I think you should be able to score nearly full marks on this one if you really try. - Term project (10%): Term project is released after recess and is due in week 13 (last week before reading week). This term the project can be done in teams of two although at the start of this semester Prof said it's an individual project. You have two options: (i) pick a dataset and run different ML algorithms and draw some insightful conclusion; (ii) pick a research paper (from a set of papers recommended by Prof) and do a critical review on it, including paper summary, defense, critic and new results. New results are very important for this option and if you aim for high scores, you should develop some non-trivial results (either theoretically or empirically). I chose the latter option and did a review on a 2008 paper and developed some improvements of it. I really think that my results are somewhat trivial but it still got me 9.5/10 in the end. If you like to do theoretical ML research, I would highly recommend you to try the second option. - Quiz (2 * 15%) and final (50%): There are two midterms each counting 15% and another final exam counting 50%. They all have similar structures and similar difficulty. The first midterm is in week 6 and the second is in week 10. Prof Tan really likes to give incremental problems where the problem consists of several smaller questions, guiding you step-by-step to solve the whole problem. Therefore, the problems come with hints themselves and if you know how to follow the logic flow of the smaller questions, they shouldn't be too hard. Usually there are no hardcore math proof questions like the lectures, but they test your understanding of the taught algorithms. The first quiz contains some proof questions, but I found it manageable because more or less you can follow the same approach taught in lectures to prove the results. Expected grade: A. Final grade: A+.

The NUS English Language (i.e. linguistics) department is full of win. Dr Yosuke Sato is a great lecturer with a superb sense of humour - I ended up tweeting a lot of the things he said. My tutor, Jian Rong, is a very chill guy who tucks in his T-shirts who asks very intelligent questions. Other than that, the guest lecturer (Dr Hiramoto) was also great,and one of the tutors sounds like a radio DJ? Yeah. Out of all the exposure modules I've taken, I think this one comes in second to Japanese Studies. As an introduction to linguistics, the material is novel enough to always be interesting, and that combined with engaging tutorials (each group takes charge of one tutorial to do a presentation) means that you really do learn things. Content covered includes micro-aspects of linguistics like the Int'l Phonetic Alphabet and phrase-structure rule formation, as well as more macro areas like Singlish and biolinguistics. I guess the most frustrating thing about this module was the group project, which is a <5000-word research paper based on some language datasets they give you, but that was just because of my group; the assignment itself was reasonable. Exams are entirely MCQ, which is amazing. It makes them quite easy while not being entirely memory-based, because Dr Sato gives you actual linguistics problems to solve during the paper. As long as you have a good head on your shoulders and review the concepts before exams, you should be totally fine. This module is a very good exposure choice if you're also taking PL1101E and NM1101E. They cover a lot of the same things - PL1101E has a chapter on language and learning, for instance. In any case, taking that particular combination made studying for the exams a lot easier for me. Difficulty: Quite easy, as long as you're prepared to memorise jargon and phonetic alphabets! Workload: Besides the exams, you only have that one group project and tutorial presentation. There isn't much actual content to review for the exams themselves either, especially when compared with psychology. Assessment: I think the group project is entirely reasonable - you're given a few datasets and some investigation tasks to perform, after which you construct a coherent research paper around your analysis. So it's not just meaningless question-answering; it forces you to think originally and also trains your writing skills. Interest Value: There's one point in the module where Dr Sato claims that linguistics is the centre of the universe, and it's a convincing argument. Teaching Quality: I like this department a lot. Grade: A+
