IS4241Social Media Network Analysis Taken in AY 14/15 Semester 1 Module Coordinator: Dr Chan Hock Chuan Lesson Structure: - 3.0 hr seminar every week - No tutorials or labs Workload: 2 x Assignments (10% each) 2 x Open-Book Quizzes (5% each) 1 x Group Project (30%) Final Exam, Open-Book (40%) Contrary to what the module title suggests, you are not going to analyse Facebook, Twitter or any social media networks. In fact, this module is more about graph theory and basic network analysis than social media. However, IS4241 is still a manageable module. Compared to most level 4000 modules, IS4241 is considerably light in terms of workload and content. If you are an IS major taking IS3102 (8MC) in Semester 1, you might want to consider taking this module as an elective to complement your other heavy modules. You are also likely to be interested in this module if you are more logically-inclined, or if you enjoy the graph theory taught in CS1231. (Ok, this makes the module sound difficult, but most of the concepts taught during the lectures are easy enough to understand and nowhere as theoretical as in CS1231.) Having a statistics background gives you a slight advantage, but it is not really a big deal, and is in fact not a pre-requisite. A few of my friends and I took this module without having taken any statistics modules beforehand, and we still did well. -------------------- Lesson Schedule -------------------- Week 1: Introduction to Networks Week 2: Network Characteristics, Theories Week 3: Introduction to NodeXL Week 4: Advance Network Metrics in NodeXL Week 5: Study Design Week 6: Filtering, Clustering Network Groups Week 7: Intro to UCINET Week 8: Important UCINET Tools Week 9: Triadic Closure & Structural Balance in Networks Week 10: Information Flow I Week 11: Information Flow II Week 12: Project Presentation (no lessons) Week 13: Project Presentation (no lessons) Each lesson usually consists of a lecture, followed by a group discussion, and a few students' impromptu presentation of what they learnt from the lesson or from readings. There are readings every week, and you might be tasked by your peers to share your 'insightful' findings from the readings, but even then there is not too much to worry about. Each presentation is chill, short and informal, and you have the freedom to discuss anything you want. There's no class participation marks to judge you, either. Each reading is an academic paper downloadable from NUS Library's e-resources, and most of them are quite dry and lengthy. I hardly have the time to read all of them, so I usually end up reading just the summary at the back of each reading. The more difficult content comes in the later part of the semester, which is about learning how to utilise the UCINET software (which has a rather terrible user interface) to perform network analysis. The only statistics-related concepts you ought to understand for this module are correlation and regression. While you are not required to manually calculate them in the final exam, you eventually need to have a i) basic understanding of what correlation or regression is, ii) how UCINET helps in the computation, and iii) the input and output involved using certain UCINET procedures. Just do a Google search if you are unsure. Regression with UCINET is one of the most pertinent topics in the final exam, so be sure to study it. It came out in almost every past year paper, and is highly likely to come out in your paper if you ever take this module. ----------------------------------- A Closer Look at the Workload ----------------------------------- 1. Assignments You will have 2 take-home assignments over the semester. Each assignment consists of 4 to 5 questions that test your understanding and ability to utilise the software taught in class (NodeXL and UCINET). The second assignment is harder than the first, but they are still quite manageable. Since they are take-home assignments, you can discuss and compare answers with your friends before submitting them to the IVLE workbin. Almost everyone will score full marks for both assignments, so make sure you're one of them. 2. Open-Book Quizzes Fortunately, the lecturer is kind enough to let you know when he intends to conduct each quiz, so you are able to plan for them better. During my semester, the quizzes were held on week 9 and 11 respectively. Both quizzes were open-book and open-laptop, but no Internet connection was allowed. Each quiz is worth 5 marks (5% of your total grade) and I think that the class average was about 4/5. Even though the quizzes are generally easy, there will be 1 or 2 trick questions that you may not get full credit for because of carelessness. Read the questions carefully and write your answers in pencil so that it is easier for you to make corrections when you check through them. Time is extremely precious in each quiz, so be quick! 3. Group Project The project is done in groups of 5 (or 6, if there are still students unable to form a group). You get the freedom to form your own team so you might want find friends to take this module with prior to the semester. Each team will be required to write a report about network analysis in a real-world environment and present it to the prof in Week 12 or 13. You will also have to utilise software such as NodeXL or UCINET to perform your analysis. You may choose to do a topic recommended by the lecturer or choose your own topic, but most groups end up choosing a topic recommended by the lecturer. Unless you are able to come up with an interesting topic and collect sufficiently useful data for your analysis later, you may want to stick to the lecturer's topic instead. The group project is the most crucial determinant for your final grade. Most students will score close to full marks in the other components such as the assignments and quizzes, but writing a rigorous academic paper is not everyone's forte, and some groups stumble in the group project. If you want to do well for this module, treat your group report like an FYP paper. Refer to your readings to get a sense of how a serious academic paper is structured. Consulting the instructor and TA is essential too. There were no rubrics given, but from what I know, the group report is graded based on (i) report logic and structure, (ii) whether you did a comprehensive and related literature review, (iii) whether you are able to provide strong arguments for your hypotheses, (iv) whether you explain your results well and (v) whether your topic/analysis is interesting. 4. Final Exam The final exam is open-book, so just bring everything that might be helpful to you. When I took this module during my semester, the paper was structured this way: 3 x 5 marks questions 1 x 25 marks question (10 marks for part 1, 15 marks for part 2) TOTAL: 40 marks Most of my peers found the paper manageable. In fact, I feel that the group project was harder than the final exam. The 5 mark questions are mostly give-away questions that you ought to score full credit in. The 25 mark question, composed of 2 parts, were basically about regression in UCINET. You can't just study the lecture notes alone. Be sure to do the practice questions given out prior to the exam. I would also recommend checking out the UCINET user guide online when you're confused while studying. If you really want extra practice, you can even try sample assignments and past year papers from similar modules offered by other universities. --------------- TEXTBOOKS: --------------- Most of the lecture notes are based on these 2 textbooks, which are freely available online. 1. Networks, Crowds, and Markets: Reasoning About a Highly Connected World (by David Easley and Jon Kleinberg) You can download the book here: 2. Analyzing Social Media Networks with NodeXL: Insights from a Connected World (by Derek Hansen , Ben Shneiderman and Marc A. Smith) To download it, go to the NUS Libraries site, click on DATABASES, select Science Direct and search for the chapters. --------------- SOFTWARE: --------------- As mentioned earlier, you will be learning how to use NodeXL and UCINET for network analysis. Both software are free to be downloaded from their respective sites, but there is NO version available for Mac OS. If you are a Mac user, make sure that your computer is able to run Windows OS in a VM or by dual booting. You can also try to run UCINET on Mac using Wine too. Alternatively, you can use one of the computers in SoC's programming labs, but that would be quite troublesome, especially if you don't stay on campus. -------------- TL;DR: -------------- Take this module if: 1. You are OK with logic & light math 2. You are interested in graph theory & network analyses 3. You don't like class participation grading 4. You want a relatively light workload You might NOT want to take this module if: 1. You only want to learn about Facebook & Twitter 2. You don't really like group projects 3. You and your potential group mates are not very comfortable with writing an academic research paper 4. You have no access to Windows OS at all Thanks for taking the time to read this! :)

Taken in 20/21 Sem 2 with A/P Li Wenhui Assessment: Midterm exam (35%), Final exam (65%) Lectures were in-person despite the COVID situation because the class size was small. The lecture notes are handwritten by Prof Li herself. Formula sheets and summaries were also provided. This is a graduate level module focusing on how lasers work, their principles and the different ways of manipulating them. Since Prof Li is an experimentalist at CQT, the module also takes on an experimental slant, with more focus on practical work, and less on detailed proofs and derivation. This module consists of 4 topics: 1. Laser Beams 2. Laser Theory 3. Laser Modulation Techniques 4. Non-linear Optics Even though Modern Optics (PC3247) is listed as a prerequisite, it is not exactly necessary. Only the first topic, Laser Beams, require some background knowledge of PC3247 but that topic was quite manageable so you’ll do probably do fine anyway. Instead, I found a good background in electromagnetism more important (see corequisites). It may help to read through your EM notes before starting this mod. The module is moderately rigorous, but does not come close to the rigour of other physics modules (think MM1). It probably is one of those modules that is 5k not because of its rigour but because of how niche the subject matter is. The midterm exam covers the first half the module (Topic 1 and 2) which consists of concepts about light-atom interaction, broadening mechanisms, lasing mechanism, and steady-state laser operation. Ray optics and Gaussian Beams are also covered i.e. finding Rayleigh length, beam waist, beam width etc. The final exam covers the second half of the module including the concepts of Acoustic-optic (AO) modulation, Electro-optic (EO) modulation and EO effects in birefringent crystals. The idea of an index ellipsoid was a particularly interesting mathematical tool in finding the different refractive indices; this could be something you may look forward to. The last chapter was quite interesting too — it was about how nonlinear responses to E-fields can allow second harmonic generation (SHG) and sum frequency generation, depending on several parameters and conditions. The midterm exam was doable; the final exam is actually not too difficult but it was difficult to study for. The questions were unprecedented and required a deep understanding of the lecture material. Students with experience working with lasers in the lab will likely have an edge. Doing extra questions from the recommended text may help (Fundamentals of Photonics by Salem & Teich). Prof Li is very approachable, and replies promptly to emails, answering questions with much detail and clarity. It was a real joy to be able to learn from her. This module is particularly suitable for people aspiring to do experimental work at CQT, and may be helpful for those who have to work with lasers. If you are like me, an intimidated undergraduate (year 3) ((not even from FOS)) sitting in a roomful of masters students, there is no cause for worry. Sit back, relax and enjoy the module :)

Took this module in Sem 1 of AY16/17 under Dr Marc Rochester. No final examination. TL;DR: Basically "Orchestras in Singapore 1101". Stickler for essay formatting with vague topics that are easily misinterpreted. Very light workload, but not guaranteed an A. Probably boring for people who already are immersed in the Singaporean "western" music scene. CA consists of four parts: CA1: Fieldwork project on the study of audience behaviour in western music concerts in Singapore OR study of music schools/teaching programmes in Singapore, with a presentation in class. Group work of about 5-8(?) people. CA2: 500 word objective individual essay on a "western music ensemble" in Singapore. CA3: 750 word subjective individual essay on the position of the Singaporean music scene in the global context. CA4: Introduced at the last minute - class discussion during week 13's class. I found that there was a huge discrepancy between what the module title and description suggests and what is actually taught in the module. While the module is titled "Western Music within a Singaporean Context" (where western basically = classical as we generally understand it), it basically can be summed up as "the history of orchestras in Singapore". As someone who comes from a choral background I found it immensely disappointing that the vast majority of content covered orchestral music, with the other major topic being the role of learning and teaching "western" music in Singaporean society. The module description also reads: "It will assess the impact of majority cultures (particularly from the Chinese, Malay and Indian communities) on the general reception of Western music, as well as on music written by Singapore-based composers. Students will be introduced to the principal figures in Singapore’s musical development." However, these issues were just touch-and-go, with Marc basically rambling on about the treatment of classical music in Singaporean households or about audience perceptions. I honestly do not recall anything about majority cultures in Singapore being mentioned, and only a very small portion was touched on regarding Singaporean composers, even solo Singaporean musicians. While Marc himself is a rather funny guy, he basically sits you down for 1.5 hrs a week and rambles on, asking more questions than he gives answers, simply because this is a field that doesn't really have much research conducted with regard to music in Singapore. While he occasionally gives you facts, he doesn't properly cite the sources that he tends to mention casually, making it seem extremely wishy-washy. Lecture slides are uploaded every week after class, along with (rather soft) audio recordings of one of the lecture slots. The guest lectures are pretty banal, with more about the orchestras like SSO and Music Makers, the history of their establishment and things like that. If you're already pretty much into the local "western" music scene there's not much you can learn from attending lectures: it's basically a reaffirmation of what you already know more or less. For the fieldwork project, since the class is split into such large groups, you are allowed to split the work by having some members exclusively do data collection and others do the presentation, or have everyone involved. However, traditional powerpoint presentations should be eschewed for more interesting and attention-grabbing methods such as skits and interactive sessions. It also helps to have a few major points from your fieldwork presented as clearly as possible rather than trying to cover all bases. For the essays, the main thing is to FOLLOW THE GUIDELINES STRICTLY! He spells them all out within the powerpoint and word documents, though both documents sometimes have things that he does not put in the other, so be wary and ensure that you put in everything and double/triple check before submission, as he has been known to drop people a few grades for not following the format. The topics tend to be VERY VAGUE and are easily subject to misinterpretation, as evidenced by the majority of my groupmates and myself. While the topics may be vague, he has a very strict idea of what should be put in the essay (which is pretty unfair), and so if you really want that A you HAVE to consult him about your ideas relating to the given essay topics, otherwise it's extremely easy to get a C for the essay component. Book him early for a consultation as he tends to be busy running around watching concerts and other stuff. You only get one chance to upload your essay, and if you don't follow the guidelines or completely misinterpret the essay he will ask you to resubmit it with a SEVERE PENALTY (25%) IN GRADING, and can only be done during the submission period. i.e. past the given deadline, no more re-submissions if you fail to interpret or follow the guidelines. Some of the criteria for formatting make sense, while others like INSISTING ON USING UK ENGLISH or COUNTING HYPHENATED WORDS AND ACRONYMS AS INDIVIDUAL WORDS are a complete pain in the ass. While this module has an extremely light workload I would honestly not recommend it for people already immersed in the "western" music happenings in Singapore as it will be boring af. Plus, the essays are a real chore which always makes you second-guess yourself. I completely regret wasting 1400 points on this module as I had to bid it under the SSY module code.

Taken in: AY20/21 Sem 2 Lecturer: Dr. Michael Yoshitaka Erlewine (mitcho) Assessment components: 10% Tutorial Attendance + Participation 10% Tutorial Quizzes 15% Tutorial Oral Presentation + Problem Set Notes 15% Essay 20% Midterm Exam 30% Final Exam I was recommended this module from a friend who said it was highly interesting and engaging, and indeed, it did not disappoint! As its name suggests, it deals with the logic behind language. You will get to learn things from how languages form words and sentences, to how reflexive pronouns (e.g. himself ) behave, or how quantifiers (e.g. a, some, all ) are actually “functions” linking sets. There is some math involved, mainly set theory, though not so much as to make the module inaccessible to those from less math-intensive majors. In other words, this module will look at certain ‘rules’ which we picked up (subconsciously or otherwise) and use in our daily speech and writing. It’s interesting to see how these ‘rules’ which we naturally apply can still be quite a challenge to break down! Examples were mainly provided in English, though there may be snippets from other languages brought in to demonstrate certain concepts. No worries if you don’t know them – the questions are well explained and broken down! Prof. mitcho is a highly engaging and passionate lecturer. Even in a Zoom semester, he keeps his content interesting (and succinct) so watching his weekly lectures were never a drag. Also he is super responsive (and his tutors were, too) – most of our questions were answered within the day itself or the following day. Lectures: Pre-recorded videos, ranging from around 30-60 minutes. There are also weekly quizzes on the topic of the week to assess your understanding of what was covered in the lecture. Tutorials: 1 hour sessions every week. There will be one week where your group will have to present your solutions to the problem set of that week (you will be briefed in the start of the semester) – this comprises 10% for the presentation and another 5% for the ‘refined’ solutions which you will submit a few days after your presentation. Essay: There are a few questions – choose one and answer the question in 1000 words and in a way that makes it “accessible to the layman” (like how you would write a blog post or newspaper article). Each question deals with an interesting observation in linguistics (I did one about verbs) so choose the topic that interests you the most personally. Also, each question comes with some readings to help give you the contextual knowledge to get your essay going, but feel free to do your own research as well. Exams: Comprises of MCQs and a few short-answer questions where you are given some examples and asked to explain them using concepts in the module. I found both exams pretty manageable. Do take time to understand the concepts behind your tutorial questions and there should not be much to worry about. Also, mine was open-book because of the online exam setting though I’m not sure if this will be the case in the future. Overall, this module was sufficiently challenging, insightful, and not too time-consuming. Coming from a technical major, it was also an interesting eye-opener to the field of linguistics and my most enjoyable experience out of all the GE modules I took. Not sure which GE pillar it will fall under for the new syllabus, but regardless I highly recommend this module :)

Taken in 18/19 SEM 2 under A/P Ho Ghim Wei, A/P Jeroen Anton van Kan and Mr Tan Huei Ming Grading: 2 x 15% midterm tests (one for each part) followed by 70% final paper This module is split into 2 parts. The first part scratches the surface of basic semiconductor physics and was taught by A/P Ho. Students who have studied NTU's H3 Semiconductor Physics and Devices (EE2003) will have no problem with the first part because a huge bulk of it is repeated content. A standard text on semiconductor physics will be sufficient for reference (personally I used D.A Neamen's) The contents covered include energy band diagrams, the semiconductor in thermal equilibrium, the semiconductor in non-equilibrium and a brief introduction on carrier physics (drift and diffusion mechanisms of conduction). The first part ends with an introduction to the direct applications of semiconductors in: p-n homojunction diodes (forward and reverse biased), metal-semiconductor contacts, bipolar junction transistors, MOS capacitors and finally MOSFETs. Tutorial questions are very computation based but the midterm and final exam questions aimed to test more on conceptual understanding. The second part focuses more on the material aspects of solid state physics and was taught by A/P van Kan. The second part follows very closely to Chapters 7-9 of S.O Kasap's Principles of Electronic Materials and Devices, so I would recommend getting a copy of the book, soft copy or not. Chapter 7 opens with Miller's indices and cubic lattice structures and continues to explore various mechanisms of polarization. Chapter 8 covers concepts of magnetism like Ampere's Law, the Bohr magneton and gyromagnetic ratio, different types of magnetism, hysteresis loops and Bloch walls. Only the last 2 lectures were on Chapter 9, where the electromagnetic wave in medium is explored, alongside the derivation of refractive index under DC and HF conditions. Tutorial questions were taken directly from Kasap's book and focuses on application of concepts. However, the test and exam questions were more "standard" in nature, bearing significant resemblance to the examples given in the lecture slides. The tutor for tutorials was Mr Tan Huei Ming. He makes the effort to give a summary of content covered in lectures and also direct applications of what we have learnt that is being used in the industry today.

by A/P Stella Tan Content: This is a content-heavy module, giving a broad overview of many concepts, including DNA, fingerprints, bloodstain patterns, hair, questioned documents, arson, drugs, firearms, forensic psychology, forensic pathology, forensic entomology, etc. There are also some lectures on law, but they're basic enough that non-law students are not disadvantaged at all. Lecture Style: There are multiple lecturers and guest lecturers for this module; lectures are not webcasted, Lectures notes are self-sufficient, and many of the lecturers merely read off what's on the notes. But it's still advisable to attend the lectures, as the lecturers drop hints here and there on what's important and what's irrelevant for the exams. Workload: Light. Lectures are once a week, no tutorials, no projects. Practical (20%): There are 3 stations: 1) fingerprint-dusting-and-lifting, 2) spot-the-human-hair and 3) match-the-fingerprints. The 2nd and 3rd stations are easy enough so it really comes down to the 1st. The funny thing is that there is no practice at all. So you either get it or you don't. I didn't; my fingerprints were a mess and I got a B for it, which was the lowest grade awarded (Highest grade A+). Mid-term (30%): 6 open-ended questions (with sub-qns), closed book. 95% testing on memory, so bell curve is quite broad since it's closed book; if you memorize everything from the lecture notes, you are bound to ace it. Which was what I did, and I got A+ (lowest grade C). Finals (50%): 100 MCQs, closed book. There are memory and application questions, less difficult than mid-terms since MCQ. Even though there are 100 questions, there is enough time to complete. Just try to memorize as much content as possible. Overall: I felt I got about 90+/100 for the finals, which would give me an A+ for the finals itself perhaps, and an overall grade of A taking into account my B for practical. And that's exactly what I got. So I guess I can say, don't worry too much if you mess up the practical, as long as you can make up for it with the mid-term and finals. And if you're aiming to get accepted into the Forensic Science minor programme, you need to get A or A+; they only accept students with A or A+.

Taken in AY 20/21 Semester 1 Lecturer: Dr Li Wei Assessment Structure: Weekly Lecture Quiz (1 question/week) and Tutorial Quiz (1 question/week from Week 3 onwards): 5% Midterm Test (Chapter 1 and 2) : 30% Quiz on Week 13 (Chapter 3 and 4): 15% Final Exam (Chapter 3-6) : 50% Module Content (will not elaborate much on this): Chapter 1: Theory of Interest Chapter 2: Bond and Term Structure Chapter 3: Expected Utility Theory Chapter 4: Mean Variance Analysis Chapter 5: Porfolio Theory and CAPM Chapter 6: Basic Option Theory While I didn't find the calculations in this module too difficult, I think the biggest challenge that most people might face would be the numerous financial jargon that will be introduced every week, so this is where conceptual understanding is key. That being said, one thing I really loved about MA3269 was how well prepared Dr Li Wei was in teaching the module, from her clear and concise lecture notes to being so prompt in email queries and even having ample practices for students to use in preparation for the assessments (we had around 2 sample papers each for the midterms, finals and quiz along with extra practice questions for the final). Class size was neither small nor big at around 130 students, with majority either Y2 QF and Y2/3 Applied Math students, with a small number of students from FoE. So I'd say one thing prospective students might want to watch out for would be the bellcurve which I think was rather steep - for our midterm test, 25th and 75th percentile was 26/40 and 35/40 respectively, with the median at 31/40. Midterm and week 13 quiz weren't too difficult as many of the questions were variations of the sample papers and tutorial discussion questions. However, time crunch was definitely a problem during the midterm which made it especially easy to commit careless mistakes. Final consisted of 4 questions, totalling 100 marks. First 2 questions were pure computational questions while the 3rd question was a mixture of computation and proof questions. The last question (~19 marks) was pure proof (apart from one subpart which was computation). Personally I didn't find the final too easy nor too difficult, but there were a few computational questions which I stumbled on before being able to do them so do spend some time thinking so far questions which you aren't 100% confident in rather than jumping right into doing the computation (or skip the question first then come back to it later!) Oh but I couldn't do the entire last question so.... :") All in all, a good introductory module that teaches the basic of financial mathematics! Highly recommend this mod for Applied Math majors who aren't sure whether to pick ORFM as your specialisation! (sorry QF majors, you guys don't have a choice HAHA) Expected Grade: A- Actual Grade: A (pleasantly surprised by this, bless the bellcurve)

Semester taken: AY19/20 Sem 2 If you're looking to fulfil your GES requirement or take a UE while simultaneously ticking off your SJW bucket list, look no further. With less balance than a punch-drunk lightweight after twenty pirouettes, the course material and its presentation during lectures appears (to me at least) designed to steer young minds towards various inexorable anti-establishment conclusions. As a politically neutral third year who had completed the 8-MC LC2007 Constitutional & Administrative Law module not too long ago, I was triggered to no end by the relentless use of pejoratives coupled with snide remarks during the lectures while course material was being taught. Constitutional and statutory provisions were cited only partially - in one particularly egregious case, different subsections from different sections in the statute were copied (without section numbering of course) onto consecutive slides, then labelled as something like "what the law says". Offence-creating provisions in the Defamation Act were presented without any mention of possible statutory defences. The cherry-picking list goes on. For a course that purports to discuss important freedom of speech issues, it neglects to even touch on the institutional separation of powers and other basic constitutional issues, as well as engage foundational moral/political justifications, all of which provide the necessary context for any freedom of speech discussion. Granted, these issues might not be suited for a level-1000 module. But doesn't that make it all the more dangerous to provide students with such flimsy and one-sided material, knowing that this will heavily influence their future political views? The illusion of knowledge is more dangerous than ignorance. Admin-wise, it was a **** show of the highest order. Graded assignments (scrapbook article commentaries) were supposed to be marked and returned before the next one was released/due (there were about 4) to allow students to incorporate feedback, but the first was only returned some time after the final one was released. The midterm take-home essay instructions were changed drastically a week after the initial release: the maximum word limit was changed to a minimum word count. Having already completed the assignment, I had to scramble to unpack my heavily-condensed essay into a full-length one. Clarifications and additional instructions came piecemeal, replete with glaring spelling and grammatical errors. I have never seen a more incompetent course coordinator in my life. Thankfully, tutorials cover content wholly separate from lectures. My tutor, Ms Farah, was pretty solid and attempted to facilitate candid discussions, but was sadly limited by the 45 minutes of contact time per week. Her tutorials were for the most part really engaging and made up somewhat for the lectures. Overall, this course is great for preaching and pretending to discuss stuff you don't actually know enough about to engage meaningfully. Unless you're a senior law student or have a keen interest in constitutional issues and have read up extensively enough on the same to see through the disingenuous lecture presentations. Then you won't end up echoing the political views the rest of the unwitting students have been manipulated into forming. You'll just get tilted real hard and end up writing a scathing NUSMods review. PSA for the law students thinking of taking this course: if you're ok with trash assignment instructions and can hold in the tilt, TAKE THIS MOD. The entire course content, readings and slides combined, is something like 10% of one single topic in LC2007. I kid you not. There is ZERO new material so you have to study absolutely nothing. If you want an easy A/A+ just parrot the political views pushed here, don't be me and take the path of most resistance by flaming the examiners by picking apart the essay questions and calling the phrasing "disingenuous" in your response. For everyone else thinking of taking this mod, be warned: take everything your learn here with about as much salt as there is in the Salar du Uyuni. There ARE very valid and important points raised, but their presentation is incredibly one-sided. Side note: I was alerted by some people that my review was taken down after I posted it. Lecturer: Mr Jonathan Sim Tutor: Mr Reeve Tham Grade: A- Course Weightage: Class Participation – 20% Pre-Tutorials – 15% Online Quizzes – 20% Video Presentation & Report (Group) – 35% Reflection Paper – 10% As a compulsory GE module for FASS students, I admit I was annoyed to have had 'GET1050 - Computational Reasoning' forced upon me. It will go down in history as my most hated module, or at least the one I can't help but hate. We were introduced to Microsoft Excel features such as pivot tables, which can be used for data analysis but a main bulk of the content focused on theories like confirmation bias, greedy rule algorithms and social network analysis. More importantly, we were taught how to do simple VBA coding on Microsoft Excel too. Coursework wise, I gotta give props to the lecturer for the well-edited online lecture videos although it was slightly too "onz" and energetic for my liking haha. There were 4 pre-tutorials that we needed to complete. The first three were written assignments and the last one was to code a simple game on Microsoft Excel. The pre-tutorials were designed to mimic real-world examples but I feel like everything was very fluff. We also had online quizzes every week, which was rather annoying to do. While we have 5 attempts for each quiz, the answer options change. They also don't show you which question you got wrong (in case people cheat); so for a slow learner like me it was actually very counter-effective, and I eventually ended up not giving two shits about the quizzes. For the group project, we had to do a report and a 8-minute video presentation on which people groups we think deserve to be vaccinated from a virus first. There were many considerations and it opened my eyes to how unreliable algorithms can be. Lastly, we had to write a simple final reflection paper on the group project; nothing too difficult. Overall, this module falls short in getting us to think and reason computationally. All I can remember is sleepless nights from trying to understand what's happening and spending hours on Excel only to forget everything. Oh well, I wish they let us choose our own GET module instead.

Lecturer: Mr Jonathan Sim Tutor: Mr Reeve Tham Grade: A- Course Weightage: Class Participation – 20% Pre-Tutorials – 15% Online Quizzes – 20% Video Presentation & Report (Group) – 35% Reflection Paper – 10% As a compulsory GE module for FASS students, I admit I was annoyed to have had 'GET1050 - Computational Reasoning' forced upon me. It will go down in history as my most hated module, or at least the one I can't help but hate. We were introduced to Microsoft Excel features such as pivot tables, which can be used for data analysis but a main bulk of the content focused on theories like confirmation bias, greedy rule algorithms and social network analysis. More importantly, we were taught how to do simple VBA coding on Microsoft Excel too. Coursework wise, I gotta give props to the lecturer for the well-edited online lecture videos although it was slightly too "onz" and energetic for my liking haha. There were 4 pre-tutorials that we needed to complete. The first three were written assignments and the last one was to code a simple game on Microsoft Excel. The pre-tutorials were designed to mimic real-world examples but I feel like everything was very fluff. We also had online quizzes every week, which was rather annoying to do. While we have 5 attempts for each quiz, the answer options change. They also don't show you which question you got wrong (in case people cheat); so for a slow learner like me it was actually very counter-effective, and I eventually ended up not giving two shits about the quizzes. For the group project, we had to do a report and a 8-minute video presentation on which people groups we think deserve to be vaccinated from a virus first. There were many considerations and it opened my eyes to how unreliable algorithms can be. Lastly, we had to write a simple final reflection paper on the group project; nothing too difficult. Overall, this module falls short in getting us to think and reason computationally. All I can remember is sleepless nights from trying to understand what's happening and spending hours on Excel only to forget everything. Oh well, I wish they let us choose our own GET module instead.

CS1010FC AY14/15 Sem 2 Taught by: Prof Ben Leong, Daryl Seah and Michelle Teo This is a brilliant course. I encourage everyone who has the chance to take it. And I'm not just saying this. I am the last person anyone would expect to like programming (because I sucked majorly at it in school). But after this course, I can truthfully say I LOVE programming :D The prof is VERY good at imparting the concepts in your head - he explains every single thing, so those with no programming knowledge whatsoever can easily understand. And he is very nice and entertaining - you will never be bored in class. Plus, assignments are done on Coursemology, which is a really effective platform to make you do work :D Submitting assignments allows you to get EXP (points) and you can level up - as though you're playing a game! For me, doing the assignments alone was quite enough to make me learn things - I didn't even have to study much outside of class. Again, definitely would recommend people to take this - I have never had any other class in which studying was so easy and effortless. That being said, I wouldn't say that you shouldn't study at all. I think the most important thing is to focus, do the practices they give you, and ask questions when in doubt. In fact, posting questions on the Coursemology Forum will get you more EXP i.e. more CA marks. Which other course gives you marks for just asking questions?? Exactly. Special shoutout to GIRLS: DON'T be afraid of programming. A lot of girls I know think programming is only for guys who game a lot or whatever but it's not. I too used to think that. But after this course I know it's not true. I assure you, it can be done by ANYONE. I did it and I'm a girl! So yeah :) Girl power woohoo! Anyway, so the structure of the course is as follows: 1st half - online video lectures (posted on Coursera/IVLE) , along with assignments (that will be submitted on Coursemology) , + tutorials and online recitations on WebEx each week(Saturday or Monday) After 1st half - Midterm Exam (15%) 2nd half - basically the same as first half, except recitations and tutorials are at COM2 at NUS. After/During the end of 2nd half - Practical Exam (15%) and 2 weeks later Final Exam (30%) The remaining 40% of your grade will be split into Coursemology (35%) and Class Participation (5%). Honestly, you should be able to get full marks for Coursemology as long as you do your homework and submit on time. As for class participation...I would say if you want to get 5% for sure, then do every single thing on Coursemology (it is not easy) and make sure you get the "OCD" badge. As for exams, I would say, study consistently and think clearly. It's not that bad - the questions are not as twisted as you would expect. Although admittedly the final exam was tough. But the midterm was easy and the practical was doable. So make sure you score decently on those. All in all, definitely take this course!! :D

Taken in: AY14/15 Semester 2 Module Lecturers: Irene Woon, Anand Ramchand Ever since AY14/15, IS1103 has been rebranded as IS1103FC (and now as IS1103X), where an FC (flipped classroom) approach has been taken. Flipped classroom just means that some of the lessons will be conducted digitally, via the Coursera platform, and students can attend them at their own pace and flexibility. Whether this change is for better or for worse, I'll leave it up to you to decide after reading this review. The module covers ethical issues in the context of technology and relevant interesting scenarios are given to students for them to analyse and discuss. Examples of such issues: If a monkey uses a photographer's camera to take a selfie, does the IP of the photos belong to the monkey or the photographer? Should drones be allowed in urban areas as they are double-edged swords? (They can provide value through delivery services, but at the same time, be misused for illegal purposes). Sorry I'm unable to provide too much an overview of the class as I can't remember what was taught after Week 4 (if anything at all)... on to the next part. Firstly, there are only around 6 physical lessons every other week. The lecturers are supposed to upload lesson video content every week so that students can view them at home. Also, there are supposed to be weekly quizzes to allow students to test their understanding of the lecture materials for each topic. However, for some reason, after Week 4, the lecturer stopped updating both lecture videos and quizzes. There was nothing left to do in between the physical lessons. The module syllabus wasn't even updated lol. I kinda slacked off after Week 4, not touching the module much. This is good if you are a slacker like me, bad if you are a good student and you are keen to learn about the ethical issues in technology. Secondly, there is the Term Paper, where you work in teams of 4/5 to explore an emerging topic related to the course. Note how vague the aim of the paper is? It's really as open as you can imagine, and you are free to research on whatever topic you like. Example of topics include internet addiction, gaming addiction, social media depression, phantom vibration syndrome, etc. My team picked Facebook Depression (FD) and we researched on the causes of FD and how they can be prevented/cured. There were a few milestones in between, supposedly to check on the progress of the team, but the module instructors did not give very useful feedback anyways. We managed to cough up 6,000 words within a week and submitted a paper, crossing our fingers and hoping the instructors have a similar tolerance for nonsense as us. Another major CA component was oral participation. There is a Coursera forums but it's not widely used. In an attempt to gain some CA marks to make up for my predictably poor Term Paper and Exam scores, I tried to gain more CA marks through being active on the forums. In class, try to speak up more also, as it's really beneficial for oneself to contribute your opinions and share them with the class. Your just might gain new insights from the lecturers and classmates! Class discussion is perhaps the most fun part of the module. Lastly, the exams. Since it was open book, I didn't prepare for the module at all, and merely printed out the lecture notes and brought in the textbook. However, in the last lecture, the module instructor did advise us on how to approach the exam questions. It's really very structured in the sense that you bring up some ethical theory or codes from "Software Engineering Code of Ethics and Professional Practice" and apply them to the exam questions. However, you have to make a stand on whether a particular decision is ethical or not. Examples of ethical scenarios given in the exam: Your friend is in a financially tight situation and you have purchased a software that he/she can benefit from, do you make a copy of the software for your friend? You have to use some of the ethical theories (consequence-based, utilitarian-based, etc) to evaluate the scenario and come up with the decision. It's my final semester and I was in the YOLO-mode, hence I just suibian answer all the questions and left the exam hall early. In retrospect, the module instructors weren't very responsible in ensuring that the students were imparted the relevant knowledge throughout the duration of the module. As lazy students who just want to get the module over and done with, my friends and I did not really chase them about it, so that everyone will be happy (: Final Grade: A (LOL.)

I did this mod in Sem 1 2020/21 under prof Anand Mohan Ramchand. Despite its low coursework, you can expect to pick up some of the most useful skills of pitching ideas and ramping up and improving business models in tech companies. This module is basically like NUS's version of the tv show "Shark Tank". You are given Harvard Business School cases to roleplay as different companies and startups in different industries, be it Google, Uber, Carousell, Career Karma and imagine what kind of strategic decisions would you be making to make it through the competition and shine with the use of technology. For example, How do you make Google Assistant win the voice wars with Alexa and Siri? How do you help Carousell stand and survive against Facebook marketplace? Who wins the race between Uber and Lyft and what lays in the future of the AI self driven car industry? How do you capitalise on that and enjoy economies of scale? In return for light coursework, this module instead is looking for a lot of innovative and unique thinking in terms of changes you would bring to a company's business model. These ideas of yours would be untried and untested for the company and hence you need to do your research with your team to demonstrate and present that your idea will work in the real world in front of the class audience, who are going to find every chance to grill you,nitpick and play the role of investors for atleast 45minutes. I did ask the prof how is it possible for us to be brilliantly creative in a possibly saturated industry with tried,tested,accepted and rejected ideas. Prof simply replied, "Well now you know that the pros aren't really smarter than you. They have more data but they still have the same struggles as you are having and the whole objective is to push your thinking ahead of them. That's a lot of hard work, but kind of seasoning and sharpening of your mind will take you the long way." Pretty well-designed mod. Prof Anand is a really cool and chill guy who treats everyone as respected peers,given he curates every group's presentations and has a lot of interaction with every classmate,since the module has no tutors. Coursework wise: 1. We had 1 HBS case a week, would have to answer 1-2 questions in a word doc and submit them. 2. Each team would present once every 3 weeks on a selected HBS case. In total, you and your team presents up to 4 cases the whole semester, with each subsequent case getting higher weightage since you're expected to improve. The 4th one has the highest weightage (25% of your grade). 3. No midterms, or quizzes. Only a final exam where prof asks 6-7 questions and these are not asking for strategic decisions like in the business case presentations. Instead they just cover off theoretical concepts like technology-S curves, strategic advantages of some companies he wants us to study about. typical market behaviours like the "Red Queen Effect", "The Chicken and Egg" situation. During my self study for the final exam, I found this blog to be immensely helpful and similar to his content and it does give you a good idea of the nature of content you will find him teaching.

Taken in: AY20/21, Semester 1 Lecturer: Dr. Leslie Lee TA: Mei Yunbo Overview: An introductory module to Linguistics. I took this module to clear my Humanities basket and took EL1101E as it seemed to be the lesser of all evils in that basket (and also because I heard the lecturer was quite cool). However, I unexpectedly enjoyed this module quite a lot through the semester due to the interactive lectures and the ability to work with my groupmates on the graded problem sets (I took this module with friends). The knowledge acquired in this module can be quite specific, especially in the start of the module where we examined the formation of sounds. Towards the end of the semester, the content got much more interesting and applicable as Dr. Lee examined the use of language in society (sociolinguistics), language shifts and death, as well as language in relation to thought and culture. Assessment Format: 10% : Lecture Participation - At the start of every lecture, we were to log in to PollEv. Using PollEv, Dr. Lee would ask questions related to the content that he would be covering in the lecture. To gain the full points, you just have to click in for at least half of Dr. Lee's questions each lecture for the whole semester. 25% : Graded Homework - During each tutorial (less week 2, 8 and 12 - those tutorials were used for Mid-Term reviews or for administrative purposes), we were given a problem set related to the previous week's lecture. We were to do these problem sets in groups of 3-4 (my TA allowed us to form our own groups) and had to spend about an hour a week to discuss the problem set. This completely replaces the tutorials for this module (again, with the exception of the aforementioned weeks). The problem sets were challenging but rewarding, and my group spent about 1.5 hours on average working through them - there were a total of 8 sets of homework to be submitted onto MS Teams. The TA would then comment on our answers and suggest areas for improvement, which was really helpful in crystallizing our understanding on the previous week's concepts. The downside is that it can be quite difficult to get clarification on the concepts since the class does not technically meet for tutorials. However, Dr. Lee and Yunbo are both extremely accessible and were willing to clarify our doubts via email or Zoom consultation, should the need arise. 45%: 2 Mid-Term Quizzes in Week 7 and Week 11 (Open-book) - It consisted of about 25 MCQs and 3 SAQs to test our understanding on the concepts taught. Each quiz was an hour long, and was conducted during the lecture slot. The quiz was administered using LumiNUS quiz, with backward navigation disallowed (to prevent cheating). The questions were straightforward if you have understood whatever that Dr. Lee has explained in lecture thoroughly. The bell curve for the quizzes was also not that insane, considering the nature of the assessment. 20%: Research Project - The last component of our assessment, which was due at the start of Week 15. In this component, we were tasked to apply what we have learned on language use by analyzing linguistic patterns when conversing in English (or any other language, since Linguistics is the study of language). The essay was not to be more than 1000 words in length. I enjoyed this part of the assessment a lot as Dr. Lee allowed us the freedom to analyze anything that was related to the lecture content in the later parts of the semester. Dr. Lee also gave us a lot of guidance by answering our questions pertaining to the project on LumiNUS forums quickly. Expected Grade: B+ Actual Grade: A

CG2271 AY2017/18 Sem 2: Sem 2 is always taught by Prof Ravi, while Sem 1 is taught by Prof He Bingsheng (the review by Jiachao may be more accurate for prospective students taking CG2271 in Sem 1). The concepts taught in this module are very high level concepts, which may not be everyone's cup of tea (not for me at least). You'll cover real-time operating systems and how they function, including processor-memory operations, interrupts, task managements & memory principles. Quite touch and go so a bit abstract. Prof Ravi does a decent job in explaining them, although reading the lecture notes alone can be sufficient as well. CG2271 has very high weightage (around 40% I believe) on the lab component, so get it done well and you'll be more or less guaranteed a decent grade. Problem is, your lab TA matters a lot. My lab TA marks the lab reports much more leniently than the other lab TA. You might use an Arduino board (subject to change for other sems), which integrates FreeRTOS in the 2nd part of the semester to carry out simple tasks. Generally quite ok as you are given the templates to work upon, and you are guided quite well, especially the setup of the software on your computer is pretty much idiotproof. Some of the later tasks may be hard since you have no idea of the algorithm needed. (Ask your friends for help!) The lab demos are once every fortnightly, so there's time to work on your code and after that, your report which generally isn't hard because the questions are concept based questions, although some questions require a bit of digging through documentation (of FreeRTOS). Unlike Sem 1, midterms and finals are completely closed book. And they are hard. The midterms tested questions that don't even appear to be covered in the lecture notes, or just totally strange questions. The finals however, is partially a joke because past year questions were completely reused. But the main killer of the finals were the programming questions which required you to write code from scratch, even though you are allowed to "invent" your own syntax so long its understandable from FreeRTOS point of view. TL;DR Abstract high level concepts. Labs are generally manageable, nail them. Prepare to die in midterms (weird questions) and finals since no cheat sheets (and coding questions in finals). Expected Grade: B- Actual Grade: B I didn't practice any past year papers and flunged the finals (while my midterms were sub-par as well), even the coding questions. However, due to my lenient lab TA, I was saved from getting a horrible grade.

(covid -- 100% zoom) Prof Damith Expected: A Received: A+ I can't remember the weightage already, but there's 3 main components: individual project, team project, and final exam. As you'll see below, the assessment is mostly a joke anyway. Again, I'll preface this by saying that I don't find Prof Damith to be a bad lecturer. As is this case with most (MOST) of the profs in NUS, they're good people, but there's just something wrong with the course content or delivery. In this case, it was a mix of both. I can't remember what I wrote for the "official" module feedback, so I'll paraphrase from memory here. In essence, this module should really be called "Object Oriented Software Engineering, Sponsored by the UML (tm) Mafia". Java, OOP, and UML really go together like flies, rotten fruit, and a bad aftertaste. Starting with a high level overview of the problems: (1) Objected Oriented. ------------------------- To put it in short: if I were an average student with not a lot of prior programming experience of *differing paradigms*, what would I walk away from this module with? I'd walk away with the idea that OOP is the One True Paradigm, because (a) all the tools and environments are already setup to be OOP-friendly and everything-else-adverse; (b) the module, the professor, the tutors, they all keep endorsing OOP, whether implicitly or explicitly; (c) the starting code given (for the TP) is written in OOP, and is even said to be "well-written"; (d) all my friends are writing OOP code. I'd graduate with a warped view of programming, with the idea that large software projects invariably end up being OOP. In fact, given the structure of the NUS compsci curriculum, all you'd graduate with is "OOP", and "Java Streams" (thanks Prof Henry). Tragic. This module completely does not cover any other kinds of programming paradigms. From day 0 and the individual project, it's all objects, classes, OOP OOP OOP. One of the deliverables for the individual project (henceforth IP) was literally "More OOP -- implement more OOP". This gets worse for the team project (TP). As you might have read from the other, less scathing reviews here, it is a brownfield project, so you start with some existing code. And let me tell you, damn is that field brown. It's not dirt, by the way. Let's just say it's... fertiliser. The code you will be given is your typical, enterprise Java OOP garbage codebase. Full of classes pointlessly abstracted out, code that is a sort of "implicit spaghetti", and classes that literally have no state (only methods), and yet are instantiated -- all for a program that doesn't do very much. About that spaghetti -- because of "abstraction" and the "Single Level of Abstraction Principle" (abbreviated SLAP, how fitting), the code *looks* neat, but you'll soon realise that in order to actually grasp the program (AddressBook 3 -- AB3 ( , you end up jumping all over the place. It's bad. In short, this mod pretends to be software engineering, but in reality it is OOP engineering. So if I don't write OOP code, am I not a software engineer? Do I not qualify for the $5k median starting pay of CS graduates? (2) Sponsored by the UML Mafia ------------------------------------- You better get used to UML, because so much of the finals will be testing UML. Guess what -- after this module, I couldn't tell you what the notation for interfaces are any more. Does it matter? No. Just like the MIPS mafia (which you will be familiar with if you took/take CS2100), the UML mafia is another shadowy organisation that somehow manages to get schools all over the world to push UML and treat it like it's the holy grail of program structure/organisation representation. (Hint: it's not). Here's my personal take: 1. for a high level overview, nobody needs such a rigorous, over-specified notation like UML. Does it matter what specific methods this specific class has? No -- that's what your IDE is for. In fact, the 2103 textbook even states that there isn't a standardised notation for architecture diagrams in UML. god bless. 2. for a low level detail, nothing beats reading well-documented code. Here's the problem with UML: it's not code. Having outdated documentation is already a massive, known problem in the software industry. If programmers can forget (and/or be lazy) to update documentation that's literally right next to the code they're changing (eg. Doxygen, Javadocs), do you think they'll update a bunch of silly UML diagrams that need to be compiled to silly pictures by a silly tool? Probably not. UML will get outdated so much faster than documentation, that the one true source of information is the program source code itself. I won't get into too much detail for the rest of the mod, as the other reviews cover it pretty well. The other thing I want to say is that the mode of assessment frankly sucks. As you might gather, there's 3 main components: the IP, the TP, and the final exam. (I think there might be class participation -- would explain why the tutor keeps name-calling us). Here's the thing: literally 90% or more of the class will get full marks for the IP. Yes, full marks. As long as you submit a working program that meets the specification (which isn't very hard), there's literally no way you can get below full marks. There's a component where you need to add a GUI with JavaFX, but guess what? There's literally a tutorial that you can copy-and-paste code from, and there you go. All you need to do is change a few pictures and you're done. Guess why 80% of the submissions for the IP literally look like reskins of each other? The IP component had weightage of ~20%. What does that mean? It means that it's literally worthless. Unless you're a good student, there's no need to put in so much effort into your IP -- just the minimum will get you that 20%. (putting in extra effort, eg. differentiating your program from the rest, probably won't get you any bonuses either). Next is the TP, which is ~45% (?) of the grade (more than the final exam). Again, given that this was a brownfield project with an existing codebase, from what I could tell, there were 2 kinds of groups -- the kind that basically came up with an entirely new program, and the kind that didn't really change the existing code too much. There was hardly any middle ground, from what I could tell. Where does that leave you? it means that even if your team really puts in a lot of effort to make a good submission, there's tens of other teams that are submitting comparable projects. and that means that this bunch will get mostly full marks for the TP component as well. Finally, the final exam. So, after getting full marks for the IP, and full or close to full marks for the TP (because you're a good student who put in a lot of effort, and had a good team to carry you, right?), you're still fighting for that A+ with lots of other people on this end of the bell curve. Remember how I said you had better dissolve UML paper in water and drink it? In the end, your grade might be determined mostly by the final exam and it's mere ~30% weightage. So what does the final consist of? UML. Yes, UML. Sure, there's other components like code style, conceptual questions on testing and other stuff, but... UML. seriously, go memorise your UML (or get a good cheatsheet). There's graded components for documentation as well -- on the CS2103 side, the developer guide. Because this isn't 2101, it doesn't need to be *THAT* polished -- just make sure your UML is correct, and it doesn't look too shabby. It's probably a good idea to designate one person in your team to be in charge of formatting and error-checking, and another to be in charge of polishing the UML. Finally, there's the bug-testing part of the assessment, which was... an interesting concept. (not a bad one, mind you). There's 3 parts -- (1) attack other people's TP to find bugs; (2) attack other people's TP documentation to find errors; (3) defend your own TP against attacks by refuting their bogus claims. The problem is that sometimes you might get a group that either (a) is simply too good that there's very few "high-severity" bugs, or (b) the group simply didn't add that much functionality that there are very few new bugs at all. (bugs from AB3 don't count). When other people file bugs against your project, your team does get to give a rebuttal (including downgrading severity, rejecting it, etc. -- with appropriate justification), and you can counter-rebut a team's justification against your bug reports. The teaching team uses some magical orb of wisdom to decide who wins, and it's not very transparent here. Sometimes you get truly stubborn people who insist that your program should work the way they want it, and not the way that you have clearly documented in your user guide. for some reason. Of course it's not all bad things; you do learn how to use git+github with a forking workflow, intellij idea (personally i didn't use that piece of bloatware), and how to write tests with junit. the textbook also does *SKIM THROUGH* some code quality fundamentals (like the SLAP thingy, as well as basic SOLID stuff from 2030), but not to a great degree. It's not *all* useless. Team wise, as others have said, it's better to get together with people you know beforehand, and try to get into the same tutorial group. You get to choose (with caveats), so choose wisely. There's some restrictions that remind me of HDB racial quotas -- can't be all the same gender, needs at least one non-singaporean, etc. -- so either have that token group member already part of your decided group, or form a group of 3-4 people and literally cold call the remaining people (that's what we did -- zoom chat and email "yo you wanna join us") to fill up the 5 people. And don't just pick people you know -- make sure they're competent too. If you end up with a bunch of people who are lackadaisical, the project won't turn out well. TL;DR: uml. it's compulsory, you can't escape this. uml. get good teammates. uml. it's not that hard in a practical sense, but the final exam is important. uml. This review was not sponsored by the uml mafia.

Taken in AY20/21, Semester 1 Professor: Prof Rajesh Rai Teaching assistant: Megan Lourdesamy GES1007 is a module unlike any other I have taken before. I had initially taken this module primarily to fulfil my General Education requirements. However, the comprehensive course curriculum and enthusiasm of my Prof and TA left me pleasantly surprised. Course content: This module explores the timeline of South Asian migration into Singapore, and their contribution to its nation-building legacy. While this may seem like a boring history lesson on the surface, the teaching team constantly strives to make connections between events of the past and their observable effects on Singapore as we see it today. This truly helps one see Singapore through a different, historical lens. For example, every time I pass landmarks such as Serangoon road or Market street, I can envisage the events that unfolded there in the past, creating the places that we love and cherish today. Teaching style: The module is taught over a course of 12 weeks, with a 2-hour lecture per week and a 2-hour tutorial every alternate week. Each lecture covers a specific aspect of South Asians in Singapore, such as their religion and geographical settlements, which is discussed further in tutorials. The lectures and tutorials are effective not only in explaining key concepts, but also in teaching how to think critically when presented with historical facts. This was extremely helpful for a Science student like me with no background whatsoever in History. Assessment and workload: This module is assessed through a combination of attendance and participation marks, a tutorial group presentation, a group project on one selected topic, and a book review. Deadlines for all submissions are well spaced and there is more than enough time to work on each submission and ask any doubts. Therefore, this module has a low to moderate workload - adequately challenging without consuming all your time. However, bear in mind that the module can get content heavy at times, so be sure to attend all lectures so that the burden to understand all the content does not fall close to the submission deadlines. Overall, GES1007 is an absolutely fun, engaging and insightful experience. I would recommend it to anyone who loves reading, writing essays and critically analysing facts Expected grade: B+/A- Actual grade: A+

However, learning these 2 concepts before the course will be very beneficial as much of the rest of the course relies on them. We covered the telegrapher equations, Smith chart usage (beyond what is taught in PC2020), Y/Z matrices and S parameters as an introduction. The pace was very slow at this point with Prof Guo spending quite an excessive amount of time on these concepts. Power dividers (Wilkinson, Coupled line) and filter design was then taught. Filter design will not be a problem if you have an analog electronics background, but the even and odd mode analysis for power dividers could take a while to get used to. These 3 chapters were covered in the first half of the course. The second half of the course was more rushed as Prof Guo effectively finished teaching chapters 4-8 in about 3-4 weeks. Content covered includes more RF devices like switches, amplifiers, mixers and oscillators. Amplifier design is a huge part of this course and many details like the non-linear effects in amplifiers, how to design matching circuitry, design for high gain/low noise figure was taught. The first lab experiment was to measure the S-parameters for different devices. Remember to take many pictures! The second lab experiment was to calculate the noise temperature and noise figure of an amplifier under bias/no bias. The first mini project required us to design a power divider at a fixed resonant frequency. The second mini project was the difficult one: designing a low noise amplifier with a single transistor. However, the GA went through all the steps from start to end, but did not explain the big picture again (seems to be the trend in this group), so I just went with the flow without understanding why some steps were done (although they magically improved the parameters). Do start early for this project as it can be quite time consuming. Tutorials are the worst: Prof Guo skipped the first 2 tutorials and basically just glossed over the rest of the 3 tutorials. Doesn’t take a genius to tell students that “this is easy, you should be able to do it” for many of the questions. The tests and final exam tested on basic concepts, and you should be fine if you understood every slide (which is not a lot anyway). Anyway I didn’t do very well for the second test and exam because I was getting destroyed by other classes. Final thoughts: I 100% would not recommend this course. Prof Guo didn’t give me the impression that he prepares for lectures and just glossed over the explanations. (Read in AY 2015/16 Sem 1) MA1505 is a requirement for all engineering students and a very important foundation mod for your math skills, especially if you need to read fluid mechanics/thermodynamics after year 1. It's usually read in year 1 semester 1. The rough flow of the syllabus goes like: functions -> (basic) calculus -> series & sequences -> vectors -> multivariate functions -> vector calculus (line & surface integrals). The assessment for the module was purely exam-based. 20% mid-terms and 80% final exam. No tutorials or assignments are graded. The mid-terms is a one hour 10 MCQ paper, no cheat sheet allowed. A formula sheet is provided instead; some standard Taylor series (e^x, sin(x), cos(x), ln(1+x), arctan(x)), the Taylor theorem, projection of a vector on another vector and shortest distance from a point to a plane. I can't remember what topics were tested; I think it only covers the start of the class up to vectors. The final exam is open-ended with eight questions for 80 marks in two hours. Each question has two parts. You can bring into the final exam a double-sided, handwritten A4-sized cheat sheet (this is very important!!!). No formulas are provided. The math department releases around 10 past year papers (like a ten year series) with solutions for the mid-terms and final exam. Make good use of this opportunity to practice solving interesting problems. Try to have some timed practices to ensure you can complete on time. Exam pro-tip: If you encounter an answer that is exactly 1505 or {the year you are in}, then it is probably the right answer. The calculator policy follows MOE's standards. You can use your A level GC and scientific calculators. I suggest you purchase the recommended Casio scientific calculator that will be shown to you in the first lecture, as it can evaluate definite integrals and solve single variable equations. I can't comment as to the nature of the grade distribution for this class exactly but I suppose it is probably skewed to the right end based on hearsay and the mid-term results. Aim to get full marks for your mid-terms and final exams to secure a good grade. Practice is really important, but make sure you also understand the underlying mathematical principles and have decent problem solving skills so you can adapt to weird, unseen problems. There's usually a pattern to the questions in the mid-term and final exams, but my final exam happened to be quite different from the previous years and caught many of us off-guard. The workload for this module is a two-hour and one-hour weekly lecture and a one-hour weekly tutorial. No graded assignments. I did not attend tutorials other than the first two times as the math department releases full worked solutions after each tutorial. My lecturer was Dr. Yap Wen Ying. Very funny guy! I never skipped math lecture because of him. He is quite clear acoustically and in explaining and analogizing which is really important as you progress to vectors, multivariate calculus and vector calculus. He also makes funny jokes and shows interesting visualizations. 7/7 would attend math lecture again. I suggest complementing the lecture materials with Khan Academy or patrickjmt if you have difficulty following the lecture. Khan Academy saved my butt many times in vector calculus. I found that almost every theorem used in 1505 is covered by either KA, patrickjmt or both. You may also want to collate a "master cheat sheet" for your reference over the semester as you complete lectures/discover new and important things. It's very helpful to consolidate the concepts. My cheat sheet for MA1505 can be found on Paperbaton or on my Github (just download the pdf): Remember that your final cheat sheet for the exam must be handwritten. Include trigonometric identities in your cheat sheet too! If there are any mistakes, please let me know via email so I can correct them. Mid-term: 8/10 (I think the mean was 7?) Final exam: ~70/80 (estimate, we don't know our final marks) Grade received: A. There is a wall of text below if you want to know more about what you'll do in 13 weeks. The first half of the module is H2 math-level stuff that is quite familiar. There are some new bits added in here and there. I will try to review the module by its sub-topics below. In functions and calculus, there are some new things like the notion of extreme and critical values, evaluating limits, indeterminacy in limits and L'Hopital's rule. Otherwise, the rest of the material is quite familiar: first derivative test (also called sign test), second derivative test for concavity, strictly increasing/decreasing functions, integration by parts, the LIATE rule and the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus. You will also need to know how to do partial fraction decomposition for integration. In series and sequences, you will see the familiar arithmetic and geometric series (both convergent and divergent) and power series (like Maclaurin series). The new stuff is: using ratio test to check for convergence, radius of convergence of a power series, Taylor series, Taylor's Theorem, and Fourier series. Taylor series is a generalized version of the Maclaurin series from H2 math. It allows you to represent any infinitely differentiable function as a power series centered around some value. A Maclaurin series is actually a special case of a Taylor series where the power series is centered around 0. Taylor's theorem allows you to determine the error of your n-th order Taylor series, i.e. how far off is the n-th order Taylor series from the actual function. This is not very difficult but can be tedious. The Fourier series is a way of representing a periodic function as a series of sine and cosine terms. Fourier series is quite an extensive part of this class and will come back to haunt you in later chapters and MA1506. It's like the periodic version of the Taylor series where you use sine and cosine terms instead. This is a huge pain in the ass as you need to have a strong foundation in calculus to evaluate the integrals for the sine and cosine coefficients. There's some stuff you need to know like the idea of odd and even functions to simplify your working because then you can use a half range expansion instead (cancels half your work! How great is that?!) There is also some foundational knowledge like piecewise functions, the behavior of their differentials (critical values from the first chapter!) and the notion of convergence of a Fourier series which is important to understand and might make you feel stupid if you do past year papers. My final exam had 15 marks of 80 on Fourier series. The next chapter is vectors. It's similar to the H2 math syllabus: dot and cross product, projection of a vector on another vector, perpendicular distance and distance between point and plane. The main new thing is the arc length of a space curve (more integrals). From this point onwards, I think everything is new. Multivariate calculus (MVC) concerns functions with multiple variables, e.g. instead of f(x) we now have f(x,y,z). The first part is partial derivatives and chained derivatives which are just simple extensions of the normal derivatives. The next part of MVC is on directed derivatives which are derivatives of the function in a certain direction, and determining if a point on the multivariate function is a maxima/minima/saddle point. This is where you need to turn to tools like Wolfram Alpha, Mathematica or get a better GC as the multivariate functions you'll see a lot are in 3D so you cannot easily visualize it. I bought a TI-nspire CX CAS off Carousell to help me out with my learning, but you can't use this during your exams. The next part is on Lagrange multipliers which is used to find the maxima/minima of a function f(x,y,z) subject to some constraints on x, y and z. The next part of MVC concerns multiple integrals. This is an extension of integrals to multiple variables, e.g. if you want to find the area of a region bounded by a multivariate function. Here you will use iterated integrals, which are definite integrals done sequentially (like the inverse of partial derivatives). You will also make use of the polar r-theta coordinate system instead of the normal x-y Cartesian coordinate system, and transforming from Cartesian to polar coordinates. It's very useful in later chapters as because it's incredible at simplifying working. The last part of this course is on vector calculus. This was the point where I had to turn to Khan Academy and patrickjmt for more help, and also what will make up the bulk of your cheat sheet because it's so damn hard to remember everything. You need a solid foundation in vectors, especially in computing dot and cross products. The first half of vector calculus is on line integrals. The introductory parts are on vector fields and gradient fields, which are extensions of multivariate functions. The next part is on the concept of a conservative field which is a property you need to be able to identify to solve certain problems. It basically boils down to "a vector field is conservative if an integral in the vector field is independent of the path taken, and is not conservative otherwise". You'll then learn how to compute line integrals of scalar functions and vector fields. Lastly you'll see the Fundamental Theorem for Line Integrals and Green's theorem which will assist in simplifying problems. The next half of vector calculus is on surface integrals. You'll learn about parametric representations of common geometrical shapes like spheres and cylinders (this is where polar coordinates come in handy). Next you'll have the notion of a tangent plane, which is like an extension of a tangent line. You'll then learn how to compute surface integrals of scalar functions and vector fields. Then you'll progress onto curl and divergence which are just vector field operations, and how they can be expressed using the del operator. Lastly, to conclude the module, you will see Stokes' and Gauss' Theorems for surface integrals. Interestingly, Green's Theorem is actually a special case of Stokes' theorem. These will allow you to simplify complicated expressions and integrals immensely. You must be able to recognize when you can use which theorems!!! I may have missed some parts or made some errors. Please take this as a loose guide! Good luck!
