Amplifier design is a huge part of this course and many details like the non-linear effects in amplifiers, how to design matching circuitry, design for high gain/low noise figure was taught. However, this part was mostly glossed over by Prof Guo and I felt like he was just explaining whatever formulas were on the slides in a “wing-it” manner instead of connecting it to the big picture. The first lab experiment was to measure the S-parameters for different devices. Remember to take many pictures! The second lab experiment was to calculate the noise temperature and noise figure of an amplifier under bias/no bias. This part was more complicated and a good understanding of how noise originates in a circuit is required. Data from both labs was taken in person, and we were given 1 week to complete the lab report. The GAs were helpful and approachable in this portion of the course. The design software that we used for both projects was ADS, and it is relatively intuitive and easy to use. The first mini project required us to design a power divider at a fixed resonant frequency. The second mini project was the difficult one: designing a low noise amplifier with a single transistor. The lab manual alone was 33 pages, and there were many steps to be completed. However, the GA went through all the steps from start to end, but did not explain the big picture again (seems to be the trend in this group), so I just went with the flow without understanding why some steps were done (although they magically improved the parameters). Do start early for this project as it can be quite time consuming. Tutorials are the worst: Prof Guo skipped the first 2 tutorials and basically just glossed over the rest of the 3 tutorials. Doesn’t take a genius to tell students that “this is easy, you should be able to do it” for many of the questions. The tests and final exam tested on basic concepts, and you should be fine if you understood every slide (which is not a lot anyway). Anyway I didn’t do very well for the second test and exam because I was getting destroyed by other classes. Final thoughts: I 100% would not recommend this course. The content covered is pretty good to me, but think of this course as a good restaurant with a really bad waiter. Prof Guo didn’t give me the impression that he prepares for lectures and just glossed over the explanations. At one point, I stopped watching the lectures entirely even though they were recorded because I simply did not understand anything he was saying. I relied a lot on my own self studying for this.

Took this on AY21/22 Sem 1 Conducted fully online Lecturers - Dr. Sayaka Chatani and Dr. Jack Chia Tutor - Dhevarajan S/O Devadas Assessment: Lecture attendance (10%) Tutorial participation + Forum posting + Individual consult (25%) Fictional report writing (10%) Media history essay (20%) Final essay (30%) + outline (5%) I took this module because of the 3 baskets requirements for FASS graduation and this module was very fun. During tutorial it was breakout room discussions about the questions and we would consolidate our answers into a google doc. After which the tutor will go over the answers all the groups had provided and discuss with us about the general consensus etc. After every tutorial there is a forum reflection post to do regarding that tutorial session. Fictional report writing is 500 - 600 words and can be about anything as long as its in the past. It is recommended that it could be a diary entry or a letter to someone. As long as it is about anything historical. (Got A-) Media history assignment. 1,000 - 1,500 words. The 5th tutorial is changed to an individual consult session which we will book around week 11-12. We have to submit an outline of our final essay to our tutor days prior to the consult. The profs and TA give amazing guidance and i highly recommend this module to those seeking to fulfil the 3 baskets requirements or just for UEMs! Expected Grade: B+/A-

Taken AY19/20 Sem 1 Lecturer: Dr NG Wei Khim Grade: A Note: Taken as GEM for H pillar. I think we were the 2nd or 3rd group to take this module, it's pretty new and the lecturer is still experimenting with the lesson plan and schedule. Review: I selected this module purely based on how the module description sounded fairly interesting and how it managed to fit into my timetable. I would have preferred to take other modules for GEH, since there are so many interesting ones out there, but at the end of this module, I think taking this module was a blessing in disguise. The module consists of: - 2x 25% Tests (Middle and end of semester, open book) - 25% Term paper (25% report + 10% video presentation) - 5% Participation (Class activity) - 10% Assignment (LumiNUS, 5 quizzes , 1 attempt each, one per chapter) There are only lectures, twice a week. Tutorial questions will be uploaded for you to complete or look through in your own time, and will be covered during lecture. The tests are approximately half MCQ and half open-ended questions. They are also open book and open laptop (no internet access). The tests are definitely easy to pass, but if you want to guarantee an A, you may have to put in a bit more effort to secure all the marks you can get. Most questions test on things that are straight out of the lecture slides, but there are some which do test your understanding of the topics. The term paper was very flexible in which topic we could write on. He was also very flexible in the groupings. For each member in your group, you will have to write 1.5k words, so the more members, the more words, and the broader your content is expected to be. He promised to take the number of members and the breadth/depth of the paper into consideration when grading, and personally I feel that he is very lenient. The video presentation does not require you to stand in front of a camera, but it is more of a trailer to the term paper. Just a screen recording of you clicking through a PowerPoint with some voice over is sufficient. This is the only project and is given at the start, and due at the end. The class activities are very simple and basically free points. He will even remind you to attend the next lecture if the next lecture will have a class activity. The assignments are online quizzes on LumiNUS. MCQ quizzes which you can refer to your notes and discuss with your friends. Just note that there is only one attempt. Very easy and almost guaranteed at least 4/5 or 5/5 for every quiz. This is the only "homework" and about 2 weeks is given to complete them, definitely more than enough time. The content touches on many real life physics questions you might expect to see answered on popular YouTube videos, such as how rainbows form, why we see colours, and why hurricanes and tornadoes spin clockwise or anticlockwise depending on which hemisphere it is in. The main topics covered include time, space, motion, temperature, sound, and sight (light). The lecturer brings props and uses many demonstration tools to help explain concepts, and these concepts are easily relatable considering they are all around us. The hardest or most abstract topics would probably be time dilation or sound interference. However, even for these "harder" topics, you mainly need to understand the key point or the effect of the concept for the test, plus it is open book so you do not need to memorise content. While some math concepts may be brought in to explain certain topics, we were not required to use math to prove anything. At most, it is just basic multiplication, such as "F=ma, if a doubles, F increases by __". Also something interesting is that the answer to a question can change depending on the time of the test, like whether the Sun is in the eastern or western part of the sky. I would consider this module very easy to score an A in, and definitely recommend it to people who are just generally interested in everyday science stuff.

. My first level 4000 Math module. I was really scared of this module halfway through the semester because I had no idea what the hell is going on. That is partly because of my weak linear algebra background (make sure you are good there or you’ll have a tough time), but oh my god. Tough. Basically it’s solving linear equations a la MA3252, but subject to restrictions that your answers must be integer. However, the module is only half-computational based, as there’s a lot of proving to be done unlike MA3252. You really must understand the concepts behind the methods used well (and that’s where linear algebra comes in). There’s also a section on computational complexity, and I find that my knowledge from CS3230 helped a lot. I really.. didn’t find Prof Sun very good.. I don’t know whether it’s the dreading Monday night 3 hours lecture, but oh man it’s boring most of the time. The worst thing is, his lecture notes are very brief, so you really have to force yourself to listen to him, copy down notes, and then try to make sense out of it during your subsequent revisions. The last chapter, which is on actual application of the optimization method, is a life-saver as it’s just blind calculation using the provided method and it’s not too hard. Tutorials are a must, since you probably can’t do the questions anyway. No, I’m not kidding, they are really hard. Okay maybe I am really weak at linear algebra. I digress. The tutor explains them rather well, but in the case that you can’t understand it on the spot, copy the answers down first, and stare at it 198349021 times after class. No assignments! So mid-term and final exam are really important. The calculation questions are the easy part of the paper – scoring full marks for them should not be a problem. As for the proofs, I think it’s really luck-based, as depending on the questions that are tested (the difficulty of proofs), you either see the answer or you don’t. Make sure you copy down as much proofs as possible from the tutorials/lectures into your one-sided cheat sheet! Some of the proof questions in the paper will be similar to them. Some are really the same. (Which I find really intriguing – if you’re gonna test the same question, then what’s the point? But then again, the module will probably kill everyone if not the case..) Summary: Difficult concepts, easy calculations. Your ability to score is really based on, to a large extent, your ability to cram in your cheat sheet.

A rather unique module. My lecturer was Dr. Sandy Lim, really engaging and entertaining. My tutor was Ms. Riwa Akiyama and kept discussions lively and fun. Assessment consisted of a group project (35%), final exam (35%), tutorial participation (20%) and subject pool (10%). The Group Project was about making a positive difference in someone's (person or organization) life and making a video and report on it. We made a system for the sustainable donation of excess/old furniture from furniture companies to needy families. Took it in AY16/17 Sem 2, under A/P Sanjay Chaudhuri Assessment: Midterms (40%) Finals (60%) I'm from the pioneer batch of students under Data Science & Analytics, a new course offered by NUS Faculty of Science. In the first few weeks, lecture content is mostly about introductions to what data science is about as well as its applications in real world context. There are also introduction to statistical terms (i.e. stuff taught in ST1131) and simple mathematical proofs in deriving statistical calculations like mean, variance and standard deviation. The module progresses on to programming in R (a programming language for statistical computing and graphics) and teaches you how to obtain and analyze simple data using RStudio, a free and open-source integrated development environment for R. Most of the codes are given to you inside the lecture slides provided so you can either get used to using them by understanding what each portion of the code does, or self-learn programming in R using the internet since codes provided in lectures are definitely not exhaustive. In fact, this part of the module feels like a crash course to ST2137 which DSA students are not required to take. In the last few weeks of school, guest speakers (2 for my batch) will be invited to give a talk on how data science is important and its application in things like genomes or manufacturing/designing. The lecture content from here on will also be more directed towards things that can help us handle big data in future (i.e. storage bases like SQL database) and a rough outline as to how these techniques/methods work. For my batch, there were two take-home midterms of which both were capped at 40 marks and a 1 week duration and only the highest score out of the two will be considered into our assessment. Take-home midterms were largely based on R programming and our ability to extract and analyze the given data in coming up with conclusions. One question has multiple parts but it is unclear how many marks were allocated to each portion because only the maximum marks that can be attained for each question (and all its parts) was mentioned. 1st Midterm: Q1) Proving Questions (10 marks) Q2) Analyzing Data (15 marks) Q3) Analyzing Data (15 marks) 2nd Midterm: Q1) Analyzing Data (20 marks) Q2) Analyzing Data (20 marks) Finals were held in the exam hall (i.e. MPSH) and most of it involved proving questions. None of the questions required you to code (since we have no access to RStudio anyway), but some required knowledge of analyzing given data (i.e. using a decision tree to determine predictions). The final paper was capped at 60 marks under a 2 hour limit. Do take my review with a pinch of salt as this module is subjected to changes easily since it has only been taught once and is still open to feedback and improvements. The module content is likely to remain the way it is, but exam formats and assessments may change in the upcoming semester. Furthermore, DSA1101 is now offered in Semester 1 only whereas it was offered in Semester 2 for my pioneer batch. Good luck guys! (:

Taken in AY18/19 Semester 1 Lecturer: Professor Zhao Gongyun Expected grade: F Actual grade: B (I thank my ancestors who have blessed me) Assessment and workload: - 20% Midterm test, no helpsheet (I got 14/50, which was absolutely depressing) - 80% Final examination, 1 A4 sized helpsheet. Experience: - This module extremely difficult. It elaborates a lot about the concepts gone through in MA3252 for linear programming, and MA3236 nonlinear programming. Proofs that were previously omitted in those 2 modules are discussed here. As somebody who has done all optimisation modules, this module is a real eye opener for me because the concepts of optimisation go pretty deep. The module starts with a very thorough discussion about convexity, convex sets and functions, then moves on to optimality conditions. Chapter 3 would be about duality and the most general form of duality, Fenchel duality, would be introduced. The following 6 chapters would be optimisation algorithms and their convergence results. The final chapter would be about nonsmooth optimisation which is really difficult but interesting. This module does complete the optimisation package in NUS. - Prof Zhao has taught this module many times and is very experienced in teaching it. He explains the concepts in the lecture notes pretty well and in a systematic way, adding his own understanding as input when he writes the concepts on the whiteboard. He is also very approachable and keen to answer questions posed by students. - There are no tutorials for postgraduate modules but Prof Zhao provides a list of recommended exercises to try, which were pretty useless because his test and exam uses techniques of a way higher level compared to the exercises. - Midterm test was a bloodbath. Prof Zhao set a pretty difficult paper, at least it was really difficult to me. The level of technique needed to do the questions is very high and it is not easy to come out with those techniques in the short span of 90 minutes. The cohort didn't fare that well, and the mean is in the low 20s out of 60 before Prof Zhao voided 1 question. Still, my coursemates, especially the Phd students, are very strong and the highest scorer got 54/60 before Q5 was void. - Final exam was another bloodbath, to the extent that I felt like crying halfway during the paper. With such a heavy weightage finals, one would expect there to be some giveaway questions to ensure that students pass, but no. There were only 7 marks out of 100 that is a giveaway, one which required students to solve an LP. The rest of the questions were all nontrivial and I just tried my best to write what I know and just submitted the answer book. I felt pretty bad after the paper, as bad as MA4252. Conclusion: - I recommend not to take this module under Prof Zhao if possible, for students who are doing postgraduate studies. It will end up becoming like a pure Mathematics module with a lot of theory and nontrival proving techniques. That being said, this module is an eye opener and it increases my understanding about the optimisation concepts learnt in the undergraduate courses. For people who want to do this module, ensure that you have background in linear programming and nonlinear programming before taking this module.

CS1010FC AY13/14 Sem 2 Taught by: Prof Ben Leong, Brian Koh and Michelle Teo Took this iBLOC from Jan to Jun 2014 under Prof. Ben Leong, You can read more about iBLOC here: ... This is essentially an introductory course on programming. Computing and engineering students have to take this since it’s a compulsory mod. NS guys who have ORDed or going to ORD between Jan to Jun can take this mod before matriculating in August. If you’re an NSF/NSman reading this, YOU SHOULD TAKE CS1010FC INSTEAD OF CS1010 (which is equivalent but starts in semester 1). WHY CS1010FC IS BETTER: 1) iBLOC is essentially a combination of e-learning and face-to-face classes. The first half of this course (Jan to mid Apr) has NO real life classes. All lessons are uploaded online as videos or conducted real-time on an online interactive platform. In the 2nd half you have real-life recitation classes where the prof reinforces what was taught in the lecture videos, and also tutorial classes where your helpful tutors would answer all your doubts. 2) If you’re completely new to programming, you get 5 WHOLE MONTHS to dedicate yourself fully to building a good foundation in programming. Since I was also new to programming at that time, I can tell you in the beginning you will STRUGGLE and spend HOURS of your weekends doing the assignments (called ‘missions’) because you will TRY and FAIL again and again until you get it. Having more time to learn and familiarize yourself with coding really helps especially for beginners. Also you are better off doing something productive in the few months, rather than just sitting around waiting for school to start. 3) If you take CS1010 in sem 1 instead, you have to learn and do the same things in a short period of only 3 months, along with 4 to 5 other mods plus your CCAs and hall activities. I am thankful that my sem 1 is free from CS1010 and you would, too X) 4) This mod teaches everything in Python, which in my opinion is a beginner-friendly language that most people can understand and pick up easily. It’s also A LOT more forgiving on syntax errors compared to other languages. 5) All assignments, quizzes, tutorials etc in this course can be 100% done and submitted online. For most practice questions and tutorials (MCQs and short coding questions), your answers are instantly marked and given feedback by the system. Missions are submitted online and graded within a few days by your tutors. 6) This mod uses a platform called coursemology (which is great) and also tries to integrate some RPG elements into its features which worked surprisingly well. Instead of simply receiving marks for your online assignments, you gain a certain amount of EXPs (depending on the difficulty) which let you level up and climb the leaderboard. By completing certain tasks you even get badges! Because of this most students were quite motivated to do as many tasks/assignments as possible. 7) Prof. Ben Leong is awesome and passionate about teaching. What I like most about him is the amount of effort he spent on designing our assignments and exams. Even though programming is tedious and frustrating in nature, the settings/backstories that he set for the tasks are interesting and lots of fun. My favourites are the ones involving Inception and X-men. XD ASSESSMENT: 35% Coursemology assignments (easy to score) 5% tutorial participation (easy to score) 15% Midterm (WRITTEN) 15% Practical exam (IN COMPUTER LAB) 30% Final Exam (WRITTEN) IMO the exams are can be quite hard but reasonably so. The written ones are particularly challenging since you cannot test out your codes on a computer. Really tests your concepts and thinking. Cheatsheet is allowed but from my experience, you won’t need one if you already know your stuffs. TL;DR – THIS MOD IS SPECIALLY CREATED FOR NSMEN WHO HAVE ORD-ED OR GOING TO ORD. IF YOU ARE ONE, TAKE THIS MOD.

Taken AY20/21 Sem 1 Lecturer: Dr FOO Maw Lin, Prof ANG Wee Han, Prof John YIP Grade: B+ The module starts off with solid state chemistry (by Dr Foo), so your crystal packing, holes and ratios, defects, band theory of metals, lattice energy, etc. Next is coordination chemistry (by Prof Ang), going from nomenclature, equilibria, isomers, chirality, electron counting, VB theory, CFT, CFSE, MO theory, LFT, Metal-CO bonds, phosphines, TEP, TCA, review of HSAB theory, ligand substitution, electron transfer, oxidative addition, reductive elimination. Second part (after recess week) is symmetry and spectroscopy (by Prof Yip), starting with symmetry elements, point groups, and character tables, to infrared, UV-Vis spectroscopy, d-d transitions, and MLCT, LMCT. There are plenty of old concepts reviewed in the module, as well as some new concepts. Most of the concepts and things taught can be absorbed fairly easily and there are not a lot of mental gymnastics to be done in the module. The most important parts/concepts are basically listed above. One of the larger part of the module involves a lot of spatial thinking. For the isomerism and symmetry elements, you do need enough practice to be able to get the answer. Most students are able to get it in the end, as observed by the ridiculously high scores of everybody in the test. Lecturer: Dr Bimlesh Wadhwa Module content: This is one of the unconventional CS modules where the focus is not on hardcore CS concepts. Instead, the whole module revolves around a problem-solving methodology called Design Thinking. Design Thinking is one of the hottest approaches in problem solving these days. SAP charges over a thousand for a Design Thinking workshop that lasts a few days. The Faculty of Engineering has a programme called Design-Centric Programme, which also emphasizes on Design Thinking through the curriculum. Students in CS3240 will be taught and brought through the various stages of Design Thinking: Empathize, Define, Ideate, Prototype, Test. Lectures and Tutorials: The lectures are highly interactive and almost every lecture involves hands-on exercises to reinforce the concepts taught in each phase of Design Thinking. The lecture content is light as there are no tough and technical CS theories to be learnt. Most theories and concepts are quite straightforward and actually makes a lot of sense. Hence they were easy to understand in my opinion. Note that the tutorials and lectures are combined together into one massive 3-hour lesson, so it might get tiring halfway. There's also no distinguishing between lectures and tutorials. But somehow time passes pretty fast during the lessons. Also, Dr Bimlesh she brings snacks (Oreo, sweets, etc) and puts them at the back of the class and they are available for any hungry/student to eat. I visit the snacks corner often (: In the last few weeks, us students took over the lectures instead. In our project groups, we were each assigned an Interaction Design-related topic and gave presentations to the class. However, the quality of the presentations is subjected to the groups effort in preparing the content. In my opinion, some groups' presentations were off-topic and did not have much valuable content. Labs: There were four lab sessions in total covering the following topics: HTML/CSS, Front-end development with Bootstrap and jQuery, HTML5 Canvas, and Chocolate Chip UI. Personally I did not attend any of the lab sessions as I had prior experience with front end development so I am unable to comment on the lab sessions. From the materials covered, the content covered is pretty basic, and students would have to really spend their own time delving into them to be proficient enough in them. Lab Assignments: There were two lab assignments for the course: Bootstrap and Chocolate Chip UI. The topics were very open and you could make any app that you wanted, as long as they made use of the various Bootstrap/ChUI elements. For the Bootstrap lab, I made a portfolio site template ( and for the ChUI lab, I made a Hacker News and Designer News aggregator ( . The final outcome can be a mockup, as long as interactions were allowed. The labs are only worth 3% each, and each small mistake will cost you 0.3%, hence really negligible impact. I spent quite a lot of time (one-two days each) on the assignments though, because I liked doing front end web development. Project: The project group is formed early in the semester and there are three deliverables spread across the semester so that progress can be seen over the semester. The project topic was to solve a problem with a technical solution by applying the Design Thinking techniques and process that we learnt in the class. For the first deliverable, we had to identify our target users, analyze the problem and draft out the requirements for the solution. For the second deliverable, we had to define the primary user persona, define key tasks that our solution will support, build a paper prototype and also get people to test and give feedback. For the third and final deliverable, adjust our prototype according to the feedback, build a final interactive prototype, and evaluate with users. It is up to the technical standard of the team for the final interactive prototype. While it is perfectly fine to build static web mockups, building real working prototypes will definitely score you more points. For my project, we built NUSMods Collab, extending upon NUSMods and adding group collaboration features, allowing group members to combine their timetables to find common timeslots to plan for future group meetings. Our project got 2nd place in the STePS (SoC Term Project Showcase)! Watch out video produced by talented videographer Darren Chua and starring my super 上镜 members Khor Poo Siang and Joan Tan: Exam: Dr Bimlesh was very kind in giving us adequate practice for the exam, and her exam questions were an altered version of the exam practice that we were given. Doing the past year papers will definitely help in managing expectations. However, there were many many exam questions, and most require a lot of writing. Know Bootstrap well, because we were asked to draw out the appearance of a webpage based on some Bootstrap-styled HTML code. Many exam questions were on the design thinking process applied to different real-life scenarios (you'll be given a sample problem/issue/scenario), so it will help if you did the project seriously. I started the exam paper from the back because the questions at the back had a higher marks/time spent ratio. In the end, I skipped questions that I knew I had to spend time thinking or didn't know how to do, and left about 8 marks blank. Overall, a light module that I enjoyed. If you are the creative kind that likes hands-on and front end web development, I would recommend it. Grade: A+

Hi (I'm sorry it's quite a late reply). Compared to background in data mining, I deem that a strong background in probability and vector calculus may help you more, as there are quite a lot of proofings, theories, etc in this module.

AY and Sem for the module taken: 2020/2021 Sem 2 Administrative: 1. Assessment breakdown: - 5 homeworks = 20% - Mid-term = 25% - Finals = 50% - Participation (Lecture attendance) = 5% 2. Exam format: Midterm/Finals = ~8-10 structured questions. Face-to-face, paper based. 3. Workload: quite theory heavy for assignments, tutorials, and lecture, but for finals and midterms are more applicative and relatively easier. This semester the module was taught by Prof. Cheung Wang Chi. He is easily one of the best probability-module professor from the various probability modules that I have taken. He is very smart - and FAST. So make sure to try to understand what is going on, and feel free to let him know when he goes too fast because if no one stops him, he will carry on. So to summarize: IE2100 could be split to three parts. The first 1/3 of the semester (up-to week 5) covers the probability theories (ST2334-computation wise, and/or ST2131-proving, theoretical-wise). Watch out, although this first half is most likely a recap (easier content), Prof Cheung deliberately made the questions more challenging to stabilise the rigor throughout the module. So it's great if you can listen carefully to what is being discussed and the new theorems (Towering Theorem, Chapman-Kolmogorov). The 2nd half of the semester (up to week 11) focuses on Markov-Chains, both discrete-time and continuous-time. Honestly it was quite challenging to fully understand the Discrete-Time Markov Chains (DTMC) at first as it was a very new concept and was accompanied with overwhelming notations and theorems. That said, after a lot of practices, actually DTMC follows a set of pattern and you will be able to master it eventually. DTMC topics include the Classes, Auxiliary Digraph, Transition probabilities, nth-step Transitional Probability, recurrence and transience of a node and a class, Periodicity and Aperiodicity, Invariant distribution, Long-term behaviours and Time Reversibility. Upon understanding the concept, Prof Cheung will introduce a slightly new concept -although somehow relatable to the previous - Counting processes. Upon understanding DTMC, and a good understanding of concepts in ST2334/ST2131, counting / poisson processes should not be a big hassle. It introduces the concepts of three definitions of counting processes and how they are applied differently to different problems, the superpositions of counting/poisson processes and the splitting of the processes. The Counting, Poisson Processes, together with DTMC would then really help in understanding the Continuous Time Markov Chains (CTMC) in which it incorporates both concepts in DTMC and poisson processes. It also introduces concepts like birth-death processes, which will also help in understanding the final part of the module (last 2 weeks) The final part of the module covers Little's Law and Queuing theories. Introduction to renewal processes and long term behaviours of the queue based on the birth rate and the death rate of the queue. Honestly this module is the heaviest module so far for me, as there are tons of concepts and practices to do to fully understand and master the concepts taught in class, but it is also interesting and fun! Any tips: Listen carefully to the lectures, do the tutorials and keep up with the weekly tutorials (can just watch recorded at x2 speed), find friends to check for answers as homeworks are very challenging compared to tutorials and exams. Grade attained: A Module Rating: 5/5

Taken in AY 2014/15 Sem 1 “What reporting verb do you use to express disagreement with someone in an academic essay? Claims. 'He claims that this and that is true, but actually it’s all a load of crap.'” Overview: ES1541 is the fairly new writing module introduced back in 2013 to develop the written and verbal communication skills of science students. As you might infer from the module name, you will be expected to write a lot, and present a lot. The popular science part comes in the form of 5 popular science books from different disciplines, and the idea is to analyse how these books communicated obscure scientific knowledge to the general public in an accessible way, then applying what you have learnt in your presentations and essay. It is compulsory for all science students to take this module, unless you are part of a programme which already offers a writing module in their curriculum, e.g. Utown programmes. You can decide whether you want to take the module in your first, second or third year, although I would recommend clearing it in your first year, not only because of the lower bid points, but also because it is a requirement to go on overseas exchange. ________ Syllabus: As this is a writing module, learning is usually done via class activities and assignments. For my cohort, these included: - Individual and group summaries - Synthesis (of multiple sources to support your thesis) - Individual and group presentations - Argumentative essay (on a topic of your choice) - Peer review (of summaries, essay drafts) - Reflections Workload: I feel that commenting on the workload (and assessment) isn’t very meaningful here, due to the fact that this is a relatively new module which is still in the process of fine-tuning. The assessment components have changed drastically in the semester since I took the module, and will likely continue to do so. The amount of workload you experience will also differ depending on who you are and who your tutor is. I know people who found the module easy, but to others (like myself), it is a major burden. In general however, having a good command of spoken and written English and being comfortable with making presentations will make things easier for you. ________ Teaching Staff: Tutor: Ms Serene Eng Ms Eng is one of the most enthusiastic teachers I’ve seen. Even though my class is at 8 am, she has the ability to make the class come alive during lessons. She brings a new meaning to walking the talk, using the presentation techniques taught in the syllabus to capture the class’s attention and engage each and every one of us. She often shares her past experiences with us, which was an eye-opener for me. It shows that she genuinely cares about her students. Near the end of the semester, she even got a director of an MNC to advise us from an employer’s point of view, highlighting why communication skills are so important in today’s globalised job market. ________ Personal Experience: I am someone who has always been terrible at presentations, from primary school all the way to the PW OP in A levels. Whenever I have an upcoming presentation, I will go almost crazy with anxiety over it, sometimes to the extent of losing sleep the entire night. So you can imagine the horror I felt when I realized I couldn’t escape from this mod which has presentations nearly every week. But you know, it turned out to be one of those times when you are pushed to your limit, your perspective changes. I realized that if I don’t do anything, this problem will plague me for the rest of my life. I decided I had to face it. I accepted that I was going to stumble and fall, but I resolved to start learning from my mistakes and find ways to improve on the next presentation. Over the course of the semester, I experimented on various strategies, e.g. memorizing the entire script, remembering the key points, using props etc. While I didn’t do well for the majority of the presentations (sometimes I will literally stun there when I forget my script), I was beginning to understand what I could or couldn’t do. I finally managed to put it together in the last 10-minute presentation, scoring (what I felt) was an amazing 78/100. I still suck at presentations, no kidding, but at least I now know why I suck. And that makes all the difference, because for the first time in my life, I felt hope in my presentation skills. So it goes without saying that I am very happy with my performance in this module, regardless of the grade I obtained. So if you find yourself in a similar situation as me, don’t give up. Most people get at least a B+ for this module (I think the bell curve is slightly modified here), so your hard work will surely pay off in the end. More importantly, if you have the positive attitude of wanting to learn as much as possible, classes will become much more bearable, even enjoyable at times. The curriculum is structured in such a way that you will have to do just as many assignments as everyone else anyway, so why not learn something while you are at it?

He uploads an updated copy based on what we covered and with answers to the in class questions after each lecture, and I think there’s no need to print notes. Grading: Assignments – 50% (25% + 25%) The 1st was to analyse 2 timetable builders based on Fitt’s Law, KLM and Cogtools. It’s partly individual work and partly pair work, and you guys need to present your findings to the class after the deadline of the project. The 2nd assignment is on experimental design and analysis of AutoComPaste. It would have been a pretty fun assignment if not for the terrible code we were given by the TA, which resulted in the prof having to extend the deadline twice cause it was just so bad and incomprehensible. You need to design and carry out an experiment, and since users are very unpredictable, I strongly suggest not faking your results. You’ll learn much more that way too. Class and workshop participation – 10% Higher than most other CS mods, but I think it’s free marks :D As mentioned above, there are in class questions in the lecture notes, for which he first asks for volunteers, before starting to arrow people. The questions are all very straight forward thought, and you shouldn’t have any trouble answering them if you paid attention. There’s also a panel discussion during one of the weeks, where HCI people from the industry are invited down. Prof Zhao had a great idea of us smsing in our questions, so there was no reason to be afraid of appearing stupid or anything (: Just sms him a question to get your marks :D In class quizzes (closed book) – 10% (5% + 5%) 5 questions for 5 marks, 15 minutes to complete. The 1st quiz is on the 1st half of the mod, the 2nd quiz on the 2nd half. Some of the questions can be a bit tricky, but other than that the questions are pretty doable. Time is also kinda tight. Final exam (1 A4 cheat sheet) – 30% 2h paper with 20 MCQs and 8 short and long answer questions. The exam for this was really easy and I actually enjoyed doing it haha :P You should have more than enough time to complete this paper if it remains at this standard (: EXTRA CREDIT – up to 2.5% There were 3 HCI experiments done by the research labs and they needed participants, so prof Zhao gives you an extra 0.5% for each one you take part in. Each experiment takes around 45-90min, and I think it’s good to experience how this is done, since you need to carry out your own experiments for Assignment 2. We were also invited to submit possible exam questions and answers. “Depending on the quality of the question, you will receive 0.5% if it is reasonable and the answer is correct or 1% if the question is not only reasonable, but also a good example of testing the understanding (instead of memorizing) of the course material.” My verdict: really interesting mod! I would love for more mods to have this style of teaching (seminar style lectures only, higher project weightage compared to exam, high class participation) actually, cause I learn best this way. Bell curve is steep, so try to do the extra credit stuff (I did all, but not sure if my exam question was good or not). Also, there are Master’s students in the class. My grade: A-

Taken in 20/21 Sem 2 Grading: 5% CA1, 25% CA2, 10% CA3, 30% CA4, 15% CA5, 15% participation Ah yes, the compulsory English class to be taken by all Computing students. There are 2x2hr sessions per week with high weightage class participation, which I'm sure contributes to the universal hate this class gets. The content of the class can be read from the other reviews so I'll just talk about the assessments. --- Assessment --- Similar to CS2101, grading is very consistent throughout the semester due to the 5 CAs. There aren't any "lull" periods where there's nothing to do (notwithstanding the 2x2hr sessions per week), so expect to put in more work than you might probably expect. For group projects, the class is split into groups at the start of the semester based on a survey done in the first class. You're stuck with this group for the whole semester so pray you get people who have the same goals as you. I was fortunate to have landed in a group with like-minded individuals who all wanted to maximise effort:reward ratio. CA1: Craft a presentation/video of a spin on a children's tale. Pretty simple, can be done in an afternoon if focused. CA2: Make a "Critical Thinking Rubric" from the Ennis reading, write a report on it (15%) and do a presentation (10%). This is the most tiring group project so I'm glad the co-ordinators put this early in the semester. CA3: Panel Discussion on an topic that was agreed upon prior to the discussion. You have to research the topic, then have an "academic conversation" that goes on for about 30-45min with your group, with 15min Q/A at the end. Can be prepared the day before. Try to be nice to your teammates and let them have their say in the discussion. CA4: Position Paper. You propose a question then write a 800-word-or-so essay on it. This is similar to writing a GP essay, except with citations. Can be done in a day assuming you already have a good question to write on. This is individual work with high weightage so if you're planning to score, better put work into this. CA5: Given a prompt, do an individual impromptu speech on the prompt in 2min. This is a luck of the draw if you get a good prompt or not. It's over within 2 minutes so if you can't think of anything to say, hey, at least you'll die quickly. Expected Grade: B/B+ Actual Grade: TBC

Took it in semester 1 2017/2018 under Vik Gopal. Format: 10% tutorial attendance (sign on a piece of paper) 10% assignments (actually just a set of free courses on datacamp on a myriad of topics stated below. appreciate this very very much) 30% midterms (in this semester it was a coding assignment done in a lecture timeslot. Pretty difficult and most people couldn't finish it, but the bell curve will save you) 50% finals (written exam with no coding. Mostly about the second half of the module which is plotting graphs and aesthetics, giving suggestions to improve plots, analysing plots provided by the examiner) This is quite possibly one of the most important modules for aspiring data scientists (beyond the mathematical statistics). This module teaches you the most important (and industry-relevant) part of data analysis - cleaning, tidying and managing your data. For students who are more resourceful, some of the content in this module is easy to find online, but for those who aren't this is a very appreciated introduction to the basics expected of a data scientist. For students in statistics, most of your ST courses only teach you the mathematical part of statistics, yet some students have no idea what to do with a given set of dirty data. Also, some elementary data scraping with APIs is introduced in this module. Many SMEs and some larger corporations collect a shit ton of data for analysis and most of the time, the data isn't formatted in an ideal format for analysis (by my personal experiences). With the techniques learnt in this course, you be able to manipulate data easily and efficiently using R and some packages. Apart from that, the second half of the module will be focused on graphing techniques in R using ggplot2 and some of the philosophy behind delivering information in an efficient and aesthetically pleasing manner. Vik Gopal is pretty legendary among statistics students. He's insanely dedicated, knowledgeable and always willing to help. It helps that he has the lecture-perfect voice which makes even 8am lectures bearable. He is very easy to pay attention to and doesn't skimp on explaining difficult concepts, nor does he go off tangent in his lectures. In general, all modules taught by him are worth attending. I've taken 2 modules under him in my 4 years and they were always pleasant and never a waste of time. However, he tends to set difficult (but fair) papers, but will be manageable for those who are consistent with their studying. Here's the outline: Weeks 1 – 2: R programming. Weeks 3 – 4: Importing data into R. Weeks 5 – 6: Data manipulation. Week 7: Principles of data visualisation. Week 8: The grammar of graphics. Week 9: The grammar of graphics + mid-term. Week 10: The grammar of graphics + de-brief. Weeks 11 – 12: Exploring data through visualisation. In addition, there is a whole suite of datacamp courses (free!) by the school that you will be automatically signed up for. I'm not sure if they are permanent though.

By Prof Al Au What is it about? You will learn about the 1) negotiation fundamentals, and 2) psychology process that drive various themes in negotiations. How’s the workload? One 3-h seminar style lecture a week + readings. 9% class participation, in-class negotiation exercise every week 16% Individual report, on the in-class negotiation exercise (choose 1) 10% Paper presentation, 20% Group presentation, 45% Finals. How *difficult is it? Best not to think in terms of module difficulty - Your experience in the module is better determined by your interest in the topic. [Below are my thoughts on that is covered in this module, by themes] Psychology of Negotiation is part-Business, part-Psychology. 1) First and foremost, this module is about Negotiation. You will learn about value-claiming and value-creation modes of negotiation. The module will also cover specific strategies and broader themes like power, motivations, multi-party negotiations. 2) This course will include cognitive biases and heuristics (read Kahneman & Tversky), motivational models and influence (e.g. SVO), emotional appeals (e.g. displays of anger), social/contextual influences (e.g. power) among other psychological themes. You will also conduct analyses at the inter-, intra- individual level and inter-, intra- group level. Individual report This is NOT a reflection exercise. Choose 1 in-class negotiation and write a 4-page (~1200 words) report. Incorporate themes and link to course content, also and offer original analysis. [This was a fun exercise. Remember to take notes during the in-class negotiation so that you can point out specific instances in the report.] Group presentation Pick a real-life case of negotiation, avoid political cases. Most of the class ended picking either business mergers or union-strikes. The trick to this assignment is to present just enough background, while focusing the bulk of the time on analysis. Especially for drawn-out negotiations (weeks/month), it is a good idea to show how the negotiation (power, motivation, multi-party) factors affect the eventual outcome. How is the Prof? Prof A. is adorable. He has the fatherly-vibe and is always checking that you understand the content. Prof A. active in his research and up-to-date with current research. This prof speaks with a Hong Kong accent. [Not a downside, by any means. But do take note.] Should you take it? If any of the above points, or a combination of them, intrigues you. Or if you are unsure where to go, but looking for a fun and practical module. I encourage you to take this module. Exam tips Essay-based. During studying, keep in mind the overarching themes. [I color-coded my notes to help me see the links between chapters.] Conclusion: I enjoyed myself thoroughly in this module. Also, I learnt things that I practice in my daily “negotiations” with friends and family. Grade obtained: B+

AY18/19 Semester 2/Special Term 1 iBLOC – Mid January to Late June Prof Ben Leong (Online Lectures) Prof Tan Tiow Seng (Recitations) TA Ayush Mitra (Tutorials) Assessment Breakdown: 35% Coursemology (Gamified assignments) 15% Midterm 15% Practical Exam 5% Participation (based on CA) 30% Final Exam CS1010X is offered as an iBLOC for RNSmen who very likely are approaching or have already passed their ORD. As such, it’s geared to letting students slowly get back into the swing of things. This version taught programming methodology using Python, with a minor amount spent on C as well. There is no bell curve. Coursemology Structure Coursemology is a gamified learning platform used by CS1010X. The grade determined from Coursemology depends on your overall level at the end of the course, capped at 35. To gain levels, completing assignments will net the student experience points, of which enough of will cause one to level up. With the multitude of assignments available, it isn’t difficult to max out the 35% available to you. All Lectures for CS1010X were online in video format taught by Prof Ben Leong. After watching the Lectures, the student is expected to complete Lecture assignments to apply what they learnt. Lecture assignments will usually net a small amount of XP. Questions on Lecture can be asked directly on the Lecture page and will be timestamped to specifically when the student asks. Afterwards, there are Tutorials to be completed which net a larger XP. The bulk of XP will come from the Missions assignments which are programming-based questions with a story background to make it more interesting for the student. They are connected to the content taught in the Lecture and Tutorials and are usually more difficult. A bulk of XP gained should come from here. For these three sections, bonus XP will be given if the assignments are completed before their cutoff dates. There are also optional Extra, Past Year, and C sections that the student can attempt to further improve their skills. These provide small amounts of XP with no bonuses. Forum A significant part of CS1010X is the availability of the Forum. If you are stuck on any assignment given, you can post a question on the Forum for help. Other students who have solved the question will be glad to assist, and if none of the students know, the Professor or the TAs will provide guidance. This section is extremely useful in letting each other know what concepts you might have misunderstood, whether you’re on the right track, or - if you have mastered the concept taught – let you share your knowledge with others. Exams For all exams given in the course, it should be no surprise that practicing past-year papers will greatly increase your chances of scoring well for them. Midterms tested content covered up to that point, Practical Exams tested the whole course (except C) and Finals tested everything including the simpler concepts in C. Generally the Midterms and Finals had the same structure of 4 sections, with everything being written (no MCQ). PE had 3 main questions. Note 1: Although the Coursemology material was still provided, C was not tested in the exams at all in AY19/20.. Note 2: Starting from AY20/21, it is likely that C will be replaced by Java. Tips Practise. Practise some more. There really isn’t much else advice with programming. You will end up finding out what you don’t know the more you code. With the forums available for this course, there is no excuse for not finding out what you don’t know. Google and ask if you don’t know. Personally, I found the course extremely liberating because of the large amount of time you have. There is little pressure in terms of deadlines since everything is spread out. Most questions were relatively manageable for me as I was already highly interested in subject matter. Overall, the course can be quite enjoyable if you put in effort to do your own practice. If your major/minor needs you to complete CS1010/S/E,CS1101S, or any equivalent it is really beneficial to take up CS1010X. Expected Grade: A/A+

As expected from social work, the MCQs were not as straightforward as psych and all the options sound correct because it's a more human subject. Despite only mugging all my social work readings the day before the exam, I still managed to answer most of the questions with confidence. I guess paying attention to lectures and tutorials really helps! Would recommend anyone who is interested in social issues to take this as an exposure mod or just a UE! :)

Semester Taken: AY2020/2021 Semester 1 (COVID sem with no S/Us) Lecturers: Prof Hanny Kusnadi (Week 1 to 6), Prof Stephen Lynn (Week 7 to 13) Tutor: Prof Stephen Lynn Module Breakdown: - 20% Class Participation (During Tutorials) - 30% Group Project - 50% Final Examination (HUGE TIP FOR BBA (NON-ACCOUNTING) STUDENTS : Take this module in Year 1 Semester 2 instead of Year 1 Semester 1, as the BAC students will be assigned ACC1701 in Semester 1. Hence, the Semester 1 bell curve will be MUCH steeper given you are competing against the Accounting Majors.) Brief Introduction: ACC1701 delves into the basics of Accounting, where you will learn how companies handle accounting in the business world as well as learn how to prepare financial statements and interpret them. The content is very heavy if you are unfamiliar with Accounting in general, as many of us understandably would be, and hence every week was a huge new chunk of content being taught. However, despite my dislike for accounting, I must acknowledge the usefulness of the content taught in this module as well as the professionalism of the teaching staff with regards to handling technical difficulties faced during the online semester and the tutorials. Lectures: There is a 2-hour lecture timing every week, where a lot of content is covered every week relating to each financial statement or element of financial statements. Prof Hanny’s slides were really useful and professional, and it really helped me to understand the content when I went back to refer to the slides, which was especially useful when starting out with accounting. On the other hand, Prof Stephen’s slides were quite unorganised and definitely not usable on its own without watching the lectures. I would say my grasp of the earlier content was much stronger, mostly due to the difference in quality of the lecture slides as I liked to make notes and reread lecture slides. I would not recommend cramming the content at the end of the semester and instead would encourage you to diligently follow each week’s lecture and syllabus as they are taught. This is because the content builds on one another and is also very heavy, so you will find yourself lagging behind drastically, especially in tutorials. Tutorials: The tutorials were mainly sessions used to go through questions and assignments related to last lecture’s content, where 20% of your grade is determined by your class participation in answering the tutor’s questions or contributing to solving the assignments. With the tutorial being held on Zoom, I felt that it was extremely easy to participate as you could just raise your hand on Zoom and answer the question. Prof Stephen was also very good at ensuring students all had equal opportunities to participate, as he would break down questions into several segments to allow as many students to answer questions and contribute to earn their class participation marks. If you raise your hand on Zoom, you will almost be guaranteed a chance to talk and participate. Thanks to the online format and Prof Stephen giving ample opportunities to participate in class, I was able to speak at least once every tutorial, which I felt contributed to a good lead before the finals started. Group Project: The Group Project was a series of questions asking about a company’s performance in the year, where you are given the company’s financial report for that year to analyse. Overall, the group project was actually extremely easy to complete, as it required basic knowledge of reading financial statements and some basic prose answers to the questions that tested our accounting knowledge. There was only one open-ended question that asked us to indicate our satisfaction with the company as an investor, where we could use external resources or metrics learnt in class to assess the company’s performance. Overall, with good teammates and good pacing, it is very easy to complete the group project on time and score well. Finals: The finals paper was uploaded and held on Examplify, where there were 20 MCQ questions and 4 open-ended questions that required you to prepare some financial statements and interpret some transactions that occurred. Overall, I felt like the open-ended questions were really difficult to do well in because they required you to get basically upwards of 15 transactions all correct to prepare correct financial statements. However, I am pretty sure marking is lenient enough to have error carry forward, so just make sure you get as many transactions correct as possible. Balancing your accounting equation is also not very important, although I have to admit that the finals paper was the first time that I had ever managed to balance my accounting equation, and the sense of relief I had was indescribable. The finals were held IRL in rooms in NUS Business School, where students would download and do the paper on Examplify. However, there were a lot of issues faced with Examplify, such as students being unable to copy and paste their workings from the inbuilt Excel or being unable to open the Examination paper. This is where I would like to commend the teaching staff for their professionalism in ensuring equity for all students affected. They were able to come up with a solution that would grade the affected students separately and took the higher marks from different permutations of mark breakdown. This accounted for students who prioritised doing the MCQ first or students who started with the open-ended questions first and encountered problems, thus ensuring the fairest judgement would be provided to all students. This is probably the mod that I found the fairest in terms of getting your deserved grade. Overall Ratings: Fairness Rating (How Fair the Breakdown is): 5/5 Satisfaction Rating : 3/5 (I dislike accounting but must admit the satisfaction from balancing your equation is unparalleled) Usefulness Rating : 5/5 (Financial ratios you learn are actually used in real life to interpret company performances for the year) Overall Rating: 4.5/5 Expected Grade: A- (I felt like I participated as much as I could in the tutorials and my group project went well, but my finals was not very good as I basically barely answered the last few open-ended questions. Seeing the Accounting students from Poly send the correct answers with perfect formats right after the finals scared me, but thankfully the number of students with this experience is probably few and far between.) Final Grade: A (Definitely got saved by my class participation and group project)

Full reviews at By Prof Tan Gek Woo Overview/workload: I think it would be less misleading if the “software” word was removed ._. Other than that, lots of team dynamics concepts which I’m already using but don’t give much thought to, let alone know their names. There’s also a lot of memorising (compared to CS mods), which is kinda annoying cause it’s like you know the concept but you can’t remember the name -.- Workload is average to slightly chill for a 2k mod, BUT again, this is compared to the CS 2k mods. A number of my IS friends have told me they consider this mod to be on the heavier side. Teaching style/lecturer: 3h seminar style classes each week, which means you shouldn't skip them. I’ll admit that it can sometimes get pretty boring, partly due to my short attention span. Prof Tan Gek Woo tries her best to make things interesting though, as well as link it back to software as much as possible. There’s only so much linking she can do though, but according to friends who have previously taken this, it’s much better now. One thing I must say: prof Tan is an incredibly nice person. She is extremely caring and has, on a few occasions, offered to help me with my FYP report/presentation stuff as she knew how worried I was about it. Prof Tan is assisted by her TA (who happened to be my friend/junior haha) in class activities and the marking of some assignments. Notes/textbook: Slides are uploaded to IVLE before the seminars. I can’t say they are very useful in class since I didn’t take any notes at all, but they do a good job of summarising the main points for revision. Textbook is Creating Teams with an Edge by Harvard Business School Press (see, nothing to do with software), with additional readings uploaded to IVLE by prof Tan. As usual, I didn’t bother with the textbook or the readings. The only compulsory reading was “The Army Crew Team” (case 9-403-131) from Harvard Business Review, which we did a *graded* debate on. That one has to be purchased from HBR (or obtained via where ever). Grading: 1. Final exam (closed book, individual) – 40% 2h paper which was waaaaayyyyy too long. I told myself to do it as slowly as possible, yet I still finished within 40min and was the first to leave the venue, which made me wonder if I missed out a page or something >< The paper had 3 sections: 1. MCQ of 0.5m each (I think) 2. MCQ with 7 options of 1m each (again, I think) 3. structured questions. When I read the very last structured question, I was like argghhh, it’s pure regurgitation from a slide in the notes which I had decided to skip cause I thought it wasn’t important -.- thankfully, everybody else also couldn’t do that question haha. 2. Midterm (closed book, group) – 10% Yes, it’s a group midterm! Which means there’s a chance of one of your groupmates being asocial loafer (concept from the mod haha), and also that you have to cater to the speed of your group. The paper consisted of 2 questions about a case study from HBR, and we had to come up with a group answer to submit. My group got 7/10 for this I think, which I felt could have been better. 3. Pop quizzes – 5% These were given at the start of a lesson. I think we had 6 or 7 in total, of which the marks of our best 5 were taken. I think these are quite useful as they force you to read the previous notes before hand or you won’t be able to remember all the terms. The questions are gone through immediately after the quiz so you can learnt from your mistakes. Unfortunately (or fortunately, depending on you), mine was the Tue class, and the Mon class was given the exact same quiz the day before us so… 4. Group project – 33% You get to choose your own group during the first class during the first lesson. Choose wisely, as this project is pretty much student driven and you want people who can match your pace of work. The interesting – and annoying – thing about this project was that the class was the subsidiary and the different groups were the sub-teams, which meant that everybody was working on different components of the same product. This was meant to mimic the dynamics of the workplace, and let me tell you, there was a HUGE coordination problem. The project consists of 3 sets of deliverables: 1. the team and subsidiary proposal, 2. the final product demo, and 3. the team and subsidiary project report. The most annoying thing was that a lot of times, you can’t start on your part cause the subsidiary hasn’t come to an agreement yet/you don’t know what info the other teams need from your group/can offer your group. Oh and I must mention that there was no coding involved – all that was required of us at the end were mockups of the product. 5. Case study debate (group) – 6% This was pretty fun! Unfortunately, the stand we took for the debate wasn’t our own personal stand, but rather, allocated to us. Thank goodness the one my group got was what I believed in! Interestingly enough, all the groups prepared so well that by the end of the debate, each team was convinced that theirs was the best option and didn’t want to switch haha. The format for the debate was: 1. presentation of arguments by the teams taking Stand A, 2. cross-examination (questioning) of the teams in (1), 3. repeat (1) and (2) for the other 2 stands, and 4. open floor where anyone can ask any team a question. 6. Individual reflection – 6% Free marks! I think. All we had to do was 2 reflections, 1 after the midterm and 1 during the last class. I’ve no idea how this is graded, or why it has such a high percentage, for that matter, but hey, one of the easiest 6% in my NUS life :D My verdict: Take if you want to improve your team dynamics skills. Those from IS don’t have a choice since this is your core mod, so take it earlier to maximise its usefulness. Also, the grades of students from the Tue class were generally better than those from the Mon class. The only reason I can think of is the 5% pop quizzes, except that 1. I didn’t do too well for those and 2. it would mean this mod has an incredibly steep bell curve. My grade: A

Interpolation and Least Squares Approximation - Cubic Spline Interpolation and Least Squares Approximation is not examinable. 4. Numerical Integration - Romberg Integration is not examinable. 5. Solution of Nonlinear Equations Finals: 60% Midterms: 15% Lab: 10% Tutorial/Lab attendance: 10% Homework: 5% Prof Chu/ Tests: Prof Chu has been the best lecturer I've had so far, he knows his stuff well and was pretty engaging during his lectures. He valued learning and the welfare of his students a lot so he kept the content simple, drop explicit hints for midterms and finals, and even directly lifted a tutorial question and set it as a 20 mark question in the finals. This module is, however, very computationally intensive, so being careful is very important, no matter how easy the computation is, don't be complacent. In numerical analysis, (a+b)+c is not equal to a+(b+c) in general, so be very careful of such computations. Content: After taking calculus modules (MA1102R, MA1104) and ST2131, I thought this module was going to be of a similar format where the lecturer introduces a bunch of senseless integration techniques and sets incredibly tricky exams that doesn't serve any purpose in learning, but hell I was wrong. This module is by far the best module I have taken throughout my 3 semesters and it sparked a lot of interest in me in other fields of computational mathematics. I took this module together with CS1010 and MA3110, which helped me derive meaning out of the content in numerical analysis and complete the MATLAB project a lot. As an applied math major, I am not a really big fan of mathematical analysis, though they are quite fun to do, and this module helped to ease that boredom a little. In pure math, we often say ''∃c ∈(a,b) such that ... or ∃a partition P such that the integral is...'', but this is unfeasible in the real world as we need working knowledge of the variables we wish to compute, rather than some arbitrary results. This is where MA2213 bridges the gap between pure math and the real world, by building on the results of mathematical analysis to produce numerical methods to approximate integrals/ solutions to equations etc. This mod would be refreshing to take for anyone who's interested in seeing the real applications of mathematical analysis. They are openbook, but you certainly won’t have time to search through the textbook for that single theorem that you have only seen once in your entire life. For some reason, I scored higher than average in both tests. 40% Final I like to think of taking the finals as playing in escape rooms. Some escape rooms are fun, others are challenging, but this one is pure scary. It is literally a collection of the hardest problem of each concept. There are simply no easy marks. At the one hour mark, I had only done 40% of the problems. After another hour, I wrote down 15% more. Of course, later I found some mistakes in some of my solutions, so my final score would be ~45/100. In conclusion, please be mentally and physically prepared if you are planning on taking this mod. I’d say that my relationship with calculus was quite nice compared to others. I’ve read other reviews that some students actually cry during the finals. I didn’t cry, I was just mildly infuriated at that time. So long, calculus, hope I can understand you better next time we meet.

under Prof Martin Henz. Modules in this semester were affected by the COVID-19 pandemic, and were required to end one week earlier than usual (i.e. week 13 was cancelled). All classes (both lectures and labs) could be attended online from early in the semester, going beyond the social distancing measures that were mandated by the school. This module starts by introducing formal specification of language semantics (inductive definitions; dynamic, static, and denotational semantics; type safety), and then moves on to virtual machines (compilation from the source language to an instruction set architecture, and execution of the compiled program), memory management (with a focus on garbage collection). The last few classes dabble with records, exceptions, lazy evaluation, and object-oriented programming. Most of the course is taught in Source, the programming language created for CS1101S. Source is a dynamically typed programming language that is mostly a subset of JavaScript. The topics in this module are mostly geared towards higher-level programming or scripting languages - for example, memory management focuses on garbage collection (instead of the implementation of C-style malloc/free), record properties are taught with the semantics of Scheme (instead of C semantics), and object oriented programming is taught in a manner that differs from Java or C++. There is a lack of focus on lower-level implementation concerns, such as stack-based records (C, C++), memory alignment, generic programming (Java, C#), templates (C++, Rust), pointers, and async/await (JavaScript, C#, Rust, Python). In this module, we are often satisfied with JavaScript-like dynamic typing. Graded components: - Test 1 (20%) - Test 2 (20%) - Lab assignments (20%) - Project (40%) There is no final exam for this module (this was decided before bidding started, and hence was not due to the pandemic). Tests 1 and 2 are scheduled approximately at the 1/3 and the 2/3 points of the module, and they test on the content covered in the lectures. There are weekly lab classes up to week 10, and some of them have graded take-home programming assignments. All labs are conducted in Source using Source Academy, the platform for teaching CS1101S, as an editor and execution environment. Familiarity with Source is not required, but it may be useful to have some background in JavaScript. The lack of a final exam is somewhat odd for a computer science module. This also means that material covered after Test 2 is effectively non-examinable. The project is pair work, and it is a programming project that spans the entire semester. Students may choose their partners, but they must be from the same lab group. There was a large range of projects to choose from - students may submit their preferences in the first week of class, but Prof Henz subsequently allocates a project to each team based on their preferences. Many of the projects are features for Source Academy, intended to be integrated at the end of the semester. This also means that many projects require TypeScript. The project culminates in a half-hour presentation in either weeks 12 or 13. Students are expected to present their projects to Prof Henz and approximately 11 other students (each student has to attend 11 presentations apart from their own).

(AY 15/16 Sem 1, Prof Ng Hwee Tou & TA Kaveh Taghipour) The textbook is of poor quality, having many serious errors, some of which he himself pointed out in class, and some of which my classmates pointed out to him, which he apparently didn't even realize. Despite that, his style of teaching is very textbook-oriented. Assignments, tests and exams do not really test true understanding of the concepts, but rather test whether you are able to parrot the textbook or the solutions he presents for his problem sets. If you do not want to be like a parrot, DO NOT take this module! There was also one occasion where two students asked him after class whether he could give them answers to past year papers. He raised his voice and told them off, saying something like that this is a university and he will of course not provide ten-year-series. He also stated flatly that he will not answer any inquiries about past year papers' questions, but only about the course materials. Of course everyone in the room heard his response. While I agree that learning is not about past year papers, I felt it was an unkind way to treat a student. After all, if he wants to assess students based on exams, it is to be expected that they would want to know how to answer his style of exam questions. Certainly he ought to be at least willing to answer inquiries of students who already show him their own serious attempts at answering the exam questions. If he is not, then he ought not to use exams to judge students' competency in natural language processing. Furthermore, he could have just told those students nicely what he felt about past year papers rather than talking down to them. This year's programming project was actually a reasonably interesting one, namely to implement a word-pair disambiguation classifier, in which the program needs to choose the right word of a given pair (like adopt/adapt) to fill in the blank in each test sentence, after learning from training data where the correct answers are provided. The word pair is of course not known in advance, so the program must be able to learn from the training data alone. We submitted both source code and a short write-up explaining our classifier. A significant portion of the marks went to our classifier's performance on the unseen test data, which is fair enough, but some marks also went to the classifier's performance on the sample test data that Prof Ng provided, which I felt was a bit wrong since some people might tune their classifier to fit best the sample test data. The weightage for the sample test data was half that of the unseen test data, so it was not really an issue for the grading, but it was still not a good marking scheme in my opinion. As an earlier reviewer already wrote, the test and exam questions are often of the type where just a slight mistake will cost you all the marks for that question, such as 5 out of 40 for the midterm, or 10 out of 80 for the final. Since the exam turns upon your carelessness during that 2 hours, you had better sleep well at least the night before! That is, if you have already chosen to be like a parrot for one semester. =P Finally, the TA, a PhD student whose supervisor was Prof Ng, was very unapproachable and many of us students who went to see him about the assignment grading felt very put off by his attitude towards us. I won't say more. Now let me make some course recommendations. For finite automata and context free grammars and related algorithms and much more, take CS4232, which teaches them properly. Prof Ng did not seem to actually have knowledge about these beyond what was in his natural language textbooks, so he couldn't confidently answer some simple questions about them that some students asked in class. For natural language processing content, you're probably better off reading online materials such as Wikipedia, which are not only much clearer but also more comprehensive, not so mistake-laden and better organized. Some reliable friends who also disliked CS4248 told me that some other modules are much worse, so I'm thankful that CS4248 is already one of the worst I've taken in SOC. Perhaps the other modules I've taken were so well taught that I had a high expectation before taking CS4248. Expected grade: A Obtained grade: A-
