Took this module in Sem 1 of AY16/17 under Dr Marc Rochester. No final examination. TL;DR: Basically "Orchestras in Singapore 1101". Stickler for essay formatting with vague topics that are easily misinterpreted. Very light workload, but not guaranteed an A. Probably boring for people who already are immersed in the Singaporean "western" music scene. CA consists of four parts: CA1: Fieldwork project on the study of audience behaviour in western music concerts in Singapore OR study of music schools/teaching programmes in Singapore, with a presentation in class. Group work of about 5-8(?) people. CA2: 500 word objective individual essay on a "western music ensemble" in Singapore. CA3: 750 word subjective individual essay on the position of the Singaporean music scene in the global context. CA4: Introduced at the last minute - class discussion during week 13's class. I found that there was a huge discrepancy between what the module title and description suggests and what is actually taught in the module. While the module is titled "Western Music within a Singaporean Context" (where western basically = classical as we generally understand it), it basically can be summed up as "the history of orchestras in Singapore". As someone who comes from a choral background I found it immensely disappointing that the vast majority of content covered orchestral music, with the other major topic being the role of learning and teaching "western" music in Singaporean society. The module description also reads: "It will assess the impact of majority cultures (particularly from the Chinese, Malay and Indian communities) on the general reception of Western music, as well as on music written by Singapore-based composers. Students will be introduced to the principal figures in Singapore’s musical development." However, these issues were just touch-and-go, with Marc basically rambling on about the treatment of classical music in Singaporean households or about audience perceptions. I honestly do not recall anything about majority cultures in Singapore being mentioned, and only a very small portion was touched on regarding Singaporean composers, even solo Singaporean musicians. While Marc himself is a rather funny guy, he basically sits you down for 1.5 hrs a week and rambles on, asking more questions than he gives answers, simply because this is a field that doesn't really have much research conducted with regard to music in Singapore. While he occasionally gives you facts, he doesn't properly cite the sources that he tends to mention casually, making it seem extremely wishy-washy. Lecture slides are uploaded every week after class, along with (rather soft) audio recordings of one of the lecture slots. The guest lectures are pretty banal, with more about the orchestras like SSO and Music Makers, the history of their establishment and things like that. If you're already pretty much into the local "western" music scene there's not much you can learn from attending lectures: it's basically a reaffirmation of what you already know more or less. For the fieldwork project, since the class is split into such large groups, you are allowed to split the work by having some members exclusively do data collection and others do the presentation, or have everyone involved. However, traditional powerpoint presentations should be eschewed for more interesting and attention-grabbing methods such as skits and interactive sessions. It also helps to have a few major points from your fieldwork presented as clearly as possible rather than trying to cover all bases. For the essays, the main thing is to FOLLOW THE GUIDELINES STRICTLY! He spells them all out within the powerpoint and word documents, though both documents sometimes have things that he does not put in the other, so be wary and ensure that you put in everything and double/triple check before submission, as he has been known to drop people a few grades for not following the format. The topics tend to be VERY VAGUE and are easily subject to misinterpretation, as evidenced by the majority of my groupmates and myself. While the topics may be vague, he has a very strict idea of what should be put in the essay (which is pretty unfair), and so if you really want that A you HAVE to consult him about your ideas relating to the given essay topics, otherwise it's extremely easy to get a C for the essay component. Book him early for a consultation as he tends to be busy running around watching concerts and other stuff. You only get one chance to upload your essay, and if you don't follow the guidelines or completely misinterpret the essay he will ask you to resubmit it with a SEVERE PENALTY (25%) IN GRADING, and can only be done during the submission period. i.e. past the given deadline, no more re-submissions if you fail to interpret or follow the guidelines. Some of the criteria for formatting make sense, while others like INSISTING ON USING UK ENGLISH or COUNTING HYPHENATED WORDS AND ACRONYMS AS INDIVIDUAL WORDS are a complete pain in the ass. While this module has an extremely light workload I would honestly not recommend it for people already immersed in the "western" music happenings in Singapore as it will be boring af. Plus, the essays are a real chore which always makes you second-guess yourself. I completely regret wasting 1400 points on this module as I had to bid it under the SSY module code.

Taken in AY15/16 Semester 1 Lecturer: Dr. Neiladri Sinhababu Grading - Tutorial attendance (5%), Short paper (20%), Term paper abstract (5%), Term paper (40%), End-of-semester MCQ test (30%) Content - Theories covered include moral realism (naturalistic and non-naturalistic variants), non-cognitivism, and error theory, among others. Criticisms and objections to these theories were also discussed. Lectures - 2-hour lectures (not webcasted), once per week. During lectures, Dr. Neil mainly explains the contents of the reading assigned for that week, and brings in additional information to supplement students' understanding. Over the course of the module, he explains how the theories of the various philosophers relate to one another (e.g. the theories may be in direct conflict, or they may be consistent with each other). Dr. Neil is humorous, speaks very well, and commands the attention of students. Tutorials - 2-hour tutorials, fortnightly. Dr. Neil is also in charge of tutorials, and he mainly conducts them in the style of question-and-answer sessions, where students raise questions to clarify their doubts and he answers them. Students who have diligently read the readings will probably benefit more from tutorials as they can ask relevant questions, and also understand the questions that other students raise. Workload - The workload for this module seemed moderate to light. There was one reading assigned every week, but I think it is possible (though probably not advisable) to get by without completing readings, since lectures provided adequate summaries of the readings. There was no final exam for this module, but there was an MCQ test (29 questions, 30% of final grade) in Week 13, which was largely manageable as long as one read the readings diligently or paid attention during lectures. Module grade: A-

GEQ1000 AY2017/18 Sem 1: Pretty much the throw-away module simply to fulfill the Q pillar of the 5 GE pillars. Probably the easiest compulsory module in NUS. Most importantly, it is CS/CU, so that explains it all. There are no physical lectures, everything is webcasted (like GER1000). But, there is simply no need to watch it. There are also tutorials which is a must to attend since a surprising large percentage of your marks come from it, JUST BY TURNING UP. Yeap, no participation required. How much you enjoy your tutorial depends on your tutor. Some make it quite interesting, some can't be bothered like you. It may help in finishing your assignments for this module though. This module is split into 6 sections representing different genres: Philosophy, Science, Computational Thinking, Engineering, Economics & Design. For each genre, there can be open ended questions to answer and/or MCQs to answer. Unfortunately, different people get different questions for MCQs, so it may not be easy to simply grab answers. I left out one of the Design assignments where you had to design a wallet, because who got time for that?! Easy peasy to pass, no reason to fail, I got that CS grade easily.

Took this in AY2017/2018 Sem 2 under Prof Vincent Tan. Applied maths majors with MMDA specialisation can take this to fulfil requirements. I think Data Science & Analytics majors too, though I suspect a lot of content in this module overlaps with some of their compulsory modules? [Any confirmation? Can't really speak for this as an AM (MMDA) major] Either way, there is a lot of rigorous maths involved in the motivation behind the algorithms to be applied, and really feels like MA2216 + MA2213 ramped up several notches (with a sprinkling of Markov chains). And there are a good number of models and methods that you should understand thoroughly, especially since you may be tested to analyse and apply slightly modified versions of these models/methods. It's a MA-prefixed module after all :p Graded components: 2 in-class quizzes (15% each), computational exercise (10%), project (10%), final (50%). At least for our batch, we had two options for the project: either compare several methods(including one not discussed in the lectures) by applying on a real life dataset, or report on one of several recommended papers. Both the comp ex and project are language agnostic, so go nuts with your favourite programming language. This module is still pretty fresh, so I suspect the curriculum will keep changing radically over the next few years. Overall though it's a good module if you're interested in the mathematical rigour behind the models and computations employed in data analysis.

under Prof Yu Haifeng. This module covers the theoretical foundation of shared-memory and distributed-memory systems. Focus is placed on the formal definitions of key concepts in such systems, as well as the algorithms associated with those concepts. Topics for shared-memory systems include: critical sections (Peterson's, Lamport's bakery, and Dekker's algorithms), semaphores, monitors, and memory consistency. Topics for distributed-memory systems include: clocks, consistent global snapshots, causal order, total order (Skeen's algorithm), leader election, consensus (FLP theorem), and self-stabilisation. Only midterms (40%) and finals (60%) are graded. Homework questions are generally given after every lecture for students to check their understanding, but they are not collected and not graded. While this module is specified to have two hours of lecture followed by an hour of tutorial, it is functionally three hours of lecture. This is an extremely proof-based module. Expect to spend most of the time (during both lectures and exams) proving or disproving statements. Typical exam questions do not tell students if a given statement is true or false - students have to decide if the statement is true on their own, and then prove (or disprove) it. As exam questions do not generally "guide" students in the correct direction, confidence in one's own answers is important. Some background in mathematical reasoning might help with this module. Lectures proceed at a reasonable pace; it is generally slower than most mathematics modules. As such, most concepts can be grasped during the lecture. Midterms are closed-book (without help sheet) while finals are open-book. There are no group projects for this module.

The second half of the module has concepts such as variance, covariance, and continuous distributions, which are concepts new to me. I made the mistake of ignoring the module because I thought the first half was easy and had to study last minute at 12am for the second midterm. You should read the notes regularly, as you cannot solely rely on the tutorials for practice. The tutorials do not cover every topic. We were assigned a group based on the alphabetical order of our name during the first tutorial and stuck with that group for the semester. During every tutorial, we were given a worksheet to complete individually, but could discuss the questions. The final grade received is dependent on both our individual grade and our group's grade, but how it's calculated is not revealed it to us. It basically became peer tutoring. All the tutorials on different days of the week had a different worksheet. There were 2 midterms for this module. The first midterm was done on our own laptops using the Examplify software, which only works on Windows/Mac. I disliked this software as we had to give it full control over our laptops. While taking the test, the software locked us from other applications in our laptops, and we couldn't even "ctrl alt del". The second midterm was a traditional written test. The first midterm was quite easy, and I felt that an excessive amount of time was given (90 mins for 15 MCQ, that's 4 mins per question!). Most people left the test early. The second midterm was harder than the first, but it wasn't too hard either. 90 mins were given for 3 questions, and counting the part (a) part (b) etc, that's about 6 parts. The paper also felt more like an algebra paper, as most of the questions can be solve by writing down expression using definitions and simplifying it. A lot of hints were given as well. I just read the notes. The video explaining the concepts were made by the prof, not recorded from an LT. Those videos felt like listening to the prof reading a script while pressing next on the PowerPoint slides. He didn't even use a marker/pointer to show which point he is at on the slides, and instead, would say stuff like "as you can see from point 2". Just reading the notes without watching the video should be sufficient. My senior recommended me to take it in sem 1 as it was taught by the math department instead of the stats department, which I unfortunately couldn't due to missing prerequisites. UTC1702E Difficulty: Easy Workload: Low Class Slot: 1900-2100 Mondays at RC4-SR5 Teacher(s): Dr BELLAM Sreenivasulu Grade weightage: 20% Class Participation 15% Mini Project 1 15% Mini Project 2 15% Major Project Report 15% Major Project Presentation 20% Test Expected Grade: CS Grade: CS Thoughts: Through this module, you will learn how to model complex systems related to energy, using causal loop diagrams, stock-flow diagrams, and observe how the different stocks change over time using behaviour-over-time graphs. You will learn how to do these diagrams on paper and also through a program called Vensim. This module will require you to work in a group of two to three people. Not many people care too much about this module because it is a CS/CU module but I feel it is important to at least care a bit if you want to know what is going on in the Senior Seminars. Teacher: Dr Bellam Sreenivasulu is a good teacher in that he can explains concepts decently. He is also quite friendly but that is probably expected of a Resident Fellow. However, I feel he spent too much time explaining things rather than moving on, often leading to us ending classes much later than usual, which is pretty annoying given how the class is already officially supposed to end at 2100 (or rather 15-30 minutes before as is customary). I wonder if he does this because somebody previously gave him feedback that he does not explain enough or maybe he finds a lot of his senior seminar students not understanding the basics of systems thinking, so he wants his junior seminar students to have solid foundations. Whatever it is, I hope he finds a balance between explaining too much and explaining too little. Still, that is just minor, he is not bad. Class participation: Just answer his questions; this component is not very hard to score. Mini project 1: Each group had to do a five-minute video on a topic related to energy. We had to use systems thinking and apply it to that topic then present on that topic through the video. You can be very creative on how the video is done, it does not need to be in a boring, professional presentation style. Mini project 2: Each group had to do a modelling task using Vensim; for our group, we had to compare using coal and its effects against using oil. Afterwards, we had to submit the model and a report on the comparison. Major project: Each group had to do another modelling task, but now we had to use sensitivity analysis to show how the behaviour of the system changes depending on certain factors. Then we had to suggest policies to push the system towards a certain optimal behaviour depending on that analysis. Afterwards, each group had to submit a report and prepare presentations individually (yes, not as a group). The presentations were unfortunately during reading week/exam week. Test: There was a test in one of the last few weeks (I think week 11 or 12) which was a test conducted for all those taking junior seminars in RC4, so it was based on systems thinking in general, not just on energy systems. It is not difficult if you understand systems thinking well. It is a written open-ended test but has a modelling component and so you had to submit a Vensim model online as well so you need to bring your laptop for this test.

“It’s great to be a physics student in a module where you can have equations dropping from the sky.” Overview: Unlike the other level-1 physics modules, PC1142 covers two distinct areas in physics, thermodynamics and optics. Thermodynamics, which is covered first, is the easier topic as some of the content had been covered in H2 physics; things like enthalpy, heat cycles, ideal gas law etc. Optics, on the other hand, was completely omitted in the H2 physics curriculum, so most of the content will be unfamiliar to most people. The module is conceptually heavy; there is a lot of new content to digest, but the good news is that the mathematics is slightly toned down relative to PC1141. Also, as this is an introductory module, many of the theorems taught are given without proof, which makes things a lot easier. Still, the emphasis remains on computational questions, and some knowledge of basic calculus is required. ________ Syllabus: 1. Temperature & Heat 2. Kinetic Theory of Gases 3. First Law of Thermodynamics 4. Second Law of Thermodynamics 5. Light & Geometric Optics 6. Image Formation 7. Interference & Diffraction 8. Polarisation ________ Assessment: 5% Tutorial attendance 10% Lab reports 10% Mastering Physics assignments 15% Mid-term test: Covers only the thermodynamics portion. The prof uploads past mid-term tests and solutions to IVLE, so this is a very good opportunity to score, especially since the questions don’t vary that much between years. 60% Final exam: Can be quite challenging, with several application-based questions. Not too mathematically intensive, however, so if you spend the time to thoroughly understand the lecture content, it shouldn’t be difficult to do well. ________ Teaching Staff: Lecturer: A/Prof Peter Ho Prof Ho does a fairly good job of conducting the module. His teaching is fine, I don’t really have any comment on it, however I do like the way he uses ‘test your understanding’ questions interspersed throughout his lecture slides to ensure that we are keeping up with the lecture. He seems to be a busy prof, and rarely has time for individual consultations. However, he does conduct mass consultation sessions he calls ‘special clinics’ before the mid-term and final exam. Tutor: Dr Ching Chee Leong Chee Leong does a great job in conducting his tutorials. He has a warm demeanour; listening to him talk makes one feel at ease. He is able to present the solutions in a clear cut way, so it is easy to grasp the concepts after his explanation. I’m not sure if he sets them, but tutorial questions are generally short and do not require excessive mathematics, and some of them reference various applications in the real world, which I felt was quite enlightening. ________ Personal Experience: I did alright for the thermodynamics part, but couldn’t revise optics properly as I was on the verge of being burnt out near the end of the semester. As a result, my understanding was rather limited and it showed in the final exam when I couldn’t do all the long questions. I ended up writing random equations down on the paper, hoping for some sympathy marks. I felt really terrible after the paper and walked out of the exam hall without talking to anyone. I was ready to S/U this module, but in the end, the grade I got was far beyond my expectations. Maybe it’s due to the bell curve, but I think that my near-perfect CA score pulled my grades up significantly. So don’t underestimate the importance of the CA component. What I’ve learnt from this experience is that it pays to be consistent, not just throughout the semester for the CA, but also through the final push at the end of the semester.

[GET1043/GEX1024: Universe, Big Bang, and Unsolved Mysteries] Review Taken during: AY2021/22 Year 2 Semester 1 (still a COVID-semester) Lectures: Twice weekly, lecturer usually completes within 1.5 hours, sometimes even less than an hour) Tutorials: NIL Assessments: 100% CA (elaborated below) Lecturer: Dr. Cindy NG Lecture style: 100% Zoom but NOT recorded. The content started off fine, learning about religious point of views on the universe, then we go on to the Greek philosophers/scientists, describing how the Earth was flat in the past and now got debunked by other scientists etc. The content for the first part of the module (before reading week) was still understandable but when it came to Einstein's theory of relativities, everything (at least for me) start to go haywire. I started to not understand a lot of things but the lecturer just kept going on and on. Then a lot of other theories came on, along with the names of so many scientists that I started to lose focus and eventually gave up trying to understand a lot of the concepts since Week 8-ish. Assessments: LumiNUS Quiz (not necessarily weekly, but released every timeafter she completes a topic): 10% Term Test 1: 20% Term Test 2: 20% Project: 45% Forum: 5% Post-topic quizzes containing between 5-9 questions on average covers the topic that she just covered. As mentioned earlier, it is password protected so don't miss it when she releases during the live and not recorded Zoom lecture. Questions are quite tricky and Google may not necessarily have the answers for you. A final average score will be given to you which I got 8.4/10 and the median for my batch is 8.24. Term Test 1 on Week 7 covers topics taught before recess week (around 6 topics). 30 MCQs (1 mark each) + 5 short response questions (which she calls essay questions) 2 marks each. MCQ questions are multi-response type and are even trickier than the quizzes. Really must scrutinize each question properly and know your content well if you want to do well. Essay questions are also quite tough/application based. I got 21/30 for MCQ and 6/10 for the "essay questions" and I thought it was actually quite poorly done until I saw the grade statistics and the median for MCQ was like 17 while the essay one was like 5. She told us anything above average is already a A- so I'm quite surprised, considering I didn't really put in much effort for revision because of my core mods. Term Test 2 on Week 13 covers topics ONLY taught after recess week (around 7 topics). Same format as Term Test 1 but much harder due to the content. I only got 16/30 for MCQ this time round and I thought I would get 0 for the essay because I had absolutely no idea what I was writing but in the end turned out to be 6 again. Median for MCQ was 19 this time but essay was still 5. Project.. gosh it was a tough ride. 45% some more.. But basically this project is really all about essay writing with minimal discussions required. 10 essay questions (totally unrelated to the topics in the module) are released in Week 1 and we were told to form groups of 3 and rank the essay choices. We got an essay question regarding wormholes and space travel (not taught in lectures, I repeat), and what we had to do was to research on our own, write our stand and submit. We need to have 3 arguments for our main essay and so just nice each of us write an argument then together write an intro and conclusion. It was damn tough trying to find arguments for our essays and often I am lost with all the scientific terms. That is only 10% by the way. PC3193 Experimental Physics II For more module reviews (and the complete review) visit (20 MCs) Lecturers A/Prof. Tok Eng Soon Dr. Ren Minqin Dr. Vajandar Saumitra A/Prof. Thomas Oscipowiz Teaching Assistants Arif Er Chow Lin Er Tan Chuan Jie Zhang WenHan Lab Staff Dicky Seah Lee Soo Mien Grade Distribution Start of Semester 90%: Lab work (Report/Summary + Viva) 3 Short Experiments 2 Long Experiments 10%: Oral Presentation End of Semester 100%: Lab work (Report/Summary + Viva) 2 Short Experiments 2 Long Experiments We don’t actually know the grade distribution for the lab work. Covid struck one of the students taking the module and one experiment was dropped. Later on, because of the rising number of cases, the oral/presentation was dropped as well. List of Experiments Experiments done are underlined Short Experiments Channelled Spectrum Comparators Diffraction & Polarization of Microwaves Eddy Current Ferroelectric Measurement Ferromagnetic Resonance Gyroscope Laue Diffraction + Duane-Hunt Relation & Planck’s Constant * Laue Diffraction + Moseley’s Law & Rydberg Constant * Magnetostriction with the Michelson Interferometer Nuclear Magnetic Resonance Peltier Heat Pump (Attempted, gave up) Plasma Physics Principles of Lasing X-Ray Crystallography X-Ray Fluorescence Analysis Zeeman Effect Long Experiments Atomic Force Microscopy Compton Scattering Digital Video Microscopy Faraday Effect Fourier Transform Infra-red Spectroscopy Kerr Effect Michelson Interferometer Mossbauer Spectroscopy Nuclear Lifetimes One-electron & Two-electron Spectra Optical Pumping of Rubidium Particles-Matter Interaction Raman Spectroscopy Silicon Nuclear Detector Laboratory Sessions Just like the PC2193, this module requires you to go down to the lab to do the experiment yourself. The main difference is that now, you work individually rather than as a pair. The experiments themselves are more in-depth than in the level 2000 module – you actually have to do quite a bit of self studying to understand the concepts behind the experiments. I was told by the laboratory staff that the experiments are designed to supplement your learning in the level 3000 modules, so you might want to pick the experiments that are directly related to the modules you’re taken (or have taken). Like before, you will have to fulfil a certain number of hours by some arbitrary deadline during the semester. Rest assured no one actually checks that – it just serves as a good pacing to follow. You will also have to fill up your lab notebook, but again, no one actually checks that. Traditionally, you should be able to go down to the lab whenever you feel like it (From 12 to 5). But because of Covid, lab hours are now restricted so that everyone can only come down twice a week during the allocated slots. They don’t really enforce this, so there are weeks I don’t bother going down at all, while there are weeks I pop in four times. The staff are quite understanding so don’t be afraid to asks them. Because the experiments are more involved, there are required pre-experiment quizzes you have to complete before you can start collecting data. Be sure to read up on the experiments first as you will definitely be a little lost when you first start. Additionally, because of the restriction on when you can go down to lab, pre-reading is important so that you know what you’re doing. If you make a mistake in collecting your data, you might have to come down again on your assigned day and that’s half the week wasted (Out of the 12 weeks you have) The first experiment is assigned to you. The others are free and easy pick-what-you-want, as long as it isn’t taken by someone else already. You can start on the next experiment while finishing up the data processing and report writing for the previous, so that you don’t waste the limited time you have. Reports/Summary Same as PC2193, just that you might need to delve a little deeper into the background information section. Viva Similar to PC2193, although in my experience, the focus on data analysis and methods is more lacking than that of understanding the concept behind the experiment themselves. (Although to be fair the questions they have are rather dependent on the report you submitted so it may differ with individuals) Experiments In chronological order Particle-Matter Interaction (Long) Was assigned to me as the first experiment. Is completely computational, so if possible, one should do this one over recess week (Lab isn’t open). The program was a pain to set up on my computer, but worth it as you can collect data anytime. Even if you cannot set it up, no worries, as there are computers in the lab that have the program installed. Note that some of the simulations are very computationally intensive and may take hours to complete. Theory-wise, I felt that it wasn’t that extraordinary. The basics of scattering (covered at the start of PC3232) and a little reading up will cover you just fine. Optical Pumping of Rubidium (Long) I chose this one because of my interest in light-matter interactions. Out of all the experiments I’ve tried, this one is definitely the hardest. The theory behind it is surprisingly involved, and the equipment is a pain to learn, with many one-of-a-kind quirks. If you have experience with AMO (atomic, molecular and optical physics) and worked with oscilloscopes before, it’ll definitely help you. I don’t regret picking this experiment, but if you do, be prepared to spend quite some time here. Principles of Lasing (Short) Has absolutely nothing to do with principles of lasing. The first part of the experiment has been removed, due to how long students tend to take to align the equipment. The second half can be done in a matter of hours, depending on how thorough you want to be in collecting data. The theory itself is not too bad, especially if you already understand the basics of lasers (from JC or otherwise). The main bulk of the required theory is covered in the latter half of PC3247, so you might want to consider doing this experiment last, while taking it alongside PC3247. A trivial experiment. To be very honest, I picked this one because of how long I spent on the previous experiment and I wanted to catch up on time. Peltier Heat Pump (Short) Initially, this was going to be my last experiment. But after playing around with the set-up and trying it out for myself, I realised that it would take too long. Minimally, you need two full days to collect ONE set of data for each segment. That is equivalent to 2 weeks of time (since lab is only open half-days twice a week), for the bare minimum if you make no mistakes. It wasn’t worth the time. Theory-wise, it is relatively simple. However, there appears to be a mistake in the theory suggested for the first part of the experiment and how the results for power and efficiency are computed. This further dissuaded me from continuing with this experiment. Zeeman Effect (Short) So I went with this experiment instead. It was really quite easy compared to the previous one. Theory-wise, not too bad, although reading up about the weird interferometer took some time. The experiment itself took two sessions to complete. Expected Grade: A- Final Grade: visit Thoughts Overall, a pretty fun module. It’s one of the few physical modules where you can interact with people, definitely making it enjoyable in the current climate.

semester-2-year-1.html CM1502 is a core module for all Chemical Engineers in NUS. You will typically be allocated this module in semester 2 of the first academic year. There are no pre-requisites for this module other than A-level chemistry, which all of you would have satisfied to qualify for this degree anyway. As the module title suggests, CM1502 is all about physical chemistry. You will be brought through the entire spectrum from acid/bases to electrochemistry to nuclear magnetic resonance. About 70% of the content have been covered in your pre-university education, assuming of course, that you remember them. The remaining 30% can be pretty tricky. The module is also split up into 2 portions, each covered by a different lecturer. This is also your first brush with lab sessions. Part A - Dr Emelyn Tan 1) Gas laws 2) First law of thermodynamics 3) Second law of thermodynamics 4) Gibb’s free energy 5) Chemical equilibra 6) Acid-base equilibra 7) Electrochemistry 8) Spectroscopy Part B - Dr Prabha 9) Chemical kinetics (2 lectures on this) 10) Quantum mechanics (4 lectures on this) 11) Theories of covalent bonding (2 lectures on this) Exam format 15% Mid-term 1 (Dr Emelyn’s parts) 15% Mid-term 2 (Dr Prabha’s parts) 20% Labs (6.67% for each of the 3 lab sessions)50% Finals Teachers Good: 1) Dr Emelyn and Dr Prabha are both tutors for this module as well so there is a high chance you could get your queries answered fairly efficiently. 2) Dr Emelyn replies emails extremely quickly. 3) Dr Leonard Perreira, who is in charge of your lab sessions, is very nice so you can approach him if you find your lab scripts unprofessionally graded. Bad: 1) Dr Prabha does not really entertain emails. 2) Depending on your luck, you could get a lazy lab tutor that just ticks your script and randomly assigns you a grade. 3) Both lecturers are new so they might confuse you on some concepts. Dr Prabha messed up VSEPR a bit and Dr Emelyn lost me in spectroscopy. However, further clarifications with them solved the problem. Workload Weekly tutorials are pretty manageable but the lab sessions add a new dimension to the entire module. With 11 topics to cover in 13 weeks, lectures are extremely rushed. There are no webcasts so my advice is to not dream during class. Overall, workload is bordering on heavy so this is potentially one of the modules in which more time has to be invested. Tips Labs are extremely time consuming so it is best to free up the weekend after each lab session. The lab reports (which typically span 6 pages to 16 pages) are due the following week. It is important to do some reading up on the topics used for lab sessions. You are randomly allocated the order of the labs so you could (as i did) end up doing your kinetics lab 4 weeks before kinetics is taught. The 3 lab topics are: chemical kinetics, acid-base equilibra (titration) and chemical equilibra (precipitation of salt). Also, don’t be fooled by the ease of the tutorial questions and 2 mid-terms! The finals is meant to segregate the good from the average so it is EXTREMELY TOUGH. There are 4 questions, each worth 25 marks with many, many parts. I did not do 4 of the parts and still ended with an A so do not be alarmed! Work hard and you should be fine. Grade obtained: A

Taken in 20/21 Sem 2 Grading: 5% CA1, 25% CA2, 10% CA3, 30% CA4, 15% CA5, 15% participation Ah yes, the compulsory English class to be taken by all Computing students. There are 2x2hr sessions per week with high weightage class participation, which I'm sure contributes to the universal hate this class gets. The content of the class can be read from the other reviews so I'll just talk about the assessments. --- Assessment --- Similar to CS2101, grading is very consistent throughout the semester due to the 5 CAs. There aren't any "lull" periods where there's nothing to do (notwithstanding the 2x2hr sessions per week), so expect to put in more work than you might probably expect. For group projects, the class is split into groups at the start of the semester based on a survey done in the first class. You're stuck with this group for the whole semester so pray you get people who have the same goals as you. I was fortunate to have landed in a group with like-minded individuals who all wanted to maximise effort:reward ratio. CA1: Craft a presentation/video of a spin on a children's tale. Pretty simple, can be done in an afternoon if focused. CA2: Make a "Critical Thinking Rubric" from the Ennis reading, write a report on it (15%) and do a presentation (10%). This is the most tiring group project so I'm glad the co-ordinators put this early in the semester. CA3: Panel Discussion on an topic that was agreed upon prior to the discussion. You have to research the topic, then have an "academic conversation" that goes on for about 30-45min with your group, with 15min Q/A at the end. Can be prepared the day before. Try to be nice to your teammates and let them have their say in the discussion. CA4: Position Paper. You propose a question then write a 800-word-or-so essay on it. This is similar to writing a GP essay, except with citations. Can be done in a day assuming you already have a good question to write on. This is individual work with high weightage so if you're planning to score, better put work into this. CA5: Given a prompt, do an individual impromptu speech on the prompt in 2min. This is a luck of the draw if you get a good prompt or not. It's over within 2 minutes so if you can't think of anything to say, hey, at least you'll die quickly. Expected Grade: B/B+ Actual Grade: TBC

Taken in AY 2014/15 Sem 1 “What reporting verb do you use to express disagreement with someone in an academic essay? Claims. 'He claims that this and that is true, but actually it’s all a load of crap.'” Overview: ES1541 (now SP1541) is the fairly new writing module introduced back in 2013 to develop the written and verbal communication skills of science students. As you might infer from the module name, you will be expected to write a lot, and present a lot. The popular science part comes in the form of 5 popular science books from different disciplines, and the idea is to analyse how these books communicated obscure scientific knowledge to the general public in an accessible way, then applying what you have learnt in your presentations and essay. It is compulsory for all science students to take this module, unless you are part of a programme which already offers a writing module in their curriculum, e.g. Utown programmes. You can decide whether you want to take the module in your first, second or third year, although I would recommend clearing it in your first year, not only because of the lower bid points, but also because it is a requirement to go on overseas exchange. ________ Syllabus: As this is a writing module, learning is usually done via class activities and assignments. For my cohort, these included: - Individual and group summaries - Synthesis (of multiple sources to support your thesis) - Individual and group presentations - Argumentative essay (on a topic of your choice) - Peer review (of summaries, essay drafts) - Reflections Workload: I feel that commenting on the workload (and assessment) isn’t very meaningful here, due to the fact that this is a relatively new module which is still in the process of fine-tuning. The assessment components have changed drastically in the semester since I took the module, and will likely continue to do so. The amount of workload you experience will also differ depending on who you are and who your tutor is. I know people who found the module easy, but to others (like myself), it is a major burden. In general however, having a good command of spoken and written English and being comfortable with making presentations will make things easier for you. ________ Teaching Staff: Tutor: Ms Serene Eng Ms Eng is one of the most enthusiastic teachers I’ve seen. Even though my class is at 8 am, she has the ability to make the class come alive during lessons. She brings a new meaning to walking the talk, using the presentation techniques taught in the syllabus to capture the class’s attention and engage each and every one of us. She often shares her past experiences with us, which was an eye-opener for me. It shows that she genuinely cares about her students. Near the end of the semester, she even got a director of an MNC to advise us from an employer’s point of view, highlighting why communication skills are so important in today’s globalised job market. ________ Personal Experience: I am someone who has always been terrible at presentations, from primary school all the way to the PW OP in A levels. Whenever I have an upcoming presentation, I will go almost crazy with anxiety over it, sometimes to the extent of losing sleep the entire night. So you can imagine the horror I felt when I realized I couldn’t escape from this mod which has presentations nearly every week. But you know, it turned out to be one of those times when you are pushed to your limit, your perspective changes. I realized that if I don’t do anything, this problem will plague me for the rest of my life. I decided I had to face it. I accepted that I was going to stumble and fall, but I resolved to start learning from my mistakes and find ways to improve on the next presentation. Over the course of the semester, I experimented on various strategies, e.g. memorizing the entire script, remembering the key points, using props etc. While I didn’t do well for the majority of the presentations (sometimes I will literally stun there when I forget my script), I was beginning to understand what I could or couldn’t do. I finally managed to put it together in the last 10-minute presentation, scoring (what I felt) was an amazing 78/100. I still suck at presentations, no kidding, but at least I now know why I suck. And that makes all the difference, because for the first time in my life, I felt hope in my presentation skills. So it goes without saying that I am very happy with my performance in this module, regardless of the grade I obtained. So if you find yourself in a similar situation as me, don’t give up. Most people get at least a B+ for this module (I think the bell curve is slightly modified here), so your hard work will surely pay off in the end. More importantly, if you have the positive attitude of wanting to learn as much as possible, classes will become much more bearable, even enjoyable at times. The curriculum is structured in such a way that you will have to do just as many assignments as everyone else anyway, so why not learn something while you are at it?

Module Review by limwj ( The Professor for this semester is Dr. Jia Lile. Weekly lecture is held at 8am, but I managed to attend every session, rain or shine. Dr. Jia engages his students during lectures by getting us to do sms polls on some social psychology experiment. He would leave some blanks on his powerpoint, so that we have to fill them in. Videos are also shown, which can be funny, perplexing, and sometimes, thought-provoking. Dr. Jia will usually invite a guest speaker in one of the lectures, as a out-of-exam-focus talk on a particular topic within social psychology. It will be good to read your textbook before attending lectures, and lectures will be like a revision, and to spot the areas in which Dr. Jia focuses more (and therefore to focus more for exams). Throughout the semester, you will keep revisiting concepts such as schema, cognitive dissonance, self-fulfilling prophecy, and self-awareness theory. Topics tested during the mid-terms are not tested in the finals. Exam format for midterms and finals are the same: MCQs + SSQs (40% and 45% respectively). The remaining 15% comes from a project presentation. Study for the exams by doing mind-maps, understanding core concepts and their definitions, and do your textbook MCQs. Overall: This is an easy module; too easy that you have to work harder to be at the top of the bell-curve! (just saying) Take this module if: you are a psychology student; this is a core module, and it isn’t heavy. Hi, there are more module reviews here too: EG2301 Case Studies in Engineering Difficulty: Moderate Grade Obtained: B+ Lecturers: Prof Koen This module is one of the modules available to DCP students in Year 2 Sem 1 and introduces students to innovation and it’s components: feasibility, desirability, and viability. The goal would be to provide a good foundation for subsequent major project modules like EG3301R and EG4301R. The alternative module would be EG2311 Introduction to Space Systems. Here is how the module is graded: CA (100%) Lectures: Lectures are held every Tuesday night 6-9pm in EA and every week has a different theme and case study. Over the weeks, the concepts of feasibility, desirability, and viability and the tools that are used to gauge them are gradually introduced to us. Assignments: Even though the case studies sometimes feel irrelevant, the workload is still quite high. Every week, there are at least 2 short (300 words) individual assignments and a group assignment with a randomly assigned group for the week. Seems like this is supposed to get us to know fellow students in the DCP cohort. These short assignments are usually relatively easy to complete but over the weeks, these assignments become more annoying as you get busy preparing for other more important modules. There are also two big projects that makeup 50% of your grade but only with slightly more time than the usual weekly assignments. The limited time we have really limited the quality of work that we student’s produce. Generally, this module the biggest complaint that I have is that the submission of the individual assignments and not the quality of the answers counts towards the grade. That really reduces the quality of answers as students give minimum effort or less for the assignments and don’t learn the concepts and practice them properly. Not that their learning is my concern but the fact that I’ll probably be working with at least some of them in the future semesters for EG3301R and EG4301R makes this trend highly unsettling. Bell curve rating: Doesn’t seem to be much to curve Helpful resources: None needed Module Rating: The lessons to be learned are worthwhile, only if you put in the time to actually learn it.

Lecturer: Wang Fei Webcasted Assessment: 5% Lab 15% Homework (3 sets of equal weightage) 20% Midterm (helpsheet provided) 60% Final (helpsheet provided) Textbook: Thomas' Calculus (lecture notes are self-contained, so textbook is really for additional reference and practice) This is an introductory course to single-variable calculus, which is compulsory for Math majors. Concepts that may be new to JC students with H2 math background include limits and continuity, as well as some theorems like IVT, EVT, Rolle's Theorem, MVT, Fundamental Theorem of Calculus. Otherwise, you'll see some old friends, including differentiation and integration, explained in far greater detail and with a bit more mathematical rigour. Even though it is an introductory module, this module can be quite difficult and unforgiving, especially if you have basically forgotten everything you learnt in JC. Make sure you do whatever practice you can get your hands on (tutorials, past year papers, etc.) Dr Wang Fei is an excellent lecturer who is able to explain concepts clearly. He likes to do a thorough review of the previous lecture's content, which can be very useful as the whole module is pretty interconnected. The labs are frankly kind of boring. You learn to use a software called Maple, but you use it to do stuff that you could probably already compute on WolframAlpha. This culminates in a lab quiz towards the end of the semester, which doesn't actually really test anything besides your ability to key things properly into the software. Quality of tutorials really depend on the quality of the tutor you end up with. My tutor basically only provided solutions for some of the more difficult questions, and I don't really think I benefited much from attending the tutorials in the long-run. Dr Wang Fei has a tendency to set very tedious homework questions, but since they are take-home assignments, most people end up getting the full marks anyway. Treat the homework as useful practice. There is a fairly significant jump from the difficulty in content from tutorials to midterms/finals, especially if you don't have a good grasp of the content. Thus, those that score well in this module tend to be those with prior experience or those who have practised a lot. Be prepared to put in the effort to get the grade.

AY21/22 Semester 1 Lecturer: Multiple Assessment Components: Weekly Quizzes (60%): 10 quizzes, best of 9 are taken In-Tutorial Participation (15%) Group Presentation (10%) Post-Tutorial Engagement (15%) Overview: A compulsory module for CHS students, this brand-new module was meant to be a high-level introduction to several disciplines (Sociology, Psychology, Political Science, Economics, etc.) within the social sciences umbrella. Lectures are given in a Zoom webinar format, and students are encouraged to ask questions both in the zoom sessions and in the forums. Tutorials are bi-weekly and compulsory (they make up a percentage of your grade), hence requires you to read (or at the very least skim) through the lecture reading(s). The assessment format does not stop there though, as you are also required to present a 10-minute group presentation on a topic selected by your tutor/TA/lecturer with predetermined groupings of 3-4 people. Furthermore, tutorial engagement is also regarded as another component, which means that students will have to generally add their own insight(s) to discussions in a Microsoft Teams group. Module Difficulty: This module has a pretty light workload relative to other modules. The introduced topics, however, may bore those that do not have an inclination towards the social sciences. Furthermore, there have been some criticism about the way the module was run, including the order of the introduction of topics, as well as the not-so-natural-science-related content. Quizzes (which are open-universe) are generally moderately difficult, requiring about 1-2 hours each week to contemplate and finish. The participation aspect (including group presentation) was more to the easier side of things, as long as you have done your due diligence in going through the given readings and/or finding more information online. Personal Opinion: Albeit quite the number of people disliking the module as a whole, I have personally found it to be pretty well-run, as the lecturers/teaching staff have given a pretty visible amount of effort to selecting the depth of the content taught in this module. Concepts in the different areas of the social science umbrella are introduced quite well (especially considering that this was the first iteration of the module), although there may be room for improvement in the order of topics. As long as you maintain an open-minded and diligent attitude towards learning, it’s generally an enjoyable module (more so with the light workload). Tips: - If you are interested in a concept within this module, try to explore more through the internet or by asking your tutor/TA! - It’s better to skim through the given readings than read it word-by-word. - Content discussed during lectures often come up in the quizzes, so it’s better to take note of the more important points Expected Grade: A-/A Final Grade: TBD

Certainly he ought to be at least willing to answer inquiries of students who already show him their own serious attempts at answering the exam questions. If he is not, then he ought not to use exams to judge students' competency in natural language processing. Furthermore, he could have just told those students nicely what he felt about past year papers rather than talking down to them. This year's programming project was actually a reasonably interesting one, namely to implement a word-pair disambiguation classifier, in which the program needs to choose the right word of a given pair (like adopt/adapt) to fill in the blank in each test sentence, after learning from training data where the correct answers are provided. The word pair is of course not known in advance, so the program must be able to learn from the training data alone. We submitted both source code and a short write-up explaining our classifier. A significant portion of the marks went to our classifier's performance on the unseen test data, which is fair enough, but some marks also went to the classifier's performance on the sample test data that Prof Ng provided, which I felt was a bit wrong since some people might tune their classifier to fit best the sample test data. The weightage for the sample test data was half that of the unseen test data, so it was not really an issue for the grading, but it was still not a good marking scheme in my opinion. As an earlier reviewer already wrote, the test and exam questions are often of the type where just a slight mistake will cost you all the marks for that question, such as 5 out of 40 for the midterm, or 10 out of 80 for the final. Since the exam turns upon your carelessness during that 2 hours, you had better sleep well at least the night before! That is, if you have already chosen to be like a parrot for one semester. =P Finally, the TA, a PhD student whose supervisor was Prof Ng, was very unapproachable and many of us students who went to see him about the assignment grading felt very put off by his attitude towards us. I won't say more. Now let me make some course recommendations. For finite automata and context free grammars and related algorithms and much more, take CS4232, which teaches them properly. Prof Ng did not seem to actually have knowledge about these beyond what was in his natural language textbooks, so he couldn't confidently answer some simple questions about them that some students asked in class. For natural language processing content, you're probably better off reading online materials such as Wikipedia, which are not only much clearer but also more comprehensive, not so mistake-laden and better organized. Some reliable friends who also disliked CS4248 told me that some other modules are much worse, so I'm thankful that CS4248 is already one of the worst I've taken in SOC. Perhaps the other modules I've taken were so well taught that I had a high expectation before taking CS4248. Expected grade: A Obtained grade: A-

: This module is an introduction to the music programming software known as Max MSP by Cycling '74. I took it as a UEM, and because i belong to a computing course as well, naturally this should be quite easy for me. It is open to ALL NUS students, regardless of whether you are a YST student or not. The prof conducting this module is Prof Peter Ivan Edwards. He is a very nice professor, explains concepts very clearly and occasionally, tells us very interesting stories about his life, totally out of nowhere. It makes lessons pretty interesting at times. :) While the module can essentially be self taught since all the materials being covered are just documentation inside the software itself, attendance is a part of the grade, so remember to turn up for lessons. There are also a few in-class activities which make up part of the grade as well. The bulk of the grade comes from the individual projects that have to be done. The projects are easily doable, all you need to know is the relevant documentation for the project and just refer to it. Since it is a programming module, I can tell you that Max MSP programming is very much like Scratch - basically visual programming, connecting a bunch of boxes to each other. Each of the boxes, however, have their own unique ports which serve a specific purpose. It is near impossible to remember each of the different box types so documentation is very important. You just need to know what each port does, and in no time you'll know how to connect them all. Because of the need to look through documentation and sometimes needing to test whether the connections are appropriate, the projects do take some time, so start early. To help you out, you will be given ALL the boxes you need for the first 2 projects already, but in the last project, you will be left to figure out how to make the sub-programs given the parameters. Debugging is quite straightforward with the use of the monitor tool which you will be taught. Ultimately there are 2 reasons why you want to take this module - to get an easy A, or because you are interested to invest some time into learning music programming by furthering in other modules that involve Max MSP / explore it out on your own. I took this module for the former, but it eventually helped me in another module i was taking that involved the same Max MSP software. I did eventually find Max MSP fun to mess with since the other module i took, MUA2271, featured Max MSP patches which could create different types of sounds. The prof had no problems giving us all an A if we showed the effort we put into the individual projects. The class is also very small at less than 10 students, so the prof isn't pressured to give a bad grade either way.

Taken in 20/21 SEM 2 under Prof Guo Yong Xin (online lessons) Grading: 5% x 2 lab experiments, 10% x 2 mini projects, 10% x 2 CA test, 50% finals This course serves as an introduction to microwave circuits and the important components that make up the circuits. Pre-requisite is EE3104Cwhich I waived, going in with PC2020 knowledge. I subsequently found out that this was doable because transmission line and S-parameter theory was taught from scratch. However, learning these 2 concepts before the course will be very beneficial as much of the rest of the course relies on them. We covered the telegrapher equations, Smith chart usage (beyond what is taught in PC2020), Y/Z matrices and S parameters as an introduction. The pace was very slow at this point with Prof Guo spending quite an excessive amount of time on these concepts. Power dividers (Wilkinson, Coupled line) and filter design was then taught. Filter design will not be a problem if you have an analog electronics background, but the even and odd mode analysis for power dividers could take a while to get used to. These 3 chapters were covered in the first half of the course. The second half of the course was more rushed as Prof Guo effectively finished teaching chapters 4-8 in about 3-4 weeks. Content covered includes more RF devices like switches, amplifiers, mixers and oscillators. Amplifier design is a huge part of this course and many details like the non-linear effects in amplifiers, how to design matching circuitry, design for high gain/low noise figure was taught. However, this part was mostly glossed over by Prof Guo and I felt like he was just explaining whatever formulas were on the slides in a “wing-it” manner instead of connecting it to the big picture. The first lab experiment was to measure the S-parameters for different devices. Remember to take many pictures! The second lab experiment was to calculate the noise temperature and noise figure of an amplifier under bias/no bias. This part was more complicated and a good understanding of how noise originates in a circuit is required. Data from both labs was taken in person, and we were given 1 week to complete the lab report. The GAs were helpful and approachable in this portion of the course. The design software that we used for both projects was ADS, and it is relatively intuitive and easy to use. The first mini project required us to design a power divider at a fixed resonant frequency. The second mini project was the difficult one: designing a low noise amplifier with a single transistor. The lab manual alone was 33 pages, and there were many steps to be completed. However, the GA went through all the steps from start to end, but did not explain the big picture again (seems to be the trend in this group), so I just went with the flow without understanding why some steps were done (although they magically improved the parameters). Do start early for this project as it can be quite time consuming. Tutorials are the worst: Prof Guo skipped the first 2 tutorials and basically just glossed over the rest of the 3 tutorials. Doesn’t take a genius to tell students that “this is easy, you should be able to do it” for many of the questions. The tests and final exam tested on basic concepts, and you should be fine if you understood every slide (which is not a lot anyway). Anyway I didn’t do very well for the second test and exam because I was getting destroyed by other classes. Final thoughts: I 100% would not recommend this course. The content covered is pretty good to me, but think of this course as a good restaurant with a really bad waiter. Prof Guo didn’t give me the impression that he prepares for lectures and just glossed over the explanations. At one point, I stopped watching the lectures entirely even though they were recorded because I simply did not understand anything he was saying. I relied a lot on my own self studying for this.

It is one of the modules that can't be practised outside of lab, unless one enjoys cooking very much. :) Which for me is not the case. :(( Whether one finds it hard or not depends largely on his or her hand-on skills and preparations. Do prepare well before lab! It's best to really spend 5 hours rehearsing everything before the lab... Sadly I didn't have that much time for each session. Report-writing is reduced to 4 pro formas, one short report and a group long report. Assessment methods are standard: reports, purity, yield (for the regular exps), viva, written test, and practical test. Skills newly learned in the module: rotatory evapourator, IR spectroscopy for solids and liquids, reflux, water-free reactions (Grignard), working with dry ice, stereoselective reactions (and resolution of enatiomers), reduction with NaBH4, green chemistry (solvent-free reactions), sample preparation and result interpretation of NMR spectroscopy, measurement of optical rotation, measurement of magnetic suseptibility, air-blowing oxidation, simple distillation (not simple at all), and for Practical Exam, low-temperature control. Skills in CM1191 reviewed: TLC, recrystallisation (always a nightmare), gravity and suction filtration (needed almost in every session), extraction (Be ultra careful if gas evolves in the separatory funnel!!! The whole solution might just burst out!!! Own experience!!!), drying agent (don't add too much), UV-vis spectroscopy, weighing and transfer of compounds (not easy at all...). Theories needed: Mostly how to determine the number of unpaired electrons in a complex from its magnetic suseptibility, and how to use this to determine the geometry of the complex. Some understanding of stereochemistry in Organic chem is needed. Warning: Don't blindly follow the manual and don't simply copy what your friends did. Even don't follow whatever the lecturer says without asking why. #justsaying Think the reason behind every step. Take notice of temperature, pressure, the constituents of the reaction mixture at all times. Watch the reaction vessels carefully to prevent topples. I once just went for a chat for 1 minute and the whole system toppled. The above sounds hollow but is ultra important! It is okay to make mistakes, but note them down to prevent making them again. Specific warning (all personal bad memories): 1. Tighten all essential screws when using the retort stand 2. Don't be hasty when doing recrystallisation. Add solvents drop by drop. Sometimes the reaction keeps going during recrys! 3. Use solid funnels to transfer solid when possible. Fold the paper well if the transfer is into a microtube. (very hard) 4. In extraction, shake the separatory funnel gently first. Remember to vent the gas inside it frequently. 5. When transferring liquid, keep the beak of the upper vessel inside the lower vessel. 6. Remember exactly where you need to weigh an empty glassware. 7. It's better to familiarise yourself with where everything is in the first session. 8. Be safe. Always wear PPEs. My hand would have been ruined by conc H2SO4 if I didn't wear gloves. Don't duck the head into the fumehood. (VERY IMPORTANT!) 9. Never come to the lab unprepared! Suggestions on how to make the module better (on the teaching side) (personal views only): Firstly, there should be more interactions between different lecturers, lecturers and TAs, TAs and students, and so on. Now they are doing pretty well but still a long way to go to achieve the level of cooperation among staff in CS1010S. #justsaying Secondly, I hope there are remedial sessions for practically ungifted students to just practice basic things like TLC, NMR sample preparation, extraction, etc. ... I understand that this is much harder than for a theoretical module but I really want to improve myself. Out-of-class practice is important anyway. Thirdly, lecturers can try to give back our reports more promptly and write some more comments on them. I know that some lecturers are very busy...... but this is work worth doing haha. Difficulty: Hard for me. Grade: Bad

Lecturer: Vik Gopal Flipped Classroom, Webcasted Assessment: 30% Tutorials (11 sets of groupwork sheets done in-class) 30% Midterms (2 midterms, each with 15% weightage) 40% Finals (1 double-sided cheatsheet allowed) Textbook: A First Course in Probability by Ross (mostly useful just for the exercises, since lecture notes are largely self-contained) Just as the textbook used for the module suggests, this is a first course in probability, and it is a compulsory module for Stats and Maths majors. However, it is considerably much harder than the probability concepts you might be familiar with in secondary school/JC, going beyond just counting events. The most difficult parts of the module are probably properties of expectation as well as joint distributions, but these concepts are key for future modules in statistics, so it is important to have a decent grasp on them. While only MA1102R is needed to take this module, you will be expected to have some familiarity with double integrals. That being said, even if you don't have familiarity with multivariable calculus, Dr Vik will guide you through the various steps needed for this module. Dr Vik is a very effective instructor, perhaps the best I've seen in the Science Faculty so far. He designs the module in such a way that concepts like expectation and joint distributions are first introduced in an easier, discrete setting, then extended to a continuous setting. This gives more time to get a better understanding of the concepts in the module. The flipped classroom format for my batch was executed as follows: 1. Watch lecture videos on the lecture topic 2. Attend lecture, where Dr Vik reinforces concepts that is covered in the lecture video and goes through a set of fairly challenging example questions. 3. Attend tutorial, where you and a group of others attempt 1-2 questions. You are free to consult notes, the tutor, or even Dr Vik if he is around. 4. At the next lecture, Dr Vik goes through the solutions to all the different tutorial questions posed for the week. There were 2 midterms. Initially, Dr Vik intended to use the Examplify software for both midterms, setting mostly MCQ questions. However, most people did very well for the first midterm which used Examplify, so Dr Vik reverted to the traditional structured question, pen-and-paper format for the second midterm, which was considerably harder. Finals is of a similar standard to the second midterm, with a mix of mechanical questions and more challenging ones. In setting questions, Dr Vik emphasises probabilistic intuition more than the math department offering of the module does, and it shows when you compare the different finals papers, with fewer proving questions appearing. Overall, I highly recommend taking the module under Dr Vik, unless you prefer a more mathematically rigorous treatment of the content.

AY20/21 Sem 1 (COVID) Lecturer: Mr Ravi Suppiah Lab TA: Khairul Iman & Tessa Tutorial TA: Sai Ganesh Assessment Breakdown 40% Final Exam 15% Midterm 5% Tutorial Attendance & Participation 10% Lab Assessments 30% Mini-Project Topics CPU & GPIO, Interrupts & Analog I/O, Timers & Serial Comms, RTOS & Processes, Scheduling & Concurrency, Task Synchronization, Communication & Data Sharing, Memory Management & Virtual Memory Note: The mod underwent major changes starting from AY19/20 Sem 2. Previously used was the Arduino Uno microcontroller with FreeRTOS, but the current iteration of the module uses the FRDM-KL25Z board with Keil RTX. Introductory mod to RTOS, which I found to be quite enjoyable and one of the modules CEG can be identified with. The module was held fully online, with the exception of the Labs where students had the option of doing their work in the DSA Lab. Some of the earlier concepts such as GPIO, Interrupts, Serial Comms should be fairly familiar from EPP2, so the main bulk of new knowledge is the RTOS concepts. Lab & Tutorial Unlike previous iterations, labs did not require reports at all, and all that was needed was attendance and demonstrations of the first 6 labs (later labs were then ungraded). However, it is important to understand the concepts used in these labs since they are used in the assessments. Tutorials also had participation marks, but only 4 of all the tutorials needed our input to get full credit. Effectively, this mod had 15% dedicated to just participation. Lab TA Iman was extremely helpful by being hands-on in understanding the practical concepts and Tutorial TA Sai Ganesh put in the effort to answer our questions, so kudos to them. Mid-Term The Mid-Term was held in Week 9 and covered a bit more than the first half of the module, up until RTOS. It consisted of 15 MCQ and was fairly manageable, especially with a few concepts already covered in EPP2. Mini-Project The star of the module this time was our very own RC car. Using an Android app, we could control the car’s movement, and based on what we programmed, the car would execute the movement, flash LEDs and play sounds according to the car’s status. The RTOS concepts learned had to be used and allowed us to design the architecture in any way as long as the minimum requirements of were met. The project just follows directly from the labs, so other than the hardware issues we faced, it was not too complicated. At the end there is a competition run and your best of two times will be used and compared with the rest of the class. Each group had two to three students, and grading consisted of requirement fulfilments, a competition run leaderboard rank, report + code, and video. Final The final was completely online, and the questions could be said to be comparable to the tutorials given. They were all open-ended, including programming questions, and tested the entire module, mainly focusing on the latter part that was not tested in the mid-term. As long as there was effort put in understanding what was going on in the tutorials and labs this should also be manageable. The past year questions before AY18/19 S2 were of very different types of questions which were irrelevant, so we only had one past year paper to really practice with. However, I believe there was enough covered in the module to make it possible to answer 95% of the questions in the exam. Overall, the module is quite manageable, and I would say it wasn’t too easy or too difficult. This tends to be the style for Mr Ravi*, try to enjoy the learning! *(You can check out his material on docr.sg ) Expected Grade: A/A-

UTC1415 was the first module I have ever taken in CAPT. As a freshmen with not much intel on this module, I decided to take up this module out of pure interest from the module description. Indeed, it was true that I took away many new insights about issues such as abortion, LGBTQ+, divorce etc to name a few and how these issues inadvertently affect the social landscape of Singapore, more specifically the traditional nuclear family unit. Lessons were fun and engaging when guest speakers were invited to share their view on the topic especially when they are actively involved in the local scene - whether it be fighting for transgender rights, building halfway houses for troubled youth or a foster parent who shared her struggles of taking care of a foster child. Prof Sue would also give a background of information of current trends, news and share with us any relevant mainstream media that concern the topic of discussion for that session. Occasional field trips were also enriching when we had external speakers share with us experiences we would not have been able to hear unless from one who has been in the industry or landscape long enough. It was both eye-opening and enriching, an experience I knew would be hard to come by without this module. This module I took in AY17/18 Semester 1 was geared towards the learning ethos of breadth rather than depth. By the end of the semester, we had managed to discuss over 10 topics that families have to tackle in today's modern society. Individual reflective writing assessments were rather manageable as it was not so much on head knowledge you have to possess to be able to complete task well but your honest and genuine response to the things you have seen in class or during field trips. As long as you regularly keep up with the readings in class and listen attentively, one hour open-book quizzes in the form of 500-word essay questions were very doable. Points raised that are well-substantiated is good enough for a good grade. There is a group project component which requires your group to do a poster presentation on an issue that affects families today whilst also suggesting possible solutions that may help to bridge current gaps. It is also expected for each group to interview a stakeholder whether a social worker, person who has had experience grappling with this issue etc. The aim of this is to also allow us to gather a new perspective and inculcate empathy while exploring familial issues in Singapore. While it seems daunting at first to interview an external party, Prof Sue's guidance and contacts aided the process greatly and turned out to be a smooth experience for my group to complete this task. The module is a compulsory S/U which very much takes away the pressure of having to perform exceedingly well for each assessment. Hence, I would like to encourage to take up this module if you are interested or even just would like to explore more on this issue. Prior knowledge is not required, only open minds :-)

Instead, I'll simplify it for you by asking you a few questions. First, is it feasible to learn how to ride a bicycle just by reading a book or watching a video about riding bicycles? Second, is it feasible to understand why flipping through a stack of papers is troublesome, as compared to simply doing a Ctrl-F on a keyboard for text search in a word document? Third, is it feasible to understand the difficulties in making ethical decisions if you have never experienced the pain and sweat and hunger and anger and frustration and jealousy and joy and happiness and love that goes into making such decisions in the real world?" What can I say, except that I completely agree? Unfortunately, this is not the reality of IS1103. It is not feasible to learn about riding bicycles by reading a book, just as it is equally impossible to learn about ethics by doing quizzes about contrived scenarios without avenues for creative discourse. Furthermore, I am sure that it can be justifiably unethical under some of the ethical frameworks, to make students flip through papers to essentially "teach them a lesson" that physical data is harder to aggregate than digital data. Also, arguably, students were not asked to make any ethical decisions, so this entire point seems barely relevant. "If you answered yes to any of the three questions stated above, you're not being truthful with yourself, and scientific research backs that up". This translates to: your personal experiences and opinions are invalid, because "scientific research" is never wrong. Is it ethical to be so condescending and dismissive towards a student like that? “Scientific research” or otherwise? ---------------------------------------------------------------------- 3. In response to the question "Why do the missions not seem to be connected with the topic?" "I can assure you that the missions are extremely connected to the topic, it's just that you need to reflect on them to see it. For example, in Mission 1 and 2, Big Data is about the 4Vs (Variety, Veracity, Velocity, Volume), and you indeed encountered a Variety of data types (eg. image vs. text, visual vs tactile, etc), with varying levels of Veracity [accuracy] (blur vs. sharp pictures, useful vs. un-useful data, etc), with different Velocity (walking to some place vs. seeing it on the internet, accessing a file online vs accessing a file physically, different barriers to the information such as the X-ray room in UHC [how to get that information? Ask someone? Search Google? Physically go to UHC to find it?]), and with varying Volume (the amount of information you get when you are walking from place to place vs. the amount of information you get by just reading the text), these are all examples of how you have experienced Big Data" I struggle to see how obtaining 5 pieces of contrived information, nor flipping through a stack of papers, constitutes big data. First of all, there was no explanation on what big data was supposed to be, in the context of this module. As one of the latest internet buzzwords, it seems that this module has taken it upon itself to introduce another interpretation of big data, in this case, "meaningless data". Perhaps it would be more effective for students to be able to "reflect on" the missions, *after* having the concepts and implications of "big data" explained to them -- would it not? ---------------------------------------------------------------------- In summary, his statements are frankly dismissive and condescending of students' experiences, and gives students the impression that their concerns are simply invalid. Is this the way that professors are supposed to respond to student feedback? See? Straight from the horse's mouth. Unbelievably condescending and dismissive.
