Prof Wang Chi-Hwa: Fundamentals of Heat Transfer, Steady and Unsteady-State Conduction, Convective Heat Transfer and Correlations, Boiling and Condensation, Molecular Mass Transfer, General Differential Equations for Mass Transfer Prof Soh Siow Ling: Steady and Unsteady-State Mass Transfer, Convective Mass Transfer, Analogies of Momentum, Heat, and Mass Transfer, Radiation This module basically discusses the different modes of heat and mass transfer and how to quantify them for (chemical) engineering purposes. This module is more like 2/3rds Heat Transfer and 1/3rds Mass Transfer, as 8/13 lectures discussed heat transfer (conduction, convection, and radiation) and only around 5/13 lectures discussed mass transfer. However, the contents are similar to each other and in the end there would be one lecture that links momentum (CN2122A), heat, and mass transfer together and it would become apparent why we spent more time understanding the heat transfer part. The assessment of this module during this iteration were as follows: 30% Midterm, contents from fundamentals of heat transfer to convective heat transfer and its correlations. 7 open ended questions within a 2 hour time limit. Average was around 76/100, 75th percentile was 89/100. 15% Quiz 2, contents included all of the mass transfer part. 19 MCQs and MRQs (no partial marks) within a 1 hour time limit, testing concepts (almost no calculations, only simple ones). Average was 8.5/19, 75th percentile was 11/19. 5% Industry Guest Lecture report + Mini Project Report. Similar to senior’s reviews, can refer to Mario Lorenzo’s post/ ilovechocolate’s post. Average was around 78/100. 50% Finals. Comprising ~ 11-12 open ended questions within a 2.5 hour time limit. In my opinion, this module is quite heavy because the amount of formulas that we need to get used to for the midterm and finals. I faced some difficulty during the first half of the module as I was still “adapting” to the sheer amount of formulas in this module, especially the heat transfer part. However, it was also rewarding because when you are already accustomed to the formulas used, the mass transfer part would be much easier as the formulas are very similar (almost exactly the same, just changing the variables). So my advice would be to get accustomed with the concepts and formulas of the first part (I did this during recess week) to ease your learning journey for the rest of the semester. I even wrote a personal 18-page cheatsheet (might as well call it a cheatbook) for this module alone, almost exclusively for the formulas, not for the concepts, to have a “quick access” to all the formulas and directly plug in all the numbers to get the answers. This module is somewhat like a continuation of transport processes that we learned in CN2122A, and as mentioned in the first paragraph, there will be like a “grand finale” to link the concepts from CN2122A with CN2125, which is quite interesting. However, this means that there would be some concepts from CN2122A (hence, the pre/corequisite of this module is CN2122/A) that would be utilized in this module such as boundary layers and Blasius and Von Karman solutions. Another (implicit) skill from CN2122A that would also be useful for this module is simplification of differential equations. In particular, your skill in simplifying the Navier-Stokes equation from CN2122A would be useful to simplify the General Heat Transfer/Mass Transfer Differential Equations. This is especially important, as prof Soh Siow Ling’s second quiz mainly tested our understanding of the General Mass Transfer Equation and what assumptions that we use to simplify the equation. Oh and don’t throw this knowledge away after finishing the module as during our batch, a question about deriving a concentration profile and molar flux equation appeared in our CN2116 Final Exam, as the concepts are quite related to the ending chapters of CN2116 (read my module review there to know more). I would also like to add a comment about the profs who taught this module during our batch. Prof Wang has taught this module many times and I would say his delivery in the lectures were decent but quite monotone. Thus, the lectures could seem to be quite boring. On the contrary, Prof Soh’s delivery in the lectures were very engaging and he liked to relate the concepts he taught with some real life examples. This makes his lectures much more lively. In the end he also showcased a bit of MATLAB to solve harder topics regarding Heat and Mass Transfer (like 2-D Heat/Mass Transfer), which for me is quite interesting and in my opinion should be showcased more throughout the module.I would say he is one of the better lecturers in the Chem Eng department (just as Mario Lorenzo said in his review). Overall, I would say that this module is not really hard, but you need to adjust to the pace and the sheer amount of formulas thrown at you every week. I would suggest creating a cheat-sheet for all the formulas and the conditions so you can refer to them quickly during the midterm/final exams.

Module taken during AY2020/2021 Semester 2, taught by Professor Loke Hung Yean Prof Loke based his lesson heavily on the book Differential Analysis on Complex Manifolds by Raymond O. Wells, whose approach differs greatly from the original syllabus. The student who is expecting to learn the inside-outs of basic manifold theory may be disappointed as this book only touches the basics of manifold theory very briefly in the first chapter and dive in pretty quickly into the geometry on (complex) vector bundles over complex manifolds. Many topics stated in the original syllabus such as immersions, submersions, orientation of manifolds, integration on manifolds, Stokes' theorem are omitted. Instead, notions fundamental to the realm of complex geometry such as sheaves, sheaf cohomology, curvature, Chern classes etc are taught. I find the content to be incredibly fun and interesting, though it is somewhat challenging and very abstract for the student learning geometry for the first time. However, one should realise that such abstractions are meant to simplify things, not complicate them. For example, the notion of sheaves is invented to capture local information of objects (say functions) on a manifold and the idea of Chern classes gives us an somewhat easier say to detect if the tangent bundle over a smooth manifold is trivial, etc. Prof Loke is a very easy-going and kind teacher who is obviously well-prepared for classes. He will explain constructions fully and fill in gaps in computations and the proofs which Wells left out in the book. Very often, he will also remind us on definitions/ideas that have been taught but we may have otherwise forgotten, like for e.g. a vector bundle, a sheaf, etc. The pace of the lecture is pretty slow for the first half of the semester, for some reason. Prof Loke covered the basics of manifold theory in the first 6 weeks (chapter 1 of Wells), which isn’t a lot of content. The pace only starts to pick up after recess week, where there are lesser distractions in class. From there on, Prof Loke dives in pretty quickly into sheaf theory, sheaf cohomology and subsequently ending the semester with a very basic introduction to Chern classes of differentiable vector bundles. As IK mentioned, one grip I have with the module is that Prof Loke does not go in depth in many topics. This is possibly due to the lack of time. For example, doing sheaf cohomology and explicit computations on sheaf cohomology would be a great supplement to learning sheaf theory. However, Prof Loke only described certain sheaf cohomologies briefly and did not provide any interesting examples of computations, which I felt was a missed opportunity. As such, unless the student is extremely motivated to read up on their own, they may leave the course with only a basic knowledge but no working knowledge of say, sheaf theory. All in all, I had a very enjoyable time taking this course under Prof Loke. Every lesson was a joy to attend and his teaching style made the otherwise supposedly difficult content a lot more digestible for students. Not only that, he is extremely friendly and is always willing to talk to students after lessons to clarify their doubts. I strongly recommend any one who wishes to have a glimpse in geometry to take this module.

GES1017 AY2016/17 Sem 1: I selected this module out of all the other GES modules due to its engineering nature. I didn't regret the decision, it's a fun and educational module. I was taught by Prof Chai Kah Hin, Prof Tan Kim Seng & Prof Vladan Babovic, who alternate teaching different case studies. I find Prof Chai Kah Hin most memorable for his teaching enthusiasm, but Prof Vladan was also memorable who being quite jovial and even speaking a slight bit of Singlish in his own accent. The module is conducted in seminar style, which spans 3 hours. I have to admit that this is very tiring, although the lecturers do give a break in-between. Before each class, it is recommended you read up the case study (you'll be told via email and IVLE) and roughly understand it. If you enjoy reading about engineering aspects, it should be no problem. Some of the case studies are simple, others are a bit more technical. The cohort is made of a wide variety of students, from many different faculties and students from different years of study. (as what you would probably from a GE module) There are class participation marks, so try your best to ask / answer questions in a few lectures (you are required to have a name stand in front of you, and there is an assistant recording down who is asking questions) There are no tutorials. It is also taught in terms of case studies. Every lecture is of a different case study, which explains the behind-the-scenes for each engineering structure (like Jurong Island, one-north & Semakau Landfill), or the background behind a certain Singapore fundamental aspect, such as Water or Manufacturing. It is very enlightening to discover the behind-the-scenes for each engineering aspect, if you are into inventions or engineering in general. The main part of the module comes in a major group project, where you have to do a report based on an interesting engineering aspect of Singapore, such as the MRT or HDB housing. This does take up quite a lot of time, as the report is quite long. You can refer to the case study materials to help you craft your report. Our group met several times for a few hours, also working on the project outside meetings for more hours. There is a presentation day where you give a brief presentation, but not all your group members need to present. I had fun with my project group, and once again if you enjoy reading up on engineering stuff, this is actually quite educational. There are also small graded assignments where you need to write a short essay about a topic on some case study. These are generally very easy to score, as so long you put in reasonable effort to write something, the lecturers will most likely give you full credit for the homework. These assignments also help in the final exam. There are no midterms but there is a final exam, but generally the preparation is not much as all you need to understand are the concepts taught in the case studies, such as the unique ways (and concepts employed in certain areas, such as work-live-play-learn concept in one-north, plug and play concept in Jurong Island) engineers used to overcome the problems. The exam is generally quite relaxed, with a few short essay questions, though I have to say that the MCQ questions were the hardest, since there can be MORE THAN ONE correct answers. Some people walked out of the exam after 1hr or so. (The exam is 2hrs) I heard some of my group mates simply wrote the essay questions in point form. The most fun part of the module is you actually get to go on a field trip! I went to the Marina Barrage for my semester. I liked the module very much and hoped for a really good grade, ended up with a B+. However, I enjoyed the module very much. I worked on the MRT for my project (more focused toward Downtown Line), and even after I finished the module, every time I step near or into a Downtown Line station, I remember all the research I've done for it for my GES1017 project.

This module requires high level of consistency since the proportions of module are equally spreaded between CAs and exams. So for non-SoC students, you may want to reconsider this option to fulfill your CS1010 requirement. This mod is not bell-curved (according to what they said which I sometimes doubt lol). Dr. Low Kok-Lim is a great lecturer that is able to deliver the concepts in simple packs so that the concepts are very easy to be digested. He is responsive to queries and patiently explains the doubts to the students. Even though the lectures are webcasted, it is strongly encouraged to come to the lectures if you feel that you are lost since it will be helpful and you can ask any queries to Dr. Kok-Lim. There are weekly studios (equivalent to tutorials) and reflections (equivalent to recitations) where attendances are taken. Additionally, there are 2% proportion of studio participation in order to make the class active. Instead we get this half-assed mode of assessment which benefits nobody except the people marking the answers, because they don't need to use their brains to actually evaluate the arguments made by students. How can you teach a module saying that ethics is up to the interpretation of the individual person, when the entire structure of the module is in such a way that nobody even gets to express their own views? Next there is the "world setup"; it feels like the profs watched john wick over winter break and decided to add artificial drama to the module, which contributed nothing to the students' learning experiences. Finally, there is the question of the absolutely condescending Lu Weiquan. After a few weeks there were expectedly people rightfully complaining about this module. In response to the question "Why not just make everything like every other written test/exam that you've ever taken in your Primary/Secondary/JC/Poly/etc school life?" "As IS1103 is an Experiential Learning module, the learning happens when you experience what you need to experience in the module. In other words, unlike other modules / classes / courses that you have taken, in which all the answers can be found in a textbook, Experiential Learning is about finding the answers through your own personal experiences when doing the missions." Third, is it feasible to understand the difficulties in making ethical decisions if you have never experienced the pain and sweat and hunger and anger and frustration and jealousy and joy and happiness and love that goes into making such decisions in the real world?" What can I say, except that I completely agree? Unfortunately, this is not the reality of IS1103. It is not feasible to learn about riding bicycles by reading a book, just as it is equally impossible to learn about ethics by doing quizzes about contrived scenarios without avenues for creative discourse. Furthermore, I am sure that it can be justifiably unethical under some of the ethical frameworks, to make students flip through papers to essentially "teach them a lesson" that physical data is harder to aggregate than digital data. Also, arguably, students were not asked to make any ethical decisions, so this entire point seems barely relevant. "If you answered yes to any of the three questions stated above, you're not being truthful with yourself, and scientific research backs that up". Is it ethical to be so condescending and dismissive towards a student like that? “Scientific research” or otherwise? ---------------------------------------------------------------------- 3. Ask someone? Search Google? Physically go to UHC to find it?]), and with varying Volume (the amount of information you get when you are walking from place to place vs. the amount of information you get by just reading the text), these are all examples of how you have experienced Big Data" I struggle to see how obtaining 5 pieces of contrived information, nor flipping through a stack of papers, constitutes big data. . Taught by Dr. Gene Segarra Navera. Grade I was fighting for: A- Actual grade: A This module has a high workload, regardless of whether you intend to S/U this module or not. Like all I&E2 modules, students will spend most of the semester researching and writing 3 papers: (1) annotated bibliography, (2) research proposal, and (3) research paper. This adds up to about 4000 words in total. On the bright side, students get to decide the topic of investigation, so do read the module description carefully and make sure that the scope of study interests you. Tutor: Dr. Gene is a great teacher who is very knowledgeable about the field of rhetoric and discourse. He is friendly and extremely understanding of the pain that students go through in I&E. To illustrate, Dr. Gene makes sure to always end his class at the 1hr 35min mark, so students have enough time to make it for the next lesson. He is also very accommodating of his students' schedules, so do approach him if you are facing any difficulties in keeping up with the deadlines. Workload: 2 x 2 hour sectionals each week. Expect to spend about an hour before each sectional to read the readings and organize your thoughts. The "normal" classes (when there is actual teaching) only make up about 30% of the sectionals. The remaining is used for peer reviews, consultations, and presentations. Assessments: Participation: This component is a combination of class participation, class facilitation and the final presentation. Normal class participation is straightforward--be sure to have some ideas and insights and share them in class and you'll do fine. You will also be expected to form a group of 3 and facilitate the class for a 1-hour session. This takes place from the 2nd to 4th instructional week. Finally, there is an informal (no slides needed) presentation near the end of the semester where students share about their research project. Annotated Bibliography (500-700 words): Life sucks. 4 weeks into the semester and you will be asked to find four academic papers to review and write about. Each of the four entries in the annotated bibliography is 150 words long. On top of summarizing the key points, try to include some insights and critical analysis to score well. Adherence to citation format is very important in this assignment. Mistakes made in this paper will result in heavier penalties. Research Proposal (750-1000 words): This is where you will be laying the foundation for your final paper. You are expected to write a literature review, list out your sources of data and your critical approach. You will get a 15 min-20 min consultation slot prior to the final submission. Let Dr. Gene know about any difficulties you face in writing and pay close attention to his advice. Pick out any ideas that he gives and consider incorporating them into your paper. Research Paper (1900-2200 words): Yes, this is a lot of words to write. Thankfully, you are allowed to reuse certain parts of the research proposal, so this should lessen the pain. Once again, you get another consultation session before your final presentation and submission, so make full use of this opportunity to get help. Students aren't required to produce a full draft during the consultation and first draft submission, but I personally advise doing so. That way, Dr. Gene will be able to have a bigger picture of what you are writing about, which is crucial for your final source of guidance which is the final presentation. Conclusion: I&E2 is a relatively high-workload module for students who aren't well-versed at academic writing like myself. As such, you might consider taking this mod with the intention of S/U-ing it. However, I would recommend at least trying to push for an A- so that you can justify the workload. I, for one, had issues with formal writing and did not originally expect to get more than B+ in an academic writing module. Dr. Gene monitors each of his students' progress carefully; your effort to improve yourself will be recognized. All the best!

Median for all assignments were 5 marks from full marks. For finals, non-linear techniques were NOT tested, which saved A LOT of revision time. The prof tested mostly concepts that were taught and interpretation or R code output. Highly recommend this module if you are interested since it's not as intense and has interesting content, however I suggest to not skip non-linear dimension techniques as they are important skills that you should know

Taken in 19/20 Sem 1. A very time consuming and honestly difficult module that could easily be worth 8 MCs. My year covered Series, Vector Analysis, Fourier Series, Integral Transforms, ODEs and Green’s Functions. I agree with the other reviewer — it is maybe not a good idea to overload with this module. Kenneth is a good lecturer, and is an even better teacher when you go to him for consultations — don’t be afraid to drop an email and knock on his door. Go for the tutorials — these are killer difficult, and sometimes you can read the solution and still not get what is going on. AY2020/2021 Semester 1 Review This module is taught by Professor Zhang De-qi. Concepts Taught: A review of group theory, ring (module) theory and a really short review on Galois theory. Most concepts are already taught in Algebra 1 and Algebra 2, as well as Galois theory. New things one would learn outside the aforementioned courses would be solvable and nilpotent groups, tensor products, module over P.I.D and a bit of injective and projective modules (self-learnt through presentation) Due to Covid-19, the module was taught over zoom, and lecture notes are provided. The reference book for the module is “Algebra”, by Hungerford. Professor Zhang strictly follows his lecture notes. Professor Zhang assumes that one already knows all the concepts in the per-requisite modules, so he skipped through the details of things that he thinks that one should already know. He finished the syllabus by week 11, the last 2 weeks was spent on presentation: each member of the class was assigned a theorem from the reference book to present on. (About injective/projective modules and duality of modules) The final exam consists of 6 questions (mirroring the qualifying exams) one on groups, 3 on ring/module theory, and 2 on Field/Galois theory. I feel more time should be allocated to teaching Galois theory, given the weightage in the finals. Professor Zhang only spend two lectures on Field/Galois theory, so I feel that people who didn’t take the Galois theory module before are severely disadvantaged. Pros: Professor Zhang has a unique sense of humor and is really entertaining. I personally enjoyed his classes. One can take this module to consolidate your learning on abstract algebra. Cons: Unfortunately, due to large amount of content covered, he didn’t cover them in great detail: If this is your first exposure to say Ring theory or Galois theory, you might have to do a lot of self-studying. Since the module is aimed to be a preparation for the qualifying exams, maybe in the future the module could be focused more on problem solving instead of just covering the content.

Taken in AY2014/15 “Did you all get that? Let me come again. … Actually, I shouldn’t be saying such things in public. … But to come again, it must be hard. … as in difficult. I don’t know what all of you are thinking about. ” Overview: MA1505 is the first of two modules which covers the mathematical fundamentals which are commonly used across the various fields of engineering. The main topic of interest here is calculus and its branches which are most relevant to engineering applications. This means learning about things like Taylor’s theorem, Fourier series and vector calculus, up and above the regular differentiation and integration techniques and applications covered in H2 math. This is not a light module. The content taught here is arguably the equivalent of 2 modules taken by math majors, as it covers both single and multivariable calculus. Therefore, much of the content is condensed with the focus on applying the theorems taught, and the proofs of said theorems given only a passing mention or else omitted entirely. ________ Syllabus: 1. Functions 2. Differentiation 3. Integration 4. Series 5. Vectors 6. Fourier series 7. Functions of several variables 8. Multiple integrals 9. Line integrals 10. Surface integrals Workload: There will be one 2-hour and one 1-hour lecture per week, plus 1 tutorial per week. Attendance is not graded, plus there is webcast, so you can self-study everything at home if you want. However, if you are an average student, be prepared to spend a lot of time wrapping your head around things like Fourier series, Stokes theorem, Divergence theorem etc. ________ Assessment: 20% Mid-term test: This 1-hour paper contains 10 MCQ questions and covers the first 5 chapters. The paper is harder than it looks (the mean score for my cohort was 6/10), as almost all questions require some form of computation. If you want to do well, attempt all the past year test papers uploaded on IVLE as the format of the papers are more or less the same. 80% Final exam: Although the exam covers only chapters 6-10, it is not easy as these chapters are the hardest in the module. Again, doing the past year papers helps a lot. You will also be allowed to bring in 1 cheat sheet into the exam. You can write whatever you want in the cheat sheet, but I recommend you include all the important formulas in case you forget them during the exam. If you have extra space, copying the past year paper solutions is a good idea as well. ________ Teaching Staff: Lecturer: Dr Yap Weng Yin Dr Yap was my webcasted lecturer. He lectures quite well; nothing spectacular, but he gets the idea across. He occasionally punctuates his lecture with some, uh, not-so-decent jokes, which always gave the class a good laugh. I felt it provided a very welcome relief from solving integrals and analysing vector fields all the time. Unfortunately, I only attended a couple of tutorials, mostly studying using the solutions provided on IVLE, so I'm not in a position to comment about the tutor. ________ Personal Experience: I did not have a pleasant experience in this module, although it is partially my fault. I only started watching webcast lectures during reading week, and cramming that much information into my brain in such a short time was very painful. If that wasn’t enough, I then realized after the exam that I hardly understood anything that I had learnt, beyond memorizing the steps to solve exam problems. Apparently what happened to me is very common for first year students. My advice is the same as that of the reviews before mine. Study consistently throughout the semester, even though most of the marks are in the final exam. And it's not just for the grade in this module. Many of the concepts taught here seem dry and abstract now, will likely appear again in future modules. Building a solid foundation now would mean having an easier time later.

Took in 17/18 Sem2, taught by Prof.Liang Zhenkai. As the name suggests, the module is a practice module. Being a "hands-on" module, it is not very intensive in content, so students who have attended CS4236/CS2105/CS3235/CS2106 before should be very familiar with the techniques used in this course, such as sql injection, binary analysis, TCP seq prediction, packet forging... etc. It is conducted in lab sessions, in each lab session the professor will bring you through a topic and you have a lab sheet to practice the techniques taught in the session. Taken in: Semester 2 AY2016/2017 Professor teaching this module: Dr. Mary Posa Dr. Posa is very friendly, especially during fieldtrips. She is also very organised and is clear in her explanations. _________________ Teaching Modes 2h lecture once a week, 4h practical session every odd week Venue: S17 LT34 Webcast: No 3 Field Trips – Avian (Pulau Ubin), freshwater (canal/coast), terrestrial (forest) _________________ Assessment CA1 - Personal Statement (2.5%) CA 2 - Ubin Report Draft 1 (5%) CA 3 – Extinction Game Quiz (2.5%) CA 4 - Ubin Report Revised (5%) CA 5 – Group Oral Presentation (15%) CA 6 – Individual Report (15%) Other tasks, participation (5%) Finals (50%) _________________ CA1 - Personal Statement (2.5%) Deadline: Week 2 Introduce yourself to the prof and staff in a conversational way, telling them about your background in Science, why you took the module, where you want to go etc. _________________ CA 2 - Ubin Report Draft 1 (5%) Deadline: Week 4 After the avian field trip to Pulau Ubin, you’ll write a report about the birds you see there. You can choose what focus to take, as long as it is about the distribution of birds on Pulau Ubin. My group did on the heterogeneity of mangrove specialist vs generalist bird species. It was quite fun, especially if you have Environmental Studies groupmate who would be very passionate about birds. Since it’s the first report and is done with your group mates, there is less pressure. _________________ CA 3 – Extinction Game Quiz (2.5%) Deadline: Week 3? (I forgot) For one of the practical session, you will play an ecology nerdy game called Extinction. It was very fun, plus we were released 2 hours early haha. The quiz opened at night if I remember correctly, so you should do the quiz asap, while the game details are still fresh in your head. Pretty simple questions like what causes species to die out etc, which you will definitely know since it is part of the game. _________________ CA 4 - Ubin Report Revised (5%) Deadline: Week 6 A revision of the draft, also as a group, based on the feedback from your TA and Dr Posa. _________________ CA 5 – Group Oral Presentation (15%) Deadline: Week 11 This has got to be one of the most nerve-wrecking presentations I’ve ever done, due to the 10 minute time limit and lack of cue cards. Depending on which group you are in, the topic will be either the freshwater sampling or terrestrial sampling. For both topics, the question is whether urban forests/waterways are homogeneous. Having to present the intro, methods, results, discussion, future developments and conclusion in 10 minutes was crazy. Personally, I felt that presenting on the freshwater sampling was so much easier (but more tedious due to the number of factors and parameters). The biotic factors for terrestrial sampling included all the diverse types of vegetation. Also, because cue cards are not allowed, memorisation and practice as a group is key. After the 10 minute presentation, a 5 minute Q&A session follow. From experience, being the first few groups to present is better as the audience have not really warmed up yet so the questions tend to be easier to answer. After that, the number and difficulty of questions start to increase. _________________ CA 6 – Individual Report (15%) Deadline: 1 week after presentation, week 12 Page limit: 6 pages (including references) Same topic as the group presentation. Based on feedback from Q&A, TA and Dr Posa, you can edit and change the focus/research question of your topic. As it is individual work, it doesn’t matter if your research questions are different from your group members. Squeezing it onto the page limit was another crazy obstacle, as they included references. So be smart about your sources and use those which you can use to cite for a lot of points. _________________ Other Tasks, participation (5%): Have no idea what this component comprises May be asking questions during the Q&A of the group presentation _________________ Field Trips: Pulau Ubin – Held on Week 2 Saturday early in the morning (pick-up point at 6.15am) to early afternoon. Objective was to spot and identify birds. Freshwater – Ulu Pandan, Pandan Gardens or West Coast. Objective was to collect water samples and do testing for parameters. Terrestrial – Dover forest, Bukit Sedap forest or Kent Ridge Park. Objective was to identify and record down the trees, and measure the abiotic parameters. Half the cohort will go to the freshwater, the other half will go to the forest. The next practical session, they will swap. _________________ Finals : 2 hours Closed book MCQ, structured questions, short essay MCQ tested on the details like calculating the biodiversity index, correct identification of the relevant keywords. Structured questions had questions on explaining the difference between 2 similar concepts (I forgot the rest). Short essay included scenario-based questions such as why it is impossible for so many large creatures to exist in Skull Island, how biodiversity would be affected if we shifted nature spots/jungles to the rooftops etc. Quite interesting. _________________ Comments: Content is easy to understand, fortunately. Webcast should be compulsory for every module. _________________ Expected grade: B+ Actual grade: B- (so unexpected)

Module Review: Overall comments: Well, what a module this was. 7-8 weeks of barely understanding anything before the light came. Breakdown is 30-30-30-10, 30% - class participation and presentation, 30% class work and assignments, 30% final assignment, 10% - for flexibility purposes she said. She deals with abstract concepts and uses scholarly articles to provide framework for discussion and only actually went into the text from week 7/8 onwards. , under Prof Zhang De Qi. Assessment: 5 Homeworks, due every 2 weeks, Prof Zhang has never change them in eons, if you really cant solve them you can refer to seniors' works/suggested answers. 1 midterm exam, tested up till Linear Transformations, tutorial 5. Prof Zhang has probably set the easiest midterm paper in the history of MA2101, close to 15/60 students got 99/100 and above lol. There is, however, an interesting 50% of the class who can score below 60/100 which firmly secures the bottom half of the bell curve. Final exam, 1 two-sided cheatsheet and calculator allowed. It covers all the lecture content, Prof Zhang does not give less emphasis on materials covered in the midterms, every topic is tested with equal weightage in the finals. Overall impression: I got full marks for every homework assignment and 99/100 for midterms, hence the distinguishing factor for A/A+ would be the finals. I was struggling a lot in the last 2 chapters, particularly on Jordan Canonical Forms and Inner Product Spaces, because I couldn't find an intuitive way of understanding those 2 long chapters that spanned close to 100 pages. Prof Zhang presents the concept of Inner Product Space in the way where he goes through the idea of Bilinear Forms, then narrowing down to inner product space, then introducing different properties of inner product spaces and linear transformations. The entire portion on Bilinear Forms can actually be ignored, it only serves to confuse the reader with irrelevant abstract concepts. Basically, the inner product space is a bilinear form with an added positivity property, that's about all you need to know about Bilinear Forms. Prof Yang Yue also has his own set of notes and explains the concepts of Jordan Canonical Form and Inner Products in a more intuitive and less technical way, which is useful in seeing the grand scheme of things after going through Prof Zhang's notes. Please do go through them to grasp the content, it helps in understanding the content better and helps in tackling seemingly abstract finals problems. After attempting a few finals paper, I realised that the main challenge wasn't the complexity of the problems, most problems are either definition questions or quite trivial given sufficient practice. However, the main challenge was to complete 7-8 problems within 2 hours. Due to the vast amount of content, it is close to impossible to document everything onto a 2-sided cheatsheet, thus one has no choice but to understand the content thoroughly and have a working knowledge of it at the back of your mind. Thus, it is imperative to hone your knowledge and get all the exam techniques up on your fingertips. Once you have that and a well-crafted cheatsheet, it shouldn't be too hard to tackle the finals paper. Expected grade: A

Many people are taken aback by the first chapter (limits, especially epsilon-delta proofs) so it is recommended to keep pace with the module and consistently work on the tutorial questions, like most math modules. There are also take-home assignments which are made to be tricky and lengthy, so do allocate enough time to work on it and discuss with friends. There are also lab sessions every other week but these are a joke, especially if you have coding experience, and are ultimately useless throughout the module except for the Lab Quiz. It still is possible to skip lectures for those with university-level mathematics background. Otherwise, it is highly important to go to lectures as Dr Wang is really good at explaining concepts and showing how to think in order to solve the equation, without referring to his notes. By Prof Leher Singh What is it about? You will learn about recent research and controversies about the advantages/disadvantages of bilingualism. How’s the workload? One 3-h seminar style lecture a week + readings. 10% class participation, Prof caters time after every class for discussion and class-sharing 30% Midterm, 25% Commentary essays, 35% finals. How *difficult is it? Best not to think in terms of module difficulty - Your experience in the module is better determined by your interest in the topic. [Below are my thoughts on that is covered in this module, by themes] Psychology of Bilingualism is part-Linguistic, part-Developmental psychology, part-Neuroscience, and part-Social Psychology. 1) This course will cover basic linguistic concepts like Morphemes, Plosive-consonants, Syntax rules in English (and other languages). Content will be taught in the course, but it is beneficial to have a working knowledge beforehand. 2) Bilingualism research is mostly on children (til adolescent). Course content will cover auditory/verbal milestones in infant and childhood development. Later lectures will cover effect of bilingualism in older adulthood. [I did NOT take PL3234 before this module, I did not have any difficulties keeping up.] 3) Models of bilingualism will include models of attention, brain bases, and cognitive processing limitations/bottlenecks. Course content will draw on research that utilize these models and apply them in experimental settings. 4) Bilingualism is collinear with other social phenomenon like immigration upper-class (*seems opposing, i know). Part of the module will be identifying and teasing out the influence of social psychology on the advantages/disadvantages of bilingualism. How is the Prof? Prof S. is a BEAST. She is well-read on the topic, up-to-date with current literature, and active in her own research. She knows the course content inside and out. Her teaching style encourages discourse over "vomitting-knowledge". She prepares interesting prompts for class discussions and will take on additional questions from the students. She is approachable after class and online. Always on time with uploading of lecture resources. Should you take it? If any of the above points, or a combination of them, intrigues you. Or if you are unsure where to go, but looking for a good educator. I encourage you to take this module. Midterm/ Exam tips [When I took the module, it was entirely MCQ. A plus point for some students, i know :) But that means the bell-curve is skewed, as well. ] Conclusion: I enjoyed myself thoroughly in this module. Also, I learnt things that I bring with me into everyday conversations. Grade obtained: B+

(another covid sem) under Prof Cindy Ng Content: The content is as outlined and described in Saad Haider 's review below, and won't be repeated here. I would again echo the point that this is a really beautiful module content wise . A couple more bits of interesting information I learnt to illustrate the point: - Why sunrise / sunset timings vary across the year - Why a "blood moon" occurs during a lunar eclipse - Why auroras occur - Various types of telescopes - Why (and that) Uranus's axial tilt is almost perpendicular to that of other planets - Feasibility and proposals for colonization on some celestial bodies (e.g. Venus, Mars, Titan, Europa) - Numerous takes on various astrological phenomena across many cultures Workload: Weekly Quizes (10%) - These are more of "attendance check" mcq / mrq quizzes. There are total of 12 quizzes, and only the best 10 are counted toward the final score. Scoring full marks is a breeze provided you attend the lectures dilligently. Each takes just about 5-15 minutes to complete. Video Project (25% - 5% participation evaluation, 15% content, 5% presentation) - The task is to pick a recent news piece (going back as far as half a year before the semester) and elaborate on the news, science, and culture aspects of it in a 8-9 minutes video. My group covered the great conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn in 2020 for example. - This is the bulk of the workload for this module, which is still very manageable, provided your team (of 2 / 3) starts early in the semester and works consistently. I took about 24 hours in total for this (50% video editing, 50% researching), which can vary depending on your grade expectations and aims. Video Critique (15%) - Simply involves viewing the videos from 7 other project groups and doing a short writeup on the content / presentation aspects of each. Dosen't take too long. Astrophotograph (10%) - Involves taking a "photograph of a celestial object / phenomenon" and doing a short writeup (photo + selfies + methodology) on it. Grading is partly based on creativity, although, I would guess that it is a very small portion as many of us only have phone cameras (see below). - If you are an expert photographer with dslr / telescopes, there are many, many options here. (e.g. the moon rabit, Jupiter, Saturn, Mars, .......) - If you are an amateur photographer with only phone cameras, this is still very doable, but your options would be limited. I simply went with the introductory lecture's suggestion of creating a collage of the Sun path across the semester. Two term tests (40%) - These are 75% mcq / mrq, and 25% open ended questions. - The content across the two tests are not repeated, which really helps with the amount of content in this module. The first test covers the first half of the module's content, while the second covers only the latter half. - These are fairly "crammable" provided you have paid attention in lectures consistently . Delivery: There are no webcast recordings, and if this trend follows there should be no webcasts in a non-covid semester as well. Some things highlighted there (mostly from student clarifications) are not mentioned in the slides, and can help clarify your doubts, so paying attention in lectures pays off. The delivery itself isn't spectacular but comfortably lands above average (your experience may vary). However, the content is really so interesting that it really shouldn't matter regardless of your perception. Contest with physics majors: Being a computing major, I came into the module a little apprehensive that physics majors would have an advantage, but that is really not the case . The explanations revolve around very easily understandable layman terms and intuitive explanations. The formation of the solar system for example, references a video of ice-skating to illustrate the conservation of angular momentum. A basic intuitive understanding of motion and gravity would do. The open ended questions in term tests (which are already 75% mcq / mrqs) also do not expect overly technical answers. Expected Grade: A- / A Final Grade: A+

Lecturer: A/P Chin Chee Whye Taken in 16/17 Sem 2 Weightage: Assignment 48% Midterm 16% Finals 36% Took this module to try-out SPM. Typically in blocks of 3 hours lecture, what you see is what you get on the timetable. No 'tutorials' per se because tutorials are integrated into lectures and he only spend times discussing material from text. There are no 'tutorial questions' allocated, only homework and style of lesson is roughly like MA1100 if you've done the module under him. Generally class size is small (my year was around 14) and can vary, so I suspect the grades for module is most likely not moderated. Course is divided roughly to 6 parts: 1. (Ordered) Fields and other preliminaries 2. Sequences 3. Construction of the Real and Properties 4. Series and various convergence tests 5. Continuous functions and properties 6. Introduction to Topology (Not really examinable but you can use concepts from topology in exam) Some parts of the course material can be dry. I often lose attention and focus. But otherwise most mathematical proofs are not entirely foreign and not difficult follow. It's good to review and revise the proofs that he produced (on the spot, hand written, A for affort) during discussion after lectures. I believe the whole point of the module (or rather of Prof Chin) is to let us learn about the whole business of analysis and more importantly, various concepts fundamental to analysis, minus the limited scope/lenses of analysis. What are the behaviours endowed to fields of with different properties? How do we extend meaning of continuity to a general context? How do we extend the meaning of continuity to other functions that are necessarily real valued? There is also an emphasis on utility for why certain concepts are developed as opposed to others. He does not go through homework questions during lecture unless requested because I think he trusts that we know what went wrong and fix it? That being said, homework questions are not impossible, just need to think carefully sometimes. Midterm questions are tough. There are no 'standard calculation questions' (i.e. showing convergence for a particular type of sequence etc.) and I think at least one or two question requires uses result (not entirely trivial) from your homework. Heuristics is important but I believe he also wants us to present the solutions rigorously. So be warned! Did quite badly for Midterms despite given 8 questions in 2.5 hours. On other hand finals is rather easy; 6 questions in 2 hours. I think only 1 question is regurgitation (reproduce the proof that the alternating harmonic series is convergent), otherwise other questions can be challenging but still considered 'humane' by his standards. Past year papers generally vary in difficulty and types of questions. But in general, I think depending on how your lecturer wants to teach the module and the pedagogical goals he wants to achieve, the types of question would be different. So doing PYP might get you super demoralised or happy, but it will not be a good gauge for your performance in your finals.

If you have any questions, please send it to my email atqhteo@gmail.com. Don't worry, there are no stupid questions! I've received many emails asking me all sorts of questions. I reply all of them :) What is it about? The title says it all - the module goes through a large variety of topics such as memory, learning, intelligence, developmental psych, abnormal psych, etcetc. If you have interest in how the brain works and what human behaviour is like, this is a module for you. How's the workload? The textbook is a monster - it was 800++ pages in total. (excluding references + appendix) Readings every week are usually one chapter, though you may have to read more in some weeks. Each chapter is about 40-60 pages. Do note that the textbook may change every sem(or year?) so it may be different. There is one mid term paper (which you know the topic from about week 3 or 4, and is due about week 8?), a 100 MCQ mid term test, and a 100 MCQ + 5 short essay finals. (both closed book) One 2h lecture per week (should be 6-8pm on monday as always) and one 2h tutorial fortnightly How difficult is it? The readings sound like alot but they are really not that bad. Firstly, the information is generally interesting to read and are not dry readings like journal articles. Next, there are many experiments and examples to aid your understanding, so it is not as long as it seems. The textbook is pretty easy to understand so there shouldnt be any problems here. The exams are almost entirely memory-based - if you are able to memorize the textbook from the first to last page, you will very likely get a close-to-perfect mark. That said, understanding the concepts is quite important (versus just memorizing definitions) as the MCQs like to rephrase certain terms and see if you can pick the correct definition. Do try to read every thing from the textbook and remember the gist of everything, because they will test everything. Miscalleneous Tips This is one module in which you cannot fall behind in your readings - everything snowballs really quickly. Also, it's all about remembering everything, so ideally try to read your textbook at least twice over. Making a summary sheet for every chapter REALLY helps in revision. Also, get started on your mid term essay early since they release the topic so early. The topic was fairly straightforward for this semester, not sure about future sems. Lectures are an absolute waste of time, I stopped going for lectures in the second half of the semester. All they do is regurgitate what is stated in the textbook, and do a rushed job (because realistically all the content cannot be covered within a short 2hr lecture) Tutorials are boring as well, but I guess it depends on which TA you get. No tutorial participation, so go ahead and switch off during tutorials :p Should you take it? A content heavy mod and should be balanced accordingly with whatever else you are taking. Not difficult at all to score if you have the time to keep up with readings. Known to be one of the most interesting exposure mods, and psychology is always interesting to read about. Go ahead and try it!

Taken in AY15/16 Semester 1 Lecturer: Dr. Ben Blumson Grading - Term paper (50%), Finals (50%) Content - The first half of the module was about existence; what exists and what they are like. Parts, numbers, properties, possible worlds, and sets were discussed. The second half of the module was about identity. Theories discussed included mind-body identity, necessity of identity, composition as identity, endurantism, perdurantism, essentialism, and theories of personal persistence. Lectures - 2-hour lectures (not webcasted), once per week. Dr. Ben does a good job explaining lecture material, making use of everyday examples to illustrate his points. He seems rather quirky but he is deeply knowledgeable about metaphysics. The lecture notes typically contain only the main points of the lecture (and on some weeks, no lecture notes were provided at all), so one needs to pay close attention during lectures to avoid missing out on important information. Tutorials - 1-hour tutorials, once per week. The tutor was also Dr. Ben. The style of the tutorial varied from week-to-week as he tried to find ways to enhance learning (there was even one week when he organised an impromptu debate between students). There was no attendance-taking, but I do recommend attending his tutorials as he often discussed things which were relevant but weren't discussed during lecture. Workload - There was only 1 assignment (the term paper) to be completed throughout the semester, so I think the module was rather light. However, there were weekly readings which were somewhat difficult to understand. Some research is probably needed to enhance learning and prepare for finals. Finals - Write 2 essays (only 2 questions provided, so students have to answer both) in 2 hours. The questions were very generic (one on existence, the other on identity). I think decent answers could be provided as long as one paid attention during lectures and tutorials. Module grade: A

They do not help you in any ways in understanding what you need to know to tackle exam questions. They are purely for your reference and interest. There were 3 projects in total. The first was a group project which your group has to research on manufacturing procedure of a product. For example, my group have to find out how to produce ethylcellulose from scratch. From scratch meaning it has to be a starting ingredient that can be bought or easily available. The second project was an extension of the first project and it is done individually. You are assigned a feedstock and you have to design your own procedures (with valid references) to your final product (in my case, ethylcellulose) without incorporation of additional organic material. My feedstock was sugarcane bagasse which is basically cellulose. To make ethylcellulose, the ethyl branch needs to be from my sugarcane as well. Basically I cant just add any ethyl substituents in. Every carbon in product has to be from the feedstock. Last project was a group tutorial presentation. Every group can choose a topic/workshop to and discuss its assumptions/validity. In a nutshell, you are pretty much on your own because the notes are often incoherent and provide very little knowledge to connect topics together. Yet the quizzes and exam questions expect you to see the connection. Unlike normal chemistry modules, this module does not really have a clear defined answer. Everything is debatable as that is the nature of green chemistry, to always improve on existing and there is no clear solution to one problem. Although it would be very different under a different professor, the key takeaway message is that you really need to have interest to read all the references/readings on your own to appreciate and understand the difficulties in green chemistry. Took this module in AY2019/20 Sem 1. This module was taught by Dr Robert and A/P Liou. LSM3244 was a rewarding and unique module. In this module, students will be exposed to a wide breath of topics that include genome editing, CRISPR, GMO and some aspects of immunotherapy. Both lecturers were very approachable. As part of our weekly reflection, Dr Robert provides weekly feedback for all our reflections individually. Moreover, before every lecture, common questions and enquires from the reflections will be summed up and some general comments will be provided. To add on, since it is a small cohort, students are constantly learning from each other during the presentation sessions. In terms of workload, this module was divided into five major components: weekly reflections (10%), field trip reports (10%), critique writing (25%), business plan (35%) and a final CA (20%). Firstly the field trips (total of 3) were tied closely to the lectures covered in the module and we get to interact with industry partners to learn about the different operations in the biotechnology industry. For this semester, Sciex (a spectrophotometer manufacturing plant), NovogeneAIT (a sequencing and bioinformatics lab) and Experimental Drug Developmental Center (a drug discovery and immunoglobin profiling lab) were visited. Secondly, the critique writing consists of a written assignment (15%) and a presentation (10%) on the applications of genome editing (in particularly CRISPR). This assignment was due after the recess week. For this assignment, student need to critically evaluate a research paper and present the findings, strengths and weaknesses to the class. More importantly, since CRISPR is gaining traction and there were many published papers, the presentation session provides a snapshot of the many applications, advancements and the medical potential of the technology. Thirdly, the business plan or a business review. Students were grouped in two (there was one student who did it individually) where they can select anything related to biotechnology to propose a business plan to the class. It was really an eye-opening session as there were many interesting ideas from agriculture, to plastic-degrading microbes to portable devices that can detect drugs in urine. But personally, the highlight was the Q&A session. There were a lot of feedback was provided by both the class and the Profs to help improve our idea before the final report submission. To summarize, this project can be started as early as Week 2 with an executive summary to be submitted after the recess week. However, if groups decided not to do the business plan, a review of the latest and emerging biotech trend can be done. (Pretty unsure how it would change for the coming semesters). Fourthly, the module has a final CA that was conducted on Week 13. The CA was based on the lectures covered and an additional two research papers which will be given weeks before the CA. Even though it was an "open universe paper", it was application-based and the CA really tests on the understanding of the concepts taught during the module. Personally, the CA gets students to think of how problems can be solved in a real-life setting. In sum, this module has a very clear objective on what it wants the students to learn. First, it is a module that emphasizes on application and how one can relate what was covered in the lectures to solve experimental problems. Second, this module exposes students to the science, business and patent application of a biotech idea or product – making it a very comprehensive module. Lastly, the constant feedback provided by the instructors and students will definitely help with identifying personal blind spots. Hence, I can safely say that this module was well-worth the time and it gives another perspective on what a Life Sciences major can offer not only in terms of research but commercially. Note: This module is only on its second run and there will be changes to the curriculum as Dr Robert takes feedback from the previous batch seriously.

Taken in AY 2014/15 Sem 2 Overview: In a nutshell, this module teaches you how to solve various differential equations and linear algebra problems, then applying these techniques to solve actual problems in the real world (albeit their simplified versions). As the reviews below mine note, the problem-solving and mathematical modelling skills acquired from this module form part of the core competencies required to tackle future engineering (or for my case, physics) modules. If you hated MA1505, here’s some good news: with interconnected topics, less abstract content, and plenty of applications, this module is much more interesting than MA1505. Most people will enjoy this module both for its relevance to engineering topics and the uniquely engaging way it is taught; or if not, at least find it less of a bitter pill to swallow. ________ Syllabus: 1. Ordinary Differential Equations (Separable, first-order, second-order linear) 2. Applications of ODEs 3. Population Modelling 4. Laplace Transform 5. Matrices 6. Linear Transformations 7. Systems of First-order ODEs 8. Partial Differential Equations The format of MA1506 is very similar to MA1505. With all the materials uploaded to IVLE, most people don’t attend lectures and tutorials, preferring to watch webcast lectures and refer to the worked tutorial solutions and PYPs instead. There is also a lab component where you learn how to use MatLab over four sessions in the latter half of the semester. As these are optional, I did not go for any of them, so I can’t give any useful info on this. Apparently it used to form part of the assessment, but has since been removed (probably so Chem engin people don’t gain an unfair advantage?). ________ Assessment: 20% Mid-term: Only Chapter 1 is tested. 80% Final Exam: Entire syllabus tested, 1 A4-sized double-sided help-sheet allowed. MA1506 uses the exact same mode of assessment as MA1505, with 10 MCQs in 1 hour for the mid-term, and 8 x 2 = 16 questions for the final. The difficulty varies very little between semesters; most are cookie-cutter type questions, which you should be able to ace by doing your PYPs, but there are always those couple of questions which require you to think out of the box, to differentiate those who really know their stuff. ________ Teaching Staff: Lecturer: A/Prof Fred Leung Pui Fai Prof Leung was the lecturer for my lecture group (Group B). You may know him as the module coordinator from MA1505, and some of you may have been taught by him before. He took two lecture slots (A & B) for this semester. He is a decent lecturer who has had quite a lot of experience teaching, he’s been in NUS more than three decades if I’m not wrong. He speaks with a Hong Kong accent which is pretty funny at times, but it gets in the way of comprehension, and I often had to concentrate hard to catch his words. He uses his own handwritten notes to supplement the ones by the module coordinator (more on him later), and it’s clear that he knows the content through and through. Maybe too much, however, as he tends to skip steps when doing calculations, often losing slower students (like myself) who are unable to see the missing link(s). Webcasted lecturer: Prof Brett McInnes I was playing around with the webcast menu, wondering where lecture group C’s lectures were, when I stumbled upon Prof McInnes’ Sem 1 lectures. It turned out to be the best thing that’s happened to me in the module. Prof McInnes is, hands down, one of the best (and coolest) lecturers in NUS. Watching his lectures is like watching a Hollywood movie. Not a bad analogy, considering that he once showed us a clip of Lord of the Rings to illustrate the mathematical modelling of warfare. How many of you can say you’ve seen something like that in your math class? J He has some sort of magical ability to keep your attention throughout his entire lecture (which is on math, that’s saying something). He is able to explain things in a succinct manner and make it entertaining at the same time. He often uses online resources, such as applets, to illustrate certain topics, which greatly helped me to visualize the math involved. As the module coordinator, he created all the lecture notes and tutorials. In both, he does his best to minimize the tedium of the mathematics by dreaming up various imaginative scenarios where your newly acquired knowledge can be put to use. Some examples include gambling in RWS, Angelina Jolie fandom, and let’s not forget about his favourite Shakespearian couple, Romeo and Juliet. My only regret is not being able to join his lecture group so I can nominate him for the teaching awards he deserves. ________ Personal Experience: I felt that I was much better prepared for this mod compared to MA1505. Firstly, I finally understood the importance of spamming past year papers, which was exactly what I did for both the mid-term and final exam, to astonishing results. Second, I attended nearly all lectures and webcasted a different lecturer during my revision to refresh my memory. Lastly, the great number of applications used to illustrate concepts just made everything easier to grasp and understand. While I believe that most people do better in MA1506 (and thus a steeper bell curve), it still holds true that because of the enormous class size and standardized format of testing, this is one of those modules where you are almost guaranteed an A if you do your due diligence.

Took this in AY19/20 Sem 1 under Dr Chin Chuan Fei This is a really interesting module offered by the Philosophy department. Highly recommended! The module is split into 4 main topics (inequality, meritocracy, multiculturalism and migration). On top of that, different approaches to examining social issues were taught. Content The pace of this module is very manageable in allowing us to dive deep into these "very Singaporean" themes that we often take for granted. Dr Chin also made it a point to clarify some concepts to any potential foreigners. In my tutorial class, there were quite a few foreign exchange students too so not to worry if you are one. Workload In terms of workload, it is quite manageable as well. Before lecture, you are required to finish the assigned reading of the week (the readings are quite straight forward too). During the lectures, Dr Chin will extract out the important parts of the reading and separate into their individual headers which makes it even clearer for those who are not used to doing readings. Assessment 20% 4xReading quizzes Alternates between this and journal entries every week. It is 5 MCQ about that week's reading. The page numbers are also provided so you just need to read through those pages that he specified to answer the question. It would be much easier to do it with other people too since the bel curve is usually quite steep for this. 20% 4xJournal entries It is a 500 words entry that you can write about anything that relates to the topic of that week. Pretty easy and you can just write whatever come to your mind. 30% Group project Pick a social issue that illustrates inequality in Singapore. Make sure that you pick an issue that your groupsmates are interested in and you should be fine. Dr Chin is not really picky on the aesthetics of the slides, having interesting insights would be more important. 30% Final exam (20 MCQs, open book) Same format as the reading quizzes and that it is open book so make sure you bring ALL the readings. Pretty unenvironmental but it is necessary! Final grade: A

AY 17/18 Sem 2 Lecturer: Prof Dinh Tien Cuong 20% Homework (5 sets to be completed every fortnight) 20% Midterm 60% Finals Content: Module split into two halves: first half focuses on the elephant in the room, Complex analysis, which is the study of holomorphic functions (which a whole lot nicer than real differentiable functions) and the second half is an introduction into Riemann surfaces. This course under Prof Dinh is really difficult for 2 main reasons: the entire complex analysis part of the module is squeezed into the first 6 weeks, which can be horrendous given that it is our first time studying complex analysis and also we spent first 2-3 weeks reviewing topology. Secondly, Riemann surfaces are not exactly the easiest things to study as an undergrad; to have a good grasp of it requires many areas of Mathematics: Complex Analysis (duh), Manifolds, Geometry, Topology, Group Theory. Its not easy trying to put everything together. So be warned! Lecture pace is really quick so you need to do a lot of revision so as to not fall behind (I fell behind quite often and I totally gave up for Riemann surfaces). Prof Dinh is a lecturer that focuses more on the big picture of the proof rather than the nitty gritty technicalities so I guess in some sense it is good because it helps to develop some intuition as to why certain results are true. Tutorial: Tutorials are not easy. But they contain many useful tricks and results essential to the study of complex analysis and Riemann surfaces respectively. The questions are not important but the way of thinking and proving are more essential than what is presented. Tests/Exams: Thankfully, Prof Dinh is quite merciful when it comes to exam/tests. Computational question usually comes out for exams and usually only 1/2 questions will be really difficult. Prof Dinh is also very lenient with his allocation for marks (even homework) I think its one of the few modules that you have to work hard consistently because it is very fast paced and the content is difficult. I think the end results can be rewarding but then again if you have no interest in learning Riemann surfaces, perhaps the iteration of S-mod under Prof Dinh is not suitable for you.

Low Kok Lim seems to care a lot about the learning outcome of the students and his lectures are super fun and interesting. GET1024 AY2017/18 Sem 2: Way too technical for a GET module. I highly recommend you do NOT take this module unless you LOVE physics, or have REAL interest in nuclear and radiation. The lectures are generally very boring since they are too technical. While Prof Chung tries his best to make his lectures more understandable, the technicality is too deep. There are midterms and a pre-finals (before Reading Week), both of which feature questions that are too focused on certain content, sometimes even content that is too trivial. Sometimes I'm not sure whether to advise you to study for it, since the content is way too much. (And you probably have other modules which are more important) There is also a group project where you must write an ~3k word report and ~3min video on any topic relevant to nuclear and/or radiation. This holds a large percentage of your grade so try to get it done well. It's hard to gauge how well you might do because the group project is way too freestyle. There are also tutorials which do count as participation so long you attend. These tutorials generally cover midterm and finals questions, so it may be useful. Other participation marks include doing in-lecture surveys, so do attend the lectures. I attended probably less than half the lectures and skipped almost all the tutorials. I missed my video submission deadline although Prof Chung was kind enough to give me an extension with penalty. I solo-ed the whole project since I couldn't find any teammates. I really wasn't expecting to pass this module at all though I'm glad I did so that I do not have to retake GET pillar.

Took this module in Semester 1 of AY15/16 under Dr. Vik Gopal. The mid-term and final allows for one double-sided A4 cheat sheet. Relevant stat tables for normal and t distributions are provided. The content of the lecture is pretty simple and Dr. Vik makes it very intuitive and relatable to life science students. The examples provided are mostly medical-related or (since it was the GE year) elections-related, but he goes through the examples in a very detailed and systematic manner. Vik also more or less explicitly states what he does or does not require you to know for the scope of this module, so it's a large burden off the shoulders especially when it comes to derivation of formulae (most of which don't need to be memorised). All the lectures are webcasted. Tutorials are 1hr but can be skipped or swapped at leisure, since the questions and answers are all posted on IVLE. The tutorials don't do anything more than what the answers do except provide the opportunity to clarify concepts or answers. Most of them are SPSS based and so will require you to use the programme if you're on top of your game and doing these tutorials as they come, but otherwise just waiting for the answers to come out and studying them to understand the concepts is sufficient. Tutorials are not graded. There are also weekly IVLE quizzes which must be taken as they account for a large portion of the grades excluding the mid-term and final tests. These quizzes have no time limit which makes referencing your notes easy. Again, the module is more concept-oriented. Vik also provides self-assessment quizzes with the explanation of answers immediately after submission, of whih the questions are usually relevant to the graded quizzes, so it is useful but not essential to do them before taking the quizzes. While the module is relatively easy, the bell curve is incredibly steep, even for a cohort of 600-ish people. Maximise the marks that you get doing the IVLE quizzes if you want to be on the top end of the curve, which would make much more sense after reading this module. :) Also, protip: don't sit at the back of the LT. Vik likes the use the handwriting function and has the tendency to write stuff obstructed by the panels on the ceiling. Of course you could always review the webcasts but you could just avoid the trouble in the first place, or just watch the webcasts and not go for the lectures at all.

Semester taken: AY19/20 Sem 2 If you're looking to fulfil your GES requirement or take a UE while simultaneously ticking off your SJW bucket list, look no further. With less balance than a punch-drunk lightweight after twenty pirouettes, the course material and its presentation during lectures appears (to me at least) designed to steer young minds towards various inexorable anti-establishment conclusions. As a politically neutral third year who had completed the 8-MC LC2007 Constitutional & Administrative Law module not too long ago, I was triggered to no end by the relentless use of pejoratives coupled with snide remarks during the lectures while course material was being taught. Constitutional and statutory provisions were cited only partially - in one particularly egregious case, different subsections from different sections in the statute were copied (without section numbering of course) onto consecutive slides, then labelled as something like "what the law says". Offence-creating provisions in the Defamation Act were presented without any mention of possible statutory defences. The cherry-picking list goes on. For a course that purports to discuss important freedom of speech issues, it neglects to even touch on the institutional separation of powers and other basic constitutional issues, as well as engage foundational moral/political justifications, all of which provide the necessary context for any freedom of speech discussion. Granted, these issues might not be suited for a level-1000 module. But doesn't that make it all the more dangerous to provide students with such flimsy and one-sided material, knowing that this will heavily influence their future political views? The illusion of knowledge is more dangerous than ignorance. Admin-wise, it was a shit show of the highest order. Graded assignments (scrapbook article commentaries) were supposed to be marked and returned before the next one was released/due (there were about 4) to allow students to incorporate feedback, but the first was only returned some time after the final one was released. The midterm take-home essay instructions were changed drastically a week after the initial release: the maximum word limit was changed to a minimum word count. Having already completed the assignment, I had to scramble to unpack my heavily-condensed essay into a full-length one. Clarifications and additional instructions came piecemeal, replete with glaring spelling and grammatical errors. I have never seen a more incompetent course coordinator in my life. Thankfully, tutorials cover content wholly separate from lectures. My tutor, Ms Farah, was pretty solid and attempted to facilitate candid discussions, but was sadly limited by the 45 minutes of contact time per week. Her tutorials were for the most part really engaging and made up somewhat for the lectures. Overall, this course is great for preaching and pretending to discuss stuff you don't actually know enough about to engage meaningfully. Unless you're a senior law student or have a keen interest in constitutional issues and have read up extensively enough on the same to see through the disingenuous lecture presentations. Then you won't end up echoing the political views the rest of the unwitting students have been manipulated into forming. You'll just get tilted real hard and end up writing a scathing NUSMods review. PSA for the law students thinking of taking this course: if you're ok with shitty assignment instructions and can hold in the tilt, TAKE THIS MOD. The entire course content, readings and slides combined, is something like 10% of one single topic in LC2007. I shit you not. There is ZERO new material so you have to study absolutely nothing. If you want an easy A/A+ just parrot the political views pushed here, don't be me and take the path of most resistance by flaming the examiners by picking apart the essay questions and calling the phrasing "disingenuous" in your response. For everyone else thinking of taking this mod, be warned: take everything your learn here with about as much salt as there is in the Salar du Uyuni. There ARE very valid and important points raised, but their presentation is incredibly one-sided. Side note: I was alerted by some people that my review was taken down after I posted it. The irony is not lost on me but here's a repost. Update: this is repost number 2.

Semester: 2020-2021 Sem 1 Lecturer: Lee Gim Hee General review: This module is tough, but rewarding at the same time. The concepts are very math heavy and can be hard to understand (especially those taught in the latter lectures), but it is obvious that Prof. Lee Gim Hee is extremely passionate about the subject, and he is very good at explaining the concepts in a clear way (at least as clear as possible). Especially if you are doing research in the ML field, I think this module will be a big help. Just be prepared to put in some work to understand the concepts. Assignments (4 * 15%): For each assignment, we had to implement some algorithm(s) we had been taught in the lectures and write a 1-page report on our implementation. In general it was quite easy, mostly just following pseudo-code for the lectures with the main job being to figure out which indices were the correct to multiply together. Most students scored top marks in these or very close to top marks. In general, I found the assignments fun to do and they helped cement my understanding. Quizzes (2 * 20%): The quizzes were quite brutal. The average score for the first quiz was 25/40 marks and for the second it was 13/40 marks. They require you to understand the concepts deeply. Due to the shift to online test assessment, Lee Gim made the questions much harder than previous years. I personally found it quite discouraging to study previous exam questions a lot, only for the final questions to look nothing like the problem sets we had seen before, especially for quiz 2. I prefer the tests where there is a mix of medium and hard questions so the excellent students can still show they are excellent, while the average students also get to demonstrate they at least know something. Here, you were destroyed if you were not brilliant. In the end though, Gim Lee was very lenient in the marking (I got a few points for quiz 2 I am not sure were deserved), and the poor class average score made it such that you would get saved by the bell curve. Expected grade: B+ Final grade: A- If you are very good at math, I agree with a previous reviewer that A+ should probably not be too difficult.
