AY19/20 Semester 1 module review here:

. Taught by Dr Alioto and Dr Chua. Expected Grade: A Actual Grade: A+ Digital Design is a compulsory mod for all Electrical Engineering and Computer Engineering students in Year 1. The bulk of the module focuses on logic gates and the design of digital systems such as finite state machines. Additionally, there is significant focus on Verilog, a Hardware Description Language. Other than the midterm and end of semester quizzes, there is a project component where we had to program an FPGA with a voice scope module. There is no final exam for this module. While midterms were generally considered by many to be easy, the 'finals' were extremely thorough in the content being tested, with excellent knowledge of the lecture materials being a prerequisite to even complete the paper. The FPGA project (which was around Week 9-11) was extremely fun and fulfilling, as the open-ended component allowed for much creativity. Verilog is an extremely restrictive language (as compared to Python/C, which the EE/CEG students are familiar with), and the project encourages students to learn more about the language and do more with it despite all its quirks and limitations. Dr Alioto and Dr Chua are extremely competent lecturers that are aided by competent teaching staff, with a special mention going to my TA Christopher, who was able to explain the tutorial and lab questions clearly and methodologically. The ease of Quiz 1 and the general creativeness for the open-ended project made me worry that the bell curve would be too steep, but Quiz 2 provided to be differentiating enough for these worries to be partially quelled. All in all, this module, while compulsory, is a fulfilling and interesting module that helped me appreciate the underlying designs of basic and more complex digital systems.

Semester Taken: AY13/14 Sem 2 Lecturer: Prof Juzar Motiwalla, Prof Wong Weng Fai, Prof Pete Kellock The course consists of 5 assignments constituting 30%, 20% class participation and 50% final project. The assignments were fun to do and didn't take up too much time. We had to review TechCrunch Disrupt finalists' ideas, generate our breakthrough ideas using the Big-W framework (a very useful idea generation framework), do a patent review exercise and a simple exercise on storytelling. For the final project, together with my friends from CS3217, we built Pomoc, a customer feedback service that mobile app vendors can integrate into their existing mobile applications. We would get useful feedback regarding our ideas which helped us polish it up. Next, I will go through the various aspects of the class. People - There were only 11 students in the class and the students were well selected and all were competent, which the insightful comments brought up made every class interesting and engaging. However, I wonder if the course can actually be scaled to accept more students when evidently, we were running short on time for many of the classes even though we only had 6 teams. It is a useful class for students interested in entrepreneurship and the trend is that an increasing number of students are paying more attention to startups and wanting to found their own startup. Hence I would encourage my peers and juniors to join this class. The course instructors were also very helpful throughout the course, with each of them having expertise in related fields. Prof Juzar and Pete were experts in startups and the experience they shared with the class was extremely insightful. Personally I enjoyed attending the two review sessions as I received helpful comments from the instructors and I took effort in implementing them so as to improve the product. Content - I found the BIG-W particularly useful as I am always interested in new ideas. In fact, I used the BIG-W approach to come up with the idea for Pomoc, to integrate live chat customer support into mobile apps. Also, after I learnt about BIG-W, I observed that that was how many successful startups came about. Hence, BIG-W is definitely an approach worth learning and adopting. I would try to adopt BIG-W in the generation of ideas for my future projects. Variety - It was good that product validation was allowed to be done via many approaches (prototyping, mockups, surveys, interviews, etc) to accommodate the lack of technical competency in the groups. In our final project presentations, we saw a variety of validation methods and it was an eye-opener for me as all of these would be useful for validating real products if we were to startup in the future. The storytelling session was also fun to attend because we saw many different approaches that the teams took to tell their story: Comics, videos, animations. I liked the variety and dynamic content that the course and its students offered. Homework - The amount of work given to us was reasonable and each deliverable’s deadlines were also mentioned to us in the first lecture so that we could manage our schedule well. I appreciate that very much. Structure - The flow of the course was very clear, from idea generation, to patents, then storytelling and validation. These are the steps that a real startup would have to go through. Hence the structure was realistic and reflective of real-life situations. In the end, Prof Juzar recommended me to pitch my project for VasCo grant. We didn't pitch in the end because not all of us had the time to pursue the project after the module. It was a great experience nonetheless. Grade: A+

Lecturer: Steven Halim PLEASE DO NOT TAKE THIS MODULE!!!! As the module title suggests, the purpose of this module is solely to train you for various programming competitions. Lectures: Every lecture begins with a 75 minute mini contest, which is worth 3% of your module grade. After that, the undergrad TA will go through the solutions. The second half of the lecture is centered around a topic written in the lecturer’s book CP3, which everyone in the module is required to buy. During the lecture, the lecturer often asks questions irrelevant and unrelated to the module content such as soccer teams and names of soccer players in exchange for participation marks, which can sometimes be very unfair to the people who have no knowledge about said questions. Homework: Every week, there is a written homework, which is mainly centered around a section of CP3. Students are required to read up on the next lecture’s material and critique and suggest improvements to the book as well as his site visualgo. Each homework is worth 1.5% of your grade. The CP3 textbook explains the required concepts rather poorly and online resources are almost always necessary to understand the required concepts instead. Luckily, there are plenty of good online resources out there. CP3 contains rather little explanation on the algorithms and why they work, as the emphasis is on knowing how to use library code, rather than actually understanding the theory. That being said, the lectures focus on the algorithms, which I find rather strange. Exams: There is no exam for this module, which is replaced by a midterm team contest and a final team contest. Most of the contest is set by the undergrad TA. As such, the lecturer is unable to solve all the problems in the contest, which are usually set by the undergrad TA, so the contest is of considerable difficulty. Hence, the lectures and the lecturer’s book will not help for the preparation of the contest. As the contests are done in teams of 3, usually the strong people will team up with the equally strong people, leading to the average and weak people faring poorly in the contests. Overall: Unless you happen to be someone like “LL” who claims to have a IOI medal (refer to other review), it might be a good idea to not take this module.

I took this module in 16/17 SEM2 with prof. Dilip Raghavan. This module is very interesting. Dr. Dilip is good at explaining the complicated idea of mathematical logic with pictures and examples. Why you should take this module: We have done proofs extensively so far in our study in mathematics (and other subjects as well). Some proofs are derived directly from the axioms, such as the proofs in elementary geometry, but others could be quite tricky, such as the proof of that same number of diamonds of each direction must be used when a hexagon is filled with diamonds, so it is reasonable to try to find a way to base our mathematical proofs on a mechanical set of rules, such that it can be tested without much intelligence involved. A large part of this course involves the study of proofs. This course starts from a mechanical logic language, and then build a relation between such language and mathematical subjects, and then reason about proofs and proof systems. The major takeaway for me is that the meaning of (the existence of) proofs become more clear to me. How to study well: You will find MA3205 Set theory very helpful before taking this module. This module helps a lot if you take CS3234 concurrently. Again, try to do the homeworks, because the homeworks in this module are particularly fun (go and explore yourself). Do not worry about the tests, because dr. Dilip will tell you exactly the exercises you need to prepare for the tests. What you shouldn't do: Do not be philosophical, but be truthful to what you know. Treat proofs as mathematical objects and just do proofs on them intuitively, and you will understand the philosophy once you get familiar with the ideas. Thinking about what it entails of doing proofs on proofs does not help in this module (it could be in future ones?). The most interesting maths module I have taken so far. There are 2 midterms, and that's all for your CA grade (40%). I missed the final exam (so sad), but I think an A grade would be possible if I had attended. ruomu.

Taken in AY 21/22 Sem 1 By Ms. Chua Jon Lin Participation - 10% Weekly Assignments - 20% Project 1 - 10% Project 2 - 30% Project 3 - 30% I want to preface this by saying that I have not had training in classical music. I was not fortunate enough to receive lessons as a child. My first exposure to music was in JC1 when I joined guitar ensemble, and I spent a couple of years after that learning piano with a teacher who only gave me fake sheets for pop music. So I'm an adult learner who can't sight-read. Most of the other students in this class, however, had classical piano lessons as children, barring one lady who I believe was a jazz pianist using her skillfuture credits. I can testify that it's passion and interest that will get you the furthest in this module, even though my interest is in more modern styles of music. This has been my favourite module in NUS so far. It basically teaches you the rudiments of music theory and composition in the framework of the Classical era. Take note that this is big C Classical, so that includes all the quirks of Mozart's and Haydn's time, including the lack of a sustain pedal on the piano. Ms. Chua is a brilliant lecturer. She conveys the concepts with ease and passion. I've personally pestered her a lot after class along with some others, and she was always very eager to answer our questions, and remarked how pleased she was to have inquisitive students. While the module description recommends a familiarity with music theory rudiments, you don't need to have had prior experience with classical repertoire on instruments. As long as you know which note is what on bass and treble clef, what accidentals, major, and minor scales are, and a basic understanding of rhythm notation and common time signatures, you're all set. This is basically less than half an hour's worth of youtube videos. There is no performance component to this module. Compositions are submitted in the form of sheet music, which Ms. Chua will then play on her own piano while marking, or to the class, if your piece is chosen for learning purposes. Weekly assignments are short exercises practicing the week's content. For example, the first few weeks' assignments involved creating five short chord progressions each in block chord form, and labeling them. Each week built upon the last and got progressively more interesting. Project 1 was a review essay of any performance of Classical music of our choosing. Project 2 was to compose a short (~16 bar) parallel period, and Project 3 was a short (~32 bar) composition in binary, rounded binary, or ternary form. The best tip I have is to use as many of the taught concepts as possible in both projects, and don't forget to make them playable, if you're composing away from an instrument ;-) In total, the workload is not super heavy, as Ms. Chua has a very busy life, it seems. The last project was due on the last day of reading week, and there are no midterms or finals. Of course, you can always write more for your assignments and projects, like I did, and give poor Ms. Chua more to mark. :-P But that means more room for mistakes, and I actually ended up with fewer marks for doing so. Oh well. Learned more. Regrettably, my lack of exposure to Classical music all my life was a hindrance when trying to compose music in that style. Both my composition projects were As, but both times I received feedback that they didn't sound super Classical, despite following everything taught in the course. It really boils down to using your ears when you're composing, and when I composed, I suppose my modern sensibilities kept showing through. Other classmates who had spent their childhoods playing/listening to Classical music followed the style much more closely, but their grades weren't necessarily better. :-P In closing, even if you haven't listened to or played much Classical music all your life, you still learn a lot in this course, and it sets up a strong foundation in music theory rudiments that will help with future learning. I'm planning to take YST's placement test in a few weeks to take more advanced modules like MUT3223 (Early Twentieth-Century Music) and MUT3113 (Orchestration) , and the concepts learned here, from what I gather, will be very helpful. Also, much of the knowledge is applicable to many other styles of music. And you can definitely succeed no matter your background, if you have a decent musical sense and a strong love for music. If you're here, take this module. You won't regret it. Expected grade: A-

Taken in AY19/20 Special Term I Taught by: Prof. Boyd Anderson (Lecturer), Goh Ka Hui/Phyo Han (Lab Tutor) Disclaimer: This module was affected by the COVID-19 pandemic, and as a result it may differ significantly from how past/future modules would/will be conducted. Assessment Structure: 22% Lab (10 Labs, first 8 2% each, last 4%) 18% Weekly Quiz (10 quizzes, 2% each) 5% Participation 25% Midterm (Examplify) 30% Final (Examplify) This is a compulsory module to many programmes in NUS. I took it to satisfy my CS minor (which would later be dropped). The module’s topics include abstraction, testability in object-oriented (OO) programming (OOP), substitutability in OO design, interfaces, generics and variance of types, other java constructs, null references, declarative programming withs streams, lazy evaluation, functional programming and asynchronous programming. Parallel streams were introduced in the last chapter but was not tested. Note that all codes are done in Java. There is no textbook of reference. There are no live lessons, with all lectures and lab sessions conducted via Zoom. While lecture and lab attendances are not compulsory, lecture attendance is accounted for when computing a student’s participation score. Lab sessions mainly involve the lab tutors explaining the lab to be done for the week, possibly including some tips on how to solve the problems. They usually do not take the full 1.5 hours. There are also no recitation sessions, but recitation problem sets are distributed approximately after every lecture, each containing about 2-4 problems. Videos explaining the solutions are uploaded to LumiNUS. Additionally, a forum was set up in Piazza (which functions very similarly to StackExchange), where students are allowed to ask and answer questions. The forum participation probably accounts for the bulk of your 5% participation score. There are two labs to be submitted per week (except for first and last, which has only one lab). Their format is similar to the missions in Coursemology for CS1010S/X students – each lab has about 4-6 levels (each level can be seen as a “question”, and usually they are of increasing difficulty), which each level having its own set of test cases. Students are to code their solutions offline then upload the files onto CodeCrunch, where they can check if they have passed all the online test cases after a few minutes (naturally, the test cases given on the question page does not necessarily include all online test cases). In addition, students are required to follow a rather strict coding style (can be checked with a script called ‘checkstyle’) to ensure consistency. If the student’s codes pass all test cases and is consistent with the required coding style, they obtain full credits immediately. Some labs require students to include Javadoc in their codes. Conceptually, this module is not difficult. Most concepts taught are intuitive and easy to pick up, but some topics require additional attention, such as generics and lazy evaluation. Despite so, the heavy amount of CA results in me putting in a lot more time on this module than expected. Most labs can be finished on the day it is released, but there were a couple which took me up to four days. The difficulty lies in knowing how to apply the concepts to solve the problem given in the lab. Dr. Boyd is a very friendly lecturer who is always available to help out his students. He responds to each of students’ questions very patiently and ensures that they understand the concepts. He also lectures well in general, but tend to stutter from time to time (sometimes understandably due to technical issues and possible lack of experience of live Zoom lectures). Furthermore, he tends to rush through some concepts, which I found it hard to follow because I don’t read the lecture notes beforehand. As such, I recommend students to read them before attending. Regardless, I’m glad Dr. Boyd is the lecturer for the module. Midterm and Final were done through Examplify, and were both open internet (communication between students is not allowed). Both follow quite closely to the past CS2030 papers, and they have the same flavour as CS1010S/X papers as well. Midterm was quite difficult, with one question requiring us to design a program skeleton which does not result in cyclical dependency. I scored pretty badly for midterm (slightly above mean/median). However, final was significantly more manageable and I believe I scored close to full marks, which was probably the saving grace to my grade. While students who need this to fulfil their major requirements have no choice but to take this module, I recommend students who have passed a CS1010 module and would like to take more programming modules to take CS2030 as a UE. Expected Grade: A- Final Grade: A

Lecturer: Dr Wu Shangyuan Tutor: Ms Sim Ee Waun Grade: B (S/U-ed) Course Weightage: Class Participation – 20% News Article Pitch – 20% Feature Story – 35% Press Release & Social Media Writing – 25% My biggest disappointment this semester has got to be 'NM2220 - Introduction to Media Writing'. We were taught the theoretical basics of media writing such as: news writing, web journalism, broadcast journalism, photo/video tips, lateral reporting, writing for public relations and advertising. We also touched on topics like ethics and media law. However, in my opinion, this module tried to cover too many things without actual guidance on how to write a news article or craft a press release, which were the main graded components. Coursework wise, as someone who is already working part-time and freelance in the media industry, I felt that this module focused too much on the nitty-gritty that is not an actual representation of the working world. Firstly, we had to do a pitch of 3 stories from one local news article. Sounds simple but the unrealistic guideline was that the angles have to be fresh and original. In the real newsroom, ideas are tweaked slightly from others because those are what get the eyeballs instead!! Next, we had to write a feature story on something interesting about NUS students. Once again, we also had an unrealistic guideline – this time that it has to be 700 words... No feature piece is 700 words in the real world. We also had to take our own pictures but in the newsroom, there are professional photographers for that. Moreover, the marking was rather strict. Lastly, we had to write a press release and several social media captions on a fictitious health campaign. This was okay if not for the fact that the tutorial on press releases was after the assignment deadline so we were basically left in the deep end of the pool. Overall, an unrealistic and poorly organised module. It is better off as two separate modules that go more in-depth – one on basic journalism (news writing) and one on writing for public relations. No wonder they said don't bother with journalism school. Now I know why...

Disclaimer: Tutored for the module last year. Highly biased towards it. Module content: This module covers both implementation and application of data structures + algorithms with equal focus. For any given data structure / algorithm, you are expected to understand/describe: input -> output (what problem it solves) variations on the problems (e.g. converting shortest path to longest path) running time guarantees assumptions made (e.g. distances are positive only) implementation flow (essentially be able to trace a program) pseudocode*. Given a problem, you are expected to be able to combine algorithms you have learnt to solve it (hopefully efficiently). There will be special topics, depending on the lecturer's mood, which will be in the recitations. *Actual programming is limited to problem sets + practical examination. You are expected to be able to read the javadocs (provided in PE) and do stuff without the use of stackoverflow (not provided in PE). Module pacing: Blazing fast and stays that way. We cover CS1020 in about... 2-3 weeks. Primarily because we assume that you will be able to learn java without the lectures. (Your tutors will help you) From memory, there are at least 8 problem sets. Expect to spend at least 4 hours each, but probably closer to 8 (technically it can be done in 30 mins, if you already know everything. But you don't, that's why you are taking the module.). Lecturer: Seth Gilbert - The star of this module. Covers difficult concepts extremely well. Very entertaining. Attend lectures and recitations. He also teaches graduate level (graph, combinatorial and randomized) algorithms, so you can throw anything at him. Cons: Java =( No lambdas yet.

What a horrible, horrendous mod. This might be the most bullshit mod you ever have the privilege of taking in your NUS education. AY19/20, Sem 2. 30% Mission Report A 60% Mission Report B 10% "marksman bonus" Profs: Lu Wei Quan, Yang Lu Here are the things that I've learned: 1. IS1103 violates my natural rights to life, because it is soul-sucking, making it unethical. 2. I have the claim right for NUS to provide me the best possible education, seeing as the school receives tuition fees from students; IS1103 is in clear opposition to this right, and so it is unethical. 3. IS1103 is not ethical under deontology, because it is not logical to force students to take this module. 4. IS1103 is not ethical under contributing to society, because it is clear that work was not done responsibly and ethically. 5. IS1103 is not ethical under the social contract theory; I have sacrificed my freedoms in an attempt to escape my state of nature, but taking this module is arguably worse than the state of nature. 6. IS1103 is unethical under utilitarianism, because my aggregate utility has drastically decreased after taking this module. The entire foundation of this module is frankly horseshit. It's branded as an "ethics" mod, but there's literally nothing applicable to ethics in relation to computer science. So why in god's name is this mod compulsory for SoC students? Why? Here are some examples of the quiz questions that they ask: According to Layer2.txt, it is mentioned that The Pawnbroker relied on Security by Obscurity. Is it ethical or unethical for The Pawnbroker to rely on Security by Obscurity? The correct answer: Under any of the ethical views mentioned in this question's suggested answers, it would be ethical ----------------------------------------------------------------- According to Layer5.txt, it is mentioned that The Pawnbroker relied on Security by Encryption. Is it ethical or unethical for The Pawnbroker to rely on Security by Encryption? The correct answer: It is unethical under Contributing to society ----------------------------------------------------------------- As you saw from Exhibit A, although many organisations require its members to abide by "strong password" policies (eg. use a mix of alpha-numeric and special characters, don't write the password down, use a different password for each website etc.), many of such policies are in fact very difficult to abide by, and if they are abided by, this tends to create difficulties for users in their daily lives (eg. forgetting the password). Is it ethical to have such policies in the first place? The correct answer: It is unethical under all the ethical views mentioned in this question's suggested answers ----------------------------------------------------------------- What kind of nonsensical Q&A is this? Encryption is a contentious subject in the world of ethics, because on the one hand you have people defending its use for privacy, but on the other hand you have people making backdoors to catch criminals or whatever. There is so much depth to a discussion about the ethics of encryption, and yet all we get is some stupid nonsense that it's unethical under contributing to society? What absolute garbage. That's just for the quiz; for the mission reports, the mode of assessment is that we need to justify *THE "CORRECT" ANSWER* of the quiz. Not the answer that you wrote, but the answer THAT THEY GIVE. What kind of backwards teaching methodology requires you to posthumously justify answers that weren't even your own? Did you submit an answer on the quiz that you felt was correct? Well good luck to you, because you have no chance to even begin to justify yourself or your point of view. How bloody ethical. Furthermore, each "justification" can only be a few sentences, because you have to literally write hundreds of them; 4 options per question, 5 ethics questions per quiz, 10 quizzes in total -- you do the math -- spread over reports A and B. I might not have come out of NIE and taken some weird course about "experiential learning" or whatever, but I do know that in the 8000-9000 words required to write out those justifications, we could've had 8-9 long-form essays, which lets people defend and expand -- with rebuttals, counterpoints, and examples -- their viewpoint of ethics. Instead we get this half-assed mode of assessment which benefits nobody except the people marking the answers, because they don't need to use their brains to actually evaluate the arguments made by students. How can you teach a module saying that ethics is up to the interpretation of the individual person, when the entire structure of the module is in such a way that nobody even gets to express their own views? Next there is the "world setup"; it feels like the profs watched john wick over winter break and decided to add artificial drama to the module, which contributed nothing to the students' learning experiences. Maybe if the questions asked about the ethical implications of the fella's actions or something, but instead we just get nonsensical labels like "adjudicators" and "high table" and whatnot applied to the quiz. If you gotta try so hard to make your module seem "cool" to a bunch of 18-20 year old adults, what does that say about your teaching methodology, and the content of the module? Finally, there is the question of the absolutely condescending Lu Weiquan. After a few weeks there were expectedly people rightfully complaining about this module. In response, he sent out an email to all students, "explaining" his motivations with so little tact, and with such a belittling tone to the students, that I really wonder what the intention of that email was. Here's an excerpt -- the email "answered" some "grievances" that students had: 1. In response to the question "Why not just make everything like every other written test/exam that you've ever taken in your Primary/Secondary/JC/Poly/etc school life?" The way the question is phrased already paints a negative picture of the response, but I digress. All these quotes are taken directly from the announcement on luminus. "As IS1103 is an Experiential Learning module, the learning happens when you experience what you need to experience in the module. In other words, unlike other modules / classes / courses that you have taken, in which all the answers can be found in a textbook, Experiential Learning is about finding the answers through your own personal experiences when doing the missions." Indeed, experiential learning means learning through experience. But, I cannot say with a clear conscience that, in the course of this module, i have actually "experienced" anything. How are our personal experiences relevant, when the only mode of assessment tests our ability to retroactively apply frameworks to an already-given answer? ---------------------------------------------------------------------- 2. In response to the question "Why do we need to physically go to places and physically handle stuff? Why so troublesome? Why not make it all online?" his response: "That's a great question, and the answer can be found in Experiential Learning scientific literature. I will not bore you with the details. Instead, I'll simplify it for you by asking you a few questions. First, is it feasible to learn how to ride a bicycle just by reading a book or watching a video about riding bicycles? Second, is it feasible to understand why flipping through a stack of papers is troublesome, as compared to simply doing a Ctrl-F on a keyboard for text search in a word document? Third, is it feasible to understand the difficulties in making ethical decisions if you have never experienced the pain and sweat and hunger and anger and frustration and jealousy and joy and happiness and love that goes into making such decisions in the real world?" What can I say, except that I completely agree? Unfortunately, this is not the reality of IS1103. It is not feasible to learn about riding bicycles by reading a book, just as it is equally impossible to learn about ethics by doing quizzes about contrived scenarios without avenues for creative discourse. Furthermore, I am sure that it can be justifiably unethical under some of the ethical frameworks, to make students flip through papers to essentially "teach them a lesson" that physical data is harder to aggregate than digital data. Also, arguably, students were not asked to make any ethical decisions, so this entire point seems barely relevant. "If you answered yes to any of the three questions stated above, you're not being truthful with yourself, and scientific research backs that up". This translates to: your personal experiences and opinions are invalid, because "scientific research" is never wrong. Is it ethical to be so condescending and dismissive towards a student like that? “Scientific research” or otherwise? ---------------------------------------------------------------------- 3. In response to the question "Why do the missions not seem to be connected with the topic?" "I can assure you that the missions are extremely connected to the topic, it's just that you need to reflect on them to see it. For example, in Mission 1 and 2, Big Data is about the 4Vs (Variety, Veracity, Velocity, Volume), and you indeed encountered a Variety of data types (eg. image vs. text, visual vs tactile, etc), with varying levels of Veracity [accuracy] (blur vs. sharp pictures, useful vs. un-useful data, etc), with different Velocity (walking to some place vs. seeing it on the internet, accessing a file online vs accessing a file physically, different barriers to the information such as the X-ray room in UHC [how to get that information? Ask someone? Search Google? Physically go to UHC to find it?]), and with varying Volume (the amount of information you get when you are walking from place to place vs. the amount of information you get by just reading the text), these are all examples of how you have experienced Big Data" I struggle to see how obtaining 5 pieces of contrived information, nor flipping through a stack of papers, constitutes big data. First of all, there was no explanation on what big data was supposed to be, in the context of this module. As one of the latest internet buzzwords, it seems that this module has taken it upon itself to introduce another interpretation of big data, in this case, "meaningless data". Perhaps it would be more effective for students to be able to "reflect on" the missions, *after* having the concepts and implications of "big data" explained to them -- would it not? ---------------------------------------------------------------------- In summary, his statements are frankly dismissive and condescending of students' experiences, and gives students the impression that their concerns are simply invalid. Is this the way that professors are supposed to respond to student feedback? See? Straight from the horse's mouth. Unbelievably condescending and dismissive. In summary: literally the biggest bullshit mod ever.

Semester taken: AY19/20 Sem 2 If you're looking to fulfil your GES requirement or take a UE while simultaneously ticking off your SJW bucket list, look no further. With less balance than a punch-drunk lightweight after twenty pirouettes, the course material and its presentation during lectures appears (to me at least) designed to steer young minds towards various inexorable anti-establishment conclusions. As a politically neutral third year who had completed the 8-MC LC2007 Constitutional & Administrative Law module not too long ago, I was triggered to no end by the relentless use of pejoratives coupled with snide remarks during the lectures while course material was being taught. Constitutional and statutory provisions were cited only partially - in one particularly egregious case, different subsections from different sections in the statute were copied (without section numbering of course) onto consecutive slides, then labelled as something like "what the law says". Offence-creating provisions in the Defamation Act were presented without any mention of possible statutory defences. The cherry-picking list goes on. For a course that purports to discuss important freedom of speech issues, it neglects to even touch on the institutional separation of powers and other basic constitutional issues, as well as engage foundational moral/political justifications, all of which provide the necessary context for any freedom of speech discussion. Granted, these issues might not be suited for a level-1000 module. But doesn't that make it all the more dangerous to provide students with such flimsy and one-sided material, knowing that this will heavily influence their future political views? The illusion of knowledge is more dangerous than ignorance. Admin-wise, it was a shit show of the highest order. Graded assignments (scrapbook article commentaries) were supposed to be marked and returned before the next one was released/due (there were about 4) to allow students to incorporate feedback, but the first was only returned some time after the final one was released. The midterm take-home essay instructions were changed drastically a week after the initial release: the maximum word limit was changed to a minimum word count. Having already completed the assignment, I had to scramble to unpack my heavily-condensed essay into a full-length one. Clarifications and additional instructions came piecemeal, replete with glaring spelling and grammatical errors. I have never seen a more incompetent course coordinator in my life. Thankfully, tutorials cover content wholly separate from lectures. My tutor, Ms Farah, was pretty solid and attempted to facilitate candid discussions, but was sadly limited by the 45 minutes of contact time per week. Her tutorials were for the most part really engaging and made up somewhat for the lectures. Overall, this course is great for preaching and pretending to discuss stuff you don't actually know enough about to engage meaningfully. Unless you're a senior law student or have a keen interest in constitutional issues and have read up extensively enough on the same to see through the disingenuous lecture presentations. Then you won't end up echoing the political views the rest of the unwitting students have been manipulated into forming. You'll just get tilted real hard and end up writing a scathing NUSMods review. PSA for the law students thinking of taking this course: if you're ok with shitty assignment instructions and can hold in the tilt, TAKE THIS MOD. The entire course content, readings and slides combined, is something like 10% of one single topic in LC2007. I shit you not. There is ZERO new material so you have to study absolutely nothing. If you want an easy A/A+ just parrot the political views pushed here, don't be me and take the path of most resistance by flaming the examiners by picking apart the essay questions and calling the phrasing "disingenuous" in your response. For everyone else thinking of taking this mod, be warned: take everything your learn here with about as much salt as there is in the Salar du Uyuni. There ARE very valid and important points raised, but their presentation is incredibly one-sided. Side note: I was alerted by some people that my review was taken down after I posted it. The irony is not lost on me but here's a repost. Update: this is repost number 2.

Taken in Semester 1: 2018/2019 Lecturer: Dr. Jose Carlos Viana Gomes We covered topics such as Electrostatics, Special Techniques (method of images, separation of variables, Laplace and Poissons equation, multipole expansions), Electric Fields in Matter, Magnetostatics and Magnetic Fields in matter, and Electrodynamics. I thought the unit was a pretty interesting extension of first year Electricity and Magnetism. The difference between 1st year and this course is that the topics are treated a lot more systematically, the problems are harder to set up, and once you've set up the problem, the Maths needed to finish the problem is usually fairly involved ( most commonly some sort of tricky multiple integral or differential equation that needs to be solved, or some sort of symmetry that has to be noticed). If you know your Vector Calculus and Differential Equations (including Fourier Series) well, then the Maths shouldn't be a big problem, but the visualisation/ geometry to set up the problem is nearly always tricky. The textbook for this course (Griffiths Electrodynamics) is really good, and it's essential for learning the material. Dr. Gomes's homework assignments (while good) are not enough to really understand everything. Usually the questions that Dr. Gomes writes won't be too mathematically involved (he is more of an experimentalist than a mathematician/theorist), but he does take questions straight from Griffiths and puts them on the exams in order to compensate for that. Reading Griffiths and doing as many problems as you possible can will serve you well and help you to do well on the tests and the final exam ( I think I solved at least a third of the final exam simply because I'd already solved the problems beforehand in Griffiths). Overall the unit was interesting, and while some of the problems were tricky, I did feel like I learned something when I completed the course. If anything, I found out what all that Maths is actually useful for :) Grade: B+

This module was a disaster because everything was webcasted as electures. The electures very rarely bring any form of clarity to the already ambiguous content in the lecture notes. There is a lack of organisation in notes, the ideas are all over the place. Physical lectures are cut short to 1 hour for going through non-graded true /false quizzes to reinforce on concept. However, the questions were so had phrased that you hardly understood what the question was asking for. The clarification during lectures often leaves you with more doubts than clarification if any because it is usually more on the phrasing of question rather than the concept. Tutorials were reserved for workshops to draw connection between theory and real life problems. They were complex and interesting if you really like and appreciate them. They do not help you in any ways in understanding what you need to know to tackle exam questions. They are purely for your reference and interest. There were 3 projects in total. The first was a group project which your group has to research on manufacturing procedure of a product. For example, my group have to find out how to produce ethylcellulose from scratch. From scratch meaning it has to be a starting ingredient that can be bought or easily available. The second project was an extension of the first project and it is done individually. You are assigned a feedstock and you have to design your own procedures (with valid references) to your final product (in my case, ethylcellulose) without incorporation of additional organic material. My feedstock was sugarcane bagasse which is basically cellulose. To make ethylcellulose, the ethyl branch needs to be from my sugarcane as well. Basically I cant just add any ethyl substituents in. Every carbon in product has to be from the feedstock. Last project was a group tutorial presentation. Every group can choose a topic/workshop to and discuss its assumptions/validity. In a nutshell, you are pretty much on your own because the notes are often incoherent and provide very little knowledge to connect topics together. Yet the quizzes and exam questions expect you to see the connection. Unlike normal chemistry modules, this module does not really have a clear defined answer. Everything is debatable as that is the nature of green chemistry, to always improve on existing and there is no clear solution to one problem. Although it would be very different under a different professor, the key takeaway message is that you really need to have interest to read all the references/readings on your own to appreciate and understand the difficulties in green chemistry. I am sure Prof Jason will do a much better job as I have taken his classes before. Yes, I hated this module and this is a biased review. Take it with a pinch of salt.

Taught by Prof Phil Chan If you have any questions, please send it to my email atqhteo@gmail.com, or leave a comment below. Don't worry, there are no stupid questions! I've received many emails asking me all sorts of questions. I reply all of them :) What is it about? First half you will be learning about Einstein's Special and General Relativity, Blackholes and some stars/planets-related stuff. Second half is about Quantum Mechanics and Particle Physics. How’s the workload? There’s no textbook. No readings. Everything you need to know is in your lecture notes. Lectures are very important, you have to attend, because the lecturer gives explicit hints about what he's going to test and what is important. (e.g. "TAKE NOTE, this this that that blabla") Assessment: Tutorial Quiz every tutorial (don't worry, the tutor goes through the answers and then asks you to do them, so as long as you have decent dictation skills you will get full marks for all of them LOL.) Star Gazing - 2 sessions - Simply go for two Friday night sessions of stargazing. If you can't be bothered just go and mark your attendance and you can leave. 2 / 3 person story project - write a 2000 (or 3000) word story, using concepts from the module Forum participation - just make 10 posts and you're fine. As long as you don't copy and paste or give one-liners, you get the full marks. One mid term test, one finals test. Both tests are MCQs, open book (just use lecture notes) (first test may have a short open ended short-answer question, which was a comprehension passage kind of thing for me) Two 2h lecture per week, one 1h tutorial every fortnight How difficult is it? Are you a geek? If you are into complicated-sounding Physics stuff, this is for you. Issues such as traversing faster than the speed of light... quarks and leptons... etc may sound foreign and scary to an ordinary non-geek but the professor is actually pretty darn good in simplifying most things to an understandable level. I have like, zero interest in these issues but I found most things fairly understandable. Plus the professor is one of the best lecturers I've had - he's witty (in a geeky way), entertaining, and explains things in the simplest ways. I enjoyed the lectures very much, even if I was confused/amazed/bewildered after many of them. The quizzes are literally giveaways, you just need to turn up for class and copy down what the tutor says (often he won't give the answer explicitly but more or less guides you directly to the answer and stops short of just saying it out). Story-writing, well, is up to your creativity. The first quiz was HELL - I had no idea how to do more than half of the MCQs and was guessing most of them. The second quiz was A JOKE - many answers could be found directly from the notes, and it just felt really easy overall. Miscalleneous Tips Go for lectures and pay attention. He gives many tips so do note whatever he asks you to note. Scientist's faces / names are important to note, he will test them in one or two questions in the first test at least (just be able to recognize them and roughly what they did. Shouldn't be that hard to remember Einstein's face, yes? And some others. It's open book anyway if you can't remember) He gives many quotes during lectures too, and apparently in previous sems he tested 1/2 questions on them too, but not for my semester. Should you take it? I had an enjoyable experience overall, and some things that I learnt during this module are certainly paradigm-changing for me. I've never knew what 'Relativity' was until this module haha. There are many who take this module to S/U, so you can expect a wide bell curve (e.g. my first test which I guessed 75% of the questions, I got a B/B+ range score) If you like learning about fascinating Physics stuff, and don't mind being confused abit, go for it. The lecturer is good, so you should enjoy the lectures. Not much Physics background is needed. Predicted Grade: B Actual Grade: B+

under Prof Chin Wei Ngan. The first half of the semester is on functional programming using Haskell, covering various concepts including pureness, abstract data types, higher order functions, functors, monads, and parsers. Haskell-specific concepts include typeclasses and the Parsec library. The remaining part of the semester covers logic programming using Prolog, an introduction to OCaml, as well as a brief introduction to Scala. The content of the module is roughly split in this proportion: - Haskell (55%) - Prolog (25%) - OCaml (15%) - Scala (5%) Graded components: - Lab/written assignment ×4 (35%) - Midterm test (15%) - Final exam (45%) - Tutorial participation (5%) Weekly tutorial sessions are carried out in a computer lab - some questions are distributed to students a few days before the session, and the TA discusses the solutions during the session. These questions are mainly implementation questions - students are expected to write code that conforms to some specified behaviour. There are four assignments - three of them are programming assignments in Haskell, and one is a research assignment on a programming language topic of the student's choice. Tutorial sessions generally discuss questions of similar nature to the programming assignments, so a good grasp of the tutorial material should make the programming assignments manageable. All four assignments are take-home assignments - students are given a few weeks to complete each assignment. Midterm and final exams are open-book. Midterms consists of approximately 80% MCQs, and finals consists of approximately 50% MCQs. Both midterms and finals scrutinise students' knowledge on the features and details programming languages covered in this module (with the exception of Scala, which is non-examinable), with questions such as "what is the inferred type and return value of the following expression" or "write a data type that implements this typeclass". Most questions were unambiguous, but there was a problem with the open ended questions in the midterm test. Lectures are conducted at a somewhat slow pace, possibly because this is a level 2 module. Prof Chin generally reads from his slides, and sometimes gives additional examples using the whiteboard. He is approachable and will explain concepts to students that ask him questions during lecture breaks or during lectures, but it may be difficult seek midterm expected answers from him after the midterm. Lectures are not webcasted, but his slides are generally sufficiently detailed for revision purposes.

Taken in AY 2020/2021 Sem 1 under Prof Aaron Tan Tuck Choy and Prof Lawrence Wong Tin Lok This module is all about Discrete Maths and it's pretty fun. Our topics included Logic, methods of proof, Sets, Functions, Relations, Induction, Divisibility, Modular Arithmetic, Counting, Probability, and basic Graph Theory. Prof Aaron and Lawrence do a great job of making the content interesting and revelatory and also teach the topics in a fairly straightforward manner. However, some of the topics can be difficult to understand, like Relations. You may have to revise a lot for Midterms and Finals for the topics you have trouble with. It's best if you're good at proving, but it's not the end of the world if you struggle with it since the assessments have quite a lot of non-proving questions as well. Also, make sure to make a cheat sheet of all the definitions/theorems mentioned in the lecture notes and the tutorials. Our TA provided a link to one for us but yours may not do the same. For the tutorials, we were given a worksheet with questions every week and we would spend the tutorials going over the previous lecture as well as the worksheets. Attendance is graded, but even if it weren't I'd recommend attending anyway since if you have a good TA it can really help clarify the topics and better your understanding. The worksheets don't take too much effort, maybe about an hour or two to do, and you don't have to complete it. Assessment Breakdown: Tutorial Attendance: 5% 2 Take Home Assignments: 20% Midterms: 25% Finals: 50% We were given a week to do the take home assignments. I'd say they're a bit longer and more difficult than the tutorial worksheets but not as hard as the midterms or finals. The general structure of our Midterms and Finals were that they started off with Multiple Choice Questions, then went on to Multiple Response Questions (which were all-or-nothing), then to the Structured questions, some of which were proofs, some of which were not. Like I mentioned before, being good at proving is helpful but there are enough non-proving questions that I think you can still manage without it. Final Grade: A+ TL;DR 1 is worst, 5 is best Enjoyment : 5/5 Usefulness : 4/5 (for CS) Prof: 5/5 Difficulty: Fairly difficult and some topics can be confusing. The curve isn't too bad, though. Workload : Some with tutorial worksheets every week and the take home assignments. Exams also require quite a bit of studying, more if you're not that good with discrete maths. Should I Take It: Not much of a choice if it's required for your degree, lol. Otherwise, take it if you like maths and are good at it.

Took this module in AY10/11 Sem 2. This module totally feels like a 4MC module, with 3 labs and tutorials every week. It starts of with a refreshment of JC electrical circuit knowledge. A few new laws will be introduced, such as KVL, Thevenin's Law, Norton's Law etc. They may seem confusing as first, but practice makes perfect. Phasors will be introduced after DC circuit concepts are covered. This is basically introducing complex numbers into AC circuits, hence solid knowledge of complex numbers learnt during JC will come in handy at this point of time. The first part of the module is relatively simple once the concepts are grasped. The second part of the module is quite simple too, it can actually be viewed as four separate topics, logic gates, transformers, diodes and motors. Logic gates are quite simple, dealing with alot of boolean algebra. Hence those who have taken CS1231 or GEK1505 will be at an advantage. The content covered in transformers, diodes and motors are quite surface level; hence memorisation of formulas is sufficient. Didnt attend most lectures and attended only a few tutorials. My tutor was very good. Before she starts on a tutorial, she will go through the topic and highlight the key important points and she explained the concepts really well. Each question is also given adequate coverage. Very useful. Midterms are quite easy. The first midterm consists of 4 questions worth 10 marks each. For the first midterm, due to the extensive amount of practice that I did, I had time to do every question twice, using a different approach to make sure the answers are the same regardless of approach. For the second midterm, it was 15 MCQs. Most of the questions are easy, with some involving one step workings. However, do not underestimate the paper as some questions, beneath its innocent exterior, hides a cruel intent. Read questions carefully. The mean was 22/30 (11 out of 15 questions) correct, which in my opinion, is quite high. Labs are long and draggy. Try to understand the experiment before going for the lab. Each lab is given a grade based on the quality of the lab report. Not difficult to get an A, just need to be meticulous and detailed. Average for labs is A,A,B for the 3 labs. The standard for the final exams differs for each semester. Some very complicated circuit diagrams are actually very simple if the correct rule/law is applied. I would advise students to do past year paper questions to get a feel of the kind of circuit questions that may appear during exams. They are usually not difficult, merely requires the candidate to see through the trick to doing the question. Phasor calculations are pretty straightforward. I would advise ALL EG1108 candidates to get a CASIO fx991ES calculator, which can do phasor/complex number calculations. This is they key to saving time during examinations, rather than doing phasor calculations manually. Most questions are similar to tutorial standard. Hence it is imperative to do your tutorials dutifully. Lastly, the motors question is A MUST DO. It's simple and has a high mark weightage. Generally, I would advise candidates against doing both the circuit questions because they are quite time-consuming to analyse and calculate. Circuit questions: 2-3 lines of working -> 1 mark Motor/Diodes/Transformer questions: 1 line of working -> 2-3 marks Hence, its much wiser to spend time doing questions from part 2 of the syllabus and the remaining time checking the paper. I would not say this module is difficult, as long as one puts in time and effort to study the notes and attempt tutorials and past year questions, a decent grade is attainable. My CA is above average, but my finals pulled me up quite abit. The only thing I’m unhappy about this module is that its only 3MCs, when the workload made it seem like a 4MC one. Grade: A+

Taken in 20/21 Sem 2 Grading: 5% CA1, 25% CA2, 10% CA3, 30% CA4, 15% CA5, 15% participation Ah yes, the compulsory English class to be taken by all Computing students. There are 2x2hr sessions per week with high weightage class participation, which I'm sure contributes to the universal hate this class gets. The content of the class can be read from the other reviews so I'll just talk about the assessments. --- Assessment --- Similar to CS2101, grading is very consistent throughout the semester due to the 5 CAs. There aren't any "lull" periods where there's nothing to do (notwithstanding the 2x2hr sessions per week), so expect to put in more work than you might probably expect. For group projects, the class is split into groups at the start of the semester based on a survey done in the first class. You're stuck with this group for the whole semester so pray you get people who have the same goals as you. I was fortunate to have landed in a group with like-minded individuals who all wanted to maximise effort:reward ratio. CA1: Craft a presentation/video of a spin on a children's tale. Pretty simple, can be done in an afternoon if focused. CA2: Make a "Critical Thinking Rubric" from the Ennis reading, write a report on it (15%) and do a presentation (10%). This is the most tiring group project so I'm glad the co-ordinators put this early in the semester. CA3: Panel Discussion on an topic that was agreed upon prior to the discussion. You have to research the topic, then have an "academic conversation" that goes on for about 30-45min with your group, with 15min Q/A at the end. Can be prepared the day before. Try to be nice to your teammates and let them have their say in the discussion. CA4: Position Paper. You propose a question then write a 800-word-or-so essay on it. This is similar to writing a GP essay, except with citations. Can be done in a day assuming you already have a good question to write on. This is individual work with high weightage so if you're planning to score, better put work into this. CA5: Given a prompt, do an individual impromptu speech on the prompt in 2min. This is a luck of the draw if you get a good prompt or not. It's over within 2 minutes so if you can't think of anything to say, hey, at least you'll die quickly. Expected Grade: B/B+ Actual Grade: TBC

by Dr. John van Whye Content: This is a HISTORY module, about the history of evolution, so being a life science major does not give you any advantage at all. First 2 lectures are a bit boring because they have nothing to do with Darwin but do bear with them as they set the historical context; a lot of names introduced will also come back in later lectures. Things get exciting from lecture 3, where we learn about Darwin's life, his famous Beagle voyage, his conception of Origin, the surprise of Wallace, etc. Along the way, there's a lot of cool myth-busting, like did you know the Galapagos finches were NOT Darwin's source of inspiration for Origin? Did you know Larmack's theory is NOT inheritance of acquired characteristics? Etc, etc... Lecture Style: This is the tricky part. Dr. John's slides are mostly pictures with very few words, and he expects students to make their own notes by taking down stuff he says during the lecture. (Lectures are NOT webcasted.) He delivers his lecture in a narrative style, so it is usually not difficult to keep up with him, but sometimes he can speak very fast when he gets excited. An option would be to do a voice recording, and play back the parts you missed, which would also be useful if you somehow manage to fall asleep during his lecture. Workload: Very light. Lectures are biweekly, no tutorials, no projects. Exams: Mid-term (50 MCQs, 50%, closed book), final (50 MCQs, 50%, closed book). Since everything is multiple-choice, it is quite easy to score if you paid attention during the lectures and studied well. One thing to note is that even though Dr. John says he does not test dates, he DOES. At least for my finals. So if it's not too much of a hassle, just try to cram in some important dates; might get you a few more marks. Expected grade: A+ Obtained grade: A+

Prof. Dilip Raghavan (Lecturer and Tutor) Assessment Structure: Homework: 4% Midterm Exam #1: 23% Midterm Exam #2: 23% Final Exam: 50% This is a pure math module that leads up to the path of mathematical logic in the pre-requisite tree (MA5219/MA5220 Logic and Foundations of Mathematics I/II require MA3205). The module’s topics include set and operations, pairing, products and relations, Russell’s paradox and proper classes, natural numbers, comparing size of sets, quasi/partial/linear/well-orders, countable and uncountable sets, ordinals and ordinal arithmetic, cardinals and cardinal arithmetic, and some applications of Axiom of Choice. There is no main textbook of reference. Class size is small so lectures and tutorials are held in a classroom without webcast. Attendance is not compulsory for both, but one needs to submit their weekly homework during the tutorial session. Tutorial sessions simply involve Prof. Dilip explaining the solutions for tutorial problems. Homework is split into 11 parts (one per tutorial session), and only the best 10 out of 11 will be graded and each are of equal weightage. Each homework consists of only one problem provided in the lecture notes (all tutorial/homework problems are contained in the lecture notes). However, I strongly recommend students of this module to try out all problems in the notes as they are very good practices which reinforce the concepts taught. Concepts taught in set theory are generally extremely intuitive, but it guess less intuitive in the second half. The first half of the course is mostly a repeat of MA1100. After that comes orders and ordinals/cardinals, which were not introduced in MA1100. This module is notorious for the difficulty of understanding ordinal/cardinal arithmetic, so students should expect to spend more time understanding them. In this academic year, Prof. Dilip rearranged the order of the chapters taught, and started ordinal/cardinal arithmetic at around week 10, making it easier for students to understand the content. Prof. Dilip is an amazing lecturer who displays very good understanding of the content (as expected since he’s taught the module for at least 4-5 years). He draws many diagrams to illustrate the concepts taught. He is generally a very entertaining lecturer, slotting in his own jokes from time to time, such as him taking a vacation in the middle of a proof. However, his lectures may still get dry from time to time due to the content taught being quite technical, and he writes on the board most of the details of the proof. One may find themselves drained after each lecture. Regardless, I believe his lectures are worth attending due to his clear explanations of the concepts taught. Due to a timetable clash, I was not able to attend his lectures on Friday, and I spent significantly more time self-studying the notes at the second half of the module. I’m very happy to have taken a module under Prof. Dilip. The two midterms and final exams were out of 23, 23 and 50 respectively (matching exactly their percentage weightage). They are all closed book with one A4-size double-sided helpsheet, which is extremely helpful due to their being lots of theorems to remember. All exams share the same format: all questions are more or less standard and similar to the problems given in the notes, with the exception of the last part of the last problem, which is very difficult and forces students to think really creatively. The standard questions in midterms were manageable, and more difficult for finals. I didn’t manage to solve the last part of last question for all the exams, yet obtained an unexpectedly good grade. Expected Grade: A Final Grade: A+

Module Review by limwj ( This is a CAPT module. It is only available for students in CAPT to take. This is the 2nd time this module is being run, and the module coordinator agrees that she will have to continue to make modifications to the module to make it better for students in the future. I am not an ‘environment' person. I took this module for the 'civil society' part. There is, however, more emphasis on the environment than civil society. In particular, we focus on Pulau Ubin alot, towards the later part of the module. The best part about this module is the fieldtrips. The worst part about this module is also about the fieldtrips, and the 4 combined sessions that is held from 6-8pm. We visited Sungei Buloh Wetland Reserve, did the International Coastal Cleanup in Pulau Ubin, and was suggested to go for another trip to ubin for our personal presentation. If not for the participation in the coastal cleanup, i would never have learnt about the existence of ICCS (don’t know what this is? google.) The guide for our fieldtrip to SBWR was a nature activist, and he tells great stories that pique our interests, not only in the natural happenings in SBWR, but also how SBWR gained its nature reserve status, and the ‘fight’ with the government over the years to protect our environment. These fieldtrips usually eat up our precious Saturdays… Combined sessions would have invited guests to speak about environmentalism and civil society (we had one speaker on civil society in sg, two speakers on environmentalism in Pulau Ubin - overkill). These combined sessions end around 8pm, which would make you exhausted if you have had a day of lessons before that. Since this is a S/U module, grades are not really important, and every section of assessment is merely like an opportunity to share what you learn with the class. This makes things more relaxed, and at the same time more interesting. Don’t worry if you don’t like Pulau Ubin; the module is a very dynamic one, and the content changes accordingly to what is the most current news on environment and civil society in Singapore. I like how Prof Joelle would go through with us news on the environment before the start of her weekly seminar sessions =) Overall: I’ve learnt alot about our environment and the struggle that happened in the past that allowed us to have our nature reserves today. these struggles are real and are still happening; the latest plans about the cross-island MRT line is going to cut through our central catchment nature reserve!! (how can we protect our remaining nature spaces?) Take this module if: you want to learn more about environmentalism in Singapore. This module is not good if: it is non-S/U, which is going to be a reality for students from AY2014/15. Idk, imo I feel that such modules are better enjoyed when it is S/U - learning for the sake of learning. Lecturer: Asst Prof. Soh Siow Ling Grading Scheme: 25% Midterm, 15% Mini-Project, 60% Final This is compulsory module for Chemical Engineering students that discusses fundamental physical phenomena such as Heat Transfer, Radiation and Diffusion. These are physical processes that occur everywhere in our daily lives and in many scenarios, so in some sense, this was quite enlightening for me. Content wise, the most annoying part of the syllabus was the empirical equations for many complicated phenomena. While these empirical equations are shortcuts for engineers, they do not develop good intuition on why the equations are true, which was rather sad. You will also get to see the parallelisms between Heat and Mass transfer which were pretty cool. Lectures were well-developed. I like Prof Soh's style of teaching and he is probably one of the better lecturers in this department. He is also very engaging. However, you should try to read up on lecture notes before coming to class because it is easy to lose track given the sheer amounts of empirical equations. Speed-running for this module towards the exam is possible but not recommended as it is stressful. Midterms was extremely easy and the average iirc was 16/20. It was almost just plugging in the correct equation and getting the answer. Marking was also extremely lenient. The project was also really fun to do. You basically have to model a real life heat/mass transfer scenario on MATLAB using the PDE solver. I had a lot of fun doing it as I modeled a piece of bread heating up. This is perhaps the most fun part of the module. And it was easy to score 10/10, just follow the criterion, but do not forget to have fun along the way. The finals were like the midterms, however, you need to manage your time well for the finals as some people did not finish the paper. My suggestion is to just leave everything in algebraic form before writing the final answer in decimals. You save alot of time from having to do tedious calculations. Also, the only hard question was some simple diffusion equation that involved some ODE at the back of the paper. In terms of just merely midterms/finals, this is really the epitome of plugging and just bashing through the questions quickly. However, this module has let me appreciate the basic physical processes in our daily lives a little more. It is actually a fun Chem Eng module because content was well-delivered by Prof Soh and you can relate to it. The hard part about this module is not about the questions. It is about the broadness of the content. There are 15 chapters and 3-4 sections in total. You would probably need to know where and what each section is, and perhaps make a summarized cheat sheet to survive for the finals. Once you are done with that, and have done all practice questions in the tutorials, you should be good to go! This module is significantly easier than CN2122, which should be a relief to hear for some people. It is well taught and questions are generally easier under Prof Soh. I really enjoyed this module the most of all the CN mods I took this sem. Difficulty: 4.5/10

UTW1001Z Difficulty: Moderate Workload: Moderate-High Class Slot: 1200-1400 Tuesdays and Fridays at TC-SR6 Teacher(s): Lect Laetitia MONBEC Grade weightage: 15% Paper 1 25% Paper 2 40% Paper 3 10% Presentation 10% Class Participation Expected Grade: B/B+ Grade: B+ Additional Remarks: COVID Sem: Became e-learning halfway through the sem Thoughts: It’s a pretty interesting module though it’s quite arts-y so if you’re a non-arts-y person like me, don’t expect to get an A. You basically just learn different interpretations of colour, how it is related to culture, how it is applied to things, and how it is used to communicate messages. Throughout the first half, you will be doing some readings of journal articles on colour so that you get familiarised with its concepts. Teacher: Dr Laetitia (actually she asks us to call her Ms Laetitia) is a very friendly teacher and her passion for the subject makes the module better. I think she teaches well. Paper 1: This is the reflective summary where you will basically be asked to read a journal article and write a summary in the first paragraph, before giving your thoughts about it in the second paragraph. This isn’t too difficult and can be done in a few days. You may be asked to do peer review on other students’ papers. Paper 2: This is the lens paper where you will be required to choose something to apply a lens on; usually you will be asked to pick among pictures such as movie posters, movie scenes or album covers. A lens, as how I understand it, is roughly a framework somebody else made for you to analyse stuff with. You will probably be asked to analyse using the lens of Van Leeuwen’s parametric theory of colour. You can use this to assign colour concepts to their interpretations to understand the message behind the picture. This isn’t that difficult if you know exactly what message is being conveyed and if your picture has a lot of things you can write about. Paper 3: This is the expository paper where you will be tasked with basically coming up with some claim/argument/thesis statement about the use of colour in society, usually through some visual work you choose (for example, a music video, or a computer game) and then you will write points supporting your claim. It is quite difficult to find journal articles to support your claims especially if the visual media you have chosen does not have that much research done on it so choose wisely. Presentation: You will be merely presenting what you wrote for paper 3 so this shouldn’t be that difficult to prepare for, just convert your paper to slides.

Taken in AY16/17 Semester One Lecturer: Dr Vitor Pereira Syllabus: - Mathematical preliminaries (Complex algebra, probability theory, matrix algebra, eigenvalue problems, linear vector spaces, Dirac notation, dual spaces and inner product, linear operators, matrix representation of operators, observables and representations) - Description of quantum systems (The state vector, observables and outcomes of measurements, probability interpretation and state reduction, compatible and incompatible observables, Ehrenfest’s theorem, uncertainty relation, spin and Stern-Gerlach experiments) - Time evolution (Time-independent Schrodinger equation [TISE], stationary states, time evolution operator, Larmor precession, general two-level system, transition probability) - Position [X] and momentum [P] representations (Continuous bases, translation operator, momentum operator and its eigenstates and action in position representation, Schrodinger equation in position representation, canonical commutation relations, X-P transition, Ehrenfest’s theorem and classical equations of motion, time dependence of wavefunctions, free-particle solutions to TISE, wavepackets, time evolution of wavepackets, local conservation of probability density) - 1D potentials (Boundary conditions to TISE in 1D potentials, bound states and energy quantization, general properties of the 1D spectrum, infinite potential well and properties, finite potential well and properties, potential step and properties, potential barrier and properties, tunnelling and scattering, transmission and reflection coefficients, Dirac delta potential and properties) - 1D harmonic oscillator (Properties of the quantum harmonic oscillator. Algebraic solution: Ladder operators, the number operator and spectrum properties, ground-state wavefunction. Analytic solution: Asymptotic behaviour of TISE, series solution. Eigenfunctions and expectation values) - 3D potentials (Composite systems, tensor product spaces and application to 3D problems in Cartesian coordinates) - Angular momentum (Separation of TISE in spherical coordinates, raising and lowering operators, commutation relations, spectrum and eigenstates of angular momentum operators, eigenfunctions of angular momentum, spherical harmonics) - Central potential (Radial equations and properties, Bessel functions, two body central potentials, the hydrogen wavefunction) - Physical invariance and rotations Assessment: - In-lecture quizzes (15%) - Tutorials (15%) - Midterms (15% + 15%) - Finals (40%) Personal Experiences: I actually took this module in Semester One, during which I found it to be rather joyless and depressing. I was too tilted back then to even consider a review. In Semester Two, I went on to take the sequel PC3130 Quantum Mechanics II, and only then did I start to appreciate this module. Here in PC2130, we learn the basics of quantum mechanics and the application of these basics to simple problems. However, such a seemingly harmless statement does not accurately convey the amount of abstraction that one will face in this module. Unlike previous modules where one may be able to understand or anticipate certain results from physical intuition, the majority of this module’s content follows from mathematics as applied to the postulates of QM and this may be initially off-putting for some. It certainly was off-putting for me, hence my earlier remark on how I found this module joyless. I can imagine a ball falling under gravity or a charged object experiencing electric forces, but the idea that a quantum particle is to be described by a state vector obeying the TISE was very jarring initially. More confusion ensues when the idea of operators appear. More often than not, I felt as if I was just doing the calculation with no idea as to what were the actual, physical consequences of the results I obtained from mathematics. This makes it difficult to feel any motivation or emotional attachment to your work. Put in another way, “do I care?” One interesting consequence of the “live by the math, die by the math” nature of this module is that it is actually very possible to perform decently just by math alone. I am not proud to admit this, but for the midterms I would only start studying the night before. Despite my half-assed efforts at studying, I wound up scoring rather decently. But this is a truly stupid way to study, and after this miserable experience I never want to do this crap again. As I had mentioned at the beginning, however, this is necessary suffering to prepare you for the more fun content in the sequel Quantum Mechanics II. It’s like learning your AEIOUs before you can start reading Enid Blyton. Hang in there and try not to get as tilted as I did.
