Took this module in Sem 1 of AY16/17 under Dr Marc Rochester. No final examination. TL;DR: Basically "Orchestras in Singapore 1101". Stickler for essay formatting with vague topics that are easily misinterpreted. Very light workload, but not guaranteed an A. Probably boring for people who already are immersed in the Singaporean "western" music scene. CA consists of four parts: CA1: Fieldwork project on the study of audience behaviour in western music concerts in Singapore OR study of music schools/teaching programmes in Singapore, with a presentation in class. Group work of about 5-8(?) people. CA2: 500 word objective individual essay on a "western music ensemble" in Singapore. CA3: 750 word subjective individual essay on the position of the Singaporean music scene in the global context. CA4: Introduced at the last minute - class discussion during week 13's class. I found that there was a huge discrepancy between what the module title and description suggests and what is actually taught in the module. While the module is titled "Western Music within a Singaporean Context" (where western basically = classical as we generally understand it), it basically can be summed up as "the history of orchestras in Singapore". As someone who comes from a choral background I found it immensely disappointing that the vast majority of content covered orchestral music, with the other major topic being the role of learning and teaching "western" music in Singaporean society. The module description also reads: "It will assess the impact of majority cultures (particularly from the Chinese, Malay and Indian communities) on the general reception of Western music, as well as on music written by Singapore-based composers. Students will be introduced to the principal figures in Singapore’s musical development." However, these issues were just touch-and-go, with Marc basically rambling on about the treatment of classical music in Singaporean households or about audience perceptions. I honestly do not recall anything about majority cultures in Singapore being mentioned, and only a very small portion was touched on regarding Singaporean composers, even solo Singaporean musicians. While Marc himself is a rather funny guy, he basically sits you down for 1.5 hrs a week and rambles on, asking more questions than he gives answers, simply because this is a field that doesn't really have much research conducted with regard to music in Singapore. While he occasionally gives you facts, he doesn't properly cite the sources that he tends to mention casually, making it seem extremely wishy-washy. Lecture slides are uploaded every week after class, along with (rather soft) audio recordings of one of the lecture slots. The guest lectures are pretty banal, with more about the orchestras like SSO and Music Makers, the history of their establishment and things like that. If you're already pretty much into the local "western" music scene there's not much you can learn from attending lectures: it's basically a reaffirmation of what you already know more or less. For the fieldwork project, since the class is split into such large groups, you are allowed to split the work by having some members exclusively do data collection and others do the presentation, or have everyone involved. However, traditional powerpoint presentations should be eschewed for more interesting and attention-grabbing methods such as skits and interactive sessions. It also helps to have a few major points from your fieldwork presented as clearly as possible rather than trying to cover all bases. For the essays, the main thing is to FOLLOW THE GUIDELINES STRICTLY! He spells them all out within the powerpoint and word documents, though both documents sometimes have things that he does not put in the other, so be wary and ensure that you put in everything and double/triple check before submission, as he has been known to drop people a few grades for not following the format. The topics tend to be VERY VAGUE and are easily subject to misinterpretation, as evidenced by the majority of my groupmates and myself. While the topics may be vague, he has a very strict idea of what should be put in the essay (which is pretty unfair), and so if you really want that A you HAVE to consult him about your ideas relating to the given essay topics, otherwise it's extremely easy to get a C for the essay component. Book him early for a consultation as he tends to be busy running around watching concerts and other stuff. You only get one chance to upload your essay, and if you don't follow the guidelines or completely misinterpret the essay he will ask you to resubmit it with a SEVERE PENALTY (25%) IN GRADING, and can only be done during the submission period. i.e. past the given deadline, no more re-submissions if you fail to interpret or follow the guidelines. Some of the criteria for formatting make sense, while others like INSISTING ON USING UK ENGLISH or COUNTING HYPHENATED WORDS AND ACRONYMS AS INDIVIDUAL WORDS are a complete pain in the ass. While this module has an extremely light workload I would honestly not recommend it for people already immersed in the "western" music happenings in Singapore as it will be boring af. Plus, the essays are a real chore which always makes you second-guess yourself. I completely regret wasting 1400 points on this module as I had to bid it under the SSY module code.

The conduction of the first online quiz was a total disaster, both assignments were delayed and also took a very long time to grade, for the final project students asked multiple times for exact submission format where Prof. Wei Wang would not really be clear and then just a few days before the submission deadline an explicit format was finally given, etc. I think the Covid-19 situation affected the module a lot, and hopefully most of these concerns regarding execution itself will be addressed in future iterations of the module. The second assignment was a bit tougher and included implementing img2col, backward function of conv, forward function of pooling, forward function of LSTM, backward function of Bi-directional RNN and finally tune a CNN and a RNN. Some parts of the implementation were not immediately obvious from the lectures. I had to read a few blog posts to understand it properly, but it was not too bad. I spent maybe 5-8x as long on assignment 2 as I did on assignment 1. But given that extra time, you should be able to score top marks. I highly recommend forming a group of the maximum size since you are not judged harsher for being more people anyway. The task was image classification. The marks were divided in two parts with the first part being the relative position on the Kaggle leaderboard (30 marks) and the second being a report (10 marks). Many groups spent a long time tuning hyperparameters, experimenting with different architectures, doing different types of ensembling, etc. Prepare to spend a significant amount of time on the project if you want to get a good score and make sure you have a good group. AY17/18 Sem 2 Lecturer: Assoc Prof Chin Chee Whye Assessment: 40% Homework 20% Midterm 40% Finals Content: Topology is concerned with the study of topological spaces continuous maps between topological spaces. Module can get quite content heavy: we covered topological spaces (standard topologies and various notions like compactness, connectedness), topological groups, compactifications, Tychonoff theorem, Urysohn Lemma and Tietze Extension and also nets (generalization of sequences), Fundamental group (and very fun results like there is continuous map from unit ball to circle that is a retraction, Borsuk-Ulam) and also briefly touched on the topology of compact convergence. Prof Chin does follow discussion in Munkres closely. Homeworks: Starts off quite chill but can get quite tough when you need to use some very very involved and non-trivial tricks. Just keep in mind some heuristics like showing a set is open you just need to show that you can write it as a union of open sets or even connectedness; if you want to show that a property holds for an entire set that is connected, you just have to show that a subset with such a property is non-empty and simultaneously closed and open. Midterm/Exams: Midterm was quite tough because of time constraint (4 questions in 1.5 hours) and questions are far from trivial (like the Lebesgue Number Lemma??) ; there were no "free-marks". Finals was much easier and merciful but I could have done better than expected. Ultimately the mod is rewarding because of the slew of applications topology has in different branches of mathematics.

Lecturer: Prof. Sanjay Jain Grading Scheme: 10% Tutorial Participation, 25% Midterm 1, 25% Midterm 2, 40% Final This module is an elective that can be taken for CS (Algorithms and Theory Focus Area) and Math majors. This module essentially covers various machines in increasing power aka types of languages that can be accepted by the machine: - Regular Languages (Deterministic Finite Automata, Non-Deterministic Finite Automata, Regular Expression) - Context-Free Languages (Pushdown Automata, Context-Free Grammars) - Recursively Enumerable and Non-Recursively Enumerable Languages (using Turing Machines and Partial Recursive Functions for proofs) At the end of this module, theory of complexity (time and space complexity and NP completeness) is also taught. By Prof Paul Reddish What is it about? You will learn about the psychological mechanism and consequence (+ve & -ve) of religion. You will analyze religion from cognitive, social, and evolutionary perspectives. How’s the workload? One 3-h seminar style lecture a week + readings. 5% class participation, Prof caters time after every class for discussion and class-sharing 15% Midterm, 30% Commentary essays, together with below 20% Group presentation 30% Finals. How *difficult is it? Best not to think in terms of module difficulty - Your experience in the module is better determined by your interest in the topic. [Below are my thoughts on what is covered in this module, by themes] Psychology of Religion is part-Neuroscience, part-Social psychology, and part-Evolutionary Psychology. Finally, a cursory view of major world religions + folk religions. 1) This course will include cognitive modules, biases and heuristics, brain bases, and cognitive processing limitations/bottlenecks. Course content will draw on research that utilize these models and apply them in experimental settings. 2) Religion is collinear with other social factors. For example, christianity is more prevalent in white, affluent societies. Islam is more prevanent in conflict-bound societies. Folk religions are more prevalent in rural and small communities. The challenge in PoR is to seperate the local effects of religion in one culture from the global effects of religion. 3) This course will include theories of evolutionary psychology. Particularly, how certain cognitive modules were adaptive in the past, but are not prone to heuristics and biases. These may or may not lead to the phenomenon of religion. This topic is covered in the later part of the module. 4) Religion. Most of the class entered this module with either strong religious views or strong non-religious views. [My own experience with my religion spurred me to look into this RELIGION from the lens of psychology. It may be the same for you, but I caution: there are no debates about which religious view is superior. This is strictly an academic exercise to apply psychology in another domain of human experience.] Group presentation + Essay Pick a topic in religion (e.g. self-control, health, prayer) [Mine was atheism]. Conduct a literature review on the current views towards that topic and share it as a formal presentation. Prof R. encourages students to generate original ideas. [The “original idea” part was somewhat vague initially. But through group discussions, we decided on a logical flow of content for the presentation. The essay portion allowed me to pick my favorite part of the presentation and write about it, in 2000 words or less. It was more interesting than you might think.] How is the Prof? Prof R. is open and friendly. He takes the course content seriously and will engage with students after class. Since this is a non-textbook module, the resources are many and up for interpretation. Prof R. does an excellent job in framing the readings into a curriculum that teaches smaller concepts that gradually build up to a holistic understanding of PoR. He is approachable after class and online. Always on time with uploading of lecture resources. Should you take it? If any of the above points, or a combination of them, intrigues you. Or if you are unsure where to go, but looking for a good educator. I encourage you to take this module. Midterm/ Exam tips Essay-based. During studying, keep in mind the overarching themes. Laplace equation is up next, followed by Green's functions. Green's functions is the most difficult part of the course because a lot of care is needed to choose the correct Green's function. Prof Yu then teaches additional things out of the syllabus: Systems of PDE, Laplace/Fourier transform, multidimensional wave/diffusion equation. He essentially almost finishes almost all the theory in the whole Strauss textbook. - Prof Yu has taught this module many times. However, as reported previously, he is not a very good lecturer, but better than the time where he taught me MA4252 Advanced ODEs. Took this module in Sem 1 of AY16/17 under Dr Marc Rochester. No final examination. TL;DR: Basically "Orchestras in Singapore 1101". Stickler for essay formatting with vague topics that are easily misinterpreted. Very light workload, but not guaranteed an A. Probably boring for people who already are immersed in the Singaporean "western" music scene. CA consists of four parts: CA1: Fieldwork project on the study of audience behaviour in western music concerts in Singapore OR study of music schools/teaching programmes in Singapore, with a presentation in class. Group work of about 5-8(?) people. CA2: 500 word objective individual essay on a "western music ensemble" in Singapore. CA3: 750 word subjective individual essay on the position of the Singaporean music scene in the global context. CA4: Introduced at the last minute - class discussion during week 13's class. I found that there was a huge discrepancy between what the module title and description suggests and what is actually taught in the module. While the module is titled "Western Music within a Singaporean Context" (where western basically = classical as we generally understand it), it basically can be summed up as "the history of orchestras in Singapore". As someone who comes from a choral background I found it immensely disappointing that the vast majority of content covered orchestral music, with the other major topic being the role of learning and teaching "western" music in Singaporean society. The module description also reads: "It will assess the impact of majority cultures (particularly from the Chinese, Malay and Indian communities) on the general reception of Western music, as well as on music written by Singapore-based composers. Students will be introduced to the principal figures in Singapore’s musical development." However, these issues were just touch-and-go, with Marc basically rambling on about the treatment of classical music in Singaporean households or about audience perceptions. I honestly do not recall anything about majority cultures in Singapore being mentioned, and only a very small portion was touched on regarding Singaporean composers, even solo Singaporean musicians. While Marc himself is a rather funny guy, he basically sits you down for 1.5 hrs a week and rambles on, asking more questions than he gives answers, simply because this is a field that doesn't really have much research conducted with regard to music in Singapore. While he occasionally gives you facts, he doesn't properly cite the sources that he tends to mention casually, making it seem extremely wishy-washy. Lecture slides are uploaded every week after class, along with (rather soft) audio recordings of one of the lecture slots. The guest lectures are pretty banal, with more about the orchestras like SSO and Music Makers, the history of their establishment and things like that. If you're already pretty much into the local "western" music scene there's not much you can learn from attending lectures: it's basically a reaffirmation of what you already know more or less. For the fieldwork project, since the class is split into such large groups, you are allowed to split the work by having some members exclusively do data collection and others do the presentation, or have everyone involved. However, traditional powerpoint presentations should be eschewed for more interesting and attention-grabbing methods such as skits and interactive sessions. It also helps to have a few major points from your fieldwork presented as clearly as possible rather than trying to cover all bases. For the essays, the main thing is to FOLLOW THE GUIDELINES STRICTLY! He spells them all out within the powerpoint and word documents, though both documents sometimes have things that he does not put in the other, so be wary and ensure that you put in everything and double/triple check before submission, as he has been known to drop people a few grades for not following the format. The topics tend to be VERY VAGUE and are easily subject to misinterpretation, as evidenced by the majority of my groupmates and myself. While the topics may be vague, he has a very strict idea of what should be put in the essay (which is pretty unfair), and so if you really want that A you HAVE to consult him about your ideas relating to the given essay topics, otherwise it's extremely easy to get a C for the essay component. Book him early for a consultation as he tends to be busy running around watching concerts and other stuff. You only get one chance to upload your essay, and if you don't follow the guidelines or completely misinterpret the essay he will ask you to resubmit it with a SEVERE PENALTY (25%) IN GRADING, and can only be done during the submission period. i.e. past the given deadline, no more re-submissions if you fail to interpret or follow the guidelines. Some of the criteria for formatting make sense, while others like INSISTING ON USING UK ENGLISH or COUNTING HYPHENATED WORDS AND ACRONYMS AS INDIVIDUAL WORDS are a complete pain in the ass. While this module has an extremely light workload I would honestly not recommend it for people already immersed in the "western" music happenings in Singapore as it will be boring af. Plus, the essays are a real chore which always makes you second-guess yourself. I completely regret wasting 1400 points on this module as I had to bid it under the SSY module code.

Here are some examples of the quiz questions that they ask: According to Layer2.txt, it is mentioned that The Pawnbroker relied on Security by Obscurity. Is it ethical or unethical for The Pawnbroker to rely on Security by Obscurity? The correct answer: Under any of the ethical views mentioned in this question's suggested answers, it would be ethical ----------------------------------------------------------------- According to Layer5.txt, it is mentioned that The Pawnbroker relied on Security by Encryption. Is it ethical or unethical for The Pawnbroker to rely on Security by Encryption? The correct answer: It is unethical under Contributing to society ----------------------------------------------------------------- As you saw from Exhibit A, although many organisations require its members to abide by "strong password" policies (eg. use a mix of alpha-numeric and special characters, don't write the password down, use a different password for each website etc.), many of such policies are in fact very difficult to abide by, and if they are abided by, this tends to create difficulties for users in their daily lives (eg. forgetting the password). Is it ethical to have such policies in the first place? The correct answer: It is unethical under all the ethical views mentioned in this question's suggested answers ----------------------------------------------------------------- What kind of nonsensical Q&A is this? Encryption is a contentious subject in the world of ethics, because on the one hand you have people defending its use for privacy, but on the other hand you have people making backdoors to catch criminals or whatever. There is so much depth to a discussion about the ethics of encryption, and yet all we get is some stupid nonsense that it's unethical under contributing to society? What absolute garbage. That's just for the quiz; for the mission reports, the mode of assessment is that we need to justify *THE "CORRECT" ANSWER* of the quiz. Not the answer that you wrote, but the answer THAT THEY GIVE. What kind of backwards teaching methodology requires you to posthumously justify answers that weren't even your own? Did you submit an answer on the quiz that you felt was correct? Well good luck to you, because you have no chance to even begin to justify yourself or your point of view. How bloody ethical. Furthermore, each "justification" can only be a few sentences, because you have to literally write hundreds of them; 4 options per question, 5 ethics questions per quiz, 10 quizzes in total -- you do the math -- spread over reports A and B. I might not have come out of NIE and taken some weird course about "experiential learning" or whatever, but I do know that in the 8000-9000 words required to write out those justifications, we could've had 8-9 long-form essays, which lets people defend and expand -- with rebuttals, counterpoints, and examples -- their viewpoint of ethics. Instead we get this half-assed mode of assessment which benefits nobody except the people marking the answers, because they don't need to use their brains to actually evaluate the arguments made by students. How can you teach a module saying that ethics is up to the interpretation of the individual person, when the entire structure of the module is in such a way that nobody even gets to express their own views? Next there is the "world setup"; it feels like the profs watched john wick over winter break and decided to add artificial drama to the module, which contributed nothing to the students' learning experiences. Maybe if the questions asked about the ethical implications of the fella's actions or something, but instead we just get nonsensical labels like "adjudicators" and "high table" and whatnot applied to the quiz. If you gotta try so hard to make your module seem "cool" to a bunch of 18-20 year old adults, what does that say about your teaching methodology, and the content of the module? Finally, there is the question of the absolutely condescending Lu Weiquan. After a few weeks there were expectedly people rightfully complaining about this module. In response, he sent out an email to all students, "explaining" his motivations with so little tact, and with such a belittling tone to the students, that I really wonder what the intention of that email was. Here's an excerpt -- the email "answered" some "grievances" that students had: 1. In response to the question "Why not just make everything like every other written test/exam that you've ever taken in your Primary/Secondary/JC/Poly/etc school life?" The way the question is phrased already paints a negative picture of the response, but I digress. All these quotes are taken directly from the announcement on luminus. "As IS1103 is an Experiential Learning module, the learning happens when you experience what you need to experience in the module. In other words, unlike other modules / classes / courses that you have taken, in which all the answers can be found in a textbook, Experiential Learning is about finding the answers through your own personal experiences when doing the missions." Indeed, experiential learning means learning through experience. But, I cannot say with a clear conscience that, in the course of this module, i have actually "experienced" anything. How are our personal experiences relevant, when the only mode of assessment tests our ability to retroactively apply frameworks to an already-given answer? ---------------------------------------------------------------------- 2. In response to the question "Why do we need to physically go to places and physically handle stuff? Why so troublesome? Why not make it all online?" his response: "That's a great question, and the answer can be found in Experiential Learning scientific literature. I will not bore you with the details. Instead, I'll simplify it for you by asking you a few questions. First, is it feasible to learn how to ride a bicycle just by reading a book or watching a video about riding bicycles? Second, is it feasible to understand why flipping through a stack of papers is troublesome, as compared to simply doing a Ctrl-F on a keyboard for text search in a word document? Third, is it feasible to understand the difficulties in making ethical decisions if you have never experienced the pain and sweat and hunger and anger and frustration and jealousy and joy and happiness and love that goes into making such decisions in the real world?" What can I say, except that I completely agree? Unfortunately, this is not the reality of IS1103. It is not feasible to learn about riding bicycles by reading a book, just as it is equally impossible to learn about ethics by doing quizzes about contrived scenarios without avenues for creative discourse. Furthermore, I am sure that it can be justifiably unethical under some of the ethical frameworks, to make students flip through papers to essentially "teach them a lesson" that physical data is harder to aggregate than digital data. Also, arguably, students were not asked to make any ethical decisions, so this entire point seems barely relevant. "If you answered yes to any of the three questions stated above, you're not being truthful with yourself, and scientific research backs that up". This translates to: your personal experiences and opinions are invalid, because "scientific research" is never wrong. Is it ethical to be so condescending and dismissive towards a student like that? “Scientific research” or otherwise? ---------------------------------------------------------------------- 3. In response to the question "Why do the missions not seem to be connected with the topic?" "I can assure you that the missions are extremely connected to the topic, it's just that you need to reflect on them to see it. For example, in Mission 1 and 2, Big Data is about the 4Vs (Variety, Veracity, Velocity, Volume), and you indeed encountered a Variety of data types (eg. image vs. text, visual vs tactile, etc), with varying levels of Veracity [accuracy] (blur vs. sharp pictures, useful vs. un-useful data, etc), with different Velocity (walking to some place vs. seeing it on the internet, accessing a file online vs accessing a file physically, different barriers to the information such as the X-ray room in UHC [how to get that information? Ask someone? Search Google? Physically go to UHC to find it?]), and with varying Volume (the amount of information you get when you are walking from place to place vs. the amount of information you get by just reading the text), these are all examples of how you have experienced Big Data" I struggle to see how obtaining 5 pieces of contrived information, nor flipping through a stack of papers, constitutes big data. First of all, there was no explanation on what big data was supposed to be, in the context of this module. As one of the latest internet buzzwords, it seems that this module has taken it upon itself to introduce another interpretation of big data, in this case, "meaningless data". Perhaps it would be more effective for students to be able to "reflect on" the missions, *after* having the concepts and implications of "big data" explained to them -- would it not? ---------------------------------------------------------------------- In summary, his statements are frankly dismissive and condescending of students' experiences, and gives students the impression that their concerns are simply invalid. Is this the way that professors are supposed to respond to student feedback? See? Straight from the horse's mouth. Unbelievably condescending and dismissive. In summary: literally the biggest bullshit mod ever.

Taken in AY 15/16 Semester 2 Lecturer: Associate Professor Ren Weiqing Tutor: Associate Professor Ren Weiqing Expected Grade: B+ Grade: A- Assessment and workload: - 5% Tutorial attendance (Free marks, I got 5%, just attend all his lectures since attendance is randomly taken 5 times.) - 20% Homework (There's 5 sets. Each homework has 2 questions. Very tedious questions that have to be done by hand. I probably got about 18.7%) - 75% final exam (I find this really heavy.) - No midterm test, which is very scary as the final exam makes or breaks your grade. - No helpsheet and no calculator allowed for the final exam, which was absolutely disastrous. - No webcast as the venue is S16-0307 which is a large sized tutorial room. Experience: - I have mixed feelings about this module. There are 6 chapters of this module, mainly vector/matrix norms, linear systems of equations, nonlinear systems of equations, initial value problems for ODEs, boundary value problem for ODEs and a short chapter on monte-Carlo methods. It is a continuation of MA2213 and explores more numerical methods to solve equations. Some of the concepts intersect with MA2213 concepts, which is a good thing, but this module explores it in somewhat greater depth. The interesting things come when ODEs are introduced. Instead of analytical methods to solve ODEs to obtain closed form expressions, numerical methods are introduced. The last chapter on Monte-Carlo methods is rather interesting as it is something totally new to me; it involves estimating quantities using expectations of pdfs. Prof Ren is an ok lecturer. It’s his 2nd time teaching this module and he explains concepts well mostly. Sometimes in some lectures, it feels like he didn’t prepare for the lesson as he stammers a lot. But most of the time he teaches rather smoothly. He derives the numerical methods for us to see on the whiteboard and tries to explain the motivation behind them. He focuses a lot on the numerical methods and results and doesn’t go deep into proofs, which may or may not be a good thing. There’s really hardly any analysis of numerical methods in this module, contrary to the name of the module. In addition, the numerical methods are taught in a Matlab way, which doesn’t appeal to me as I’m really bad at programming in general. The algorithms taught are pseudocodes to be coded into Matlab to do the approximations for us. Prof Ren also takes the 2 Matlab tutorial slots personally and marks assignments personally. No solutions uploaded so we don’t really know what he looks out for in marking… - Tutorials aren’t very useful. This module has no written tutorial questions. In the entire semester we only had 10 assignment questions + past year paper questions to refer to for the exam. The tutorials are actually Matlab coding sessions. Every single tutorial is done in the Matlab computer lab. Prof Ren is really kind to provide us the codes to implement and modify to solve the tutorial questions. It’s very helpful if you’re good at Matlab programming or want to see how Matlab implements the methods. These questions don’t help at all in the final exam. I attended all the tutorials and watched how my friend does the coding as I’m bad at coding. - Midterm test doesn’t exist. Final exam makes or breaks your grade. - Final exam gave me a lot of pressure since it weighs 75% of the course grade. Being unable to use a calculator is terrible. It gives us a huge handicap as this is a numerical module after all! No helpsheet as well. This is pressurising as we had to memorise all the algorithms except for the really complicated ones, variable by variable, index by index. Surprisingly Prof Ren set a manageable paper this time round. He smiled and said there would be MCQs and fill in the blanks and he really made it happen. Furthermore, instead of the 3x3 matrices in the past year paper, he gave us 2x2 matrices which are much easier to work with. In the exam I used the first 10 mins to write down all the formulae/algorithms I memorised, so as to ease my memory load. This worked out well as I was able to do the paper in a more relaxed manner. The exam used almost all of the stuff taught in the 6 chapters. Conclusion: - I have mixed feelings about this module. The content isn’t difficult as it’s just numerical methods. I believe anybody can do it since it’s just application of formulae and algorithms. The difficult part would memorising all the formulae/algorithms for the final exam, and the tutorial questions which require modifying Matlab code. Other than that, it is an eye opener as we’re exposed to many numerical methods which vary in efficiency to solve equations, as well as the introduction to Monte-Carlo methods. I would recommend this module to people who are interested in numerical methods.

AY2020/21 Sem 2 Lecturer: Mr Ravi Suppiah Assessment Tutorial Attendance & Participation (5%) Midterm (15%) Project (40%) Final Exam (40%) Overall Experience I personally found CG2271 to be a very enriching CEG module that went deeper in covering the intersection between software and hardware applications. The module not only covered the course content in great detail, but also gave us significant hands-on experience where we could regularly apply the learned content in the lab sessions and our project. Real-time operating systems are very important and fundamental in applications such as embedded systems and robotics, and the module enabled us to learn and appreciate how it is used in the context of a vehicle robot. Course Content The course was split into two different parts. The first half of the course covered fundamental embedded system concepts. The second half built on the concepts taught in the first half in the context of RTOS concepts. The Keil µVision IDE was used for programming on the FRDM KL25Z micrcontroller board. 1st Half: Software Design Basics, CPU, GPIO, Interrupts, Timers & Serial Communications 2nd Half: Scheduling, Concurrency, Context Switching, State Transition, Priorities, Messaging & Task Synchronisation (Introduction to data types used in RTOS such as Flags, Semaphores, Mutexes, Message Queues, etc), Memory, Address Decoding and Direct Memory Access. Do check out to learn about the various task synchronisation methods and data types that we regularly used throughout the second part of the module. Lectures During the weekly once two-hour lecture sessions, Prof Ravi would introduce the course content (mentioned above) and explain the individual concepts in detail. I personally liked his teaching style as he would include polls for students to answer and test their concepts and learn from them, in addition to pausing during the lectures to explain how the different concepts (even content covered across weeks) would interact with each other using annotations. He would also regularly use the FRDM KL25Z board data sheet to explain how the concepts will work. Towards the end of the lecture, he would introduce us to what we will do for that week's lab session including demos and review how the concepts we learned earlier in the lecture are applied here. I would recommend not skipping the lectures as it actually helps in understanding the content and clear common misconceptions. Lab Sessions The lab sessions were very useful in enabling us to apply the concepts that we learned during the lecture. This is a good opportunity to truly test your understanding of the concepts and experiment with what is expected to work. The sessions are two hours long and provide sufficient time in collaborating with your project team-mates (discussed in the next session). Project The lab sessions were definitely useful in helping me learn the necessary concepts that I later applied during the project component in this module. For our project, we can choose our members (groups of three) and we will be required to assemble and program a robot based on the RTOS concepts that we learned. We were required to develop a simple Android App using the MIT App Inventor to use serial communications to control the RC car's functions that we programmed, namely movement, LEDs, audio etc. At the end of the module, students will be graded based on how fast their robot moves through two challenges of a competition run (we were ranked on a leaderboard and our grading is based on our rank in the individual challenges). We also had to submit a report detailing the software architecture of our robot, the code we wrote to program the robot, and a video that reflects our entire project learning experience. Working on the project takes more time than the other components of this module, but this is where the application of the theory to practice comes into the picture. Tutorials The tutorials enabled us to internalise what we had learned in both the lectures and the labs and apply them in the form of worksheet problems. They were held for an hour on a weekly basis, and attendance is taken. Your participation (sharing screen to show your answers) during tutorials are counted towards your grading for the module. The tutorials always helped me to resolve any misconceptions that I had. Mid-terms The closed-book midterms were in the format of a LumiNUS quiz with 15 multiple-choice questions that tested your understanding of the concepts covered in the first half of the module. Do note there are questions in the mid-terms that are tricky and really test your understanding of the concepts. You are allowed to refer to the KL25Z data sheet during the mid-terms. You are also allowed to bring in your own one-page cheat sheet. Finals The closed-book finals on LumiNUS have just as high of a weightage as your project, so do ensure that you have revised your concepts well before taking them. You are not allowed to bring in your cheat sheet to the exams but a reference sheet with the documentation of the RTOS data types is provided. All the questions are open-ended, unlike the mid-terms. The finals tested the RTOS concepts covered in the second half of the module in greater depth. There were also questions where we had to write code in the solution boxes. The programming of the robot during my project helped me in answering these questions. All in all, CG2271 is a module with a manageable workload that I personally found quite exciting. I have also been able to apply what I learned in this module in my other extracurricular robotics projects - this mod is indeed quite useful! Also, big thanks to Uncle Jalil in the lab for helping us whenever we needed assistance.

Took this on AY20/21 Sem 1 Lecturer - Dr Priya Jaradi Experience: (10/10) Workload: Seminar Participation (20%) Seminar Presentation (20%) Mid-Term Paper (30%) - 3000 words Final Test (30%) - 2 hours plus, open book, no word count limit This 3k module definitely was the highlight for this semester because I really love the way Dr Priya teaches and articulate clearly about her content. Her slides are loaded with lots of information but also necessary and useful for me to understand the different concepts revolving around the idea of collecting as an activity and collections in the museum. Even the topic was very intriguing because normally, one would not associate the action of collecting as something important or worth learning in an university setting but its definitely an eye opener for me to learn that there are dedicated scholars in the world that spend their life researching on a seemingly trivial action. Another plus point for me was that the structure of the lessons was really well executed. We first started off with the introductory lesson on learning why humans collect and went on to learn about various modes of collecting such as the souvenir, fetishistic and the systematic. We were also introduced to case studies of collections from the Habsburg Kunstkammer, Emperor Rudolf II’s collections, Jehangir’s collections, Ming China collecting activities, The Louvre collections, Baroda’s collection, Kemal’s fetishistic collections in Orhan Pamuk’s novel “The Museum of Innocence” etc. We were also told to use theories of collecting to understand these case studies collecting practice such as Pierre Bourdieu’s theory of taste, theory of liminality and ritual etc. Perhaps the only downside to this module was that there was a lot to read. We had to complete the whole book written by Craig Clunas’s “Superfluous Things: Material Culture and Social Status in Early Modern China,” finish Orhan Pamuk’s novel along with other readings. But I guess this was pretty normal in a history module… Advice: Start your reading early, try to finish all the readings so that you know what to say in the seminar. Grade: A

under Prof Yair Zick. This module is a so-called "mezzanine" module - it is dual-coded, undergraduate students take the module as CS4261 and postgraduate students take this module as CS5461. CS4261 students take a final exam, while CS5461 students do a pair project in place of the final exam. (I did CS4261.) This module covers the basics of game theory (Nash equilibrium, social optimality), cooperative games (core, Shapley value), and some mechanism design. Various types of games (routing games, various instances of cooperative games, Nash bargaining) and mechanisms (stable matching, allocation of indivisible goods, rent division, auctions, facility location on a line) are discussed. Graded components: - Assignments ×8 (30%) - In-class quizzes ×2 (30%) - Final exam (35%) - Class participation (5%) There are eight graded assignments throughout the course of this module; these assignments are take-home assignments and students generally have at least one week to complete each assignment. There are two in-class quizzes and one final exam (CS5461 students do not have a final exam, but still need to complete the two quizzes). The weekly tutorials are mainly used to discuss the solutions of the graded assignments, and are generally quite interactive due to the small size of tutorial groups. Quizzes have similar structure to the final exam, so one may consider them to be "midterms" instead. Quizzes and finals are closed-book (with help sheet). There are no group projects for those taking CS4261. There is a significant amount of mathematical proofs in this module. Lectures contain some proofs (or general ideas of the proofs), and students are expected to prove various statements in the graded assignments and exams. Students may have an advantage if they are comfortable with general proving techniques, calculus (differentiation), combinatorics (permutations, counting), probability (expectation), mathematical analysis (metrics, compactness, limits), and the max-flow min-cut theorem. About 50-80% of each graded assignment comprises of proof-based questions; the rest are computation questions. Quizzes and exams have slightly less proof-based questions. Prof Yair is a good speaker and his lectures are quite engaging. With sufficient attention, most of his lectures can be readily followed. He focuses more on the intuition of the proofs rather than the details. There were a few mathematical/logical errors in his lectures, which may be a source of confusion for students who try to work out the details of the proofs. Overall, I've quite enjoyed Prof Yair's lectures.

SC2216 AY2015/2016 SEMESTER 2 I don't major in Sociology and took this module as a UE because its content sounded very relevant and applicable to real life, and I was interested to learn more about something so integral to daily life, and living in general. I had no prior experience with sociology modules, so I didn't really know what to expect. 1) GRADING: Tutorial attendance and participation - 20% Three Response Papers - 30% Final Exam - 50% 2) WORKLOAD: Readings were quite tough to cope with, which was surprising for me because they're usually manageable. There were about 2-4 sets per week, and each set had 10-20ish pages. Some of the readings were written by philosophers, and I found myself re-reading things twice or thrice just trying really hard to fully comprehend each statement. I also tend to do a lot of highlighting and annotating when covering readings, which is probably why I took so long and found myself struggling to finish them. Having said that, those that I did plough through were very insightful, and thought provoking. Some readings were from biographies, and anecdotes tend to be easier to read and digest. Regurgitation of readings isn't very helpful; they're more to guide you in understanding theories that you are then expected to apply to your own examples. 3) TUTORIALS: My tutor was Ms Ambika Aiyadurai. Tutorials were 2 hours fortnightly, and for my tutorial they would be split into two segments. The first hour is spent with your small group, discussing answers to questions that the tutors will email you with regards to the readings (the worksheets are about three pages long). You won't need to present them to the class, but you'll just be expected to contribute to the discussion. The second hour is used by Ambika to consolidate the discussions and elaborate on the theories and examples raised. Tutorials went by pretty fast for me, unlike some tutorials that tend to just drag on. I found them pretty useful because I got to clarify theories or definitions that I didn't understand with my classmates, and sharing our personal examples made it a lot easier to understand things that were previously unclear out of context. Ambika is familiar with the content, and quite eloquent with her explanations, so I enjoyed listening to her. (Sidenote: I realised in tutorials that the struggle with readings was not entirely universal, as many classmates managed to keep quite on task, so don't let that scare you off! It really depends on the individual.) 3) LECTURES: Lectures were conducted weekly by Dr George Radics, with the exception of one guest speaker. Like the tutorials, time flew quite quickly, and lectures were professional but relaxed. He'd frame each lecture based on the readings we were assigned, without repeating the contents too straightforwardly. There would be additional information - writers' background, videos, personal stories, data and all sorts of things that provided me with a more well-rounded understanding of each reading. He's quite an amiable presence, and funny as well, which made people quite receptive to his presentations. 4) ASSIGNMENTS: Three response papers, the questions of which are made available to you from the beginning of the semester (although you might not necessarily know how to answer the second two because of unfamiliarity with the relevant readings, and also the inability to link your arguments to previous readings). They're spread out about a month apart, which makes churning them out very doable. I found that my better essay had solid personal examples, and also managed to interweave explanations about theories learnt without repeating what is already in the readings. I was really shooting blind when it came to writing essays for this module, but I made a friend who was a Soci major and he very kindly sent me soft copies of papers he wrote when he was in his first year. If you manage to, do get a good friend to help you with that and thank them profusely because it really clears a lot of questions if you're as blur as I am. Writing response papers was generally quite a fun experience for me though. 5) FINAL EXAM: 4 short essays in 2 hours, each weighing 25%. One is a compulsory question, probably about a reading from one of the first few lectures (the fundamental theories that kind of set the basis for your understanding of subsequent readings), and then you can choose three other questions from nine options. Preparing for the exam was a kind of madness because of how content heavy everything (seemingly) is, but I think you just need to consolidate all your notes neatly and understand the theories and definitions, and how to apply them, rather than memorise the endless examples provided to you. I found the time given, and expected essay length, quite reasonable. It wasn't an exceptional rush. 6) OTHERS: Overall I did alright - possibly pulled down slightly by the response papers while I was still trying to navigate my way around how to write them. I was really impressed by how, despite the fact that we are given quite a wide scope of content, each week presented us with meaningful and applicable information. My favourite classes were those towards the end, where we started to apply the theories on our study of emotions (Love, Humor, Anger).

I don’t know what all of you are thinking about. ” Overview: MA1505 is the first of two modules which covers the mathematical fundamentals which are commonly used across the various fields of engineering. The main topic of interest here is calculus and its branches which are most relevant to engineering applications. This means learning about things like Taylor’s theorem, Fourier series and vector calculus, up and above the regular differentiation and integration techniques and applications covered in H2 math. This is not a light module. The content taught here is arguably the equivalent of 2 modules taken by math majors, as it covers both single and multivariable calculus. Therefore, much of the content is condensed with the focus on applying the theorems taught, and the proofs of said theorems given only a passing mention or else omitted entirely. ________ Syllabus: 1. Functions 2. Differentiation 3. Integration 4. Series 5. Vectors 6. Fourier series 7. Functions of several variables 8. Multiple integrals 9. Line integrals 10. Surface integrals Workload: There will be one 2-hour and one 1-hour lecture per week, plus 1 tutorial per week. Attendance is not graded, plus there is webcast, so you can self-study everything at home if you want. However, if you are an average student, be prepared to spend a lot of time wrapping your head around things like Fourier series, Stokes theorem, Divergence theorem etc. ________ Assessment: 20% Mid-term test: This 1-hour paper contains 10 MCQ questions and covers the first 5 chapters. The paper is harder than it looks (the mean score for my cohort was 6/10), as almost all questions require some form of computation. If you want to do well, attempt all the past year test papers uploaded on IVLE as the format of the papers are more or less the same. 80% Final exam: Although the exam covers only chapters 6-10, it is not easy as these chapters are the hardest in the module. Again, doing the past year papers helps a lot. You will also be allowed to bring in 1 cheat sheet into the exam. You can write whatever you want in the cheat sheet, but I recommend you include all the important formulas in case you forget them during the exam. If you have extra space, copying the past year paper solutions is a good idea as well. ________ Teaching Staff: Lecturer: Dr Yap Weng Yin Dr Yap was my webcasted lecturer. Taken in May-Aug 2018. This module is taken over the summer break, but MCs are credited in semester 1 of the following year. This module is "independent" to the fullest extent of the word. It is pair work (you can choose your partner), and you have the freedom to work on any software project that you would like to do, and with any kinds of technologies. You can choose how easy or how difficult you want your project to be - it really depends on what you are interested in and what you want to achieve. Most students choose to do web apps, but you can also do mobile or desktop applications or games, or even hardware projects that work with micro-controllers. This module is graded on a CS/CU basis, and (barring exceptional situations) nobody is given a CU grade - you can drop the module at any time during the summer break with no penalty. This means that you can experiment and explore various technologies without the fear of getting a bad grade. There are two compulsory face-to-face sessions in this module - "Liftoff" (the start of the journey) and "Splashdown" (the end of the journey). Some optional sessions are available during the summer break, and these sessions focus on particular technologies (e.g. iOS development, web app deployment) that might be useful. More information can be found here: There are three "levels of achievement" that are awarded depending on how complex your project is, and some prizes to be won for the top projects. However, peer voting is used for the prizes, and hence it is largely dependent on your team's popularity and the poster location that you have been assigned. I recommend that you sign up for Orbital so that you can work on something that you enjoy, rather than for the awards or prizes. Three "milestones" are spread across the summer break; for each milestone, teams have to submit a poster, video, readme, and project log. (Typically the readme will contain instructions on how to download or access the product and use it, so that evaluators can try out the product on their own computers.) These items will be used by an assigned "advisor" and some peer evaluators to evaluate your project, and evaluations determine your level of achievement. (Advisors are students that have taken Orbital before, and they are randomly assigned to teams.) The sole deliverable for Splashdown is a project poster, but it is useful to bring your functional product for demonstration. Prof Zhao Jin was the module coordinator in 2018, but the module coordinator has little impact on what students learn and do, due to the self-directed nature of this module. The module experienced an extremely high demand in 2018 - if you are interested, look out for the registration email in the second half of semester 2, and sign up immediately upon receipt of the email. Lecturer: Mr. Aaron Tan Expected: A+. Actual: A (messed up the finals) Mr. Aaron said that nobody has ever said they liked both parts of the module, so let me be the first to say that, yes, I actually enjoyed both parts of it. The first half of CS2100 starts with boolean logic and algebra, numerical system and encoding (turning numbers into binary), and tools like K-maps which are used to tackle complex boolean expressions. With this foundation, we learn logic gates (AND, OR, XOR, etc.) and how they can be used to implement basic components such as Adders, and from these very basic building blocks create medium and large scale logic and processor units. This is the lowest level you'll go to as part of a CS degree, unless you take an Electrical Engineering module, and it is very enlightening, because it shows how from fundamental components we can build complex thinking machines - functional abstraction turns up a lot in logic design. Boolean algebra is also useful, since binary will come up again in a lot of places in CS, and it pays to be familiar with them. The second half of the module covers MIPS processor design, architecture and programming. This part starts with learning the MIPS instruction format and how they correspond to certain high(er) level language constructs - in essence, learning very basic compiler design. Then, using a simplified model of the MIPS processor we are shown how the processor translates MIPS assembly language into binary which the processor then executes (the datapath). Finally pipelining (executing multiple parts of different instructions simultaneously), branch prediction and caching is introduced to speed up the processor. All of these are important concept because they are applicable elsewhere - HTTP pipelining is used by browsers speed up the loading of websites, for instance, and caching reappears as memoization in higher level programming. under Prof Ooi Wei Tsang. This is the first time this module is offered. Prof Ooi is able to illustrate the programming concepts of this module clearly and with adequate examples. This module seeks to familiarise students with various programming paradigms, such as abstraction, object-oriented programming, functional programming, and task-based parallelism. It is taught in Java, but does not expect students to have prior Java knowledge. This module is relatively manageable, and should be extremely simple for anyone who has worked on a small- to medium-sized Java, C#, or Visual Basic project before. For those with no experience with those three languages, some work may be needed to appreciate object lifetime management in Java (a sound understanding of Java's reference vs. value types is necessary for the later part of the module). A large portion of the grade for this module comes from weekly lab assignments that require students to write code based on concepts taught during the lecture. Lab assignments from the first half of the module (object-oriented programming) may be tedious, but lab assignments from the latter half of the module were mostly interesting. under Prof Leung Ka Hin. The primary focus of this module is algebraic structures such as groups, rings, and fields. Despite what the module description might suggest, most of the module is taught like a conventional algebra module (i.e. with focus on proofs related to groups, rings, and fields). Only about three weeks of lectures deal with coding theory and the applications of these algebraic structures. As compared to MA2101 (which is a prerequisite for this module), the content of MA3218 is somewhat easier to grasp. The first half of the semester (which covers groups) are generally quite intuitive. The second half of the semester (which covers rings and fields) require more effort to attain the same level of proficiency. As this module has a very small class size (6 students in my semester), the lecturer is able to give additional help to students that struggle with the content. Lectures are conducted in a classroom so there are no webcasts, but the lecture slides alone usually contain sufficient detail to understand the proofs covered during the lecture. Like most other mathematics modules, each lecture builds upon the previous lectures, so it is strongly recommended to attend all lectures. There are weekly tutorials, and they are conducted by Prof Leung himself. Students are expected to have attempted the tutorial questions before coming for the tutorial session, and they will need to present their solutions to their peers during the tutorial session. Prof Leung reads through the solutions attempted by each student (students submit their solutions via IVLE a few hours before the start of the tutorial), and during the tutorial he highlight the errors made by each student. The need for students to submit their solutions provides them with an added disincentive to fall behind in their learning. Prof Leung's accent may take some time getting used to, but there should be no significant communication difficulty in his lectures and tutorials. Midterms and finals are a mix of proof-based questions and computational questions. As the exams may be rather lengthy, practising on past year papers is important to ensure speed and accuracy.

PC2193 Experimental Physics I For the full review and more, visit Taken in AY20/21 (Post Circuit Breaker Semester) Physics Major (24 MCs) Module Coordinator: Dr Wang Xuesen Lecturers: Dr Wang Xuesen Dr Eda Goki Dr Nikolai Yakovlev Dr Ariando Ariando TA: Various (Unimportant, they do nothing at all) Grade Distribution: 2 Presentations 1 Report + Viva 3 Summaries + Viva Experiments: • Basic Diode Electronics • Ultrasonics • Magnetic Moment in Magnetic Field • X-Ray Diffraction of Crystals • UV-Vis Absorption Spectroscopy • Propagation of Laser Light • Pohl’s Pendulum • Absorption of Gamma and Beta Rays • Electron Spin Resonance • Franck Hertz • Hall Effect in P/N Type Semiconductors • Band Gap of Germanium • Brewster’s Angle • Diffraction of Circular Aperture Laboratory: The whole module is own-time-own-target, with deliverables every two weeks or so. You may choose to do any six experiments, and use them accordingly for presentation, report or summary. In total, we have to complete 2 presentations, 1 report and 3 summaries. Both the report and summary require a viva to be done as well. There are several constraints on which experiments you can use for the deliverables, which will be briefed on the first day of lab. The module is usually done in pair-work, although you can choose to do it alone. Viva: The profs will ask you on different aspects of the experiments you conduct and your report/summary. These questions can range from how you calculate errors, how you account for them or even conceptual questions about the experiment themselves. Not too challenging or scary, it is conducted as more like a personal conversation with the prof who is in charge of that particular experiment. Just have knowledge of the experiment that you conducted, the working physics behind it and the reasoning for the data analysis that you performed on your results, and you’ll pull through easily. Presentation: The presentation is held in the lab, with all the professors in attendance as graders. Each student is given 10 minutes to present, and 5 minutes for QnA. All students who are taking PC2193 are allowed to come in and spectate the presentation. The presentation is likely the first of its kind of content-grading for physics majors. It is a good opportunity to test the presentation skills of the students. I think what’s important for presentation is knowing how much to include in your slides. A brief overview of the experiment and the concepts behind it, the aim of the experiment, results and conclusion, and potential future work. You should have a good sense of the kind of data analysis needed in each experiment, and justification for every step you take in processing the results. The presentation QnA is trickier than the viva, simply because there are now more graders to bounce their questions off you to really test your understanding of the experiment. Don’t be too rushed to answer the questions, clarify and think through first before giving your answer. For my presentations, I did X-Ray Diffraction and UV-Vis Spectroscopy. Summary: Nothing much. A quick write up of the experiment, concepts, methods and results. Not too difficult. Make the font size larger to help reduce the strain on the professors’ eyes. For the summary, I did Brewster’s Angle, Magnetic Moments and Absorption of Gamma & Beta Radiation Report: An extended version of the summary. Usually for the report, more experiments would have to be done, or in further/greater detail. Here is where you can put in a lot more effort into researching the phenomena involved, and thoroughly investigate every little detail of your experiment. (If you haven’t already been doing so) For the report, I did Hall Effect in Semiconductors. Expected Grade: A-/B+ Final Grade : A- Thoughts: The most enjoyable physics module I have taken. Perhaps it is because it is the online semester, having a module that requires me to go school helped to freshen up my days and provide me an outlet to interact with people. The experiments themselves were pretty fun to do, but can be extremely frustrating at the same time. Part of the challenge of this module is troubleshooting. Sometimes, the data you obtain from the experiments can be extremely different or have very large error bars, and you would have to either find an unresolvable justification for the results or return back to the lab to attempt to get better results. This problem is especially prominent in light-based experiments, which are very sensitive and twiddly in general. Troubleshooting is a very tiring process. Fixing the experimental set-up/procedures can take hours or days, depending on how fast you arrive at the solution. Examples that I’ve encountered include swapping of samples with the lab coordinator, interchanging parts between the machines set up for our use, and redoing the experiment in more controlled settings or running them in reverse. Despite all this, I assure you the feeling of finally figuring out what went wrong and getting good results is extremely fulfilling. Personally, my favourite experiment was Hall Effect, simply because of the richness of the experiment. With many different parameters to investigate, you find that there are many different concepts and phenomena interplaying with each other that you can exploit in your report for completeness. This was the first experiment done by me and my partner, but ended up being the last deliverable to hand up. The different professors each have their own quirks and priority for learning outcomes for the module. Nikolai focuses more on experimental methods (and troubleshooting), and data analysis. Ariando usually tests concepts related to the experiment, and understanding of the student. Xuesen and Goki asks hypothetical scenarios which tests the students understanding of concepts and ability to extrapolate to different cases. I feel that this shouldn’t affect how you choose the experiments you want to do. Either way, you will have to go through all of them and the quirks of the prof-in-charge doesn’t really matter. I think choosing experiments based off your understanding would be for the best. Experiments such as Hall Effect require some knowledge of semiconductors and the different energy bands, while ESR requires knowledge on electron spin and how it interacts with external applied fields. If you lack the required background knowledge, or are a little rusty, you might want to pass up on that experiment. Understanding of the physics behind each experiment would aid you in troubleshooting, data processing, and viva/QnA later. Don’t be afraid to ask people for help. Although the TAs can be seen doing nothing and lazing about in the lab, they can be (slightly) helpful if you approach them. The lab coordinator and the supervising prof in the lab can also be approached for more directed and meaningful assistance. Teamwork is key here. Do talk to the other people doing experiments in the lab. There are some experiments that are straight up a waste of time, or simply ridiculously tedious to finish. Some experiments have tips and tricks that you need in order to get good results from. Problems that you may be facing in your experiment may have already been solved by someone else. Talking to other people and helping each other will make this module a more enjoyable one. Even for presentation, going to each other’s presentation for support (Or just to banter, the profs won’t mind too much) would make everything a lot more fun and less stressful. Get a lab partner that you are comfortable talking with. It really helps to have someone working alongside you that you can bounce ideas off and think through problems with.

He frequently brings in examples from both his clinical practice and from real-life mental health campaigns, which makes it easy for us to see the practical applications of the content being taught. Midterms consisted of about 40 MCQs, which ranged from content knowledge to diagnosis based on symptoms. Some of the diagnosis questions are quite tricky. Even so, the symptoms may be quite ambiguous, so do make sure your justifications are clear. under Prof Sanjay Jain. All lectures were recorded, and one of the tutorial groups was conducted online. This module can be roughly split into four parts (in chronological order): - Regular languages (deterministic finite automata, nondeterministic finite automata and regular expressions) - Context-free languages (context-free grammars and pushdown automata) - Turing machines - Computational complexity (time and space complexity, NP-completeness) Graded components: - Midterm 1 (25%) - Midterm 2 (25%) - Final exam (40%) - Tutorial presentations (10%) There is no group work in this module. The midterms and exam are open book (though this may be a result of conducting them online over Zoom). The midterm tests and exam contain a mix of construction and proof questions. Construction questions are those that ask for an explicit automaton or grammar that exhibits a certain property (e.g. accepts a given language), and are generally simpler. Proof questions are generally tougher, and require formal proofs. This module is taught rather rigorously -- formal proofs are covered during the lectures, and some questions in the tests and exam require students to prove given statements. However, Prof Jain seems to be rather lenient with awarding partial marks for proof questions -- if the general idea of the proof is correct, the student should obtain most of the marks for the question. Most of Prof Jain's lectures are moderately paced, and he explains each concept well, mostly without making assumptions about students' prior knowledge. This makes his lectures quite manageable most of the time. CS1010FC AY13/14 Sem 2 Taught by: Prof Ben Leong, Brian Koh and Michelle Teo Introduction: CS1010FC (CS1010 Flipped Classroom) is part of NUS’ internal Massive Online Open Course series, or iMOOC for short. It is intended to cover programming methodology and is targeted at Returning National Servicemen (RNSmen) who have served their compulsory two years of National Service. CS1010FC is intended to cover all the basics to computing, by using Python; an easy to understand high level language that is written using C. You will cover a wide variety of topics and understand what it means to use a computer that to translate a “Human Readable Essay” into reality, or as it is termed; functional abstraction to create something that emulates reality. Lecturer: Professor Ben Leong, School of Computing, National University of Singapore. Professor Ben Leong taught this module for AY2013/2014 iMOOC Semester, and on an interesting note for those who are interested, he is a Masters in Electrical Engineering and a PhD in Computer Science from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, and on a side note is the person in NUS who sends Computing Science majors to Google. Aside from that he is also employed as the Director of Experimental Systems and Technologies Laboratory as of July 2014. Professor Ben Leong began this initiative of establishing CS1010FC as a means to allow fresh incoming students exposure to actual computing over a comfortable period of time intended to accommodate to a variety of students, and actually does this in his free time because he believes strongly in teaching and teaching to the masses; he is also continually looking for ways to improve the iMOOC system on CS1010FC’s end, and will always be friendly to students and help them enthusiastically. On a personal note, Professor Ben is a very intriguing individual. He has shown great enthusiasm as well as initiative in taking time off his schedule to come and give consultation slots, along with his Teaching Assistants. If you get him in your normal semesters, you are very blessed. What content is covered, what are the delivery methods, and how is it graded? The content covered will be exactly as that of a normal semester CS1010X (X can be any code) module; except it is held over January to June. Content delivery is via a series of Online Lectures which you will have to download (fret not about where to go – they will direct you) and attend online tutorials, discussions, recitations, and complete missions. Missions being assignments which you have to complete online. The content covered is short and sweet, and viewable anytime due to the cyberspace medium, which is so because the intended objective is understanding in a short time anywhere! During my iMOOC, the iMOOC started using face-to-face (FTF) sessions to cover the best of both worlds: Online and FTF, to cater to a variety of students. Furthermore towards the end of the course, CS1010FC will cover two things not covered in CS1010X during normal semesters: Object Oriented Programming, and Basic Introduction to C. For those in Engineering who have to take CS1020E, CS1010FC covers literally (in Python language) CS1010E (C) and CS1020E (C++). How cool is that? For the grading portion we have a midterm exam, a practical exam, online assignment portion and a final exam, all contributing to your grade. The weightage may be subject to change, so I will not publish that information here lest it conflicts with the NUS SoC’s arrangement. How can I be prepared for this iMOOC CS1010FC? The content covered is very thorough and you need not go to take additional classes to try and be ahead. Even if you have had prior experience in computing in Junior College, Polytechnic or external course, few would usually come close to the content that is being covered, or the depth, and so people are more or less on equal footing when they begin. Bluntly put – computing at the university level is not easy to learn. So come with an open mind and learn. But if you want to be prepared, the only thing you can do is purchase a computer and download Python. But even so, please wait until Professor Ben announces which version of Python you have to do. Or for all you know he may be using a very different language! What if I am still serving NS during the period of iMOOC? Don’t worry – the intention of iMOOC itself is to specifically cater to RNSmen, especially those who are still serving. As long as you have your interest, the teaching staff can accommodate, and their online sessions are usually held such that you will be able to attend; be it at night or on weekends when you are free. Furthermore, the staff are very helpful and will do their best to answer any queries or assist you in any problem that comes up. After all that is the purpose of iMOOC. (Or at least, rest assured Professor Ben Leong will make them helpful; but generally they are very helpful.) Recommendation is STRONG for Four reasons: 1 – If you clear this iMOOC early you need not take it in the subsequent semester as an Advanced Placement Credit with Grade (APG), which is 4 Modular Credits. 2 – If you are not planning to use it as an APG you can still pick it up so you can learn a new language in the future. 3 – The content covered is very thorough and extensive: it will definitely help you in shaping your perspective before entering NUS, and also Professor Ben will cover on higher level concepts such as thinking about Life. (No, I am serious, he will cover that as well. You’d be surprised at what life should be like and where one is now.) 4 – Period of time is over 6 months. That allows people to slowly get back into the habits they need. How do I apply for this iMOOC? Look out for a letter from NUS for incoming undergraduate students to participate in iMOOC. If you do get it (all RNSmen should get it) you can follow the instructions to enrol and request for the modules, including CS1010FC as well. The letter should come a few months short of the calendar year which you enrol in. (You are matriculating in year 2015, so the letter should come in year 2014.) What if I intend to drop it halfway, let’s say I lose my interest as I do not want to continue it any further? I cannot say if this will apply to all iMOOC years, but for my experience iMOOC allows us to take the module until the halfway mark period and then we have to start paying fees; this allows us to gauge whether we do want to take it – a mercy compared to semester module dropping.

Taken in AY 2016/2017 Sem 1 Lecturer: A/Prof Chin Chee Whye Grade: A+ Unlike what many of what my friends have said, I believe that you do not need a huge background of Mathematics to do well in this module. Personally, I did not even complete any JC Math courses (i.e. I did not have a prerequisite of H2 Math, neither have I participated in any competition math either). Nevertheless, what you do need is a (very) open mind, as well as to let go of your intuitionistic ideas about mathematics. Lectures in this module are dry, but they are very informative. Prof Chin really takes pride in the rigourous treatment of Mathematics and he doesn't appreciate leaps in logic. He also emphasises that one cannot use a result he has not proven yet. As many people noted, homeworks are noticeably challenging, but I urge people to seriously take the time to figure it out on your own. It is ok to take 3-4 hours on one homework (anyways we always have 2 weeks to complete it). It is crucial because it really trains your mind to solve future math problems one may encounter. Tests and the final exam are, in my opinion, quite manageable, provided that one has diligently and consistently done his homework. As usual, there was negative marking on the true/false questions but it wasn't really a big deal in my opinion. The proving questions were a little on the hard side, so one must prepare thoroughly before the tests and exams. A little word of warning: this module is not easy, and don't think you can get away by slacking or doing last minute revisions. The concepts taught are very abstract and one must consistently be on your feet. Complacency is a big killer for this module, as with sticking with your intuitionistic understandings of Mathematics. Many of my friends who have taken H3 Math or have done competition math fell into this trap and did not do as well as they had hoped to. Nevertheless, if one wants to get a feel of abstract mathematics, this is an excellent eye-opener module. I highly recommend this module to anyone who is passionate about mathematics.

Overview German 2 is a continuation of German 1 and uses the same textbook, proficiency level A1. German 2 is the same as what you would expect in German 1. Maybe catch up on some German media during the break so that resuming your German lessons won't come too much as a shock. This consists of a short forum post, reading (voice record), writing, and video project. These should each take 1-2h. There are 2 semester tests, one in week 8 and one in week 13, which tests on listening, comprehension, grammar, and conversation structuring. Workload Prof Chan is a very experienced teacher and frequently engages students in conversation so this keeps us on our toes. He also shares various nuggets of information from his personal experiences in Germany and this keeps lessons interesting. You should come to tutorials prepared with your completed Hausaufgaben, which should take max 1h for each tutorial. The biggest workload imo is having to attend 4 hours of tutorials every week. As an Engr student, the workload on the whole is acceptable. Conclusion With a higher level mod, students tend to be more enthusiastic about learning the language. While this can spur learning, it can also make it harder to score. I wasn't as enthusiastic and had other mods to contend with, thus I studied less and scored worse for semester tests (bottom 25%) as compared to German 1, even though I was learning and handling tutorials just fine. Despite expecting a B-, I ended with a B+. Not sure what happened to the bell curve, but more importantly was to participate in tutorials actively and enjoy learning a new language.
