ME1102 Difficulty: Easy especially if you can get the new topics down Workload: Low Studio Slot: 1200-1400 Thursdays at LT2 Tutorial Slot: 1600-1800 Thursdays at E3-06-03 Tutor(s): Lect ONG Eng Teo Grade weightage: 50% Studio 10% Mid Term Test 40% Final Exam Expected Grade: B+/A- Grade: A+ Additional remarks: Tutorial Compulsory: No but the mid term test was during that slot Flipped Classroom: Yes Open book: Yes for both the mid term test and final exam Topics Covered: Week 1: Introduction lecture by Dr TAN Danielle S, no studio or tutorial Week 2: Guesstimation, significant figures, units and dimensions, and safety Week 3: Forces Week 4: More on forces and Newton’s laws of motion Week 5: Work, energy and power, and momentum part 1 Week 6: Work, energy and power, and momentum part 2 Week 7: Stress and strain Week 8: Deformation in structures Week 9: Deflection of beam Week 10: Heat transfer Week 11: No classes due to Deepavali Week 12: Buoyant force Week 13: Fluid mechanics Final exam topics: All Thoughts: Most of this module felt very unnecessary; only the topics in weeks 7-10 and 13 were new to anybody who never took A level H2 physics (let’s call these “the new topics”) with the rest of the module seeming like a big waste of time, having to revise A level physics all over again. It would have been fine if there were people who really needed the revision but it is quite unnecessary because I believe engineering students who need to know physics but did not take A level physics have their own bridging module (if I am wrong then please correct me). I could rant about that but moving on, most people would definitely not know much about new topics so I would advise everybody to just read up on that at the start of the semester to get familiar with it if you take a long time to master subjects. There are not much practice questions provided so mastering these concepts now could be a challenge. If you did A Level physics, you should not need to read up on the reading materials even though the teaching faculty strongly encourages everybody to unless you have really forgotten the concepts in physics. Tutor: Dr Ong Eng Teo is very friendly and he is a good teacher. He is also very open to helping you out if you need advise on things out of this module. Studio: This is basically just lab but in groups of four to five where you perform experiments which are not at all difficult, it is just time-consuming. You have to gather the results and process them through Excel (calculations and graphs) then type up a report/worksheet using that and submit it at the end of the session. There are guiding questions for the report so no need to worry about not knowing what to write. Most people should get close to if not full marks for this component. The teacher facilitating your studio is the same as your tutor and there are TAs assisting him. You can ask them any questions throughout, even sometimes on what to write for the report because the report has a lot of weird questions in which you may not know what answer the questions is expecting even though you may understand everything that is going on in the experiment. So when in doubt, just ask, if not you will not get the full marks although they are very lenient with their marking already anyway. Tutorials: There are questions to be done before these with answers provided but they are not really necessary to do. The tutorial does not have enough time to cover some of the questions so the tutorial is mostly for covering gaps, like if you could not obtain the answer provided or if you do not understand that week’s topic. Mid term test: Given how only A level topics are covered before recess week, this test is basically just an A level revision test, only easier with an attempt to increase the difficulty through trick questions (using weird units, irrelevant/redundant information, etc.). There are 15 MCQs and each question answered correctly is worth 2 marks, those left blank 0 marks, and those answered wrongly -1 marks; they are to be completed in 45 minutes during your tutorial which is more than enough time. Given how the studio is not at all difficult for everybody to score in, this is one of the things that can differentiate the skilled from the less skilled, or rather it is supposed to but it really does not; with how easy the test is and how many trick questions there are, it only differentiates those who are careful/check properly from those who do not. Final exam: There are 40 MCQs to be done in 2h with the same negative marking scheme as in the mid terms. The only difficult part of this are the new topics if you are not fully familiar with them with the rest of the questions being of moderate difficulty, or maybe even slightly easier than that. The time limit and the lack of practice with the new topics are what can make this a killer.

CS1010FC AY13/14 Sem 2 Taught by: Prof Ben Leong, Brian Koh and Michelle Teo CS1010FC serves as a good stepping stone for (just about) anyone who is going to enroll in NUS soon, especially for those whose brains have collected dust and dirt after their numerous field camps in NS. Trust me, at first your thought processes may feel slow and cumbersome, but after awhile, they'll get faster. The online course was spread out over a duration of 6 months for me, so workload was easily managed. It utilizes an online system called Coursemology for homework distribution/submission, lecture slides, past year exam questions, a forum for Q&A, contests, and other paraphernalia. Video lectures are used, as well as WebEx tutorials and recitations, so mostly everything can be done from the comfort of home, except for exams (which allow for 1-2 cheat sheets anyways) and the class-based Recitations/Tutorials. A part of the final grade will be based on how much participation was done in Coursemology - so do everything. Professor Ben is a very good and experienced teacher. Not only does he keep the in-class sessions interesting, he imparts life lessons too. His flexible Teaching Assistants are dedicated to our development in this course, and extra help is definitely given when needed. Homework is graded quickly, and occasional comments are given for self-improvement. The programming language used in this class is Python, which is very syntactically light when compared to others. This is to allow for easier problem solving, avoiding a lot (A LOT) of unnecessary trouble searching for that missing semicolon at the end of code statement, hence keeping our focus towards formulating a solution. Later on there will be some C, but the problem solving methods are usually more important than the syntax (unless stated otherwise). The whole idea of this class is to manage complexity. Not just the complexity of the problem itself, but to sort through an infinite number of solutions to find the most efficient one. Problem solving skills and methods that are taught in this class can also be implemented in other applications besides computing. To summarize, this module is a must do, especially if this is one of your core modules. The basic material is important, and the long duration of this class will help to strengthen your understanding of them better than a regular-length module would.

Lecturer: Mr Jonathan Sim Tutor: Mr Reeve Tham Grade: A- Course Weightage: Class Participation – 20% Pre-Tutorials – 15% Online Quizzes – 20% Video Presentation & Report (Group) – 35% Reflection Paper – 10% As a compulsory GE module for FASS students, I admit I was annoyed to have had 'GET1050 - Computational Reasoning' forced upon me. We were introduced to Microsoft Excel features such as pivot tables, which can be used for data analysis but a main bulk of the content focused on theories like confirmation bias, greedy rule algorithms and social network analysis. More importantly, we were taught how to do simple VBA coding on Microsoft Excel too. Coursework wise, I gotta give props to the lecturer for the well-edited online lecture videos although it was slightly too "onz" and energetic for my liking haha. There were 4 pre-tutorials that we needed to complete. The first three were written assignments and the last one was to code a simple game on Microsoft Excel. The pre-tutorials were designed to mimic real-world examples but I feel like everything was very fluff. We also had online quizzes every week, which was rather annoying to do. While we have 5 attempts for each quiz, the answer options change. They also don't show you which question you got wrong (in case people cheat); so for a slow learner like me it was actually very counter-effective, and I eventually ended up not giving two shits about the quizzes. For the group project, we had to do a report and a 8-minute video presentation on which people groups we think deserve to be vaccinated from a virus first. There were many considerations and it opened my eyes to how unreliable algorithms can be. Lastly, we had to write a simple final reflection paper on the group project; nothing too difficult. Overall, this module falls short in getting us to think and reason computationally. All I can remember is sleepless nights from trying to understand what's happening and spending hours on Excel only to forget everything. Oh well, I wish they let us choose our own GET module instead.

under Prof Damith Chatura Rajapakse. This module is the first group software project for computer science students. For most computer science students, this module is twinned with CS2101. Some students that are enrolled in special programmes (such as the University Scholars Programme, or a double degree programme where SoC is not their home faculty) often do not need to take CS2101. CS2103T is the twinned version of this module, while CS2103 is the non-twinned version. Lectures and exams are combined and they are identical for CS2103 and CS2103T students. However, CS2103T students form project groups with other CS2103T students only, because the same project group is required for CS2101. Project groups are typically formed during the first CS2101 class. The main reference material for this module is on this website ( ). There are two parts to this module - the lectures (which closely follow the reference website) and the group project. For most students, the group project takes up the bulk of time spent on this module. Students were required to either enhance an existing address book application ( ) or morph (i.e. convert) it for a different use case. The "morph" route is considered the high-risk-high-reward option, because a failure to complete morphing the product is likely to result in an unusable application. The address book application is written in Java, and students will only be graded on the Java code that they have written. This project is graded on a number of aspects, including: product testing by peers and tutors, review of code and coding style, difficulty of your contributions (listed in your project portfolio page), and quality of documentation. The project group must consist of students from the same tutorial group; when I took the module, each group was required to contain at least one male, one female, one Singaporean, and one non-Singaporean student. I recommend that you find a group of 3-5 people whom you are comfortable working with before the semester starts, and ballot for the same tutorial group. This helps to alleviate much of the uncertainty with group work. Despite what CS2101 tutors might suggest regarding group formation, having more groupmates who are experienced in writing medium-scale software is beneficial to the amount of polish you can give to the product (which results in better project grades). The lectures are about programming practices and design patterns (with a focus on OOP in Java), as well as working in a software development team. They are geared towards working with medium- to large-scale software projects, and those intending to work in software engineering in the future. The content for the final exam comes from the lectures and reference materials. Being sufficiently acquainted with the main reference material (the CS2103/T website) will allow you to do well for finals. There are no midterms. Finals are closed-book (with help sheet). The finals come in two parts - the first part is 100 True/False questions to be answered within an hour, and the second part is four open-ended questions to be answered within another hour.

Taken in AY18/19, under Prof Nina Powell. 15% Response paper 1 15% Response paper 2 10% Group project 20% Participation and professionalism 40% Finals First off, I just want to say that I LOVED this module. Morality in itself is such an interesting topic, and Dr. P's take on it is really eye-opening. Easily my favourite module of all time. Readings: This is Dr. P's 5th semester teaching this module. She has made tremendous changes to the syllables over the years. For one, the reading list has been shortened considerably, about 3 papers a week. Some weeks she only prescribed 1 paper. The most number of readings was 5, and that was only for one particular week. The papers are all easy to understand, so I'd say overall the workload was very manageable. 20% participation + professionalism: The module was conducted entirely flipped. You watch the e-lecture before coming to class (about 15-20mins long), then class time is used for discussion. This is where you get your participation points. She has this system where every time you speak, you're awarded 5 points. If you say something that impresses her, she'll give 10 points. And if you say something really mind-blowing it'll be 15 points. At the end of 13 weeks you add up all the points, and that's one portion of your class part + professionalism marks. The other portion comes from 5 online quizzes that you have to complete. The quizzes are marked for completion, not content. Complete quizzes add to your class part + professionalism marks. If you don't complete them then points are deducted. Points are also deducted if you display unprofessional conduct, such as plagiarising or being a nuisance in class, that kinda thing. But I don't think anyone got their marks deducted. It's just there to serve as a deterrent. 30% response papers: 500 words. One due before reading week and the other in week 12/13. The response papers were a little tricky at first, I'll admit. She doesn't want you to present a balanced argument like most other arts mods. She wants you to argue a point and defend it with your life. There's no need to be balanced or on-the-fence. You have to be really in-depth. Present just one or two pieces of evidence and keep fleshing them out. She'll give some example papers for you to follow their writing style. I struggled with the first RP and got a B-, but I expected that. I worked harder at delivering the kind of writing she wanted for RP 2 and managed to get an A :) 10% group project: Present on any topic related to morality (LGBT, incest, euthanasia). Dr. P doesn't care about fancy slides or presentation styles. She even said it's fine if just one person stood in front of the class and read off a script. It's the content she cares about. She wants you to use that moral situation you picked and relate it back to things you learnt in class. My advice would be to pick a topic that is novel and interesting. That way you can probably pique her interest as well. My group did our presentation on lab-grown meat (look it up, it's really cool) and we got an A+. 40% final: 10 short-answer questions, choose 7. 2 essay questions, choose 1. The SAQs are basically quiz questions. So if you've been doing the quizzes then you're good to go. Literally some of the questions on the finals were exactly the same as the ones on the quiz. The essay questions are like response papers. 500 words, pick a stand and defend it with your life. The essay questions are the big philosophical questions that have no right or wrong answer. E.g. "Where does morality come from?" If you have done the response papers properly you should be prepared for the essay question. Overall, I really liked this module. I loved coming to class, and I really wish we could have more time discussing morality. The content is just mind-blowingly interesting, the workload was manageable, and Dr. P really challenges you to not just learn the content, but develop a deep understanding of morality. Be prepared to think hard about moral issues, embrace that you won't have any of your questions answered, just because those answers don't exist right now (e.g. nobody knows exactly where morality comes from, there's just loads of theories but no one concrete answer), and engage in lots of discussion! Good luck :)

Took CS2030S in AY 2020/2021 Sem 2 under Prof Boyd Anderson and Prof Ooi Wei Tsang, not sure how much of this applies to CS2030 This module is all about teaching you how to make your code 'good' e.g. readable, flexible, and scalable. The language we used was Java, so it's not a bad idea to take this mod at the same time as CS2040S. The topics covered included OOP, Data Hiding, Generics, Typing, Nested and Local Classes, Lambdas, Streams, Lazy Evaluation, Monads, Asynchronous Programming, and Parallel Programming. The content was personally not interesting but it is definitely useful for coding in general. It starts off fairly simple but topics like Generics, Lazy Evaluation, and Asynchronous Programming can get very confusing. Lectures would have the profs go through the topics and show examples using programs. They were ok but not enthralling and the profs were a bit monotone. However, the profs are very responsive on Piazza and it's a great place to clarify any questions you have. Aside from lectures, we also had Recitations and Labs. For recitations, we were given a worksheet with questions beforehand. Then, in the recitation class itself, the TA would go through the worksheet. Attendance isn't compulsory IIRC but I'd recommend going anyway since they can help clarify any misunderstandings you have with the topic. The worksheets are short with only 3-4 questions and you aren't required to complete them so the recitations add little to the workload. They're also only an hour long. Labs I'll cover in the next section. IMPORTANT!! In this mod, we were required to SSH into the school computers and use Vim in our assessments and labs. I highly recommend learning how to use Vim beforehand since it saves you time learning it during the semester. vimtutor is a pretty good tutorial for it, and you should do a bit of actual programming in it to get the hang of it. Having some basic knowledge of Linux terminal commands is good too. Assessment Breakdown: Labs: 30% Midterms: 15% Practical Exam 1: 10% Practical Exam 2: 20% Final Exam: 25% The labs are where most of the workload in this course comes from. All in all, they are also Every week, we were required to implement a class with certain specified functionality. We were given the specifications, files, the class/method names, and test cases, but we had to code the functionality of the classes and their methods. During the Lab sessions, we would meet with the TA who would give us an overview of what we were supposed to do and then leave us to work on the lab on our own. I personally enjoyed these labs but they do take a long time, probably about 3-4 hours each week. Like the content, they start off simple but some of them can get very confusing, especially the ones involving Lazy Evaluation. The Practical Exams are like the labs but you have to do them in 2 hours which can be pretty stressful. We were allowed printed notes for these. It's a good idea to print out your Lab code since sometimes the code you have to write in the Practical Exams will be similar to the ones you wrote for the Lab. Practical Exam 1 wasn't too bad but most people got destroyed in Practical Exam 2, including me. The midterm and final exams both allow notes but they had to be printed out even though the exams were online. They start off with MCQ questions and then later on become short answer questions with a few short essay questions (like "Explain why..."). These were generally easier than Practical Exam 2 and nothing difficult if you understood the course content. Final Grade: A+ TL;DR 1 is worst, 5 is best Enjoyment: 3/5 Usefulness: 5/5 (for CS) Profs: 3.5/5 Difficulty: Some of the topics are difficult to understand. Practical Exam 2 is hard, the other assessments are easier but can still be tricky if you don't understand the topics. Workload: Quite a lot with the weekly labs. You also have to study for the exams. Should I Take It: It's required for CS. If it's not required for you but you're interested in doing coding, I recommend taking it since it's very useful.

AY 17/18 Sem 2 Lecturer: Prof Dinh Tien Cuong 20% Homework (5 sets to be completed every fortnight) 20% Midterm 60% Finals Content: Module split into two halves: first half focuses on the elephant in the room, Complex analysis, which is the study of holomorphic functions (which a whole lot nicer than real differentiable functions) and the second half is an introduction into Riemann surfaces. This course under Prof Dinh is really difficult for 2 main reasons: the entire complex analysis part of the module is squeezed into the first 6 weeks, which can be horrendous given that it is our first time studying complex analysis and also we spent first 2-3 weeks reviewing topology. Secondly, Riemann surfaces are not exactly the easiest things to study as an undergrad; to have a good grasp of it requires many areas of Mathematics: Complex Analysis (duh), Manifolds, Geometry, Topology, Group Theory. Its not easy trying to put everything together. So be warned! Lecture pace is really quick so you need to do a lot of revision so as to not fall behind (I fell behind quite often and I totally gave up for Riemann surfaces). Prof Dinh is a lecturer that focuses more on the big picture of the proof rather than the nitty gritty technicalities so I guess in some sense it is good because it helps to develop some intuition as to why certain results are true. Tutorial: Tutorials are not easy. But they contain many useful tricks and results essential to the study of complex analysis and Riemann surfaces respectively. The questions are not important but the way of thinking and proving are more essential than what is presented. Tests/Exams: Thankfully, Prof Dinh is quite merciful when it comes to exam/tests. Computational question usually comes out for exams and usually only 1/2 questions will be really difficult. Prof Dinh is also very lenient with his allocation for marks (even homework) I think its one of the few modules that you have to work hard consistently because it is very fast paced and the content is difficult. I think the end results can be rewarding but then again if you have no interest in learning Riemann surfaces, perhaps the iteration of S-mod under Prof Dinh is not suitable for you.

As a politically neutral third year who had completed the 8-MC LC2007 Constitutional & Administrative Law module not too long ago, I was triggered to no end by the relentless use of pejoratives coupled with snide remarks during the lectures while course material was being taught. Constitutional and statutory provisions were cited only partially - in one particularly egregious case, different subsections from different sections in the statute were copied (without section numbering of course) onto consecutive slides, then labelled as something like "what the law says". Offence-creating provisions in the Defamation Act were presented without any mention of possible statutory defences. The cherry-picking list goes on. For a course that purports to discuss important freedom of speech issues, it neglects to even touch on the institutional separation of powers and other basic constitutional issues, as well as engage foundational moral/political justifications, all of which provide the necessary context for any freedom of speech discussion. Granted, these issues might not be suited for a level-1000 module. But doesn't that make it all the more dangerous to provide students with such flimsy and one-sided material, knowing that this will heavily influence their future political views? The illusion of knowledge is more dangerous than ignorance. Admin-wise, it was a **** show of the highest order. Graded assignments (scrapbook article commentaries) were supposed to be marked and returned before the next one was released/due (there were about 4) to allow students to incorporate feedback, but the first was only returned some time after the final one was released. The midterm take-home essay instructions were changed drastically a week after the initial release: the maximum word limit was changed to a minimum word count. Having already completed the assignment, I had to scramble to unpack my heavily-condensed essay into a full-length one. Clarifications and additional instructions came piecemeal, replete with glaring spelling and grammatical errors. I have never seen a more incompetent course coordinator in my life. Thankfully, tutorials cover content wholly separate from lectures. My tutor, Ms Farah, was pretty solid and attempted to facilitate candid discussions, but was sadly limited by the 45 minutes of contact time per week. Her tutorials were for the most part really engaging and made up somewhat for the lectures. Overall, this course is great for preaching and pretending to discuss stuff you don't actually know enough about to engage meaningfully. Unless you're a senior law student or have a keen interest in constitutional issues and have read up extensively enough on the same to see through the disingenuous lecture presentations. Then you won't end up echoing the political views the rest of the unwitting students have been manipulated into forming. You'll just get tilted real hard and end up writing a scathing NUSMods review. PSA for the law students thinking of taking this course: if you're ok with trash assignment instructions and can hold in the tilt, TAKE THIS MOD. The entire course content, readings and slides combined, is something like 10% of one single topic in LC2007. I kid you not. There is ZERO new material so you have to study absolutely nothing. If you want an easy A/A+ just parrot the political views pushed here, don't be me and take the path of most resistance by flaming the examiners by picking apart the essay questions and calling the phrasing "disingenuous" in your response. For everyone else thinking of taking this mod, be warned: take everything your learn here with about as much salt as there is in the Salar du Uyuni. There ARE very valid and important points raised, but their presentation is incredibly one-sided. Side note: I was alerted by some people that my review was taken down after I posted it. The irony is not lost on me but here's a repost. Update: this is the THIRD repost.

For those who are thinking of taking CS3216 in AY2014/15 Sem 1, I have written a more detailed post-mortem of my CS3216 experience here: This module has been FUN. Never have I built so many products within a span of a semester before. We had the freedom to do whatever we wanted in our assignments and final project, unlike other software engineering modules where students had to build to-do lists. However, this freedom and flexibility meant that the scope of the project depends on you. You can choose to simply meet the bare requirements or aim for the sky with a large-scale project. In my projects, my team(s) and I aimed to meet these three criteria: usable, polished, valuable. This is much unlike my past hackathon projects where I could only achieve polish-ness. A small, robust application that really works has more impact than an ambitious one that cannot be completed within the timeframe of the project. CS3216 is a huge test of versatility and my versatility was stretched near its limits throughout the course. The final project really drained me out. I was wearing multiple hats and it was tough to juggle them. In my opinion, the most important factor is good teammates. Form your team fast before they get snapped up by other people. In the first few weeks, I kinda already knew who I wanted to work with for the final project: My assignment 1 team. We knew each other well and enjoyed working with each other. Hence we did not mind spending time together hacking the final project. For the grade conscious, this module is not graded based on a bell curve, hence easily half the class will be awarded A-range grades. It was an awesome experience thanks to the great classmates around and the committed teaching team, Dr Colin Tan, Su Yuen and the TAs. Grade: A+

I really don't have much to say about this module, but here goes: Very boring, but it's not the module's fault. It's just that if you've taken literature for six years straight, you'll feel like you've gone back to Sec 1. This module is pitched at students of all levels of experience and analytical skill, and it shows. As a prospective literature major it was honestly hard to stay awake in this class. Otherwise it should be manageable, though it'll still be a leap from four ("A"s) /fifteen (IB) texts in two years. The texts aren't difficult, and neither is the analysis. Exams should be fairly easy if you've taken literature as an examinable subject before, and if you haven't, you'll usually have guiding questions to help you along. I've heard that others were better, though. Overall, this is a pretty good exposure module, but if you're already been sufficiently exposed, you're likely to be quite bored. Difficulty: if you've taken literature at O/A/IB level before, you should breeze through this. if not, should still be ok? I don't know anyone who took this without prior experience Workload: depends on how quickly you read, but there's only one take-home 1500-word essay, so I'd say pretty light Assessment: as literature exams go, these ones are pretty fair. everything is an essay. if you can't write essays, don't take this Interest Value: I honestly don't know if anyone not interested in studying literature would be any more interested after taking this module, but I kinda doubt it Teaching Quality: meh. Taken in Sem1, AY18/19. This module has 2 weekly lab slots (3h each) and 1 tutorial slot (2h). The lab sessions were really quite fun and I was looking forward to each lab session. Although there are graded lab reports and a journal to keep log of whatever you learnt in the lab, it was actually quite manageable as lab reports are expected to be submitted within the lab timing, hence the questions asked are direct and short since there isn't much time to do a full proper report. Keeping a log was very useful as you could easily review what you did in previous lab studios since many tools will be used very often (like how to get min/max, FFT in oscilloscope, etc). The basics of DC and AC circuits will be taught with a strong focus on practical application (eg: we built our own 5V DC phone charger using a power supply, capacitor and voltage regulator) and later on applications of Op-Amp circuits will be covered as well. In the final 4-5 weeks of the semester, the mbot project will be given to you and you have to design the software and hardware to make your robot traverse a maze and perform some challenges autonomously. This was easily the most fun part of the module and there was even some friendly competition to see who could finish the maze the fastest. Some tips for doing well: - Make sure to read up the lab sheet before going to the lab or you will spend a lot of time just trying to understand what's going on. Reading up before hand will make the studio more fun and exciting - Ask your TA's during the lab studio literally any doubt you have. They are very knowledgeable (Yr 2 CEG students) - Once you receive your mBot, ensure to split the workload between the 4-6 teammates evenly and don't rush everything last minute as other modules will also have submissions towards the end of semester - For the 2 graded quizes, just ensure to review all the tutorial material as the quiz is usually around the same standard as the tutorial questions

Taken under Prof Holbo in AY 2014/15 Don't be afraid to take this because it's a philosophy module. The major part of it is actually reading short science fiction (SF) stories! There are also writing assignments such as ' Turn a SF into a fairy tale, or vice versa' kind or philosophical kind like 'Would it matter if fatalism is true' (one genre in SF is time travel/predestination) Basically there are many assignment topics and you are supposed to choose and do 6. Recommended to be 2-3 pages long, though technically there is no word limit but 1 page can't get you anywhere. 5 of the 6 will be graded, with the worse being 'S/U-ed' MCQ tests are actually very idiot proof if you read the stories. Taken in 20/21 Sem 1 (remote learning) Lecturer: Prof. Victor Tan Textbook: Linear Algebra Concepts and Techniques on Euclidean Spaces, 2nd Ed. Workload: medium (6 hrs/week) Expected Grade: A Actual Grade: A Assessment: 15% Luminus online quizzes (best 10 of 12) 15% Practice*4 20% Homework*2 50% Final I enjoyed this module throughout the whole semester. Prof. Tan’s web lectures were super entertaining and relaxing. This module taught topics like linear systems, matrices, vector spaces, orthogonality, diagonalization, and linear transformations. The subjects were introduced one by one, in a very detailed manner. When I watch his 2~3 hour weekly web lectures, I feel like I was not “learning” many new things. But at the end of each week, I will always be surprised about how many new skills I have acquired and how they relate to everything I have learned so far. You’ll definitely fall in love with “The map of linear algebra.” Together with a few other theorems, you can solve almost all problems in every practice session. There are also live lectures on zoom every week, though attendance is optional. During the live lectures, you can ask question 15% Luminus online quizzes (best 10 of 12) By the Sunday of each week, we have to complete a quiz to check our understanding. They do not make up a big part of the final grade, so you shouldn’t spend too much time checking answers with multiple classmates. If you don’t finish the quiz by 1600 on Sunday, you will receive a thoughtful reminder from your TA. Luckily, my best ten quizzes are all full marks, and this is also quite common. 15% Practice*4 This is where things get interesting. We all get one hour to rush through a worksheet. In the hour, we can use MATLAB, communicate with friends, use google search. Basically, there are no restrictions. But by the end of the hour, we all have to submit our solutions. My practice sessions are 1700~1800, so I’m super tired every time. In my last practice session, I accidentally submitted the original worksheet instead of my answer file!!! I only found out about that after the results of the practice are released. After a few late-night emails, I was forgiven and was only punished by deducting 10% of my score on that practice. Thank you, Prof. Tan! 20% Homework*2 The homework problems are way more challenging and exciting than those in quizzes, practices, or even the final exam, probably because it is not timed. We were given about two to three weeks to work on ten to twelve problems with parts. In contrast to practices, we have to do them independently, and we can check our answers with friends later. About a little fewer than half of homework problems are proving problems, and they are graded by attempt rather than correctness. In other words, you can get points just by giving the problem a decent shot. As a result, two-thirds of students score 90+ on each homework. 50% Final The final was 2 hours long, and it had 5 problems with parts. Only a quarter of the problems required some proving, while the rest were purely computational. MATLAB can be used to find RREF and stuff, so it was helpful. However, the problems were way harder than past years’ finals. It might be because of the remote learning, though I’m not sure how harder problems are supposed to prevent cheating. Anyway, great mod. It gave me a totally different perspective of numbers and matrices. Also, someone in the live lecture mentioned that Prof. Tan looks like Blathers from Animal Crossing (the owl). We all had a great laugh and I couldn’t unsee it from then on.

Offence-creating provisions in the Defamation Act were presented without any mention of possible statutory defences. The cherry-picking list goes on. For a course that purports to discuss important freedom of speech issues, it neglects to even touch on the institutional separation of powers and other basic constitutional issues, as well as engage foundational moral/political justifications, all of which provide the necessary context for any freedom of speech discussion. Granted, these issues might not be suited for a level-1000 module. But doesn't that make it all the more dangerous to provide students with such flimsy and one-sided material, knowing that this will heavily influence their future political views? The illusion of knowledge is more dangerous than ignorance. Admin-wise, it was a **** show of the highest order. Graded assignments (scrapbook article commentaries) were supposed to be marked and returned before the next one was released/due (there were about 4) to allow students to incorporate feedback, but the first was only returned some time after the final one was released. The midterm take-home essay instructions were changed drastically a week after the initial release: the maximum word limit was changed to a minimum word count. Having already completed the assignment, I had to scramble to unpack my heavily-condensed essay into a full-length one. Clarifications and additional instructions came piecemeal, replete with glaring spelling and grammatical errors. I have never seen a more incompetent course coordinator in my life. Thankfully, tutorials cover content wholly separate from lectures. My tutor, Ms Farah, was pretty solid and attempted to facilitate candid discussions, but was sadly limited by the 45 minutes of contact time per week. Her tutorials were for the most part really engaging and made up somewhat for the lectures. Overall, this course is great for preaching and pretending to discuss stuff you don't actually know enough about to engage meaningfully. Unless you're a senior law student or have a keen interest in constitutional issues and have read up extensively enough on the same to see through the disingenuous lecture presentations. Then you won't end up echoing the political views the rest of the unwitting students have been manipulated into forming. You'll just get tilted real hard and end up writing a scathing NUSMods review. PSA for the law students thinking of taking this course: if you're ok with trash assignment instructions and can hold in the tilt, TAKE THIS MOD. The entire course content, readings and slides combined, is something like 10% of one single topic in LC2007. I kid you not. There is ZERO new material so you have to study absolutely nothing. If you want an easy A/A+ just parrot the political views pushed here, don't be me and take the path of most resistance by flaming the examiners by picking apart the essay questions and calling the phrasing "disingenuous" in your response. For everyone else thinking of taking this mod, be warned: take everything your learn here with about as much salt as there is in the Salar du Uyuni. There ARE very valid and important points raised, but their presentation is incredibly one-sided. Side note: I was alerted by some people that my review was taken down after I posted it. The irony is not lost on me but here's a repost. Update: this is the THIRD repost.

Taken in AY15/16 Semester 1 Tutors: Dr Anand Ramchand, A/P Irene Woon I hate this module with a passion. It is probably going to be one of the most useless modules I will ever take and was a total waste of time in my already packed semester. For those in School of Computing who are not yet matriculated and happen to chance upon this, take this module as early as possible (best during iBLOCs or your first semester so you can exercise your S/U option). The module is not useless for its content (its actually quite important for ensuring we solve moral dilemmas appropriately when we enter the workforce) but for the way it is taught which makes it useless. The module co-ordinators seem to not care about this module halfway through and makes me question why they have such a module if even the teaching staff seem disinterested in it. Basically the module seeks to teach us (i say seek because I doubt whether it actually really taught us all these things) about various ethical issues specifically arising from technological advancement. The first half of the module on ethical theories, forming sound arguments and teaching us about professional ethics at the workplace as well by teaching us the Software Engineer's Code of Ethics and Professional Practice (SECEPP). This part is taught by A/P Irene Woon. She teaches the content in a rather dry manner, but it is always clear about what she is trying to teach to the class. The next half deals with various ethical issues in the IT industry including privacy, copyrights, censorship etc. This was taught by Dr.Anand and although his teaching is slightly interesting, he does tend to go off tangent once in a while. However both tutors have a problem when answering questions from students. Questions in the forum take weeks before a tutor answers them and sometimes they are left unanswered (as is the case of some questions currently). In fact we did not even know the format of our final paper until one week before the actual exam. Assessment Components: 30% Quizzes (Coursera and Edutech) Best to do this with a group of friends so you can discuss answers. I regret not giving this more importance as I totally flunked the first few quizzes resulting in a lower overall grade for this part. Do pay attention on what is required to score as much as possible during these quizzes (e.g. quiz must be done multiple times, only highest attempt/ last attempt will be taken into consideration etc.) 20% Group Project Another area where the tutors seemed not to care. I actually questioned what the relevance was of the topic of E-Waste and how it had any relation with cyberethics. Sure there are ethical issues that may arise from it but none of those were required in the open letter we were supposed to write. Also we were assured on regular feedback from the TAs regarding this by submitting milestones on the stated deadlines. But we never got ANY comments from them, ( at least in my group's case). Nothing. Zero. Zilch Nada. Really disappointed that this was the case. 15% Class Participation Probably the easiest to score in. Just talk as much as possible in class, makes sure the tutor notices you (but make sure you don't talk for the sake of talking). Active class participation will be probably the thing that can bring you closer to an A, so do participate as much as possible in class. In my case, my class was quite active as a whole so maybe did not do as well as I had hoped for in this part. 35% Final Exam If you can "fluff" very well (i.e. make up stuff and elaborate on it in a way that seems legit) this will be a breeze. And it is also open book so all your lecture materials and tutorial materials are at your disposal. Personally found the exam quite easy and its probably going to be the only paper in my university life in which I dared to leave before the exam is over. Mostly scenario and conceptual questions, copying some answers straight of your lecture notes and making up stuff for the rest of the paper. Very easy to score if you have got those "skills". Overall its sad such a module has such a lack of commitment from the teaching staff. Personally I feel that such a module should be just self-studied, unless serious restructuring is done to make the module less of a waste of time and less of a waste of 4 MCs for non-IS students who are have this module as a core requirement. Expected Grade: A Final Grade:A- (still not too bad in my opinion given the effort I put in :X )

I took this module as part of my major in Political Science. Nature of the module: This module covers the details of the causes and nature of war in a thematic fashion, and the syllabus attempts to link the theories with contemporary events, the war on terror. The module is moderately heavy, with around 4 journal readings per week. Even though the lecturer (Prof Terence Lee) advises that the readings should be done prior to lectures, I felt that sitting through the lecture helps me filter out the less important bits of the readings. Then again, you may also follow his advise to read prior to the lecture if that works better for you. The lecturer: Prof Lee injects humour and passion into his lectures, and his lectures are really focused on the readings assigned and of him drawing links to current affairs. As he covers the content rather fast during the lectures, it is highly recommended that you surface questions either in the lecture, in tutorials or email questions to him or the TA. Assessment modes: Class part (20%): Students had to send in 2 questions 2 days before the start of every tutorial, where the TA will aggregate the questions into a broad question that will be discussed in tutorials. Term Paper (30%): 10-page essay answering 1 question from a list of 3 essay questions. As the question looks for cross-topic analyses from 2 or more lectures, you need to grasp the crux of each argument and use them to back your arguments. Highly advisable to consult your TA on what he/she is looking out for. Final exam (50%): There are two parts to finals. For the first part, similar to PS1101E, students will need to answer any 5 of the 10 ID terms printed. However, as Prof Lee does not release which terms that will be tested on, you will need to gauge which terms will be coming out. For the second part, students will need to answer 1 out of 2 long essay question. Similar to the term paper, the long essay question will test on your cross-topic understanding, so be prepared. Overall: This module is really interesting due to its close reference to current affairs, as well as the commendable teaching style of Prof Lee and the TA(s). However, your choice for taking this module should be weighed against your ability to write according to how the Prof/TA wants it. Grade attained: A

Semester: 2020-2021 Sem 2 Lecturer: Yang You When I took this module, the following topics were covered, each as one lecture: ◾ Adversarial Machine Learning ◾ Deep Reinforcement Learning ◾ GANs ◾ Neural Architecture Search ◾ Mixture of Experts ◾ Self-Supervised Learning ◾ Latest on Transformers ◾ Advanced deep learning optimizers and convergence ◾ Background for distributed deep learning ◾ Distributed Optimization (LARS & LAMB) The lectures were pre-recorded and uploaded to LumiNUS and YouTube. The grading consisted of 8 labs worth 40% in total, project poster (20%) and project report (40%). No tests. The labs were often tutorials that had been taken straight from the internet with no accredition and then removed a few lines of code that the student had to implement. As such, I had a few times where I was stuck and tried to google in general to understand the problem, and by mistake stumbled into the exact solution. I think this is quite bad. Two of the labs took very long time to complete while the remaining were completed in ~1 hour. The project is what you make it to, but it is expected that it is almost original research. You can choose almost whatever topic you'd like as long as it is relevant to neural networks. You can form groups of up to 4 people. In general, I wouldn't advise to take this module because ◾ Since so many different topics are covered, they are only covered very shallowly. ◾ Since there are no tests, there is nothing "forcing" you to understand the concepts in detail. ◾ Most assignments are taken directly from the internet. ◾ The assignments were graded extremely late. As an example, we waited for over 45 days from submission deadline until the first assignment was graded. ◾ Even though the project made up 60% of the grade, we never got any feedback and didn't get to see our marks for this. It feels quite lackluster to work on something for so much time and not get any direct feedback at all. In general I got the impression that the lecturer and TAs didn't really care about the students too much. To perform well in the module, I'd advise ◾ Finish your assignments by yourself and then double check with the internet solution you can easily google to catch any silly mistakes ◾ Make sure you are in a good project group and start early on the project Expected grade: A Final grade: A

Taken in AY2015/2016 Semester 2 Taught by: Prof Wu Jie Assessment: 10% Class Attendence 10% Tutorial Participation 30% Report (2 Book Reviews 15% each) 50% Finals (Open Book) Textbook is mandatory because the final examination is open book. Taken in A18/19 Sem 2 Lecturer: Associate Professor Sun Rongfeng Assessment Structure: Homework: 15% , Midterm: 35%, Final Exam: 50% I am a student from Engineering, and I decided to try out SPM because I wanted to to test myself. Even though MA1511 is a prerequisite for this module, please do not take this module just because you got A+ for MA1511 because this module assumes you are familiar with proof techniques. This is a very challenging (but definitely not impossible) module, and it was easily the hardest module of my semester. As aforementioned, this module is an entry point into SPM. The 4 main topics in this module are the Real and Complex Number systems, Metric Space Topology, Sequences and Series, Continuity, and there is a small introduction to convergence of functions. While the normal MA2108 focuses mainly on Real Analysis, MA2108S under Prof Sun will cover general metric spaces, which may not have some of the nicer properties that the real numbers do. This was one of the main difficulties of this module. Do not let the topics fool you, there is quite an in-depth discussion into these topics. If not for my prior experience in Math/Physics, I would probably have drowned in this module. One might also notice that this module is similar to that of MA3209 albeit MA3209 being broader in content. Lectures are a must go. Prof Sun is a good lecturer, who helps the students' intuition by discussing the heuristics before going in-depth into the proof. Furthermore, given the difficulty of the module, one should diligently go for lectures in this module to prevent oneself from lagging behind, since the pace of this module is quite fast. Tutorials are also a must go. In the tutorials, some new concepts and problem solving strategies that are not taught in the lecture are also introduced to aid our understanding of the topics. The tutorials were also very enlightening, even though they were challenging. Tutorials were generally harder than most of my modules, and would require a few hours to finish. Homework was relatively easier, just do them diligently as they may require some time. Typically, I take a few hours to complete one piece of homework. Proofread the homework several times before submitting, and do it very meticulously. The problem sets were collected in groups of 3, with one set issued after each week. Midterms and finals were both difficult 5-question sets, and I struggled to even finish 3 questions for the midterm. Prof Sun was a lenient grader, perhaps to ensure that we do not lose out too much by taking this module. Still, while there might be 2 questions which have a straightforward answer, the other 3 are not intuitively very obvious and require a lot of thinking. As such, do not be surprised by the level of difficulty of the questions in this module. Practicing on MA3209 past year papers helped me and my friends prepare for the difficulty too. Overall, I must say that if you genuinely like math with proofs, and are intellectually curious, you should take this module because Prof Sun is a very good lecturer for this module and he will enhance your understanding of analysis. While one might struggle, especially in the first part of the semester, once I understood the basics of metric space topology, many of the proofs became a lot easier! If you like MA1102 and MA1100 and are the type who likes a challenge, this module is for you. However, bear in mind that you will have to work harder for this module as compared to other modules. In addition, I advise anyone taking this module to read other material relevant to the topics to be better prepared. I guess for me, this module was a rewarding experience despite all the struggles. What doesn't kill you makes you stronger :)

Taken in AY19/20 Semester 2 Taught by: Prof. Dinh Tien Cuong (Lecturer and Tutor) Disclaimer: This module was affected by the COVID-19 pandemic, and as a result it may differ significantly from how past/future modules would/will be conducted. Assessment Structure: 20% Homework (4 sets total) 20% Midterm (In-Class) 60% Final (Online) This is one of the five S modules, and also usually the last one which SPM students would take. The module’s topics include metric spaces and topologies, and MA3111 Complex Analysis I contents (complex and contour integration, Cauchy’s theorem and its consequences, power series and Taylor’s theorem, Laurent series), MA4247 Complex Analysis II contents (Identity theorem, Riemann’s removable singularity theorem, Casorati-Weierstrass theorem, maximum modulus theorem, winding numbers, Residue theorem, Rouche’s theorem). Additional topics include sequences and series of holomorphic functions, complex manifolds and distribution theory (only first is tested). The notes of reference prior to additional topics is Further Analysis, W. T. Gowers. Similar to other S modules, class size is relatively small so there is no webcast for live lessons. Lecture and tutorial attendances are not compulsory. Tutorial sessions usually involves Prof. Dinh presenting the solutions, but he actively engages the students to think about how to approach the problem from various perspectives, and how to solve if the hypothesis was slightly changed. Tutorial questions are generally very difficult, and it appears that many students spend a lot of time on tutorial questions but end up not finishing them. Regardless, they are extremely important as this module is a lot about knowing many different tricks to solve problems. Furthermore, many concepts not covered in the lecture notes but tested in the exams originate from tutorial questions. Concept wise, this module is of average-moderately difficult difficulty. Complex analysis requires a lot of heuristics and intuitive understanding, for otherwise the proofs may look very cryptic. Do not expect to understand everything in this module. Many theorems in the later part of the module require theorems/lemmas from the earlier part, so I strongly advise students to understand the concepts taught (or at least be really familiar with it). It took me a long time before I could appreciate the Cauchy integral formula, in which then many other theorems at the back become clear. As expected of an S module, one should not have time to slack off in this module. Homework is split into 4 parts, each of equal weightage. Homework questions are generally more manageable but they can still be quite difficult sometimes. As the course goes on, one may realise that many questions in tutorial/homework are similar, with them applying the same theorem/concept but on different functions, numbers etc. This is important to note, as exams will be of this type as well. Prof. Dinh is a brilliant lecturer whose key strength is his ability to convey his ideas pictorially. He focuses a lot on the big picture, drawing many pictures to illustrate the ideas instead of focusing on the technical parts of the proofs. While he does omit some details ultimately, these are generally parts which are easy to fill in. Furthermore, he explain concepts in an excellent pace, making it not feel rushed despite the heavy amount of contents covered in this module. This also makes his classes relaxing to attend. This is especially evident in the second half of the course, we he explained manifolds and distribution theory, and most proofs were omitted for this part. Note that, as mentioned above, manifolds and distribution theory were not tested in the final. Overall, taking a module under Prof. Dinh’s instruction is a truly memorable experience. Midterm is closed book (with calculator but no helpsheet), and both consist of 3 questions (+1 optional question, which is NOT credited to your midterm score if you attempt it, so it’s just for fun). The format is standard: The first question consist of multiple parts of standard questions which would have been covered in class, the second question is less standard and requires some creativity, and the last question is extremely difficult, with most people failing to attempt even one or two parts (out of four). Final is of similar format with only two questions, second being the less standard one. Despite the questions being difficult, Prof. Dinh heavily inflates the scores and has repeatedly (though implicitly) mentioned in class that he’s very lenient on giving good grades, so one need not be worries as long as he did fine for both exams. Despite not being listed as a strict requirement, students are encouraged to take both MA2108S and MA3110S before taking this module (instead of the normal variants) as Prof. Dinh expects everyone to have a decent understanding of metric spaces at the start of the module. Expected Grade: A/A+ Final Grade: A+

under Prof Cristina Carbunaru. This module is an expository module to parallel computing and the various parallel architectures in use today. Many topics are covered, but with little depth in each topic. In the earlier part of the semester, threads and synchronization are covered, and this overlaps somewhat with CS2106. Different parallel programming models are discussed to give students an overview of the current state of parallel computing. OpenMP, MPI, and CUDA programming are covered (with a programming assignment in each of these paradigms). A basic overview of memory consistency and network interconnections is also covered, but without any formal mathematical proofs. This module is one of the most content-heavy computer science modules that I have taken (this means that lots of memory work and help sheet optimisation is required). However, it does not require any significant amount of algorithmic or mathematical knowledge - secondary school mathematics is sufficient. There are two major programming assignments in this module. The first assignment requires the use of OpenMP and MPI, and the second assignment requires the use of CUDA. C and C++ are allowed for these assignments, and students are expected to know at least one of those languages (or learn them on their own). While C is sufficient for all assignments, using C++ is likely to reduce implementation difficulty as C++ is more high-level than C. These programming assignments may be done individually or with one other student, and there is no penalty for pair work. There are weekly tutorials or labs (tutorials and labs share the same timeslot, and it usually alternates between tutorials and labs). Tutorials are useful for clarifying the concepts taught during the lectures. However, the tutorial questions may not be representative of the midterms or finals, so preparation by trying out past year exam papers is recommended. Prof Carbunaru is a patient lecturer that tries her best to ensure that students understand the lecture content, and clarifies doubts with students when they arise. I find the slides on memory consistency to be somewhat confusing, but most other lectures are relatively easy to understand and should not pose a problem to the majority of students. Her midterms and finals are closed-book (with help sheet), and they are very open-ended in nature - questions generally have many different possible answers - so during the exams it is sometimes difficult to tell if your answer is one of Prof Carbunaru's intended solutions. As there are often many acceptable answers, it is recommended to answer all questions even you are not confident of your answers. Time management is also important in the exams as the exam paper is rather lengthy. There are no group projects for this module, apart from the option to do the assignments as pair work.

Year Taken: AY2020/2021 Semester 1 (COVID) Lecturer: Prof Ryan P A BETTENS Tutor: Prof Michael Yudistira Assessment Mode: 10% Weekly Homework Quizzes (Best score of 5 attempts recorded for each weekly quiz) 30% Mid-Term Quiz (80 questions in 62 minutes) 30% Thermodynamics Assignment 30% Kinetics Assignment Difficulty of this Mod: 7/10 (I was a H2 Bio student, without any H2/O level Physics Background) Possibly one of the toughest Year 1 Chem Mods to take, with a total of 40 lectures spanning over the course of 11-12 weeks (excluding reading week). Students who have taken H2 Physics may find the content of this module easier/more manageable, but that doesn't mean those without physics background are heavily disadvantaged in anyway whatsoever. In sum, CM1131 is a further extension of H2 Chemistry Reaction Kinetics and Thermodynamics/Chem Equilibrium with greater depth and further breadth. For Reaction Kinetics, the depth/breadth is 80% similar to what was already taught at JC, whereas for thermodynamics, the depth and breadth is a huge jump from what one has learnt for thermodynamics/chem eqm for JC Chem (I would only say the content has only about 10% similarity), spanning from coverage of basic terms like isochores, isotherms, first/second/third law of thermodynamics (covered mostly in H2 Physics) to other stuff such as equipartition theorem, Henry/Raoult's Laws, ideal/non-ideal solutions and also chem equilibrium calculation questions which can be way more complex as what you may have been used to in JC. Prof Bettens is a very knowledgeable professor in Physical Chem, and even though the speed of content/concepts covered in this module may make this seem like an 8 MC mod, the way he explains concepts in the recorded lecture videos does make the seemingly complicated content much more digestible and easy to understand. The use of analogies at times to reiterate/outline certain concepts were instrumental too. However, the rather frequent ''You should already know this by now'' which gets repeated once every 5 to 10 minutes in most lecture videos made me slightly sad/disconnected when I get lost at times understanding the content initially as he assumes every student taking this module to have H2 Physics Background. Prof Yudistira also puts in his utmost effort during tutorials to explain the tutorial questions very clearly, and without fail, tends to ask us thought-provoking questions at times during tutorial to check on our understanding of the content for this module. Despite not having a physics background, through putting in effort to try and understand the content/concepts being taught in this module and applying them, I ended up enjoying this module. To future students taking this module, especially those without any prior physics knowledge, don't be disheartened. As long as you put in consistent effort in revising whatever has to be done on a weekly basis, and know your stuff well and able to apply the concepts across different chapters, this will be a rather manageable mod overall. Edit: Assessment portions wise were rather doable as a whole in my opinion. As long as you know your stuff, and proactively seek to clarify your doubts (if any) during tutorials, you should be fine. However, due to COVID, we had 2 assignments, one on thermodynamics and another on kinetics. The thermodynamics assignment was rather doable, whereas the kinetics assignment was deceptively simple, especially a question which asked students to provide 2 examples of other mechanisms similar to the general mechanism shown at the start, whereby one also had to supplement their explanations on whether the mechanism explained follows steady state/pre-equilibrium approximation, on top of explaining how the general mechanism works. Expected Grade: A Actual Grade: A+

Taken in AY1516 Sem 2, by Prof Henry Chia Module Breakdown: - 50%: Group Project - 40%: Final Exam - 10%: Tutorial Participation This module covers the basics of software engineering. Unlike the basic programming modules taken (i.e. CS1010, CS1020 and CS2010), the content taught in the lectures are not technical. Instead, a lot of emphasis is based on how to design the software, as well as how to test code systematically. The problem with lectures being non-technical is that the technical knowledge is assumed. A considerable amount of time will have to be spent to learn independently. Coding will be done on IDEs – Eclipse (Java coders), or Visual Studio (C++ coders). Usage of Java is highly recommended even if you have no prior knowledge, as the amount of support for your code is much higher, and the libraries are much more extensive. Tutorials are mainly to make sure that your group is up to date with the project, and that each team member does his part to stay updated on the content covered in lectures. I recommend tutorials to be taken seriously not just for the participation points, but also to benchmark your own progress to prevent scrambling at the very last minute. Depending on the lecturer teaching this module, the requirements for group formation varies. A good group will go a long way in making your life easier, as the project requires a lot of coordination and communication. As for the finals, the focus is testing on how you would approach a software engineering project, and again, very little technical knowledge is tested. Despite the amount of effort expected of you to put in, this module is easily one of the best modules I have taken in NUS thus far. Another plus point for this module is that it is not bell curved, so students tend to get a better grade for this module on average. (Note to ISE students: Although this module is no longer compulsory, I highly recommend it because you are still clearing a technical elective (Category A) by taking this module, and there are a number of internship openings which require software engineering experience. Learning Java is not that difficult because the OOP knowledge from C++ helps in understanding faster.)

ME1102 Difficulty: Easy especially if you can get the new topics down Workload: Low Studio Slot: 1200-1400 Thursdays at LT2 Tutorial Slot: 1600-1800 Thursdays at E3-06-03 Tutor(s): Lect ONG Eng Teo Grade weightage: 50% Studio 10% Mid Term Test 40% Final Exam Expected Grade: B+/A- Grade: A+ Additional remarks: Tutorial Compulsory: No but the mid term test was during that slot Flipped Classroom: Yes Open book: Yes for both the mid term test and final exam Topics Covered: Week 1: Introduction lecture by Dr TAN Danielle S, no studio or tutorial Week 2: Guesstimation, significant figures, units and dimensions, and safety Week 3: Forces Week 4: More on forces and Newton’s laws of motion Week 5: Work, energy and power, and momentum part 1 Week 6: Work, energy and power, and momentum part 2 Week 7: Stress and strain Week 8: Deformation in structures Week 9: Deflection of beam Week 10: Heat transfer Week 11: No classes due to Deepavali Week 12: Buoyant force Week 13: Fluid mechanics Final exam topics: All Thoughts: Most of this module felt very unnecessary; only the topics in weeks 7-10 and 13 were new to anybody who never took A level H2 physics (let’s call these “the new topics”) with the rest of the module seeming like a big waste of time, having to revise A level physics all over again. It would have been fine if there were people who really needed the revision but it is quite unnecessary because I believe engineering students who need to know physics but did not take A level physics have their own bridging module (if I am wrong then please correct me). I could rant about that but moving on, most people would definitely not know much about new topics so I would advise everybody to just read up on that at the start of the semester to get familiar with it if you take a long time to master subjects. There are not much practice questions provided so mastering these concepts now could be a challenge. If you did A Level physics, you should not need to read up on the reading materials even though the teaching faculty strongly encourages everybody to unless you have really forgotten the concepts in physics. Tutor: Dr Ong Eng Teo is very friendly and he is a good teacher. He is also very open to helping you out if you need advise on things out of this module. Studio: This is basically just lab but in groups of four to five where you perform experiments which are not at all difficult, it is just time-consuming. You have to gather the results and process them through Excel (calculations and graphs) then type up a report/worksheet using that and submit it at the end of the session. There are guiding questions for the report so no need to worry about not knowing what to write. Most people should get close to if not full marks for this component. The teacher facilitating your studio is the same as your tutor and there are TAs assisting him. You can ask them any questions throughout, even sometimes on what to write for the report because the report has a lot of weird questions in which you may not know what answer the questions is expecting even though you may understand everything that is going on in the experiment. So when in doubt, just ask, if not you will not get the full marks although they are very lenient with their marking already anyway. Tutorials: There are questions to be done before these with answers provided but they are not really necessary to do. The tutorial does not have enough time to cover some of the questions so the tutorial is mostly for covering gaps, like if you could not obtain the answer provided or if you do not understand that week’s topic. Mid term test: Given how only A level topics are covered before recess week, this test is basically just an A level revision test, only easier with an attempt to increase the difficulty through trick questions (using weird units, irrelevant/redundant information, etc.). There are 15 MCQs and each question answered correctly is worth 2 marks, those left blank 0 marks, and those answered wrongly -1 marks; they are to be completed in 45 minutes during your tutorial which is more than enough time. Given how the studio is not at all difficult for everybody to score in, this is one of the things that can differentiate the skilled from the less skilled, or rather it is supposed to but it really does not; with how easy the test is and how many trick questions there are, it only differentiates those who are careful/check properly from those who do not. Final exam: There are 40 MCQs to be done in 2h with the same negative marking scheme as in the mid terms. The only difficult part of this are the new topics if you are not fully familiar with them with the rest of the questions being of moderate difficulty, or maybe even slightly easier than that. The time limit and the lack of practice with the new topics are what can make this a killer.

CG2271 AY2017/18 Sem 2: Sem 2 is always taught by Prof Ravi, while Sem 1 is taught by Prof He Bingsheng (the review by Jiachao may be more accurate for prospective students taking CG2271 in Sem 1). The concepts taught in this module are very high level concepts, which may not be everyone's cup of tea (not for me at least). You'll cover real-time operating systems and how they function, including processor-memory operations, interrupts, task managements & memory principles. Quite touch and go so a bit abstract. Prof Ravi does a decent job in explaining them, although reading the lecture notes alone can be sufficient as well. CG2271 has very high weightage (around 40% I believe) on the lab component, so get it done well and you'll be more or less guaranteed a decent grade. Problem is, your lab TA matters a lot. My lab TA marks the lab reports much more leniently than the other lab TA. You might use an Arduino board (subject to change for other sems), which integrates FreeRTOS in the 2nd part of the semester to carry out simple tasks. Unlike Sem 1, midterms and finals are completely closed book. And they are hard. The midterms tested questions that don't even appear to be covered in the lecture notes, or just totally strange questions. But the main killer of the finals were the programming questions which required you to write code from scratch, even though you are allowed to "invent" your own syntax so long its understandable from FreeRTOS point of view. TL;DR Abstract high level concepts. Labs are generally manageable, nail them. Prepare to die in midterms (weird questions) and finals since no cheat sheets (and coding questions in finals). Expected Grade: B- Actual Grade: B I didn't practice any past year papers and flunged the finals (while my midterms were sub-par as well), even the coding questions. However, due to my lenient lab TA, I was saved from getting a horrible grade.
