under Prof Wong Weng Fai. This module acts as a deep dive into the Intel x86 build of the Ubuntu Operating System. This can be seen as a deeper version of CS2106. You will explore the x86 Ubuntu, learning more about stuff like the intel x86 instruction set (no need to memorise), linux scheduler (how it evolved from O(n) to O(1) to CFS and BFS), linux memory management, filesystems (briefly about ext2, 3, 4, and btrfs). During my semester, there were 4 assignments, 9 pop quizzes (during lectures), and final exam. The 4 assignments were all done via VirtualBox. It is advisable that you use VirtualBox to run the Ubuntu version specified so that whatever you did is replicable by Prof Wong. - Assignment 1: Explore configuring Ubuntu kernel options. This assignment requires you to complete a set of tasks related to configuring the Ubuntu kernel. The assignment is relatively straightforward except for the part where you need to try and compile a smaller (or the smallest if you want) kernel. The speed of this assignment is dependent on how many cores your computer has as compiling a default configuration kernel on a duo core computer took me 2+ hours. I was able to procure a virtual machine with 16 cores to speed up to around 10~mins. Of course if you knew exactly which configuration were not needed, your builds would also be faster since there is less to compile. However, if you do not know then you would end up trial and error, slowly building and testing the kernel you built. I probably built around 40 kernels before giving up and settling with a kernel build that was only slightly smaller than the default 1. The 2nd part of the assignment is answering some questions regarding the Intel x86 instruction set. The approach for this part is to download the volume (I think volume 2) of the x86 instruction set and find the instruction of interest and try and understand how each segment of the instruction works. It takes awhile to understand this so do not start last minute. - Assignment 2: Tracing the kernel. The first part is learning how to print kernel messages then using ftrace to trace the call stack of kernel functions. The assignment requires does not teach you everything so you need to find a guide that shows you how to do the tracing. It is not difficult but you need some time to understand how to use ftrace. Part 2 is about the GOT and PLT. The lectures don't cover in detail how it works. Prof Weng does attempt to show it live for a simple program but it is not enough to answer this part. I found a youtube video that explained in a little more detail which helped. - Assignment 3: Build a device driver. The assignment provides a template for which you need to complete it to create a device driver that functions as per the small test case provided. This is not too difficult although it was somewhat ambiguous due to how simple the test case was. Part 2 is CS2106 scheduling questions and 'Draw the red black tree'. If the lecture's explanation of insertion into red black tree is ambiguous, google the insertion algorithm (note that there seems to be 4/5 insertion cases depending on who you ask). - Assignment 4: Build a buddy allocator, paging system, and LRU cache. This is probably the hardest assignment as it required significantly more programming than the other 3 assignments. This assignment, as usual, is ambiguous as you can't really tell if the output is correct or wrong. If your program handled input in a manner that seems reasonable to Prof Wong, which he doesn't really say what is reasonable, then you will get your marks. Otherwise, you will be deducted marks if your output 'seems unlikely' with no further justification from Prof Wong. We were supposed to use C but we were also allowed to use C++ after requesting. C++ helped as I did not want to create the common data structures needed (e.g. list, map). The pop quizzes are essentially small tasks released during the lectures and normally to be done before the end of the day unless the task is big (e.g. trace the linux scheduler). The pop quizzes normally test the lecture's content that day. They should not take more than 1 hour to do. The final exam for my semester was physical and open book. However, note that open book in this case meant that you had to print every lecture slides (few hundred slides) if you want to be able to check concepts. The slides may be ambiguous so try your best to interpret it in the way Prof Wong understands the concept. The approach for this exam was to answer every question even if you don't know enough about it. If the questions asks for 3 things, try to give 3 things even if they kinda say the same thing. Try to give your justifications for every answer as they are probably all ambiguous and hope he reads and accepts those justification if your answer differs from his answers. The exam answers released after were terribly unclear and I could not understand how it answered the questions. Prof Wong's lectures are not the best. He pretty much reads off the slides and also skips stuff in his slides during lecture. What is worse is that it seems to me that Prof Wong misunderstood some of the content he is teaching. This was regarding how a B-Tree works. He claims that a B-Tree can have a node inserted, however, the actual claim should have been that you can insert a key and if the node the key was inserted to is full, it will split up and create another node. This behaviour is not the same as 'inserting a node into a B-Tree'. However, during the pop quiz, we are require to insert a node which does not make sense. But we still 'inserted' it since he was the 1 marking. So in case of ambiguity, try to think what Prof Wong would think. Ideally, try to clarify early with Prof Wong and try to insist that the ambiguity be clarified. There is a tutorial slot but it is actually just for the lecture which is why it is back to back with the lecture. Prof Wong is friendly like a Singapore Uncle would be. However, he is not the best at detailing requirements and expectations, resulting in, as you may know by now, a lot of ambiguity. Prof Wong normally answers emails but sometimes he will miss your email. Prof Wong's answer to queries are not exactly helpful as he sometimes misunderstand the question or handwaves the issue, which means that you will probably will not have an answer for your queries. Overall, I would not recommend taking this module under Prof Wong as the ambiguity was too much for me to deal with. If you are interested in learning more about the Ubuntu Operating System, you could take the module but it is to an extent, just a small dive into Ubuntu. The content is interesting but I think that the module kinda made it not so interesting. Expected Grade: B+/A- Actual Grade: A+ (Despite all the ambiguity in the exam, I somehow scored well for it)

Prof Farooq Shamsuzamman: Flash Distillation (Binary and Multicomponent), Binary Multistage Distillation and Special Cases, Absorption and Stripping, Multicomponent Multistage Distillation, Column Sizing Prof Suraj Vasudevan: Extraction (Immiscible Systems and Partially Miscible Systems), (Revision) Mass-Transfer Analysis, Rate-Based Design for Distillation, Absorption, and Stripping, Humidification, Cooling Tower Design TLDR (long review ahead): THIS. MODULE. IS. HARD. Might be one of the HARDEST CN mods you will face in your candidature as a chemical engineering student (excluding hard project mods like CN3101A and CN4123R Design Project). However, it is also one of the most critical modules you will learn in your candidature if you are an aspiring chemical engineer, as it deals with separation units, arguably one of the most common and critical unit operations in Chemical Engineering. This module will make you reconsider your interests in Chemical Engineering again. This module will form the bulk of your study workload in the semester. Consistent revision is needed to understand loads of concepts taught in class, BOTH the lectures and tutorials. LOTS of conceptual details within each separation process unit and you need to have a really strong grasp of Mass and Energy Balances to master this module well. Exams are tight on time, both the quizzes and final exam, and you REALLY need to master the concepts well to ace them. PRACTICE through the past sample papers that they give for quizzes and final exam. This module discusses the different separation process units that are commonly used in chemical industries. For our batch, the main separation process units that were discussed were distillation, absorption, stripping units, extraction, and cooling towers. Prof Farooq will teach the first part of the module, which deals with mostly equilibrium-based separation processes. He started off with binary and multi-component flash distillation, which is the foundation to understand the subsequent topics which are multistage distillation and its special cases. The finale of this topic would be multicomponent, multistage distillation columns, which would be the foundations for you if you are really interested to enter the oil and gas industry. This is more like an “introductory”, as understanding the operating temperature and pressure of distillation columns and the preliminary calculations to determine the required number of stages for the distillation column was the highlight for this module. Further understanding of distillation column calculation would need HYSYS simulations which would be taught in CN4122 Process Synthesis and Simulation. Prof Farooq will also discuss distillation column design and sizing. Next, Prof Farooq would discuss binary and multicomponent absorption and stripping. The second part of the module discusses other separation units like extraction and the relations between separation units and cooling towers. Prof Suraj will start with extraction, both immiscible (which you will find surprisingly similar to stripping) and partially miscible systems. You will hurt your eyes and brain understanding both the equilateral and right triangular diagrams for partially miscible extraction. Then, Prof Suraj will move on to explaining rate-based separation processes for distillation, absorption, and stripping and how the concepts correlate with the equilibrium-based concepts that we have learned in the first part of the module. Prof Suraj also discussed column diameter calculations for rate-based design. As rate-based design uses concepts from interface mass transfer (from CN2125), a quick online video gave a recap on this and there was a small quiz regarding this topic. Lastly, he touched upon humidification and psychrometric charts (from CN2101) to explain cooling tower design, which although does not sound like a separation process unit, the graphs are similar to stripping and it is also one of the most common unit operations in Chemical Engineering. Topics from Week 1-6. 18 MCQs/MRQs in 50 minutes using Examplify, no backward navigation . Average: 15.65/22, 75th Percentile: 19/22. 3% Mass Transfer Quiz : Held during Week 10 lecture. 5 MCQs/MRQs within 5 minutes using LumiNUS Quiz, no backward navigation . Average: 4.5/7. 75th Percentile: 6/7. 20% Quiz 2 : Held on Saturday of Week 12. Topics from Week 8-11. 18 MCQs/MRQs in 50 minutes using Examplify, no backward navigation . Average: 16/24, 75th Percentile: 20/24. 57% Final Exam : 10 questions (with sub-questions), within 2.5 hours. Physical exam but we used Examplify, no backward navigation . All topics were tested. I would consider this module as the hardest CN module you will encounter (with the exception of CN4123R Final Year Design Project) throughout your candidature as a Chemical Engineering student and in my opinion, this module will test all your fundamental basics regarding your Chemical Engineering knowledge. The analogy is this: For Computer Science (CS) people, they have a hardcore big brain core module which is CS3230 (Design and Analysis of Algorithms). For Data Science and Analytics (DSA) people, they also have a hard big brain core module which is DSA3102 (Convex Optimization). For Computer Engineering (CEG) people, they have a very important but taxing and heavy core module which is CG3207 (Computer Architecture). In the case of Chem Eng people, we have our own big brain and extremely crucial module, which is CN3132. Understanding the contents of this module is essential for aspiring chemical engineers as in this module, you will learn about one of the most important chemical engineering process units, which are separation units. If you see the list of TEs and Pathway modules, you can also see that CN3132 (together with CN2116) are prerequisites for a LOT of TEs and Pathways. I would go as far as to say that CN2116 (Chemical Kinetics and Reactor Design) and CN3132 would be two of the most important modules you need to master to be an aspiring chemical engineer, as these two modules are the modules that separate Chemical Engineering from other engineering disciplines. Thus, these two modules are conceptually challenging (if you read my module review in CN2116, I considered that module as the hardest CN 2k module in NUS). In this module, you will integrate what you have learned from CN2101, CN2121, and CN2125 (Material Energy Balances, Chemical Thermodynamics, and Mass Transfer) to learn about separation process units and integrate them with knowledge from CN2122A (Fluid Mechanics) and CN2125 (Heat Transfer) for the pumps, reboilers, and condensers operating conditions, using some tools to help in calculations from CN3421A (Numerical Simulation). This module really has LOTS of details and concepts, mostly based on thermodynamics and mass transfer and understanding various graphs regarding operating and equilibrium lines of several separation process units. To be honest, the calculations are not really too extensive, but I was overwhelmed with the tons of concepts introduced in this module. If you made it this far into your Chemical Engineering degree and not really enjoying it, this module will make you reconsider your life choices by making you ask yourself: Why am I in Chem Eng? During the module feedback exercise, I describe what I liked/disliked about this module as follows: “This module has the difficult conceptual understanding approximately the same level as CN2116, integrating concepts from CN2101, CN2121, and CN2125 and giving them steroids to understand separation units, integrating them with knowledge from CN2122A and CN2125 to design the pumps and reboiler/condenser and touched upon safety concerns from CN3135, with also a sprinkle of CN3421A added to the mix.” There’s one 2-hour lecture slot and a 2-hour tutorial slot every week, with tutorials starting from Week 2. Lectures are recorded, but the tutorials are NOT recorded . As the tutorials are not recorded, you NEED to come to the tutorials, as the tutorial questions are set in such a way that it gives extra insights regarding what you have learned in the lectures. The tutorial solutions are longer compared to other CN mods like CN3121 as the professors wanted to give extra insights regarding what they have taught in the tutorials. Once you lag behind, you will DIE (like I did during the second half of the sem :”) ). In addition, you need to watch some extra videos (they call it online lectures) before the lecture timing as it serves as a “prelude” to the lecture. Practically speaking these online videos felt like another 1-hour lecture that you need to watch in your free time (although the videos take at most 30 minutes) as these videos always introduce new concepts and (at least for me) need some time to digest. Please revise and don’t be afraid to ask questions when in doubt, as sometimes the concepts inside this module make your brain ache hard, and you better get your concepts right before getting NUKED in the quizzes and final exam. Again, I should emphasize that the difficulty of this module is in the tremendous amount of details and concepts that you need to understand. The calculations are not really very tedious, and if you’re more of a math person, you might find CN3121 and CN3421A much more of a breeze compared to this extremely difficult module. The reason you need to get your concepts right is because of the examination format. The quizzes and final exam are done using Examplify without backward navigation . For thee quizzes, you will have approximately 2.5 minutes per question, and these questions test regarding your conceptual understanding and a bit of calculations. Thus, again, if you don’t get your concepts right by the time of the quizzes, you will DIE . The final exam was basically a speed run. Compared to much older batches, our questions were a LOT easier, where you can roughly see what should be done. If you try to see past papers from 19/20 Sem 1 and older, you will realize that this module’s final exams were MUCH tougher. They kid you not when seniors say CN3132 Final Exam has been one of the most KILLER final exams throughout their candidature back then during non-COVID days. However, now there were MUCH MORE questions for our batch, and if you need to flip the lecture notes a lot to find the right concepts, you will waste lots of time and won’t finish the entire final exam (in other words, get NUKED ). So I would guess that the professors now want us to understand the concepts thoroughly and quickly remember them to solve the problems. I would suggest making a cheat sheet for all the details and formulas so that you can get quick access to them during the final exam (personally I made another 18-page cheat sheet for this module like CN2125). I find that a lot of people didn’t manage to finish the final exam as they flipped their lecture notes round and round to find the required formula/procedure to use. The professors give sample papers for the quizzes and final exam so you have something to practice to prepare for the quizzes and/or final exam. My reaction when I saw 2019/2020 CN3132 Final Exam PYP for the first time the day before the final exam: “... if these questions come up tomorrow, I will surely die . Let’s just assume that the final exam was similar to 20/21 PYP as the format is similar.” Thank God it did. I guess profs or tutors could offer more assistance on this. Finals were pretty manageable as well. This constitutes 40% of your final grade. As this is introductory module to Business Analytics, I think this is a really good module for new beginners and seniors to clear your UEs and it really helps to interest students to learn more about analytics. Overall, a very good module! Expected Grade: A-

Taken in AY 14/15 Sem 1 Lecturer: Assistant Professor Chin Chee Whye Tutor: Lim Wei Quan Grade: B+ Assessment and workload - 24% homework - 26% midterm tests (2 midterm tests) - 50% final exam - NO CALCULATORS allowed for all tests/exams - No helpsheets all for tests/exams Experience: - First few lectures were fine with mathematical induction being taught in a rigorous manner. Things escalate very very quickly after set theory is introduced. Strongly NOT recommended for people who don't like doing rigorous mathematical proofs or people who have no talent for writing such proofs. I fall into the 2nd category. - Prof Chin is a good lecturer if you're naturally good at mathematics and can follow his arguments. His slides and mathematical proofs are very rigorous. He manages lecture time very well and always ends on time at 1.30pm or earlier except on 1 occasion. - However, Prof Chin sometimes lectures in such a way that I feel he is treating us as gifted students like those in the special programme. - Homework is the killer. They can be incredibly difficult such that you have no idea how to write the first step, or even understand the question. Make some friends and discuss the problems to learn together. He gives 5 sets of homework, 6 questions each and takes the best 4 out of 5 homework to compute the 24%. We have approximately 1.5 to 2 weeks to complete each set. That being said, homework marking is generally lenient. - Tests and exam standards are pretty manageable, with exception to test 2. Test 2 really demoralised many people. Questions in test 1 and the exam are modified tutorial questions so learn the answering techniques well. Prof Chin implemented negative marking for both midterms to give us a valuable lesson about mathematical precision. This was eventually scrapped. I found his anti-copying strategy hilarious. No calculators for tests and exams can be annoying especially when calculating permutations and combinations. - Tutorials are quite important. I recommend going for tutorials to copy tutorial solutions as tutorial solutions are not uploaded. More importantly, learn the answering styles properly, which I still have yet to grasp fully. My tutor isn't good at explaining concepts because he tends to use lots of programming language. He is also not very approachable and is quite argumentative towards students' questions. Conclusion: - Despite having H3 mathematics background, I found this module difficult and rather demoralising. No doubt, it is incredibly satisfying to finish a mathematical proof to a 'difficult' question and to learn about how simple axioms we assume can be that rigorous Prof Chin demonstrated to us why a+b = b+a for integers and how rational numbers are constructed, which I found interesting. If you like abstract algebra, this module is for you if taught by Prof Chin. Not recommended for other faculty students to take as a breadth module unless you enjoy mathematics in its purest form.

Taken in A18/19 Sem 1 (First Half) Assessment: 65% Finals, 35% Tutorial Attendance and Assignments Tutor: Ms Chen Lin, Lecturer: Dr Ng Wee Seng This module teaches 2-Dimensional Calculus, path integrals, conservative vector fields, integration with respect to area, Green's Theorem, Taylor/Maclaurin Series etc. Honestly, this module did not have a lot of proofs, and was purely computational. I studied Multivariable Calculus before taking this module since I knew I was going to need it. So to those who are thinking of joining Engin, studying Multivariable Calculus will help a lot, in this module + other Level 2 modules. Assignments were quite easy since we were allowed to discuss. Check your answers before submitting and the 35% is yours. The bell curve separation occurred in the finals. The exam difficulty mainly lied in the time limit. I trained myself by attempting to finish past year 1511/1505 papers in 40 minutes. That proved to be very useful, in the finals, I finished the paper, and I overhead many people not being able to finish it. Some basic integrals like anti-derivatives of 1/(x^2+1), log x , x e^(x^2) etc, would be good to know by hand. Overall, I feel that this module is essentially a speed run. Practice a few times and you should be fine. Also, try to be open-minded, there was a question in my finals that required the calculation of the area of a hexagon after applying Green's Theorem. This module is a toned down version of MA2104, so if you like this module take MA2104 too. Expected Grade: A/A+ Final Grade: A+

Taken in AY 21/22 Sem 1 Lecturer: Sufatrio Component breakdown: 2 CTF-style assignments (10% + 15%) Midterms (15%) LumiNUS revision quiz (5%) Group presentation (5%) Tutorial attendance (5%) Finals (45%) TL;DR: + Has cool and fun CTFs - Module scope leaves much to be desired - Lecturer is not good (I rolled a not so good tutor, which made the experience even worse) As someone who loves information security, I went into this module with great excitement. I was NOT prepared to be let down this hard. Module scope: Iffy. About half of the topics covered felt very touch-and-go; they were briefly glossed over and then rarely, if ever, cropped up again. Many sub-chapters are treated merely as "vocabulary" and their sole purpose in the module is to serve as possible answers for the fill-in-the-blank/MCQ section in the midterms and finals; nothing more than a cursory understanding is required. Lectures & lecturer: Lectures were conducted live over Zoom and recorded. Dr Sufatrio proceeds at a glacial pace, reading off the slides for the most part and circling random words while he speaks. His voiceover adds negligible value to the slides themselves and you're better off reading them on your own. He also has a tendency to waste time; around 10 minutes at the start of each lecture for "announcements". I couldn't attend the lectures live as I was typically travelling to NUS for another in-person tutorial during that timeslot, but I stopped bothering to watch the recorded videos a few weeks in because they're that slow even at 2x speed. Dr Sufatrio takes weeks to respond to email queries, and his responses are typically not helpful. I'm not even sure if he fully understood the questions being asked before replying with unrelated stock responses such as "this is how we defined it in the notes". Tutorials: My experience with tutorials was not great because I got a questionable tutor (who I will not name). On at least one occasion, he stated that he "didn't remember ever seeing" something despite literally having just gone through a question about it in the previous tutorial session. He also has a tendency to give wrong answers or explanations to questions posed by students, and usually doesn't bother correcting himself afterwards. This was not very beneficial to the understanding of many students in my tutorial group. To his credit, though, he provided us with a definition list/cheatsheet, which was quite helpful as quick reference during the finals. The tutorial questions themselves are generally okay, though some of them have a tendency to be somewhat tedious (e.g. given the following list of requirements, list all the firewall rules you would implement). Group presentation: This component felt like an afterthought. You pick a topic from a list and do a short presentation on it during the tutorial timeslot. This is something you can get done in a single night, but the grading is completely opaque and it's up to your tutor's discretion whether you get a 4/5 or a 5/5. Assignments: The highlight of this module. Assignments are CTF-style and the challenges are set by the NUS Greyhats. It's very hands-on, so you will probably learn more from trying these challenges than from the rest of the module put together. They are pretty time-consuming though, and can be pretty difficult if you don't already have some background and need to pick everything up from scratch. I found this pretty enjoyable, and I think it was the one redeeming part of this module. LumiNUS quiz: This is just a MCQ quiz you can do at your own time. It's meant to serve as revision before the final exam. There's no time limit so make sure you get full marks for this. Midterms/finals: Midterms and finals were conducted over Examplify with Zoom proctoring. Format was open book but no internet. Dr Sufatrio reuses questions a lot and the format of his papers is always the same. The first half of his paper (fill-in-the-blanks + MCQ) often has questions which are ripped word-for-word from previous years' papers. Even the open-ended questions are incredibly formulaic; all 3 final papers I did that were set by him (2 PYPs and the actual finals for this sem) had secure programming questions with similar code and identical vulnerabilities. The papers' difficulties are generally not high. It's entirely possible to get 100% if you understand what's going on in the module and don't make careless mistakes. The question wording can be pretty bad, though, and sometimes it's not really clear what the question wants from you. All you really need to do to prepare for his midterms/finals are to do any past papers set by him. Lecture content barely gets tested, and if they do, it's stuff that you can just look up in the notes anyway. Conclusion: If you're looking for a neat introduction to information security, this module (at least under Dr Sufatrio) isn't it; it barely covers anything interesting. If you must take this module, consider taking it under a different lecturer instead. If you just want to learn more about information security or play CTFs, you'll probably get a lot further by getting to know a few Greyhats members.

under Prof Cristina Carbunaru. This module is an expository module to parallel computing and the various parallel architectures in use today. Many topics are covered, but with little depth in each topic. In the earlier part of the semester, threads and synchronization are covered, and this overlaps somewhat with CS2106. Different parallel programming models are discussed to give students an overview of the current state of parallel computing. OpenMP, MPI, and CUDA programming are covered (with a programming assignment in each of these paradigms). Basic overviews of memory consistency and network interconnections are also covered, but without any formal mathematical proofs. This module is one of the most content-heavy computer science modules that I have taken (this means that lots of memory work and help sheet optimisation is required). However, it does not require any significant amount of algorithmic or mathematical knowledge - secondary school mathematics is sufficient. There are two major programming assignments in this module. The first assignment requires the use of OpenMP and MPI, and the second assignment requires the use of CUDA. C and C++ are allowed for these assignments, and students are expected to know at least one of those languages (or learn them on their own). While C is sufficient for all assignments, using C++ is likely to reduce implementation difficulty as C++ is more high-level than C. These programming assignments may be done individually or with one other student, and there is no additional penalty for pair work. There are weekly tutorials or labs (tutorials and labs share the same timeslot, and it usually alternates between tutorials and labs). Tutorials are useful for clarifying the concepts taught during the lectures. However, the tutorial questions may not be representative of the midterms or finals, so preparation by trying out past year exam papers is recommended. Prof Carbunaru is a patient lecturer that tries her best to ensure that students understand the lecture content, and clarifies doubts with students when they arise. As the content in this module is not primarily algorithmic or mathematical in nature, lectures are mostly relatively easy to understand and should not pose a problem to the majority of students (the slides on memory consistency are somewhat confusing, but the confusion is confined to that single topic). Her midterms and finals are closed-book (with help sheet), and they are very open-ended in nature - questions generally have many different possible answers - so during the exams it is sometimes difficult to tell if an answer is acceptable. As there are often many acceptable answers, it is recommended to answer all questions even you are not confident of your answers. Time management is also important in the exams as the exam paper is rather lengthy. There are no group projects for this module, apart from the option to do the assignments as pair work.

Lecturer: Ms Angela Li Ke Tutor: Mr Ho Weiyang Grade: B (S/U-ed) Course Weightage: Class Participation – 20% Media Diary – 20% Interview Guide – 10% Visual Analysis – 20% Digital Ethnography Presentation – 10% Digital Ethnography Paper – 20% Like most university students, I hate research. Thankfully, 'NM2104 - Qualitative Communication Research Methods' changed my perspective and I actually felt like research isn't as daunting as it sounds. We learnt different qualitative research methodologies such as digital ethnography, interviews, visual analysis and textual analysis; and were introduced to research concepts such as self-reflexivity, thick description and semiotics. The module also covered a small bit on research ethics and how to code qualitative data. Coursework wise, we had to do four individual media practicums, and I was surprised that there was no group component. Firstly, we had to write a media diary that tracks our media usage over a two-day period. This was relatively easy and the whole exercise was to practice collating both quantitative and qualitative data and coming up with thick descriptions. We were also tasked to come up with an interview guide of 10 questions for a media research. This was also relatively easy and there was a proper brief on how to segment the guide too. The third practicum was a visual analysis of a print advertisement. This was slightly trickier as we had to highlight the different power relations and interpretations (dominant, negotiated & oppositional) of the advertisement. Lastly, we had to do an actual digital ethnography of our choice – by giving a 5 minute presentation on our topic, then actually conducting the research and writing a report paper on it. I wish there was more guidance to this as I was quite confused over what to do, but thankfully managed to squeeze out an interesting research. Overall, it was unexpectedly interesting for a research module and I enjoyed the scope of qualitative research. There was a progressive flow in the lessons, although it was at a way quicker pace towards the end of the semester. Definitely more excited to try sister module NM2103!

Under Prof Cristina Carbunaru. This module acts as an introduction into parallel computing; covers threads, processes, CUDA (nvidia gpu computing), OpenMP (cpu parallel computing), MPI (computer node parallel computing). CS2106 overlaps with CS3210 but it not necessary to do CS2106 before taking CS3210. For my semester, there were 3 assignments, 1 mid term and 1 final exam coupled with labs/tut every week. The 3 assignments were all programming assignments using C. - Assignment 1: Parallelising Longest Common Subsequence with pthreads, processes, then OpenMP. For this assignment, it was not difficult finding a parallel implementation that works but if you are gunning for the highest speedup, then it might take quite awhile. - Assignment 2: 'Cryptocurrency mining'. I say this as the assignment was about finding a nonce that would result in the hash being below a certain threshold using CUDA. An implementation for this is not difficult but benchmarking the results should had to be done with care as the results are somewhat random. - Assignment 3: Scheduling work across a network. Create a work scheduler using MPI to send the work to different nodes in the network. This assignment is somewhat difficult due to the nature of debugging what went wrong in the implementation. All assignments require a report (no format defined then) which details how the assignment was implemented and benchmarks (mainly speedup). There are essentially 2 parts to each assignments: Implementing the solution and writing the scripts to collect results of the solution for the report. The time taken is roughly 60% - 70% implementing the solution and 30% - 40% writing the report depending on how much data you want to collect (write bash scripts to help automate as much as possible). Furthermore, all assignments are to be runnable on nodes provisioned for the module (no need to worry that you don't have a nvidia card for CUDA). This causes an issue where you constantly need to monitor when someone else is using the node you are currently using, especially when the deadline is close. If someone else is using your node, then the data you are collecting would not be accurate. Thus, it is advisable to start each assignment early. Another advise is to work in pairs so that you need to suffer through debugging alone and also to leverage on pair programming. Try to take this module with a friend for the assignments. The assignments are a time sink (possibly the same amount of work as CS1101S?) so please set aside enough time for this module if you are intending to get a good grade. The midterm and final exams are all testing on your understanding of the concepts with some simple math involved. Due to the nature of the questions asked by Prof Cristina, there can be multiple answers to it, thus if your answers make sense and are justified, you may be awarded marks. When I was doing the module, it was rather worrying as I never really knew if my justifications were valid until the results came back. The only advise here is make sure you really know the concepts so that you can justify properly as it is common that the answer is 'It depends'. The best way to prepare for midterm and finals are to do past year papers so that you have practice justifying. Prof Cristina's lectures are pretty good as she puts in the effort to be interactive with the students during the lecture. When I was doing the module, it was during Covid so all lectures were via Zoom. The tutorials and labs kinda alternate each week. The tutorials are to test the contents of the lectures. The labs are for exploring the different technology (e.g. play around with CUDA by following a simple lab). Prof Cristina is a very approachable teacher. She tries her best to clear any doubts students have and also allows students to arrange a meeting with her to discuss anything related to the module. Overall, I recommend taking CS3210 under Prof Cristina as it was an enjoyable module and it is pretty accessible as an introduction to parallel computing. Expected Grade: A-/A Actual Grade: A

Taken in AY15/16 Semester 1 Tutors: Dr Anand Ramchand, A/P Irene Woon I hate this module with a passion. It is probably going to be one of the most useless modules I will ever take and was a total waste of time in my already packed semester. For those in School of Computing who are not yet matriculated and happen to chance upon this, take this module as early as possible (best during iBLOCs or your first semester so you can exercise your S/U option). The module is not useless for its content (its actually quite important for ensuring we solve moral dilemmas appropriately when we enter the workforce) but for the way it is taught which makes it useless. The module co-ordinators seem to not care about this module halfway through and makes me question why they have such a module if even the teaching staff seem disinterested in it. Basically the module seeks to teach us (i say seek because I doubt whether it actually really taught us all these things) about various ethical issues specifically arising from technological advancement. The first half of the module on ethical theories, forming sound arguments and teaching us about professional ethics at the workplace as well by teaching us the Software Engineer's Code of Ethics and Professional Practice (SECEPP). This part is taught by A/P Irene Woon. She teaches the content in a rather dry manner, but it is always clear about what she is trying to teach to the class. The next half deals with various ethical issues in the IT industry including privacy, copyrights, censorship etc. This was taught by Dr.Anand and although his teaching is slightly interesting, he does tend to go off tangent once in a while. However both tutors have a problem when answering questions from students. Questions in the forum take weeks before a tutor answers them and sometimes they are left unanswered (as is the case of some questions currently). In fact we did not even know the format of our final paper until one week before the actual exam. Assessment Components: 30% Quizzes (Coursera and Edutech) Best to do this with a group of friends so you can discuss answers. I regret not giving this more importance as I totally flunked the first few quizzes resulting in a lower overall grade for this part. Do pay attention on what is required to score as much as possible during these quizzes (e.g. quiz must be done multiple times, only highest attempt/ last attempt will be taken into consideration etc.) 20% Group Project Another area where the tutors seemed not to care. I actually questioned what the relevance was of the topic of E-Waste and how it had any relation with cyberethics. Sure there are ethical issues that may arise from it but none of those were required in the open letter we were supposed to write. Also we were assured on regular feedback from the TAs regarding this by submitting milestones on the stated deadlines. But we never got ANY comments from them, ( at least in my group's case). Nothing. Zero. Zilch Nada. Really disappointed that this was the case. 15% Class Participation Probably the easiest to score in. Just talk as much as possible in class, makes sure the tutor notices you (but make sure you don't talk for the sake of talking). Active class participation will be probably the thing that can bring you closer to an A, so do participate as much as possible in class. In my case, my class was quite active as a whole so maybe did not do as well as I had hoped for in this part. 35% Final Exam If you can "fluff" very well (i.e. make up stuff and elaborate on it in a way that seems legit) this will be a breeze. And it is also open book so all your lecture materials and tutorial materials are at your disposal. Personally found the exam quite easy and its probably going to be the only paper in my university life in which I dared to leave before the exam is over. Mostly scenario and conceptual questions, copying some answers straight of your lecture notes and making up stuff for the rest of the paper. Very easy to score if you have got those "skills". Overall its sad such a module has such a lack of commitment from the teaching staff. Personally I feel that such a module should be just self-studied, unless serious restructuring is done to make the module less of a waste of time and less of a waste of 4 MCs for non-IS students who are have this module as a core requirement. Expected Grade: A Final Grade:A- (still not too bad in my opinion given the effort I put in :X )

Took this module in AY2021 Sem 2 First of all, if given the opportunity, please do not take this module under Prof Bryan Low unless you already have an intuitive understanding of machine learning concepts like concept learning, neural network, etc. For the most part, throughout the module, we went through quite a bit of stuff that were theoretical, abstract and sometimes even mathematical in nature. This sounds fine but Prof Bryan has this habit of making things seem a lot more difficult than it actually is. There are several instances during the lecture when he could actually use diagrams to explain certain concepts but decides to use very technical words to explain. And don't get me started on the analogies he gives. This tends to make things very confusing since it is very difficult to understand what he was trying to get at. And to further make things worse, every so often, you will meet some tutorial questions you have no idea how to start on. And when you eventually look at the tutorial answers, it's like they are pulling answers from the air (looking at you information theory). And guess what, the tutorials are graded, so glhf if you are soloing the module and not strong in the theories. Last but not least, when it comes to the exams, it appears that what is taught in the lecture != what is taught in the tutorial != what is tested in the finals. Honestly, I have no idea why he focusses sooooooo heavily on concept learning. It just isn't interesting nor useful at all in the practical sense. Also, the neural network question was quite useless and pointless. It's already made known to us that most of the time, neural network is a black box model, yet he wants students to list down the weights that make the neural network consistent. Just extremely pointless. I guess one thing that is great (for experienced students) is that the exams are very grindable (except for the Find-S/ Find-G concept learning questions), making it very possible to get good marks. Ultimately, a few takeaways for someone like me who is not very interested in the underlying math and concepts are EM algorithm, Naive Bayes, Decision Trees. Apart from that, the other topics are just extremely boring and sometimes pointless. End of the day, please consider if you are willing to put yourself through the mental torture before signing up for the module. Taken in 15/16 Sem 1: "Ever wondered how do computers work?" Granted this module will not teach you that, but it is the foundation of learning more about the lower level hardware and software that makes computers tick. It is compulsory for most Computing students and I suggest only taking this as an elective if you are intending to minor in Computer Science or Computer Engineering. There are two distinct halves of this module, which are separated by recess week. Before recess week, we learn about logic circuits which includes binary arithmetic (and other bases as well), Hamming codes, Logic and logic gates, logic function expressions, Karnaugh Maps, MSI components, Combinational Circuits and Sequential Circuits. Very interesting and it is quite important for labs when you are designing your own logic circuits. The second half goes more on the software side, albeit a much much lower level, clsoer to the hardware implementation. Here we learn a language which is at a lower level than C, which is Assembly. We used the MIPS architecture in this case, and other topics include Performance, Instruction Set Architecture, Datapaths, Control flow, Pipelining (very important) and lastly ending off with learning about the cache. Lecturer: Aaron Tan This was the first time Aaron Tan was taking the module alone. Usually he would teach the first part, involving logic circuits and then Dr. Soo would come in after the mid-sem break to teach the second part of the module. The content was always quite heavy in the module so a lot of reading, understanding and memorizing will be involved (Memorization will be much less if you have a good cheat sheet :)) The lectures are generally well paced and Aaron likes to hold interesting demonstrations using the students to illustrate concepts more clearly. (Pay attention to these demonstrations, these demos may be bonus questions!) There are also practice questions which we are meant to do on the spot, and some other which he likes to call "3 second quizzes". Again, as I mentioned in another module Aaron Tan teaches, be sure to take down notes because Aaron's slides always leave blanks meant for students to fill on their own. However, these lectures are webcasted so it is not that bad if you missed something. Just watch the webcast to catch it again. The lectures are 3 hours per week, with one two hour slot and another one hour slot. Generally they are well paced even though sometimes Aaron squeezes too much into the Friday lecture (and too little into the Monday ones). Recommended you attend so you can bug him with your numerous questions. Continual Assessment Breakdown: 5% Tutorial Attendance Tutor: Zhou Jun Tutorials are held weekly with one hour slot. The tutorials are generally quite easy to do, with maybe one or two tricky questions. It is split into two parts. The first part, is meant for discussion on the forums and the rest will be gone through during class. Zhou Jun is very efficient in covering our tutorials and he expects people to come out write the solutions and asks the class to crtique answers accordingly. It is recommended you attend tutorials for two reasons: 1) There are marks allocated for tutorial attendance 2) Tutorial solutions which are uploaded are often incomplete. You will only get the full solutions by copying down whatever your tutor goes through during class! 15% Labs Lab TA: Guo Zi He This is probably the best part of this module. As a physics loving guy, I love to play around with circuits , and making our own logic circuits in this module was a fantastic experience. During the second half of the module, we created circuits using a software called Logism, and we also played around with basic Assembly programming (seriously quite fun, although you write lines and lines of code). You are advised to do as much of the lab as possible (designing circuits, testing out programs) at home and then do the execution during your lab period. This way you are more than likely to finish your labs on time, and in most cases very early, giving you more free time to catch up on whatever you like. Do take note though, don't be careless, as I found out to my cost. It pays to be careful and to bring up your CA mark as much as possible here 10% Assignments We had a total of three assignments (supposed to be 4 but Aaron decided there was no time for the fourth one). The assignments are generally manageable, so yet again do check your answers thoroughly and discuss with friends before handing them in, and try to get close to full marks as possible (it is definitely doable). You normally have about a week to do each assignment, so try and finish as quickly possible. 20% Mid terms Mid-terms were generally ok. A 1 page hand-written cheat sheet is allowed. Use it wisely to write down things you normally would need to memorize (e.g. Truth Tables for various functions, Excitation tables for Flip flops etc.). The more you squeeze in, the less you need to memorize and are able to focus on the concepts which are key to doing well in this module. Do organize your information well as time is of the essence. Only downside is no calculators (if I remember correctly). Do score highly as well (my batch's mean was about 30 out of maximum of 40 marks). Do watch out for the bonus question too :) 50% Finals Like the mid-terms, the finals were generally manageable with a few tricky bits here and there. Your cheat sheet becomes even more important here especially for assembly language functions, datapath diagrams and pipelining. At this point I would like to reiterate that you SHOULD NOT copy paste your entire lecture notes into the cheat sheet (You only have one page (both sides) which you are allowed to bring in). Put stuff that will make you rely less on memory and more on application of concepts. It greatly aids your studying and will be handy reference in your examinations. Calculators are allowed for finals. I only had one regret after the paper of not drawing my own datapath diagram on my cheat sheet despite the ample space avaialble TLDR; This module's content is generally easy (given you put in effort), with the exception of pipelining. That stuff, though important to computer science, is bloody confusing and irritating even till now. Get as many marks as you can in your CA components and examinations and such consistent performance should guarantee you an A. And most importatntly, prepare your cheat sheet SMARTLY. Expected Grade: A Final Grade: A

This module is a first course in linear algebra, dealing with Euclidean vector spaces. It is compulsory for many different quantitative majors. The module starts fairly innocently, introducing augmented matrices as a means of representing systems of linear equations, but advances fairly quickly afterwards, dealing with matrix operations, invertible matrices, determinants, vector spaces and their bases, matrices associated with vector spaces, orthogonality, diagonalization and linear transformations. Everything in the module is built-up knowledge, so you really cannot afford to slip up at any point in time. There is a good mix of computational as well as proving questions in the tutorials, homework, and the textbook exercises, both of which are essential. Computational questions allow you to get a good feel of how to work with matrices and vectors, and proving questions help to ground your intuition regarding the concepts in the module. There’s a serious lack of reviews about EC2205 online (partially because it’s a relatively new module that only began in AY 18/19), hope to bridge part of that gap with this module review! Taken in AY 20/21 Semester 2 Lecturer and Tutor: Dr Connie Chung EC2205 is a module on managerial economics. Unlike some of the more foundational EC modules like EC2101 and EC2102 which still have computations, EC2205 is more qualitative in nature. Took this module to satisfy my Economics minor, plus I took EC1301 the previous sem under Dr Connie and I really liked her teaching style. Class size was slightly lesser than 90 students. The mixture of students taking this module is quite balanced – around half my tutorial classmates were Econs majors (mostly Y2s and Y3s) while the other was spread across various faculties with the majority either from Science, Computing or Engineering. Module Content Chapter 1: Economics and Management – basic economic principles in business Chapter 2: The Power of Markets and the Wealth of Nations – trade, allocation mechanisms and private ownership Chapter 3: Spontaneous Order, Markets and Market Failure – sources of market failure and the role of government in MF Chapter 4: Spontaneous Order and the Firm – what is a firm, why does it exist and how does it operate? Concepts like a firm’s supply chain and governance and supply chain are also covered here Chapter 5: Organisation of the Firm – the different structures a firm can take (hierarchical form, U-Form, M-Form etc.) Chapter 6: When Other Firms Don’t Respond – this chapter analyses how individual firms can raise their competitiveness. Key focus is on two economic models, the Five Forces Model and Resource Based Model. Chapter 7: When Other Firms React – introduction to Game Theory (just some of the basics, there are other modules like EC3101 and EC3312 which I believe will cover GT more in depth) Chapter 8: The Knowledge Economy – covers the importance of knowledge workers in today’s economy and key issues in a knowledge economy. Chapter 9: Strategies With Respect To Government – government intervention in businesses (taxes, subsidies, tariffs). Also covers less commonly talked about policies like antitrust laws and different regulations (economic regulations, social regulations, international regulations etc.) Assessment Structure Tutorial Particpation (10%) Lecture Quiz Participation (10%) – 2 quizzes per week for 10 weeks from week 3 to 12, do both quizzes during lecture to get full credit. I forgot to do the first 2 weeks lecture quizzes so I lost 2% here.... :") Midterm (25%) – Closed book exam on Examplify (chapters 1 to 5) 50 MCQ questions in 1h with no backward navigation. Very important to do well for midterms because the bellcurve for this is super steep, median was 43/50! Group Assignment and E-Presentation (15%) – Dr Connie will assign you to a group of 3-4 students and you’ll work together on a group assignment of about 9 to 10 questions. Each question is answered as a short essay no more than 1 page long, and relevant examples should be cited (diagrams not as necessary). Following that your group will have to present your answers in the form of powerpoint slides in one tutorial session. Finals (40%) – Open book exam on Examplify with backward navigation, 10 short-answer questions covering all 9 chapters. This is the part that really determines who does well because it tests your understanding on the module content in a very comprehensive manner as you have to cite relevant examples or hypothetical scenarios to back up your explanations (simply regurgitating the lecture slides here is NOT enough) Concluding Remarks Overall, while the content in EC2205 is not heavy, it is very theoretical (apart from chapter 7) and can be rather abstract at times (this is not helped by most of the slides being in point form), so personally I took quite some time to digest the content and see how all the different concepts link up to one another. Would recommend this module for those who prefer the JC Econs type of assessment (more qualitative), not so much for those who are only comfortable with computations because there is virtually zero calculations in EC2205. Grade expected: B+/A- , midterm was above median while my group assignment got an A- , so really depended on my finals performance which I wasn't too optimistic about... Grade obtained: A (thanks Dr Connie heh)

GEQ1000 AY2017/18 Sem 1: Pretty much the throw-away module simply to fulfill the Q pillar of the 5 GE pillars. Probably the easiest compulsory module in NUS. Most importantly, it is CS/CU, so that explains it all. There are no physical lectures, everything is webcasted (like GER1000). But, there is simply no need to watch it. There are also tutorials which is a must to attend since a surprising large percentage of your marks come from it, JUST BY TURNING UP. Yeap, no participation required. How much you enjoy your tutorial depends on your tutor. Some make it quite interesting, some can't be bothered like you. It may help in finishing your assignments for this module though. This module is split into 6 sections representing different genres: Philosophy, Science, Computational Thinking, Engineering, Economics & Design. For each genre, there can be open ended questions to answer and/or MCQs to answer. Unfortunately, different people get different questions for MCQs, so it may not be easy to simply grab answers. But you can simply google them, PDF search the keywords, or just skim through the videos, jumping as you wish. Or anyhow answer. It doesn't matter that much, just make it up in the open ended questions. (You are given your marks scored frequently, so just check often to see how far are you) There is also Final Reflections, which is worth a large percentage, so just write some BS to get some marks. Finally, you need to post 6 IVLE forum posts, so just aim for at least 2 genres you are good at and whack. Pick the topics with less posts since it's easier to BS since more posts means more BS and thus less BS for you to type. You can omit 1 or 2 assignments as you wish, but definitely attend tutorials and do the Final Reflections. I left out one of the Design assignments where you had to design a wallet, because who got time for that?! Easy peasy to pass, no reason to fail, I got that CS grade easily.

Taken in AY 2013/2014 Sem 1 (Dr Han Fei) Basically a more in depth version of MA1102R ( cover limit , sequence, function). It studies an in depth proof of many theorems, this module will use epsilon-delta analysis to basically, everything... Textbook is not compulsory. Content : Epsilon - Delta approach to all kind of stuffs. Expect little calculation, what matters is how you rigorously proof results / corollary. Assesment : Tutorial Presentation : Prof Han Fei doesn't specify how many times we should go and present, but encourage us to present at any ocassion. He then makes it like a "sectional style", where he asks the class to debate your answer. If there is a mistake at your proof ( which will happen often) he wants the class to find out, in the end if no one finds out about your mistake, he'll clarify it with the class. Basically there are many different approaches to solve one question, the most common way is to use epsilon delta , which can be used to solve almost any question. Some questions are direct application of theorems ( root test , ratio test, etc) Midterm : Before the midterm, he posted a practice question. the midterm is VERY SIMILAR to the practice, so ensure you can do them. at the very least, memorize the answer if you don't understand. Many people score full mark because the practice is similar to midterm. Final : It is much more difficult and challenging than the midterm. It tests your understanding, as there are many questions which require a lot of in depth thinking. General comment : Prof Han fei is very kind lecturer, sometimes his explanation in class is a bit hard to catch, do attend all lectures and tutorials as they are very useful in understanding the content of this module. Difficulty : Moderate Grade : A+

AY2014/2015 Semester 2 Review Professor Chu Delin has been teaching this module for 2-3 times alternating with Andy Yip sometimes in the recent years. AY20/21 Sem 2 Lecturers: Prof. Dilip Raghavan and Prof. Jonathon Teo Yi Han Assessment: 15% Weekly Quiz (best 10 out of 12) 15% Practice Questions (4x throughout the sem) 20% Midterm 50% Final Exam Module Difficulty I do not know if most of the content was covered during JC but it was during my high school. Therefore I did not spend too much time struggling during the first half of the sem. However, during the second half of the semester the difficulty increased noticeably but not dramatically, but still manageable. Overall, as one of the introductory math mods, it is not that much of a killer. Probably the bell curve will do the job for you, whether it is against you or not. TLDR, an easy module in terms of understanding the content. The workload below is measured weekly. Lectures - 2h The live session was taught to me under Prof. Jonathon. We had a bunch of prerecorded lectures by Prof. Dilip to watch every week before Prof. Jonathon's live lecture. The prerecorded lectures cover everything from the lecture slides and is OTOT, so the duration may very. Some sped the video into 2x speed or maybe 6x speed, if they are quite pro. The live lectures are pretty much the recap of the webcast lectures with some practice PollEv questions. Democracy is much loved during his lecture so feel free to answer anything. I think it should be 4 hours but one of the sessions was cancelled so we only had 2h of live lecture every week. Personally I think Prof. Jon did very well on his lectures. Despite the fast pace that he had warned us before, he always makes sure his students are on track. Therefore, he won't be hesitated to be consulted a lecture part with, such as the common misconceptions and tips on proving questions. Tutorials - 1h In this module there is a provided handbook (the same over time, check other reviews) which consists of lots and lots of practice questions. Feel free to consult these during the tutorial sessions. Some of these sessions are actually for all of us to be assessed on the graded practice questions having 3-4 questions every session. MATLAB We're allowed to use MATLAB for any of these assessments. The Profs gave us four OTOT lab sessions (every 2-3 weeks) for us to practice on. There wasn't any special MATLAB quiz like the past semesters probably did, but it is probably useful to speed up your matrix operations or to check your final answer. Personal Opinion To me, the pressure is actually the bell curve rather than the material, probably because I have learnt the first two out of seven chapters before in high school. If you are taking this as an elective module, I think it is fine as long as you can find the connection between one topic and another, e.g. you will use matrix in the final chapters but matrix was taught on Chapter 2. Otherwise, it is a core module and that means you have to take this, just like me. Make sure you do well on the quiz although they will pick the best 10 out of 12. You have unlimited attempts to do this so check and review thoroughly, and do not miss the submission deadline. Final exam was one of the most "okay" exams that I took during the sem. Not too easy yet not too hard as well. The format of the final exam is very likely to be the same over time so do practice from PYPs, anywhere you can find it. One more thing, spend enough time for the prerecorded lectures and the textbook if you think you won't do well in this module. Repeating the video or slowing it down will take time for your better understanding. Every question other than the proving question is MATLAB-able , so spend most of the time on proving questions. This can be done by reading all the PYPs and recognizing the secret jutsus applied on them. They usually are the last questions on the final exam or the final part of a question, if not the last question. Expected grade : A Final grade : Somewhere around the expected

Full Module Review available here: CG3207 was one of the most informative, educational modules I have taken. This module answered many of the questions which was always running in my head: "How computers function so smoothly managing several tasks simultaneously?", "How do the building blocks of computers actually come together in building a computer?", "How does a processor function?" etc. That being said, it was definitely and undoubtedly a challenging module. Took this mod in special term (Jun – Aug 2014) under Dr Abel. Overall this is quite an easy mod. You would enjoy what you learn in this mod if you are at least somewhat curious and interested to find out more about the universe. You would learn the answers to questions such as ‘Why do stars and planets form?’, ‘Why are some planets larger than others’, ‘How do scientists measure the distance of stars from Earth?’ etc ASSESSMENT: Midterm Test – 30% (Mostly MCQ, and a few short answer questions, closed book) Final Test – 30% (Same as midterm, mostly MCQ) Tutorials – 10% (easy to score) Project – 30% From the other reviews that I’ve read about this mod, the project set by Dr Abel is different from the one set in the normal semesters. First, it’s not a group project but a solo project. Second, instead of doing an experiment, the project requires you to go to this website called zooniverse where you would do simple tasks such as identifying galaxies or monitoring the moon's surface, then write a report about what you did. Overall I’ll say the project is pretty manageable and can be done in a short time. CONTENT: Because I took this in special term, the pacing of this course is quite fast (four 2-hrs lectures per week, covering 20 chapters within a month). The contents cover pretty much everything, from Earth to Sun to planets and to stars. However I think most of the contents are very straightforward (i.e. you can literally just read the lecture slides, google what you don’t understand, and go straight for the exams). Mostly facts to memorize, and not much calculation to do, despite being a physics module (good news if you don’t like maths :)) The lecturer is okay, he speaks clearly and his lecture notes are pretty comprehensive. However I do find the lectures a bit dull sometimes. The tests are fairly easy as long as you study for them, except for a few trick questions and questions that test on obscure facts in the lecture notes. BONUS: There usually will be 1 or 2 optional stargazing session held during the term, for students who are interested. TL;DR – One of the easier and more interesting science mods in NUS. (You get to learn about stars and planets! And the tests are MCQ!). If you need to take a science GEM, I recommend this one.

Took this in AY2017/2018 Sem 2, and I believe it's the first time Prof Sun Yeneng lectured this module? It can definitely be daunting for someone completely new to game theory to jump into this module and be greeted by so much new terminology, but a lot of the mathematical concepts formalise ideas that can be intuited, I think. Having additional econs background isn't a must, but it may help you grasp the concepts better. (The lectures also go through several economic models too) Nevertheless, this module gives you a useful toolkit to examine lots of examples of human behaviour in the real world. Also those prereqs related to optimisation (MA3236/MA3252/DSC3214/DSN3701) aren't *too* critical. You'll lightly rely on optimisation concepts when it comes to maximising rewards / minimising losses in certain games. And at times you'd need to rely on geometric series for certain infinite-stage games. Otherwise the calculations aren't too tedious, I feel. Both midterm and final tests were closed book, but final allowed 2-sided helpsheet while midterm didn't. The questions you'll encounter often depend heavily on your question comprehension skills, so it's important to get a good grip on the game theory ideas and know how to reason through the problems thoroughly. On the flip side, you also don't have to remember too many specific formulae or algorithms.

Taken in Semester 1 (AY 2021/2022) Prof : Noor Aisha Binte Abdul Rahman Difficulty: Easy Workload: Manageable Contents: 10% Class Participation 10% Class Presentation (Automatically assigned partners from Tutorial groups) 25% Midterm Essay (1000 words on a given topic relating to key concepts and methodology introduced in the module) 25% Image-Based Essay (800 word essay comprising 20 images on any topic that tells a story on any theme relating to Islam and the Malays in Singapore or the region.) 30% Final Essay (1500 words on a given topic) (Any referencing/bibliography style can be used for the essays) Lectures and Tutorials were held online. Weekly Lectures pertaining to a new topic relating to the religious orientations of the Malays and how they evolved overtime. Module is not an examination of Islam as a religion, but rather an analysis of its socio-historical significance. Prof is extremely well-versed in the material, and often goes into long and thoughtful discussions about the lecture topics. I would recommend this module to those who emphasize knowledge over grades, although the workload is very manageable. Many readings are provided that can provide more insight into the topics, and they can be used to help formulate the essays. Tutorials were held every odd week (until Week 11). Tutorials were used for Class Presentations, where each session a different group would spend 40 minutes presenting on a given Tutorial Question. The Prof would host these tutorials too and provide their own insight into the given question after the end of the presentation, and would engage in discussions not only with the group members, but also the tutorial participants. If you are a Muslim interested in taking this module, the Prof makes sure to notify us that our knowledge of the religion will not help in this module, as it is not an analysis of the religion. In fact, it can become a handicap of sorts, as you may have lingering biases that make writing the essays a bit more challenging. Although, I would still encourage you to take this module anyway as I found that the lingering biases only slightly affected my writing style and information processing. In fact, this module helped provide me with practical experience on how to better formulate informative essays when there could be bias involved. Overall, I found this module to be quite interesting. The lecture material is highly informative, and the Prof is very engaging with the class. Workload is very manageable. I would recommend this module to those looking to fulfil their GES/GESS pillar and/or those who are interested in the material (especially if you are Muslim).

AY2016/17 Semester 1 Dr. Zhao Yu. A new module separated from CM4225 Organic Spectroscopy. Workload: Light, no assignments. Only around 4 tutorials in total. Skip Lecture?: You can if you are good enough. There is often extra stuffs in the live lecture that are important as well, because the lecture notes were newly prepared under tight time constraints. EE2027 AY2017/18 Sem 1: EE2027 is a rebranded version of EE2021. They basically took most of the chapters from EE2021, and remodeled the content in them. TL;DR, this module is unnecessarily dense in content. If you know how to nitpick the correct content to study, this module is actually not very difficult and quite easy to understand. Also do your tutorials to drill in the methodology. Except that you wouldn't feel that at first. The amount of slides in each set of lecture notes doesn't help at all. You will unfortunately need to scorn through them. However, take particular note of the calculation portions and the modelling parts where you take a component/portion of the circuit and remodel it as simpler and more understandable stuff. The miscellaneous content such as how it works is bonus and don't carry much marks in exams. When studying for the midterms or finals, work your way from the provided cheat sheet given in exam. (You are not allowed to bring your own) Know how to use them, and chain your memory of thoughts/draw connections from the formulae and models given. Nail the calculation questions to score. And if the format stays the same, do not answer the T/F questions if you are not sure as a wrong answer earns NEGATIVE marks. There are 2 lab sessions, the first one is easy. The second one is anything but. Get help from your friends, those who have done it (if you are a later week lab session). And get intel on what questions are being asked in that session too. You are supposedly graded on your understanding as well. Lectures are packaged lectures and tutorials. (Some lessons are lectures, some are tutorials) One is taught by Prof Hong Minghui, who has a difficult to understand accent. However, he is very patient in consultations, even after class. The other is taught by Prof Choy who in my opinion, explains concepts very clearly and her explanations during any consultations are crystal clear (but sometimes does beat about the bush). The tutorials are essential to scoring well due to the need to nail the method in calculations. The problem is, because they go through the slides linearly, lectures do get very boring, and are sometimes not exactly necessary to attend. Topics covered are: Basic Concepts from CG1108 (KVL, KCL, Thevenin, Norton, Superposition, Phasors, Transient Circuits), Real/Apparent Power, Diode, BJT, MOSFET, Opamp, Single & Multi Stage Amplifiers. Opamp is extremely difficult to understand and often contain the hardest questions, study it last after Single & Multi Stage Amplifiers.

Tutorials took place periodically (every 2 weeks) during the lecture timings. The labs were enjoyable (it is exciting to see your system actually execute the sequence that you have designed for) and supplemented the lectures well.

I took this module in Sem 1 AY15/16 under Professor Tan Sun Teck. This is definitely not an easy module, and even with background it is a struggle at times. Expected Grade: A- Actual Grade: A Most of the cohort is made up of polytechnic students who are exempted from CS1010 and typically have a background in Java. For students who took CS1010 and need to transition from C to Java the transition may be tougher. But for those already familiar, the first few lectures would be similar to topics taught in Polytechnic but later topics have much more depth. The pacing is somewhat tough even for those with background. The concepts taught require much practice and the lecture does not help you to visualize too well. Tutorials taught by Ivan helped to concretize and better visualize many of the concepts taught during the lecture, Ivan is by far the best TA I had this sem, he is well versed in the module and is great at teaching. Workload is basically 1 lecture, 1 lab and 1 tutorial a week. Each week would rotate between a Take-home lab and a Graded lab. Take-home lab typically consists of 5 exercises with the final one being graded. The Graded Lab is like a lab test whereby you have to come up with a solution within the lab session. There is also a Practical Exam which is like 2 Graded Labs back to back, a midterm and a final exam. The midterm was killer for most students as the MCQ had a high weightage, 4 marks per question, and 2 massive open ended questions where you had to write code. Problems faced by most were carelessness during MCQ, as the answers were similar, ambiguity in the open ended questions whereby you didn't know what the Prof wanted and the lack of time to write out so much code in so little time. A retest was offered to students, a large majority of students took up the retest. Final Examination was a great deal easier than the Midterms possibly due to the cohort's performance at the Midterms. Overall, with consistent practice it is possible to do reasonably well in all the practical components. Midterms and Finals are harder to prepare for, and you must get used to writing code on paper. This module is definitely doable with consistent work put in.

Semester: AY2015/2016 SEMESTER 1 Teaching: DR HEEJIN HAN style of teaching is really structured and it worked very well for me. Being a module on China,Japan, South/North Korea and Taiwan there is a wealth of historical context behind the interactions in the region. I had prior knowledge of the histories of China and Japan but I think even students without such knowledge can do well because her lectures mainly consist of facts/figures. I definitely enjoyed the module and I honestly don't think her expectations are very difficult to meet Just put in consistent effort, turn up for lectures/tutorials and start EARLY on the research paper.
