The second part of a year-long module which significantly improves on the first part, which was just a series of lectures that absolutely no one listened to. This time, you have to draft and complete a mock research proposal according to NUS guidelines. Over the course of the semester, you submit a few drafts to an assigned supervisor who you meet twice for consultations, followed by the final deadline in Week 12. This was a lot more useful and a lot more enjoyable than the previous semester. Mainly because it forces you to actually do something, rather than just sit there and fall asleep continuously. It also won't take up too much time; my supervisor (Dr Leung) actually reminded me outright that the module was pass/fail, advising me not to attempt anything too ambitious. One huge plus point about this project is that you can use it to think about what you want to do for your Independent Study Modules (i.e. research projects) and honours thesis. Even if you don't, it's still really valuable to familiarise yourself with the proper protocol. Difficulty: Not too bad. Depends on how good you are at writing essays. Also, it's pass/fail, so you shouldn't have to worry too much about it. Workload: I spent about 2-3 hours on each draft, tops, and I only had three submissions. You will have to do quite a bit of background research, since all academic research builds on previous literature (I was reminded of this multiple times), but Google Scholar is always your friend. Thinking of a viable topic might take some time, but again, it's pass/fail so it doesn't matter too much. Assessment: Your supervisor marks your final draft on a pass/fail basis, which is great because s/he will spend up to 40 minutes with you beforehand going through exactly what they want. It shouldn't be too hard to pass. Interest Value: Very relevant to USP students especially, since they'll be doing a lot of these proposals in the future. Teaching Quality: Dr Leung, my supervisor, gives very targeted advice and isn't long-winded in the slightest; my last consultation took all of five minutes. She's also very understanding, and often reminded me that I only needed to aim for a pass, hehe.

Semester taken: AY19/20 Sem 2 If you're looking to fulfil your GES requirement or take a UE while simultaneously ticking off your SJW bucket list, look no further. With less balance than a punch-drunk lightweight after twenty pirouettes, the course material and its presentation during lectures appears (to me at least) designed to steer young minds towards various inexorable anti-establishment conclusions. As a politically neutral third year who had completed the 8-MC LC2007 Constitutional & Administrative Law module not too long ago, I was triggered to no end by the relentless use of pejoratives coupled with snide remarks during the lectures while course material was being taught. Constitutional and statutory provisions were cited only partially - in one particularly egregious case, different subsections from different sections in the statute were copied (without section numbering of course) onto consecutive slides, then labelled as something like "what the law says". Offence-creating provisions in the Defamation Act were presented without any mention of possible statutory defences. The cherry-picking list goes on. For a course that purports to discuss important freedom of speech issues, it neglects to even touch on the institutional separation of powers and other basic constitutional issues, as well as engage foundational moral/political justifications, all of which provide the necessary context for any freedom of speech discussion. Granted, these issues might not be suited for a level-1000 module. But doesn't that make it all the more dangerous to provide students with such flimsy and one-sided material, knowing that this will heavily influence their future political views? Graded assignments (scrapbook article commentaries) were supposed to be marked and returned before the next one was released/due (there were about 4) to allow students to incorporate feedback, but the first was only returned some time after the final one was released. My tutor, Ms Farah, was pretty solid and attempted to facilitate candid discussions, but was sadly limited by the 45 minutes of contact time per week. Then you won't end up echoing the political views the rest of the unwitting students have been manipulated into forming. You'll just get tilted real hard and end up writing a scathing NUSMods review. The entire course content, readings and slides combined, is something like 10% of one single topic in LC2007. I shit you not. There is ZERO new material so you have to study absolutely nothing. Teaching Modes: Lectures every week, tutorials once every 2 weeks Assessment: Tutorial Attendance and Participation: 20% CA1 Take Home Essay: 10% CA2 Research Essay: 20% Final Exam: 50% Lectures Lectures are webcasted but are released only during Recess Week and Reading Week, so it is highly recommended to attend lectures. Lecture 2: Singapore Society: From Colonial to National Lecture 3: Writing the Singapore Story Lecture 4: The Impact of War and Occupation Lecture 5: Merger and Separation Lecture 6: Residues after Separation Lecture 7: Immediate Needs: Jobs and Security Lecture 8: Education for a Nation Lecture 9: Making Singapore a Home Lecture 10: Society’s Role in Nation-building Lecture 11: Film Screening of Tan Pin Pin’s ‘To Singapore With Love’ Lecture 12: Becoming Singaporean Tutorials (20%) Tutorials are held once every other week, and attendance is taken. There are marks for class participation so make sure to speak up every tutorial, seeing as there are only 4. Prepare for tutorials by reading the readings (can be quite a lot) and discuss the questions in groups. Short group presentation and comments from the tutor Assignment CA1 (10%) Supposed to be timed on IVLE but was changed to a take-home test instead. Given around 7 days to complete, submit on Turnitin, complete with in-text citations and bibliography. You are staffing the SG60 Diamond Jubilee (for the year 2025) working committee. As part of a collection of key historical moments in Singapore’s national history, you have been asked to put together a first-hand account (by a witness or participant) of Separation, and its immediate aftermath. The committee expects a history that highlights the immediacy of the event through personal voices and experiences, and not a mere regurgitation of published books and / or articles. The committee also expects a separate submission explaining the main messages of your history and the choices of primary sources. Question 1 Using no more than two primary sources, write a brief account of the immediate and underlying circumstances that led to Singapore’s separation from Malaysia, and the immediate tasks the people of Singapore felt they have to address after 9 August 1965. Taken in 18/19 SEM2 under Dr Yeo Ye and Prof Yeo Tat Soon. Grading: 2 x 12.5% midterm tests, 2 x 2.5% class participation, 2 x 10% laboratory, 50% finals. This module is split into 2 parts. Recommended reading: Field and Wave Electromagnetics by David K Cheng (I only used it for the 2nd half; used Introduction to Electrodynamics by Griffiths for the first half) The first part is a somewhat compressed form of FOS' PC2131 (Electricity and Magnetism 1). Electrostatics and magnetostatics in both vacuum and medium are first taught before culminating in the electromagnetic wave and Maxwell's equations in their full, generalised, time dependent glory. A huge focus of this module is the solving of Laplace and Poisson's equations for electrostatics and magnetostatics. A strong background in multivariable calculus and vector calculus will be very helpful because the transformation of Maxwell's equations from integral to differential form requires understanding of Divergence and Stokes' Theorems. The content became rather rushed after Week 4 because quite a fair bit of time was spent on the first chapter on electrostatics in medium. However, the part on magnetism bears an uncanny resemblance to the part on electricity (such is the beauty of the symmetry of electrodynamics!) so it will be easier to understand for the second time. Dr Yeo is extremely enthusiastic in delivering and clear in his explanations, so as intimidating as those inverted triangles, dots and crosses may seem at first glance, he breaks it down into bite-sized bits for us to absorb. Pay close attention to tutorials though, because things that are in the tutorials can very well not be covered in lecture. Personally, I struggled quite a fair bit with the tutorials because a very limited coverage of the framework used for the solving of Laplace and Poisson's equations was introduced in the lecture. Furthermore, with a huge emphasis being placed on the solving of these equations, paying attention becomes even more important. We performed 3 experiments in the first lab session (3 hours): Electric field profile of wires submerged in baby oil by spinning a Whimhurst wheel and spraying sesame seeds into the oil, variation of electric field strength of a plasma ball with distance and lastly, swinging pendulums of different materials through a magnetic field. A lab report was to be submitted 1 week after the session containing results and explanations for the experiments. The first midterms was an MCQ test of 20 questions without cheatsheet. Being familiar with the various expressions and committing them to memory is highly encouraged to save time, given the factual nature of some questions. Be careful though, as a few questions are very tricky. The second part builds upon the electromagnetic wave and its interaction with different media before ending in an introduction to the transmission line model. The phasor form of the electromagnetic wave is first introduced alongside its relevant parameters such as amplitude of E/H fields, wavevector and frequency (time to revise all the complex number manipulations). The case is then generalised to a case where the medium causes loss during propagation (lossy medium) and also when the wave is crossing from 1 medium to another (only normal incidence is in the syllabus) focusing on wave reflection and transmission. Finally, the transmission line is introduced, drawing upon everything learnt before. Personally, the transmission line was highly non intuitive because of all the different differential circuit components that make up small segments of the line. A good mathematical command of complex numbers and exponentials will be very helpful because of the phasor nature of the EM wave. Finally, the Smith Chart is introduced. The second lab session involved determining the components that are within sealed boxes by using a device that measures the reflection coefficient and subsequently using the Smith Chart to calculate the complex impedance. It is recommended to be very familiar with how to use the Smith Chart prior to the lab session (even though it is taught from scratch) because it can be a little rushed if one is unfamiliar. The second midterms tested on everything up to basic transmission line questions. There were 4 questions of 25 marks each. If you are familiar with the tutorials it should be relatively similar. A cheatsheet was allowed. Equal weightage for each part (50 marks) was allocated for the final paper. A cheatsheet was allowed. The first half of the paper contained 5 short questions from each part while the second half was a "2 choose 1" structure for each part. I CANNOT EMPHASISE THE IMPORTANCE OF KNOWING HOW TO SOLVE LAPLACE AND POISSON'S EQUATION, since it is almost guaranteed that one of the 2C1 for the first part will be on the solving. The second 2C1 is likely to be 1 question on propagating wave in medium/free space and 1 question on transmission line theory. I wasn't able to tally my Laplace equation during the exam. Comments: I felt that this module was a little ambitious in combining the physics and EE aspects of electromagnetics. I would have liked to learn more about the physics part (multipole expansion, method of imaging) but I guess that is not the focus of the module. Note that this is still a relatively new module so some substantial changes can still be made. For those proficient in using Gauss and Ampere's Law to exploit symmetry (thereby bypassing the entire use of Laplace/Poisson's equation), only use it as a backup if you are not able to solve it. The focus of the module (as mentioned by Dr Yeo himself is not the usage of symmetry, and I am not sure how marks will be allocated if Gauss/Ampere's Law is used and DONE WRONGLY.

Taken in: AY 15/16 Sem 2 “If you thought that science was certain - well, that is just an error on your part.”- Richard Feynman A similar thing could be said for this module, for nothing is certain within it, except for its difficulty(which is surprisingly hard). If you are doing this module, and you are not a Physics major, I would sincerely wish you all the best. The good thing is that this module is rather popular module among non-Physics majors, so you can hope for someone to carry you on that front. But if you are taking the module hoping the bell curve to carry you to a glorious A, that might be a bit of stretch. So you best be sure to have a good mathematical foundation as well as abstract Physics concepts before you wish to commit to this module. As the module name suggests, Introduction to Modern Physics covers an array of topics related to recent Physics discoveries, most of which have occurred within the last century. The topics covered in the syllabus include: - Relativity (only Special Relativity) - Basic Quantum Theory (Photoelectric Effect, Compton Scattering, Lasers, X-Rays, Wave-Particle Duality) - Quantum Mechanics (Schrodinger's equation, Potential Wells and Barriers, Simple Harmonic Oscillation etc.) - Atomic Physics (Schrodinger's equation in 3D, Hydrogen Atom, Zeeman effect, Spin etc. ) - Nuclear Physics (Nuclear properties and models, nuclear stabilities and reactions, fissions and fusions) - Particle Physics (Accelerators and detectors, Classifications, Conservation Laws, Quarks, Leptons, Mesons) There is also a short chapter that touches on Mathematical methods that are essential for certain calculations throughout the duration of this module. One can think of this module as an extension of H2 Physics, but with a lot more extra information. And if you thought H2 Physics' modern physics content was manageable, this is a whole new different ball game, especially with all the Mathematics involved in all the topics. Word of advice: If your Calculus is weak, you would be better off doing another module instead. Also, do note that there are H3 students taking this subject as well. But don't get your hopes up, they are graded on a separate bell-curve. And as an added disadvantage, because it is an A Level subject, no past year papers are available :( Also no cheat sheets are allowed for assessments which leads to quite a bit of memorization that is required. Lectures: 4 hours per week (Two 2 lecture slots) Lecturer: Ng Wei Khim Wei Khim is an OK lecturer. He is clearly someone who is extremely familiar with the advanced concepts being taught, but often fails to bring them to a level low enough to be understood by first years, let alone the H3 students. The fact that his lectures are not webcast means you are often compelled to attend his lectures and be lost half the time he is trying to explain concepts. He can clarify them well during consultations but the fact that he was not able to convey across these concepts clearly is a disappointment to most. It is of course not easy to explain a multitude of counter-intuitive concepts of abstract matters of physics to beginners in the field, and hence this makes a lot of self-study necessary. As mentioned by another review, the textbook is a good starting point. There are also numerous Youtube videos and other resources online denoted to the various things explained during lectures. They certainly helped me understand the content better. A benefit of the lectures however was the fact that Wei Khim often gives Lecture practices. These lecture practices are extremely useful in checking your understanding of various topics. It is especially useful when there are no past year papers available. So these are the best substitute available in this case. Do attempt them diligently, your performance in the module might well depend on it. Tutor: Dr Ching Chee Long Tutorials happen once every two weeks. Chee Long is a fantastic tutor, and if often makes you wish you had tutorials more frequently since he covers advanced topics very well. Since tutorials happen fortnightly, it is advised that you attend them as much as possible as Chee Long normally does a review of the tutorial's topics before going into the tutorial questions itself. Just make sure you do remember which week you have tutorials as they are not a weekly affair. He also allows people to consult him after the tutorial and its best you attend them. Assessment: 5% Tutorial Attendance Just don't forget to mark your attendance. If you are ill, try and come for a make-up tutorial. Dr Ching will understand. 10% Mid-Terms Mid-Terms tested us from relativity to quantum mechanics. It was manageable if you picked up on the various hints dropped by the lecturer (and therefore yet another reason to attend lectures), then you would have fund it fairly easy to do. Another good thing is that Wei Khim normally focuses on your methods, so he will not penalize carelessness that heavily. That being said, it is best to avoid such carelessness anyways. 15% Lab This is probably the most interesting part of the module in one aspect, but the lab reports made it extremely irritating. As it is also held in alternate weeks, just like the tutorial, there are only 5 experiments to conduct. A normal lab includes a demonstration by the lab technicians/ lecturer with comments on how the experiments we are doing relate to what we are doing. After the demonstration, you will carry out the experiment with your lab partner. If you have a friend doing the module with you, it is advisable that you take this timeslot. Once you are done with your experiment, it is extremely important to get the lab demonstrators to approve your results before you leave (otherwise you might have screwed up results and not know it :P) During that time lab demonstrators will also give you a viva (short pop quiz relating to the experiment) before letting you leave. Do note you will not always get perfect results, and with the limited time you have for the experiments (you will result 3 hours is not a lot of time) you might have to live with those imperfect results. At least that gives you much more to talk about in your sources of error in your report! On that note, make sure you know which errors affect which measurements and how they affect your results, because stating any source of error without explanation might lead to your report being penalized. Overall, these practicals are quite easy to score on, so try to do well in them. 10% Assignments Assignments are normally quite easy to score in. The math can get a little hectic, but besides that it is quite manageable. Personal advice: Type your assignment's out in LaTeX. Easy to handle the math, and much more neater and pleasant to mark! 60% Finals Like the midterms, Wei Khim will drop numerous hints for the finals. So yet again, pay attention during the lectures to at least catch these hints. It will tell you directly what to study for the finals. Normally consultations are held before the actual paper. You would do well to attend them and clarify any final lingering doubts. I screwed up my finals quite badly, but still hoped that the bell curve would save me in the end. Like the midterms, no helpsheets are allowed (since it is also an A Level Examination). Overall, despite the difficulty of the module, I found the module extremely interesting. Being highly interested in Physics, the things I learnt in this module slightly made up for how badly I did in them. Learning about relativity and quantum theory in depth was very enjoyable for me. An interesting way to satisfy your requirements for a Science module if your major requires it. But it will not be CAP puller especially if you hate calculus (integration of complicated functions especially). Expected: A-/B+ Actual: B+

Taken in AY2016/17 Semester 1 under Dr Soon Yuen Jien. General thoughts: It's an exposure module to Operating Systems, where you learn to (hopefully) appreciate the design of an Operating System. The topics covered can be roughly split into three parts: process, memory and file management, all of which are covered in general detail (not specifics or in-depth), with a few case studies (mostly UNIX/POSIX implementations). I really enjoyed the course and the content that is thought would most likely be new /interesting to most CS students (no matter if you have prior programming background). Lectures: Uncle Soo knows how to teach and he knows what he is teaching. He makes use of a lot of analogies while teaching the module (sometimes using himself as the analogy :P). Tutorial: Held weekly, most of the time there would not be enough time to cover the whole of the week's tutorial sheet. Solutions are uploaded online, though it's only limited to content that has not been covered in class. My tutor, Marc, is quite a knowledgeable tutor, but he tends to ramble a lot and he is sometimes hard to follow. Labs: Lab exercises are quite fun, it's mostly emulation of the various OS features. All labs are in C (as is the case of any OS course). Unless you are competent in programming/debugging, I highly recommend that you do not do the labs at the last minute, as due to the nature of the course and C, you may run into unexpected bugs that would only manifest itself every X executions (e.g. timing/race problems). Midterms/Finals: One handwritten cheatsheet for midterms and two handwritten cheatsheets for finals. Since I took it under Uncle Soo, it's the classic Uncle Soo-style exam paper. You have to be EXTREMELY careful of working out the solution, as there is almost NO room for error. His style is such that the answers are the only thing that matters and not your working/method of derivation. In his defense though, the questions are crafted such that it guides you along a certain way of approaching the problem. Also, he likes to set extremely tricky questions, which will leave you scratching your head after the exams are over (though it's not of the nitpicking variety). Overall, I would say that this module may be difficult to some, but not many people would seriously dread it (especially if Uncle Soo is the one teaching). Expected grade: B+ Actual grade: A+

Taken in AY18/19 Semester 1 Lecturer: Professor Zhao Gongyun Expected grade: F Actual grade: B (I thank my ancestors who have blessed me) Assessment and workload: - 20% Midterm test, no helpsheet (I got 14/50, which was absolutely depressing) - 80% Final examination, 1 A4 sized helpsheet. Experience: - This module extremely difficult. It elaborates a lot about the concepts gone through in MA3252 for linear programming, and MA3236 nonlinear programming. Proofs that were previously omitted in those 2 modules are discussed here. As somebody who has done all optimisation modules, this module is a real eye opener for me because the concepts of optimisation go pretty deep. The module starts with a very thorough discussion about convexity, convex sets and functions, then moves on to optimality conditions. Chapter 3 would be about duality and the most general form of duality, Fenchel duality, would be introduced. The following 6 chapters would be optimisation algorithms and their convergence results. The final chapter would be about nonsmooth optimisation which is really difficult but interesting. This module does complete the optimisation package in NUS. - Prof Zhao has taught this module many times and is very experienced in teaching it. He explains the concepts in the lecture notes pretty well and in a systematic way, adding his own understanding as input when he writes the concepts on the whiteboard. He is also very approachable and keen to answer questions posed by students. - There are no tutorials for postgraduate modules but Prof Zhao provides a list of recommended exercises to try, which were pretty useless because his test and exam uses techniques of a way higher level compared to the exercises. - Midterm test was a bloodbath. Prof Zhao set a pretty difficult paper, at least it was really difficult to me. The level of technique needed to do the questions is very high and it is not easy to come out with those techniques in the short span of 90 minutes. The cohort didn't fare that well, and the mean is in the low 20s out of 60 before Prof Zhao voided 1 question. Still, my coursemates, especially the Phd students, are very strong and the highest scorer got 54/60 before Q5 was void. - Final exam was another bloodbath, to the extent that I felt like crying halfway during the paper. With such a heavy weightage finals, one would expect there to be some giveaway questions to ensure that students pass, but no. There were only 7 marks out of 100 that is a giveaway, one which required students to solve an LP. The rest of the questions were all nontrivial and I just tried my best to write what I know and just submitted the answer book. I felt pretty bad after the paper, as bad as MA4252. Conclusion: - I recommend not to take this module under Prof Zhao if possible, for students who are doing postgraduate studies. It will end up becoming like a pure Mathematics module with a lot of theory and nontrival proving techniques. That being said, this module is an eye opener and it increases my understanding about the optimisation concepts learnt in the undergraduate courses. For people who want to do this module, ensure that you have background in linear programming and nonlinear programming before taking this module.

CG2271 AY2017/18 Sem 2: Sem 2 is always taught by Prof Ravi, while Sem 1 is taught by Prof He Bingsheng (the review by Jiachao may be more accurate for prospective students taking CG2271 in Sem 1). The concepts taught in this module are very high level concepts, which may not be everyone's cup of tea (not for me at least). You'll cover real-time operating systems and how they function, including processor-memory operations, interrupts, task managements & memory principles. Quite touch and go so a bit abstract. Prof Ravi does a decent job in explaining them, although reading the lecture notes alone can be sufficient as well. CG2271 has very high weightage (around 40% I believe) on the lab component, so get it done well and you'll be more or less guaranteed a decent grade. Problem is, your lab TA matters a lot. My lab TA marks the lab reports much more leniently than the other lab TA. You might use an Arduino board (subject to change for other sems), which integrates FreeRTOS in the 2nd part of the semester to carry out simple tasks. Generally quite ok as you are given the templates to work upon, and you are guided quite well, especially the setup of the software on your computer is pretty much idiotproof. Some of the later tasks may be hard since you have no idea of the algorithm needed. (Ask your friends for help!) The lab demos are once every fortnightly, so there's time to work on your code and after that, your report which generally isn't hard because the questions are concept based questions, although some questions require a bit of digging through documentation (of FreeRTOS). Unlike Sem 1, midterms and finals are completely closed book. And they are hard. The midterms tested questions that don't even appear to be covered in the lecture notes, or just totally strange questions. The finals however, is partially a joke because past year questions were completely reused. But the main killer of the finals were the programming questions which required you to write code from scratch, even though you are allowed to "invent" your own syntax so long its understandable from FreeRTOS point of view. TL;DR Abstract high level concepts. Labs are generally manageable, nail them. Prepare to die in midterms (weird questions) and finals since no cheat sheets (and coding questions in finals). Expected Grade: B- Actual Grade: B I didn't practice any past year papers and flunged the finals (while my midterms were sub-par as well), even the coding questions. However, due to my lenient lab TA, I was saved from getting a horrible grade.
Frankly speaking, there were a few mistakes in his notes, finals were easier than the previous years.

Overview: MA1104 is a straightforward, content-covering module. It essentially explores what happens if a function were dependent on more than one variable. And it turns out that this simple change opens up a whole new realm of mathematics. The module is unique in that it is one of the few math modules taken by math majors which has direct applications to physics and engineering (that’s just the impression I get about math modules in general; math majors, do correct me if I’m wrong). Consequently, it is also not as abstract as many other math modules, with less emphasis on proofs. Physics and engineering students should seriously consider taking this module to strengthen their mathematical foundation. ________ Syllabus: 1. Vectors 2. Functions of multiple variables 3. Partial derivatives 4. Directional derivative, Gradient vector 5. Extrema of functions, Lagrange multiplier 6. Double, triple integrals 7. Plane transformation 8. Line integrals 9. Surface integrals Workload: Quite manageable for a core module. With 2 x 2 hour lectures which are webcasted, and 1 (optional) tutorial a week, much of your learning is self-directed. So the amount of time you will be spending on this module will be a function of both your desire to get good grades and your prior mathematical background. ________ Assessment: 15% Assignments – 4 sets of worksheets. Assignment questions are quite easy by most standards, so you should be getting full marks or close to full marks for them. 20% Mid-term test - For my cohort, the mid-term test was ridiculously easy, the median score being 44/50. Most of the questions were taken from the practice questions posted by the prof before the test, so really, all one has to do is copy them down on the (2-sided) cheat sheet and score close to full marks without even studying. 65% Final exam – Typically has a mixture of simple questions and challenging ones, which are conveniently arranged in order of difficulty. Make sure you score full marks for the simple questions by attempting the past year papers and copying the solutions you think you might forget into your 2 cheat-sheets. ________ Teaching staff: Lecturer/Tutor: Dr Ku Cheng Yeaw Dr Ku is great at both lectures and tutorials. He explains stuff slowly and methodically, and I was able to follow his logic quite easily. He’s also very patient, willing to repeat himself and explain basic concepts for slower students like myself. Also, I particularly liked the way he handled the more…enthusiastic elements in the class. Those who took the module with me would know what I mean. :) ________ Personal Experience: I found this module to be both manageable and helpful. As a core module for math majors, it was easier than I expected. My math major friends also found it easy compared to their other more proof-intensive modules. That is not to say it’s a walk in the park, however. It’s still content heavy, and you have to really understand the content if you want to score well in the final exam. As mentioned above, this module provides good training to tackle the multi variable problems that appear in both physics and engineering. I can’t speak for the various fields of engineering, but you can’t run away from partial derivatives and vector calculus from year 2 physics onwards. A few days ago, I was looking at some old tests for PC2132 Classical Mechanics when, to my shock, I realised I could do a couple of the questions without referring to any of the lecture notes, all thanks to the stuff I learnt here. So heads-up to all physics majors out there: please take this module, or you will lose out. Especially so for the cohort after mine, as MA1505 is no longer part of the physics curriculum for you guys.

AY1617​ Semester​ 2 Lectures: Dr Abel Tutorials: Leong Qixiang Grade: A This module is pretty mind-blowing and will really give you a different understanding of the universe we love in. But it can also be very boring as the content can get rather technical and dry. Dr Abel lectures very clearly and has very good and succinct PowerPoint slides. There was a recommended textbook but not compulsory at all and not necessary. The content of the lectures can sometimes be more detailed than what would be covered in tests. So no need to worry if you find yourself getting lost in lecture. Just hang on to the fundamental principles. Lectures are twice a week so there is a lot of content covered over the semester. Tutorials are great. Qixiang ties Dr Abel's lectures together really neatly and gives a really good big picture overview to whatever has been happening in lectures. He also answers random questions very competently and really allows space to explore the content of the module. A pity tutorials are rather short at 45 mins every alternate week. But that's a good thing too for the busy student. Tests are mcq and not difficult. A bit of effort is required to capture a photo for the assignment since you'll have to go down for stargazing sessions (dependent on weather). Hi, there are more module reviews here too: EE2020 Digital Fundamentals Difficulty: Moderate Grade Obtained: B+ Lecturers: Prof Alioto and Prof Chua This 5MC module is done in 2 parts by 2 Professors. The first part is taught by Prof Alioto and focuses on the fundamental topics like counting in binary and converting between different radixes and an introduction to logic gates. The second part is taught by Prof Chua and focuses more on the different systems we can build with the logic gates like Signal generators and Finite State Machines. This module is graded this way: Sit in lab (12.5%) Design Project (20%) Midterm quiz (20%) Final quiz (20%) Lectures: Most of the content has been mentioned above. Lectures are all webcasted, so there’s no need to attend all the lectures if your schedule doesn’t allow for it. But Prof Chua usually sets up kahoot quizzes and gives out prizes at the end of her lectures so you might want to attend her lectures. Tutorial: Held weekly, Prof Chua tutored my class so most of the time would be to cover the week’s tutorial questions. And if there was more time, we will have play kahoot in class so that was fun! All solutions are uploaded on IVLE and they were enough to help us understand the method of solving those questions. The design questions later in the sem will take more time but are generally still doable. Labs: Chris takes us for our weekly labs. Labs exercises are done in Verilog on Vivado and uses an FPGA provided by the lab. Labs will take up quite a lot of time because of how long it takes to generate a bitstream. So any errors you make will cost you quite a lot of time. Midterm quiz: No cheatsheet and no calculators. Really the basics and fundamentals e.g counting in binary, converting between radixes and 1’s and 2’s complements. Midterms are easy and so the bell curve is steep here. Final quiz: No cheatsheet and no calculators. Moderate difficulty. The concepts tested in the finals is similar to the questions in the tutorials. I disliked the arrangement that final quiz is held in week 13 as that is also the week of our CS2103 Project submission. That means that most of us only had less than 2 days to catch up with exam prep and the content of the paper. Bell curve rating: Moderate Helpful resources: Apparently, theres is a EE2020 wiki that I didn’t know about then (that cost me quite a few hours in debugging) Module Rating: Moderately chill because of special term, this module is a lot more CA than you think

AY21/22 Sem 1 Lecturer: Prof. Wang Fei Assessment Components: 25% Homework Assignments @ 6.25% x 4 assignments 25% Midterm Exam 50% Final Exam Overview: The module starts off with a review of functions and the intuitive definition of a limit. Immediately after is when people usually start dozing off in lectures as the precise definition of the limit is introduced, which carries on during the chapters of continuity, differentiability, theorems related with calculus, as well as applications of differentiation. Computationally-oriented individuals should be wary of the initial half of the module, since it might present a 'roadblock' in their learning. Afterwards, definite integration (and Riemann sums) are introduced, which leads to indefinite integration, inverse functions, and ordinary differential equations (ODEs). The lecturer additionally often gives out SageMath handouts (which are optional to learn and do), which covers using the language to do computer-aided calculations. Module Difficulty: This module shouldn't be an issue if you have learnt and passed H2 Mathematics with a better score than most, as most of its content is already introduced in that level. However, as mentioned previously, this module has a different approach to tackling calculus in that mathematical rigor is paramount (concepts are introduced from first principles, so the initial half of the module is very important). The assessments are pretty standard, with homework assignments of normal difficulty and harder midterm/final exams. Be sure to review ALL tutorials if you wish to do well during the exams, since a lot of the questions are of similar format to them. There will always be a major time pressure in the exams, as well as one question that is noticeably more difficult than the rest. Homework assignments are usually easier (albeit can take a lot of time to solve), but people usually still score in the 80-100/100 (standardized for easy calculation) range. Average and median marks for the exams are in the 50/100 range. Personal Opinion: This module is a very good module to introduce yourself to the mathematical rigor that might often come up in higher-level modules. The lecturer (Prof. Wang Fei) is a very enjoyable person to learn from (in lectures and tutorials), and he is very approachable (he usually replies emails within the hour, even at night). Overall, he is able to introduce concepts clearly, and would stay back after the main lecture is done to gladly attend to questions. Homework should be manageable with proper time management, even if you have forgotten the concepts you've gotten in H2 Mathematics. Exams are the real test of whether you can quickly think through the concepts needed to solve a problem, hence the low average and median standardized scores. Tips: - Solve (or at least try to solve) all tutorial questions before the sessions themselves. - Redo every tutorial question in preparation for exams (you already have the solution, so it's much easier to do). - Contact the lecturer immediately if you have any questions, since the concepts learnt (especially in the first half of the semester) will be used later on. Expected Grade: A Final Grade: TBD

Lecturer: Dr Vikneswaran S/O Gopal This module is compulsory for all CS/Math DDP students. The first half of the module is on counting and discrete probability, which is basically primary 5/6 Math Olympiad, and can be mostly solved using P and C techniques. However, there are some new terms and notations that you need to know the meanings of, such as "decreasing events" or "disjoint pmf". The second half of the module has concepts such as variance, covariance, and continuous distributions, which are concepts new to me. I made the mistake of ignoring the module because I thought the first half was easy and had to study last minute at 12am for the second midterm. You should read the notes regularly, as you cannot solely rely on the tutorials for practice. The tutorials do not cover every topic. Tutorials are compulsory as they account for 30% of the final grade. We were assigned a group based on the alphabetical order of our name during the first tutorial and stuck with that group for the semester. During every tutorial, we were given a worksheet to complete individually, but could discuss the questions. The final grade received is dependent on both our individual grade and our group's grade, but how it's calculated is not revealed it to us. It basically became peer tutoring. All the tutorials on different days of the week had a different worksheet. There were 2 midterms for this module. The first midterm was done on our own laptops using the Examplify software, which only works on Windows/Mac. I disliked this software as we had to give it full control over our laptops. While taking the test, the software locked us from other applications in our laptops, and we couldn't even "ctrl alt del". The second midterm was a traditional written test. The first midterm was quite easy, and I felt that an excessive amount of time was given (90 mins for 15 MCQ, that's 4 mins per question!). Most people left the test early. The second midterm was harder than the first, but it wasn't too hard either. 90 mins were given for 3 questions, and counting the part (a) part (b) etc, that's about 6 parts. The paper also felt more like an algebra paper, as most of the questions can be solve by writing down expression using definitions and simplifying it. A lot of hints were given as well. For example, they gave you the identity needed to simplify the equation, so you just had to modify your expression to fit the hint's identity. Lectures were webcasted. In fact, half the time, live lectures weren't even available as only a video was available. The LT would be empty. It's a flipped classroom kind of module, so the prof would go through some questions on alternate lectures and webcast them as well. I did not go for lectures, and neither did I watch the videos. I just read the notes. The video explaining the concepts were made by the prof, not recorded from an LT. The video is usually about 10-20 mins, which is much shorter than a traditional lecture, but it's also a bit boring. Those videos felt like listening to the prof reading a script while pressing next on the PowerPoint slides. He didn't even use a marker/pointer to show which point he is at on the slides, and instead, would say stuff like "as you can see from point 2". Lecturer: Dr Wu Shangyuan Tutor: Ms Sim Ee Waun Grade: B (S/U-ed) Course Weightage: Class Participation – 20% News Article Pitch – 20% Feature Story – 35% Press Release & Social Media Writing – 25% My biggest disappointment this semester has got to be 'NM2220 - Introduction to Media Writing'. We were taught the theoretical basics of media writing such as: news writing, web journalism, broadcast journalism, photo/video tips, lateral reporting, writing for public relations and advertising. We also touched on topics like ethics and media law. However, in my opinion, this module tried to cover too many things without actual guidance on how to write a news article or craft a press release, which were the main graded components. Coursework wise, as someone who is already working part-time and freelance in the media industry, I felt that this module focused too much on the nitty-gritty that is not an actual representation of the working world. Firstly, we had to do a pitch of 3 stories from one local news article. Sounds simple but the unrealistic guideline was that the angles have to be fresh and original. In the real newsroom, ideas are tweaked slightly from others because those are what get the eyeballs instead!! Next, we had to write a feature story on something interesting about NUS students. Once again, we also had an unrealistic guideline – this time that it has to be 700 words... No feature piece is 700 words in the real world. We also had to take our own pictures but in the newsroom, there are professional photographers for that. Moreover, the marking was rather strict. Lastly, we had to write a press release and several social media captions on a fictitious health campaign. This was okay if not for the fact that the tutorial on press releases was after the assignment deadline so we were basically left in the deep end of the pool. Overall, an unrealistic and poorly organised module. It is better off as two separate modules that go more in-depth – one on basic journalism (news writing) and one on writing for public relations. No wonder they said don't bother with journalism school. Now I know why...

CG2271 AY2017/18 Sem 2: Sem 2 is always taught by Prof Ravi, while Sem 1 is taught by Prof He Bingsheng (the review by Jiachao may be more accurate for prospective students taking CG2271 in Sem 1). You'll cover real-time operating systems and how they function, including processor-memory operations, interrupts, task managements & memory principles. Quite touch and go so a bit abstract. Prof Ravi does a decent job in explaining them, although reading the lecture notes alone can be sufficient as well. You might use an Arduino board (subject to change for other sems), which integrates FreeRTOS in the 2nd part of the semester to carry out simple tasks. Generally quite ok as you are given the templates to work upon, and you are guided quite well, especially the setup of the software on your computer is pretty much idiotproof. Some of the later tasks may be hard since you have no idea of the algorithm needed. (Ask your friends for help!) The lab demos are once every fortnightly, so there's time to work on your code and after that, your report which generally isn't hard because the questions are concept based questions, although some questions require a bit of digging through documentation (of FreeRTOS). Unlike Sem 1, midterms and finals are completely closed book. And they are hard. The midterms tested questions that don't even appear to be covered in the lecture notes, or just totally strange questions. The finals however, is partially a joke because past year questions were completely reused. But the main killer of the finals were the programming questions which required you to write code from scratch, even though you are allowed to "invent" your own syntax so long its understandable from FreeRTOS point of view. TL;DR Abstract high level concepts. Labs are generally manageable, nail them. Prepare to die in midterms (weird questions) and finals since no cheat sheets (and coding questions in finals). Expected Grade: B- Actual Grade: B I didn't practice any past year papers and flunged the finals (while my midterms were sub-par as well), even the coding questions. However, due to my lenient lab TA, I was saved from getting a horrible grade.

Taken in AY19/20 Semester 1 Taught by: Asst. Prof. Bao Huanchen (Lecturer and Tutor) Assessment Structure: Homework: 20% Midterm Exam: 30% Final Exam: 50% This is one of the five S modules, and the earliest possible semester to take this module is Y2S1 (as is the case with MA3110S). On top of the topics listed on MA2202 NUSMods page, we were taught group actions, Sylow theorems, semidirect product, nilpotent & solvable groups, group series (derived, upper/lower central) etc. We were also taught (but not graded on) introductory category theory. The textbook of reference is Abstract Algebra, Dummit and Foote. Similar to other S modules, class size is relatively small so there is no webcast. Both lecture and tutorial attendances are not compulsory, but I would recommend students to attend them all. Tutorial merely involves Prof. Bao going through tutorial questions, but he occasionally encourages students to present in front of the class. No lectures notes are provided, and Prof. Bao has his own set of hand-written notes (which are not uploaded) that do not follow the flow of the textbook, so I typed what he wrote during class. Homework is split into 10 parts, with first issued in week 3 and last issued in week 12. Each homework holds equal weightage of 2%. This is probably the easiest S module. Homework questions are generally manageable but hard questions pop up from time to time, so it’s perfectly normal to search for help online. Contents are generally easy to understand, but concepts from Sylow’s theorem onwards become difficult to understand. Unlike analysis, do not expect to have good intuition and geometric interpretation to everything you learn. In this module, it is normal to be able to prove a statement without knowing why it is true outside of algebraic manipulation. Despite so, students should put in their best effort to understand what is going on in a statement. Prof. Bao is an amazing lecturer who shows deep care for his students. He provides thorough explanation to all the concepts taught. He started off slow but the pace picked up in the second half of the semester, as expected of an S module. He is willing to make time during the lecture break/after lecture to further clarify the students’ doubt. Overall, taking this module under Prof. Bao had been a fantastic experience. Midterm and Final exams are closed book (with no helpsheet and calculator), with them consisting of 6 and 8 questions respectively. Both papers are very manageable, with the mean of midterm being 88/100. I recommend students who want to “test water” on S modules to start with MA2202S. Expected Grade: A/A+ Final Grade: A+

Took this module in Sem1 AY15/16 This is one of the compulsory GET modules for CS majors (the other one is get1021 critical thinking and writing). There is no lectures for this module but two 2-hour tutorials each week. Weightage: 5% penal discussion 10% oxford tutorial discussion 30% oxford tutorial essay 5% midterm 15% group project 10% group project presentation 15% reflection of group project 10% wild card (I will explain what they all are in the later parts) As the title of this module suggests, it teaches how to question the information sources we see everyday from the Internet or other media. You will be taught different fallacies and ways to identify them. In my personal opinion (and my opinion only) this module does not introduce much interesting content. I myself found it quite boring most of the times. As there is no final exam for this module, the final grade will go as the components i listed above. Penal Discussion: Students will be grouped into groups of 3 or 4 and each groups will be given a topic. Each team will have 15-25 minutes (depending on how many students per group) to discuss their given prompt. every member will speak for 2 to 3 minutes first and the rest of the team will discuss what he or she has said for 2 to 3 minutes. Oxford Tutorial: Each group will be given a question to write an essay (individual work). And they will read out their own essays in front of their teammates and the teammates will discuss the essay (basically picking out the fallacies). You will have 24 hours from the end of the discussion to submit the essay. The discussion will take up 10% of the final grade and the essay you submit will take up 30% of the final grade. Midterm test: only mcqs and took about 10 minutes to finish. very easy. Group project: You are to make a game about critical thinking. The game doesn't have to be a very complicated one. I made the game using powerpoint. At the presentation you have to demo the play of the game and how the game has shown the critical thinking process of the player. Taken in AY19/20 Semester 2 Taught by: Assoc. Prof. Zhang Tengren (Lecturer and Tutor) Disclaimer: This module was affected by the COVID-19 pandemic, and as a result it may differ significantly from how past/future modules would/will be conducted. Assessment Structure: 10% Tutorial Participation 20% Homework (2 sets) 20% Midterm (In-Class) 50% Final (Online) This is a module under the MA4 list, allowing Pure Math majors to take this to satisfy their core requirements. The module’s topics include basics and definitions of topological spaces, connectedness and compactness, countability and separation axioms, Tychonoff’s theorem, complete metric spaces and function spaces. Prof. Zhang also spent the last few lectures on an introduction to algebraic topology, which was not tested. The textbook of reference is Topology (Second Edition), James Munkres. Lecture attendance is not compulsory but tutorial attendance is. Tutorials involve students presenting their solutions in the front, and their tutorial participation grade will depend on their presentation. Prof. Zhang opened a forum for students to indicate their interests to present certain problems, and he ensures that every student is given mostly equal chance of presenting. Tutorial problems are often tested topics which he decides is best left for students to figure out themselves (and hence are not explained in lecture, but may be brought up in lectures after the tutorial). Topics raised include order topology, topological groups (due to COVID-19 situation, last few weeks of tutorials were dropped, so topological groups were no longer tested), and construction of various counterexamples in topology. Tutorial questions are often very difficult, so do not be surprised if you need to seek much online help for them. Homework is split to 2 sets, and questions from homework are significantly more manageable than that of tutorial questions. Homework questions mainly serve to reinforce concepts taught in lectures (unlike tutorial questions). This module was really difficult. By generalising metric spaces to general topology, many heuristics become blurred, and many results that are true in metric spaces (from MA3209) become either false or non-trivial results in general topological spaces. To master the concepts in topology, I believe that one must have very strong visualising skills and grasp of the concepts to understand the theorems. Many counterexamples in topology are very artificial – in short, this means that it’s probably impossible for one to come out with such a counterexample without studying the statement for months, or maybe years. Furthermore, after seeing such a counterexample, the first impression is usually “oh, I guess it’s false” instead of “right, no wonder it’s false!”. I always refer the topology as “set theory with analysis”, but ironically, I find topology one of the least intuitive modules of the semester (I mentioned in my previous reviews that both set theory and analysis are intuitive). Prof. Zhang is a top-notch lecturer whose strength lies in his clear and fluent delivery of concepts taught. His lectures are often very well-prepared, and as such lectures often flow smoothly. However, he gets slightly repetitive at times and his lecture pace is somewhat fast, so one may find it hard to catch up if they lost their attention for a few minutes. However, he recognises concepts which are less intuitive, and he will slow down at these times and draw various pictures to ensure that we understand what is going on. He is very approachable any entertains almost any question, even those which may seem trivial once you realised the answer. Finally, he admirably includes a lecture summary after every lecture and disseminates it via an announcement, to cater to students who missed the classes. Overall, MA4266 under Prof. Zhang is a very worthwhile module to take. Midterm is closed book (with no helpsheet) and consists of 4 questions. First question was split to six T/F questions and is manageable in difficulty, as long as one has good intuition of the concepts. It requires one to be familiar with counterexamples as well (e.g. path connected set does not imply closure is path connected). Second question was an easy repeat of a homework question. However, Q3 and Q4 were both very difficult, especially in exam setting, and as a result the test was done rather poorly (fortunately, I did really well for it). Final is open internet and is extremely easy (given that we are allowed to search for any resources, both online and notes), and I believe was not a good indicator of the students’ familiarity of the concepts, as the questions were most covered in lectures, so as long as one took notes these questions are trivial. I believe topology is one of the most important fields in pure mathematics, so I strongly encourage interested math students to take them. More interested students would need topology to take the graduate modules Algebraic Topology and Differential Manifolds. Expected Grade: A/A+ Final Grade: A+

Taken in AY 15/16 Sem 2 Lecturer: Dr Ng Wei Khim Expected Grade: C / Actual Grade: B tl;dr: Don't take this module if you're a CS student wishing to fulfil your science requirements, or for that matter anyone who's not a physics major. It is almost impossible to fail this mod, thanks to the bell curve, but unfortunately it is also not very easy to score well for it, especially if you don't major in physics. If you do want to take this module, it is highly recommended that you take a introductory calculus module before this one, such as MA1521 for computing students. As its name suggests, PC1144 covers a good deal of topics in modern physics in a brisk 13 weeks. The breadth of topics combined with the fact that modern physics is rather counter-intuitive means that module is not easy to keep up with. Unfortunately, the lecturer is really not very good. Dr. Ng frequently fails to explain concepts clearly, and doesn't appear to understand what his students know and don't know before the start of the module, thus spending large amount of time explaining things that are trivial, while skimming over topics which require more explanation. He also has a bad habit of pausing mid-sentence, as if realizing that the next half of his sentence will likely be too advanced for the students sitting in front of him. I frequently find myself exiting the lecturer theatre feeling more confused about the subject matter than when I entered. The recommended textbook, University Physics with Modern Physics, is very good and quite readable. I would recommend reviewing it thoroughly before each lecture, because otherwise it becomes very difficult to keep up due to the aforementioned problems with the lecturer. Lectures are not webcast on IVLE, so attendance is a must (though paying attention is optional). The math used in this module is H2 level calculus (differentiation, integration by parts, substitution, etc.) plus 1st and 2nd degree ordinary differential equations, probability, Fourier transformation (not tested) and a little of complex numbers and Taylor series. Although the math is suppose to be taught during the course of the module, it is best that you have prior knowledge of all of these, since knowing them will help in understanding the physics as a lot of modern physics seem more based in math than empirical results, and also because learning math from physics professors is an exercise in frustration. Tutorials are one hour fortnightly, and it is highly recommended that you do the questions beforehand, since this and the very few lecture practise sessions are the only chance you get at doing actual questions to practise for exams. No exam papers are released by the faculty, but that doesn't mean you can't find them. No help sheets are allowed for the exams, and while the topics covered are broad and sometimes confounding, the exams are surprisingly fair (though still quite brutal). On the whole it is difficult to recommend this module. While the subject matter is interesting, it is hard to score well for, and I found myself learning more by reading the textbook myself than listening to the lectures.

Taken in AY 15/16 Semester 2 Lecturer: Associate Professor Lim Tiong Wee Tutor: Associate Professor Lim Tiong Wee Expected Grade: B- Grade: C+ (That’s it, I quit minoring in stats) Assessment and workload: - 20% Homework (3 assignments, 5%, 5%, 10%) - 10% Presentation of tutorial solution - 10% Midterm test (I got 34.8/40 for homework and midterm tests combined) - 60% Final exam - 1 A4 size helpsheet allowed for both midterm test and final exam. No calculators however. - No webcast since LT34 doesn’t seem to have webcast facilities. Experience: - This module is difficult. The concepts aren’t that difficult but applying the concepts are difficult. It is a continuation of ST2131/MA2216 probability. The module begins by revising the stuff taught in probability for about 2 to 3 weeks. Things start becoming really difficult after the chapter on estimation starts. The algorithms to follow for estimation are straightforward but are often difficult to apply. After that, the module teaches hypothesis testing in depth. It is quite eye opening to how hypotheses tests are derived through the maximum likelihood ratio and it showed me that I knew nothing about hypothesis testing that I learnt in JC. - Prof Lim is an excellent lecturer. He teaches concepts in a clear, concise manner and has a dark sense of humour. He knows the module very well such that he can answer students’ questions and address misconceptions at a fast speed. He uses the whiteboard to illustrate concepts as well. Prof Lim also does recaps of previous lecture at the start of each new lecture and summarises each chapter after each chapter is done. I find that quite useful since there are no webcasts. Prof Lim is also very approachable and always tells us not to hesitate in looking for him to ask questions since that’s what he is paid to do. - Tutorials are quite useful in illustrating concepts and a wide variety of questions are provided in the tutorial sheets uploaded. Prof Lim takes on all tutorial groups and explains the questions well. Each student has to present tutorial solutions at least once and it carries 10% of the course grade, quite a significant bit. Prof Lim then collects the solutions, scans them and uploads them to IVLE. This method is quite useful in teaching since it allows us to learn from others’ mistakes. - Homework is manageable and can be discussed with friends. No solutions provided so teamwork is needed to maximise the likelihood of getting full marks for them. No solutions uploaded, but comments will be given in a pdf near the end of the semester, so we don’t know what Prof Lim looks out for in marking… - Midterm test is manageable but I screwed it up big time. Made a bad decision on the last question not to trust my mathematical instincts. The level of difficulty in the midterm test is similar to tutorial questions. No calculator is a handicap since I couldn’t check my definite integral properly. - Final exam was a killer. It was a total massacre of the cohort. I would say that even if it was open book and open internet, most people still wouldn’t be able to do the exam. The A4 size helpsheet allowed was useless as the examples copied had little relevance to the exam questions. Throughout the exam I heard rigorous shaking of tables due to frantic erasing of answers. I left the exam feeling terrible since I was confident of only 3/60? Conclusion: - I have mixed feelings about this module. On one hand I got to learn in depth hypothesis testing which is amazing, but on the other hand, the final exam was just depressing. Also the 8am lecture slot on Mondays and Thursdays is terrible, although Prof Lim starts lectures at 8.15am instead. Math and applied majors have the option to do this in place of a level 2000 math module, but I would suggest not taking this module unless interested in statistics.

The first half of the module on ethical theories, forming sound arguments and teaching us about professional ethics at the workplace as well by teaching us the Software Engineer's Code of Ethics and Professional Practice (SECEPP). This part is taught by A/P Irene Woon. She teaches the content in a rather dry manner, but it is always clear about what she is trying to teach to the class. Personally found the exam quite easy and its probably going to be the only paper in my university life in which I dared to leave before the exam is over. Mostly scenario and conceptual questions, copying some answers straight of your lecture notes and making up stuff for the rest of the paper. Very easy to score if you have got those "skills". Overall its sad such a module has such a lack of commitment from the teaching staff. I like his style as he doesn't emphasize rote learning but encourages us to understand the material instead of memorizing it - for example he cites many studies to show certain points in his lectures but his description of the study is always very brief and succinct - he doesn't require you to remember the name of scientists, exact methods, etc, but just the variables and the results and what it shows - the gist of it. Taken in 20/21 SEM 2 under Prof Guo Yong Xin (online lessons) Grading: 5% x 2 lab experiments, 10% x 2 mini projects, 10% x 2 CA test, 50% finals This course serves as an introduction to microwave circuits and the important components that make up the circuits. Pre-requisite is EE3104Cwhich I waived, going in with PC2020 knowledge. I subsequently found out that this was doable because transmission line and S-parameter theory was taught from scratch. However, learning these 2 concepts before the course will be very beneficial as much of the rest of the course relies on them. We covered the telegrapher equations, Smith chart usage (beyond what is taught in PC2020), Y/Z matrices and S parameters as an introduction. The pace was very slow at this point with Prof Guo spending quite an excessive amount of time on these concepts. Power dividers (Wilkinson, Coupled line) and filter design was then taught. Filter design will not be a problem if you have an analog electronics background, but the even and odd mode analysis for power dividers could take a while to get used to. These 3 chapters were covered in the first half of the course. The second half of the course was more rushed as Prof Guo effectively finished teaching chapters 4-8 in about 3-4 weeks. Content covered includes more RF devices like switches, amplifiers, mixers and oscillators. Amplifier design is a huge part of this course and many details like the non-linear effects in amplifiers, how to design matching circuitry, design for high gain/low noise figure was taught. However, this part was mostly glossed over by Prof Guo and I felt like he was just explaining whatever formulas were on the slides in a “wing-it” manner instead of connecting it to the big picture. The first lab experiment was to measure the S-parameters for different devices. Remember to take many pictures! The second lab experiment was to calculate the noise temperature and noise figure of an amplifier under bias/no bias. This part was more complicated and a good understanding of how noise originates in a circuit is required. Data from both labs was taken in person, and we were given 1 week to complete the lab report. The GAs were helpful and approachable in this portion of the course. The design software that we used for both projects was ADS, and it is relatively intuitive and easy to use. The first mini project required us to design a power divider at a fixed resonant frequency. The second mini project was the difficult one: designing a low noise amplifier with a single transistor. The lab manual alone was 33 pages, and there were many steps to be completed. However, the GA went through all the steps from start to end, but did not explain the big picture again (seems to be the trend in this group), so I just went with the flow without understanding why some steps were done (although they magically improved the parameters). Do start early for this project as it can be quite time consuming. Tutorials are the worst: Prof Guo skipped the first 2 tutorials and basically just glossed over the rest of the 3 tutorials. Doesn’t take a genius to tell students that “this is easy, you should be able to do it” for many of the questions. The tests and final exam tested on basic concepts, and you should be fine if you understood every slide (which is not a lot anyway). Anyway I didn’t do very well for the second test and exam because I was getting destroyed by other classes. Final thoughts: I 100% would not recommend this course. The content covered is pretty good to me, but think of this course as a good restaurant with a really bad waiter. Prof Guo didn’t give me the impression that he prepares for lectures and just glossed over the explanations. At one point, I stopped watching the lectures entirely even though they were recorded because I simply did not understand anything he was saying. I relied a lot on my own self studying for this.

with Kenneth The module covers (in order) special relativity, tensor analysis, particle and photon geodesics, black holes, even more tensor analysis (covariant derivatives, curvature, parallel transport), and finally the field equation is derived. If you have taken a module with Kenneth before, you know his style. There’s the lecture worksheets and the weekly (difficult!) assignments, and his two (also difficult!) midterms and a final. Thanks to covid we had no finals, fortunately. But it meant that assignments were super high weightage, and there was a lot of stress about getting these right. I further made the incredibly stupid decision of a couple of assignments to be done “later”, which meant I spent a good chunk of reading week finishing this stuff up. The module follows quite closely Hartle’s book on general relativity. Interestingly, not even a little “real” differential geometry has to be developed to get all the way up to the field equations, and for the most part, there is still a logical flow from first principles. The only thing you really have to accept is that every curved space is locally flat (this in fact is true for any manifold: they locally look like Rn). Personally, I think this is the right way to learn GR from the physics side — it gave us lot of time to think about what trajectories outside a Schwarzchild black hole actually look like instead of just developing some mathematical tools and building einstein’s equations. I learnt the most physical intuition from the assignment questions: like how is time measured on a spaceship orbiting a black hole? Is there really a singularity at R=2M? Workload is heavy, or atleast it is supposed to be. As I mentioned, my procrastination made it not so heavy, but I had to feel the bite later. Kenneth’s lecture is a lot slower here than in MM, because he is not rushed to complete some fixed syllabus (as this is an elective course). I guess minimally he just wants to get to the field equations (he has some extra section on the Kerr geometry if your class goes fast enough). As for tips, **revise the section on curvilinear coordinates** before the module, it will help you infinitely to have a good grasp on standard coordinate transformations before you go to transform coordinates where your space is not flat anymore. Hartle’s book is good. Also there’s this book by Ta-Pei Cheng in the science lib which is nice. Personally I didnt really use any books a lot, just attending his lectures was enough. NB: There is also a book by Wald, which I actually have, and you can use if you are brave and want to learn differential geometry by the side. For me it just lay unopened in my bookshelf. Hoping to read it over the holidays... Overall, if you are a physics major (or even a math major) I recommend you take this mod, because its really something different that is hard to learn by yourself. Instead of taking your third course on EM or something, it might be nice to take this! EDIT: I should mention, there is not much discussion about cosmology and hubble’s constant and whatnot. This is a pure relativity module other than the secrion on black holes.

Overview/Workload: Ethics mod, very light especially for a year 3. Teaching style/lecturer: 3h sectional teaching group every week. However, aside from the first couple of weeks, most of the other sectionals are split into 2 groups of 1h 30min, and you only need to go for yours. The sectionals are seminar style, where learning takes place through discussion. The 2 profs, Irene Woon and Anand Ramchand, were both really really nice! Just that sometimes prof Anand forgets to upload stuff (not that I download them anyway OOPS). Notes/textbook: 1 page handouts are given out during most of the sectionals. However, they are pretty bare, and almost all the content comes from the class discussion. I didn’t really take a lot of notes though, since most of it was common sense/application. The textbook used was Ethics For the Information Age by Michael J. Quinn. I strongly recommend not buying the book (or at least get 2nd hand); just download the softcopy. It’s good to read I guess, though I gave up after getting to the part on the different ethical theories lol. Grading: Final exam (open book) – 40% 2h (too much time!), consists of MCQ and open ended questions. I found the final exam really easy, and some of the MCQ questions/options were hilarious! “What is the Great Firewall of China? a) A tourist attraction” LOL. Also, even though it’s open book, I didn’t refer to any of my notes. For the open ended application questions there’s no right or wrong answer as long as you can argue using any ethical theory. I only used Kantianism, Act and Rule Utilitarianism for the entire paper. Group assignment – 30% Form a group of 4-5 and write a report based on a particular theme (my group did cyber warfare). Each person does a ~5 page case study on an incident which falls into your chosen theme (I did Stuxnet), and as a group analyse the ethical dilemas/similarities and differences of each case. My group did mostly individual work though, only the intro was discussed as a group. Class discussion – 10% This is important! As mentioned previously, this is where the bulk of the learning takes place. Taken in AY 15/16 Sem 2 Lecturer: Dr Ng Wei Khim Expected Grade: C / Actual Grade: B tl;dr: Don't take this module if you're a CS student wishing to fulfil your science requirements, or for that matter anyone who's not a physics major. It is almost impossible to fail this mod, thanks to the bell curve, but unfortunately it is also not very easy to score well for it, especially if you don't major in physics. If you do want to take this module, it is highly recommended that you take a introductory calculus module before this one, such as MA1521 for computing students. As its name suggests, PC1144 covers a good deal of topics in modern physics in a brisk 13 weeks. The breadth of topics combined with the fact that modern physics is rather counter-intuitive means that module is not easy to keep up with. Unfortunately, the lecturer is really not very good. Dr. Ng frequently fails to explain concepts clearly, and doesn't appear to understand what his students know and don't know before the start of the module, thus spending large amount of time explaining things that are trivial, while skimming over topics which require more explanation. He also has a bad habit of pausing mid-sentence, as if realizing that the next half of his sentence will likely be too advanced for the students sitting in front of him. I frequently find myself exiting the lecturer theatre feeling more confused about the subject matter than when I entered. The recommended textbook, University Physics with Modern Physics, is very good and quite readable. I would recommend reviewing it thoroughly before each lecture, because otherwise it becomes very difficult to keep up due to the aforementioned problems with the lecturer. Lectures are not webcast on IVLE, so attendance is a must (though paying attention is optional). The math used in this module is H2 level calculus (differentiation, integration by parts, substitution, etc.) plus 1st and 2nd degree ordinary differential equations, probability, Fourier transformation (not tested) and a little of complex numbers and Taylor series. Although the math is suppose to be taught during the course of the module, it is best that you have prior knowledge of all of these, since knowing them will help in understanding the physics as a lot of modern physics seem more based in math than empirical results, and also because learning math from physics professors is an exercise in frustration. Tutorials are one hour fortnightly, and it is highly recommended that you do the questions beforehand, since this and the very few lecture practise sessions are the only chance you get at doing actual questions to practise for exams. No exam papers are released by the faculty, but that doesn't mean you can't find them. No help sheets are allowed for the exams, and while the topics covered are broad and sometimes confounding, the exams are surprisingly fair (though still quite brutal). On the whole it is difficult to recommend this module. While the subject matter is interesting, it is hard to score well for, and I found myself learning more by reading the textbook myself than listening to the lectures.

Taken in 20/21 Sem 2 Grading: 5% CA1, 25% CA2, 10% CA3, 30% CA4, 15% CA5, 15% participation Ah yes, the compulsory English class to be taken by all Computing students. There are 2x2hr sessions per week with high weightage class participation, which I'm sure contributes to the universal hate this class gets. The content of the class can be read from the other reviews so I'll just talk about the assessments. --- Assessment --- Similar to CS2101, grading is very consistent throughout the semester due to the 5 CAs. There aren't any "lull" periods where there's nothing to do (notwithstanding the 2x2hr sessions per week), so expect to put in more work than you might probably expect. For group projects, the class is split into groups at the start of the semester based on a survey done in the first class. You're stuck with this group for the whole semester so pray you get people who have the same goals as you. I was fortunate to have landed in a group with like-minded individuals who all wanted to maximise effort:reward ratio. CA1: Craft a presentation/video of a spin on a children's tale. Pretty simple, can be done in an afternoon if focused. CA2: Make a "Critical Thinking Rubric" from the Ennis reading, write a report on it (15%) and do a presentation (10%). This is the most tiring group project so I'm glad the co-ordinators put this early in the semester. CA3: Panel Discussion on an topic that was agreed upon prior to the discussion. You have to research the topic, then have an "academic conversation" that goes on for about 30-45min with your group, with 15min Q/A at the end. Can be prepared the day before. Try to be nice to your teammates and let them have their say in the discussion. CA4: Position Paper. You propose a question then write a 800-word-or-so essay on it. This is similar to writing a GP essay, except with citations. Can be done in a day assuming you already have a good question to write on. This is individual work with high weightage so if you're planning to score, better put work into this. CA5: Given a prompt, do an individual impromptu speech on the prompt in 2min. This is a luck of the draw if you get a good prompt or not. It's over within 2 minutes so if you can't think of anything to say, hey, at least you'll die quickly. Expected Grade: B/B+ Actual Grade: TBC
