Taken in AY17/18 Semester 1 Lecturer: Dr Nils Hassan Quittineh (Guest lecturer for entire semester) Tutor: Dr Nils Hassan Quittineh Expected grade: B Actual grade: B+ Assessment and workload: - 10% Homework assignments (I got 96/100 for the first and 100/100 for the second) - 5% Computer Laboratory exercise (I got 92/100) - 25% Midterm test, no helpsheet and no calculator allowed. (I did very badly and scored 63/100, median was 69) - 60% Final exam, 1 A4 sized helpsheet and calculators allowed. Experience: - This module is pretty manageable. The focus of this module is the theory and the computational aspect of nonlinear programming. The course begins with a very simple introduction to terminology used in optimisation, followed by convex sets, convex functions, tests for convexity, tests for min/max/saddle point. The first highlight of the course would be the KKT conditions, which can be very computationally intense due to the many combinations of possible situations. The course then introduces numerical methods for nonlinear programming problems and that would be interesting for people who love implementing algorithms on the computer. I can only marvel at the geniuses who created these algorithms. The last and final highlight of the course would be Lagrangian duality. This is the most interesting part of the course to me because I am interested in optimisation and I have taken all the optimisation courses in NUS. For those who studied MA3252 before this module, this part of the syllabus will make a lot of sense of duality in the LP sense, because you can use Lagrangian duality to derive the dual of LPs. - Dr Quittineh is a good lecturer. He teaches the concepts in a very digestible manner and explains proofs in a very logical manner, adding on to the lecture notes where needed. He does have the tendency to make careless mistakes when calculating numerical stuff, which confuses us to a small extent sometimes. In addition, he included a computer exercise for numerical methods for NLP, something which previous lecturers did not do. I really appreciated that because it allowed me to visualise how those methods work in the computer lab. The program he coded had diagrams where we can visualise the descent directions. He also gave us very interesting insights about optimisation used in actual industrial applications. He showed us some of his presentations of the seminars that he spoke in, the most interesting one was about optimising steel production in a steel plant in Sweden, where the factory wants to maximise the output of steel subjected to lots of constraints. With those examples, I was in awe at how large the problems are in real life. - Dr Quittineh is a good tutor as well. His way of teaching the tutorial is different from the typical NUS style. He asks us if we have any questions and will explain any question that students ask. As such, we usually pose harder problems and he will explain the problems on the whiteboard. He also answers theoretical questions in class to the best of his ability. I asked if coerciveness can be applied to a smaller subset of R^n and he took a while to answer it. He also uploads a very detailed solution for the tutorials. - Assignments are very manageable, discuss with friends to make sure the numerical answers are correct before submitting. - Midterm test was manageable but I fared really badly. Carelessness kills in this module. I made extremely stupid careless mistakes which I can never forgive myself for. In addition, the handicap of being unable to use a calculator to check answers did not help. He also set a very unconventional modelling problem worth 20 marks, which I did not like, simply because it requires a great deal of comprehension skill, and I tend to overcomplicate a simple problem. - The computer assignment was also manageable as it required us to run the program, key in a few things and observe the numerical method's convergence. We then had to submit a worksheet on it. - Final exam was surprisingly manageable as well. Again, carelessness kills in this module, and I have no idea if I made any grave careless mistakes or not. A fair bit of the questions were tutorial style questions, while the last 2 questions were on the strange side, with the final question requiring us to submit the question paper together with the answer booklets because we needed to draw on a diagram how the steepest descent works. Conclusion: - I took this module as a UE, I recommend this module to any kind of math major to fulfill their level 3000 basket. In addition, it also provides a nice insight about nonlinear optimisation. This module also helped me out a bit on my Honours project, an added bonus for myself.

Taken in AY 20/21 Sem 1 (Covid Semester) Lecturer and Tutor: Christian Go Workload: Low Difficulty: Low Grading: Exam 50%, Final Luminus Quiz (one week time-limit) 20%, Homework 2x15% Contents: Chapter 1: First order ODEs (separable ODE, integrating factors, Bernoulli, with some applications on radioactive decay and Newton's Law of Cooling) Chapter 2: Second order ODE (Method of Undetermined Coefficients and Variation of Parameters with application on oscillations and pendulums) Chapter 3: Application of ODE on Population Growth Model Chapter 4: Laplace Transform Chapter 5: Basic separable partial differential equations, with some emphasis on one-dimensional heat equation and wave equation. Resources (Recommended Text): Differential Equations For Engineers by Cambridge University Press. Only parts of chapters 2,3,4,5,6,11 of this book is used for MA1512. I personally used this book for practice questions only as the practice problems are classified nicely behind every chapter based on the techniques used. Personal opinion: Workload is low for me because I self-studied the contents prior to taking the mod, and did not watched any lecture videos/attended any lecture or tutorials. That being said, there are only around less than 5 videos for every week, each around 10 minutes or less. The notes pretty self-explanatory and suitable for self-study for more mathematically-inclined person. Lecturer and tutor Christian Go is also very knowledgeable and able to deliver the contents clearly (I have many friends who are not in his tutorial but went for his online tutorial slot, although I didn't attend his lessons personally). For every type of differential equation, apply the following 2 simple steps: 1. Learn to quickly identify the type of differential equation (even if it is disguised) 2. Understand / Memorize the steps to solve it (from lecture notes) If you want to Ace this module, personally I recommend doing A LOT of practice problems instead of revising concepts again and again there aren't much concepts. Expected Grade: A+ Actual Grade: A+

Taken: AY2021/2022 Semester 1 (Fully online, zoom tutorials, pre-recorded lectures) Co-Lecturers: Dr Kamalini Ramdas, Dr Lin Ziqiang, Shaun (and other lecturers who take over a few weeks) Assessment: 20% - E-tutorial participation: students will be graded for participation during Zoom class discussion or zoom chat posts. 10% - Individual written assignment: 500-word write-up 30% - Group Project - Audio-visual material (e.g. Camtasia, e-poster, voice-over slides, mini-video) and 800-word abstract. 40% - Individual Final Assignment: Open book take home assignment comprising 1 essay (1000 word) and 3 short-answer (300 words each) questions. To be completed over 48 hours Took this module because I thought it was an interesting one. But I would say that out of all the modules I have taken, this is the module that I regret taking the most. If you're not an avid football fan, it will likely be a struggle for you. Though they say that anyone can take the course, lecturers (especially towards the end of the semester - Dr Shaun Lin) teach with the assumption that you know all the footballers in the world and all the games and all the clubs. While Dr Kamalini explains most examples in a clear way, it is not always the case for the other lecturers / co-lecturers. Even if you are an avid football fan, you might find it difficult to follow, and this might be the nature of geography itself. While the links between football and geographical concepts are interesting, non-superficial, and quite substantial, these links are often presented in a sort of 'fun-fact' manner. If I could visualize it, it would sort of be a mind map, where the lecture covers one topic, then talks about anything and everything that is related. Sometimes, we even have separate mindmaps for each powerpoint slide, so it's really difficult to find a sense of structure and bigger picture from the whole module, other than the fact that 'space and place' are just constantly being reiterated throughout the whole module. On the bright (?) side, there are many lecturers who teach this module, so naturally, each lecturer has a different teaching style. Some did not follow this 'mindmap with no structure' style at all, and instead delievered content in a very clear-cut and digestable manner, while others felt like they were saying whatever came to mind in that particular moment. I would suggest taking this module if you really love football and care more about learning football fun facts. If you wanted to sincerely learn what the link between football and geography could be, you can also take this module, but it might take a bit more work for you to form your own structure and sieve out important points in the sea of fun facts and content that is covered. With all the said, all this is coming from the perspective of a non-avid football fan who only wanted to explore more about geography in a non-dry way and also understand what the relationship between football and geography is. Also, this is still an interesting module that isn't offered anywhere else, and lecturers and TAs put in a lot of effort to make this module as fun as possible. Perhaps this is the nature of a module with multiple lecturers, and also the nature of geography.

If you have any questions, please send it to my email atqhteo@gmail.com. Don't worry, there are no stupid questions! I've received many emails asking me all sorts of questions. I reply all of them :) Prof: Dr Bernard Tan What is it about? First half you learn more or less basic aspects of music theory, such as the notes on a musical score (EGBDF, etc), time signatures, sharps/flats , semitones, etc. Second half you learn about the technological part of music such as MIDI systems and stuff. One concert review (attend any concert of your choice, write a 800 word review), one MIDI composition (compose 1 minute MIDI piece), and one mid term test, one finals test. Both tests are 25 MCQs, open book (lecture notes) If it sounds like a joke, you are right. It's a freaking joke. It's probably the lightest module in NUS. You can more or less skip the entire first half of the lectures if you have some music theory background. In fact, you can more or less skip all the lectures, and just read his lecture slides, they aren't that hard to understand. But if you are afraid of comprehension problems, go for lectures then. The problem is that he is VERY long winded, and always starts lectures at like.. 40 minutes past the hour. What does he do for the first 40 minutes? Just nag and nag about things he's said before already or recap previous lecture and just random pointless things. I would say it's quite possible to skip all lectures and still know how to do the tests. Some basic Math knowledge would be good, such as knowing how to apply simple formulas and doing simple calculations with a calculator. Miscalleneous Tips The best tip I can give you is - understand the tutorials, DO PAST YEAR PAPERS. He basically does not change the format of the tests, so if you do the past year papers and know how to do all of them, you basically will breeze through the tests. Tutorial questions are more or less gearing you up to do the tests, if you can't find past year papers then do the tutorial questions and understand how to find the answers. Should be pretty easy. Should you take it? If you want the slackest module in NUS, yes. Do note that being 'an easy module' does not make it an 'easy to score module'. These are very different concepts. How did I do for it? I got 23/25 for both quizzes, for the first quiz the median was actually 23.something with a mode of 25 -_- The 2nd quiz the median was 22.something with a mode of 24. So you can see the bell curve is pretty steep. What sets you apart will be your MIDI projects and essay, I believe. Do not make careless mistakes for your quiz. Predicted grade: B+ Actual grade: A-

AY1415 Semester II Under AP Maribeth Erb (For both lectures and tutorials) Overall I enjoyed this module a lot even though I ponned lectures a lot (it's webcasted, the temptation to do so is overwhelming). I could really relate to some of the ideas in my personal experience as a tourist, and I don't think I will be the same as a tourist again haha. --- Lectures: Prof Erb tells great narratives during lectures that I really liked listening to. She also does a good explanation of readings during lectures so take down notes (actually, write a transcript) and it will make your studying life a lot easier if you plan to skim through readings. But people who like more structure in their content may find lectures a bit wanting. Lectures are webcasted which can be both a good and bad thing. Tutorials: Except for the first tutorial, the rest were all group presentations. Which also means that you don't need to prepare for the tutorials except the one you are presenting for. Write down notes during tutorials too because groups usually tend to take apart and put back together various readings in the course, which is helpful if you plan to read selectively. Post-presentation discussions are also very enjoyable. Workload: Workload is not a lot, and fairly manageable. But timing is important. If you group presentation and paper falls late in the semester, where everything else from every other module is due, then it's going to be hard to manage. Readings: There are a lot of readings for each topic. But it's not necessary to read everything, there are papers which Prof Erb uploads so that we can take a look if we are interested. Still, I think getting a grasp of each author's key arguments and points is vital to doing well in finals. So, don't need to read everything, but need to understand everything. Finals: 2 out of 6 questions (3 choose 1 and 3 choose 1) means a lot of choice and a lot of room for spotting topics. However, some topics are easier to answer than others, obviously, so just manage your risk taking well. Whichever topic, I would think it is highly pertinent to bring in the ideas of the various authors that were introduced during lecture and in readings, and even better, use one author to comment on the ideas of the other.

Taken in AY20/21 Semester 2 Taught by : Professor Chan Heng Huat (Lecturer + Tutor) Assessment Structure : Tutorials : 19% Three tests : 27% each This module provides a "historical overview" of how number theory is developed in the 17th and 18th century. Under Prof Chan, the examinable topics include divisibility, Fermat's Little Theorem and Euler's Theorem, multiplicative functions, congruence equations, primitive roots, quadratic reciprocity law, Jacobsthal sums, binary quadratic forms, form class groups, continued fraction and Pell's equation. Prof Chan also covered some extra non-examinable topics such as group actions and the isomorphism between the form class group and the narrow class group. Both lectures and tutorials were conducted face-to-face with no webcast. For most of the tutorials, we were required to choose 4 questions (out of 7-8) to submit for grading. The best 5 out of 9 scores will then be used to compute the tutorial component. Thus the theoretical minimum workload is quite low, as one can simply choose the 4 easiest questions from the 5 easiest tutorials to submit. Nevertheless, I still recommend students to attempt all questions, as the style of tutorial questions and the style of exam questions are very similar. Prof Chan is quite a friendly lecturer and tries to get to know the names of all of his students. There are many occasions in which he stayed back after class, either to answer questions from students or just to chat about mathematics in general. Prof Chan is also quite a good teacher. This is complimented by the fact that he is very passionate about teaching and frequently insert jokes to liven up the class. However, I feel that Prof Chan can also be really intense at times. Despite not being listed as pre-requisites, Prof Chan sometimes dive into MA3201 and MA3111 territory in order to explain certain concepts. Some of the non-examinable stuff he covers are also really deep (I was completely lost when he explained the link between the form class group and the narrow class group). The three tests are conducted throughout the semester, with the final one being held on week 13. As expected of a pure mathematics module, the emphasis is on proving techniques rather than computation. Thus the performance of the cohort can be rather polarising. Professor Chan tries to level the playing field by giving a disproportionally high weightage to the "giveaway" computational questions. He also gives out additional hints DURING the exam to students who were stuck. I originally took this module simply for enrichment since many of the core modules I wanted to take had timetable clashes. Despite that, I have zero regrets taking this module. Classes are generally very lively and many students are quite enthusiastic during lessons. The class also have some hilarious reactions whenever Prof Chan drops a big theorem or demonstrates an elegant way to solve a tutorial problem and I personally enjoyed every second of it. (This paragraph applies to most pure math modules) Unfortunately, due to its nature of being a pure math module, the cohort is generally very strong (over one-third of the students are in SPM). To students who are interested to learn about number theory, I would encourage you to still take this module and not let the high performing students intimidate you. This is because the grade distribution is adjusted accordingly to reflect the strength of the cohort. I estimate roughly half of the class got A and above. Final Grade : A+

Taken in AY 16/17 Sem 2 I went for this module with high expectations for it, believing that a module about critical thinking and writing would entail a myriad of topics for us to analyse and dissect. To my dismay, the scope of this module was sadly limited to the context of saving/preserving the environment. The readings that they provided got quite boring and repeated at times. Most of the time we were forced to follow a specific format of paragraph opening sentences....which kinda defeats the nature of critical thinking (which is a topic for another day). Nonetheless, it's a compulsory module for me as an engineering student. Assessment: 3 Assignments, 1 Finals and Tutorial participation. A1 is about summary and evaluation (very similar to A Level GP but you gotta follow the dept's writing guidelines), A2 is a group project (3 people) about addressing a UN development goal and coming up with a written report detailed with your background of the problem, current measures in place and how your new engineering solutions would build upon them. The group project is the most time-consuming part of this module and make sure you find good teammates to work with! Make sure to start early and delegate roles well. There is an oral defense segment included with this but it's pretty easy if everyone worked hard in the project (unless you are a slacker...then you would be clueless). A3 is an individual reflection about the module, and like all module reflections, just remember to link back to the learning objectives of this module. Finals is basically like Assignment 1 with the bonus of evaluating 2 more key arguments. Time's the factor here so write fast. Tutorial participation depends on how friendly your tutor is. Overall, this is a manageable module if you have good foundations in GP. Teammates-wise, we had a slacker but we still managed to get a A grade for project. If this module isn't compulsory, I definitely wouldn't recommend taking this module.

Taken in AY2016/17 Semester 2 under Dr Leslie Lee Also coded as EL1101E Teaching mode: Lectures & tutorials once per week. Contents: The module covered speech sounds (consonants & vowels), morphology (how words are formed), syntax (rules for forming phrases & sentences), semantics (meaning) and pragmatics (inferred meanings). Some memory work is required, as you’d need to remember the sounds of consonants & vowels, definitions and rules. Test and exam questions may be straightforward if you remember what was taught in lectures, but a few of them can be rather tricky as they test your understanding and ability to apply the concepts learned. E.g. the question may ask you to identify any word relationships in a set of words/sounds (of a foreign language!). Overall, the workload was fine, the module was enjoyable and it served as a nice introduction to linguistics studies. The lecturer Leslie often explains new concepts in a straightforward manner, and his lectures were not dry or boring!

Semester: 2020-2021 Sem 1 Lecturer: Bingsheng He General review: This is a fun module! It is maybe also the most applied module I have taken during my studies. Prof. Bingsheng is very good at explaining the concepts clearly and the TA's were also quite good. Furthermore, I would not say the concepts taught are that difficult to understand (for example, it is not math heavy at all). The most difficult part of this module is definitely the project. Prof. Bingsheng also seemed genuinely interested in our learning, and would typically respond fast and in great detail over email and in the forum. This is also the module where I have experienced the most elaborate feedback, and i.e. for the project that consisted of multiple parts to be submitted he would give feedback on stuff to improve for the next part which was extremely nice. In-class quiz (5%): True/False questions. You were not awarded marks based on whether or not you answered correctly though, this was solely for taking attendance. I personally believe it is weird to give marks based on attendance, but none the less, these marks are easily obtained. Assignments (2 * 10%): First assignment was on Hadoop MapReduce and we had to implement it in Java. I had no prior coding experience in Java, but the assignment focuses mostly on MapReduce concepts and I had no trouble. Assignment 2 was on Spark and had to be implemented in Scala. Again, a language I had no experience with. If you for some reason have difficulty quickly learning new languages, this might pose a problem for you, but for graduate computing students it should be very easy to pick up what you need to do. Overall I would say the assignments are quite easy and you should be able to score top marks with little effort. System Survey (10%): This part is for CS5425 students only. We had to write a survey on three different NoSQL database systems. For a good grade, this requires you to read a lot of research papers and present them well. Test (35%): Consists of a lot of questions where some were easy and some were difficult. Prof. Bingsheng gave a lot of tips on how to perform well and what to prepare for. There were also previous exams to train on that were quite similar in format. Most students did well in the first part but not that well for problem solving and performance analysis, so make sure to focus on those. Project (40%): You have to propose, implement and present a project for this module which makes up a significant part of the final grade in a project group of up to 5 people. My group did a CBIR (Content-Based Image Retrieval) system that we hosted on Microsoft Azure. Microsoft was kind enough to sponsor each group with $500 worth of credits on Azure. Be aware that this can be quite tough if you have no previous experience with working with cloud providers. MapReduce and Spark is taught during the module, but a lot of what we did with Azure etc. is not taught at all. For the project, make sure you have a good group. Overall for the project, I would say that it is quite fun but also can take up quite some time. Also, if you do not propose that good a topic I imagine it would drag you down as well for the presentation and final report. My group were lucky that it seemed like prof really found our proposed project interesting. Project Proposal (10%): A report that proposes your project. Make sure to put effort into thinking about what you would like to work on, since 1) you have to spend a lot of time actually working on it and 2) you cannot suddenly change the project a lot after having submitted the proposal. Focus especially on previous work in this proposal, citing quite a few articles to make sure to demonstrate you have actually researched your area. Project Presentation (10%): A ∼15 min presentation on your project. You should have implemented most of it prior to the presentation, have interesting findings and make nice slides and be sure to present it well. Final Report (20%): Prof. Bingsheng was nice enough to mark the presentation very fast, so we could use the feedback to improve the report. if you did well in the presentation, you should be able to do so as well in the report. The report could be up to about 20 pages including figures and tables. NB: You will notice the percentages sum to 110%. This is due to the system survey being an assignment solely for the CS5425 students. Therefore the real weightages of the different items are actually a little lower (i.e. 20/110 ≈ 18% for the assignments). Final grade: A+

Taken in AY19/20 Semester 2 Taught by: Gan Wee Teck (Lecturer and Tutor) Disclaimer: This module was affected by the COVID-19 pandemic, and as a result it may differ significantly from how past/future modules would/will be conducted. Assessment Structure: 10% Homework (4 sets) 20% Midterm 1 (In-Class) 20% Midterm 2 (In-Class) 50% Final (Online) This is a module under both lists MA4 and AM4-General, hence both Pure Math and Applied Math majors can take this module to satisfy their core requirements. The module’s topics include recap of vector spaces, linear maps, Banach spaces, Stone-Weierstrass Theorem, spectral theory, dual spaces, Baire’s Category Theorem, Principle of Uniform Boundedness, Fourier analysis, inner product spaces and Hilbert spaces, and further spectral theory of compact, self-adjoint operators. There is not a main textbook of reference. Lecture and tutorial attendance are not compulsory, and lectures are initially not webcast due to small class size. When the COVID-19 pandemic forced all lectures to be suspended, Prof. Gan uploaded videos explaining the final few chapter (no Zoom lectures were carried out). Tutorial sessions just involve Prof. Gan going through selected solutions. Difficulty of tutorial questions usually range from average to quite difficult, with only a few exceptions being very difficult. Homework questions are taken from tutorial sets, and Prof. Gan like to take the more difficult questions as homework, so one should not be surprised if they need to search for online help in completing their homework. Generally, tutorial questions did well on showing how one can apply the concepts taught to solve certain problems. This is especially important for questions that rely on the same tricks, such as applying Baire’s Category Theorem or Principle of Uniform Boundedness. As such, I strongly recommend students to do and redo all the questions in the tutorials. This is one of the most difficult modules I’ve taken so far. Quoting from Prof. Gan, functional analysis is probably better called “linear analysis”, the analytic contrast to linear algebra. Many concepts generalise matrices in linear algebra to linear maps and operators, and applying analysis to linear algebra concepts such as dual spaces. Many theorems in this module are highly non-trivial, and which proofs are also messy (as with many advanced proofs in analysis) and thus difficult to understand and/or appreciate. In my opinion, Fourier analysis was the most difficult as they are the hardest to visualise. Despite so, it is possible to at least see heuristically/pictorially why many concepts are true, and one should expect to spend a good amount of time doing that. Prof. Gan is one of the best lecturers I have had so far. He excels at explaining the concepts fluently and clearly on the board as he writes on the board, an important skill that not many lecturers hold. When writing proofs, he often explains the idea behind each step to make the proofs feel less cryptic. However, his lectures tend to be quite fast, and if one just loses attention for a short moment, they may find it difficult to catch up with the lecture. Outside of lectures, Prof. Gan is a very friendly and approachable individual who encourages student to ask him questions (offline or via email) should they have any queries. Overall, it was an absolute treat to take a module under Prof. Gan. Both midterms are closed book (with 2-sided A4 helpsheet), and both consist of 3 and 4 questions respectively and total of 20 marks, while final is open internet with 6 questions total of 80 marks. Prof. Gan is known to set hard problems for his exams, and this was indeed the case for both midterms and the final exam. Despite so, he usually includes some standard and simple questions (especially at the start), in which students should grab those marks as they can. I took this module without MA3209 as I took MA2108S and MA3110S, and had no issues understanding the terms used and background knowledge assumed. I strongly recommend students interested in graduate analysis to take this module (especially under Prof. Gan) for a rich, rigorous introduction to functional analysis. Expected Grade: A-/A Final Grade: A

Grade: A+

Hi, there are more module reviews here too: CS2103T Software Engineering Difficulty: Hard Grade Obtained: B+ Lecturers: Prof Damith This is a 4MC core module for CEG students so there's no escaping this. CS1020 is a prerequisite for this module. This module is basically an introduction to group programming projects. The content is all online and you are expected to be self-learn it and attend tutorials to go through the content and clear up doubts. All the content is here Here's the high-level overview of the topics taught: Software Engineering Requirements - for the project Design - design principles, modeling, architecture and design patterns Implementation - IDEs, code quality, documentation, integration Quality Assurance - testing Project management - revision control, project planning, teamwork Tools - UML diagrams, IntelliJ, Git, Java, JUnit This module is graded this way: Project (50%) Participation (10%) Final Exam (40%) The project component refers to Phase B. This will be a major pain to your team and suck up all of your free time for the second half of this semester. In groups of 4, you're supposed to set your own the requirements for the final product you want to have at the end of the module, modify existing features and add new features to an existing code base: addressbook4 to make those features happen. And at the same time, each person will play different roles in the group e.g. project lead, code integrator, project management, documentation. You're also expected to apply the content mentioned above (design principles, design patterns, proper project management, maintaining high code quality, write good documentation) with deadlines on a weekly basis (your v1.0 to v1.5 project milestones) There are way too many things for a single person to do but that's why you have 3 other group mates to work with. And that bring us to the next point, choosing team members. It's best to choose teammates that are motivated and capable. Finally, with 40% of the grade in finals, your team can only help you so much. You'll still have to depend on own effort. This module is normally seen as the pinnacle of all the S mods, and it's not hard to see why. Content: First 3 weeks were just a revision of topology. If you took any course with metric spaces inside you should be fine for this part. Next 3 weeks, we start complex analysis, and go through basic theorems such as Cauchy Integral Formula and Laurent Theorem. Pretty much covered the whole of MA3111 here. Next 3 weeks, we go through stuff taught in MA4247, such as Rouche Theorem, Open Mapping Theorem etc. After that, there was a short introduction to Riemann Surfaces and the theory of Distributions and Currents. Fortunately, these topics were not tested. Lectures: Prof Dinh is the best lecturer I have ever had. This is perhaps why you should take this module. He gives very good insights, and his presentation of ideas is extremely clear. He tends to focus on the big idea on why the theorems are true rather than the smaller details, which is good for a person with more Physics/Engineering than Math background like myself. And even if you aren't taking this module I think you should try to sit in for some lectures to learn Complex Analysis from him, since this subject has many,many applications. Tutorials: Tricky. Very tricky. But many useful tricks hidden in these problems. Assessments: Homework was doable. But questions were slightly tricky. Not as tricky as tutorials so it was alright. Midterms and Finals were extremely hard. Fortunately Prof Dinh is very lenient with grading. Just keep an open mind going into exams. We had to prove the great Picard Theorem in the midterm (it was guided with parts) and I couldn't do anything. Overall: This module is really, really tough but you will gain a lot from the experience. I HIGHLY RECOMMEND this module if you like math or if you want to learn a bit more. If you didn't take MA2108S/MA3110S maybe try to learn some topology first before coming in. Prof Dinh is a great lecturer, so this module was an excellent experience for me. Difficulty: 10/10 How fun was this module: 5/5

under Prof Jonathan Mark Scarlett. Due to the COVID-19 pandemic, there were no physical lectures, and webcasts of the previous semester were provided instead. Tutorials were conducted on Zoom and recorded. This module is an introduction to machine learning. It starts off with linear binary classification (perceptron algorithm, support-vector machines, logistic regression), and then moves on to linear regression. The latter half of the semester covers non-linear machine learning, such as the kernel method, convex optimisation, and boosting (AdaBoost algorithm). Towards the end of the semester, there is a small chapter on "probably approximately correct" guarantees, and another small chapter on k-means clustering. The module does not go very deeply into most of the topics covered, and most of the chapters in the latter half of the semester are relatively self-contained. Graded components: - Midterm test (25%) - Project (25%) - Final exam (50%) The midterm test and final exam are open book, and are conducted under usual timed conditions. The project is completed individually, and it requires students to read up on a topic not covered in the module. The topic is chosen by the student from a short list of topics provided by Prof Scarlett. Students are to write a report (in the style of his lecture notes) about the topic that they have chosen. The style of the project was somewhat different from the previous year, perhaps because the module was conducted online this semester. Prof Scarlett's style of teaching and exams are rather different from the typical mathematics module. Instead of focusing on proofs or calculations, Prof Scarlett prefers giving students an intuitive understanding of the module content. This is also reflected in the test and exam — most questions only require students to "explain briefly" the given phenomena or their answers, and one or two sentences are sufficient explanation. Formal proofs are almost never required in the test and exam. Workload for this module seems to be relatively light, apart from the project. However, the project was released quite early into the semester, so students had the flexibility to plan their time appropriately.

Took this module in Sem 1 AY15/16, taken by Prof Emi Morita. 3 hour seminars weekly, usually with a break after 1 hour. Graded components include weekly assignments, a group project and essay, 2 CA exams and a final exam (which is roughly the difficulty and length of the CA exam). Prof Morita is a quirky and interesting lecturer who has an interest in social linguistics and has ways of making the lectures interesting and fun. Perhaps the most memorable portion of the module would be learning onomatopoeia by eating food she bought for the class from the supermarket. This also happened for one of the CA exams, so it was quite interesting to have people legitimately eating during an "official" exam. She is quite a pleasant personality to study under and is willing to sit down and discuss the problems you have, especially regarding the group project. She is, however, very strict on deadlines for assignments, though they are usually quite interesting and sometimes painful to do. While the module prerequisites state that students should have at least completed Japanese 2 or equivalent, the playing field was obviously not equal, with some students coming in at Japanese 5/6 or with JLPT N1/N2 and as such, it would definitely be advantageous to have a friend in the upper brackets to help you out. This is helpful when doing things like morphological analysis where students who are not as well-versed in the language might interpret a word in a different manner from native speakers due to the lack of contextual knowledge. Jisho.org is your friend in this module, though it can get confusing after a while. Ultimately, if you are taking the CLS LAJ modules or learning Japanese on your own, this module helps you realise the logic behind certain basic fundamentals of the Japanese language which will enlighten you and most likely aid in your understanding of things you once had to brute-force your way through studying like verbal conjugations, on/kun readings, accents and inflections etc. Understanding English linguistics prior to taking this mod or taking EL1101E before this module will help slightly in the understanding of linguistic concepts and terminology, but you are not at a disadvantage if you have not studied linguistics before. Readings are not too heavy, and both books are available as RBRs, with one of the books being available in PDF online. What she covers in lectures is strictly limited to what she assigns in readings, except that she provides more examples, so don't be too worried if you haven't done any of the readings, though they really help because you know what is going on during lectures. The group assignment requires one to find a problem in the Japanese language which non-native speakers usually have issues learning, such as the differences between onomatopoeia (in food, pain, etc), the use of Osaka dialect, or the differences in locative/dative/allative particle usage. You then have to design a short lesson to solve this problem. Usually these problems are not extensively covered in literature, or if so then not so much in english-language sources. Dr. Morita really likes empirical analysis of native usage in order to solve the problems that the groups submit, so don't shy from data-gathering and analysis because that is what she wants. The essay is basically a very short summary of the entire study and project, and she provides a pretty clear rubric to follow, with a pretty flexible word limit. People with a strong interest in the Japanese language who want to understand the rules behind what they learn would most definitely find this module enlightening.

AY 17/18 Sem 2 Lecturer: Prof Dinh Tien Cuong 20% Homework (5 sets to be completed every fortnight) 20% Midterm 60% Finals Content: Module split into two halves: first half focuses on the elephant in the room, Complex analysis, which is the study of holomorphic functions (which a whole lot nicer than real differentiable functions) and the second half is an introduction into Riemann surfaces. This course under Prof Dinh is really difficult for 2 main reasons: the entire complex analysis part of the module is squeezed into the first 6 weeks, which can be horrendous given that it is our first time studying complex analysis and also we spent first 2-3 weeks reviewing topology. Secondly, Riemann surfaces are not exactly the easiest things to study as an undergrad; to have a good grasp of it requires many areas of Mathematics: Complex Analysis (duh), Manifolds, Geometry, Topology, Group Theory. Its not easy trying to put everything together. So be warned! Lecture pace is really quick so you need to do a lot of revision so as to not fall behind (I fell behind quite often and I totally gave up for Riemann surfaces). Prof Dinh is a lecturer that focuses more on the big picture of the proof rather than the nitty gritty technicalities so I guess in some sense it is good because it helps to develop some intuition as to why certain results are true. Tutorial: Tutorials are not easy. But they contain many useful tricks and results essential to the study of complex analysis and Riemann surfaces respectively. The questions are not important but the way of thinking and proving are more essential than what is presented. Tests/Exams: Thankfully, Prof Dinh is quite merciful when it comes to exam/tests. Computational question usually comes out for exams and usually only 1/2 questions will be really difficult. Prof Dinh is also very lenient with his allocation for marks (even homework) I think its one of the few modules that you have to work hard consistently because it is very fast paced and the content is difficult. I think the end results can be rewarding but then again if you have no interest in learning Riemann surfaces, perhaps the iteration of S-mod under Prof Dinh is not suitable for you.

Lecturer: Dr Eldin Lim Assessment: • 2 Quizzes (20%) • 2 Assignments (20%) • 2 Term Papers (20%) • 1 Project Report (20%) • 1 Project Presentation (20%) General Comments: This is easily one of the most rigorous and well-taught chemical engineering modules I have taken. There is a huge diversity topics involved, and the project is rather challenging, so I think you would have to put in some effort. Other than that, it is really well-taught, and Prof Eldin is good at delivering the material. Lectures and Tutorials: The lectures mainly focused on some key concepts in mathematical modelling, such as continuum modelling, using Finite Fourier Transform to solve simple PDE, and method of variations in PDE. These are some nice things to know when solving problems in applied mathematics. As a math major, I personally did not know these things myself. I think this is probably the coolest part of the module. Even though there aren't many proofs involved, it was quite fun to know these techniques exist in case I need it. The tutorial sessions also involve going through some of the supplementary material from the lectuers, as well as learning Python and Matplotlib. That was pretty cool too. The only weird thing is that there is a large variety of topics involved that don't really seem interconnected except that they all relate to Mathematics and modelling in Engineering. Nonetheless, there will not be a deep discussion on each topic- so it wasn't that hard after all. Asssessments: The quizzes are just a recap of the lectures, so just don't make careless mistakes and practice the PYPs provided. They are quite doable. The first assignment was using numerical analysis to solve some simple problems while the second assignment involved the use of Matplotlib. The two term papers involve looking at a couple of research papers in ANY academic field regarding mathematical modelling and proposing a new general idea to improve the current status quo. For example, I talked about how some researchers used Algebraic Topology was used in Neuroscience, and what could be done to improve the model of the brain they used. It was quite fun and there is no need to be absolutely rigorous about the research plan. * Each term paper is only at most 2 pages long* The final project is the most fun part. Basically, we are allowed to investigate literally ANY mathematical modelling technique in ANY academic field and write a report and full presentation. It does not need to be related to chemical engineering at all. This was really fun, some people decided to talk about stochastic processes in finance and my group did chemical plume tracing. This was really quite fun as our ideas were allowed to go completely free. Project groupings range from 1-5 people. Overall comments: I think you should take this module if you are interested in Mathematical Modelling. Not only are the lectures well-taught, the project gives you an avenue to just let your mind decide what you wanna do. It was really fun and I highly recommend this module to anyone considering, Difficulty: 4/5 How fun was this module: 9/10

CS1010FC AY13/14 Sem 2 Taught by: Prof Ben Leong, Brian Koh and Michelle Teo Summary: For NSmen, this is a great way to "de-rust" your brain after 2 years in NS. Strongly recommended! [Info] Took the module from January to June 2014, lecturer was Prof Ben Leong and TAs were Mr Brian Koh and Ms Michelle Teo. [Content] For those who has not done programming before, it can be quite a steep learning curve. Then again, since CS1010 is a compulsory module for all Computing and Engineering students, I'd recommend you to take CS1010FC since this module spans 5-6 months instead of the usual 18 weeks for CS1010/CS1010E, which means you will have more time to learn (and of course pester the lecturer/TAs for consultations). This module is taught in Python, nonetheless the skills taught in this module can be easily applied in other programming languages. As the name of the module suggests, this module teaches you the different methods of programming, and does not focus on Python-specific functions. Having done programming in C before, I find that Python is easier to use as it is closer to the human language in terms of syntax and key words. At the end of the module, basic C programming was covered and it was mainly about coding some simple programs that were already covered but in C this time. [Delivery] Video lectures were uploaded weekly, and the lectures were uploaded in parts based on sub-topics, usually 5 videos of approximately 10 minutes each. This was very beneficial during revision as you need not have to scroll through an entire hour of video just to replay the lecture on a specific topic. On certain weeks when students had difficulty understanding concepts covered in the previous week, the lecturer took time to recap those concepts before moving on with the lecture proper. In addition, the lecturer and TAs were very helpful and were always more than willing to stay behind after the class has ended to clarify any doubts. Recitations/tutorials were conducted online for the first three months, and physically for the next three months. Online recitations/tutorials were conducted "live" using WebEx, and if you have a microphone can speak to your lecturer/TAs (instead of having to type your queries). The lecturer and tutors were very engaging and it will be difficult to doze off during their lessons! While the online recitations/tutorials were recorded, it is best to attend them instead of watching the webcast as you can clarify your doubts with the lecturer/TAs "on-the-spot". Assignments are given and graded through a portal called Coursemology, a "Gamified Online Education Platform". In fact, everything from lecture slides to announcements and administrative information are uploaded onto Coursemology. When you complete assignments, tutorials and (optional) practices, you are given EXP points. Earn EXP points to reach the next level, and your level at the end of your course determines your CA grade. The assignments are designed to be like games, there will be a background storyline (for your own reading pleasure) and a number of tasks to complete. The few assignments which I remember the most are Facebook stalking (count the number of likes, comments, etc. on a FB post), 2048 (to create a 2048 game which you can play on your computer) and Hungry Games (a variant of the Hunger Games). Tutorials are meant to test your understanding and should be done before the assignments (which test your knowledge application). Grading for tutorials were instant and gradings for assignments were usually by 24 hours, if not 2 days! Helpful comments were also provided by the graders, who are our seniors, when they grade our assignments. Besides assignments and tutorials, there are also many optional practices for you to reinforce your knowledge. By many I do mean a lot, only 2 people in the entire class completed all the assignments, tutorials and practices! There are also achievements and levels for the more competitive ones to compare with your fellow course mates. [Workload] Practise, practise, practise. Consistency is the key to doing well for this module, you will find yourself falling behind once you miss a week or two of lessons. Help is always available, from the lecturer, TAs and fellow course mates, and there is a Forum on Coursemology for you to ask questions. Consultations (both online and offline) were also readily conducted for students who require them. [Examinations] One mid-terms, one practical test and one finals. AY2020/2021 Sem 1 Review A/P An Xinliang ODE stands for Ordinary Differential Equations This module is taught via E learning given the Coronavirus period. A variety of topics pertaining to ordinary differential equations is taught in this module. The first half of the module includes solving first, second, third and higher nth order ODEs. All these are done so by determining the particular solution to the ODE and the general solution to its corresponding homogeneous ODE. Then the general solution to the particular ODE is “ a particular solution + the general solution to its corresponding homogeneous ODE “. To master this portion, one must be well versed in multivariable calculus, complex numbers (from JC) and higher order differentiations. This portion may seem easy to some but it is quite prone to carelessness. Moreover, Some ODEs are tricky and will require students to think out of the box to solve (probably by factorization, trigonometry, product rule, quotient rule, chain rule etc). The challenge in this part is that some methods which work for certain ODEs may not work for other ODEs. For instance using the variation of parameters method or the Euler equation/ formula may work for some ODEs but not for other ODEs. Hence, to master this portion, one may need continuous and kaisu practices from many past year papers and textbook problems. In fact I practiced problems from past year papers dated back as early as 2003. Then the 2nd part of the module is on solving a linear system of first order ODEs with x, y and a parameter t. It is in the form of dy/dt=f(x,y,t) dx/dt=g(x,y,t) Here the linear algebra concepts on Eigenvalues, eigenvectors and diagonalization comes in only for linear systems in the form of dy/dt=ax+by dx/dt=cx+dy Where a,b,c,d are real numbers. But for other linear system of ODEs in other forms apart from this, one may need to think out of the box to solve it. The hard part of this portion is on the properties of fundamental matrices which are useful in solving many of such ODEs. Carelessness kills in solving a non homogeneous linear system and repeated eigenvalues where many workings come in. The sign of the Eigenvalue will then determine the nature of the critical point associated to the system. This content requires students to sketch a phase portrait, a graph of y against x for a linear system of ODE mostly in the form of dy/dt=ax+by dx/dt=cx+dy Where a,b,c,d are real numbers. The sketching is tedious. This is where I wasted many foolscap papers and dirtied my bedroom. Hence do prepare yourself with sufficient foolscap and a dustbin next to your working table if you are solving such problems. The hard part is when exponential, logarithmic and trigonometric functions are introduced in a linear system of ODEs where one needs to deduce the critical points from a system of first order ODEs in the form of dy/dt=f(x,y,t) dx/dt=g(x,y,t) especially if more than one critical point exist in such a system and sketch a phase portrait. Drawing is hard and one needs an artistic sense to connect the lines to construct a beautiful art piece. Afterwards the mathematical analysis portion comes in which is applied in proving the existence and uniqueness of a solution to an ODE with given initial conditions. The lecturer goes through the standard procedure of doing so. The final does have a question which requires students to reproduce such proves from their lecture notes. Such question is a giveaway but the hard part is in deriving the Lipschitz Condition which may require one to apply concepts such as the mean value theorem The procedure is: 1. Determine the lipschitz condition 2. Establish the Picard's Iteration 3. Deduce the boundedness of the Picard's Iteration 4. Prove the uniform convergence of the Picard's Iteration to prove the existance of the ODE solution 5. Apply the Gronwall's inequality to check the uniqueness of the solution. Do note that series convergence tests (ratio test, comparison test), Lipchitz condition and uniform continuity are concepts introduced in mathematical analysis I. But Prof An Xinliang retaught and goes through them in much details, thoroughly as compared to MA2108 which goes through them in brief details. Other concepts taught too in the analysis portion are the osgood condition, stability of solutions and more rigorous proves on a system of ODEs. Prof An Xinliang is a kind and open lecturer. He encourages students to share their answers and approaches during lectures and tutorials as certain ODEs have many different approaches in solving. He really deserve the teaching awards as he is flexible in his teaching style given the contents in the module are challenging and abstract. He is able to tweak his teaching schedule to accommodate to his students’ moods and obligations too such as turning zoom lectures into face to face office hours nearer to the exam periods. This enables healthy human interactions. Sometimes he even end his lecture of the contents earlier before the official end time of his zoom lecture so that he can use the rest of his time to interact and engage with us and check on us too if we can understand the contents. He has a really fatherly figure here. Tutorial are just about 3 to 5 questions long. Tutorials are mainly like an informal discussion session. He does not summon and force students to present their solutions if they are uncomfortable doing so. Instead he gets students who can solve to share their own solutions so that others can learn. He even engages the shyer ones too. Midterms wise is doable with some challenging problems while the finals are hard. Phase portraits are surprisingly not tested in the finals. To do well one should revise through the tutorial problems. Prof An Xinliang do drop some hints in the finals too especially for the difficult problems. They are handy in solving them. His TAs are good. They are committed and patient in answering to my doubts though I have a lot of misconceptions in the sketching of phase portraits and the proving portion. I also have lunch with him and his TAs too and learned some valuable insights from them. Hopefully he can retain the same awesome TAs too when he is teaching partial differential equations next semester All in all, I learn that Ordinary Differential Equations is a wide and abstract topic and the A level knowledge is just the tip of the ice berg which never melts. I learn to appreciate the blend of linear algebra, calculus and mathematical analysis in this abstract topic of ODEs. ODE comprise of two parts. The computational half which emphasize on linear algebra and calculus techniques. The proving half which implements the convergence theorem of series and the continuity Lemmas from mathematical analysis to prove the existence and uniqueness of ODE solutions. In a nutshell, the study of ODEs is like the study of a complex art piece, implementing the many different fields of mathematics.

Taken in 20/21 Sem 2 Grading: 5% CA1, 25% CA2, 10% CA3, 30% CA4, 15% CA5, 15% participation Ah yes, the compulsory English class to be taken by all Computing students. There are 2x2hr sessions per week with high weightage class participation, which I'm sure contributes to the universal hate this class gets. The content of the class can be read from the other reviews so I'll just talk about the assessments. --- Assessment --- Similar to CS2101, grading is very consistent throughout the semester due to the 5 CAs. There aren't any "lull" periods where there's nothing to do (notwithstanding the 2x2hr sessions per week), so expect to put in more work than you might probably expect. For group projects, the class is split into groups at the start of the semester based on a survey done in the first class. You're stuck with this group for the whole semester so pray you get people who have the same goals as you. I was fortunate to have landed in a group with like-minded individuals who all wanted to maximise effort:reward ratio. CA1: Craft a presentation/video of a spin on a children's tale. Pretty simple, can be done in an afternoon if focused. CA2: Make a "Critical Thinking Rubric" from the Ennis reading, write a report on it (15%) and do a presentation (10%). This is the most tiring group project so I'm glad the co-ordinators put this early in the semester. CA3: Panel Discussion on an topic that was agreed upon prior to the discussion. You have to research the topic, then have an "academic conversation" that goes on for about 30-45min with your group, with 15min Q/A at the end. Can be prepared the day before. Try to be nice to your teammates and let them have their say in the discussion. CA4: Position Paper. You propose a question then write a 800-word-or-so essay on it. This is similar to writing a GP essay, except with citations. Can be done in a day assuming you already have a good question to write on. This is individual work with high weightage so if you're planning to score, better put work into this. CA5: Given a prompt, do an individual impromptu speech on the prompt in 2min. This is a luck of the draw if you get a good prompt or not. It's over within 2 minutes so if you can't think of anything to say, hey, at least you'll die quickly. Taken in 20/21 SEM 2 under Prof Guo Yong Xin (online lessons) Grading: 5% x 2 lab experiments, 10% x 2 mini projects, 10% x 2 CA test, 50% finals This course serves as an introduction to microwave circuits and the important components that make up the circuits. Pre-requisite is EE3104Cwhich I waived, going in with PC2020 knowledge. I subsequently found out that this was doable because transmission line and S-parameter theory was taught from scratch. However, learning these 2 concepts before the course will be very beneficial as much of the rest of the course relies on them. We covered the telegrapher equations, Smith chart usage (beyond what is taught in PC2020), Y/Z matrices and S parameters as an introduction. The pace was very slow at this point with Prof Guo spending quite an excessive amount of time on these concepts. Power dividers (Wilkinson, Coupled line) and filter design was then taught. Filter design will not be a problem if you have an analog electronics background, but the even and odd mode analysis for power dividers could take a while to get used to. These 3 chapters were covered in the first half of the course. The second half of the course was more rushed as Prof Guo effectively finished teaching chapters 4-8 in about 3-4 weeks. Content covered includes more RF devices like switches, amplifiers, mixers and oscillators. Amplifier design is a huge part of this course and many details like the non-linear effects in amplifiers, how to design matching circuitry, design for high gain/low noise figure was taught. However, this part was mostly glossed over by Prof Guo and I felt like he was just explaining whatever formulas were on the slides in a “wing-it” manner instead of connecting it to the big picture. The first lab experiment was to measure the S-parameters for different devices. Remember to take many pictures! The second lab experiment was to calculate the noise temperature and noise figure of an amplifier under bias/no bias. This part was more complicated and a good understanding of how noise originates in a circuit is required. Data from both labs was taken in person, and we were given 1 week to complete the lab report. The GAs were helpful and approachable in this portion of the course. The design software that we used for both projects was ADS, and it is relatively intuitive and easy to use. The first mini project required us to design a power divider at a fixed resonant frequency. The second mini project was the difficult one: designing a low noise amplifier with a single transistor. The lab manual alone was 33 pages, and there were many steps to be completed. However, the GA went through all the steps from start to end, but did not explain the big picture again (seems to be the trend in this group), so I just went with the flow without understanding why some steps were done (although they magically improved the parameters). Do start early for this project as it can be quite time consuming. Tutorials are the worst: Prof Guo skipped the first 2 tutorials and basically just glossed over the rest of the 3 tutorials. Doesn’t take a genius to tell students that “this is easy, you should be able to do it” for many of the questions. The tests and final exam tested on basic concepts, and you should be fine if you understood every slide (which is not a lot anyway). Anyway I didn’t do very well for the second test and exam because I was getting destroyed by other classes. Final thoughts: I 100% would not recommend this course. The content covered is pretty good to me, but think of this course as a good restaurant with a really bad waiter. Prof Guo didn’t give me the impression that he prepares for lectures and just glossed over the explanations. At one point, I stopped watching the lectures entirely even though they were recorded because I simply did not understand anything he was saying. I relied a lot on my own self studying for this.

Taken in AY 15/16 Sem 1 under Dr Connie and Dr Georgios Grade Received : A Having heard about the steep bell curve, I was initially a little worried about taking this module given that I had no prior economics background. Looking back however, I can firmly say that this was one of the most interesting modules I had all semester. The module deals with the basic concepts of economics, using the first half of the semester for microeconomics and the second half for macroeconomics. Assessment comprised of online mcq quizzes(pre and post lecture), lecture participation, tutorial attendance, a midterm exam and a final exam. Dr. Connie served as the lecturer for the first half of the semester. Personally, I found her lectures boring, as her slides and explanations were mostly straight out of the text book. I therefore attended her lectures only to ensure that I received full marks for attendance. To learn and understand the concepts, I spent my time reading the text book, which was extremely lucid and interesting. Dr. Georgios, on the other hand, was an absolutely fantastic professor. He lit up the hall with his enthusiastic explanations, and heavily encouraged class participation during the lectures. Apart from spending a lot of time on explaining the various concepts of macroeconomics, he showed us how the concepts applied in the real world through examples such as the Greek Debt Crisis and the Argentine Great Depression. If that wasn't all, he even spent time showing us World GDP data, and on one occasion showed us videos of Margaret Thatcher and Bernie Sanders. His lectures, coupled with the text book, were instrumental in developing my understanding of macroeconomics. The steepness of the bell curve was reduced in our year due to the introduction of short answer questions in the examinations alongside the erstwhile MCQs. Such questions were plentiful in the tutorials, ensuring that we received a good amount of practice. The online quizzes were places where almost everyone scored full marks, and provided ample practice for MCQ based problems. The exams were not difficult, and involved direct application of the concepts covered in class. TLDR: Great module. Read the textbook.

The workload is terrible, if you were to diligently read up everything that Prof Teo uploads. Can poverty really be eradicated? What are the other ways of helping and empowering people in a sustainable way? What is ABCD and how does it differ from NBCD? Who are social entrepreneurs? Can I be one? This module is not good if: you are taking it to pull up your grades. Nope. Review for 19/20 Sem 1 Lecturer: Prof Chan Heng Huat Assessment breakdown: 20% Weekly Homework (pick any 4 questions to do) 20% Midterm Test (2 Midterm Tests, one in week 6 the other in week 11) 60% Finals Galois Theory is the study of fields, field extensions and field automorphisms. The highlight of the course is the famed Abel-Ruffini theorem, which says that in general, there is no solution in radicals for polynomials having degree 5 or larger. Another central tool to Galois Theory revolves around groups, or more specifically Galois Groups. The correspondence between intermediate extensions and Galois Groups makes issues less abstract and more tractable. The main difficulty of the course is the sheer number of terminology. So be prepared to be bombarded by them. Try to revise consistently and have a good mental picture of them.

Taken in AY2014/15 “Did you all get that? Let me come again. … Actually, I shouldn’t be saying such things in public. … But to come again, it must be hard. … as in difficult. I don’t know what all of you are thinking about. ” Overview: MA1505 is the first of two modules which covers the mathematical fundamentals which are commonly used across the various fields of engineering. The main topic of interest here is calculus and its branches which are most relevant to engineering applications. This means learning about things like Taylor’s theorem, Fourier series and vector calculus, up and above the regular differentiation and integration techniques and applications covered in H2 math. This is not a light module. The content taught here is arguably the equivalent of 2 modules taken by math majors, as it covers both single and multivariable calculus. Therefore, much of the content is condensed with the focus on applying the theorems taught, and the proofs of said theorems given only a passing mention or else omitted entirely. ________ Syllabus: 1. Functions 2. Differentiation 3. Integration 4. Series 5. Vectors 6. Fourier series 7. Functions of several variables 8. Multiple integrals 9. Line integrals 10. Surface integrals Workload: There will be one 2-hour and one 1-hour lecture per week, plus 1 tutorial per week. Attendance is not graded, plus there is webcast, so you can self-study everything at home if you want. However, if you are an average student, be prepared to spend a lot of time wrapping your head around things like Fourier series, Stokes theorem, Divergence theorem etc. ________ Assessment: 20% Mid-term test: This 1-hour paper contains 10 MCQ questions and covers the first 5 chapters. The paper is harder than it looks (the mean score for my cohort was 6/10), as almost all questions require some form of computation. If you want to do well, attempt all the past year test papers uploaded on IVLE as the format of the papers are more or less the same. 80% Final exam: Although the exam covers only chapters 6-10, it is not easy as these chapters are the hardest in the module. Again, doing the past year papers helps a lot. You will also be allowed to bring in 1 cheat sheet into the exam. You can write whatever you want in the cheat sheet, but I recommend you include all the important formulas in case you forget them during the exam. If you have extra space, copying the past year paper solutions is a good idea as well. ________ Teaching Staff: Lecturer: Dr Yap Weng Yin Dr Yap was my webcasted lecturer. He lectures quite well; nothing spectacular, but he gets the idea across. He occasionally punctuates his lecture with some, uh, not-so-decent jokes, which always gave the class a good laugh. I felt it provided a very welcome relief from solving integrals and analysing vector fields all the time. Unfortunately, I only attended a couple of tutorials, mostly studying using the solutions provided on IVLE, so I'm not in a position to comment about the tutor. ________ Personal Experience: I did not have a pleasant experience in this module, although it is partially my fault. I only started watching webcast lectures during reading week, and cramming that much information into my brain in such a short time was very painful. If that wasn’t enough, I then realized after the exam that I hardly understood anything that I had learnt, beyond memorizing the steps to solve exam problems. Apparently what happened to me is very common for first year students. My advice is the same as that of the reviews before mine. Study consistently throughout the semester, even though most of the marks are in the final exam. And it's not just for the grade in this module. Many of the concepts taught here seem dry and abstract now, will likely appear again in future modules. Building a solid foundation now would mean having an easier time later.

Took this module in Sem 1 of AY16/17 under Dr Marc Rochester. No final examination. TL;DR: Basically "Orchestras in Singapore 1101". Stickler for essay formatting with vague topics that are easily misinterpreted. Very light workload, but not guaranteed an A. Probably boring for people who already are immersed in the Singaporean "western" music scene. CA consists of four parts: CA1: Fieldwork project on the study of audience behaviour in western music concerts in Singapore OR study of music schools/teaching programmes in Singapore, with a presentation in class. Group work of about 5-8(?) people. CA2: 500 word objective individual essay on a "western music ensemble" in Singapore. CA3: 750 word subjective individual essay on the position of the Singaporean music scene in the global context. CA4: Introduced at the last minute - class discussion during week 13's class. I found that there was a huge discrepancy between what the module title and description suggests and what is actually taught in the module. While the module is titled "Western Music within a Singaporean Context" (where western basically = classical as we generally understand it), it basically can be summed up as "the history of orchestras in Singapore". As someone who comes from a choral background I found it immensely disappointing that the vast majority of content covered orchestral music, with the other major topic being the role of learning and teaching "western" music in Singaporean society. The module description also reads: "It will assess the impact of majority cultures (particularly from the Chinese, Malay and Indian communities) on the general reception of Western music, as well as on music written by Singapore-based composers. Students will be introduced to the principal figures in Singapore’s musical development." However, these issues were just touch-and-go, with Marc basically rambling on about the treatment of classical music in Singaporean households or about audience perceptions. I honestly do not recall anything about majority cultures in Singapore being mentioned, and only a very small portion was touched on regarding Singaporean composers, even solo Singaporean musicians. While Marc himself is a rather funny guy, he basically sits you down for 1.5 hrs a week and rambles on, asking more questions than he gives answers, simply because this is a field that doesn't really have much research conducted with regard to music in Singapore. While he occasionally gives you facts, he doesn't properly cite the sources that he tends to mention casually, making it seem extremely wishy-washy. Lecture slides are uploaded every week after class, along with (rather soft) audio recordings of one of the lecture slots. The guest lectures are pretty banal, with more about the orchestras like SSO and Music Makers, the history of their establishment and things like that. If you're already pretty much into the local "western" music scene there's not much you can learn from attending lectures: it's basically a reaffirmation of what you already know more or less. For the fieldwork project, since the class is split into such large groups, you are allowed to split the work by having some members exclusively do data collection and others do the presentation, or have everyone involved. However, traditional powerpoint presentations should be eschewed for more interesting and attention-grabbing methods such as skits and interactive sessions. It also helps to have a few major points from your fieldwork presented as clearly as possible rather than trying to cover all bases. For the essays, the main thing is to FOLLOW THE GUIDELINES STRICTLY! He spells them all out within the powerpoint and word documents, though both documents sometimes have things that he does not put in the other, so be wary and ensure that you put in everything and double/triple check before submission, as he has been known to drop people a few grades for not following the format. The topics tend to be VERY VAGUE and are easily subject to misinterpretation, as evidenced by the majority of my groupmates and myself. While the topics may be vague, he has a very strict idea of what should be put in the essay (which is pretty unfair), and so if you really want that A you HAVE to consult him about your ideas relating to the given essay topics, otherwise it's extremely easy to get a C for the essay component. Book him early for a consultation as he tends to be busy running around watching concerts and other stuff. You only get one chance to upload your essay, and if you don't follow the guidelines or completely misinterpret the essay he will ask you to resubmit it with a SEVERE PENALTY (25%) IN GRADING, and can only be done during the submission period. i.e. past the given deadline, no more re-submissions if you fail to interpret or follow the guidelines. Some of the criteria for formatting make sense, while others like INSISTING ON USING UK ENGLISH or COUNTING HYPHENATED WORDS AND ACRONYMS AS INDIVIDUAL WORDS are a complete pain in the ass. While this module has an extremely light workload I would honestly not recommend it for people already immersed in the "western" music happenings in Singapore as it will be boring af. Plus, the essays are a real chore which always makes you second-guess yourself. I completely regret wasting 1400 points on this module as I had to bid it under the SSY module code.

Taken in AY18/19 Special Term I & II Supervisor: Assoc. Prof. Wong Yan Loi Title: On a Class of Diophantine Equations with Floor Function Assessment Structure: Written Report: 50% Oral Presentation: 20% Interview: 30% This is first of the two UROPS modules that math students can take to experience research at an undergraduate level. To take this module, students are to either choose a project from the list provided on the online portal, or are to find a supervisor and propose a topic themselves. I was fortunate enough to find a project that aligns well with my interest on the portal, and thus did not need to go through the trouble of finding a supervisor myself. Students should also note that it is rather rare for professors to be willing to supervise a UROPS project over the summer break, and I am thus also one of the fortunate few who were able to do so. Math UROPS projects are typically split into two rough categories: One that involves the student self-studying mathematics outside the NUS math curriculum (e.g. studying probability theory in finance at graduate level), and one that involves the student attempting to establish results on open, but usually small problems. My project revolves around (what I believe to be) an open problem, and more precisely finding solutions to an equation. The ideal outcome is to produce an explicit solution for the problem but it is way too difficult due to a large number of parameters in the problem. My biggest results in the report includes providing a general bound to solutions, providing an extremely sharp non-linear bound to solutions under a special case, and proving the existence of non-trivial solution under some conditions. As expected of research, students are expected to work independently on this project to produce results. Furthermore, as expected of a math research, most of my time on the project were spent thinking, conjecturing results and checking if they are true, and even more thinking. Expect lots of ups and downs in the process – I established many results in the first month of the project, but was stuck for quite a while in the second month. It is thus important to remain resilient and not give up easily. However, students should not be stubborn either – the supervisor is there to guide the student when they face obstacles, so it’s recommended to have regular meetings with the supervisor. I had about 3-4 meetups (excluding the interview) over the holiday. Assoc. Prof. Wong is a good supervisor who provided constructive feedback during our meetups. However, due to the open (?) nature of the problem, both of us do not have an absolutely clear idea of where the project is heading towards. As such, an important part of meetup for me was to explain clearly what can be established and what can’t, such as highlighting the difficulty of explicitly solving the equation under certain circumstances. Once again, it is important for the student to recognise what can be done and what can’t, so that they won’t spend unnecessarily excessive time in working on problems which are way too difficult for typical undergraduates. Though not stated explicitly, most professors expect students to write their reports in LaTeX. As such, it is strongly recommended for students to familiarise themselves with LaTeX before taking up UROPS. My report consists mostly of propositions, and proofs followed by one after another, just like a typical math research paper. Once the report is complete, students are required to provide a presentation and interview to the supervisor. While it is open for anyone to attend, it usually ends up with just the student presenting to the supervisor. Here, the student is to present the main results of the report. As such, this makes the module relaxed in the sense that there is no competition – as long as you put in the effort to this research and are able to establish good results, the supervisor would be pleased. Expected Grade: A/A+ Final Grade: A+
