Took it in AY16/17 Sem 2, under A/P Sanjay Chaudhuri (Pioneer Batch for NUS Data Science & Analytics Major) In the first few weeks, lecture content is mostly about introductions to what data science is about as well as its applications in real world context. There are also introduction to statistical terms (i.e. stuff taught in ST1131) and simple mathematical proofs in deriving statistical calculations like mean, variance and standard deviation. The module progresses on to programming in R (a programming language for statistical computing and graphics) and teaches you how to obtain and analyze simple data using RStudio, a free and open-source integrated development environment for R. Most of the codes are given to you inside the lecture slides provided so you can either get used to using them by understanding what each portion of the code does, or self-learn programming in R using the internet since codes provided in lectures are definitely not exhaustive. In fact, this part of the module feels like a crash course to ST2137 which DSA students are not required to take. In the last few weeks of school, guest speakers (2 for my batch) will be invited to give a talk on how data science is important and its application in things like genomes or manufacturing/designing. The lecture content from here on will also be more directed towards things that can help us handle big data in future (i.e. storage bases like SQL database) and a rough outline as to how these techniques/methods work. For my batch, there were two take-home midterms of which both were capped at 40 marks and a 1 week duration and only the highest score out of the two will be considered into our assessment. Take-home midterms were largely based on R programming and our ability to extract and analyze the given data in coming up with conclusions. One question has multiple parts but it is unclear how many marks were allocated to each portion because only the maximum marks that can be attained for each question (and all its parts) was mentioned. Finals were held in the exam hall (i.e. MPSH) and most of it involved proving questions. None of the questions required you to code (since we have no access to RStudio anyway), but some required knowledge of analyzing given data (i.e. using a decision tree to determine predictions). The final paper was capped at 60 marks under a 2 hour limit. Assessment: Midterms (40%) Finals (60%) Do take my review with a pinch of salt as this module is subjected to changes easily since it has only been taught once and is still open to feedback and improvements. The module content is likely to remain the way it is, but exam formats and assessments may change in the upcoming semester. Furthermore, DSA1101 is now offered in Semester 1 only whereas it was offered in Semester 2 for my pioneer batch. Good luck guys! (:

Furthermore,the lecture seems to be teaching people who had some understanding of python but at the same time tries to lower down the standard so that people can understand even if they just started coding. Tutorial: The tutorial is a good place to revise, learn some additional new information about that topic and ask your tutor about any questions you may have. However, due to the time constrain in the tutorial, you may want to test out unfamiliar functions after tutorial to understand properly. Assignment: There are 7 assignments. The first few assignments are quite easy and the rest is quite interesting. For example, assignment 5 has a theme for finding treasure by decoding a map. There are even additional challenges that are not graded to spark interest in those who want to learn more about the coding. Exam: I have mixed feelings about the examination for this course mainly due to the fact for Mid Terms, PE2. In Practical Examination(PE), everyone is required to install Examplify to block out your Internet however, you are allowed to download manuals, notes, and course material and read them during the exam. Everyone can use their own program to code for python but, it is recommended that you use IDLE. PE1: PE1 has 3 question and was quite easy in general. The first two question for PE1 is easier than the assignment itself but the third question requires some thinking if you have not seen this type of question before. Mid Terms: Midterm exam was an MCQ test of 25 questions. Due to the lack of practice paper with the same format, I really flunk this paper and got almost the worst score in the cohort when they showed the statistic.( I was only 1 mark higher). The questions is more of debugging and code tracing than actual problem solving. If I am not wrong, this paper killed many people in cohort. The worst part was when they announced that all the result is not bell curved but a sigh of relief when they say they going to reduce the max mark scored. PE2: PE2 has a 3 question and similar question type than PE1 just like other PE for CS1010S which just follows a pattern. (Maybe next sem will have the same pattern?) The first question is about Iteration/Recursion, followed up by a normal question that was from assignment and then a REALLY challenging question. In general, this would have been a normal examination if and only if there is no problem with Examplify at that time. (I am going to point out that I never verified if anyone else had this problem that I faced) Examplify (windows) at that time had a bug where when you launch IDLE while using Examplify the sub-processor for IDLE cannot connect causing the IDLE to sent out an error message. Hence, to bypass this we are taught on how to suppress its sub-processor so that we can still code. The problem is if you run to an infinite loop/ if you tried to change the code to relaunch, it doesn't work. Therefore, you need to copy your code, open CMD, type python –m idlelib –n, open a new file, paste your original code again every time you run to this problem. (Hopefully they solve this issue already) Final Examination: The final exam was a MCQ test of 20 questions and four open-ended questions. The last question is also part of an assignment question. Overall, my advise for this mod is to keep practicing daily and if possible learn some coding beforehand. You can try python tutor to either troubleshoot your own code/ ask people to help figure out what is the problem with your code or help other people so that you can improve in coding yourself. Expected grades: B-/B Actual grades: A-

CN2116 is a core module taught by Prof Lee Jim Yang (Head of Chem Eng Dept) and Dr Xie Jianping. A caveat - be prepared to throw everything you know (well almost) about reaction ratesout of the window. This module takes an empirical stab at reaction kinetics while all we have learnt in pre-university deals with theoretical rates. There are 2 mid-terms, weekly graded assignments and 1 final exam. The mid-terms are very challenging - typical of Prof Lee's style. The final examination was also tremendously challenging so be prepared to study hard for this module. Prof Lee likes to ask questions that are non-conventional so mugging past year papers are not as effective. There are 2 text-books: Chemical Reaction Engineering by O. Levenspiel and Elements of Chemical Reaction Engineering by H. Fogler. I got both of them and used them rather sparingly - i believe most of the stuff necessary is in Prof Lee's and Dr Xie's notes. If you want to purchase just 1, i suggest the latter. Topics covered (Prof Lee): 1) Representing Chemical Reactions, Types of Reactions 2) Definition of Reaction Rates, Rate Laws, Types of Reactors 3) Mole and Mass Balances, Design Equations 4) Analysis of Kinetic Data 5) Design of Single Ideal Reactor, Concept of Partially Converted Feed 6) Series and Parallel Arrangements of Reactors 7) Recycle Reactor 8) Instantaneous and Overall Yield Functions 9) Product Distributions 10) Energy Balance Equation 11) Design of Adiabatic Reactors Topics covered (Dr Xie): 1) Residence Time Distribution and its Moments 2) Models to Predict non-Ideal Reactor Performances 3) Elements of Heterogenous Catalysis 4) Catalyst Deactivation 5) External Mass Transfer Resistance 6) Diffusion and Reaction (Internal Mass Transfer Resistance). Prof Lee is very witty and sharp - expect humorous barbs now and then. This makes the lectures, which tend to have very challenging material, more palatable. Dr Xie is a very nice lecturer who goes out of the way to help students understand the course material - write to him and he responds rapidly. Effort has to be put in to get fairly decent grades for this course.

Taken in AY19/20 (COVID-19 year) Supervisor: A/Prof Ma Siu Lun Examiner: A/Prof Leung Ka Hin Expected grade: B+ Actual grade: A Topic: Variants of Bit-Flipping algorithm for the QC-MDPC McEliece Cryptosystem I had a 28 MCs workload during the COVID-19 semester and coped with it pretty well, FYP need not be time-draining if you manage it well :) Experience: I had done my UROPS in the area of cryptography previously and I have gotten an A+ so my FYP was a continuation of my UROPS. I very much liked how A/Prof Ma was quite patient with me during my UROPS, so I decided to continue researching in this field under his supervision. At the very beginning, A/Prof Ma set a very vague FYP topic for me, it was entitled ``Code-Based Post-Quantum Cryptosystems". He said it was to ``keep the scope of the FYP generic first, the exact title can be changed afterwards when we get an idea of what I want to work on" and I completely agree with him on hindsight. Initially he proposed that we meet every week where I share my research findings with him and discuss about them, but in reality, it was hard to churn out new research ideas or make progress on a weekly basis especially when I first started and when exams are coming. I was then given some reading materials (textbooks and research papers) to read and had complete freedom on the choice of problems to work on. Prof Ma was very quick with his thinking despite his old age. When I encountered research papers that appealed to me, I would send them to Prof Ma for some advice and he could always give me a thorough feedback in a few days. Prof Ma is also surprisingly good at programming too, a significant portion of my FYP required scientific computing and he actually guided me to implement some of the algorithms in Python. I had learnt so much from Prof Ma from this FYP. In my thesis, I tried to analyse and improve the QC-MDPC cryptosystem in two unrelated ways. The first half of my thesis was an expanded version of my UROPS project -- using graph theoretic properties of the QC-MDPC code to construct decoding algorithms. The second half was an analysis of another variant of the decoding algorithm using Markov Chains, it was motivated by a paper I've read (Sendrier, Nicolas & Vasseur, Valentin. (2019). On the Decoding Failure Rate of QC-MDPC Bit-Flipping Decoders) link at: There were many ideas that I have tried to explore but not all of them were successful or substantial enough to be noted down in the thesis. It was only at the end of the first semester that I started implementing the algorithms in Python, with some help from A/Prof Ma. I had only finalised the title for my thesis 2 weeks before the submission. Overall, I became better at thinking about math after this FYP, it led me to think more critically whenever I see a piece of work citing a certain claim and I also became more innovative in terms of generating new research ideas. Tips: - If you want to get into a good grad school, you might want to pick a more established professor, the recommendation letter that he can write can greatly value-add your application. You can also source for your own external supervisors from other departments (like SoC) or even from other research institutes like ASTAR. Note that grad schools typically require 2 or more letters of recommendation, so pick your supervisors carefully. - Some professors might be too busy with his work to impart you any skills, so choose your supervisors wisely. Don't expect the supervisor to craft out a nice research outline for you and guide you along the way, there is not much critical thinking done on your end if he handholds you all the time. - For projects that require substantial amount of programming, note that the professors are mainly researchers by profession and will likely not spend time scrutinising your algorithms with thousands of lines of code, especially if they have multiple PhD, Masters, FYP research students and are actively teaching modules lol. So don't be too concerned in submitting subpar programs.

Taken in: AY18/19 Sem 2 Lecturer: A/P Stuart W.G. Derbyshire Assessment format: 50% Midterms + Tutorial Participation 50% Final Exam (see below for exam format) Textbook used (if any): Sensation and Perception (10th Edition) by E. Bruce Goldstein One of various Level-3000 psychology elective modules. It covers, well, sensation and perception, with a focus on vision. Topics include the perceptual pathway (i.e. how information travels from the sense organs to the brain), how we perceive movement, color, depth and size, hearing and speech perception, and the cutaneous and chemical senses (that’s the feely stuff like touch and pain and the tasty stuff like taste and smell respectively). Bio-heavy, but I surprisingly found it easier to deal with than PL3232, maybe because all of it’s topics are related. It is highly recommended that you take PL3232 (Biological Psychology) before you take this mod (but I didn’t). Prof Derbyshire is a very clear and precise lecturer, and he spices up the biological focus of the module’s content with occasional detours of a philosophical nature, like asking what it means for us to actually see something. Definitely one of the better lecturers within the department, in my humble opinion. Tutorials: Tutorials were held as two-hour sessions once every two weeks. Each tutorial serves as discussion sessions on studies or current affairs related to the week’s topics. An example: discussing what it would take to build an artificial eye, as related to the topic of visual perception. Exams: Prof Derbyshire gives an interesting format: his exams consist of Very Short Answer Questions, Short Answer Questions, and an Essay. * Very Short Answer Questions are to be answered in one line, kind of like an MCQ question where you provide the correct option. (Example: Name three perceptual cues that help in depth perception.) * Short Answer Questions are 5-6 sentences. You get to choose a few out of many. * Essays are essays, with 3-4 paragraphs. You choose one out of many. Tip: practice by thinking of possible questions and answering them. There’s only so many possible topics that can be used as short-answer or essay questions. Simple mathematical models were being employed, so a good foundation in physics and mathematics would come in very handy. The laboratory exercises were relatively easy compared to the ones I had in Chemistry. The difficulty comes from the reports. Every week, you will be given ample time (about 8-10 days) to complete a lab report with your group. Try and finish this ASAP. CELC focuses mainly on your presentation and writing skills. As long as you can write coherently and have a good command of the English Language, this should not be an issue for you, albeit the fact that it might be hard to score extremely well for this portion. Quizzes were difficult, and they were pretty much the determinant for your grade. Each quiz consisted of 10 MCQ questions, which means that each question constituted 2% and 3% for quiz 1 and 2 respectively. They were open book, but the questions required some higher order thinking. These are not similar to questions that you see everyday in A levels. In fact, for quiz 1, I clearly remember having to solve an ODE and doing several manipulations to get the final answer for question 9. I was pretty sure such questions came as a surprise to many, so make sure your mathematical skills are decent. Overall, I felt that the idea behind this module was very good. I like how it exposes the students to using models to explain observed phenomena. But the quizzes definitely need some improvement, the pressure that it gave me was rather intense, given that every question wrong would a greatly reduced chances of an A. Probably my most scary exam! Scoring full marks for both quizzes will guarantee you an A+ given that the questions were relatively difficult. If you like physics, I think you will like this module. Revise your A level differential equations before coming in though. Expected Grade: A/A+ Final Grade: A+

AY2020/21 Semester 2 Professor Dr. Henry Mok Opinion I cannot be more than glad that I happened to find this module to fulfil my faculty requirement when I browsed through NUSMods. Sem 1 AY21/22 Lecturer: Chin Wei Ngan Tutorial TA: Ernest I will start with the TL;DR: don't take this module. If you're planning on going down the Programming Language focus area (for CS kids) (ie. this becomes a requirement), don't do it either. It's not worth it -- go spec in something else. The selection of PL mods in NUS is trash anyway. The bunch of reviews from this sem (Sem1, AY21/22) that basically diss this mod are entirely justified. It isn't because of the final paper either (it hasn't happened yet, as I write this). Heed our advice. Don't do it. If you remember my IS1103 review, I mentioned that it was perhaps one of the worst mods I've had the privilege of paying school fees for. CS2104 is a close second. At least it's not a graduation requirement. Seriously; if you need 4MCs, go take CFG, or some UEs -- anything else. Really. This module purports to teach "Programming Language Concepts", but none of those concepts were even taught to any degree worthy of a university education. CS2104 "covers" 4 languages: Haskell, OCaml, Prolog, and Scala. The first half (up to recess week, possibly till week 7) focuses on trying to teach students Haskell. Topics covered include the basic functional programming stuff (higher order functions [which should be OK if you took 1101S under Henz], list comprehensions, other Haskell features like pattern matching and ADTs), and of course Monads (and monadic parsers via Parsec). It doesn't do a good job, mind you, but the slides are there. The next language is Prolog. If you haven't used Prolog before, it's a language with quite a unique paradigm... and it definitely can't be covered in 1 set of slides over 1 or 2 weeks. (by the way, a large part of the slide deck just focuses on those dumb "logic puzzles" like SEND + MORE = MONEY...). The core tenets of Prolog programming (eg. the tree structure of terms, SLD resolution, etc.) are only briefly mentioned and not really elaborated in detail. It is not really feasible to expect students to gain a good understanding of these concepts when explained so poorly in such a short amount of time. OCaml and Scala are given much the same treatment; just an afterthought in this module. Based on past year papers, students are somehow expected to have a good grasp on these languages in order to answer questions. This year, it was said that students "there is no need to memorise language syntax". We shall see about that (will update this review if I remember). By the way, if you're reading the description on nusmods (above) and wondering whether this module covers "various implementation issues, such as pseudo-code interpretation, static and dynamic semantics...", the answer is NO. Assessments Speaking of assessments, there are some graded lab assignments as well as some "participation mark" tutorial questions that you have to submit. They're mostly run-of-the-mill CS labs/assignments, nothing too special or tragic on that front. For tutorials, somehow participation is graded. The TA for my tutorial was a PhD student who, on the first lesson, openly stated that he had no idea what was going on, and that we should "all learn together" (paraphrasing). Doesn't inspire much confidence, does it? The level of nonexistent confidence only continued to drop after each tutorial was basically him reading off the answers for each tutorial question, with the occasional confusion as he doesn't know what the answers were talking about. Furthermore, students are expected to form groups of 2-3 to make 2 presentations about various proglang topics over the semester. These are graded, and form part of the 10% "tutorial participation" marks. You can either choose from one of the topics suggested by the prof, or suggest one subject to approval. There is 1 midterm and 1 final exam; both are open-book. The midterm is mostly MCQ -- this round it was ~20 MCQs and 2 open-ended questions in 30 minutes. What do the questions ask? Basically, you need to be GHCI. If you cannot compile and interpret Haskell code in your head, good luck to you. Each question basically presents you with a messily-written Haskell function with nondescriptive argument names, and asks you what it does (or how to use it). I suspect the final exam (at least the MCQ portion) will be more of the same recipe. Conclusions There's really only one thing to conclude, and I already stated that at the top; don't take this module. Really, don't. The lack of prerequisites might seem tempting, but don't. Even if you love Haskell or Prolog or FP, don't do it. If you are thinking of going down the Prog Lang focus area, don't. Choose something else. In most of my other reviews (except IS1103 -- lu weiquan really deserves nothing but a dismissal from NUS) I generally attack only the course content, and not the professor. Unfortunately I can't do that here. I don't think Prof Chin is a Bad Person (tm), but being a good person doesn't make you a good lecturer. Lectures were conducted over Zoom (attendance was "mandatory" for participation marks); tutorials were either in-person or over Zoom (depends on the slot you choose). Lectures are quite dry, and often have no sense of flow; they are conducted in a very "rambly" style. Some particular concepts will be gone over very quickly, while some other concepts will somehow get a 20 minute explanation (which is actually just 2 10-minute ones repeated). Most of the time, he is just reading off the slides. Slides which, I might add, often have typos. Sometimes students point it out and he corrects them, but when he closes the slide deck, he clicks "discard changes", so next year students get the same typos again. Fun. Prof is responsive to audience questions which is good I guess. In case there was any confusion, let me state this again: DO NOT, UNDER ANY CIRCUMSTANCES, TAKE CS2104.

(AY 15/16 Sem 1, Prof Ng Hwee Tou & TA Kaveh Taghipour) The textbook is of poor quality, having many serious errors, some of which he himself pointed out in class, and some of which my classmates pointed out to him, which he apparently didn't even realize. Despite that, his style of teaching is very textbook-oriented. Assignments, tests and exams do not really test true understanding of the concepts, but rather test whether you are able to parrot the textbook or the solutions he presents for his problem sets. If you do not want to be like a parrot, DO NOT take this module! There was also one occasion where two students asked him after class whether he could give them answers to past year papers. He raised his voice and told them off, saying something like that this is a university and he will of course not provide ten-year-series. He also stated flatly that he will not answer any inquiries about past year papers' questions, but only about the course materials. Of course everyone in the room heard his response. While I agree that learning is not about past year papers, I felt it was an unkind way to treat a student. After all, if he wants to assess students based on exams, it is to be expected that they would want to know how to answer his style of exam questions. Certainly he ought to be at least willing to answer inquiries of students who already show him their own serious attempts at answering the exam questions. If he is not, then he ought not to use exams to judge students' competency in natural language processing. Furthermore, he could have just told those students nicely what he felt about past year papers rather than talking down to them. This year's programming project was actually a reasonably interesting one, namely to implement a word-pair disambiguation classifier, in which the program needs to choose the right word of a given pair (like adopt/adapt) to fill in the blank in each test sentence, after learning from training data where the correct answers are provided. The word pair is of course not known in advance, so the program must be able to learn from the training data alone. We submitted both source code and a short write-up explaining our classifier. A significant portion of the marks went to our classifier's performance on the unseen test data, which is fair enough, but some marks also went to the classifier's performance on the sample test data that Prof Ng provided, which I felt was a bit wrong since some people might tune their classifier to fit best the sample test data. The weightage for the sample test data was half that of the unseen test data, so it was not really an issue for the grading, but it was still not a good marking scheme in my opinion. As an earlier reviewer already wrote, the test and exam questions are often of the type where just a slight mistake will cost you all the marks for that question, such as 5 out of 40 for the midterm, or 10 out of 80 for the final. Since the exam turns upon your carelessness during that 2 hours, you had better sleep well at least the night before! That is, if you have already chosen to be like a parrot for one semester. =P Finally, the TA, a PhD student whose supervisor was Prof Ng, was very unapproachable and many of us students who went to see him about the assignment grading felt very put off by his attitude towards us. I won't say more. Now let me make some course recommendations. For finite automata and context free grammars and related algorithms and much more, take CS4232, which teaches them properly. Prof Ng did not seem to actually have knowledge about these beyond what was in his natural language textbooks, so he couldn't confidently answer some simple questions about them that some students asked in class. For natural language processing content, you're probably better off reading online materials such as Wikipedia, which are not only much clearer but also more comprehensive, not so mistake-laden and better organized. Some reliable friends who also disliked CS4248 told me that some other modules are much worse, so I'm thankful that CS4248 is already one of the worst I've taken in SOC. Perhaps the other modules I've taken were so well taught that I had a high expectation before taking CS4248. Expected grade: A Obtained grade: A-

Taken in 18/19 Sem 1 under Asst Prof Yair Zick This is the first time the module is offered, though it was taught under CS6283 Topics in Computer Science IV: Computational Social Choice in 16/17 Sem 2, with the same syllabus. Cozy class size of 10 students. The first half of the course is on game theory (Nash equilibrium pure/mixed strategies, regret minimisation, routing games, the core, Shapley value), and the second half was on fair allocation/mechanism design (stable matching, allocation of divisible/indivisible goods, auctions, facility location). The course takes a mathematical approach with lots of proofs - improved my proving skills! Expect no programming at all. Pre-requisite: No knowledge of mathematical statistics is required, only basic probability (expected value) is needed. Some multivariable calculus knowledge (Lagrange, partial derivative) is needed. Linear programming is referenced but not tested. Lecture: Once a week. Lecture notes are concise, so you can’t really self-study it. Highly recommended to go for lectures to have more in-depth explanation on the concepts, and illustrated examples on the whiteboard. Prof Yair was really clear (and super passionate) in explaining the concepts. Do also read the additional readings (textbook/research papers). Assignments (30%): A total of 7 assignments, of which the top 6 were taken to be counted. Generally we have 2 weeks to complete the assignments. Some questions are non-trivial, while others were straightforward. Assignment questions are mainly proofs and are similar/slightly harder than what you can expect in the assessments. Tutorials (5%): Class participation was 5%. Tutorials were used to go through assignment questions (which we were to hand in at the start of the tutorial) and all tutorials were taken by the prof. Review of concepts relevant will be gone through, and a really good platform to ask questions regarding the class, especially since there were only 5 people in the tutorial. Some tutorial sessions where there were no assignment due was used to play some games. Really fun. Midterms (30%): Restricted open book (1 cheatsheet, textbook, lecture notes, assignments, readings). Being the first time this module was run, there are no PYP to practice. Although the topics to be tested (and hence types of questions you can expect) were quite obvious, it was tedious. The questions were not difficult conceptually, just many questions within 1.5h. Being super fast and careful is key. There was subsequently a re-midterms/quiz with just 3 questions - I think most people found it easier and had increased marks (80% from original + 20% from the best of the 2), not me though. Exams (35%): Restricted open book (1 cheatsheet, textbook, lecture notes, assignments, readings). Again since there were no PYP to practice, we could only hope for the best. Some of the later topics were based on cutting-edge research, so don’t expect to find any practice questions for those apart from the assignments and practice exam questions given in class. Revise thoroughly and you should be able to score really well for the exam - prof was kind - there were no unexpected questions, mainly computational/light proofs, with no hard proofs. There were not that many questions like the midterms, and there was more than sufficient time to do all of them with time to check. The only topic pre-midterms tested was Nash equilibrium. This was my most enjoyable module in NUS thus far. Really interesting and fun module introducing game theory and mechanism design. The Prof is excellent. Highly recommended to those interested in learning more interesting topics beyond standard game theory. Grade: A+

Taken in 20/21 Sem 1 (remote learning) Tutor: Mr. Maurice Chng Textbook: None Workload: really low (2 hrs/week) Expected Grade: A Actual Grade: A- Assessment: 10% Tutorial*5 30% Luminus online quizzes (best 8 of 10) 60% Project DSA student here. This was a chill mod for me because the stuff they teach in this mod are either already taught in high school or really intuitive. The course briefly covers topics such as the design of studies, association, sampling, observational studies, and laws of probability. Each week we have to watch about 30 minutes of pre-recorded lecture, then do an online quiz of 10 questions. Tutorial sessions are once every two weeks. Each session is 90 minutes long. There are 25 students in a session, and they are split into five groups of five. The tutor is a nice guy. 10% Tutorial*5 Before each tutorial session, we need to complete a worksheet individually. They take about 1 hour to do. During the sessions, we would have time to discuss and then share our answers with the class. If you watch all the lecture videos, you should be able to finish the worksheets in no time. After that, we can ask the tutor questions regarding the content of the lecture videos, or literally anything else. Like, one time, a student asked for advice for freshmen, and the tutor gave a really sophisticated reply. Even though you can leave right after the discussion of the worksheets, most of us stayed connected until there are no more questions. 30% Luminus online quizzes Each week we have to do a quiz with ten MCQs on Luminus. Some of them are tricky, so you might want to check your group mates’ answers before submitting them. The worst two quizzes are omitted in the calculation of the grade. According to my tutor, it is common for a student to get all 30%, so there is no stress. 60% Project The group project is the biggest deal of this module. It is not an exaggeration to say that the project is the sole deciding factor of your final grade because almost everyone gets full or nearly full marks on the rest 40%. The project consists of two parts. In Part A, we have to choose one of the six research papers and apply what we learned quantitatively to analyze the findings. Then, we have to give a presentation of about 15 minutes in the last tutorial section. Part B is just some calculations done in excel. The hardest part of the project is to find a time that all five of us are available. Thankfully, all my teammates are super cooperative. In conclusion, teamwork is critical for this module. You definitely don’t want to let your group mates down because there is a peer evaluation form at the end of the semester.

Prof Namala Lakshmi Tilakaratna, if you are reading this I just want to say thank you for trying very hard to simplify an extremely complex topic despite this being your first time! Semester: AY 19/20 (Sem 1) Lecturer: Prof Namala Lakshmi Tilakaratna Advice: If you're staying in CAPT, Tembusu or RC4 you have no choice but to do a IEM1; if you aren't there's no way to apply... Take this module if you are interested in 1) how national identity is constructed and maintained, and 2) how you can analyse text and images in posters to uncover the hidden intent (and link back to nationalism). Assessment: Participation 10% Presentation (of your paper 3) 10% Paper 1: Reflective summary 15% Paper 2: Lens paper 25% Paper 3: Expository Essay 40% Content: First few weeks covers the big theories on nationalism that explore how a national identity is constructed and maintained from different angles. Paper 1 is based on an assigned text, and the key is to distil a couple of arguments from it, and link them to the big theories covered, and critically evaluate their usefulness. Following which, a couple of weeks is then spent on introducing several frameworks that can be used to deconstruct text and images to sieve out their deeper meanings. Paper 2 is based on an assigned poster, and the key is to objectively analyse how its text and images are framed to convey a holistic meaning. Paper 3 then builds on the skills learnt from paper 1 and 2, in that you are given free reign to choose your own poster/campaign/song/ad and 1) analyse its text + images to uncover the meaning, and 2) link to nationalism. It is, however, in an expository style, and so the key is on proving your stance, rather than just demonstrating a fact. It can be framed from the top-down or bottom-up approach. It should not just acknowledge, but also problematize the way the poster is used to create a form of nationalistic identity. Interestingly enough, the GRADED presentation precedes your paper 3 consultation, and thus serves as an initial proposal to the Prof and the class for your topic of choce. Review: The content was kind of complicated at first, and the readings seemingly heavy, but once distilled by the Prof, the key concepts became much easier to digest. As the Prof is of a linguistics background, the middle portion would involve some linguistics terminology in unpacking the intents. However, the enthusiasm of the Prof far outweighs the difficulties in surpassing the technical nature of the module. I personally gained a deeper insight into how propaganda is constructed and how patriotism is invented.
Expected: B+/A- Actual: A+ A/Prof Ma told me he actually only gave me an A but the system moderated me up O_O

under Prof Zhao Jin and Prof Bimlesh Wadhwa. Overview: This module is a software engineering module, and it revolves around a team software engineering project that spans the entire semester. This team project is to be written in C++, and it forms 60% of the final grade. Prior C++ experience is likely to be useful. There are no final exams. Workload: This is an 8MC module, so twice of the usual workload is expected. The workload is still rather high, and it varies significantly across teams due to the different amounts of programming experience and different grade expectations of each team. Team formation: Students work in teams of six for this module in a hybrid group formation system - students first form groups of three (where they can choose their own groupmates), and the groups are paired up at random to form the final team that comprises of six people. After forming the team of six, the original groups of three are immaterial. As the team project forms the majority of the final grade, it is important to choose appropriate groupmates to form the group of three. Project: Teams are required to build a command-line static program analyser from scratch. Unlike CS2103, the requirements are specified clearly by the teaching team (so all teams produce prototypes that have the same functions), and all teams start from scratch (i.e. there is no pre-written code to begin with). Because of this, there are many design decisions that need to be made, and the overall workload is much higher than CS2103. A small portion of the project marks is awarded to extensions, where teams can implement additional features (that may differ from those implemented by other teams). Project Grading: Around 55% of the project marks are awarded by testing the team's prototype using test inputs supplied by the teaching team - this component is solely based on the correctness and efficiency of the team's prototype. The rest of the project marks come from a few written reports and a final presentation (all are team work). There are three development checkpoints (called "iterations") - at each iteration, teams must submit deliverables such as their source code and written report. Project Consultations: There are weekly compulsory team consultation sessions with an assigned TA. These sessions seek to ensure that students do not lag behind in the development of their prototype. They may also be used for discussion of their design decisions and written report. Lectures and Tutorials: Lectures and tutorials are geared towards the project. They cover the project specification (e.g. syntax of the program that is being analysed, and meaning of queries for the static program analyser), design decisions, basic optimisation, and general guidelines for managing a project at this scale. Student participation and in-class discussions/presentations are expected. Non-project Graded Components: Non-project components include two tests (18% of final grade), some online quizzes, attendance, and participation. Both tests contain questions that check your understanding of the project specification. The second test also contains questions about the other topics covered in the lectures and tutorials. Programming Language: C++ must be used for this project. Modern C++ (C++11/14/17) may be used to the extent that Visual Studio is able to compile. Third-party libraries (e.g. Boost, Abseil, Flex/Bison) are prohibited (but if you understand how they work and like the design abstractions they provide, you can of course implement them yourself). While C++ is mandatory for this project, this module does not teach C++ at all. Students are expected to pick up C++ on their own. As C++ is a rather difficult language to learn and debug (due to its performance-centric design), a lack of experience with C++ (or other languages with similar paradigms like Rust and D) might therefore pose a challenge to students. Familiarising yourself with C++ before the start of the semester might be a good idea. Development Environment: Grading is done on Windows and code is compiled with Visual Studio, so teams must ensure that Visual Studio is able to compile their code properly. Teams may either use a Visual Studio Solution (easier, but works on Windows only), or use CMake (harder, but works on Windows, Mac, and Linux). There is no requirement on the use of any particular IDE for development, but Visual Studio is recommended. Lecturers: Prof Zhao and Prof Bimlesh are relatively easy-going, so lectures are usually quite casual. They also respond within a reasonable time on the IVLE forums.

Disclaimer: I have not taken CS2010. At this time of writing, I have been part of Dr. Steven Halim's CS2010 teaching staff twice - once as a lab TA (2011/2012 sem 1) and once as a tutorial TA (2012/2013 sem 1). I will be helping out for a final time in the upcoming semester (2014/2015 sem 1) but for CS2010R. This upcoming semester will be the 4th year that Steven's CS2010 is conducted in semester 1. tldr: Just take Steven's CS2010. CS2010 focuses on graph algorithms and dynamic programming. If these topics invoke the thought of abstract (and difficult) theory, then I'm glad to tell you that Steven's CS2010 module takes a more implementation-leaning stance - there are 8 problem sets (programming assignments using Java), each of which gives you a chance to implement an algorithm covered in the class (and maybe some more). So it's not just theory - you get to see your knowledge put into action. From the other reviews, you can probably gather that this is not an easy module if you do it when Steven is teaching it . My experience as a TA confirms this. Now, before you run away, I'll try to convince you why you should do Steven's version of the module: I. Steven is one of the best lecturers I've encountered at NUS. I have personally taken his CS2020 and CS3233 courses, the latter of which I highly recommend as a follow-up to CS2010. Maybe I just like his teaching style and I may be biased, but many other people agree with me: II. A lot of effort has been put into the teaching material to make it beginner-friendly AND comprehensive. It is entirely possible for someone encountering an algorithm covered in the module for the first time to implement the original algorithm based on the lecture notes alone, something which may or may not be possible in general for algorithms textbooks, wikipedia pages, research papers and similar (very much dependent on your level of skill and knowledge). Believe me, once you've tried implementing something from other sources, you will appreciate how good Steven's teaching material is. III. Very active discussions on the problem sets (programming assignments), previously on the IVLE discussion forums and now on the CS2010 Facebook group - (join if you haven't!!!). It is a tradition for people to contribute tricky test cases and compare the outputs of their program as a means of testing correctness. Even if you do not wish to participate in the discussions, you can learn a lot just by following the discussions. IV. Use of novel teaching methods, such as algorithm visualization using the VisuAlgo system: . You don't find this in most other modules. V. Solid teaching staff. Former CS2010 students who totally understand where you're coming from, former CS3233 students who eat this material for breakfast, ACM ICPC participants and sometimes ACM ICPC world finalists (there is one this coming semester). We are very friendly and open to questions =) I even "pressure" students to ask questions through email or similar means if they are too shy to ask in person; sadly the effect only kicks in when the semester is drawing to a close - don't make the same mistake!!! Steven also has office hours, so make use of them! There's a lot that I didn't cover to not spoil your fun. A lot more information is available at the IVLE page (also something very unusual for a module). I do not know much about how the module is conducted in semester 2 so I cannot speak on that. However, if I were you and I'm deciding whether to take Steven's CS2010, I will do what the other reviews have mentioned, that is, take a look at the reviews here and ask people. To end this rather long review, I believe that Steven has come up with a very good algorithm for teaching CS2010. How do we measure this? Not in terms of time or space efficiency, but probably in terms of how much students will learn and their satisfaction with the module.

Taken in AY 21/22 Sem 1 Lecturer: Sufatrio Component breakdown: 2 CTF-style assignments (10% + 15%) Midterms (15%) LumiNUS revision quiz (5%) Group presentation (5%) Tutorial attendance (5%) Finals (45%) TL;DR: + Has cool and fun CTFs - Module scope leaves much to be desired - Lecturer is not good (I rolled a not so good tutor, which made the experience even worse) As someone who loves information security, I went into this module with great excitement. I was NOT prepared to be let down this hard. Module scope: Iffy. About half of the topics covered felt very touch-and-go; they were briefly glossed over and then rarely, if ever, cropped up again. Many sub-chapters are treated merely as "vocabulary" and their sole purpose in the module is to serve as possible answers for the fill-in-the-blank/MCQ section in the midterms and finals; nothing more than a cursory understanding is required. Lectures & lecturer: Lectures were conducted live over Zoom and recorded. Dr Sufatrio proceeds at a glacial pace, reading off the slides for the most part and circling random words while he speaks. His voiceover adds negligible value to the slides themselves and you're better off reading them on your own. He also has a tendency to waste time; around 10 minutes at the start of each lecture for "announcements". I couldn't attend the lectures live as I was typically travelling to NUS for another in-person tutorial during that timeslot, but I stopped bothering to watch the recorded videos a few weeks in because they're that slow even at 2x speed. Dr Sufatrio takes weeks to respond to email queries, and his responses are typically not helpful. I'm not even sure if he fully understood the questions being asked before replying with unrelated stock responses such as "this is how we defined it in the notes". Tutorials: My experience with tutorials was not great because I got a questionable tutor (who I will not name). On at least one occasion, he stated that he "didn't remember ever seeing" something despite literally having just gone through a question about it in the previous tutorial session. He also has a tendency to give wrong answers or explanations to questions posed by students, and usually doesn't bother correcting himself afterwards. This was not very beneficial to the understanding of many students in my tutorial group. To his credit, though, he provided us with a definition list/cheatsheet, which was quite helpful as quick reference during the finals. The tutorial questions themselves are generally okay, though some of them have a tendency to be somewhat tedious (e.g. given the following list of requirements, list all the firewall rules you would implement). Group presentation: This component felt like an afterthought. You pick a topic from a list and do a short presentation on it during the tutorial timeslot. This is something you can get done in a single night, but the grading is completely opaque and it's up to your tutor's discretion whether you get a 4/5 or a 5/5. Assignments: The highlight of this module. Assignments are CTF-style and the challenges are set by the NUS Greyhats. It's very hands-on, so you will probably learn more from trying these challenges than from the rest of the module put together. They are pretty time-consuming though, and can be pretty difficult if you don't already have some background and need to pick everything up from scratch. I found this pretty enjoyable, and I think it was the one redeeming part of this module. LumiNUS quiz: This is just a MCQ quiz you can do at your own time. It's meant to serve as revision before the final exam. There's no time limit so make sure you get full marks for this. Midterms/finals: Midterms and finals were conducted over Examplify with Zoom proctoring. Format was open book but no internet. Dr Sufatrio reuses questions a lot and the format of his papers is always the same. The first half of his paper (fill-in-the-blanks + MCQ) often has questions which are ripped word-for-word from previous years' papers. Even the open-ended questions are incredibly formulaic; all 3 final papers I did that were set by him (2 PYPs and the actual finals for this sem) had secure programming questions with similar code and identical vulnerabilities. The papers' difficulties are generally not high. It's entirely possible to get 100% if you understand what's going on in the module and don't make careless mistakes. The question wording can be pretty bad, though, and sometimes it's not really clear what the question wants from you. All you really need to do to prepare for his midterms/finals are to do any past papers set by him. Lecture content barely gets tested, and if they do, it's stuff that you can just look up in the notes anyway. Conclusion: If you're looking for a neat introduction to information security, this module (at least under Dr Sufatrio) isn't it; it barely covers anything interesting. If you must take this module, consider taking it under a different lecturer instead. If you just want to learn more about information security or play CTFs, you'll probably get a lot further by getting to know a few Greyhats members.

Taken in AY15/16 Special Term Lecturer: Dr Yeo Ye Syllabus: - Complex numbers (Euler’s formula, de Moivre’s theorem and applications, complex logarithms and complex powers.) - Differential multivariable calculus (Partial derivatives and differentials. Cylindrical and spherical coordinate systems. The del operator - gradient, divergence, curl.) - Integral multivariable calculus (Parameterisation of curves. Line and surface integrals. Green’s theorem, divergence theorem, Stokes’ theorem.) - Preliminaries to 2nd order ODEs (Exponential and hyperbolic functions. Fourier series and Fourier transforms. Parseval’s theorem, convolution theorem and Dirac delta function.) - 2nd order linear PDEs (The wave equation and separation of variables. Solution of Laplace’s and Poisson’s equations.) - 2nd order ODEs, part one (General theory of ODEs. Euler’s equation. Green’s functions. Laplace transforms.) - 2nd order ODEs, part two (Series solutions of ODEs. Regular and singular points. Fuch’s theorem.) - 2nd order ODEs, part three (Important ODEs in physics – Hermite equation, Legendre equation, Bessel equation, Laguerre equation.) - Sturm-Liouville theory (Hilbert space of functions. Hermitian operators. Sturm-Liouville equations, Green’s functions revisited.) Assessment: - Assignments (20%) - Midterm (20%) - Finals (60%) Personal Experiences: I took this module when Physics department decided to offer it under Special Term for the first time. I have written my thoughts on Special Term modules in my review for PC2132 if one’s interested. This was a very fun module, in no small part due to Dr Yeo’s teaching. Dr Yeo is constantly in an excited state which is very beneficial to the overall morale of the class at early in the morning. His explanations can make otherwise troublesome concepts seem so easy, and he effectively accommodates students of different enthusiasm levels. Visual aids are employed to draw attention to noteworthy points and his occasional musings on life are interesting and uplifting. This module serves to supply the budding physics major with the mathematical tools that will be useful over the course of one’s candidature. The main difference between this module and other mathematics modules that one might have taken prior (MA1101R, MA1102R, MA1104) lies in the emphasis on application of mathematics to physical scenarios. For instance, most of the vector calculus concepts in this module had already been covered in MA1104 but here we see how they are employed in areas such as electromagnetism or the wave equation. The assignment, midterm and final are all very manageable, especially if one paid sufficient attention during lectures. Being a course on mathematical ‘methods’, the focus is on computations above proofs which may come as welcome relief after going through the mathematics modules of Year One. To score well, one may wish to diligently practice tutorials although this isn’t strictly necessary to do so.

AY20/21 Sem 2 (all online) (TLDR is last body paragraph) Lecturers: Prof Menusha De Silva and A/P Elaine Ho Lectures are weekly, and are recorded; you should only skip them if you're confident in your "smoking" abilities. Some graded activities will take place in a few specific lectures. Tutorials are bi-weekly, and must be attended. Assessment criteria (not in chronological order) Online tutorial participation - 20% Padlet posts, Tutorial short-answer essays - 10% Group project - 30% Online MCQ quiz - 10% Final assessment part 1: In-lecture short-answer questions - 10% Final assessment part 2: Take-home final essay - 20% Details on assessment Online tutorial participation -- Tutorial activities are mostly done in groups. You will get to choose your own groups, so if you wanna join with friends, make sure to go for the same tutorial slot. The tutorials will involve reading/watching some stuff before hand, and then coming into class to discuss some topics together as a group. Padlet and tutorial essays -- The padlet posts comprise of only two 50-word (with an accompanying image) blog posts, which are a chance for you to apply the concepts from the lectures. It's not difficult; just a surface0level analysis of some landscape of your choice with your new-learned concepts. My memory's hazy, but I think there weren't many in-tutorial essays; and they're not long (300 words thereabouts) -- it's simply a chance for you to shine and show off deeper analyses relative to the blog posts. Group project -- Due to COVID, we did an online version. The gist of it is, find 3 images of a certain landscape, then analyse it. (e.g., in terms of the power being exercised by the landscape's regulators, in terms of the purpose of the image chosen, etc) The 3 images' analyses should tie into one another, to form a big "photo essay" of 2000 words, with citations included for any external claims. It's kinda fun once you decide on a landscape and direction to analyse towards. Online MCQ quiz -- this should be the least of your worries lmao In-lecture short-answer questions -- they mean it when they say short. As long as you haven't been absent for the whole semester you should be fine. Take-home final essay -- Watch a video, and write a 1.2k word essay tangentially based on it. The time given for this was around 2.5 weeks if I recall, so you can opt to focus on your exams first, if they take place early-ish. Due to the relative easy-ness of the assessment criteria, where you end up on the bell curve will probably largely depend on your group project, and your final essay , so this is your only chance to tout your bona-fide worth on a solo scale for those seeking a full A and above. Try to take it seriously -- 1.2k words is actually already very merciful by GE module standards! How was the module ( TLDR is last paragraph ) This first para is the politically incorrect one; skip if you're a "good" student. Now, firstly, the workload is light; so dummy light it's insane. You can triple the time I personally spent on this module, and it'll still be less time overall than I spent on MA1102R/MA2002 Calculus... which I went into already knowing the content of . As an additional boon, for those whose BS skills are up to the mark (especially in writing), if you're a not-so-model student like me, you can skip 80% of the lectures and still nab an easy distinction. The only lecture I went to that didn't have a graded assessment was the first one. This is a nice mod to take if you just want to SU away GES quickly, or if you want a reasonably light mod to overload with while still wanting to do well. That's what I personally did, and I got to have my cake and eat it too. As far as content goes, we will learn about landscapes, and not just obvious physical ones like Chinatown and your neighbourhood park, but also temporary ones like National Day festivities, and imaginary ones that exist in the mind and fabric of social imagination. From there, we will learn the two major focuses of this module: The first is power -- displays of power present in these landscapes; namely, the promotion of ideals espoused by the governing party, the prohibition concepts deemed undesirable by the governing party, and the projection of a good image towards some 3rd party, as intended by the governing party. The second is geographical concepts -- studying something by thinking about it as a space (a physical domain), as a place (a space with psychological significance), or by thinking about the scale (on what level does the subject have influence? regional? national?), the flows (of people, or of ideas, etc), and the networks (of transport, of communication, etc). These concepts of power and geography will be your main analysis tools throughout this module, and are introduced as early as the first lecture. Other content taught about includes discussions of diversity or ethnicity and demographics, such as landscapes targeting the elderly, heritage landscapes, landscapes built for tourists, landscapes of public housing and the community, and so on. A lot of focus is given to the "people" aspect of it -- caring for those who are disadvantaged or left out, rather than on the history of it, for example. Anyway, even though the module is inherently Geography-styled, you can do very well (say, A-?) even if you're worried your "geog sucks" or your "writing is crap" or you "hate humans subjects", as long as you put in your due diligence, to attend lectures, and genuinely set aside focused time when writing your answers etc. If you simply want to do a little work and cruise through with an S grade, that's very easy to pull off, too. Tutorial activities aren't "cringe" imo -- the topics are important, such as how living spaces should be designed to accommodate those whose mobility is impaired, and the pros and cons of spaces heavily associated with a single ethnicity, and so on. Almost all the activities will be done as a group, so if you join the same tutorial group as your friends you'll probably enjoy it very much. Me personally, I knew no one from my tutorial group at all... but it was still fairly enjoyable. The lecturers and TAs are great: knowledgeable, patient and willing to help, and also keenly aware of the students' difficulties, especially given that 1. this is a COVID sem, 2. this is a GE mod, so most people will admittedly not want to put in much effort. The teaching staff will keep this in mind and try their best to both be educational and accommodating regardless, and I greatly enjoyed my time with them. (Man, I wish FoS staff was this good. Seriously.) They are open to answering your doubts (academic or administrative), so don't hesitate to consult them. TLDR I can confidently say that the execution of the mod was well-planned, and this is a mod suitable for 1. those who just want to put in the minimal effort to pass and SU; 2. those who are genuinely fond of (human) Geography, environments, History, politics etc, and want to explore these disciplines in a Singaporean context; 3. those who have good writing and speaking skills, and want a relatively easy distinction to boost their CAP; 4. those who want to overload with a relatively easier mod, especially if you want to overload but would still like an A- and above; and 5. those who want an essay mod where their effort is *actually* likely to produce good results. I thoroughly enjoyed this mod, even though I went in expecting little (it IS a GES module, after all. Of course I was jaded). Awesome staff, very light workload, fair assessment criteria, interesting content... stuff's great man, it gets my wholehearted recommendation. My performance Personal effort put in: embarrassingly low, I hope the staff don't see this review MCQ score: Full marks, which I believe most people got Group Project grade: A, which not many I knew got Expected grade: A- Actual grade: A+ This is my first time reviewing a mod, so pardon any typos or whatnot. Taken AY20/21 Sem 1 Lecturer: Dr Hanny KUSNADI, Elaine TAN Grade: A I took the module as a UE out of interest. As of writing this review, I’ve heard that the textbook being used in AY20/21 Sem 2 is different from the one used in AY20/21 Sem 1. The one I used while taking it was Fundamentals of Financial Accounting (6th ed) by Phillips, Libby & Libby (PLL). The one used in AY20/21 Sem 2 is Financial Accounting: Information for Decisions (REVISED 3rd ed), so note the differences, there may be difference in syllabus, since the syllabus was basically following chapter by chapter the PLL book. As all introductory modules, it has to cover the basics. There is quite a lot of fundamentals being covered that may overwhelm students, so you do need to put in some extra time making sure you understand the concepts, especially because the concepts will build upon itself over the weeks. The amount of math required in the module is very minimal, and is mostly algebraic manipulation (x + y = z, where you have 2 of the values, find the last unknown), interest calculation (sub in formula), and calculation of various ratios (sub in formula). The more difficult part of the algebraic manipulation is knowing where/how to find the unknowns, and knowing whether it is a positive or negative value. The group project is basically answering some questions and displaying your answer in a report format. Nothing really difficult but does require you to read through some financial statements, search for financial statements of some companies, and make the necessary calculations for comparison. You will also apply your knowledge of the topics by interpreting the results of your calculations, and explaining how you make your informed decision based off the calculations. In tutorials, we just went through the answers (you’re expected to have completed your tutorials beforehand) and asked questions if we had any. Every week, a different group will present their answers. The schedule is determined at the start of the semester (like week 1-2) so you can plan and prepare in advance. For the presenting you just explain how you got the answer, simple as that. Note that for both the group project/report AND the tutorial presentation, both are completed and graded AS A GROUP. The entire group will receive the same score for the component. Separate appeals are to be submitted for peer evaluation (non-compulsory, only submit if have complaints). The module was really informative and I felt that the concepts learnt were useful. The workload was relatively low. The concepts were somewhat easy to understand. And the vacancies of the module was so high that you’re basically guaranteed a slot. The lecturers made the lessons quite enjoyable to be in. Dr Hanny’s pre-lecture music was quite chill and brought a good mood in the morning. Slides are also super slick and aesthetic. Exam started around 6PM and ended around 8PM. After checking if everyone have submitted, dismissal around 8:15PM. Email was sent out for students to submit/respond if they (the student) have experienced difficulties due to disruptions in the exam. Special arrangement was done to grade their papers separately for fairness, which I feel was one of the better ways they could have dealt with the situation. Module breakdown: 10% Class participation 10% Tutorial presentation (in group of 4) 30% Group project/report (same group of 4) due week 13 50% Final exam

A/P Aaron Chia: Introduction to Project Management, Systems Thinking, Modelling and Simulation and Systems Dynamics, Stocks and Flows, Modelling and Data, Systems Dynamics, Modelling Delays and Decision Making, Testing and Validation Overview: The module mainly revolves around modelling a system using software called Stella Architect. The first few lectures are about project management, which encompasses several topics such as scope, schedule, cost management, and project control. The module then progresses towards building models using causal loop diagrams (CLD) and Stock-Flow diagrams (SFD). Subsequently, the module also discusses model testing and validation as well as delays and decision making. The module was conducted in full e-learning mode with pre-recorded lectures as well as online tutorial and lab sessions held in alternate weeks. Every lab session requires a submission of the completed task related to the respective lab one week after the lab is conducted. There is also optional homework given following the tutorials sessions which is meant for self-study and not to be submitted. The group project is a semester-long project which depicts and elaborates a problem using modelling and systems thinking. This module has a quite evenly distributed grading scheme. The individual quizzes (40%) held on Week 6 and Week 10 consist of 50 MCQ in LumiNUS quiz format. The questions were almost entirely based on the lecture notes given. Another part of the assessment is the graded group assignments (30%), which consist of two lab assignments and one Yellow Fever assignment, each worth 10%. Finally, the group project (30%) is assessed from several categories, namely the interim report (5%), final report (10%), and presentation video (10% group, 5% individual). To be honest, I don't know what I learned in this mod. The materials were like, a bit of "common sense" but at the same time quite vague as well. The parts about project management and introduction to systems thinking, CLDs, and SFDs were okay but the rest were… vague without much explanation on how we should apply the concepts. The only learning point that I got from this module was that everything happens for a reason, which (might) link into a grand causal loop that we might not be aware of. It's like GER1000 that talks about how "correlation does not imply causation" but on steroids, resulting in a nested causation that somehow creates these big loops of causal relationships. The tutorial and lab sessions were quite okay. They showed you how you apply the concepts of CLDs and SFDs with the help of software called Stella Architect. To be honest I quite enjoyed (some of) the sessions as I started to understand how and why things happen/change because of complex causal relationships. However, there was this 1 tutorial where the prof just explained about stakeholders and perceptions, which was, no joke, literally filled with memes and/or optical illusions that you might usually see in Instagram or boomer WhatsApp groups. The tutorial slides were literally filled with random videos and random optical illusions and then… "Thanks! Do you have any questions??". Throughout that session I literally just cringed at the tutorial slides and wondered why I spent 1.5 hours looking at optical illusions and cringy videos. The quizzes were quite funny as well. If not, try your best in doing the assignments and final project and hope that the tutor/prof that you get would be lenient enough to give you a good score. I fortunately got very good teammates and they were ambitious enough to make our stock-flow model quite decent and robust for the project. I heard some groups had MIA teammates, most probably because they didn’t understand the mod itself. In conclusion, I think that this module could be improved for future batches. The organisation was still quite messy and the instructions given for the final project were not that clear until Week 12-13, where the prof urgently blasted emails to explain things that he never taught in class. Hopefully the prof could improve the content and organisation of the module so that future batches could appreciate what they are learning in this module.

Taken in AY15/16 sem2 Lecturer: Dr. Tang Weng Hong Note: you might become a sceptic by the end of the module Topics: What is Knowledge (Justified True beliefs + 4th condition) Do we actually know ( Problems of Scepticism and Solutions to it) What is Justification (Evidentialist vs Reliabilist theories) Sources of Justification (Perception, Testimony, Memory) Assessment/Grading: Class Part: 20% Term Paper: 40% Finals: 40% Dr. Tang really makes you think if you actually know anything at all. As the module name suggest, Epistemology is the study of knowledge and goes into the basics in the study of knowledge. The aim of the module is that by the end, you will be able to think critically about questions concerning knowledge such as: what does it mean to know? do we actually know we are not a brain in a vat? How are we justified from our senses? For people with no formal philosophy background, not to worry. Most of the topics covered is merely the basic of epistemology. Having said that, this module does go beyond what one learns from TOK in IB or KI for A's. (I have asked friends who have taken such subjects and while they did learn topics like the Gettier Problem, they did not specifically go in depth the solutions to such problems like no false lemma or sensitivity/safety theories) As such, it is a fairly even playing ground. Do note that readings for the course can be quite complex at times. As such, I would suggest that you read and "attempt" to understand the arguments and ideas before attending the lectures where the prof will simplify the readings making it more understandable. Having said that, Tutorials are also important, not only because of a 20% class part, but that is when the bulk of philosophical discussion and learning will take place. Do try to contribute ideas of your own while taking notes of what is discuss as many ideas shared will add insight into what you learn from lectures/readings (also very good info/examples for your essay and finals) Dr Tang usually spends time going though the more challenging theories in the module in lectures. For example, Safety and Sensitivity theories in resolving the Gettier problem, Dretske and relevant alternatives, Coherentism theory of justification. As for tutorials, he usually comes up with 1-2 starting questions before the class takes over and "discuss" whether we agree or disagree before the he shares his viewpoint or clarifies any misconception. Term Paper: For the Term paper, it is a 6 choose 1 question. The questions are fairly simple as the topics have been taught in class like what is knowledge or analyzing Unger's argument for scepticism. The challenging part of the essay is to show that you actually understand the topic as well as critically analysing each argument that you propose. Don't be too dishearten if you see a B/B-, it is rare to even see an A- paper for philo. Finals: Fortunately, or unfortunately, finals was an open book examination. Thus, it is entirely possible for you to write and entire essay and bring it into the examination hall just to copy-paste. Like most art modules, prepare for your hands to ache as you have 2 hours to write 2 essays from 4 questions. Each relating to 1 of the 4 topics mentioned above. Conclusion: Overall, the module's workload is very manageable but that does not mean that it is easy to understand. A lot of people struggled with understanding scepticism and the arguments for/against it. Having said that, you ultimately become more knowledgeable about knowledge (pun intended). To do well in this module, not only should you attend lectures and tutorials but to actively take part in them and to read your readings beforehand.

CG2271 AY2017/18 Sem 2: Sem 2 is always taught by Prof Ravi, while Sem 1 is taught by Prof He Bingsheng (the review by Jiachao may be more accurate for prospective students taking CG2271 in Sem 1). The concepts taught in this module are very high level concepts, which may not be everyone's cup of tea (not for me at least). You'll cover real-time operating systems and how they function, including processor-memory operations, interrupts, task managements & memory principles. Quite touch and go so a bit abstract. Prof Ravi does a decent job in explaining them, although reading the lecture notes alone can be sufficient as well. CG2271 has very high weightage (around 40% I believe) on the lab component, so get it done well and you'll be more or less guaranteed a decent grade. Problem is, your lab TA matters a lot. My lab TA marks the lab reports much more leniently than the other lab TA. You might use an Arduino board (subject to change for other sems), which integrates FreeRTOS in the 2nd part of the semester to carry out simple tasks. Generally quite ok as you are given the templates to work upon, and you are guided quite well, especially the setup of the software on your computer is pretty much idiotproof. Some of the later tasks may be hard since you have no idea of the algorithm needed. (Ask your friends for help!) The lab demos are once every fortnightly, so there's time to work on your code and after that, your report which generally isn't hard because the questions are concept based questions, although some questions require a bit of digging through documentation (of FreeRTOS). Unlike Sem 1, midterms and finals are completely closed book. And they are hard. The midterms tested questions that don't even appear to be covered in the lecture notes, or just totally strange questions. The finals however, is partially a joke because past year questions were completely reused. But the main killer of the finals were the programming questions which required you to write code from scratch, even though you are allowed to "invent" your own syntax so long its understandable from FreeRTOS point of view. TL;DR Abstract high level concepts. Labs are generally manageable, nail them. Prepare to die in midterms (weird questions) and finals since no cheat sheets (and coding questions in finals). Term Test 2 on Week 13 covers topics ONLY taught after recess week (around 7 topics). Same format as Term Test 1 but much harder due to the content. Median for MCQ was 19 this time but essay was still 5. Project.. gosh it was a tough ride. 45% some more.. But basically this project is really all about essay writing with minimal discussions required. 10 essay questions (totally unrelated to the topics in the module) are released in Week 1 and we were told to form groups of 3 and rank the essay choices. We got an essay question regarding wormholes and space travel (not taught in lectures, I repeat), and what we had to do was to research on our own, write our stand and submit. We need to have 3 arguments for our main essay and so just nice each of us write an argument then together write an intro and conclusion. It was damn tough trying to find arguments for our essays and often I am lost with all the scientific terms. That is only 10% by the way. The next 10% is to read another group's essay (different topic) and counter their arguments totally. Then the next 10% is to review other group's counterarguments on our essays then make a presentation for our essay topic, either counter their counterarguments or substantiate on our original arguments. The next 10% is to view FOUR other groups' presentations and give useful feedback for each argument they provide for their topic. Last 5% is peer feedback, rating your own group mates and their efforts. So as you can see, the project part at least to me, is tedious as all of it mainly kicks in after the reading week and every week we have to meet to discuss about how we are going to the next part of the project. And it's 45% some more, so cannot anyhow do if you want to do well. As the concept of wormholes is quite abstract to me, I had much difficulty doing our project and scared that the arguments might not be very well-written. Summary: Difficulty rating: 8/10 Should you take this mod?: Only if you are really really into astronomy and our universe. Comments: If you want an easy A with little effort, this is not a mod to take. I had some regrets taking this module due to the workload of the project and the abstract contents of the module that I did not expect. But I still went on with it, tried my best and hoping for the best. Results for the project were not released so I'm not sure how I did in that aspect.
