by Dr John Van Wyhe To preface this review, I will not be discussing whether this module is "easy to score" or "should i take this module as I heard there is a steep bell curve" as that has been discussed and this module is so much more than that. Dr John is THE world expert on Darwin and it was a privilege to be able to attend his lectures, which were by the way, always a delight to attend. Attending his lectures were, in my opinion less of a chore, and more akin to storytelling sessions by the enigmatic grandpa you never had. It also helped that his pronunciation and delivery were flawless, which was a refreshing change to my other lectures. Out of all the modules (22 in total) I have taken in my 2 years in NUS (I'm from Mechanical Engineering), this was by far the most interesting and thought provoking module I have ever taken. Dr John is humorous and constantly encourages us to think critically, and not just to accept contemporary dogmas at face value. The unique thing about this module is that it teaches one HOW to think and not just WHAT to think, as so many other modules often do. As a general overview, this module address some key misconceptions that most individuals have today regarding Darwin and evolution in general: 1. Did Darwin steal the idea of natural selection from Alfred Russel Wallace? Is Alfred Russell Wallace the pitiful, forgotten hero of evolution? 2. Did Darwin start a war on religion and the church in 19th century England? 3. How could evolution make something so perfect like the eye? Or how could 2 totally different animals, like a moose and a toad, possibly be related? 4. Did we really come from apes? Why are there then still apes? 5. Did the people of 19th century England still believe the Earth was 6000 years old and that all animals and plants were created in 7 days? 6. Isn't evolution just a theory? 7. Did Darwin get his inspiration for evolution from the galapagos islands and it's finches? 8. Did Darwin delay publishing Origin of Species for 20 years as he was afraid of getting executed? 9. Did the death of his daughter cause him to lose faith in christianity? 10. Was Darwin an atheist, an agnostic or a theist? All of these questions will be answered in this module. I found the earlier half of the module to be extremely interesting. The module starts by immersing you in the life of a typical victorian in 19th century England. Their opinions on evolution, the role of God in their day to day lives, and general things like the age of the Earth, the fossil record which seemed to contradict biblical text and whether there was a great flood or not as per the Bible. Next, the module delves into the life of young Darwin, his life in Cambridge, his voyage and adventures around the world on the beagle and finally his publications on plants, evolution and even earthworms . The way that Dr John expertly narrates the life of Darwin really transports you back 200 years and allows one to experience the life of Darwin vicariously. The way they wrote, the way they spake, and their biases and religious beliefs are all presented in his lecture notes and readings, which make for very interesting, albeit high browed reading. Dr John is the world expert on Darwin, hailing from the same college (christ's college) as Darwin in Cambridge and it shows in his lectures. The delivery is effortless, and this allows him to inject humour into his lectures, which is a far cry from the other lectures I have taken. One should not be too concerned if ones interests lie elsewhere apart from history or evolution, for this module caters to a wide variety of interests. From geography, history, religion and scientific jealousy, to tall tales and rumours, myth busting and even philosophy. For example, when trying to understand how evolution was accepted as fact in a mere 10 years in the 1870s, our attention was focused on the victorian crisis of faith, which was a period in Victorian times where most people were questioning their faith. This was not solely caused by Darwin's origin of species, but rather the cumulative effects of biblical criticism, victorian naturalism and even the french revolution. This tied in beautifully with Nietzsche's famous statement that "God is dead, and we have killed him". This perhaps triggered the start of nihilism and Nietzsche's prediction that people would face a feeling of utter hopelessness once their strong rooted beliefs in an almighty God came crashing down due to scientific advancement and the disbelief in revelation and miracles and gives one a comprehensive overview of how different historical events and opinions tie in with one another. The last 1/4 mainly dealt with the evolution of man and all beings in general, covering concepts that shook my view of the world, such as the consumption of cooked food leading to big brains in man, and the lack of domesticated plants and animals leading to some civilisations lagging behind others and that there was once a period in prehistory where there were multiple human-like species roaming the Earth that did cave paintings, made fire and even buried their dead. Overall, this module was a refreshing change to the standard approach of cramming, regurgitation and abandonment I am so used to in other modules and I would highly recommend it.

under Prof Tan Ser Peow. This is a module where the lecturer uses umbrellas, tennis balls, and (significantly) multiple types of cake as teaching tools during lecture. Prof Tan tries to give physical meaning to the mathematical quantities that are investigated, and this is helpful in giving students some intuition of what the mathematical quantities represent. (Also, we get to eat the cake.) This module covers three main topics - differentiation (partial differentiation, critical points, Lagrange multipliers), integration (area & volume integrals, line & surface integrals), and the links between them (divergence, curl). Brief introduction on vectors and surfaces is made at the start of this module, as these concepts will be used throughout the module. In general, this module is very gentle in its introduction of new concepts, and the pace is very manageable. Unlike some mathematics modules, most questions in tests and exams require calculations instead of proofs. While proof-based reasoning is not as important here, students need to be careful in the accuracy of their calculations (some of which may be slightly tedious). Some skill in algebraic manipulation is assumed. Assessment for this module is via midterms (20%), finals (65%), graded homework assignments (12%), and tutorial participation (3%). Midterms and finals are closed-book (with help sheet), and non-graphing and non-programmable calculators are allowed.

AY15/16 Sem 1 A/P Arthur Tay & A/P Abdullah Al Mamun Builds on EE2023's Systems part (Laplace transform, zeros, poles & stability) and is split into two parts covered by separately A/P Tay and A/P Mamun. The two big new topics coming from EE2023 are Nyquist Stability Criterion and the design of a controller to meet desired specifications. The module is highly mathematically intensive and practice is key. Since past year papers and most answers are provided, there is no excuse not to do so. The textbook is not really required for this module. Knowledge of Laplace transforms, Euler's identity and trigonometric identities will also come in useful. Both professors teach well, take lots of questions after lectures or via email and write a lot on screen, so paying attention and attempting the exercises in lecture is a good way to quickly learn the syllabus contents. A/P Mamun also provides 0% optional but graded 'homework' question(s) after nearly every lecture which succinctly summarizes what he just taught, but not many seem interested in submitting them. There is a midterm (20%), two labs (2 x 10%) and a final exam (60%). The midterm is easy while the finals tend to be very challenging and difficult to complete even though it is already 2.5hrs long. The finals in recent years come provided with more and more formula so there are fewer things to memorise. tl;dr: stay away if you're weak in maths

Taken in AY14/15 Sem1 By Dr Ng Kien Ming This module introduced intermediate concepts used in Optimization, such as Integer Programming, Advanced Linear Programming, Game Theory, Dynamic Programming and Heuristics. The difficulty peaked at Advanced Linear Programming (which involved quite alot of 'code-tracing' and mastery of the algorithms introduced), eased at Game Theory, picked up a little with dynamic programming, finishing off with the easiest topic: Heuristics. In this course, A popular industrial-rate software, AIMMS, was introduced in the class, and it proved to be very useful for our group project and our respective FYPs. The classes covered a good balance between theory as well as applications, covering not only efficient algorithms/methods for solving the mathematical program, but how to formulate and extend the formulation to different scenarios. Tutorials were not graded, although we had a weekly assignment to submit that kept us on our toes and up to speed with the class. I would recommend this course to ISE students in their 3rd year, as it would be a very useful tool in your belt whenever you need to optimize something, be it for SDP, or even for one's FYP. Grading wise, we had weekly assignments in which almost everyone got full marks, a mid-term which was a time rush (I got the median score), a group project where I had the honour of working with some of the brightest minds in ISE, and of course a finals. Given my lacklustre performance for my mid-terms, I expected at best an A-, but got an A finally.

Taken in AY2014/15 “Did you all get that? Let me come again. … Actually, I shouldn’t be saying such things in public. … But to come again, it must be hard. … as in difficult. I don’t know what all of you are thinking about. ” Overview: MA1505 is the first of two modules which covers the mathematical fundamentals which are commonly used across the various fields of engineering. The main topic of interest here is calculus and its branches which are most relevant to engineering applications. This means learning about things like Taylor’s theorem, Fourier series and vector calculus, up and above the regular differentiation and integration techniques and applications covered in H2 math. This is not a light module. The content taught here is arguably the equivalent of 2 modules taken by math majors, as it covers both single and multivariable calculus. Therefore, much of the content is condensed with the focus on applying the theorems taught, and the proofs of said theorems given only a passing mention or else omitted entirely. ________ Syllabus: 1. Functions 2. Differentiation 3. Integration 4. Series 5. Vectors 6. Fourier series 7. Functions of several variables 8. Multiple integrals 9. Line integrals 10. Surface integrals Workload: There will be one 2-hour and one 1-hour lecture per week, plus 1 tutorial per week. Attendance is not graded, plus there is webcast, so you can self-study everything at home if you want. However, if you are an average student, be prepared to spend a lot of time wrapping your head around things like Fourier series, Stokes theorem, Divergence theorem etc. ________ Assessment: 20% Mid-term test: This 1-hour paper contains 10 MCQ questions and covers the first 5 chapters. The paper is harder than it looks (the mean score for my cohort was 6/10), as almost all questions require some form of computation. If you want to do well, attempt all the past year test papers uploaded on IVLE as the format of the papers are more or less the same. 80% Final exam: Although the exam covers only chapters 6-10, it is not easy as these chapters are the hardest in the module. Again, doing the past year papers helps a lot. You will also be allowed to bring in 1 cheat sheet into the exam. You can write whatever you want in the cheat sheet, but I recommend you include all the important formulas in case you forget them during the exam. If you have extra space, copying the past year paper solutions is a good idea as well. ________ Teaching Staff: Lecturer: Dr Yap Weng Yin Dr Yap was my webcasted lecturer. He lectures quite well; nothing spectacular, but he gets the idea across. He occasionally punctuates his lecture with some, uh, not-so-decent jokes, which always gave the class a good laugh. I felt it provided a very welcome relief from solving integrals and analysing vector fields all the time. Unfortunately, I only attended a couple of tutorials, mostly studying using the solutions provided on IVLE, so I'm not in a position to comment about the tutor. ________ Personal Experience: I did not have a pleasant experience in this module, although it is partially my fault. I only started watching webcast lectures during reading week, and cramming that much information into my brain in such a short time was very painful. If that wasn’t enough, I then realized after the exam that I hardly understood anything that I had learnt, beyond memorizing the steps to solve exam problems. Apparently what happened to me is very common for first year students. My advice is the same as that of the reviews before mine. Study consistently throughout the semester, even though most of the marks are in the final exam. And it's not just for the grade in this module. Many of the concepts taught here seem dry and abstract now, will likely appear again in future modules. Building a solid foundation now would mean having an easier time later.

Taken in AY1516 Sem 2, by Dr Aimee Shih Module Breakdown: - 40%: Final Exam - 30%: Mid Term - 20%: Group Project - 10%: Tutorial Participation, Presentation This module introduces the concepts of financial accounting. It covers the four basic financial statements each company has to produce, the accounting equation, and goes into key components of assets, liabilities and stockholders’ equity. Dr Aimee Shih is probably one of the best lecturers around in NUS. Although the concepts covered are boring, she presents well enough to make sure that it is not too difficult to stay awake or to follow the content. The textbook is a must, as tutorial questions are from there and the lecture content follows very closely to what is being taught in the textbook. Mid term was 40 MCQs, with some questions coming together as a problem set, i.e. question 1 – 5 uses the same background info. The catch is that question 3 often requires question 2’s answer, and question 4 requires question 3’s answer and so on. Get one wrong and all five might be wrong. However, contrary to the popular belief that the bell curve was extremely steep, the mid term results did not reflect that. There is room to make a number of careless mistakes, so there is no need to worry over the bell curve. The final exam is essentially another mid term, 40 MCQs with the addition of 1 more structured question. Getting the structured question right helps a lot in obtaining a good grade for this module. The group project was to answer a set of questions based on the financial statements of some companies, and although it doesn’t require a lot of effort to do it, it requires a considerable amount of thinking to produce good answers for some questions. The key to doing well for this module is to practice, but there aren’t many practice questions around. The lecturer typically posts one set of questions for mid term and finals, which might not be sufficient.

Taken in 20/21 Sem 2 Grading: 5% CA1, 25% CA2, 10% CA3, 30% CA4, 15% CA5, 15% participation Ah yes, the compulsory English class to be taken by all Computing students. There are 2x2hr sessions per week with high weightage class participation, which I'm sure contributes to the universal hate this class gets. The content of the class can be read from the other reviews so I'll just talk about the assessments. --- Assessment --- Similar to CS2101, grading is very consistent throughout the semester due to the 5 CAs. There aren't any "lull" periods where there's nothing to do (notwithstanding the 2x2hr sessions per week), so expect to put in more work than you might probably expect. For group projects, the class is split into groups at the start of the semester based on a survey done in the first class. You're stuck with this group for the whole semester so pray you get people who have the same goals as you. I was fortunate to have landed in a group with like-minded individuals who all wanted to maximise effort:reward ratio. CA1: Craft a presentation/video of a spin on a children's tale. Pretty simple, can be done in an afternoon if focused. CA2: Make a "Critical Thinking Rubric" from the Ennis reading, write a report on it (15%) and do a presentation (10%). This is the most tiring group project so I'm glad the co-ordinators put this early in the semester. CA3: Panel Discussion on an topic that was agreed upon prior to the discussion. You have to research the topic, then have an "academic conversation" that goes on for about 30-45min with your group, with 15min Q/A at the end. Can be prepared the day before. Try to be nice to your teammates and let them have their say in the discussion. CA4: Position Paper. You propose a question then write a 800-word-or-so essay on it. This is similar to writing a GP essay, except with citations. Can be done in a day assuming you already have a good question to write on. This is individual work with high weightage so if you're planning to score, better put work into this. CA5: Given a prompt, do an individual impromptu speech on the prompt in 2min. This is a luck of the draw if you get a good prompt or not. It's over within 2 minutes so if you can't think of anything to say, hey, at least you'll die quickly. Expected Grade: B/B+ Actual Grade: TBC

Taken in AY20/21 Semester 2 Taught by: Assoc. Prof. Zhang Lei (Lecturer) Disclaimer: This module was conducted in the third semester affected by the COVID-19 pandemic, and as a result it may differ significantly from how past/future modules would/will be conducted. Assessment Structure: 60% Homework (6 sets, 10% each) 40% Presentation (Zoom) This module introduces commutative algebra at a graduate level. The module’s content include Noetherian rings, affine algebraic sets, Grobner bases, radicals and The Zariski Topology affine varieties and primary decomposition, integral extension, Noether’s normalization, Hilbert Nullstellensatz, localizations, localizations of modules, localizations of affine algebraic varieties, the prime spectrum of a ring, Artinian rings, discrete valuation rings, Dedekind domains, modules over a Dedekind domain, Hilbert functions, dimension theory of Noetherian local rings, project and injective Modules, flat modules and exact sequences, homological algebra, Ext and Tor functors. The main text of reference is Abstract Algebra, Dummit and Foote (approximately chapters 10 and 15-17), and occasionally side-tracking to Introduction to Commutative Algebra, Atiyah and MacDonald (chapter 11). All lectures were held in a hybrid setting – that is, lectures were conducted face-to-face with a zoom meeting being opened meanwhile, so students were free to choose to attend lectures live or via zoom. Like most graduate modules, this module has no tutorial classes. Prof. Zhang provides his own sets of lecture notes (which are all handwritten), but they follow very closely to the textbook he refers to for that chapter. As with all my past reviews on algebra modules, I have once again failed to establish any reasonably solid form of intuition to any of the concepts taught, except for some more elementary concepts (at this point I have given up doing so). I did not pay lots of attention in lectures, but Prof. Zhang’s notes are quite neat and can be self-studied with. Thus, I am not able to judge the difficulty level of this module. Homework is split into 6 parts. The questions are very doable, and a reasonably understanding of what is taught in the class/lecture notes would suffice to do all the questions. Prof. Zhang also strongly recommends students to discuss the problems among themselves, as long as one eventually writes/types out the solutions themselves. Furthermore, Prof. Zhang gives bonus points (≤1 point per homework set) to students with noteworthy submissions, such as good detail, interesting alternative approach to a problem etc. These bonus points will be added to their presentation grade. Prof. Zhang is a brilliant lecturer in pretty much every aspect – he lectures fluently and explains the concepts in detail especially in parts which many may find difficult to understand. He occasionally side-tracks to other fields (especially algebraic geometry) to explain the relevance and importance of the concepts taught. He is also very friendly and approachable, so one shouldn’t hesitate to ask him questions or clarify with him any questions regarding the assessments. Overall, it’s been a great pleasure taking this module under him. The presentation involved students choosing a topic themselves that’s related to commutative algebra, then presenting their findings at the end of the semester. Prof. Zhang also indicated at various points of his lecture notes that students may explore further in that topic for their project. Specialising in logic, my project involved providing a proof of Ax-Grothendieck theorem using model theory. Commutative algebra has close ties with algebraic geometry, so people familiar with algebraic geometry would find it much easier to appreciate the concepts taught (though, to my understanding, people usually take algebraic geometry as a follow-up to this course). I think this course would be suitable and accessible to all undergraduates interested in algebra. Expected Grade: A+ Final Grade: A+

AY2020/2021 S1 (Full Online Sem) Cristina CARBUNARU Module difficulty/contents: This module is difficult, no doubt. Took this module in Sem 1 of AY16/17 under Dr Marc Rochester. No final examination. TL;DR: Basically "Orchestras in Singapore 1101". Stickler for essay formatting with vague topics that are easily misinterpreted. Very light workload, but not guaranteed an A. Probably boring for people who already are immersed in the Singaporean "western" music scene. CA consists of four parts: CA1: Fieldwork project on the study of audience behaviour in western music concerts in Singapore OR study of music schools/teaching programmes in Singapore, with a presentation in class. Group work of about 5-8(?) people. CA2: 500 word objective individual essay on a "western music ensemble" in Singapore. CA3: 750 word subjective individual essay on the position of the Singaporean music scene in the global context. CA4: Introduced at the last minute - class discussion during week 13's class. I found that there was a huge discrepancy between what the module title and description suggests and what is actually taught in the module. While the module is titled "Western Music within a Singaporean Context" (where western basically = classical as we generally understand it), it basically can be summed up as "the history of orchestras in Singapore". As someone who comes from a choral background I found it immensely disappointing that the vast majority of content covered orchestral music, with the other major topic being the role of learning and teaching "western" music in Singaporean society. The module description also reads: "It will assess the impact of majority cultures (particularly from the Chinese, Malay and Indian communities) on the general reception of Western music, as well as on music written by Singapore-based composers. Students will be introduced to the principal figures in Singapore’s musical development." However, these issues were just touch-and-go, with Marc basically rambling on about the treatment of classical music in Singaporean households or about audience perceptions. I honestly do not recall anything about majority cultures in Singapore being mentioned, and only a very small portion was touched on regarding Singaporean composers, even solo Singaporean musicians. While Marc himself is a rather funny guy, he basically sits you down for 1.5 hrs a week and rambles on, asking more questions than he gives answers, simply because this is a field that doesn't really have much research conducted with regard to music in Singapore. While he occasionally gives you facts, he doesn't properly cite the sources that he tends to mention casually, making it seem extremely wishy-washy. Lecture slides are uploaded every week after class, along with (rather soft) audio recordings of one of the lecture slots. The guest lectures are pretty banal, with more about the orchestras like SSO and Music Makers, the history of their establishment and things like that. If you're already pretty much into the local "western" music scene there's not much you can learn from attending lectures: it's basically a reaffirmation of what you already know more or less. For the fieldwork project, since the class is split into such large groups, you are allowed to split the work by having some members exclusively do data collection and others do the presentation, or have everyone involved. However, traditional powerpoint presentations should be eschewed for more interesting and attention-grabbing methods such as skits and interactive sessions. It also helps to have a few major points from your fieldwork presented as clearly as possible rather than trying to cover all bases. For the essays, the main thing is to FOLLOW THE GUIDELINES STRICTLY! He spells them all out within the powerpoint and word documents, though both documents sometimes have things that he does not put in the other, so be wary and ensure that you put in everything and double/triple check before submission, as he has been known to drop people a few grades for not following the format. The topics tend to be VERY VAGUE and are easily subject to misinterpretation, as evidenced by the majority of my groupmates and myself. While the topics may be vague, he has a very strict idea of what should be put in the essay (which is pretty unfair), and so if you really want that A you HAVE to consult him about your ideas relating to the given essay topics, otherwise it's extremely easy to get a C for the essay component. Book him early for a consultation as he tends to be busy running around watching concerts and other stuff. You only get one chance to upload your essay, and if you don't follow the guidelines or completely misinterpret the essay he will ask you to resubmit it with a SEVERE PENALTY (25%) IN GRADING, and can only be done during the submission period. i.e. past the given deadline, no more re-submissions if you fail to interpret or follow the guidelines. Some of the criteria for formatting make sense, while others like INSISTING ON USING UK ENGLISH or COUNTING HYPHENATED WORDS AND ACRONYMS AS INDIVIDUAL WORDS are a complete pain in the ass. While this module has an extremely light workload I would honestly not recommend it for people already immersed in the "western" music happenings in Singapore as it will be boring af. Plus, the essays are a real chore which always makes you second-guess yourself. I completely regret wasting 1400 points on this module as I had to bid it under the SSY module code.

Lecture/Tutor: A/P Dlip Raghavan I really enjoyed this module. For those unfamiliar with what linear algebra means, it is basically derived from the term linear and algebra. Linear is associated to representations of mathematical objects by straight lines, planes and algebra is basically representing unknown variables with letters. This module focuses mainly on vector fields, spaces. However, given the crononavirus outbreak, the content of this module is scaled down up till 6.3. This module started off with analyzing on how to solve a systems of linear equations without the use of a graphing calculator, GC. In A levels, we are used to understand the GC commands to aid us in solving a system of simultaneous linear equations of 3 or more variables. Now, in linear algebra, it teaches us the trick on how to solve such a linear system manually without the use of a GC: Gauss Jordan Elimination. How cool it is? Afterwards, the module goes on to recap on matrices operations such as addition, subtraction, multiplication. This is nostalgic as it brings back to me memories of how we were introduced to the use of matrices in o level elementary mathematics in statistics and set notations. But the difficulty level escalates in this topic where new alien terms are introduced such as elementary matrices, application of gauss jordan elimination in finding inverse, proving the properties of matrix operations and lastly determinants. Then, the 3rd chapter is on vector spaces. The first half is a recap on vector addition, subtraction which is first introduced in o level mathematics. Then concepts such as linear combinations, spans, sub spaces , linear independence and bases are derived from the addition operations of vectors. Concepts in the 1st chapter on solving simultaneous equations and gauss jordan elimination will be useful in understanding, answering and proving the concepts discussed in the 3rd chapter. Except for transition matrices which is the most alien term for me lol. The 4th chapter is on matrices associated to vector spaces. Row space, Column space, ranks are introduced in this chapter. Simple to say, row space is the set of all linear combinations of all the rows in the matrix. Column space is the set of all linear combinations of all the columns in the matrix. Important fact to understand is the techniques of deriving the bases for the row and column spaces respectively from a given matrix. Basically an extension of contents from chapters 2 and 3 Chapter 5 and 6 I can basically understand the techniques and apply the formulas but I do not deeply understand the proves behind them. It is basically an extension of common concepts covered in A levels such as dot and cross products of vectors which will be useful in proving concepts and properties on orthogonal bases. Hence for this chapter, it is best to take note of the key formulas covered in them. This will aid you in answering computation questions efficiently. The weightage is not applicable to other semesters. It is 35% mid terms, 35% finals, 24% homework, 6% take home lab assignment. It is taught under Associate Professor Dilip Raghavan. A/P Dilip is a good prof. He is warm and friendly and perhaps a great fan of star wars given that he liked my Darth Vader shirt which I wore once for his tutorial. He is willing and happy to clarify me and my friend's doubts on orthogonal and transition matrices which we have most difficulty in comprehending. He uses diagrams to aid us in his explanation and his tutorials is focused on explaining all the suggested solution to the tutorial questions. The tutorial questions are worth to practice as some questions are from past year paper. He does not call students to present their answers and he explains everything from scratch during tutorials and lectures. I really love him. He is strong in the force. I scored below my expectations for mid terms as I made a careless mistake. I misread one of the question and lose alot of marks. So linear algebra though may seem easy to some, but it is very prone to making careless mistakes given the many computations involved in this subject. The finals is one of the harder ones among the many past year papers. With careful thought, one could grasp the concepts and formulas to apply in each question and when in doubt, use the force. All in all, though linear algebra sounds like a really new subject to study, it is basically an extension of the topic of vectors, equations and inequalities, sets and matrices covered in O levels and A levels. All the best in your pursues. Stay safe and strong!! May the force be with you.

It gives you a solid foundation in cognition, covering many topics from the fundamentals of attention and memory to the higher-level processes such as mental categorization and decision-making. Definitely one of the more rigorous and technical modules in psychology, but don’t let that scare you: it’s not as hard as it seems. Highlights include: learning why the number seven is the most powerful magic number is significant in memory, and why people tend to be uncomfortable when they need to take one step back to be able to take two steps forward in problem-solving. It almost makes you feel smart, but then you realize that you weren’t the one that came up with those explanations. Lectures were a rundown of the most important concepts in each topic/chapter, and basically told you what your key takeaways should be. Tutorials: Tutorials were held as one-hour sessions once per week. During each tutorial, you’ll be required to discuss and analyse a (published) paper pertaining to the prior week’s lectured topic. What it does is to teach you how to critically think about a paper’s hypothesis, experimental method, results, and the importance of the results. Definitely a good skill to acquire, since you’ll definitely need to read papers on your own in the future for higher-level modules. Exams: Each midterm consisted of about 50 MCQs pertaining to content knowledge, which will be relatively straightforward provided that you studied the material beforehand. The finals consist of choosing a 3 essay questions out of 4, plus an additional compulsory question. Again, relatively straightforward if you studied. The key skill you’ll need here is to be able to turn your own shorthand notes into a coherent essay, and synthesize knowledge from across chapters if need be. Expected grade: A- Final grade: A- (See reviews of psychology and other modules at

Took this module in Sem 1 AY19/20. Lecturer: Nagami sensei. TA and TB tutors: Nagami sensei and Shirakawa sensei. I took the module as a natural continuation to Jap 1. I will try to highlight as many of the main differences between Jap 1 and 2 as I can. One of these is that the vocabulary quizzes now begin from the first week of tutorials, and are scored upon 10. (I remembered the earlier quizzes for Jap 1 are only scored upon 5, and are rather easy) You jump into the normal pace of lessons similar to the later part of Jap 1 from the get-go of Japanese 2, so be prepared for that. Lessons 11-20 of the Nihongo Textbook will be covered in Japanese 2. Attending Lectures is compulsory (unless you don't care for losing marks) because you have to submit your answers to lecture quiz questions every lecture, which is basically used to take attendance. When I was taking Jap 1 this was not implemented. However, the lectures are really useful for preparing you for next week's grammar and vocabulary, so it's best to attend them anyways. Also, do not expect the dialogue performances to be something that can be perfectly rehearsed like that of Jap 1. While some of them are the same as Jap 1 style (where you just need to correctly recite the scenarios in the textbook), the tutor changes things up by giving the students different pictures of scenarios on the screen where you have to think quickly and adapt accordingly. Usually, after a round of normal dialogues, the teacher gives every pair time to come up with their own personalized version of the same dialogue, where the structure of the dialogue is maintained but the specific activities and objects in question can be altered at your own discretion. Don't be afraid of making mistakes into your dialogues. Just be as flexible as possible and if you can, make it humorous so you can get more marks and it keeps things from becoming stale. Another addition to Jap 2 is the Show-and-tell component about a hobby you have. I did have a show-and-tell presentation in the final tutorial of Jap 1, but it was not graded. In Jap 2, it is a graded component, and I think it carries a significant portion of marks since time is allocated in at least 3 tutorials for you to craft your show-and-tell speech. Cue cards were allowed, but of course referring to them too much will result in a deduction of marks. I brought my 21.1 km half-marathon medals and some pictures. I think choosing something you really have an interest in gives you more motivation to write the speech and deliver it. Try to decide what your speech is going to be about earlier, so when time is given to write your speech in your tutorials, you can work your way up to the final version. I know people who changed their speech multiple times and that's quite a waste, especially since the show-and-tell happens in the final TB tutorial in the last week of school. (where you might have a lot of deadlines from other modules as well) The mid-term exam is harder than my Jap 1 mid-term exam, as you will have to work under significant time constraints. My Jap 1 mid-term was scored upon 50, while Jap 2 mid-term has a total of 70 marks for about the same amount of time given to finish the paper. However, the structure of the paper is very similar to how it was in Jap 1 so that's a good thing. There was a passage with blanks where you can choose from a provided selection of words to fill them with the correct form of the word. I suspect most people lost their marks here since you have to really be creative (you cannot use the same word twice) After that, there was a one-page long passage you have to read in order to answer 10 T&F questions. This part I rushed through quite a bit since I already spent too much time on the previous section. My suggestion is to revise all of the homework from the textbook at the minimum and do all the Main textbook chapters to be fully prepared. Try to finish the earlier parts of the paper as quickly as possible since they are the easiest and you will have more time for the harder sections. Overall, I recommend putting in consistent work and effort into Jap 2. If you just put in 30-45 minutes every day, you would be able to better assimilate the information into your memory. For myself, I got a ton of rough paper that I could write on. Every day I wrote out the vocabulary for the lessons to practise hiragana and katakana. Write kanji for as many words as you can (even go beyong the syllabus for the taught kanji if you want) so that all the kanji in Jap 2 becomes super easy. Talk out loud when doing the execises in Minna no Nihongo. For myself, I was not very good at the listening components, so I made up for it by making sure I did well at all written components. I screwed up my oral (super badly) and but managed to get A for Jap 2, so don't get discouraged... Overall, just enjoy the tutorials (we got to play many games during TA, it was very fun) and the process of learning Japanese. Make new friends, meet new people from varying years of matriculation and degrees! Undoubtedly Jap modules are the most fun out of all the modules I've taken despite all the hard work I had to put in. Expected Grade: A- (Since I messed up my oral) Actual Grade: A For reference, CA: lecture attendance homework vocabulary quiz 4x listening quiz dialogue performances mid-term test show-and-tell oral test final test

Taken AY19/20 Sem 2 Lecturer: Dr John van Wyhe Grade: B+ Review: I took this module after hearing good things about it from my peers and seniors. The content was really interesting and I strongly recommend everyone to take it if they’re interested in learning about what evolution is, and how this guy Darwin became so popular/well known. Taken in Semester 1 2018/2019: Lecturer: Professor Lee Soo Teck Disclaimer: I am an exchange student. This module was one of the best Mathematics modules I have ever taken. The pacing of this module was just right (not too fast and overwhelming and not too slow either), and it made the content very manageable. Professor Lee Soo Teck was an excellent teacher, and his style made the lectures and tutorials interesting and exciting. The assessments were also very well designed. We were issued a set of graded homework assignments to complete once every three weeks, which helped us to keep on top of the material and ensured that very little cramming had to be done for the final exam. We also received some marks for presenting solutions to allocated tutorial problems on the whiteboard. The questions on the mid semester exam ranged from easy to difficult. Most of the questions (probably 4-5 out of 7) could be solved using similar ideas taught in lectures and tutorials, while the last few were mainly for students who wanted to get A's. The final exam was probably the most challenging assessment and was worth 67%. The difficulty level of the final was higher than the mid semester exam, but the main difference was that there were a lot more questions to be done in (2 hours), so you had to work fast in order to get close to finishing the exam. Finishing about 75-80% of the final, along with perfect scores in homework and tutorials and a 90% on the mid semester exam was enough to get me an A in the course. If this is your first proof based course in Maths, the module may be a bit challenging. However, if you've already taken a proof based course like I did (e.g proof harder Linear Algebra, Abstract Algebra, harder Discrete Maths), then this course should be fairly straightforward once you understand the ideas and proof techniques. Grade: A

under Prof Tang Wai Shing Prof Tang was both the lecturer and tutor for all tutorial groups Expected: A/A+ Actual: A+ Assessment: Midterms: 25% (75 mins test, I got 48/50, mean was 39/50) Tutorial participation: 5% (just show up twice and present some tutorial solutions) Finals: 70% This module was quite a breeze to me, probably because I liked linear algebra related modules and had done well in them previously. This module focused on developing algorithms to compute eigenvalues/singular values and eigenvectors/ singular vectors. It was done by introducing various matrix decomposition/factorisation, like Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), QR factorisation, Schur factorisation etc and subsequently theorems and algorithms were developed to compute the eigenvalues and eigenvectors by applying the matrix decomposition in different ways. The Householder transformation was used almost throughout the lectures after the mid-terms but wasn't formally introduced in the notes so I had to read it up on my own, it turned out to be a pretty intuitive and useful concept. I think knowing how the Householder transformation works in the general case was a differentiating factor between the A's and B+'s. I reckon the majority of the cohort still don't understand how this technique works, as evident from the tutorial presentations I sat through, and also my A+ even though I didn't think I did that well. The finals wasn't that difficult, the bulk of the exam was computational, and the proving questions were similar to the tutorial ones. I was quite diligent in completing the tutorials independently, so I could easily replicate the answers to some of the similar questions during finals. I couldn't prove a theorem resembling the Bauer-Fike Theorem worth 4 marks and got stumped by a computational QR algorithm question due to my lack of understanding of the algorithm. Somehow I still managed to get A+, I guess the rest of the cohort understood less about the module content than I already did.

AY19/20 Sem 1 Y1 FASS student, declared Social Work as second major Lecturer: Dr Esther Goh and Dr Alicia Pon Took this module as an exposure for my declared second major and thoroughly enjoyed it. The content shared was very interesting to me, including the ethics of social work practice and a range of groups such as the elderly, children, youths, addiction, trauma and dating violence, each taking up one lecture. Sounds very content-heavy but it was manageable to me. Had a few readings every week, although honestly I gave up on them after a while. Some of them were interesting reads though. Breakdown: 15% reflection paper after social service visit 25% group project 20% participation in tutorials and discussion forum 40% final exam We had to sign up for social service visits (one to a family service centre, one to another centre such as an dementia daycare) which would take place during our recess week. We had no idea which centres we were signing up for, only the date and time, so the locations and the beneficiaries they served came as a surprise. You get to learn more about social work in Singapore and appreciate the system better. Also you learn some cool soft skills regarding therapy and conflict management! Expected grade: B+ Final grade: A-

ME2102 Difficulty: Easy Workload: Low Lecture Slot: 1000-1200 Wednesdays and 0900-1000 Thursdays at LT7 Lecturer(s): Assoc Prof LEE Kim Seng, Assoc Prof SEAH Kar Heng, Assoc Prof LAI Man On Tutorial Slot: 0900-1000 Weeks 9, 11, Mondays at E3-06-05 Tutor(s): Mr TAN Shing Liang Lab Slot: 1500-1800 Weeks 2, 4-6, Mondays at E2-0309PC6 Lab Instructor(s): (I don’t remember their names, sorry) Grade weightage: 30% Engineering Drawings Quiz 10% CAD Labs/Tutorials 10% CAD Test 50% Design Calculations Test Expected Grade: A-/A Grade: A+ Additional remarks: Lecture Webcasted: Yes Tutorial Compulsory: No Open what: Open book but not open communication COVID Sem: Became e-learning halfway through the sem Thoughts: The first half is taught by Prof Lee and is on engineering drawings. Prof Lee’s part is assessed through the drawing quiz, the CAD tutorials and the CAD test. The next part was taught by Prof Seah and is on the physics and calculations behind engineering design. The last part was taught by Prof Lai and is on bearings, shafts, and fatigue IIRC. Prof Seah and Prof Lai’s parts are assessed in the design calculations test. It’s a very easy module, just that there’s a lot of stuff to learn. Luckily it was open-book but the slides for the engineering drawings part aren’t very good for quickly searching for the answer you want (it’s not very summarised IMO), so it would be best to compile everything into a more summarised help sheet (which is a pain to do). This is very crucial because the engineering drawing quiz has so many questions but so little time to do them. Lecturers: They were alright, they seemed friendly. I took this module before I took ME2162 Manufacturing Processes in AY20/21 Sem 1 so I had no idea who Prof Seah was but most of you taking ME2102 will probably have already done ME2162 and you will definitely know who he is and that he’s a good prof (well IMO). Lectures: The content itself was usually kind of boring, especially the engineering drawings part but try your best to pay attention especially that part, because there’s a lot of stuff to remember. Tutor: I only saw him twice since there were only two tutorials but he was alright, not exceptional but not bad either. He gave some advice on the test which was cool. Tutorials: These are only for the design calculations part. It’s not that useful unless you really don’t know how to do any of the questions, which is probably unlikely because the questions are really easy. The main useful thing I got from these are the advice the tutor gives based on how the test will be like (since they tend to be seniors and probably did the module before). Lab Instructors: There were instructions to build each CAD part on the course website so all they needed to do is to read and demonstrate those instructions and maybe help fix your mistakes here and there, which they did so they were good enough. Engineering Drawings Quiz: This test will probably be on week 6 or week 7. This tests everything in the engineering drawings part. There are 50 MCQs which need to be done in 25 minutes so there’s only a short amount of time to do each question. This test is conducted at a PC lab so you can use soft copy notes to refer to because it’s open-book but some of the questions ask you about symbols which you cannot use ctrl-F for so you have to manually scroll through the slides and that takes a lot of time because there’s a lot of slides. That’s why despite it being open-book, it would be best to compile a help sheet to be able to do it fast. Most of the questions in the front can be answered by just referring, while those in the back are on interpreting 3rd angle projection drawings, so you will not need to think for the front part and but you will need to for the back part. This means it would be ideal to do the questions you only need to mindlessly refer to notes for in as little time as possible so that you have more time for the back questions for thinking. CAD Labs/Tutorials: This will be tagged as a lab session but the prof calls it a tutorial. Here, you will be taught how to use the Solidworks CAD software. For the seen ones, you will basically be guided step by step to build parts that can be found on the course website. You will also be taught to make an assembly from many parts in one of the tutorials. This implies you can try to do it yourself before coming to class because you can access the course website outside of class too. If you already know how to do CAD, you can probably just do it on the spot for the tutorial (or even way before) and you will definitely finish before the tutors finish teaching because they go through slowly for those who are new to CAD. At the end of the CAD 3D modelling, you will need to create a softcopy drawing of the model through Solidworks. They have a certain style on how they want the drawings to end up so even if you know how to do CAD and can finish the model quickly, you still need to wait for them to go through the drawing portion (the drawing instructions are also on the course website but the tutors sometimes give different instructions from the website IIRC). The first one is not graded but the second and third are graded. It would definitely make your life a lot easier if you learn some Solidworks (any other CAD probably works fine too; they’re all almost the same anyway) before the tutorials. CAD Test: This will be during the tutorial slot. In fact, it’s basically the tutorial but now the tutors will no longer be guiding you. This is quite easy if you know how to do CAD. Just make sure you check things properly. You will probably be tasked to do an assembly, but you will not have to model all the parts because some will already be modelled and provided to you. The assembly might be difficult because they may not explicitly state how it is assembled but just use your common sense for how the parts fit together, it’s just like a very simple jigsaw puzzle but in 3D. Do not forget parts during assembly, especially the ones you did not model which are usually things like screws or washers. Design Calculations Test: This test will probably be on week 13. It is quite straightforward because questions tend to be quite standard and you just need to go through the motions. In fact, there will be a shaft question testing on what Prof Lai has taught and the question is usually more or less the exact same question he has gone through in class (at least from what my tutor said, and my experience with the test was the same). I also remember one question was worth 10 marks but required just one equation so it took up just a few lines despite being worth 10 marks. I wouldn’t be surprised if most people did well in this test because of how straightforward it is so you should probably do your best to do as well as possible.

Taken in 2016/17 Sem1. The syllabus has changed considerably compared to past semesters, and I think it is for the better. It now focuses on simplifying scientific concepts and terms for the mass audience. Tutorials: 2 tutorials of 2 hours every week for this module. The first half is similar to the old format. The tutorial discusses on selected articles and examine how the writers (attempt to) appeal to the masses. This portion of the tutorial is relaxing as there are no assignments due in the first half of the semester. So just read the article before the tutorial every week, and there should be no problem. Readings include selected pages from Napoleon's Button, Statistic in Courtroom and many more! (It's the same as the previous syllabus). The second half kicks things up a notch. Immediately the week after the recess week, the first written assignment is due. There will be a peer review for this assignment along with a tutor consultation for this write-up. (In my semester there is a 2 week break for these consultations to take place, no promises though) The second written assignment is then due at around Week 11-12, and there will be an oral presentation in Week 12-13. More on the assignments below. Written Assignment: There are 2 written assignments for this module. It is essentially selecting a scientific paper from a professional scientific journal and write a popular science article (or Popsicle as my tutor says) based on that. Focus is on simplifying scientific concepts and capture the reader's attention through various techniques taught in the first half of the semester. There is no restrictions for the first writing. The second writing needs to be a topic that is OUT of your discipline. Chemistry cannot write chemistry articles, Physics cannot write physics articles, etc. A reflective commentary is also part of the 2 assignments, where we need to discuss about the choices that we made in the writing itself. Oral Presentation: Similar to the old syllabus. We need to prepare a solo 10 minutes presentation. However as now we have 2 write-ups, there is a luxury of choice here. We can choose between the 2 topics which we wrote in the 2 past assignments. We examine how speakers captivate the audience's attention in TED talks, and tries to apply them into our presentation. Tips: Select a paper that is newsworthy and easy to explain. The choice of paper is quite important as you will be using it not only for your assignment, but also your presentation as well. Read other popular science articles online and examine how they write. Having more references is a good thing when writing the assignment. Do not rush your assignment. Rather than spending 1 full day doing the assignment, spend 1 hour over a span of a few days. A fresh mindset can help in spotting errors. Ask friends and classmates to review your articles. For me, I kind of cheated by asking my ES1102 (now ES1103) tutor to review my writing, but you can do that too if you want. Conclusion: I found this syllabus to be much more interactive compared to the previous one. So for all the future students taking this module, we got lucky. Most importantly, this is probably one of the only few modules that you will mix with all other scientific disciplines, so just make friends, talk with your classmates more and have fun in the tutorial. Final Grade: A

Took this module in AY14/15 Semester 2 Lecturer: Nil Tutor: Ms Denise This is a seminar style module. The class size was slightly under 20. Taken in AY21/22 with Prof Paul Lim We covered the rest of Griffiths (after E&M1) other than some topics which he decided to skip (some parts in radiation, the EM field tensor F and its hodge dual *F, etc.) For me, this was one of the easiest PC modules I have taken since year 1, and certainly the one with the least workload (feels like 2MC). There's roughly an hour's worth of lectures to watch every week, and no homework or anything like that. The assessment weightage is that same as it was six years ago: two tests, 15% each and a 70% finals. The tests are very easy and generally directly borrowed from tutorials and lecture notes. I guess the point is to make sure you are keeping up with the content, rather than to challenge you. The finals is also very manageable IMO but certainly a bit more difficult than the tutorials. Taken in 18/19 Sem 1 Taughy by Prof Terrence Sim and Prof Aaron Tan Assessment Structure Final 50% Midterm 25% Two assignments (10% eacg) 20% Tutorial attendance 5% Well, personally I think that this mod is no-joke, i.e. difficult. At first, this mod focused on various type of proving techniques, then turned the focus to various mathematical fields that are related to CS like number theory and graph theory. Personally, I think this mod lays an important foundation for other cs mods like algorithm analysis, so try your best to understand what is taught to you even you can't solve the questions, don't just simply choose to s/u the mod and then neglect about the things that are taught to you. I would suggest that if you don't know how to solve a particular question when doing the tutorial, just refer to past year tutorials or google for the question to save you the time of doing the questions cuz sometimes I think that the solutions are mind-blowing XD. All the best to those who gonna take this mod! :D

Taken in AY17/18 Semester 2/Special Term (Part I) under iBLOC Taught by: Prof. Ben Leong (Lecturer), Oana (Tutor) Assessment Structure: 35% Online Assignments (Coursemology) 15% Midterm Exam 15% Practical Exam 5% Tutorial/Participation 30% Final Exam As Prof. Ben said in the module, CS1010X aims to teach students programming. This module focuses mostly on Python, but also has a small component on C. The CA component (apart from midterms and practical) is run entirely on Coursemology, where you need to complete assignments (called Missions/Trainings). Students start off as Level 1, and completing these assignments will reward them with experience points required to level up. The level of the student at the end of the course will determine their score for the Online Assignments component. As many iBLOC students were still serving NS, the first half of the course was completely online. There are no lectures, but there is an hour of recitation and an hour of tutorial on one weekday in the second half of the course. There is a big contrast in the perception of difficulty of this module. Students with prior experiences in programming will find this module a breeze, and many of such students had completed assignments weeks before deadlines. On the other hand, there are students without prior programming experiences who struggle with completing assignments on time. There is an online forum section on Coursemology, where students may discuss about problems in various assignments. Prof. Ben and the tutors are also very responsive on the forum. Midterm and Final exams are written and have a structured format. This includes reading codes and identifying outputs and writing programs. One must be familiar with how each Python functions work to answer the identifying outputs correctly. There is no bell curve in this module due to small cohort size, but one must be very careful to score a good grade. Expected Grade: A+ Obtained Grade: A, despite scoring 92% overall for the module

If you have any questions, please send it to my email atqhteo@gmail.com, or leave a comment below. Don't worry, there are no stupid questions! I've received many emails asking me all sorts of questions. I reply all of them :) Prof: Dr John Elliot What's it about? The development of an individual in the various domains such as emotions, moral reasoning, cognition, etc, from infant to adolescence. How's the workload? One mid term essay, one 'mid term' MCQ test (was in week 13), one essay finals (two sections, 6 choose 3 short answer and 3 choose 1 essay) One 2 hour lecture weekly, one 2 hour tutorial fortnightly. Textbook is a typical Psych textbook, 40-60 pages a chapter a week. Some weeks 2 chapters. How difficult is it? Do you like memorizing things? If you do this is the module for you! Enjoy memorizing everything in the textbook as well as everything he says during lectures as well as everything in the tutorial. Any miscellaneous tips? Lectures are important - he tests things that he talks about during lectures and his lectures cover his areas of focus, which he is likely to test in the finals. (you probably still have to know everything for the MCQ though) This made spotting rather easy - all his past year questions are available (just look for the distinctive style of 6C3, 3C1 format) and he doesn't really repeat questions, so based on what he covers in lectures as well as what's been asked in the previous year (s), you can spot some topics that will be tested. Tutorials are not worth any CA, but some things that you discuss during class is important. Just have a clear idea of how to argue for/against the prominent issues and be aware of the various points/studies that you can use. He does test details, such as age of learning how to walk and whatever crap, in the MCQ, so... happy memorizing. Do also know the studies that he cites in his lectures, he tested quite a few questions on those too (not in textbook). To sum up, memorize the textbook and his lectures, and when you revise for finals use his 'focus points' based on what he touches on in lectures to think more deeply about those topics so you can write stuff in the essay. Should you take it? It's a compulsory mod, so Psych majors don't really have a choice. John Elliot is like a super old fellow who has been around for ages, so if you're looking for a knowledgeable old man, he is the one. If you're looking for an entertaining lecturer... look elsewhere. I didn't like it as it was very content heavy, but then again those with good memorization ability should be able to do well. Predicted Grade: B Actual Grade: B-

Taken in AY 16/17 Sem 2 I went for this module with high expectations for it, believing that a module about critical thinking and writing would entail a myriad of topics for us to analyse and dissect. To my dismay, the scope of this module was sadly limited to the context of saving/preserving the environment. The readings that they provided got quite boring and repeated at times. Most of the time we were forced to follow a specific format of paragraph opening sentences....which kinda defeats the nature of critical thinking (which is a topic for another day). Nonetheless, it's a compulsory module for me as an engineering student. Assessment: 3 Assignments, 1 Finals and Tutorial participation. A1 is about summary and evaluation (very similar to A Level GP but you gotta follow the dept's writing guidelines), A2 is a group project (3 people) about addressing a UN development goal and coming up with a written report detailed with your background of the problem, current measures in place and how your new engineering solutions would build upon them. The group project is the most time-consuming part of this module and make sure you find good teammates to work with! Make sure to start early and delegate roles well. There is an oral defense segment included with this but it's pretty easy if everyone worked hard in the project (unless you are a slacker...then you would be clueless). A3 is an individual reflection about the module, and like all module reflections, just remember to link back to the learning objectives of this module. Finals is basically like Assignment 1 with the bonus of evaluating 2 more key arguments. Time's the factor here so write fast. Tutorial participation depends on how friendly your tutor is. Overall, this is a manageable module if you have good foundations in GP. Teammates-wise, we had a slacker but we still managed to get a A grade for project. If this module isn't compulsory, I definitely wouldn't recommend taking this module.

AY2015/2016, Y1S1 Lecturers: Dr Ong Ee Cheng (Micro), Mr Chan Kok Hoe (Macro) Weightage: 6% Pre-lecture Quizzes, 9% Post-lecture Quizzes, 10% Tutorials, 25% Mid-terms, 50% Finals Exam format: MCQ + Short-answer This module is the pre-requisite to most higher-level economics modules, and since I am intending to major in Economics I had to take it. Having done H2 Economics in JC would be of significant help, particularly for microeconomics content. However, this module introduces newer concepts for macroeconomics, so do not let your guard down even if you have done Economics in JC before. Lectures by Dr Ong were generally more interactive and engaging, and she moves along at a pretty decent pace so there shouldn't be much problem following the lecture. At the same time, going through a mental recap of H2 microeconomics content would be good as well. Tutorials for microeconomics were generally simple and manageable, as the problem sets were mostly to help us understand the content taught in lecture, with a couple of further-thinking questions and 1 real-world application question to help us understand how to explain and apply the relevant concepts to real-world case studies. Lectures by Mr Chan tend to be more difficult to follow due to 2 main reasons (in my opinion). One, macroeconomics in EC1101E brought in a lot more new concepts that H2 did not cover. Two, to cover the significant amount of new content, the lecture had to move along faster with less time for on-the-spot internalizing. So, do review the webcast and lecture slides, and seek consultation if any of the content seems foreign after the lecture. Also, make sure to watch the extra videos put up by the lecturer as they cover content that the lecturer expects you to have known, for the next lecture. Tutorials were generally in the same format as microeconomics tutorials, but try to understand the application question as they really help to put the concepts in a context for better understanding and revision. There are 2 types of graded quizzes - pre-lecture and post-lecture quizzes. Do remember to do this quizzes on IVLE when they open, even if the weightage seems low. These quizzes are easy (some of them at least) and repeatable, so complete them with a 100% score for free marks. Mid-terms and finals had manageable questions, but the crux of the examination difficulty was the time constraint. A lot of calculations have to be done even for the MCQs, all within a short time of 1 hour (mid-terms) and 2 hours (finals). Starting from either the MCQ or short-answer questions first makes little difference; managing the time spent per question is more important to completing the paper. it doesn't help that the bell curve is super steep due to the large proportion of students having H2 knowledge, so finishing the paper (even by guessing tougher MCQs) is a must. Overall, this module isn't particularly difficult, however time must be spent on internalizing the concepts introduced to be able to keep pace with the lectures.

Taken in AY18/19 Semester 1 Lecturer: Assistant Professor Zhou Chao Expected grade: B+ Actual grade: A- (Pleasant surprise) Assessment and workload: - 10% Homework (3 homeworks, best of 2, I got 10/10 for this component) - 30% In-class tests, open book (3 of them, best of 2, I got 25/30 for this component) - 60% Final examination, 1 A4 sized helpsheet. Experience: - This module is manageable, provided that you have taken MA4269 before this. This module could be renamed Mathematical Finance 3 due to its nature. This module goes deep into the stochastic calculus parts in MA4269 that were previously skipped or discussed very briefly. The structure of the course is also similar, starting with a detailed review about probability concepts, followed by an in-depth discussion about Brownian motion. Lecture 3 onwards is where it gets more theoretical. The quadratic variation of brownian motion would be derived in a rigorous way, which is different from 4269. Stochastic integrals would then be elaborated on, along with its properties. Ito's lemma would be used again, and in this module, if in doubt, apply Ito's lemma. Stochastic differential equations would be introduced, followed by the Black Scholes PDE. Next, Girsanov's theorem would be elaborated on, followed by change of numeraire. The concepts are the same as 4269 but the notation is quite different. The module ends with barrier options and pricing of exchange options, greeks. - Prof Zhou has been teaching this module for 4 to 5 times in a row now. He is very experienced in teaching this module and even tries to inject humour into the lecture. Prof Zhou explains concepts in a clear manner and tries his best to use analogies from simpler mathematical concepts to explain the more advanced concepts in this module. The lecture notes are also quite comprehensive and I recommend reading them before attending the lecture because some parts can get a little confusing. - There are no tutorials for postgraduate modules but Prof Zhou provides some small exercises in each set of lecture notes to practice on applying the concepts. He also assigns homework which allows us to practice the concepts learnt. - The in-class tests are about 20 minutes each and Prof Zhou sets relatively doable questions for them. The in-class test is also done in quite a relaxed setting and some people even discuss secretly. Therefore, befriend some people and sit next to them haha. - Final exam was surprisingly manageable, considering the fact that Prof Zhou set a really difficult MA4269 finals last academic year. Prof Zhou had given us a list of sample questions that he claimed to be similar to the final exam questions and he kept his word. The final exam questions were similar in content, but longer in length and more tedious, to ensure students spend 2.5h in the examination venue. Applying Ito's lemma alone nets you about 25 marks, so writing Ito's lemma for single variable and multivariable cases in the helpsheet is essential. Prof Zhou also collected the final exam question paper back so there's a chance that he reuses the same question template, but with different values and functions. Conclusion: - Although I don't really like Mathematical finance, this module is quite manageable and I recommend people to take this module to have a taste of what basic stochastic calculus is like. The workload is also not heavy, which is a bonus. It is a good module to take to fully grasp the concepts introduced in MA4269.

, taken under Prof Chow Jun Yan: This is a module where you get to design cool sound effects in a virtual environment known as Max MSP by Cycling '74. You also learn to pick up how to use different type of sound effects using a very easy to learn environment which comes from Syntorial. (It is a paid software with a trial version but you'll be provided a full license for free in this module!) Practically, it is your first step if you want to be an SFX designer, or perhaps even a Sound Designer. This module is open to ALL NUS students, regardless of whether you are a YST student. As a person who enjoys sounds and music as an interest / hobby, and not looking to learn it professionally to do it as a career, I highly recommend this module to anyone who shares the same traits as me. I took this module as a UEM, as a lost NUS student who has no idea what cool UEMs are out there. Throughout the course of this module, you will be learning about different sound effects. These effects include amplitude envelope, filter envelope, resonance, distortions, ring modulation, reverb, chorus, effect wheels (on a keyboard), low frequency oscillators (LFOs), frequency modulation (FM), etc. Now that's a lot! The first part of the semester is just about using the learning software Syntorial to learn about some effects, and every week you will be expected to complete the assignments inside Syntorial itself. Eventually, you'll finish all of them, so if you want, you can finish ahead of time (in view of the later part of the semester, you'll have a lot more assignments to finish from other modules). Unfortunately, if you are like me, you will have a lot of trouble distinguishing between minor differences in sound from a small parameter change, especially in some of the harder integration exercises. There are 2 ways you can go about this: First, start early and do only 1 or 2 chapters a day, and reserve one day for the integration exercises, less you get a headache and start having your ears ringing. Or, if you are lazy like me and a bit fed up with the minor differences that always cause your score to drop below perfect, there is sort of a hack which will guarantee full marks without the need to hear anything at all. It is a Syntorial software setting that allows you to retry the same patch even as you get the patch wrong. This allows you to screenshot the patch settings and duplicate it in the next attempt, resulting in full marks every time. Even though I was lazy to keep retrying and getting the perfect score, the lessons interested me a lot and i continued to listen to the lessons. Occasionally, where i have the time, I tried out some of the exercises but without the pressure to score well, i simply just enjoyed the sounds and just tried my best to match it. The second part of the semester was where it gets more exciting and you actually get to design sounds using provided Max MSP patches (which the prof has already prepared for you), playing around with the parameters yourself and just experimenting what tweaking each of the settings will give you. The prof is very relaxed about the rules, and so long you document the experimentation process and you state your sound preferences, Prof Chow will give you great marks for all your effort. Every week after the Recess Week would see you designing 5 sounds from different types of settings to play with, finally culminating in a final project where you have to design 15 sounds with all the settings from previous weekly assignments available to you. It was a lot of fun experimenting different degrees of sound effects for me. Every week's lessons are an extension of what you learned in Syntorial. Some lessons also include fun things to do, such as designing a patch from scratch in Max MSP to create a patch where you can tweak around with various types of settings you learned in Syntorial (not all can duplicated, sadly, with the limited time in the lessons). Prof Chow is a great prof who is passionate and will go the extra mile to help us out in learning new stuff, as well as trying his utmost best in preparing lessons and making them great to attend. He isn't always able to do everything he wishes or what everyone wants, but his passion to teach us is what captivates my attention to this module and sound design in general. I had a lot of fun learning and applying what I learned in this module, especially when everything is so loosely defined and so long you put in the effort to show it, you will definitely get the marks. I had utmost confidence in getting an A for the module, which i ultimately did. This is not only a fun module, but an easy one to get an A. You will definitely need to invest some time into this module, especially when designing the sounds for the assignments in the later part of the semester. Expected / Actual Grade: A / A

Took this module in AY2017/18 Sem 2 under Prof Michael Yoshitaka Erlewine. Overall this is an interesting and manageable module. The contents of the lectures are well-organised, with a coherent flow to it. Each lecture slowly builds up on what is covered in the previous lecture. Even though some of the readings provided can be very technical, they are intended to provide alternative ways to think about various problems and the explanations given by Prof Erlewine will eventually help in understanding the content. The examples provided during the lecture illustrate how linguists construct and refine their hypotheses with increasing data, which I feel is the main takeaway from this module. Handouts are provided for each lecture and they contain the most important points, which are really what is needed for the mid-terms and finals. As long as you understand the material in the handouts, the exams should be manageable. Basic set theory will be used for the semantics part of the module, which should not be a problem for those who have at least taken O level Maths or equivalent. The workload for this module is light for a 4 MC module as well, with short problem sets (at most 3 problems) for weekly tutorials, an essay around the middle of the semester and a mini project at the end of the semester. The essay requires reading a scientific paper, out of a few possible choices, in the linguistics field and communicating the main findings in a laymen manner. On the other hand, the project explores some fun and relevant topics, such as the Singlish "what" and formulaic language e.g. coffee shop orders like Teh O, by applying concepts that have been covered earlier in the module. While this module mainly focuses on the logic of the English language, Prof Erlewine also provides examples for other languages such as Chinese or Japanese, since certain things like conversational implicatures depend on what is available in that language. This module is highly recommended for those who are interested in the inner workings of language and serves as a starting point perhaps for understanding how languages have evolved, how language is being processed by the brain etc.

AY2015/2016 Semester 1 Review This new module is being taught by 3 different people, Dr Ji Hui, Dr Zhao Gongyun, Dr Zhang Louxin. Concepts Taught: Dr Ji Hui: Discrete Fourier Transform, Convolution, Basic Signal Processing Techniques, Conjugate Gradient Method Dr Zhao Gongyun: Modelling for Optimization, Proximal Gradient Algorithm, LP Relaxation Dr Zhang Louxin: Machine Learning, Principal Component Analysis, Data Visualization Lectures Dr Ji Hui: He does not have any notes of any kind, and you are required to be diligent in writing down your own notes from the whiteboard. He is a fairly decent teacher, not the best, not the worst either. Dr Zhao Gongyun: Dr Zhao always gives excellent notes, regardless of the module he is teaching. One fine example is Game Theory. However, his teaching fails to convey the message at times. Feels like he is beating around the bush too often and not getting to the point. Dr Zhang Louxin: His notes are decent, but his lectures are a snoozefest due to the way he speaks. Not a great teacher, but thankfully, the concepts he teaches are fairly easy. In general, this was quite a poorly taught module, so you will need to be independent. Tutorials (5% Participation) 9 tutorials, roughly 4-5 questions per tutorial. Questions range from simple to difficult. As with every module, please practice your tutorials well for your exams. Assignment (45%, 15% per lecturer) 3 Assignments, set by each of the lecturers on the topics they have taught. Dr Ji Hui's was the hardest, you had to use MATLAB to restore a signal using DFT. Dr Zhao Gongyun's was fairly easy, 1 question on modelling and solving with Gurobi in MATLAB, and another question on proximal gradient method. Dr Zhang Louxin did not set a programming assignment, but instead, a very tedious set of 5 questions from machine learning, which was annoying and had no learning value. Exams (50%. Open Book) Be prepared for a difficult exam. Each lecturer sets 2 questions each, so 6 questions in all. Dr Ji Hui tend to set the same questions as he does in MA4268 Visual Data Processing, so get the finals paper from V.D.P and try some of them. Dr Zhao Gongyun set a very difficult modelling problem (I swear, it was nothing I have seen before), and 1 question on proximal gradient algorithm. Dr Zhang Louxin set an essay question on the benefits of machine learning (LOL wut) and also another question on clustering (which takes you 30 minutes to do, because of all the manual work involved). My grade is A+. I recommend you have a friend at least, that is good in programming, so you can check your assignment answers with him (or copy from him, whatever). 50% of the grades in this course is almost free if you do your due diligence. As for the finals, practice your tutorials well, since its a new module, there is little to no past year references.
