Taken in AY21/22 SEM 1 Taught by: Sun Rongfeng (The God of Probability!) Module Description: This module is divided into 2 parts: Review of Probability & Countable State Space Markov Chain. The first part can be regarded as a new course if you did not take MA2216/ST2131 under Prof Sun. It must be the most rigorous undergraduate probability course in Singapore (maybe even in Asia? who knows :>). Highly recommend taking this module under Sun Rongfeng! Topics in the first part: Probability Measure, Random Variable, Expectation, Variance, Correlation, Law of Large Numbers, Central Limit Theorem, Poisson Limit Theorem, Generating Functions, Laplace Transformation, Branching Processes, Conditional Independence and Conditional Expectation. Topics in the second part: Irreducibility, Transience, Recurrence, Stationary Distribution, Stationary Measures, Period of Markov Chains, Long Time Behavior of Markov Chains, Renewal Processes, Reversibility and Loop Condition, Hitting Problems. Difficulty: 10/10 Toughest module I’ve taken in NUS. I took Prof Sun’s course on purpose because I was very confident in my Probability foundation. Unfortunately, this was an illusion. Your A+ from ST2131 is just an admission ticket for the game of Prof Sun’s Stochastic Processes especially when your ST2131 was taught by the Department of Statistics in SEM 2. Prof Sun is trying to push the level of abstraction to the limit of undergraduate students. Everything here is very precise, rigorous and abstract, which I really enjoy. Such depth of Probability and Stochastic Processes can only be achieved by Prof Sun in NUS. Professor: Genius! The God of Probability! He must be one of the top experts in Probability at least in Asia, even worldwide. It is my great honor to study Stochastic Processes under him. From his lectures, I can feel he is so familiar with those tough stuff and his logical reasoning is very sharp and each sentence is densely packed with information. He is indeed a man who can make a living through Probability. The proofs involve a lot of shortcuts/tricks, especially the use of indicator random variables. You can fully experience the power of indicator functions and conditional expectation in this course. Since Prof Sun is so familiar with these stuff, sometimes it may be too fast for many students. I cannot follow him very well if I did not go through the materials beforehand, so from the second half of this module, I gave up watching the live lectures. Taken in AY 21/22 Sem 1 Lecturer: Sufatrio Component breakdown: 2 CTF-style assignments (10% + 15%) Midterms (15%) LumiNUS revision quiz (5%) Group presentation (5%) Tutorial attendance (5%) Finals (45%) TL;DR: + Has cool and fun CTFs - Module scope leaves much to be desired - Lecturer is not good (I rolled a not so good tutor, which made the experience even worse) As someone who loves information security, I went into this module with great excitement. I was NOT prepared to be let down this hard. Module scope: Iffy. About half of the topics covered felt very touch-and-go; they were briefly glossed over and then rarely, if ever, cropped up again. Many sub-chapters are treated merely as "vocabulary" and their sole purpose in the module is to serve as possible answers for the fill-in-the-blank/MCQ section in the midterms and finals; nothing more than a cursory understanding is required. Lectures & lecturer: Lectures were conducted live over Zoom and recorded. Dr Sufatrio proceeds at a glacial pace, reading off the slides for the most part and circling random words while he speaks. His voiceover adds negligible value to the slides themselves and you're better off reading them on your own. He also has a tendency to waste time; around 10 minutes at the start of each lecture for "announcements". I couldn't attend the lectures live as I was typically travelling to NUS for another in-person tutorial during that timeslot, but I stopped bothering to watch the recorded videos a few weeks in because they're that slow even at 2x speed. Dr Sufatrio takes weeks to respond to email queries, and his responses are typically not helpful. I'm not even sure if he fully understood the questions being asked before replying with unrelated stock responses such as "this is how we defined it in the notes". Tutorials: My experience with tutorials was not great because I got a questionable tutor (who I will not name). On at least one occasion, he stated that he "didn't remember ever seeing" something despite literally having just gone through a question about it in the previous tutorial session. He also has a tendency to give wrong answers or explanations to questions posed by students, and usually doesn't bother correcting himself afterwards. This was not very beneficial to the understanding of many students in my tutorial group. To his credit, though, he provided us with a definition list/cheatsheet, which was quite helpful as quick reference during the finals. The tutorial questions themselves are generally okay, though some of them have a tendency to be somewhat tedious (e.g. given the following list of requirements, list all the firewall rules you would implement). Group presentation: This component felt like an afterthought. You pick a topic from a list and do a short presentation on it during the tutorial timeslot. This is something you can get done in a single night, but the grading is completely opaque and it's up to your tutor's discretion whether you get a 4/5 or a 5/5. Assignments: The highlight of this module. Assignments are CTF-style and the challenges are set by the NUS Greyhats. It's very hands-on, so you will probably learn more from trying these challenges than from the rest of the module put together. They are pretty time-consuming though, and can be pretty difficult if you don't already have some background and need to pick everything up from scratch. I found this pretty enjoyable, and I think it was the one redeeming part of this module. LumiNUS quiz: This is just a MCQ quiz you can do at your own time. It's meant to serve as revision before the final exam. There's no time limit so make sure you get full marks for this. Midterms/finals: Midterms and finals were conducted over Examplify with Zoom proctoring. Format was open book but no internet. Dr Sufatrio reuses questions a lot and the format of his papers is always the same. The first half of his paper (fill-in-the-blanks + MCQ) often has questions which are ripped word-for-word from previous years' papers. Even the open-ended questions are incredibly formulaic; all 3 final papers I did that were set by him (2 PYPs and the actual finals for this sem) had secure programming questions with similar code and identical vulnerabilities. The papers' difficulties are generally not high. It's entirely possible to get 100% if you understand what's going on in the module and don't make careless mistakes. The question wording can be pretty bad, though, and sometimes it's not really clear what the question wants from you. All you really need to do to prepare for his midterms/finals are to do any past papers set by him. Lecture content barely gets tested, and if they do, it's stuff that you can just look up in the notes anyway. Conclusion: If you're looking for a neat introduction to information security, this module (at least under Dr Sufatrio) isn't it; it barely covers anything interesting. If you must take this module, consider taking it under a different lecturer instead. If you just want to learn more about information security or play CTFs, you'll probably get a lot further by getting to know a few Greyhats members.

. Tutored by Ms Diana Chung; module coordinated by Ms Anita Toh. This module is taken by computer science students together with CS2103T to fulfil SoC requirements. It is coordinated and run by staff from the Centre for English Language Communication (CELC). The first half of the semester teaches general communication and workplace interaction skills, while the second half of the semester is heavily linked to the software engineering project from CS2103T (such as writing user/developer guides and making presentations for the CS2103T project). The module is conducted in a similar style to ES2660 - contact time is via sectional groups of 20 students each, and class participation is expected. The 20 students in each sectional group will be in the same CS2103T tutorial. There are no midterms or finals, and the S/U option can be exercised on this module. Students need to form two sets of groups in this module: in the first half of the semester (for work and assessment not directly related to CS2103T), and in the second half of the semester (this will be the grouping for the CS2103T software engineering project). When I took the module, each group was required to contain at least one male, one female, one Singaporean, and one non-Singaporean student, and no more than two people in the same group for the first half of the semester were allowed to share a group for the second half. Generally, students optimise for their CS2103T group (i.e. the second half of the semester) as it would have an impact on their CS2103T grade. At the end of the semester, students are required to produce a project portfolio page (PPP) that summarises their contributions to the CS2103T project. This PPP is an extract of relevant sections from the user and developer guides of the CS2103T project, and is graded by both CS2103T and CS2101, but to different requirements. As the length of the PPP is limited to ten pages, there is some contention as to which module's requirements the limited PPP real estate should be allocated to. Since the S/U option can be used for CS2101 but not CS2103T, the choice is clear for many. There are at least three in-class presentations (on content of a non-technical nature) for this module, and some amount of preparation work is required for each of them.

Module taken: 2016/2017 Year 4 Sem 1 Lecturers: Dr Saroja Dorairajoo, Dr Lou A. Antolihao Tutor: Mr Muhammad Kamal Jauhari Bin Zaini (J for short) WEGHTAGE --> Tutorial Attendance & Participation (15%) --> Written Assignment (15%) – Deadline end of Week 5 --> Mid-term Test (20%) – Week 9 --> Final Exam (50%) FINAL EXAM FORMAT --> MCQs (Multiple Choice Questions) and an Essay Question --> Closed book, covers all topics WORKLOAD There are readings assigned for each week, uploaded onto IVLE. Not too heavy in my opinion, usually only 1-2. I strongly suggest reading them before coming to lecture as they help consolidate the concepts and help you understand better what is being mentioned because the lectures seldom venture deeply into the topics. Lectures are conducted in alternate turns between the two professors. One week Dr Saroja would conduct the lecture, the next week Dr Lou, and so on. Tutorials are biweekly, so you can pick to come either on odd or even weeks. For the first tutorial, everyone was divided into 5 groups, and each group was assigned a question to discuss. Say you get assigned question 2 – for the rest of the semester, that will be the question number you will be tackling for each tutorial. You conduct your own discussions with your own group members, and the tutor joins in a group at a time, and then you share your findings on the whiteboard for the entire class. The written assignment is entitled ‘Weirding the Normal’, due on end of Week 5. You had to upload a soft copy up onto IVLE for plagiarism check, and also a hard copy to be submitted to the tutor’s mailbox. This assignment is based on reading an article about following norms, and writing about a selected activity you often participate in (must involve at least 2 people) in a similar format to the article and using the concepts it covers. COMMENTS I took this module sort of last minute for two reasons – it was cheap (only 1 bid point) and the module name piqued my interest. I initially planned to take another UE module to clear my requirements (cannot remember what it was already now) but the bidding was too competitive, and this seemed a good alternative from what the information I could glean from the Internet. Because it’s a level 1 module, I would say the workload is quite manageable and interesting, to say the least. According to Dr Saroja, this semester was the lowest enrollment they have ever had for the course – about 470 students compared to the usual 700-800 they get every semester. What I would critique is the lecture pace – I noticed that the lecturers often take too much time elaborating on each and every bullet point in the lecture slides. What results is that they often run over the time and students leave for their next class, and/or they rush the remaining slides and you end up having to read the remaining slides yourself anyway. My tutor was really interesting – teaching assistants of a minority ethnicity are under-represented so I was glad to meet someone like him. He made a really great impression in the first tutorial. When everyone was already mostly present, he entered the tutorial room and sat down at the very back, pretending to be a student himself. No one suspected a thing (but I already recognized him HAHA). Then he started counting the number of attendees and started asking for our names one by one, beginning with those nearest to him. Everyone looked back one by one with a bewildered face wondering what’s going on till it dawned on them. Tutorials themselves are pretty laid back, from the 3rd onwards, you just need to prepare your own assigned question and present them to the whole class. For the rest of the questions, you just need to listen to other groups present and take notes (if you wish), then it ends with the tutor providing his own comments and closing remarks. So preparation is minimal, but best not to go in empty handed because your group mates will expecting at least some contribution from everyone. For the mid-term test, there are five short answer questions given, but you only need to answer FOUR OUT OF FIVE within an hour. For each question, only ten lines are provided, and you are not allowed to write more than the space provided (it won’t be counted towards your answer). So stick to the point, answer the question as concisely as possible. If you accidentally answer all five questions, only the first four will be marked, so make your choices wisely! EXPECTED GRADE: B+ ACTUAL GRADE: A If you have any questions or want to know more about the resources, you can contact me at ishallsucc33d@yahoo.com. All the best!

Sem 1 AY21/22 Lecturer: Chin Wei Ngan Tutorial TA: Ernest I will start with the TL;DR: don't take this module. If you're planning on going down the Programming Language focus area (for CS kids) (ie. this becomes a requirement), don't do it either. It's not worth it -- go spec in something else. The selection of PL mods in NUS is trash anyway. The bunch of reviews from this sem (Sem1, AY21/22) that basically diss this mod are entirely justified. It isn't because of the final paper either (it hasn't happened yet, as I write this). Heed our advice. Don't do it. If you remember my IS1103 review, I mentioned that it was perhaps one of the worst mods I've had the privilege of paying school fees for. CS2104 is a close second. At least it's not a graduation requirement. Seriously; if you need 4MCs, go take CFG, or some UEs -- anything else. Really. This module purports to teach "Programming Language Concepts", but none of those concepts were even taught to any degree worthy of a university education. CS2104 "covers" 4 languages: Haskell, OCaml, Prolog, and Scala. The first half (up to recess week, possibly till week 7) focuses on trying to teach students Haskell. Topics covered include the basic functional programming stuff (higher order functions [which should be OK if you took 1101S under Henz], list comprehensions, other Haskell features like pattern matching and ADTs), and of course Monads (and monadic parsers via Parsec). It doesn't do a good job, mind you, but the slides are there. The next language is Prolog. If you haven't used Prolog before, it's a language with quite a unique paradigm... and it definitely can't be covered in 1 set of slides over 1 or 2 weeks. (by the way, a large part of the slide deck just focuses on those dumb "logic puzzles" like SEND + MORE = MONEY...). The core tenets of Prolog programming (eg. the tree structure of terms, SLD resolution, etc.) are only briefly mentioned and not really elaborated in detail. It is not really feasible to expect students to gain a good understanding of these concepts when explained so poorly in such a short amount of time. OCaml and Scala are given much the same treatment; just an afterthought in this module. Based on past year papers, students are somehow expected to have a good grasp on these languages in order to answer questions. This year, it was said that students "there is no need to memorise language syntax". We shall see about that (will update this review if I remember). By the way, if you're reading the description on nusmods (above) and wondering whether this module covers "various implementation issues, such as pseudo-code interpretation, static and dynamic semantics...", the answer is NO. Assessments Speaking of assessments, there are some graded lab assignments as well as some "participation mark" tutorial questions that you have to submit. They're mostly run-of-the-mill CS labs/assignments, nothing too special or tragic on that front. For tutorials, somehow participation is graded. The TA for my tutorial was a PhD student who, on the first lesson, openly stated that he had no idea what was going on, and that we should "all learn together" (paraphrasing). Doesn't inspire much confidence, does it? The level of nonexistent confidence only continued to drop after each tutorial was basically him reading off the answers for each tutorial question, with the occasional confusion as he doesn't know what the answers were talking about. Furthermore, students are expected to form groups of 2-3 to make 2 presentations about various proglang topics over the semester. These are graded, and form part of the 10% "tutorial participation" marks. You can either choose from one of the topics suggested by the prof, or suggest one subject to approval. There is 1 midterm and 1 final exam; both are open-book. The midterm is mostly MCQ -- this round it was ~20 MCQs and 2 open-ended questions in 30 minutes. What do the questions ask? Basically, you need to be GHCI. If you cannot compile and interpret Haskell code in your head, good luck to you. Each question basically presents you with a messily-written Haskell function with nondescriptive argument names, and asks you what it does (or how to use it). I suspect the final exam (at least the MCQ portion) will be more of the same recipe. Conclusions There's really only one thing to conclude, and I already stated that at the top; don't take this module. Really, don't. The lack of prerequisites might seem tempting, but don't. Even if you love Haskell or Prolog or FP, don't do it. If you are thinking of going down the Prog Lang focus area, don't. Choose something else. In most of my other reviews (except IS1103 -- lu weiquan really deserves nothing but a dismissal from NUS) I generally attack only the course content, and not the professor. Unfortunately I can't do that here. I don't think Prof Chin is a Bad Person (tm), but being a good person doesn't make you a good lecturer. Lectures were conducted over Zoom (attendance was "mandatory" for participation marks); tutorials were either in-person or over Zoom (depends on the slot you choose). Lectures are quite dry, and often have no sense of flow; they are conducted in a very "rambly" style. Some particular concepts will be gone over very quickly, while some other concepts will somehow get a 20 minute explanation (which is actually just 2 10-minute ones repeated). Most of the time, he is just reading off the slides. Slides which, I might add, often have typos. Sometimes students point it out and he corrects them, but when he closes the slide deck, he clicks "discard changes", so next year students get the same typos again. Fun. Prof is responsive to audience questions which is good I guess. In case there was any confusion, let me state this again: DO NOT, UNDER ANY CIRCUMSTANCES, TAKE CS2104.

Taken in 19/20 SEM 1 under A/P Ho Ghim Wei, A/P Jeroen Anton van Kan Grading: This module is split into 2 parts. First part: 1 x 10% midterm test, 1 x 20% project (presentation and report) Second part: 1 x 15% midterm test, 2 x 7.5% projects 40% Finals PC3242 is a renaming of ESP3102 (From Making Nano to Probing Nano), a compulsory technical core module for ESP students intending to do the nanoscience and nanotechnology specialisation. Due to the small class size, it was renamed a PC module for Physics majors to take as well. However, the content was not changed at all. Physics majors taking this module will find it different (refreshing I would say?) from traditional physics courses because of the lack of emphasis on mathematics and proofs. Rather, I would almost classify it as a GE module on steroids due to the sheer amount of information. A/P Ho taught the first half of the module, which focused mainly on a bottom-up approach of nanosynthesis. DLVO theory alongside colloid stabilising mechanisms (steric and electrostatic) were first introduced. Next, vapour and liquid phase methods of synthesis like PVD, CVD, MBE, liquid colloidal synthesis, sol-gel synthesis, VLS and VS mechanisms are introduced along with their pros and cons. Do pay attention to which structures can be synthesised most easily with which methods, as a single nanostructure can have many ways of synthesis (theoretically) but not all can be done practically. The last 2 chapters discussed SEM and TEM characterisation, as well as cantilever-based AFM imaging. There was a 10% test which was 30 minutes long. One question was explaining the different models for an electric double layer and the other was explaining possible synthesis methods for 2 different structures. Note that a combination of methods can be used so do gain a good understanding of the process flow of each method. On alternate weeks, there will be a 1 hour lab session for us to synthesise some nanoparticles. This is for the 20% pairwork project, where we had to characterise the nanoparticles using SEM and XRD as well as identify the synthesis method used. The second half taught by A/P van Kan focused on a top-down approach of nanosynthesis, with a large part emphasising on different beams (photons, electrons, ions) and their interactions with different types of photoresists. Rutherford backscattering is introduced as well as its spectra. Finally, fringe topics such as 3d printing, nanoimprinting (hot embossing, step and flash lithography) and etching conclude the course. Tutorials were basically simulation labs which were done in the class itself (no traditional pen and paper questions basically) and had to be used for the simulation assignments There was a 15% test which was 50 minutes long. The questions involved drawing the resist profile after exposure under a mask with a certain dose, fabricating a certain structure, some factual questions regarding ion beams and describing different lithography methods to fabricate greyscale microlenses. A good understanding of the advantages and disadvantages of each lithography technique was needed to identify what could or could not be done in practice. The other two simulation assignments were 7.5% each and took up a huge amount of time. The first assignment involved fabricating structures and characterising them using electron and proton beams. SRIM and CASINO were the software used for this. The second assignment involved fitting an RBS spectrum and hence deducing the thickness, stoichiometry and other parameters. Be prepared to spend a huge amount of time if you want to get a near perfect fit for the spectrum because of the sheer number of variables to be tuned. For me I did not bother much about the fit because I didn't have the time. The 40% finals took most of us by shock, mainly because of the extremely “trivia” based questions in the second half such as which plane in silicon etches fastest and to draw an RBS detector system. This was radically different from past year papers which had more “unseen” questions like identifying the RBS spectrum when the ion beam was not aligned to the substrate at normal incidence. A different kind of difficulty emphasising more on the details I would say. The questions from the first half were still alright and similar to those in past year papers.

under Prof. Denny Leung I really loved this module, even though a few of my classmates didn't enjoy it as much. It really builds things from ground up and everything is proved rigorously. Stuff like the Intermediate Value Theorem and Extreme Value Theorem are finally proven as well. The beginning I admit is quite slow, especially on series and sequences, but it's also pretty important becuase it is used pretty much everywhere. Things get fun when we go on to metric space topology and learn cool ways to work with compactness, total boundedness, completeness, connectedness etc. . I love that it's not too hard to visualise things in this module compared to more abstract modules as well. We then go on to learn about sequences and series of functions, analytic functions and the metric space C[M1, M2]. Normally I believe the text used for this mod is Walter Rudin's Principles of Mathematical Analysis, but Prof Denny decided to use Method's of Real Analysis by Richard Goldberg which I find is a much better introductory text that goes into greater details. There is also alot of cool tidbits in this book, as well as outside, that the prof liked to give us, for instance discussions about path-connectedness. One very cool bit I liked was the discussion of discontinous functions on R. It turns out that you can't have a fuction from R to R which is only discontinous on the irrational numbers, and the proof of it is pretty elegant too. So far I've only taken two SPM mods, this and MA2101S, and I found this significantly easier. I think it's a good mod to start off SPM with and is all round pretty fun.

under Prof Sun Rongfeng. This module starts off by introducing metric spaces, and then covers concepts such as limit points, compactness, connectedness, and convergence. These concepts are taught using general metric spaces (not specifically real or complex numbers), and hence overlap somewhat with the content of MA3209 Mathematical Analysis III. A good intuition and an ability to make sense of abstract concepts will be useful in this part of the module. The second part of this module covers subsequential limits and various tests for convergence (of real and complex numbers). This part is somewhat content-heavy due to the number of convergence tests; as it is rather time-consuming to derive these results and it is difficult to intuitively grasp some of the convergence tests, these tests are best memorised. Finally, the module covers the continuity of functions, as well as how it relates to compactness and connectedness. As expected from an S-module, this module is heavily proof-based, and covers more topics than the normal version. However, it should not feel rushed as long as one can maintain an intuition of the topics covered throughout the semester. This module has midterms (35%) and finals (50%), both of which are closed-book (without help sheet). The remaining portion of the grade comes from weekly homework questions. Prof Sun is able to give students a good intuition of the abstract concepts involved in this module, which is rather useful for appreciating these abstract concepts. Most concepts were illustrated clearly in his lectures. He also clarifies students' doubts after every lecture, which helps ensure that students do not fall behind in understanding the key concepts. There are no lecture notes and no webcasts - Prof Sun solely uses the whiteboard for teaching. As such, it is important to attend lectures and take down notes during the lectures. The main reference book is Principles of Mathematical Analysis by Walter Rudin, and it is followed closely throughout the module, allowing students to do revision by using the relevant chapters of this book. Tutorials generally consist of 4-6 questions of varying difficulty, and students are expected to have completed all the tutorial questions before the session. Students are usually chosen during the tutorial session to present their solutions to the class. Personal note: I took this module after being persuaded by a friend (who has also written a review of this module), and I've no regrets taking it!

Sem 1 AY21/22 Lecturer: Chin Wei Ngan Tutorial TA: Ernest I will start with the TL;DR: don't take this module. If you're planning on going down the Programming Language focus area (for CS kids) (ie. this becomes a requirement), don't do it either. It's not worth it -- go spec in something else. The selection of PL mods in NUS is trash anyway. The bunch of reviews from this sem (Sem1, AY21/22) that basically diss this mod are entirely justified. It isn't because of the final paper either (it hasn't happened yet, as I write this). Heed our advice. Don't do it. If you remember my IS1103 review, I mentioned that it was perhaps one of the worst mods I've had the privilege of paying school fees for. CS2104 is a close second. At least it's not a graduation requirement. Seriously; if you need 4MCs, go take CFG, or some UEs -- anything else. Really. This module purports to teach "Programming Language Concepts", but none of those concepts were even taught to any degree worthy of a university education. CS2104 "covers" 4 languages: Haskell, OCaml, Prolog, and Scala. The first half (up to recess week, possibly till week 7) focuses on trying to teach students Haskell. Topics covered include the basic functional programming stuff (higher order functions [which should be OK if you took 1101S under Henz], list comprehensions, other Haskell features like pattern matching and ADTs), and of course Monads (and monadic parsers via Parsec). It doesn't do a good job, mind you, but the slides are there. The next language is Prolog. If you haven't used Prolog before, it's a language with quite a unique paradigm... and it definitely can't be covered in 1 set of slides over 1 or 2 weeks. (by the way, a large part of the slide deck just focuses on those dumb "logic puzzles" like SEND + MORE = MONEY...). The core tenets of Prolog programming (eg. the tree structure of terms, SLD resolution, etc.) are only briefly mentioned and not really elaborated in detail. It is not really feasible to expect students to gain a good understanding of these concepts when explained so poorly in such a short amount of time. OCaml and Scala are given much the same treatment; just an afterthought in this module. Based on past year papers, students are somehow expected to have a good grasp on these languages in order to answer questions. This year, it was said that students "there is no need to memorise language syntax". We shall see about that (will update this review if I remember). By the way, if you're reading the description on nusmods (above) and wondering whether this module covers "various implementation issues, such as pseudo-code interpretation, static and dynamic semantics...", the answer is NO. Assessments Speaking of assessments, there are some graded lab assignments as well as some "participation mark" tutorial questions that you have to submit. They're mostly run-of-the-mill CS labs/assignments, nothing too special or tragic on that front. For tutorials, somehow participation is graded. The TA for my tutorial was a PhD student who, on the first lesson, openly stated that he had no idea what was going on, and that we should "all learn together" (paraphrasing). Doesn't inspire much confidence, does it? The level of nonexistent confidence only continued to drop after each tutorial was basically him reading off the answers for each tutorial question, with the occasional confusion as he doesn't know what the answers were talking about. Furthermore, students are expected to form groups of 2-3 to make 2 presentations about various proglang topics over the semester. These are graded, and form part of the 10% "tutorial participation" marks. You can either choose from one of the topics suggested by the prof, or suggest one subject to approval. There is 1 midterm and 1 final exam; both are open-book. The midterm is mostly MCQ -- this round it was ~20 MCQs and 2 open-ended questions in 30 minutes. What do the questions ask? Basically, you need to be GHCI. If you cannot compile and interpret Haskell code in your head, good luck to you. Each question basically presents you with a messily-written Haskell function with nondescriptive argument names, and asks you what it does (or how to use it). I suspect the final exam (at least the MCQ portion) will be more of the same recipe. Conclusions There's really only one thing to conclude, and I already stated that at the top; don't take this module. Really, don't. The lack of prerequisites might seem tempting, but don't. Even if you love Haskell or Prolog or FP, don't do it. If you are thinking of going down the Prog Lang focus area, don't. Choose something else. In most of my other reviews (except IS1103 -- lu weiquan really deserves nothing but a dismissal from NUS) I generally attack only the course content, and not the professor. Unfortunately I can't do that here. I don't think Prof Chin is a Bad Person (tm), but being a good person doesn't make you a good lecturer. Lectures were conducted over Zoom (attendance was "mandatory" for participation marks); tutorials were either in-person or over Zoom (depends on the slot you choose). Lectures are quite dry, and often have no sense of flow; they are conducted in a very "rambly" style. Some particular concepts will be gone over very quickly, while some other concepts will somehow get a 20 minute explanation (which is actually just 2 10-minute ones repeated). Most of the time, he is just reading off the slides. Slides which, I might add, often have typos. Sometimes students point it out and he corrects them, but when he closes the slide deck, he clicks "discard changes", so next year students get the same typos again. Fun. Prof is responsive to audience questions which is good I guess. In case there was any confusion, let me state this again: DO NOT, UNDER ANY CIRCUMSTANCES, TAKE CS2104.

Taken in AY19/20 Semester 1 Taught by: Assoc. Prof. Han Fei (Lecturer and Tutor) Assessment Structure: Tutorial Participation: 10% Homework: 20% Midterm Exam: 20% Final Exam: 50% This is one of the five S modules, and the earliest possible semester to take this module is Y2S1 (as is the case with MA2202S). The module’s topics include differentiation, integration, sequence of functions and power series. This corresponds to chapter 5, 6, 7 and first section of chapter 8 of Principle of Mathematical Analysis, Walter Rudin. Similar to other S modules, class size is relatively small so there is no webcast. Lecture attendance is not compulsory but tutorial attendance is. Tutorial sessions include students presenting their solutions on the whiteboard, which usually make it a rather fun experience. Tutorial questions are generally difficult, and are meant to push the students’ abilities. Many students spend a lot of time on tutorial questions but end up not finishing them. Prof. Han explicitly mentioned that if a student presents their solution, he can use this as a reason to push a student’s grade to an A should they barely missed the cutoff. Homework is split into 4 parts, each of equal weightage. Unlike tutorial questions, homework questions are generally very manageable. This is because homework questions are graded, and Prof. Han tries to set graded questions (i.e. homework and exam) of standard parallel to MA3110. Prof. Han provides a brief set of notes which flow follows closely to that of Rudin. He teaches concepts both within and outside of content taught in MA3110. Additional concepts taught include differentiation and integration in multivariate settings, rectifiable curves and density of polynomials in the space of continuous functions, but none of these are tested. Concepts within exam scope are generally intuitive and easy to understand. To deal with the vast number of theorems to remember, Prof. Han allows one double-sided A4 helpsheet for both midterm and final exams. Prof. Han is a good professor who, similar to Prof. Sun in MA2108S, tries to provide a heuristic idea to each concept taught in class. He values geometric interpretations, so his explanation of the heuristics usually revolves around that. From time to time, he also introduces various concepts related to differential geometry (but not explained in depth) due to his research interests, and also some history of mathematics. However, he tends to not be rigorous with his proofs in class, with several times filling in the proof with workings that might fail to convince some students. All in all, his classes are generally relaxing to attend. Midterm and final exams are closed book (with no calculator but helpsheet is allowed), and both consist of 6 questions. Both have five extremely manageable questions, and one difficult question (not necessarily the last question). Similar to homework, Prof. Han aims to set manageable questions to prevent us from losing out by taking MA3110S instead of MA3110. It’s noteworthy that Prof. Han values geometric interpretations, so one can earn lots of partial credits by drawing diagrams to explain geometrically why the statement posed by a problem is true. Since this module refers closely to Rudin, students who want to take this module are encouraged to take MA2108S first. Expected Grade: A/A+ Final Grade: A+

Taken in Sem 2 AY 18/19 under Prof Seth Gilbert As the module description states, this module mainly focuses on randomized algorithms which are more efficient and/or simpler than their deterministic counterparts. Some topics covered include analysis of quicksort and hashing with linear probing. In CS2040, I was told that "we should always analyse the worst case", but somehow randomized quicksort runs in O(n log n), which doesn't make sense. Over here, we go through the proof and really understand the analysis. The same thing goes for hashing with linear probing, which is non-obvious why it should use O(1) probes. It is really interesting to go through the analysis of "standard" algorithms which we take for granted. Although CS3230 is the only pre-requisite for this module, it is recommended to have a good understand of (discrete) probability- ST2131 might come in handy. In terms of the algorithms used, I would say that most of the algorithms are simple. The algorithms used are much harder to describe than those in CS3230. However, the difficult part lies with the analysis. This module focuses quite a lot on the proofs, and the proofs often involve significant amount of inequalities manipulation (typically to bound the failure probability, or sometimes the expected run time of algorithms). The lectures are really great as Prof Seth keeps the class alive even at night. My favorite module taken at SoC so far.

Lecturers: Prof Jiang Jianwen: Fundamental Concepts, Dimensional Analysis, Fluid Statics, Conservation Laws and Control Volume Analysis (Mass, Energy, Momentum), Energy Loss (Fluid Flow Through Closed Conduits) Prof Chen Po-Yen: Differential Equations for Fluid Flow, Creeping and Inviscid Flow, External Viscous Force, Fluid Machinery (Pumps and Turbines) The module discusses static and dynamic fluid behaviour and analyses them in engineering applications, mainly about pipes and pumps. The module introduces basic concepts such as shear rate and viscosity, and dimensional analysis. The module then proceeds to cover static fluids, which mainly resembles high-school-level material. The next few chapters revolve around the conservation laws, primarily mass, energy, momentum conservation, and energy loss in pipes. The latter part of the module focuses on the continuity equation, highlighting several approaches such as Navier-Stokes and von Karman analysis. Finally, the module ends with a brief introduction to the fluid mechanics found in centrifugal pipes and turbines. This semester, the assessments were based on two quizzes at the end of the first part (Week 7) and the end of the second part (Week 12) worth 20% each and a final examination worth 60%. The first quiz, which comprises Chapters 1-3, was relatively doable as the questions given were straightforward and similar to the tutorial questions given. The format of the first quiz was an online paper with three open-ended questions. The second quiz, which consists of Chapters 1-3 was more challenging than the first quiz as the materials were tougher. The quizzes are online with four sections of varying formats. The first section was a True-False section consisting of 20 statements. The second section was a theoretical section consisting of 5 open-ended conceptual questions. The third and the fourth were Navier-Stokes’ equation on a rectangular plane and von Karman analysis respectively. The final exam, which consists of six open-ended questions was not that challenging as the questions set were not particularly difficult and less tedious than the second quiz. In my opinion, this module is manageable as long as you study consistently and keep up with the new concepts thrown at you every week. This module was notoriously known to be difficult for decades, as the previous professor who taught the first half of the module, was known to set 5 MCQ midterms that should actually be open-ended questions. Fortunately, since our batch, he has retired, and he has been replaced with another professor, Prof Jiang Jianwen (review below), that made the first half of the module much more manageable. I want to make comments on the quizzes and the Final Exam. The first quiz was quite straightforward, as the questions are similar to that of the tutorials. Thus, the bell-curve for this quiz was steep, with a mean of 16.8/20. However, the second quiz was much tougher, as the True/False Questions and open-ended theory questions really tested your conceptual understanding of the material, and the material for the second part was conceptually heavy and grounded on calculus. Some people in the second quiz didn’t manage to do the calculation questions as they were stuck on finding the right answers for the True/False questions. Thus, I suggest revising some calculus (mainly MA1511 stuff, like Gradient and Divergence) to better understand the concepts in the second part of the module. Because the second quiz results were not that great, the Final Exam was made much more manageable, as there were no calculus-intensive questions like deriving Navier-Stokes and Von-Karman Boundary Layer Analysis. Thus, I expected the bell-curve for the finals to be quite steep. Lastly, I want to provide a review of the professors who taught this module in 20/21 Sem 1. Prof Jiang Jianwen is a kind and student-centred professor that always wants to make sure that all of his students understand the basic concepts and get good marks. Thus, he often set many consultation sessions before the midterm quiz and the final exam. The second prof, Prof Chen Po-Yen, teaches the latter part of the module that focuses on harder topics such as Navier-Stokes Equation and Von Karman analysis. He taught the concepts very well, but in my opinion, because the materials were quite tough, some people didn’t like his part of the module. Nevertheless, in my opinion, both professors were great and quite understanding of their students.

Taken in 20/21 Sem 2 Grading: 5% CA1, 25% CA2, 10% CA3, 30% CA4, 15% CA5, 15% participation Ah yes, the compulsory English class to be taken by all Computing students. There are 2x2hr sessions per week with high weightage class participation, which I'm sure contributes to the universal hate this class gets. The content of the class can be read from the other reviews so I'll just talk about the assessments. --- Assessment --- Similar to CS2101, grading is very consistent throughout the semester due to the 5 CAs. There aren't any "lull" periods where there's nothing to do (notwithstanding the 2x2hr sessions per week), so expect to put in more work than you might probably expect. For group projects, the class is split into groups at the start of the semester based on a survey done in the first class. I was fortunate to have landed in a group with like-minded individuals who all wanted to maximise effort:reward ratio. CA1: Craft a presentation/video of a spin on a children's tale. Pretty simple, can be done in an afternoon if focused. CA2: Make a "Critical Thinking Rubric" from the Ennis reading, write a report on it (15%) and do a presentation (10%). This is the most tiring group project so I'm glad the co-ordinators put this early in the semester. CA3: Panel Discussion on an topic that was agreed upon prior to the discussion. You have to research the topic, then have an "academic conversation" that goes on for about 30-45min with your group, with 15min Q/A at the end. Can be prepared the day before. Try to be nice to your teammates and let them have their say in the discussion. CA4: Position Paper. You propose a question then write a 800-word-or-so essay on it. This is similar to writing a GP essay, except with citations. Can be done in a day assuming you already have a good question to write on. This is individual work with high weightage so if you're planning to score, better put work into this. CA5: Given a prompt, do an individual impromptu speech on the prompt in 2min. This is a luck of the draw if you get a good prompt or not. It's over within 2 minutes so if you can't think of anything to say, hey, at least you'll die quickly. Expected Grade: B/B+ Actual Grade: TBC

under Prof Wong Weng Fai. This module acts as a deep dive into the Intel x86 build of the Ubuntu Operating System. This can be seen as a deeper version of CS2106. You will explore the x86 Ubuntu, learning more about stuff like the intel x86 instruction set (no need to memorise), linux scheduler (how it evolved from O(n) to O(1) to CFS and BFS), linux memory management, filesystems (briefly about ext2, 3, 4, and btrfs). During my semester, there were 4 assignments, 9 pop quizzes (during lectures), and final exam. The 4 assignments were all done via VirtualBox. It is advisable that you use VirtualBox to run the Ubuntu version specified so that whatever you did is replicable by Prof Wong. - Assignment 1: Explore configuring Ubuntu kernel options. This assignment requires you to complete a set of tasks related to configuring the Ubuntu kernel. The assignment is relatively straightforward except for the part where you need to try and compile a smaller (or the smallest if you want) kernel. The speed of this assignment is dependent on how many cores your computer has as compiling a default configuration kernel on a duo core computer took me 2+ hours. I was able to procure a virtual machine with 16 cores to speed up to around 10~mins. Of course if you knew exactly which configuration were not needed, your builds would also be faster since there is less to compile. However, if you do not know then you would end up trial and error, slowly building and testing the kernel you built. I probably built around 40 kernels before giving up and settling with a kernel build that was only slightly smaller than the default 1. The 2nd part of the assignment is answering some questions regarding the Intel x86 instruction set. The approach for this part is to download the volume (I think volume 2) of the x86 instruction set and find the instruction of interest and try and understand how each segment of the instruction works. It takes awhile to understand this so do not start last minute. - Assignment 2: Tracing the kernel. The first part is learning how to print kernel messages then using ftrace to trace the call stack of kernel functions. The assignment requires does not teach you everything so you need to find a guide that shows you how to do the tracing. It is not difficult but you need some time to understand how to use ftrace. Part 2 is about the GOT and PLT. The lectures don't cover in detail how it works. Prof Weng does attempt to show it live for a simple program but it is not enough to answer this part. I found a youtube video that explained in a little more detail which helped. - Assignment 3: Build a device driver. The assignment provides a template for which you need to complete it to create a device driver that functions as per the small test case provided. This is not too difficult although it was somewhat ambiguous due to how simple the test case was. Part 2 is CS2106 scheduling questions and 'Draw the red black tree'. This is probably the hardest assignment as it required significantly more programming than the other 3 assignments. This assignment, as usual, is ambiguous as you can't really tell if the output is correct or wrong. If your program handled input in a manner that seems reasonable to Prof Wong, which he doesn't really say what is reasonable, then you will get your marks. Otherwise, you will be deducted marks if your output 'seems unlikely' with no further justification from Prof Wong. We were supposed to use C but we were also allowed to use C++ after requesting. C++ helped as I did not want to create the common data structures needed (e.g. list, map). The pop quizzes are essentially small tasks released during the lectures and normally to be done before the end of the day unless the task is big (e.g. trace the linux scheduler). The pop quizzes normally test the lecture's content that day. They should not take more than 1 hour to do. The final exam for my semester was physical and open book. However, note that open book in this case meant that you had to print every lecture slides (few hundred slides) if you want to be able to check concepts. The slides may be ambiguous so try your best to interpret it in the way Prof Wong understands the concept. The approach for this exam was to answer every question even if you don't know enough about it. If the questions asks for 3 things, try to give 3 things even if they kinda say the same thing. Try to give your justifications for every answer as they are probably all ambiguous and hope he reads and accepts those justification if your answer differs from his answers. The exam answers released after were terribly unclear and I could not understand how it answered the questions. Prof Wong's lectures are not the best. He pretty much reads off the slides and also skips stuff in his slides during lecture. What is worse is that it seems to me that Prof Wong misunderstood some of the content he is teaching. This was regarding how a B-Tree works. He claims that a B-Tree can have a node inserted, however, the actual claim should have been that you can insert a key and if the node the key was inserted to is full, it will split up and create another node. This behaviour is not the same as 'inserting a node into a B-Tree'. However, during the pop quiz, we are require to insert a node which does not make sense. But we still 'inserted' it since he was the 1 marking. So in case of ambiguity, try to think what Prof Wong would think. Ideally, try to clarify early with Prof Wong and try to insist that the ambiguity be clarified. There is a tutorial slot but it is actually just for the lecture which is why it is back to back with the lecture. Prof Wong is friendly like a Singapore Uncle would be. However, he is not the best at detailing requirements and expectations, resulting in, as you may know by now, a lot of ambiguity. Prof Wong normally answers emails but sometimes he will miss your email. Prof Wong's answer to queries are not exactly helpful as he sometimes misunderstand the question or handwaves the issue, which means that you will probably will not have an answer for your queries. Overall, I would not recommend taking this module under Prof Wong as the ambiguity was too much for me to deal with. If you are interested in learning more about the Ubuntu Operating System, you could take the module but it is to an extent, just a small dive into Ubuntu. The content is interesting but I think that the module kinda made it not so interesting. Expected Grade: B+/A- Actual Grade: A+ (Despite all the ambiguity in the exam, I somehow scored well for it)

(repost since the old one is uneditable) AY20/21 Sem 1 Lecturer: Prof. Leong Wai Kay and Prof. Ben Leong Assessment: 25% Coursemology 5% Participation (Tutorials and Forums) 15% Midterms 15% Practical Exam 40% Final Exam Overview This module teaches the programming methodology with Python starting from the primitives (data types and simple Python operators), functional abstractions, recursion, higher-order functions, data abstraction (ADT), sequences (tuples and lists), searching, sorting, dictionaries, object-oriented programming (class), memoization, dynamic programming, exception handling, and data visualization (using matplotlib and some other mentioned packages). Module Difficulty For those who are new into programming, you might want to spend much more time on getting familiar with the Python environment. But don't worry, the CS1010S tutors are there to help you, also possibly your fellow peers through the Coursemology forum, which is the platform where CS1010S is using for submitting missions. I also suggest to look for more external references which other reviews have provided (I suppose so). The workload below is measured weekly. Lectures - 2h This was taught to me under Prof. Leong Wai Kay. I feel that some lectures have an extremely high pace due to the content quantity but mostly they're fine. If you missed anything from the lecture, the recording will be posted on Coursemology, so nothing to worry about! Feel free to adjust your pace at your own will. Plus, you can also type in some reflections from each lecture in the Coursemology forum which may help you for both the Participation grade and the Coursemology grade. (do once in a week and you might gain 4/5 participation grade) Recitations - 1h Basically a recap of what's taught in the lecture. From here I learn something new from Prof. Ben Leong which I didn't realize during the lecture. Tutorials - 1h It's a smaller group discussion which may provide support for those who are shy at asking questions during both lectures and recitaions. It's also a very very final recap of the latest lecture content so make sure you understand it before the next lecture (this my suggestion or else you'll be overwhelmed?) Missions (and Trainings) It may seem to be more coding but it's actually more thinking and less coding. Therefore it may take a while to finish a single missions. Take most of your time for this and possibly ponder over the tasks in the missions. Try to complete your mission as early as possible as they might come in a faster pace as it goes to the end of the module. Otherwise, procrastination might take the wheel. From my personal experience, the missions were easy at the start, then the difficulty reached its peak at the middle of the semester, then it goes down again to somewhat doable. For the hardest mission, you might spent 4h-3d (depends on you) and for the easiest it may take 1h-1d. The trainings section consists of Lecture trainings which is like a pre-test for the lecture content, Tutorial trainings which is the main questions discussed during tutorial (feel free to ask more than this during tutorial) and Extra Practice which is basically for those who have spare time for it or those who consider missions as a piece of rainbow cake, full of journey but easy for them, or for those who are aiming for the OCD badge/achievement, hearsay one of the tasks of Hercules in CS1010S. Personal Opinion The heart of CS1010S is the gamification of this module through Coursemology, which gave me incentives to do the components of this module really well, such as the missions and the trainings such as extra practices. Make sure you reach level 50 in Coursemology because almost everyone will get it. Also, this module is not bell-curved, so do your best and do not get intimated by competitive vibes. Final Comments (or maybe the TLDR part :v) All in all, I think every step of my journey in CS1010S is worth the time, and I would recommend you guys to experience the same. CS1010S profs and tutors are trying their very best to help you, it's your turn to do your best effort too. Consistent and reaching out is key! Expected grade : A Final grade : *inhales*

AY2020/21 Semester 1 Lecturer: Mr. Ravi Suppiah Lab TA: Khairul and Tessa Tutorial TA: Daniel Assessment Final Exam (40%) Midterm (15%) Tutorial Attendance & Participation (5%) Lab assessments (10%) Mini-Project (30%) There has been a change in the curriculum since AY2019/20 Semester 2 where ARM and RTX were introduced instead of Arduino Uno. Daniel always tried to break down a question into smaller ones so that everyone can have more chances to participate. Don't be afraid to raise your hand as there is no penalty for incorrect answer. The tutorial is also very helpful as the questions typically follow exam style and test your understanding about a concept in different scenario with different conditions. Labs and Project You'll have to do a demo once every 2-3 weeks and answer TA's questions relating to your code. Taken in AY 20/21 with Prof Edward Teo. We covered Feynman path integrals, Identical particles, Relativistic single-particle QM, and Quantum field theory (Scalar fields, Spinor fields, and EM field). Note scattering and appoximation theory are listed in the description but not really covered. One of only three physical modules I had in the sem! I can proudly say that for once I attended very nearly every lecture. Mostly because a) the lectures are good, and b) because the lecture notes only really have an outline of the topics, and have typos here and there, so you basically *have* to be present to take physical notes. Almost all the derivations are done on the board, line by line, so you don't miss out on your understanding. We had two term tests and a finals, along with weekly homework. The homework is only one, usually straightforward question. None of the tests were too difficult per se, although the exam was definitely the hardest of the lot. Practice all the tutorial questions well and you should be able to handle the assessments relatively well. The module also complements GR well, in that in both modules you will spend quite some time playing with indices. If you had the pleasure of taking CFT with Dr. Yeo Ye, go through as much of it as you can. In particular, the parts on rotations, Hamiltonian mechanics, and Noether's theorem are useful. I used these notes as a reference throughout this module. It is not strictly necessary, all of this is covered again here but it's nice to know. I really enjoyed this module, one of my favourite so far in the physics department.

Ger1000 Module review and some study advice Taken in AY16/17 Sem1 Prof: Victor Tan Final grade: A+ Warning: Either you find my writing style fun or full of crap. You might want to grab some snack when you read this. Above all: What is GER1000 about: Use number and rationality to design studies, check if other research methods are reliable…Instead of saying it’s like stats, I would say it’s more like source based questions (SBQ) in social study. (Yea, the one in secondary school) Basic information about the module: Lectures videos on IVLE, you can either watch the videos or read the scripts and slides if you find the facial expression of your professor too dramatic for you to concentrate. Don’t worry; you won’t miss anything unless you want to decide if there is some sarcasm in the tone when the Profs read them XD. Department is obviously worried that some students don’t actually commit enough effort when left unsupervised, therefore they advise you to set aside a fixed slot in the calendar to do the online study. Well, I guess this module demand less time on lectures than other 4 MC modules (especially taken the time for travelling into account); so fair on your side not to miss the videos/scripts. Quizzes, Online quiz every week. 10% of the final grade. My thought is that percentage is one thing to look at; the other thing is how distinguishing they can be. (If the answer can be found online and everyone gets full marks unless they got butter hands, I guess it’s unwise to pay too much attention on this kind of quiz like those on PC1431…….) I think GER1000 quizzes are distinguishing. They are not hard but they can be tricky. Sometimes they play with the language…too bad my England is not so good. You should check your answer with your friends before submitting. (Shouldn’t be hard given nearly every NUS student gotta take this module in year 1) The system allows infinite attempts so don’t be afraid to try. Of course, you should not rely on your friends for the answers. These quizzes help with your learning tremendously. Tutorials: 10% Tutorials in alternative weeks. Attendance taken. Performance during tutorial counted towards final grades. It’s in fact quite chill so don’t be anxious. Firstly, your contribution during team discussion is observed. Yea, the prof does work around the class room to see if you are speaking. I guess they don’t care about the quality of what you are saying so just make sure you simply don’t look at your teammates and your prof with a pair of very innocent eyes and refuse to say anything, unless you are very cute. Okay…. Seriously, some foreign students (if any in your group) may need longer time to formulate their sentences, try to give them some chance to at least say something if you don’t see this session as a 0 sum game. You guys gotta do project together anyway. Secondly, each group will have one representative to answer a question from the assignment given to you days before the tutorial. This means everyone will have to answer one question by the end of the semester. (Or two if you are as unlucky/lucky as me….ops maybe this is the secret road to A+, don’t tell others) The assignments you need to do before the tutorials are not easy enough to do on the spot so better prepare them.’’ Midterm: 20%; first two (most interesting and relatively difficult chapter according to me) chapters tested. Design of studies and association. 14 MCQ questions (or maybe 14, weird number anyway); shouldn’t take long to study for it. One day should be enough…..if you were consistent that is. All I know is that I got 12/13 for midterm but I guess many people did as well for our year (Guessing only, sorry if the bell curve don’t look nice). I will talk about how (I think) you can do well in this module later. (Provided you are not bored by the length yet) Final; 40% still MCQs only. 28 questions. More time than you needed given. Sampling, uncertainty, Network, Association plus the two fellows in midterm tested. The chapter on uncertainly is the most mathematical chapter in this module. Maybe, you want some extra love for it if your math foundation is pretty weak. Project: 20%; Use what you were taught (Quantitative frame work) to critic one piece of news about research findings and the research papers itself. Are smokers more likely to remain unemployed? Does more reading bring longevity? Many people make a living on doing research of all kinds. You should have many potential topics to choose from. Try to find those with numbers, charts, and graphs. They are good for your health as they make you happier later. Analysis on those stuffs is easier to apply and looks more systematic (more pro). Our professor said our project was good several times and I will accredit this simply to the fact that we managed to have more meetings aka spent more time on the project. (For your information, we had one meeting each week for 4 weeks and we carry on what is left with clear division of labour after the meeting) After PW in JC and even more projects in polys, I guess everyone has their own theories on how to contribute towards an effective team work. I don’t think I am smarter on this topic. However, I always have this thought in mind. I feel many people are too obsessed with full attendance to a degree that the benefits of insisting so do not justify its cost. Too many meetings were cancelled because one person cannot (maybe he really cannot) make it. Unless it is this very person that is absent every time, I think it’s okay and fair to have one missing person. How to do well in this module; This module is not content heavy. The summary side provided during tutorials should contain 80% of the facts you need to know about GER. Perhaps you can save the time on making your own summary notes. To do well in this module, you need to think hard instead of memorising hard. Find out which question you are wrong for the quiz and understand why you made a mistake. Don’t overlook this module just because everyone says it is easy. Easy or hard you face the bell curve and your more difficult modules are 4 MCs as well. I believe this is the smart way to use your free S/U in year1. This is a module you will be rewarded equally handsomely for comparable less effort. You should be smart to put your eggs in the right basket. I’m not saying you should prioritise your GER., but you should never give up on it. If you really find yourself in a situation where you don’t like your team, you can work on making them like you first. Everyone will do better in a delightful (group) working environment.

under prof Seth Lewis Gilbert. Assessment: 25% Midterm (closed book with helpsheet), 30% Finals (closed book with helpsheet), 6 homeworks + a mini-project with a presentation component. Skills required: Proof writing, combinatorics & graph, probability. Being proficient with probability is especially important! If you're not decent in probability, I wouldn't suggest taking this module. Content covered: sub-linear time algorithms, streaming algorithms, cache-efficient data structures and algorithms, parallel algorithms (both fork-join model and Map-Reduce model). This is a lot of content in my opinion, more than any other module I've ever taken. There're 2 or 3 new algorithms every week, and the proof techniques are very diverse too. You can still access the contents here: Class format: There are 2 hours of lecture, and 1 hour of tutorial every week. They're arranged into 1 contiguous 3-hour block from 6.30 pm to 9.30 pm. Lecture pace before recess week were sian @.@, but became ok after that. The 1-hour tutorial at the end is optional: prof Seth writes a few problems on the board, gives the class around 45 mins to solve them and then show the solutions. His problems are nice, I'll recommend you to stay back for extra practice. There'll be weekly homework in the first 6 weeks, and then the mini-project will play the role of homework in the remaining weeks. The homework was quite easy if you revise well and have a good grasp of probability techniques. Mini-project would be something like pick an algorithm, test it on a real (large) data set, see how it performs and suggest some (ad-hoc) improvements if have. You need to submit a report and make a presentation for your mini-project. This, together with CS3233 by Dr Steven Halim, are the best algorithm modules I've ever taken in NUS! The algorithms taught this module and their analysis are unlike any classic or linear time algorithm. There'll be lots of randomisation, lots of probability bounds, lots of expectation, quite a bit of variance. Prof Seth is also a very good lecturer. He's humorous, enthusiastic, and is very polite when he responds to questions. He explains things quite well. His midterm is 1 hour long on paper, but he allowed us to take as long as we want lol. Idk if I'm allowed to do this, but I want to include here an email he sent to the class after the final exam, just to show how nice he is and how much effort he puts into setting the questions for the exam " Hi, Congrats! You're done! Hope everyone enjoyed the exam and did great! You can now find the exam and the solutions on the web page. Be aware that for some problems there were alternative acceptable solutions, so your answer might be right even if it is different than the sketch that I included. (And apologies for any typos.) I included a little commentary below on the questions (and why I think they're interesting). It's been a fun semester, and do drop by to say hi if you're in the neighborhood. Take care, Seth " With regards to exams, both the midterm and the finals were hard to me. Prof Seth was aware that the papers are hard, so he would give us (near) full credit as long as we get the right idea. So make sure not to leave anything empty! In short, an awesome module with lots of interesting data structures/algorithms! Take it if your probability is decent!

Taken in AY20/21 Semester 1 Taught by: Assoc. Prof. Han Fei (Lecturer) Disclaimer: This module was conducted in the second semester affected by the COVID-19 pandemic, and as a result it may differ significantly from how past/future modules would/will be conducted. Assessment Structure: 30% Homework (4 sets total) 20% Presentation 50% Final (Online, Open Book, Open Internet) This is a follow-up of MA4266 Topology, obviously in the direction of algebraic topology. The content includes fundamentals of algebraic topology (e.g. homotopy and CW complexes), fundamental groups (including van Kampen theorem and covering spaces), and homology (including simplicial homology, singular homology, and some basic computation techniques). The textbook of reference is Algebraic Topology, Allen Hatcher. The topics above are basically whole of chapter 0, whole of chapter 1, and chapter 2.1. All lectures were held via zoom (and were of course recorded). Lecture attendance was not compulsory. Like most graduate modules, this module has no tutorial classes. Prof. Han’s lectures mostly follow the textbook (skipping some examples in the middle), inserting some additional explanations in the middle where he deems necessary. He also inserted a few lectures on category theory in around week 3-4. Algebraic topology can be a rather intuitive subject, but a lot of effort is needed to make it happen (unfortunately I did not put in the required effort to make it happen). Although personally weak at algebra, I did not find the algebra part of this module too disastrous (compared to say MA5211 Lie Theory), as they mostly stem from the basic/intuitive part of group theory (e.g. very basic representation theory/generators, free groups etc). The most difficult part of this module, however, is applying the concepts taught to solve the exercises. There were many instances which I thought I understood the theorems (and even the proofs) well, but I was completely lost when I turned to the exercises. This is worsened by the fact that Hatcher’s exercises are known to be very difficult. Another issue with algebraic topology is that it is not rigorously taught, with many “proofs” provided being just proof by pictures (e.g. the “proof” that suspension of S^n is S^{n+1} is usually provided as follows: geometrically clear for the case of n = 1 and n = 2, and “therefore” true for all n). Students must be prepared to either 1) black box many things and accept the intuition or 2) spend lots of time making everything rigorous. Personally, I suggest the first option. Homework was split into 4 parts. Homework questions were very difficult and one should not expect to be able to solve them without extensive help from peers/internet. Most of the questions were either taken from Hatcher’s book or can be found in some online problem sets, so googling for solutions should not be too much of an issue. This was the second time I took a module under Prof. Han, first time being MA3110S. His teaching style remained more or less the same – he generally tries to provide a heuristic idea of the concepts taught, especially if a geometric interpretation can be provided. However, his workings are not always rigorous, and usually he usually leaves students to complete the details if troublesome rigor is required. This is worsened by the above remark that algebraic topology is usually not very rigorous taught, so students should be mentally prepared to black box many concepts. The presentation involves students finding a topic on their own, then presenting to other students for about 20 minutes (usually barely leaving time for Q&A). Finals was zoom-proctored, open internet, and had 8 questions (100 marks in total). Almost all questions are not doable unless you google-ed, which can mostly be done (I didn’t manage to google some but my friend managed to google all). Regardless, one should have a good foundation of the concepts taught in order to process and translate the solutions found online. All in all this module provides a very good introduction to the world of algebraic topology, and I recommend anyone interested in this field to take up this module. Expected Grade: A- Final Grade: A

Taken in AY 21/22 Sem 1 Lecturer: Sufatrio Component breakdown: 2 CTF-style assignments (10% + 15%) Midterms (15%) LumiNUS revision quiz (5%) Group presentation (5%) Tutorial attendance (5%) Finals (45%) TL;DR: + Has cool and fun CTFs - Module scope leaves much to be desired - Lecturer is not good (I rolled a not so good tutor, which made the experience even worse) As someone who loves information security, I went into this module with great excitement. I was NOT prepared to be let down this hard. Module scope: Iffy. About half of the topics covered felt very touch-and-go; they were briefly glossed over and then rarely, if ever, cropped up again. Many sub-chapters are treated merely as "vocabulary" and their sole purpose in the module is to serve as possible answers for the fill-in-the-blank/MCQ section in the midterms and finals; nothing more than a cursory understanding is required. Lectures & lecturer: Lectures were conducted live over Zoom and recorded. Dr Sufatrio proceeds at a glacial pace, reading off the slides for the most part and circling random words while he speaks. His voiceover adds negligible value to the slides themselves and you're better off reading them on your own. He also has a tendency to waste time; around 10 minutes at the start of each lecture for "announcements". I couldn't attend the lectures live as I was typically travelling to NUS for another in-person tutorial during that timeslot, but I stopped bothering to watch the recorded videos a few weeks in because they're that slow even at 2x speed. Dr Sufatrio takes weeks to respond to email queries, and his responses are typically not helpful. I'm not even sure if he fully understood the questions being asked before replying with unrelated stock responses such as "this is how we defined it in the notes". Tutorials: My experience with tutorials was not great because I got a questionable tutor (who I will not name). On at least one occasion, he stated that he "didn't remember ever seeing" something despite literally having just gone through a question about it in the previous tutorial session. He also has a tendency to give wrong answers or explanations to questions posed by students, and usually doesn't bother correcting himself afterwards. This was not very beneficial to the understanding of many students in my tutorial group. To his credit, though, he provided us with a definition list/cheatsheet, which was quite helpful as quick reference during the finals. The tutorial questions themselves are generally okay, though some of them have a tendency to be somewhat tedious (e.g. given the following list of requirements, list all the firewall rules you would implement). Group presentation: This component felt like an afterthought. You pick a topic from a list and do a short presentation on it during the tutorial timeslot. This is something you can get done in a single night, but the grading is completely opaque and it's up to your tutor's discretion whether you get a 4/5 or a 5/5. Assignments: The highlight of this module. Assignments are CTF-style and the challenges are set by the NUS Greyhats. It's very hands-on, so you will probably learn more from trying these challenges than from the rest of the module put together. They are pretty time-consuming though, and can be pretty difficult if you don't already have some background and need to pick everything up from scratch. I found this pretty enjoyable, and I think it was the one redeeming part of this module. LumiNUS quiz: This is just a MCQ quiz you can do at your own time. It's meant to serve as revision before the final exam. There's no time limit so make sure you get full marks for this. Midterms/finals: Midterms and finals were conducted over Examplify with Zoom proctoring. Format was open book but no internet. Dr Sufatrio reuses questions a lot and the format of his papers is always the same. The first half of his paper (fill-in-the-blanks + MCQ) often has questions which are ripped word-for-word from previous years' papers. Even the open-ended questions are incredibly formulaic; all 3 final papers I did that were set by him (2 PYPs and the actual finals for this sem) had secure programming questions with similar code and identical vulnerabilities. The papers' difficulties are generally not high. It's entirely possible to get 100% if you understand what's going on in the module and don't make careless mistakes. The question wording can be pretty bad, though, and sometimes it's not really clear what the question wants from you. All you really need to do to prepare for his midterms/finals are to do any past papers set by him. Lecture content barely gets tested, and if they do, it's stuff that you can just look up in the notes anyway. Conclusion: If you're looking for a neat introduction to information security, this module (at least under Dr Sufatrio) isn't it; it barely covers anything interesting. If you must take this module, consider taking it under a different lecturer instead. If you just want to learn more about information security or play CTFs, you'll probably get a lot further by getting to know a few Greyhats members.
