Taken in AY 15/16 Semester 1 Lecturer: Associate Professor Chu Delin Tutor: Associate Professor Chu Delin Lab assistant: Miss Teng Dan Expected Grade: B+ Grade: A (Pleasantly surprised by this grade) Assessment and workload - 10% Tutorial and lab attendance (Nearly everybody gets this) - 10% Matlab assignment (This was challenging) - 5% Mega homework (Because there's many questions, all on cubic spline and a few proving questions covered in lecture, just copy what he says) - 15% mid-term test (I got 83/100, which many of us got very high for) - 60% final exam - GC not allowed at any test or exam. Only SC allowed for both mid-term test and final exam. - NO helpsheet allowed for mid-term test - 1 A4 size helpsheet written on both sides for final exam - No webcast. Experience: - This module is extremely interesting to me. It puts many (if not all) of us to shame for taking our calculators for granted. It begins with rounding/chopping arithmetic and errors. It sheds light to why some ancient calculators like those used in coffee shops/money changers are inaccurate when you try to evaluate decimals. Linear systems is next, putting us to shame and tormenting us with 3 digit rounding/chopping arithmetic incorporated into Gaussian elimination. Careless people like myself have a very hard time here. Then it was interpolation polynomials, followed by numerical integration. Ever wondered how our GC does integration? That's the answer. It is very interesting and yet technical. Lastly we look at solutions to non-linear equations, examining how our GC solves funny equations like sinx + x^2 = 0, for example. - Prof Chu is an excellent lecturer. He knows his stuff very well at the back of his hand, and is able to prove theorems right from scratch. Some people may think he has a very strong Chinese accent, but hey, we're all here to learn Mathematics and not criticise a professor's English isn't it? Moreoever, his speech sounds perfectly intelligible to me. Prof Chu also takes the effort to interact with students before and after lectures and asks for feedback about that lecture. He is approachable so consultations work fine with him. He is also passionate and enthusiastic about the things he teaches. The only grouse I have is that he occasionally goes very fast over harder concepts, but luckily they aren't tested in the mid-term test nor final exam (yet). In addition Prof Chu is also extremely kind and helps all students with the best of his ability to pass mid-term tests and exams. He goes through past year paper questions during lectures after each topic and gives obvious hints as to which questions have high chances of appearing in the assessments. That being said, will make the bell curve steep. So carefulness is important in this module. - This module also requires MATLAB programming, at a rather advanced level at that. There are 5 MATLAB lab sessions, which teach the very basic of MATLAB programming. The assignment in on a whole new level, which I couldn't do since I'm bad at programming. I sought help from friends to finish this assignment. - Tutorials are important in my opinion, as the past mid-term tests and final exams have questions very similar to the tutorials. In addition Prof Chu takes on all tutorials and he explains very well, although sometimes fast. His solutions uploaded can have gaps, so attend the tutorials, absorb as much as possible and write solutions again. - Lab sessions are well conducted by Miss Teng. She knows MATLAB well and adds her own inputs to the notes Prof Chu provides. She spots students' coding mistakes while patrolling the computer lab as well, and corrects them on the spot politely and professionally. - The mid-term test was scary as no helpsheet is allowed. So we had to memorise a few formulae which were rather difficult. Fortunately or unfortunately, the questions that came out were exactly the same as previous tests, which is advantageous to students who have access to their seniors' papers. I was lucky to scrape 83/100 since I did the 1st question wrongly with big conceptual errors. - Final exam is somewhat difficult and tedious. 5 questions, 20 marks each, 2h to do. Heavy question weightage. I managed to do Q1, 2 and 3 properly, and tried my best to do Q4 and Q5, which were difficult. I probably got credit for my answers to those questions. Again, the questions are similar to tutorials/lecture notes with modifications, except Q4 and 5. Take his advice and revise his lecture notes seriously as Q3 was entirely lifted from lecture notes (fixed point method). Conclusion: - This module is extremely enjoyable. The content is interesting and I learnt a lot from it. Plus an excellent lecturer who knows his stuff at the back of his hand. I recommend this applied mathematics module. Just remember that it could end up being a test of carefulness..

Lecturer: Dr Henry Chia Synopsis: CS2030 introduces various programming paradigms to students, beginning with object oriented programming and design principles, followed by some functional programming and ending with a bit on threading and parallelism. The module is taught in Java and assumes no prior knowledge of Java, but a solid understanding of basic programming constructs is required. Assessment: Comprised of weekly take-home labs (20%), two practical exams (20% each) and a written final exam (40%), all of which are open book. Doing well for the weekly take-home labs and practical exams is crucial in securing a good grade. Note that the labs and two practical exams are not graded by the TAs, but by an automated script developed by the lecturer, which is rather ruthless, and hence having a clear understanding of the requirements for every lab and following them as closely as possible is important. The written final exam is a practical exam in disguise, thus familiarity with Java and having documentation on hand is crucial to doing well. Lecturer: Prof Henry tends to do lots of live coding demos during his lectures, and his lectures are generally not hard to follow if you know what's going on. Other than that, his administration of the module is a mess this sem, with random cancellations of lectures and tutorials, uncertain TAs due to lack of information from him, and almost no feedback (in terms of marks) for work submitted, so hopefully that improves in future iterations of this module conducted by him.

Taken in AY19/20 Semester 2 Taught by: Choi Kwok Pui (Lecturer) Disclaimer: This module was affected by the COVID-19 pandemic, and as a result it may differ significantly from how past/future modules would/will be conducted. Assessment Structure: 20% Homework (3 sets total, 6%-6%-8%) 20% Midterm (Take-Home) 60% Final (Online) This is a compulsory module for Statistics majors/second majors, and Math majors may also take this module to satisfy their optional major requirements. The module’s topics include review of MA2216, and the remaining topic revolves mainly around Markov chains. This includes first step analysis, Gambler’s Ruin, transient and recurrent states, basic limit theorems, regular transition matrices, double stochastic matrices, reducible Markov chains, time reversible Markov chains, generating functions and branching processes. The main textbook of reference is Introduction to probability models, Sheldon Ross. Attendance is not compulsory for both lecture and tutorials. All lectures are webcast and recorded, especially due to the COVID-19 pandemic forcing all lectures of modules with >50 students being suspended. I only attended two of the lectures and none of the tutorials. There is a total of three sets of homework, and about 1/3 to 1/2 of the total questions test on MA2216. Probably due to a large portion of the students taking this module being from the statistics department, while many theorems were introduced, little proofs were explained. As a result, this module is not difficult in the sense that not much understanding is required in order to be able to do the homework and exam questions, much similar to ST2132. Hence, I spent very little time outside homework studying for this module. Thus, this is another “methods” module, but unless one is truly interested, they may not have much takeaway from this module. Midterm and Final were both open book exams. A well-known fact (which holds true for this semester as well) is that this module includes lots of questions that only require knowledge from MA2216 in their exams. As a result, the exams are generally very easy to score high (perfect score requires one not to commit careless mistakes). This is worsened by the fact that the exams are open-book, so the bell curve for this module is extremely high. I scored mostly full marks for HW and 56/60 for midterm, and performed very well in final. Regardless, I scored a disappointing grade. While this module provides a gentle introduction to Markov chains (which is pivotal for those interested in more advanced probability theory), do not expect a very rich and rigorous course from this module. Further self-study may be needed to prepare oneself for more advanced theory. Expected Grade: A-/A Final Grade: A- (S/U-ed, only possible due to unforeseen COVID-19 situation)

Taken in AY2014-15, Semester 2. Lecturer was Dr. Scot Hislop, Tutor was Gao Yang (a doctoral student.) Dr. Hislop is a very passionate lecturer and he conveys that passion in quirky, interesting ways (such as his barefoot lectures, the copious amounts of oolong that he drinks and the hat that he wears to class). It is quite difficult to fall asleep during his lectures as he makes the content interesting by linking the points of interest in a topic (and between topics in the later lectures) to each other. While his lectures are basically summaries of the reading material, it is a good idea to attend as he does share repeated quotes and other material such as movies and video clips that emphasise the points which he likes to focus on. The readings themselves are really heavy, and while they start off on a very historical note, the packet itself contains pieces of literature and cultural analyses. They can be dry at times, and the detail can be overwhelming as well, but the impression that Dr. Hislop gave is that he wanted us to have a broad view of Japan from this module (it is, after all, an exposure module). As such, take the readings and make the notes with the broad perspective in mind, picking up interesting details as you go along. While he did not test things like the name of the fourteenth emperor (which was written in one of the early texts, Okagami), he did test things like the plot of stories that appeared in the texts (if I remember correctly) and other small details. Apparently this is a trend in most JS1101E examinations. Tutorials also went on without a hitch, and especially so if you did your readings and formed an opinion before going to class (the questions are posted the week before classes). Because they are 45 minute discussions, there was not enough time for counterarguments and rebuttals to be made, with each group just having a representative give a summary of their discussed pointers. Also, I think because it was Gao Yang's first (or second?) semester facilitating this module, the classes themselves were not very much free-flowing. It would have been nice to have a bit more of a debate going around. The paper that we had to write as part of a group project was probably the most irritating and taxing, but rewarding portion of the module. The more group members you have, the larger a word allowance you are granted (up to 5 members for 5000 words, 1000 words per member). It is NOT helpful if you go into the module without knowing what exactly it is about Japan that you are interested in: have some specifics in mind, don't just say things like "food, anime and manga". This is meant to be an academic ARGUMENTATIVE paper, and while the topics of food, anime and manga could shape an argumentative essay, it is usually not the case. As usual, if your topic is chosen, be ready to be the one steering research and editing/writing of the paper. Dr. Hislop was already made a disclaimer at the start of the module about members who do not contribute or go missing, and one of my group members did not contribute (at all), and got a (minor, imo) penalty in her final mark from the essay. There is also a forum component where you have to consistently post questions or topics relevant to the topics being taught in JS1101E. Almost anything goes, but as with the paper component, this is a place for you to shape discussions around your interests and find people who share the same interests. Citations are nice here, and frankly while I did catch a few people lifting directly from websites without citing them, I'm not sure if it made a difference in their marks (forum gives 10% of overall grade). Sometimes, people just post things that they answer themselves within a single post (usually the foreign exchange students) and it seemingly defeats the purpose of the forum, but people tend to steer away from those posts. Overall, Dr. Hislop frames this module as a giant questioning session about identity: what exactly is Japan? Does "Japan" even exist? What is "history" and who says so? While these ideas and questions that he discusses are seemingly irrelevant, they do appear on the final exam, and they can be pretty enlightening.

This mod is highly recommended for anyone keen to delve deeper into South Asia. This is not a formal classification of Asia by any means but in my mind I think of Asia as divided very broadly into 3 main areas, South Asia, Southeast Asia and Manchurian Asia. I think that because of the cultural predispositions of Singapore students, ASEAN Southeast Asia and countries like Japan, China tend to be better understood. However, I would argue that a truly grounded understanding of Asia can only be acquired through a rigorous study of South Asia as well. No one should call herself or himself a citizen of Asia without understanding South Asia on a deeper level. Through this mod, i was introduced to the key forces, nationalist or other wise that shape and continue to shape South Asia. South Asia actually is a subcontinent on its own, understanding the powers that be that shape this critical and volatile region is a worthy endeavour. For example, India is the worlds largest democracy but in recent years the secular flavour of her democracy has acquired a Hindutva flavour. As a GE module that is supposed to help students better understand human cultures, this module is perfect and insightful. So this module is exceptional in 2 ways, one it raises key questions, not just pertaining to nationalism or nationhood, that make us think. Secondly, it allowed me to see the world and the political choices from a South Asian lens, whether it be an Indian, Pakistani, Bangladeshi, Sri Lankan lens. This cultural immersion of sorts was something i could not have gotten from other modules. This mod raises several key questions that are worth answering, questions like are the bonds of a common religion sufficient to hold a nation together? What are the key ideas underpinning nations that once undone, can lead to secession and fragmentation? My lecturer was A.P. Gyanesh Kudaisya, he is a witty lecturer who is patient enough to clarify any doubts that you have. His lectures were informative and gave a succinct overview of the topics covered. His lectures coupled with the carefully selected readings will be enough to give a brief but deep dive into South Asia!

Full review at: This is a new mod i think. My friend introduced it to me and I found the module description really interesting so I decided to take it. Review for AY20/21 Sem 2 here:

A/P Aaron Chia: Introduction to Project Management, Systems Thinking, Modelling and Simulation and Systems Dynamics, Stocks and Flows, Modelling and Data, Systems Dynamics, Modelling Delays and Decision Making, Testing and Validation Overview: The module mainly revolves around modelling a system using software called Stella Architect. The first few lectures are about project management, which encompasses several topics such as scope, schedule, cost management, and project control. The module then progresses towards building models using causal loop diagrams (CLD) and Stock-Flow diagrams (SFD). Subsequently, the module also discusses model testing and validation as well as delays and decision making. The module was conducted in full e-learning mode with pre-recorded lectures as well as online tutorial and lab sessions held in alternate weeks. Every lab session requires a submission of the completed task related to the respective lab one week after the lab is conducted. There is also optional homework given following the tutorials sessions which is meant for self-study and not to be submitted. The group project is a semester-long project which depicts and elaborates a problem using modelling and systems thinking. This module has a quite evenly distributed grading scheme. The individual quizzes (40%) held on Week 6 and Week 10 consist of 50 MCQ in LumiNUS quiz format. The questions were almost entirely based on the lecture notes given. Another part of the assessment is the graded group assignments (30%), which consist of two lab assignments and one Yellow Fever assignment, each worth 10%. Finally, the group project (30%) is assessed from several categories, namely the interim report (5%), final report (10%), and presentation video (10% group, 5% individual). To be honest, I don't know what I learned in this mod. The materials were like, a bit of "common sense" but at the same time quite vague as well. The parts about project management and introduction to systems thinking, CLDs, and SFDs were okay but the rest were… vague without much explanation on how we should apply the concepts. The only learning point that I got from this module was that everything happens for a reason, which (might) link into a grand causal loop that we might not be aware of. It's like GER1000 that talks about how "correlation does not imply causation" but on steroids, resulting in a nested causation that somehow creates these big loops of causal relationships. The tutorial and lab sessions were quite okay. They showed you how you apply the concepts of CLDs and SFDs with the help of software called Stella Architect. To be honest I quite enjoyed (some of) the sessions as I started to understand how and why things happen/change because of complex causal relationships. However, there was this 1 tutorial where the prof just explained about stakeholders and perceptions, which was, no joke, literally filled with memes and/or optical illusions that you might usually see in Instagram or boomer WhatsApp groups. The tutorial slides were literally filled with random videos and random optical illusions and then… "Thanks! Do you have any questions??". Throughout that session I literally just cringed at the tutorial slides and wondered why I spent 1.5 hours looking at optical illusions and cringy videos. The quizzes were quite funny as well. Both quizzes consisted of 50 MCQs that should be done within 50 minutes. As the quizzes were done on LumiNUS, it was set such that there was no backward navigation. The prof also said that these tests were "closed-book" tests. However, no proctoring was held for the quizzes, thus I expected that statement won't hold up much. The quiz materials were also easy to ctrl+F (find) on the lecture notes as well, thus you can expect how the bell-curve went for these quizzes. If you want to score well in this mod, pray that you get decently good teammates. The project and assignment components made up the majority of your marks, and they literally depend on your teammates. If not, try your best in doing the assignments and final project and hope that the tutor/prof that you get would be lenient enough to give you a good score. I fortunately got very good teammates and they were ambitious enough to make our stock-flow model quite decent and robust for the project. I heard some groups had MIA teammates, most probably because they didn’t understand the mod itself. In conclusion, I think that this module could be improved for future batches. The organisation was still quite messy and the instructions given for the final project were not that clear until Week 12-13, where the prof urgently blasted emails to explain things that he never taught in class. Hopefully the prof could improve the content and organisation of the module so that future batches could appreciate what they are learning in this module.

Taken in AY17/18 Semester 2 Lecturer: Associate Professor Tang Wai Shing Tutor: Associate Professor Tang Wai Shing Expected grade: B+ Actual grade: B+ Assessment and workload: - 5% from participating in class twice and attending tutorial class 6 times. Conclusion: - I took this module as a UE, which is absolutely crazy since not many people are willing to take high level Math modules as UE. I enjoyed this module because it is quite eye-opening for me. I learnt quite a bit of theory about why approximations can be done from this module. For MMDA Applied Math majors, this module is one of the level 4000s to choose from, I recommend it. For other Math majors, take this module to learn Applied Math in a Pure Math flavour.

Taken in AY 15/16 Sem 2 Lecturer: Dr Ng Wei Khim Expected Grade: C / Actual Grade: B tl;dr: Don't take this module if you're a CS student wishing to fulfil your science requirements, or for that matter anyone who's not a physics major. It is almost impossible to fail this mod, thanks to the bell curve, but unfortunately it is also not very easy to score well for it, especially if you don't major in physics. If you do want to take this module, it is highly recommended that you take a introductory calculus module before this one, such as MA1521 for computing students. As its name suggests, PC1144 covers a good deal of topics in modern physics in a brisk 13 weeks. The breadth of topics combined with the fact that modern physics is rather counter-intuitive means that module is not easy to keep up with. Unfortunately, the lecturer is really not very good. Dr. Ng frequently fails to explain concepts clearly, and doesn't appear to understand what his students know and don't know before the start of the module, thus spending large amount of time explaining things that are trivial, while skimming over topics which require more explanation. He also has a bad habit of pausing mid-sentence, as if realizing that the next half of his sentence will likely be too advanced for the students sitting in front of him. I frequently find myself exiting the lecturer theatre feeling more confused about the subject matter than when I entered. The recommended textbook, University Physics with Modern Physics, is very good and quite readable. I would recommend reviewing it thoroughly before each lecture, because otherwise it becomes very difficult to keep up due to the aforementioned problems with the lecturer. Lectures are not webcast on IVLE, so attendance is a must (though paying attention is optional). The math used in this module is H2 level calculus (differentiation, integration by parts, substitution, etc.) plus 1st and 2nd degree ordinary differential equations, probability, Fourier transformation (not tested) and a little of complex numbers and Taylor series. Although the math is suppose to be taught during the course of the module, it is best that you have prior knowledge of all of these, since knowing them will help in understanding the physics as a lot of modern physics seem more based in math than empirical results, and also because learning math from physics professors is an exercise in frustration. Tutorials are one hour fortnightly, and it is highly recommended that you do the questions beforehand, since this and the very few lecture practise sessions are the only chance you get at doing actual questions to practise for exams. No exam papers are released by the faculty, but that doesn't mean you can't find them. No help sheets are allowed for the exams, and while the topics covered are broad and sometimes confounding, the exams are surprisingly fair (though still quite brutal). On the whole it is difficult to recommend this module. While the subject matter is interesting, it is hard to score well for, and I found myself learning more by reading the textbook myself than listening to the lectures.

Semester taken: AY19/20 Sem 2 If you're looking to fulfil your GES requirement or take a UE while simultaneously ticking off your SJW bucket list, look no further. With less balance than a punch-drunk lightweight after twenty pirouettes, the course material and its presentation during lectures appears (to me at least) designed to steer young minds towards various inexorable anti-establishment conclusions. As a politically neutral third year who had completed the 8-MC LC2007 Constitutional & Administrative Law module not too long ago, I was triggered to no end by the relentless use of pejoratives coupled with snide remarks during the lectures while course material was being taught. Constitutional and statutory provisions were cited only partially - in one particularly egregious case, different subsections from different sections in the statute were copied (without section numbering of course) onto consecutive slides, then labelled as something like "what the law says". Offence-creating provisions in the Defamation Act were presented without any mention of possible statutory defences. The cherry-picking list goes on. For a course that purports to discuss important freedom of speech issues, it neglects to even touch on the institutional separation of powers and other basic constitutional issues, as well as engage foundational moral/political justifications, all of which provide the necessary context for any freedom of speech discussion. Granted, these issues might not be suited for a level-1000 module. But doesn't that make it all the more dangerous to provide students with such flimsy and one-sided material, knowing that this will heavily influence their future political views? The illusion of knowledge is more dangerous than ignorance. Admin-wise, it was a **** show of the highest order. Graded assignments (scrapbook article commentaries) were supposed to be marked and returned before the next one was released/due (there were about 4) to allow students to incorporate feedback, but the first was only returned some time after the final one was released. The midterm take-home essay instructions were changed drastically a week after the initial release: the maximum word limit was changed to a minimum word count. Having already completed the assignment, I had to scramble to unpack my heavily-condensed essay into a full-length one. Clarifications and additional instructions came piecemeal, replete with glaring spelling and grammatical errors. I have never seen a more incompetent course coordinator in my life. Thankfully, tutorials cover content wholly separate from lectures. My tutor, Ms Farah, was pretty solid and attempted to facilitate candid discussions, but was sadly limited by the 45 minutes of contact time per week. Her tutorials were for the most part really engaging and made up somewhat for the lectures. Overall, this course is great for preaching and pretending to discuss stuff you don't actually know enough about to engage meaningfully. Unless you're a senior law student or have a keen interest in constitutional issues and have read up extensively enough on the same to see through the disingenuous lecture presentations. Then you won't end up echoing the political views the rest of the unwitting students have been manipulated into forming. You'll just get tilted real hard and end up writing a scathing NUSMods review. PSA for the law students thinking of taking this course: if you're ok with trash assignment instructions and can hold in the tilt, TAKE THIS MOD. The entire course content, readings and slides combined, is something like 10% of one single topic in LC2007. I kid you not. There is ZERO new material so you have to study absolutely nothing. If you want an easy A/A+ just parrot the political views pushed here, don't be me and take the path of most resistance by flaming the examiners by picking apart the essay questions and calling the phrasing "disingenuous" in your response. For everyone else thinking of taking this mod, be warned: take everything your learn here with about as much salt as there is in the Salar du Uyuni. There ARE very valid and important points raised, but their presentation is incredibly one-sided. Side note: I was alerted by some people that my review was taken down after I posted it. The irony is not lost on me but here's a repost. Update: this is the THIRD repost.

Taken in 20/21 SEM 2 under Prof Guo Yong Xin (online lessons) Grading: 5% x 2 lab experiments, 10% x 2 mini projects, 10% x 2 CA test, 50% finals This course serves as an introduction to microwave circuits and the important components that make up the circuits. Pre-requisite is EE3104Cwhich I waived, going in with PC2020 knowledge. I subsequently found out that this was doable because transmission line and S-parameter theory was taught from scratch. However, learning these 2 concepts before the course will be very beneficial as much of the rest of the course relies on them. We covered the telegrapher equations, Smith chart usage (beyond what is taught in PC2020), Y/Z matrices and S parameters as an introduction. The pace was very slow at this point with Prof Guo spending quite an excessive amount of time on these concepts. Power dividers (Wilkinson, Coupled line) and filter design was then taught. Filter design will not be a problem if you have an analog electronics background, but the even and odd mode analysis for power dividers could take a while to get used to. These 3 chapters were covered in the first half of the course. The second half of the course was more rushed as Prof Guo effectively finished teaching chapters 4-8 in about 3-4 weeks. Content covered includes more RF devices like switches, amplifiers, mixers and oscillators. Amplifier design is a huge part of this course and many details like the non-linear effects in amplifiers, how to design matching circuitry, design for high gain/low noise figure was taught. However, this part was mostly glossed over by Prof Guo and I felt like he was just explaining whatever formulas were on the slides in a “wing-it” manner instead of connecting it to the big picture. The first lab experiment was to measure the S-parameters for different devices. Remember to take many pictures! The second lab experiment was to calculate the noise temperature and noise figure of an amplifier under bias/no bias. This part was more complicated and a good understanding of how noise originates in a circuit is required. Data from both labs was taken in person, and we were given 1 week to complete the lab report. The GAs were helpful and approachable in this portion of the course. The design software that we used for both projects was ADS, and it is relatively intuitive and easy to use. The first mini project required us to design a power divider at a fixed resonant frequency. The second mini project was the difficult one: designing a low noise amplifier with a single transistor. The lab manual alone was 33 pages, and there were many steps to be completed. However, the GA went through all the steps from start to end, but did not explain the big picture again (seems to be the trend in this group), so I just went with the flow without understanding why some steps were done (although they magically improved the parameters). Do start early for this project as it can be quite time consuming. Tutorials are the worst: Prof Guo skipped the first 2 tutorials and basically just glossed over the rest of the 3 tutorials. Doesn’t take a genius to tell students that “this is easy, you should be able to do it” for many of the questions. The tests and final exam tested on basic concepts, and you should be fine if you understood every slide (which is not a lot anyway). Anyway I didn’t do very well for the second test and exam because I was getting destroyed by other classes. Final thoughts: I 100% would not recommend this course. The content covered is pretty good to me, but think of this course as a good restaurant with a really bad waiter. Prof Guo didn’t give me the impression that he prepares for lectures and just glossed over the explanations. At one point, I stopped watching the lectures entirely even though they were recorded because I simply did not understand anything he was saying. I relied a lot on my own self studying for this.

Lecturer: Dr Vikneswaran S/O Gopal This module is compulsory for all CS/Math DDP students. The first half of the module is on counting and discrete probability, which is basically primary 5/6 Math Olympiad, and can be mostly solved using P and C techniques. However, there are some new terms and notations that you need to know the meanings of, such as "decreasing events" or "disjoint pmf". The second half of the module has concepts such as variance, covariance, and continuous distributions, which are concepts new to me. I made the mistake of ignoring the module because I thought the first half was easy and had to study last minute at 12am for the second midterm. You should read the notes regularly, as you cannot solely rely on the tutorials for practice. The tutorials do not cover every topic. Tutorials are compulsory as they account for 30% of the final grade. We were assigned a group based on the alphabetical order of our name during the first tutorial and stuck with that group for the semester. During every tutorial, we were given a worksheet to complete individually, but could discuss the questions. The final grade received is dependent on both our individual grade and our group's grade, but how it's calculated is not revealed it to us. It basically became peer tutoring. All the tutorials on different days of the week had a different worksheet. There were 2 midterms for this module. The first midterm was done on our own laptops using the Examplify software, which only works on Windows/Mac. I disliked this software as we had to give it full control over our laptops. While taking the test, the software locked us from other applications in our laptops, and we couldn't even "ctrl alt del". The second midterm was a traditional written test. The first midterm was quite easy, and I felt that an excessive amount of time was given (90 mins for 15 MCQ, that's 4 mins per question!). Most people left the test early. The second midterm was harder than the first, but it wasn't too hard either. 90 mins were given for 3 questions, and counting the part (a) part (b) etc, that's about 6 parts. The paper also felt more like an algebra paper, as most of the questions can be solve by writing down expression using definitions and simplifying it. A lot of hints were given as well. For example, they gave you the identity needed to simplify the equation, so you just had to modify your expression to fit the hint's identity. Lectures were webcasted. In fact, half the time, live lectures weren't even available as only a video was available. The LT would be empty. It's a flipped classroom kind of module, so the prof would go through some questions on alternate lectures and webcast them as well. I did not go for lectures, and neither did I watch the videos. I just read the notes. The video explaining the concepts were made by the prof, not recorded from an LT. The video is usually about 10-20 mins, which is much shorter than a traditional lecture, but it's also a bit boring. Those videos felt like listening to the prof reading a script while pressing next on the PowerPoint slides. He didn't even use a marker/pointer to show which point he is at on the slides, and instead, would say stuff like "as you can see from point 2". Just reading the notes without watching the video should be sufficient. My senior recommended me to take it in sem 1 as it was taught by the math department instead of the stats department, which I unfortunately couldn't due to missing prerequisites. By the end of the module, I felt like I didn't learn much because I just copied everything to my cheatsheet without understanding. Multivariable calculus is required for a deeper understanding, which I have not taken. Final grade: A

I took this mod in 2015/16 Sem 1 and Dr Tania Roy taught it. She's clearly a very very smart and knowledgable professor who's extremely enthusiastic about the topic of post-colonialism and attitudes towards race. I think this module is one that all Lit students should take because it was a great opportunity for me to work with non-white (and not all male at the same time) and (some) contemporary texts, finally! I know lots of people complain about the diversity in texts in Singapore, so this is the module that specially looks beyond that limited range! We had some very philosophical texts to ground us with post-colonial politics, like essays from Hannah Arendt, Frederic Jameson, Fanon, Homi Bhabha and more. And the literary texts came from Jean Rhys, Albert Camus, Assia Djebar, Tayen Salih, Mohsin Hamid, Tash Aw and Ayi Kweh Amah and more. It was a very invigorating seminar-style class and sometimes because the discussions are so smart I could get so lost! But Dr Roy is so friendly, I think we all felt free to ask her questions if we needed to. I think this class grounded me in very integral post-colonial foundations that prepare me for other modules I will take in NUS, like Singapore lit and anything regarding European imperialism.

Taken in AY17/18 Semester 2 Lecturer: Associate Professor Leung Man Chun Tutor: Nan Yuesong Expected grade: B+ Actual grade: A+ (Baffles me fully) Lectures are webcasted, lecture skippers rejoice! Assessment and workload: - 20% midterms, open book. (I got 17%) - 80% finals, 1 A4 sized helpsheet. Experience: - As an Applied Math major, this module is pretty easy, no doubt. The focus of this module is the intuition behind many concepts that were possibly forsaken in JC when we learnt it. The name of this module is essentially what it is about: Games. Throughout this module, card games, dice games, combinatorial coefficient, normal approximation will be introduced. The highlight of this module is basic game theory, which is not easy by any means because of its abstraction. However, because this is a math GEM, the mathematical concepts are not fully rigourous, which is my only grouse of this module. - Prof Leung has taught this module many times and knows the content at his fingertips. Prof Leung is very passionate about his teaching philosophy, which is centered around intuition and simplicity. He emphasises that countless times during the lectures, which is quite entertaining. Prof Leung is also very approachable and willing to listen to different kinds of intuition that students think of. - Nan Yuesong is my tutor for this module and he's very good. He explains the concepts in an easy to understand manner, and at a level that even people with little Math background can understand. He is also very approchable to questions, even to those out of the syllabus. There was one instance where my tutorial mate asked him about solving recurrence relations for a closed form formula. To my surprise, Nan Yuesong taught him how to do it despite it being out of the syllabus. - Midterm test was pretty manageable. Prof Leung is kind for the midterms this round, with the median being about 15/20. Listening to the lecture (webcast or not), and attempting the tutorial questions is enough to score for this part. - Final exam was really difficult. Prof Leung set a pretty difficult paper this academic year, maybe due to the midterm test being too well done. There were not a lot of giveaway questions for the finals as compared to previous years. I recommend doing the tutorials and copying the lecture examples into the helpsheet if possible. Conclusion: - I took this module as a UE, and also because I had 1 more s/u left. The lecture timeslot is pretty ungodly but there is webcast provided so it's not all that bad. Prof Leung also gives entertaining lectures. Thus I recommend this module to anybody who wants to learn about probabilities of card games, casino games and introductory game theory in a lighter manner compared to taking the associated ones with the MA code.

Taken in AY2013/14 Semester 1 Module taught by: Dr Wang Qinghai Grade obtained: B As you can see from the grade, this review is speaking from a view of an average Physics student. If you do find tutorial and past year questions too hard to attempt, do not despair. Try out some textbook practice questions first to gain some confidence and grasp in the understanding of the content. Lecturer: Zhang Yang Webcasted, with some pre-lecture flipped classroom content Assessment: 3% Online Quiz (Pre-Lecture, on flipped classroom content) 10% Tutorial Participation 15% Group Homework (2 sets with equal weightage) 25% Midterm (6 MCQ for 30%, 3 structured qns for 70%) 47% Final (5 MCQ for 20%, 5 structured qns for 80%) Textbook: Microeconomics, 5th Ed by Besanko and Braeutigam, with additional readings from Intermediate Microeconomics, 9th Ed by Varian. (Textbook not really required as lecture notes are fairly stand-alone, although some of the elaboration might be useful) This is the first of the 2 intermediate microeconomics modules offered in NUS, mostly covering the foundations of consumer and producer theory, as well as other topics like exchange economy and partial competitive equilibrium. This is a core module for the Econs major that cannot be S/U-ed, so take this as a UE only if you're interested in Economics, or have sufficient quantitative background. Knowledge of basic calculus (mostly just use of partial derivatives) is assumed, and more advanced concepts (specifically the method of Lagrange multipliers to solve constrained optimization problems) will be elaborated upon in class. If you're a math or engineering student, or if you're an Econs major that has done well in EC2104, the math in this module shouldn't be that taxing. Dr Zhang has taught this module since 2012(?), and her experience teaching this module really shows. Her explanations of concepts in lecture are very clear and easy to understand. She is also very approachable if you wish to seek clarification, with fixed weekly office hours and additional office hours before midterms/finals. Tutorial problem sets are fairly straightforward applications of concepts introduced in lecture, and are meant to reinforce these concepts. You will be expected to present your solution to 1-2 questions at least once during tutorial. You will also form groups of 2-3 in tutorial to complete 2 graded homework assignments, which are slightly more challenging than the tutorial content but still fairly manageable. Midterms and Finals are definitely more challenging. There will be questions are set differently from the tutorial/homework content, with an emphasis on your own mastery of the concepts in the module. Do the practice problem sets released by Dr Zhang before Midterms/Finals to get used to doing the algebraic manipulations quickly (especially for exchange economy and producer theory questions which can be very messy from my experience), but don't expect to get too far during the exams just by doing the problem sets.

To be completed over 48 hours Took this module because I thought it was an interesting one. But I would say that out of all the modules I have taken, this is the module that I regret taking the most. If you're not an avid football fan, it will likely be a struggle for you. Though they say that anyone can take the course, lecturers (especially towards the end of the semester - Dr Shaun Lin) teach with the assumption that you know all the footballers in the world and all the games and all the clubs. While Dr Kamalini explains most examples in a clear way, it is not always the case for the other lecturers / co-lecturers. Even if you are an avid football fan, you might find it difficult to follow, and this might be the nature of geography itself. While the links between football and geographical concepts are interesting, non-superficial, and quite substantial, these links are often presented in a sort of 'fun-fact' manner. If I could visualize it, it would sort of be a mind map, where the lecture covers one topic, then talks about anything and everything that is related. Prof. Li Cheng (Lecturer and Tutor) Disclaimer: This module was affected by the COVID-19 pandemic, and as a result it may differ significantly from how past/future modules would/will be conducted. Assessment Structure: 10% Tutorial Submission and Presentation 20% Midterm (Take-home) 35% Data Analysis Project 35% Final (Take-home) This is a ST4xxx module that Statistics major/second majors can take to satisfy their major requirements. The module’s topics include basics of Bayesian statistics, one-parameter model, normal model, Monte Carlo approximation, normal/Laplace approximation, Markov chain Monte Carlo and hierarchical models. The textbook of reference is A First Course in Bayesian Statistical Methods, Peter D. Hoff. Lecture attendance is not compulsory. Each tutorial set is assigned to a group of students (which is assigned around the start of the module. Students get to choose who they want to team up with), and each group only need to be present for the week in which their tutorial is presented. Prof. Li mentioned explicitly that the grading only looks at completeness instead of correctness. Tutorial questions generally are standard questions which apply techniques already demonstrated in lecture, so as long as one pay attention in class, they should not spend too much time on tutorial sets. The tutorial problems also require extensive coding in R, and students are generally assumed to be somewhat proficient in R before enrolling in tis module. Due to the COVID-19 situation, attendance to tutorial was no longer compulsory, but Prof. Li strongly recommended each group to send at least one person to present their solutions. The data analysis project was just a slightly extended version of a tutorial set, covering concepts across multiple chapters. It was issued near the end of the semester, and we were given about 2 weeks to complete it. I call modules like this a “methods” module: Many techniques and concepts are introduced in order to solve many practical problems, but rarely are these concepts explained in depth or even proven. As such, one does not need an excellent understanding in order to do well in this module – as long as they practice the tutorial problems consistently and know what step to carry out in each scenario, they should score decently well. I found this somewhat unfortunate, as many concepts look interesting enough to be explored further. Regardless, the concepts are still not easy to understand at the surface level, so one should prepare to spend quite some time on this module (while I think it is possible to do well in this module without really knowing what is going on, it is much more difficult and painful and is probably not worth it). Prof. Li is the best statistics lecturer I’ve encountered so far. He has a good intuitive grasp of the concepts and is able to deliver them in a reasonably fluent manner. He’s also a highly approachable and friendly professor who helps his students whenever they are in need, both offline and via email. However, his lecturing voice tends to be monotonous, so it’s easy to lose attention in the middle of his classes. Regardless, taking this module under him was a good experience. The COVID-19 situation forced Prof. Li to change both midterm and final to take-home assignments. Just like the project, the problems in the exams are very similar to the tutorial sets. While I was disappointed again with the lack of in-depth exploration of statistical theory, this module is probably much more theoretical than the other ST4xxx modules offered. I recommend math students who are highly theoretical to take this module if they need to take a ST4xxx module to clear whatever requirements. Expected Grade: A-/A Final Grade: A- (S/U-ed, only possible due to unforeseen COVID-19 situation)

We were lucky to not really need to do things that manually in that we could use excel or internet calculators to do Karnaugh maps from Boolean algebra/simplification and stuff like that for our online exam but in a physical exam, it would probably take a long time because it needs to be done manually. Regardless, there were still a lot of things that needed to be tediously done by hand step by step like pipelining and cache. Still, these felt like mostly mindless routine tasks, kind of like being a human calculator; you don’t really need to thing that much, they’re just tedious. Probably the only one where you really need to think is the combinational circuits/MSI components part where given a desired mapping from some inputs to some outputs, you need to figure out how to combine circuit components that would give those outputs when fed the respective inputs, but that’s probably one of the only hard topics. So I consider this mod easy because it’s mostly mindless, but it’s kind of moderate difficulty because it’s tedious and time-consuming stuff, and you might get careless because of the numerous steps involved. Lecturers: Both the lecturers are very good, always helpful and friendly, and they explain really well. I had no issues with either of them. So the first lab was just some C programming, the next three were on MIPS (actually a simulation called SPIM), then one on processors (simulation designed by Prof Ad), three on building simple circuits using components and a breadboard (but fancier) called the Logic Trainer, then two on building more complex circuits using a simulation software called Logisim (likely because doing this by hand would be really cumbersome). Honestly, it was quite fun, and kind of made me want to do Comp Eng to get more of these hands-on kind of stuff. Just make sure to check your answers for the labs, they’re really easy, and your Lab TA may hint whether you got it wrong or not, so that you don’t lose out in this component because it’s quite easy to score full marks for the lab component. Also, because it was open everything yet the test could be done alone, the average score was pretty high, which was why I was only above average. Assignments: This was not open-collaboration but they weren’t difficult so doing them alone was alright. I got full marks for the first one but not for the last two; I just had a few careless mistakes while doing them, mostly because I did them, then didn’t have the time to check again because I was overloading and I had no time. Regardless, I still scored almost full marks because they weren’t difficult. The first assignment was on C, number systems, and MIPS; the second was on Boolean algebra, logic gates, simplification, and combinational circuits; the third extends the topics in the second with additional topics of MSI components and sequential logic. IIRC, we were given 1 week to do each assignment and they were given in weeks 5, 9, and 11. Most people probably score full marks here so if you have time, just check your answers properly. CS4244 Knowledge-Based Systems - 15/16 Sem2 This is the one of those modules that I took without knowing what to expect. It was one of area primaries for the focus are of Artificially Intelligence (AI) so I thought it would be good to know what it is about. It turns out that this module dramatically expanded my knowledge of AI as well as writing programs in general. The module is mainly focused on expert systems and more specifically rule-based expert systems. In terms of the theoretical content, it has three main parts, knowledge representation, tool (clips rule-based programming language), and knowledge management. Now this may sound very confusing so let me explain the overall idea a bit. Basically in expert systems, you use knowledge to solve domain-specific problems, like airport control, medical diagnosis or floor planning. You can acquire knowledge by querying database, consulting experts (human experts) or searching for information from everywhere, anything that helps you solve the problem, this is called knowledge acquisition which is part of knowledge management. Then you also need to represent this knowledge in some form that can be used in the expert program, this problem is solved by knowledge representation, which is mainly about how to transform knowledge into facts, rules or frame-like structures (like OOP) and store them in the knowledge base. With the knowledge base, the rules and the problem at hand, we can use tools like clips, which has an inference engine to solve the problem by firing the rules opportunistically with minimum control logic. In this module, you mainly learn about the features and characteristics of expert systems and how to write programs in clips, which is not only a feature-complete rule-based programming language, but also a functional language at the same time (like lisp). Definitely unlike any other languages in the sense that the entire flow is controlled by the built-in inference engine instead of the programmer, and the programmer’s job is just writing the rules that waits to be fired when conditions are met. For the project in this module, our team developed a knowledge-based module planner, the featured image of this post (at the beginning) shows the screenshot of the software planning exact modules that I have taken. In terms of practical use of the module, it is quite debatable. Knowledge-based systems used to be a hot topic but the interest decreased drastically following the second AI winter. Nowadays people are more interested in hot topics like machine learning, neural network or tensor flow, but knowledge-based systems are still being used in specialized areas, and it may prove to be useful again in the future. I would not delve too deep into the content or assessment of this module as I am aware of a change of teaching staff for this module in the next iteration, but I hope you have some idea of what this module is all about and the topics to expect in general. Sem 1 AY21/22 Lecturer: Chin Wei Ngan Tutorial TA: Ernest I will start with the TL;DR: don't take this module. If you're planning on going down the Programming Language focus area (for CS kids) (ie. this becomes a requirement), don't do it either. It's not worth it -- go spec in something else. The selection of PL mods in NUS is trash anyway. The bunch of reviews from this sem (Sem1, AY21/22) that basically diss this mod are entirely justified. It isn't because of the final paper either (it hasn't happened yet, as I write this). Heed our advice. Don't do it. If you remember my IS1103 review, I mentioned that it was perhaps one of the worst mods I've had the privilege of paying school fees for. CS2104 is a close second. At least it's not a graduation requirement. Seriously; if you need 4MCs, go take CFG, or some UEs -- anything else. Really. This module purports to teach "Programming Language Concepts", but none of those concepts were even taught to any degree worthy of a university education. CS2104 "covers" 4 languages: Haskell, OCaml, Prolog, and Scala. The first half (up to recess week, possibly till week 7) focuses on trying to teach students Haskell. Topics covered include the basic functional programming stuff (higher order functions [which should be OK if you took 1101S under Henz], list comprehensions, other Haskell features like pattern matching and ADTs), and of course Monads (and monadic parsers via Parsec). It doesn't do a good job, mind you, but the slides are there. The next language is Prolog. If you haven't used Prolog before, it's a language with quite a unique paradigm... and it definitely can't be covered in 1 set of slides over 1 or 2 weeks. (by the way, a large part of the slide deck just focuses on those dumb "logic puzzles" like SEND + MORE = MONEY...). The core tenets of Prolog programming (eg. the tree structure of terms, SLD resolution, etc.) are only briefly mentioned and not really elaborated in detail. It is not really feasible to expect students to gain a good understanding of these concepts when explained so poorly in such a short amount of time. OCaml and Scala are given much the same treatment; just an afterthought in this module. Based on past year papers, students are somehow expected to have a good grasp on these languages in order to answer questions. This year, it was said that students "there is no need to memorise language syntax". We shall see about that (will update this review if I remember). By the way, if you're reading the description on nusmods (above) and wondering whether this module covers "various implementation issues, such as pseudo-code interpretation, static and dynamic semantics...", the answer is NO. Assessments Speaking of assessments, there are some graded lab assignments as well as some "participation mark" tutorial questions that you have to submit. They're mostly run-of-the-mill CS labs/assignments, nothing too special or tragic on that front. For tutorials, somehow participation is graded. The TA for my tutorial was a PhD student who, on the first lesson, openly stated that he had no idea what was going on, and that we should "all learn together" (paraphrasing). Doesn't inspire much confidence, does it? The level of nonexistent confidence only continued to drop after each tutorial was basically him reading off the answers for each tutorial question, with the occasional confusion as he doesn't know what the answers were talking about. Furthermore, students are expected to form groups of 2-3 to make 2 presentations about various proglang topics over the semester. These are graded, and form part of the 10% "tutorial participation" marks. You can either choose from one of the topics suggested by the prof, or suggest one subject to approval. There is 1 midterm and 1 final exam; both are open-book. The midterm is mostly MCQ -- this round it was ~20 MCQs and 2 open-ended questions in 30 minutes. What do the questions ask? Basically, you need to be GHCI. If you cannot compile and interpret Haskell code in your head, good luck to you. Each question basically presents you with a messily-written Haskell function with nondescriptive argument names, and asks you what it does (or how to use it). I suspect the final exam (at least the MCQ portion) will be more of the same recipe. Conclusions There's really only one thing to conclude, and I already stated that at the top; don't take this module. Really, don't. The lack of prerequisites might seem tempting, but don't. Even if you love Haskell or Prolog or FP, don't do it. If you are thinking of going down the Prog Lang focus area, don't. Choose something else. In most of my other reviews (except IS1103 -- lu weiquan really deserves nothing but a dismissal from NUS) I generally attack only the course content, and not the professor. Unfortunately I can't do that here. I don't think Prof Chin is a Bad Person (tm), but being a good person doesn't make you a good lecturer. Lectures were conducted over Zoom (attendance was "mandatory" for participation marks); tutorials were either in-person or over Zoom (depends on the slot you choose). Lectures are quite dry, and often have no sense of flow; they are conducted in a very "rambly" style. Some particular concepts will be gone over very quickly, while some other concepts will somehow get a 20 minute explanation (which is actually just 2 10-minute ones repeated). Most of the time, he is just reading off the slides. Slides which, I might add, often have typos. Sometimes students point it out and he corrects them, but when he closes the slide deck, he clicks "discard changes", so next year students get the same typos again. Fun. Prof is responsive to audience questions which is good I guess. In case there was any confusion, let me state this again: DO NOT, UNDER ANY CIRCUMSTANCES, TAKE CS2104.

Full review and more at blackforestcheesecakeandcoffee.wordpress.com Taken in AY20/21 (Post Circuit Breaker Semester) Physics Major (24 MCs) Lecturer : Dr Hong Chong Ming Kenneth TA: Dr Hong Chong Ming Kenneth Grade Distribution: Lecture Worksheets Assignments CA 1 (Midterms) CA 2 (Finals) Contents: • Infinite Series • Vectors • Complex Variables • Partial Differentiation • Multiple Integrals • Second Order Linear Differential Equations (2ODE) • Partial Differential Equations • Fourier Series • Gradient, Divergence, and Curl • Line, Surface, and Volume Integrals • Integral Theorems • Curvilinear Coordinates • Fourier Transform • Dirac Delta Distribution • Laplace Transform • Sturm Liouville Theorem (Untested) Lecture (Two 2 hr Lectures / Week): This semester, lectures are held over zoom. Although you may not have attempted or completed the tutorials, I would recommend attending. He often has funky tricks which he uses to solve problems, which may come in handy in future problems. The many different (and unusual) methods you can approach a problem are quite interesting and you can learn a lot from just attending his classes. Through the roof spiciness levels. Lecture Worksheets: He goes through the lecture worksheets in class, so you just need to follow along and copy them down. He also uploads a copy of the annotated lecture questions after each chapter. The deadline for us was the end of the semester, so you can take your time in submitting the lecture worksheets. Although I would recommend doing them on the spot, which would really help in learning, and because the large amount of module content can make last minute work extremely painful. The questions themselves are usually an example of a concept that was covered in the chapter or a derivation of a theorem. Not particularly challenging. Mildly spicy. Assignments: Spicy. Very spicy. Kenneth’s assignments are not as difficult as his tutorials, but are very challenging nonetheless. Every assignment usually has one or two simpler questions, then a killer question that can take days to solve. I must say that the questions are NOT IMPOSSIBLE to solve, although they can feel very overwhelming at times. Do them continuously. This is not work that you can pull off any last-minute miracles on. Even if you can’t solve the problem, write something and Kenneth will be able to give you some method marks. Like the lecture worksheets, Kenneth allows us to hand up all assignments by the end of the semester, which really helps to ease our workload and make learning more enjoyable and effective. Exams: In most years, Kenneth’s exams are abysmally difficult, leaving many students floundering at every question. This year, he has kindly opted to make the exams doable at least. The questions are not the kind that would leave you completely stunned when you look at them, leaving the time pressure as the only constraint. The questions are definitely doable, given time and an open textbook. The exams are open-book, but only for hard-copy materials. CA 1 tests content up to 2ODE, and CA 2 tests content after 2ODE. Kenneth is quite a generous grader, giving marks for students who are on the right train of thought. As such, you should write down all your trains of thought during the exam in order to score these method marks. Expected Grade: A+/A/A- Final Grade: A Thoughts: One of the most meaningful modules I have taken. Everything I’ve learnt from this module has applications elsewhere in my other physics modules. It very nicely bridges the gap between theoretical understanding of more challenging math, and direct applications where we can use them. Although the content covered is extremely heavy, I feel that the module itself is not very difficult. I had more problems with PC1142 than this module. 10/10 would take again.
